chapters.title: Approach To Patients With Emergency Conditions

sections.title: The Concept of Emergency Care and Resuscitation
sections.text:
Emergency care and resuscitation involve rapid assessment and early intervention. The approach to Emergency care and
resuscitation needs to be systematic; hence the use of the ABCs. The ABCs approach provides the framework for evaluation
and treatment of severely ill patients.

Primary survey

i. Airway
     •   Assess the airway to establish patency of the airway. This includes: Looking for signs of airway obstruction (signs
         of trauma, swelling, secretions, presence of foreign body).
     •   Listening for abnormal sounds like a stridor and snoring.

If there are signs of airway obstruction, intervene by positioning, opening and clearing the airway. Perform a chin lift or jaw
thrust maneuver to open the airway (If suspecting cervical spine injury, use the jaw thrust maneuver). Use suction to remove
secretions. Airway adjuncts, such as oropharyngeal or nasopharyngeal airway can be used.

  Note
      •     Remember to reassess the airway after performing interventions.
      •     Some patient may require use of advance airway devices like endotracheal intubation or surgical airway.
      •     Use video laryngoscopy over direct laryngoscopy helps to improve first-pass success.
      •     emergency intubation

ii. Breathing
Upon completing airway assessment and intervention, assess for the presence of breathing, signs of respiratory distress such
as tachypnea, hypoxia, cyanosis, apnea and abnormal breath sounds. Provide oxygen when oxygen saturation is below 92%
or when the patient is dyspneic. Oxygen can be administered using the nasal prong, simple face mask, non-rebreather mask
or Ambu bag. Advanced interventions include mechanical ventilation.

iii. Circulation
Check for pulse (central pulse) for not more than 10 seconds. If absent, start CPR (Refer cardiopulmonary resuscitation
section 1.3). Assess for signs of poor peripheral perfusion (shock) such as cold extremities, prolonged capillary refill, dry
mucous membrane and hypotension. If there are signs of shock, establish two (2) IV large bore cannula and give IV fluids
(crystalloids) bolus (2lts in adults and 20mls/kg in pediatrics). Limit fluids to individuals whom you suspect of having heart
failure, renal failure or malnourished children.

iv. Disability
This involves a rapid assessment of neurological status. This includes assessment for the level of consciousness (use of
AVPU or Glascow coma scale), signs of convulsions, random blood glucose level, examination of the pupils and presence of
focal neurological deficit. Interventions that can be performed during the disability assessment include correction of
hypoglycemia, airway protection, stopping the convulsions by administering anticonvulsant.

v. Exposure
This involves fully exposing the patient and rapid assessment of the body for signs of trauma, rashes or infection.

Secondary survey

After assessment and stabilization of ABCs during the primary survey, focus is turned into secondary survey. The secondary
survey is a systematic assessment of the rest of the body to identify injuries and illnesses. Common approaches include a
head-to-toe or organ –system-based assessment. It is important to note that the secondary survey is performed after the
primary assessment and interventions.
When performing a secondary survey, if the patient condition changes, then you must stop immediately and redo the primary
survey and necessary interventions.

   Note:
   All patients with compromised airway, breathing, circulation or disability must be attended in the resuscitation rooms. (Refer
   Triage overview section)

sections.title: Triage Overview
sections.text:
Triage is the process of determining the priority of a patient to medical care based on the acuity (severity of condition) and
capacity of the system to address the condition to optimize outcome.

Importance of Triage

Triage enables quick identification of patients who need immediate attention and hence improves patient outcomes by avoiding
potential delays. It helps in organizing, monitoring, evaluating and determining the department resources that patients might
need.

Triage system

The triage system is based on recommendation of Emergency Medicine expert’s basic principles of triage, which uses specific
criteria to categorize patients into three main levels of acuity:

Emergency

All patients with immediate life or limb threats who are deemed salvageable, but likely to further decompensate without
immediate intervention will be triaged in this level. This category can also be labeled as RED. Priority: those seriously
injured/ill patients with potential to decompensate if not treated within 1 hour are triaged as priority cases. This category can
also be labeled as YELLOW.
Queue: this level includes all the walking wounded or those with less serious injury/sickness who are unlikely to decompensa
te. Patients in this category can safely wait for their turn. However, they should be monitored as their conditions may change
and warrant immediate care. This category is also labeled as GREEN.

sections.title: Cardiac Arrest and Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation
sections.text:
Cardiopulmonary resuscitation is an emergency lifesaving procedure performed when there is a sudden cessation of
heartbeat. It involves the combination of chest compression and artificial ventilation to preserve blood flow to the organs
including the brain function. Early initiation of CPR can double or triple the chances of survival after cardiac arrest.

 Note: HIGH QUALITY CPR
     •    Compressions:
          •    Infant: heel of one hand (if alone) or thumb encircling technique (if you have assistance)
          •    Child: 1 or 2 hand
          •    Adult: Two hands
          •    Compression rate: 100-120/min
          •    Compression depth: approximately 1/3 antero-posterior diameter of the chest
          •    Compression/ventilation ratio: 30:2 (adults and children), For Infants-30:2 (if alone) and 15:2 (if you have
               assistance), for neonates’ compression/ventilation ratio 3:1
     •    Allow chest recoil
     •    Minimize interruptions
     •    Adequate ventilation

Clinical Presentation

    •    Unresponsiveness (sudden loss of consciousness)
    •    Absence of central pulse (carotid pulse/femoral pulse or brachial pulse in infants)
    •    Loss of spontaneous respiration

Investigations

While continuing with CPR, point of care (POC) tests are conducted while looking for the reversible causes of cardiac arrest
(Hypovolemia, hypoxia, hypo/hyperkalemia, acidosis, hypothermia, hypoglycemia, tension pneumothorax, toxins, thrombi,
cardiac tamponade). These include:
     •    Blood gases
     •    Bicarbonates
     •    Electrolytes- Potassium, sodium, Calcium, Chloride,
     •    Creatinine, POC urea
     •    RBG
     •    Bedside ultrasound- looking for pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade or thrombi
     •    Toxicology serum blood and urine screens (If available)
     •    ECG (if there is return of spontaneous circulation)
     •    Lactate
     •    Troponin

Non- Pharmacological Management

    •    HAZARDS- ensure safety and use of PPEs
    •    HELLO- Check for responsiveness, Carotid pulse (not more than 10 seconds) and breathing
    •    CPR starts with early recognition (unresponsiveness, loss of spontaneous breathing and absence of carotid pulse.
    •    In infant’s CPR is initiated when the heart rate is below 60 beats/min
    •    Call for HELP and immediately start chest compression. As more members arrives to help assign different roles
         including airway and breathing management, time recording, documentation, AED/monitor operation and
         medications administration
    •    Open the airway by performing chin lift or jaw thrust (if suspecting C spine injury). Use airway adjuncts to open the
         airway.
    •    Give 2 breaths using bag valve mask connected to oxygen source and observe for chest rise
    •    Establish IV access for administration of fluids and medications; if failed, perform Intraosseous access
    •    After FIVE cycles of compression/ventilation (2 minutes), check for pulse and use AED/Defibrillator to analyze
         rhythm if there is a need to deliver shock
    •    If no need for shocking, continue with CPR for another 2 minutes (FIVE cycles)
    •    Use capnography (ETCO₂ monitoring) during CPR to assess quality. Maintain ETCO₂ >10 mmHg as a marker of
         effective compressions
    •    Double sequential defibrillation (DSD) may be considered for refractory VF/pVT

Pharmacological Management
For Adults

A: epinephrine (adrenaline) (IV) 1mg, (repeat every 3-5 minutes)
                   AND
A: sodium chloride 0.9% (IV) 2000mls, if suspecting hypovolemia as a cause of the arrest
                   AND
A: dextrose 5% (IV) if needed to correct hypoglycemia
                   OR
B: dextrose 10%, 25% or 50% (IV) if needed to correct hypoglycemia
                   AND
D: sodium bicarbonate 1mmol/kg (IV) push (if needed to correct acidosis)
                   AND
S: esmolol IV bolus 500 mcg/kg then infusion 50–200 mcg/kg/min

For Pediatrics

A: epinephrine (adrenaline) (IV) 0.01mg/kg (repeat every 3-5 minutes)
                   AND
A: sodium chloride 0.9% (IV) 20mls/kg; if suspecting hypovolemia as a cause of the arrest
                   AND
A: dextrose 5% (IV) if needed to correct hypoglycemia

*Additional medications may be required depending on the cause of the cardiac arrest (the
reversible cause)

    Note: Upon achieving return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), a definitive airway is achieved by
    performing endotracheal intubation for mechanical ventilation and patients must be admitted to the ICU or
    transferred to a facility with an ICU capacity.

sections.title: Rapid Sequence Intubation (RSI)
sections.text:
Rapid sequence intubation (RSI) is an airway management technique that is focused on inducing immediate
unresponsiveness by the use of induction agent followed by relaxation of the muscles using a neuromuscular
blocking agent. RSI is the fastest and most effective method of controlling the airway.
Use this checklist to make sure all equipment is ready (Mnemonic: SOAP ME).
    •    Suction - suction apparatus, Yankauer, suction catheter
    •    Oxygen - working oxygen, non-rebreather mask (NRBM), BVM
    •    Airways – Nasal Pharyngeal Airway, Oral pharyngeal airway, Endotracheal tube, Laryngeal mask airway,
         surgical airway kit
    •    Pre-oxygenate - 15L/min via NRBM
    •    Medications / Monitor – prepare & decide on RSI drugs
    •    Equipment - stylet, bougie, laryngoscope, glidescope

ETT Size for Children: (Refer to Broselow Tape)
      OR
Age in years/4 + 3 (Cuffed)
Age in years/4 + 4 (Uncuffed) ALWAYS HAVE DIFFERENT SIZE TUBES AVAILABLE
 LMA size                    1                        1.5                     2                         2.5
 Weight (Kg)                 <5                       5-10                    6.5-20                    20-30
 Age (yrs)                   <6 months                < 12 months             1-5                       5-10

 Note: The INTUBATING TEAM should be a minimum of 3 people. Physicians performing intubation should verbalize the
 intubation plan to all team members. The most experienced person available should be the one performing the procedure.

Pharmacological Management
First line Choose one sedative

B: ketamine (IV) 2mg/kg (ketamine is the preferred agent for intubation for asthma and anaphylaxis)
                             OR
D: midazolam (IV) 0.2mg/kg; intubation doses are higher than sedation doses (15 – 20mg)
                             OR
D: propofol (IV) 2-2.5mg/kg onset: 10-15 seconds; suitable for patients with seizures or status epilepticus
                             OR
S: etomidate (IV) 0.3mg/kg (0.15mg/kg if hypotensive); not to exceed 20 mg

Second line: Choose one paralytic
Always give sedation before paralytics

B: suxamethonium (IV) 1-2mg/kg; onset of action: 30-60 seconds, duration of action: 10 minutes. (Note: Use with caution:
may cause hyperkalemia)
                            OR
S: rocuronium (IV) 0.6-1.2 mg/kg; onset of action: 1-15 minutes, duration of action 30-60 minutes.
Post Intubation Care

B: pethidine (IV) 1mg/kg 4hourly (always remember to monitor the patient’s pain response)
                              OR
C: morphine (IV) 0.05-0.1 mg/kg every 30 minutes (maximum: 10 mg per dose). Always remember to
          monitor the patient's pain response)
                              OR
S: fentanyl (IV) 1-2mcg/kg bolus; then 25-250 mcg hourly (titrate every 20 minutes)

Give continuous sedation

C: lorazepam (IV) 1-4mg bolus; then 0.01-0.1mg/kg hourly (titrate every 1 hour)
                           OR
D: midazolam (IV) 1-5mg bolus; (0.05-0.1 mg/kg) then 0.04-0.2mg/kg hourly (titrate every 1 hour)

   Note: Remember to confirm ETT placement and NGT insertion.

sections.title: Approach to Stridor
sections.text:
Stridor is an abnormal, high-pitched sound produced by turbulent airflow through a partially obstructed airway.
Stridor is a dangerous finding and may indicate imminent airway obstruction. It can be inspiratory, expiratory or
biphasic.
Clinical Presentation:
    •       Hypoxia
    •       Respiratory distress
    •       Altered mental status
    •       Inability to speak
    •       Inability to swallow

Differential diagnoses
Infectious causes- croup, epiglottitis, peri-tonsillar abscess, retropharyngeal abscess, non-infectious causes- Foreign body
obstruction, burns, trauma, anaphylaxis, malignancy, laryngotracheomalacia, stenosis.

Note: Assess the airway (If unstable, consider surgical intervention/consult; if stable, consider imaging or direct
visualization of larynx with fiberoptic scope or video laryngoscope

Investigations
Blood gases analysis, Lateral neck X-ray (for foreign body, masses or soft tissue swelling), CXR (foreign body,
evidence of aspiration), CT- scan Neck, Blood Sugar, Lactate, Electrolyte analysis, and/or Serum creatinine and urea
Non-Pharmacological Management
Keep the patient calm by allowing the patient to assume their most comfortable position. Give oxygen if there are
signs of increased work of breathing.
Pharmacological Management
It will depend on the underlying cause. The following medications can be used in the management of stridor;

A: epinephrine (adrenaline) (nebulization) 0.5mls/kg
         AND/OR
B: dexamethasone (PO/IV/IM) 0.15- 0.6mg/kg stat (Max 10mg)

 Note:
        •    Since stridor can be as a result of various causes, management should be focused on the
             underlying causes
        •    Administer IV fluids (if signs of shock) – refer section on the management of shock
        •    All patients with stridor whose cause have not yet been established must be referred to higher
             health facilities

sections.title: Cough
sections.text:
Cough is a common reflex action that clears the throat of mucus, allergens, dust or other foreign irritants. A cough can be
caused by several conditions, both temporary and permanent. Frequent coughing indicates the presence of a disease.
Characteristics of cough/sputum
    •       If cough is dry without sputum and fever, it is probable an allergic condition or mild upper respiratory
            illness (e.g., allergic rhinitis or allergic bronchitis)
    •       If cough is dry without sputum or fever and is associated with other congestive symptoms, it may be due
            to Congestive Cardiac Failure (CCF)
    •    If it is a repeated attack cough with wheezing but without fever, it is likely to be bronchial asthma
    •    If it is a cough with fever, rapid breathing, and chest in-drawing, it is likely pneumonia
    •    If it is cough with sputum that is yellowish pus-like and there is fever, it is likely acute bronchitis or
         pneumonia
    •    If it is cough with blood in sputum and/or irregular fever with loss of weight and appetite, it is suspected
         tuberculosis
    •    If it is cough with a large quantity of foul-smelling sputum, very foul-smelling it is likely a lung abscess or
         bronchiectasis

Non-Pharmacological Management
Ensure the patient is positioned in a comfortable and supportive posture
Pharmacological Management
Causative/precipitating factors, e.g., CCF, asthma, and allergies, must be established and treated accordingly. (Refer
respiratory disease condition chapter 9)

 Note: Refer to a high facility with expertise when a cough persists and fails to establish the cause or when
 associated with fever.

sections.title: Approach to dyspnea (Shortness of breath)
sections.text:
Shortness of breath or breathlessness may result from a range of pulmonary, cardiac, and central nervous system
causes. It is important to look for the underlying cause for immediate intervention.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Increased work of breathing
     •    Altered mental status
     •    Diaphoresis
     •    Additional sounds- stridors, wheezes

Differential diagnosis
     •   Pulmonary embolism                                                •     Tension pneumothorax
     •   Pulmonary oedema                                                  •     Cardiac tamponade
     •   Myocardial infarction                                             •     Acute chest syndrome
     •   Asthma                                                            •     Pneumonia
     •   Anaphylaxis                                                       •     Pericarditis
     •   Airway obstruction
Investigations
Blood gases, Serum Electrolytes, Serum Creatinine and Urea, Troponins, Chest X-ray, POC ECG, Bedside Ultrasound,
Lactate, Troponin, Random blood glucose, CT- PA

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Obtain a thorough history and perform both primary survey (ABCs) and secondary survey, and provide
       necessary interventions
    •  Obtain Vital signs
    •  Position the patient
    •  Give Oxygen if hypoxic or increased work of breathing

Pharmacological Management
Pharmacological Management depends on the underlying cause of difficulty in breathing. (Refer respiratory disease
condition chapter 9)

sections.title: Approach to Upper Gastrointestinal Bleeding
sections.text:
Upper GI bleeding is any GI bleeding originating proximally to the ligament of Treitz.

Clinical Presentation
Hematemesis and coffee-ground emesis suggest a UGI source. On physical examination, vital signs may reveal
    •    Hypotension
    •    Tachycardia.
    •    Cool, clammy skin as a sign of shock.
    •    Abdominal examination may disclose tenderness, masses, ascites, or organomegaly.
    •    Presence of blood and its appearance on rectal examination, whether bright red, maroon, or melanotic.
    •    Spider angiomas, palmar erythema, jaundice, and gynecomastia, which may suggest liver disease.
    •    Petechiae and purpura may suggest an underlying coagulopathy

Differential diagnosis
Peptic ulcer disease, upper GI malignancy, oesophageal or gastric varices, esophagitis, Mallory- Weiss tear, Boerhaave
syndrome and arteriovenous malformation
Investigations
ABO Grouping and cross-matching, Complete Blood Count, Hemoglobin Level, Blood Urea Nitrogen and Creatinine,
Electrolytes, (Sodium, Potassium, Calcium Chloride), PT, PTT, INR, Liver Function Tests, Lactate levels, Obtain an ECG in
patients with underlying coronary artery disease and/or Bedside Ultrasound, CXR (If suspecting perforation)

Non-Pharmacological Management
Maintain ABCs, give oxygen if needed

Pharmacological Management
Give blood if severe pallor, ongoing bleeding, Hb < 5g/dl, and Hb < 7g/dl (with active bleeding)
Adults: 2 units within 1 hour and Pediatrics: 20ml/kg 1 hour (whole blood) or 10ml/kg (pRBC), If ongoing indication
for blood, start transfusion in the following ratio: 1unit pRBCs (20ml/kg
Pediatric: 1unit FFP (20mls/kg in Pediatric): 1unit PLT (20ml/kg in Pediatric)
          THEN
A: sodium chloride 0.9% (IV)
           OR
A: sodium lactate compound (ringer’s lactate)(IV); Adults 2000mls and Pediatrics 20ml/kg
           AND
C: pantoprazole (IV); Adults 80mg stat, then infusion 8mg/hour for 3days, Paediatrics1mg/kg stat (max 80mg) then infusion
1mg/kg/hour for 3days
           OR
S: esomeprazole (IV) 40mg 24hourly for 3days
For patients with suspected variceal bleeding,
S: octreotide (IV) Adults 50mg slow bolus, then infusion 50mcg/hour for 5days; Paediatrics1mcg/kg/hour
(maximum 50mcg/hour) for 5days
If features suggestive of cirrhosis;
B: ceftriaxone (IV) 1g 24hourly for 7days
           OR
C: ciprofloxacin (IV) 400mg 12hourly for 7days

Definitive Care: Early endoscopy and Intensive care unit admission (Refer to the Gastrointestinal disease chapter)

sections.title: Approach to Seizure and Status Epilepticus
sections.text:
Status epilepticus is a single seizure ≥5 minutes in length or two or more seizures without recovery of consciousness between
seizures. Status epilepticus is a neurologic emergency, and treatment should be initiated in all patients with continuous seizure
activity lasting more than 5 minutes.
Clinical Presentations
    •    Abrupt onset seizures
    •    Altered mental status
    •    Postictal drowsiness
    •    Tongue biting

Differential diagnoses
Epilepsy, meningitis, encephalitis, malaria, space-occupying lesion, alcohol withdrawal, isoniazid toxicity, intracranial
hemorrhage, metabolic abnormalities- hyponatremia, eclampsia, acute hydrocephalus.
Investigations:
Blood Glucose, Electrolytes: (Sodium, Potassium, Chloride, Magnesium, and Calcium), ECG, Bedside ultrasound, Blood
gases, Malaria Test, Serum creatinine and urea, Lactate levels, Pregnancy test (females), Toxicology screening and/or CT
Head
Non-Pharmacological Management
     •    Protect the patient from injury (If possible, place in left lateral position to reduce aspiration risks), Don’t
          place tongue depressor
     •    Perform both primary and secondary assessments and provide necessary interventions
     •    Give Oxygen if needed
     •    Do a bedside random blood sugar test
     •    Establish IV access for administration of anticonvulsants; if unable, use the rectal route
     •    Connect the patient to the cardiac monitor to obtain vital signs

Pharmacological Management
Active seizure 0-5minutes.

sections.title: Approach to Altered Mental Status
sections.text:
This is the acute alteration in brain function and may include alteration of arousal or awareness, thought content, memory or
attention.

Clinical Presentation
Depending on the cause but may include agitation, Restlessness, Hemiparesis, visual deficit, dysphasia
Differential diagnosis
The mnemonic AEIOU TIPS is widely preferred in the emergency department when considering a broader differential.
Alcohol/acidosis, Epilepsy/Electrolytes, Insulin/Inborn Errors of Metabolism, Oxygen/Overdose, Uremia, Trauma, Infection,
Psychiatric/Poisoning, Stroke/Subarachnoid Hemorrhage/Shock
Investigations
POC Glucose, Rapid Malaria test, Blood gases, Serum Electrolytes, POC ECG, Bedside ultrasound, Serum Creatinine and
Urea, Lactate, Complete Blood Count, Liver function tests, Head CT-scan, Chest Xray and/or Toxicology screening (If highly
suspicious of intoxication)
Non- Pharmacological Management:
    •    If aggressive/ restless, consider restraining- mechanical or chemical (medications)
    •    Obtain a set of vital signs, including random blood glucose
    •    Perform both primary and secondary assessments and provide necessary interventions.
    •    Give Oxygen if Hypoxic or dyspneic
    •    Connect the patient to the cardiac monitor to obtain vital signs

Pharmacological Management
Treatment will depend on the cause of the altered mental status. For agitated patients, if needed to sedate, use:
A: diazepam (IV): Adults 5-10mg loading dose, maintenance 0.03-0.1mg/kg every 30 minutes to 6 hours;
Pediatrics 0.1-0.15mg/kg stat, may repeat after 3-5 minutes
          OR
B: haloperidol (IV): Adults 0.5-10mg (If concerned about psychiatric disorder) Child: safety and effectiveness not
established
          OR
B: ketamine (IV) 1-2mg/kg and 2-4mg/kg for (IM)
          OR
D: midazolam (IV): Adults 5mg stat, maintenance 20-100mcg/kg/hr. infusion; Pediatrics 0.05-0.1mg/kg stat.

   Note: Consult/refer to a higher center with a psychiatrist if concerned about a psychiatric disorder

sections.title: Anaphylaxis
sections.text:
Anaphylaxis is a severe, life-threatening, generalized or systemic hypersensitivity reaction characterized by rapidly developing
life-threatening airway (pharyngeal or laryngeal edema) and/or breathing (bronchospasm and tachypnea) and/or circulation
(hypotension and tachycardia) problems usually associated with skin and mucosal changes.
Clinical Presentation
    •    Hives
    •    Angioedema
    •    Wheezes
    •    Difficult breathing
    •    Diarrhea
    •    Hypotension

Anaphylaxis is a clinical diagnosis and should be suspected when:
    •    Acute onset involving skin, mucosal tissue, with either respiratory compromise or blood pressure
         reduction (or syncope)
    •    Hypotension after exposure to a known allergy for the patient (SBP <90mmHg or >30% from baseline)
    •    Respiratory compromise (i.e., dyspnea, stridor, wheeze, hypoxemia)
    •    Exposure to a likely allergen causes involvement of the skin, mucosal, respiratory compromization or
         blood pressure reduction

Investigations
Blood gases, Serum Electrolytes, POC ECG, Troponin, CXR and/or POC USS

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •    Perform both primary and secondary assessments. If the patient has signs of severe respiratory distress,
         perform early intubation/surgical airway
    •    Give oxygen if hypoxic (spO2 below 95%) or severe respiratory distress
    •    Insert TWO large-bore IV cannulas or obtain intraosseous access

Pharmacological Management
For Adults
A: epinephrine (adrenaline) (IM) 0.3-0.5mg (maximum 0.5mg) every 5-15min as soon as possible.
If inadequate response, start.
A: epinephrine (adrenaline) (IV) 2-10mcg/min in 0.9% sodium chloride or Ringer Lactate
If hypotensive.
Repeat IV fluids as needed;
For Pediatrics 0.01mg/kg, every 5-15min as soon as possible.
If inadequate response, start.
A: epinephrine (adrenaline) (IV) 0.05- 1mcg/kg/min in 0.9% sodium chloride or sodium lactate compound (ringer’s
lactate)20mls/kg
If hypotensive.
Repeat IV fluids as needed.
         OR/AND
A: hydrocortisone (IV)200mg stat
         OR/AND
B: salbutamol nebulizer10mg and equal volume of water for injection (This is useful to patients with refractory
   bronchospasm).
         OR/AND
D: methylprednisolone (IV) 1-2mg/kg/day

  Note: All patients with severe and moderate symptoms which required repeated doses of epinephrine
  (adrenaline) or do not respond to treatment must be admitted or referred to a higher health facility. Those
  with mild responses who responded to IM epinephrine (adrenaline) may be discharged after 4 hours’
  observation at the health facility.

sections.title: Cardiac Tamponade
sections.text:
Cardiac tamponade is the result of compression of the myocardium by fluid, gas, pus, blood, or a combination of substances.
It occurs in a physiological continuum reflecting the amount of fluid, the rate of accumulation, and the nature of the heart.
The result is increased pericardial pressure, which causes decreased ventricle compliance and decreased flow of blood into
the right ventricle, which eventually leads to decreased cardiac output. Conditions that may predispose a patient to pericardial
effusion and tamponade include trauma, radiation exposure, Tb pericarditis, renal failure (uremic pericarditis), autoimmune
diseases, drugs that induce a lupus-like syndrome, hypothyroidism, or ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome.
Clinical Presentations
      •    Chest pain and dyspnea
      •    Pulsus paradoxus >10 mm Hg
      •    Beck’s triad includes low blood pressure, elevated jugular venous distention, and decreased heart
           sounds.
      •    In the absence of hypotension and tension pneumothorax in a patient with PEA, consider the diagnosis
           of cardiac tamponade.

Investigations
Bedside ultrasound and ECHO, POC, ECG, Blood gases, Serum Electrolytes, Troponins, Pericardial fluid
analysis- biochemistry, microbiology and cytology, Serum creatinine and urea, and/or Chest X-ray

Non- Pharmacological Management
    •   Perform both primary and secondary assessments and provide appropriate interventions.
    •   Give oxygen if hypoxic or increased work of breathing
    •   Connect the patient to a cardiac monitor and obtain vital signs
    •   Pericardiocentesis is the definitive management

Pharmacological Management
A: sodium chloride 0.9% (IV): Adults 1-2 litres; Pediatrics 20ml/kg to increase right-sided filling pressure

 Note
     •    The definitive treatment for cardiac tamponade is pericardiocentesis. A cardiology consultation or referral is strongly
          recommended. In emergency settings, pericardiocentesis may be performed by a qualified and experienced
          medical practitioner in the emergency department.
     •    All patients with cardiac tamponade require inpatient management in an intensive care unit setting/HDU.

sections.title: Pulmonary Edema
sections.text:
A life-threatening condition that occurs due to abnormal fluid build-up in the lungs, leading to impaired gaseous
exchange, acute respiratory distress and may cause respiratory failure. Can be classified as cardiogenic
pulmonary edema, due to increased hydrostatic pulmonary pressure (HF) and non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema,
due to increased permeability (acute lung injury and allergic alveolitis).

    Note: Cardiogenic and non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema have no clear-cut differences in Clinical
    Presentation, however identifying the specific underlying cause of pulmonary edema is significant for
    therapeutic and prognostic purposes.
Clinical Presentation
Shortness of breath, use of accessory muscles, diaphoresis, tachypnoea and crepitations
Investigations
Chest X-ray, Blood gases, Serum Creatinine and Urea, POC ECG, POC troponin, BNP, Serum electrolytes and/or
Bedside Ultrasound
Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Perform both primary and secondary                                 •    Position the patient at a 45° angle or
       assessment and provide necessary                                        in the sitting upright position
       interventions                                                      •    Perform ECG (rule out ischemia,
    •  Give high-flow oxygen therapy                                           dysrhythmia). Perform bedside
    •  Put the patient on a cardiac monitor                                    ECHO (to rule out cardiac causes-
       (if available) and obtain vital signs                                   contractility, pericardial effusion)
                                                                          •    Perform chest ultrasound (comet
                                                                               tails and B lines)

Pharmacological Management
Control hypertension (Maintain SBP>90mmHg,
S: nitroglycerin (IV): Adults loading 100mcg/min titrate rapidly to 400mcg/min over 2 minutes

 Note:
     •     Beware of pre-load sensitive condition example inferior or right ventricular myocardial infarction, and
           phosphodiesterase inhibitors use.
      •    Don’t give Nitroglycerin if SBP< 90mmHg)

Reduce intravascular volume if fluid overloaded

A: furosemide (IV/IM) 0.5-1mg/kg over 20minutes (maximum 120mg) or infusion IV 5-10mg/kg (maximum 120mg).

 Note: Beware of renal insufficiency and volume-depleted patients; check the size of the IVC

Ventilation
Oxygen therapy (target saturation>95%); CPAP or BiPAP (for persistent respiratory distress, hypoxia or acidosis despite high
flow oxygen therapy); Intubation and mechanical ventilation (for respiratory failure despite CPAP/BiPAP)
Goal of treatment - Relieve hypoxemia (improve oxygenation); reduce pulmonary capillary pressure and improve perfusion.
Admit all patients with pulmonary edema to HDU/ICU or transfer the patient to a health facility with ICU/HDU capacity

sections.title: Approach to Shock
sections.text:
Shock is a state of acute circulatory failure leading to decreased organ perfusion, with inadequate delivery of
oxygenated blood to tissues and resultant end-organ dysfunction and it is an emergency condition. Adherence to
evidence-based care of the specific causes of shock can enhance a patient’s chances of surviving.
Clinical Presentation
     •    Low blood pressure (systolic BP below 80 mmHg) is the key sign of shock
     •    Weak and rapid pulse
     •    Rapid and shallow breathing
     •    Restlessness and altered mental state
     •    Weakness
     •    Low urine output

Table 1.1: Types of shock & Additional Symptoms

The following investigations can be performed depending on the type of shock;
    •     Basic serum chemistry (including renal function)            •    Troponins

    •     POC Ultrasound- lungs, IVC, Cardiac                         •    Lactate

    •     CSF analysis if a patient is
          suspected of meningitis
Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Prompt diagnosis of the underlying cause is essential to ensure optimal treatment.
    •  Perform the ABCD approach. Intervene when needed
    •  Maintain an open airway
    •  Administer oxygen with a face mask and, if needed, after intubation with assisted ventilation
    •  Check for and manage hypoglycemia
Pharmacological Management
Treatment depends on the type of shock. Intravenous fluid therapy is important in the treatment of all types of
shock except for cardiogenic shock.
A: sodium chloride 0.9% (IV): Adults give 2 litres bolus infusion. Repeat bolus until blood pressure is improved.
Transfuse blood and plasma expanders in hemorrhagic shock. Paediatrics give 20ml/kg as a slow infusion.
All children with shock that is not obviously due to trauma or simple watery diarrhea should receive antibiotic cover
for probable septicemia.
If the pressure doesn’t improve after two boluses of IV Fluids (4lts in adults and 40mls/kg in pediatrics), administer
Inotropes/vasopressors (Refer to the Sepsis and septic shock topic section)

     Note:

                 administering ceftriaxone
             •   Do not administer IV fluids in case of cardiogenic shock, but maintain the IV line
             •   If the patient develops respiratory distress, discontinue fluids but maintain the IV line
             •   Ceftriaxone is contraindicated in neonatal jaundice

Referral: Refer the patient urgently with the escort of a nurse to high level facility to establish the cause and
address all medications given in the referral letter.

sections.title: Sepsis and Septic Shock
sections.text:
Septicemia (Sepsis) is defined as life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to bacterial
infection (commonly) and fungal or viral infections. Organ dysfunction can be represented by an increase in the Sequential
[Sepsis-related] Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score of 2 points or more, with an in-hospital mortality greater than 10%.
Septic Shock is defined as a subset of sepsis in which particularly profound circulatory, cellular, and metabolic abnormalities
are associated with a greater risk of mortality than 40%.
Clinical Presentation
     •    Temperature of >38oC or <360C; Heart rate of >90/min; Respiratory rate of >20/min or PaCO2 <32 mm Hg
     •    Above features plus evidence of organ dysfunction (hypotension, jaundice, oliguria, or altered state of
          consciousness from altered sensorium like drowsiness/lethargy
Investigations
Blood gases analysis, Bedside ultrasound- assessing the inferior vena cava and the lungs, POC ECG, Urine dipstick, Chest
X-ray if suspecting pneumonia, Complete blood count, Qualitative or quantitative CRP or Procalcitonin in centers available,
Serum Electrolytes, Creatinine and Urea, Liver function tests- liver enzymes, bilirubin, clotting time, Blood culture and
antimicrobial susceptibility testing. Primary source of infection’s clinical sample culture (e.g., urine, pus, sputum CSF etc.) and
antimicrobial susceptibility testing and/or RNA/DNA PCR for viral pathogens (where indicated).

Diagnostic criteria
Sepsis: Q-SOFA in settings with limited laboratory infrastructures: two or more SOFA scores, namely: Respiratory rate
≥22/min, altered mentation, and Systolic blood pressure ≥100 mm Hg) ± bacteria or fungal proven blood culture and
susceptibility testing are recommended to make a definitive diagnosis.
Other scoring criteria include SOFA, NEWS (National Early Warning Score), and MEDS (Mortality in Emergency Medicine
Department Sepsis
Septic shock: Sepsis diagnostic criteria above and vasopressor therapy needed to elevate MAP ≥65 mmHg and lactate >2
mmol/L (18 mg/dL) despite adequate fluid resuscitation.
Non-Pharmacological Management
    •      Nutritional support
    •      Control measures focused on the primary focus of infection.
    •      Perform primary and secondary assessment and provide necessary interventions
    •      Ensure patency of the airway and give oxygen if hypoxic or increased work of breathing
    •      Connect the patient to the cardiac monitor and obtain vital signs

Pharmacological Management

A: sodium chloride 0.9% (IV) Adults: 2litres; Paediatrics: 20mls/kg.
                OR
A: sodium lactate compound (ringer’s lactate)(IV): Adults 2litres; Paediatrics 20mls/kg in 20 minutes as a first bolus followed
by a second bolus of 2litres/20mls/kg (use small boluses in CCF).
                   OR
S: dobutamine (IV) 2-20mcg/kg/min can be given for patients in shock not responding to fluids or when there is
poor cardiac output.
                   OR
S: norepinephrine (IV) 5-20mcg/min for patients in septic shock not responding after the first 30mls/kg of IVF bolus
to maintain the mean arterial pressure (MAP) of ≥ 65mm Hg
                   AND
A: hydrocortisone (IV) 200mg stat.
                   OR
S: albumin 60g of 20% running for 2-3 hours

   Note:
       •      Transfuse blood (If hemoglobin is < 7g/dl)
       •      Lactate clearance should be used as a resuscitation target.

Antimicrobial therapies (broad-spectrum antibiotics must be started within the first hour):

A: ampicillin (IV) 150-200mg/kg/day divided 6 hourly a day
                     AND
B: cloxacillin (IV) 50-100 mg/kg/day 6 hourly a day
                     AND
A: gentamicin (IV) or (IM) 120mg, 7.5mg/kg 24hourly for 5 days for children.
If there is no improvement in vital signs within 24 hours (Temp, HR, RR and altered state of consciousness), give:
B: ceftriaxone (IV) 1 gm, 100mg/kg (IV or IM) 24hourly for 4-14 days for children
                     AND
A: gentamicin (IV) or (IM) 120mg [For children 7.5mg/kg] 24hourly for 5 days
    Refer immediately.

D: ceftriaxone + sulbactam (FDC) (IV) or (IM) 75-120 mg/kg 24hourly for 4-14 days
                     AND
A: gentamicin (IV) or (IM) 120mg [For children 7.5mg/kg] 24hourly for 5days
                     OR
S**piperacillin + tazobactam (FDC) (IV) (4g+0.5g) administered 8hourly [For children 100 mg Piperacillin+12.5mg
Tazobactam per kg body weight 8hourly] for 7-10days
                     AND
A: gentamicin (IV) or (IM) 120mg [For children 7.5mg/kg] 24hourly for 5days.

Alternatively, (for patients who have evidence of not improving on the treatment above and referred to a
zonal/tertiary hospital with judicious decision from a medical specialist or medical super- specialist):

S**meropenem 2g (IV) 8hourly in adults and adolescents [40 mg/kg 8hourly in children] for 7-14days
                  OR
S**vancomycin (IV) 15 to 20 mg/kg body weight 8 -12hourly (not to exceed 2 g per dose) for 7-14days.
 Note: In renal insufficiency, vancomycin can be adjusted for dose and dose interval. These antimicrobial agents
 are usually reserved for Gram-negative and Gram-positive pathogen(s), respectively, supported by culture and
 antimicrobial susceptibility testing

For suspected co-existing anaerobic infections, an additional regimen to all regimes above

B: metronidazole (IV) 500mg 8hourly [In children 7.5 mg/kg 8hourly] for 7days
                   OR
S: clindamycin (IV) 600mg 1.2g/day diluted infusion in two or three doses; In children 15-25mg/kg/day in three
equal doses for 7-10days is recommended.
For the rare cases of sepsis or septic shock due to carbapenem-resistant Gram-negative bacteria or vancomycin-
resistant Gram-positive bacteria, give:
S** colistin (IV) 2.5-5mg/kg/day 8-12 hourly for 5days
                    AND
S** linezolid (PO/IV) 400-600mg 12hourly for 10-14 days, respectively or other non-beta-lactam antibiotics may
be considered based on culture and antimicrobial susceptibility testing results.
In case there is/are risk factors for invasive candida infections, such as in immunocompromised states, prolonged
invasive vascular, necrotizing pancreatitis, then antifungal therapies should be added.
C: fluconazole (IV) 800mg 24hourly on the first day, then 400mg 24hourly for 14days [In children 6-12mg/kg/day
for 14days]

sections.title: Approach to Pain
sections.text:
Pain is an unpleasant sensation or emotional experience associated with actual or potential tissue damage, or described in
terms of such damage. Any pain of moderate or higher intensity is accompanied by anxiety and the urge to escape or terminate
the feeling. Pain is subjective and unique perceptual experience with multiple dimensions that may not directly be observed
by others or measured by physiological tests. Assessment is almost entirely self-reported.
Assessment of pain.
Self-report is the key to pain assessment. In non- or preverbal children, facial expression is the most valid indicator
of pain; therefore, use the faces pain scale to assess severity. Pain should be assessed by:
     •     Duration                                                         •    Relieving or aggravating factors
     •     Severity, e.g., does the patient wake                            •    Accompanying symptoms
           up because of the pain                                           •    Distribution of pain
     •     Site                                                             •    In children, pain can be assessed by
     •     Characteristics,     e.g.    stabbing,                                a child’s crying voice, posture,
           throbbing, crushing, cramp-like                                       movement and colour
     •     Persistent or intermittent

sections.title: Approach to Chest Pain
sections.text:
The approach to non-traumatic chest pain requires early recognition of life-threatening conditions. Patients with
life-threatening conditions may have stable initial vital signs.
For a patient presenting with chest pain, the following are the differential diagnoses
     •    Acute coronary syndrome                                           •    Tension pneumothorax
     •    Cardiac tamponade                                                 •    Acute chest syndrome (sickle cell
     •    Pericarditis                                                           patients)
     •    Myocarditis                                                       •    Lung infection (pneumonia)
     •    Myocardial infarction                                             •    Esophageal perforation
     •    Aortic dissection                                                 •    Reflux Esophagitis
     •    Pulmonary embolism                                                •    Musculoskeletal pain

   Note: Refer to the relevant chapters for detailed management of the specific disease condition.

Investigations
Depending on the Clinical Presentation, the following investigations may be required:
POC ECG, Bedside USS- (cardiac, lungs, pleural, IVC, Abdominal aorta, kidneys, etc.), Serum electrolytes, POC
Troponin, Blood gases, Serum creatinine and urea, Urine pregnancy test, Radiological investigations- Chest X-
ray and/or CT scan- chest.
Pharmacological Management
Treat the underlying cause as indicated in specific chapters. The following analgesics may be used to relieve the
pain:
Mild pain:

A: paracetamol (PO) 1g 6hourly for 24 hours
          OR
A: ibuprofen (PO) 400mg 8hourly for 24 hours
          OR
A: diclofenac (IM/IV) 50-100mg stat

Mild to moderate pain:

A: paracetamol (PO/IV) 1g 6hourly for 24 hours
          OR
A: ibuprofen (PO) 400mg 8hourly for 24 hours
          OR
A: diclofenac (IM/IV) 50-100mg stat
          AND
B: tramadol (PO/IV) initially 100mg, then 50-100mg every 4-6 hours; usual maximum 400mg for 24 hours

Moderate to severe pain:

S: fentanyl mcg/kg q1-3h
         OR
C: morphine (IV) 0.1mg/kg stat
         OR
D: paracetamol (IV) 1g stat
If myocardial ischemia is highly suspected, give:

A: acetylsalicylic acid (PO)325mg stat
          AND
D: clopidogrel (PO) 300mg stat

   Note: Refer to a higher facility with expertise when failed to establish the cause of the chest pain.

sections.title: Approach to Abdominal Pain
sections.text:
Abdominal pain is among the common complaints of patients presenting to the Emergency Department. While the
majority have benign and self-limited etiologies, the goal is to identify those with serious or life-threatening
etiologies to perform early intervention.
Differential Diagnoses:
                                                                     Genito-urinary causes;
Surgical causes;

                                                                          •   Ureteric and kidney stones
    •    Upper GI bleeding
                                                                          •   Urinary tract infection
Medical causes;                                                           •   Pelvic inflammatory disease
                                                                          •   Lower GI bleeding
    •    Myocardial infarction
                                                                          •   Splenic rupture

    •    Gastroesophageal reflux disease

    •    Inflammatory bowel syndrome

Investigations
Depending on the Clinical Presentation, the following investigations may be required:

Blood gases, Lactate, Serum Creatinine and Urea, Urine pregnancy test, Radiological investigations (Chest and
Abdomen X-ray and/or CT scan- Abdomen).

Pharmacological Management
Refer to the above section (Chest pain)

For those patients who are unable to take oral medications

sections.title: Headache
sections.text:
Approach to acute headache
Headache is a challenging complaint as it requires balancing symptomatic control with rapid assessment for life-threatening
diagnoses. Headaches can be categorized into primary and secondary. Primary causes are neurologic and include tension,
cluster and migraine. Secondary headaches are a result of an underlying pathological process such as malignancies,
infections and other organic causes.
Differential diagnoses
                                                                     Altered
Sudden onset of severe headache
                                                                          •    Meningitis
    •    Subarachnoid hemorrhage                                          •    Encephalitis
    •    Cerebral venous thrombosis                                       •    Space-occupying lesions
    •    Hypertension emergency                                           •    Stroke
    •    Adrenal and pituitary emergencies                                •    Subarachnoid hemorrhage
                                                                          •    Intracranial tumor

  Note: Refer to specific chapters for the management of the specific disease condition

sections.title: Other Pains
sections.text:
Other pains may include:
    •    Generalized body ache                                            •    Pains due to injury
    •    Joint pain                                                       •    Eye pains
    •    Pain due to local infections                                     •    Ear pains

Non-pharmacological
Perform the primary and secondary assessment with interventions when needed.
Pharmacological Management
For generalized pain give analgesics, advise the patient to rest and make a follow-up. For joint, infections, injury,
eye and ear pains treat as for main disease.
Refer patients if:
     •    Children with moderate and acute severe pain
     •    No response to oral pain control
     •    Uncertain diagnosis
     •    All acute abdominal pain accompanied by vomiting and no passing of stool
     •    Pain requiring definitive treatment for the underlying disease
     •    Pain requiring opioids

sections.title: Approach to Fever (Pyrexia)
sections.text:
Fever is an abnormal elevation of body temperature that occurs as part of a specific biologic response that is
mediated and controlled by the central nervous system and is usually a symptom of an infection. It is characterized
by an elevation of body temperature above the normal range of 36.5–37.5 0C
Clinical Presentation
     •    Depression                                                      •    Inability to concentrate
     •    Lethargy                                                        •    Feeling cold
     •    Anorexia                                                        •    Increased muscle tone
     •    Sleepiness                                                      •    Shivering
     •    Hyperalgesia                                                    •    Irritability

Investigations
    •    Will be specific based on the Clinical                           •    POC Urine dipstick
         Presentation. These may include:                                 •    POC ECG
    •    Rapid Malaria test                                               •    Radiological investigations- X-ray,
    •    Blood slide for malaria parasites                                •    CT scan
    •    Rapid dengue test                                                •    Complete blood count
    •    Lactate                                                          •    Serum Electrolytes
    •    Blood culture                                                    •    Serum Creatinine and Urea
    •    Bedside USS- Gall bladder, Liver,                                •    Urine Culture
         spleen, Abdominal aorta, kidneys                                 •    CRP

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •       Perform both primary and secondary assessment. Intervene whenever necessary.
    •       Advise the patient to rest in bed
    •       Ask patient to take plenty of fluids (If able to take orally)

Pharmacological Management
A: paracetamol (PO) Adults 1g 6hourly when required, Pediatrics 15mg/kg 6hourly when required or suppository
125mg–250mg, 6hourly
                     OR
A: ibuprofen (PO) Adults 400mg 8hourly when required; Pediatrics 5-10mg/kg 8hourly when required
For patients who are unable to take oral medications, give:
D: paracetamol 1gm (IV) when required
Referral
 Note: Refer the patient to the next facility with adequate expertise and facilities.
        •    If no diagnosis is established
        •    If no improvement of fever after the use of antibiotics
        •    Fever that recurs

sections.title: Approach to the Trauma Patient
sections.text:
Table 1.2: Approach to Trauma Patient
  Preparation
  Mobilize medical emergency team                       High Risk Mechanisms of Injury
  Prepare    equipment,   examples;   monitors,         •              High speed motor vehicle accident
  ultrasound, Consider high-risk mechanisms of
  injury                                                •              Pedestrian accidents
                                                        •              Ejection
                                                        •              Fall > 3m in height
                                                        •              Penetrating injuries

  Initial Resuscitation
  Airway: Protect as appropriate and ensure Cervical-spine immobilization.

  Breathing: Give oxygen and titrate to SpO2 (above 92%). If no air entry or if hyper-resonance is present, insert a chest
  drain. If the patient is showing signs of obstructive shock or a deviated trachea, needle decompression can be used initially
  before definitive decompression with a chest drain.

sections.title: Approach to Dehydrated Patient
sections.text:
It refers to the loss of body water, with or without salt at a rate greater than the body can replace it. The cause of dehydration
is a combination of physiological and disease processes. Persons at greatest risk for dehydration include persons with
diarrhoea, vomiting, fever, diabetes or infections, impaired level status.
Table 1.3: Types of Dehydration

 Skin pinched up                Becomes normal                Takes two seconds for              Remain in folds f o r
                                immediately                   folds to disappear                 over two seconds

                                present                       absent
 Mouth                          Not dry                       Is dry                             Is dry

 Fontanel                       Normal                        Depressed                          Sunken
 Blood Pressure                 Normal                        Normal but orthostasis             Decreased
 Capillary refill               2s                            2-4s                               More than 4s
Investigations
     •    Blood chemistry (to check electrolytes, especially sodium, potassium, and bicarbonate levels)
     •    Blood urea nitrogen (BUN) and creatinine
     •    Bedside USS- IVC
     •    Complete blood count
     •    Urine specific gravity
     •    Blood Gas analysis
     •    Lactate

Other tests may be done to determine the cause of the dehydration (for example, blood sugar level to check for
diabetes).
Non-Pharmacological Management
     •    Perform both primary and secondary assessments and provide the necessary interventions.
     •    Give oxygen if hypoxic or increased work of breathing
     •    Put TWO large-bore IV cannulas for fluid resuscitations

The treatment for minor dehydration, often considered the most effective, is drinking water and stopping fluid loss.
Pharmacological Management
In more severe cases, correction of a dehydrated state is accomplished by the replenishment of necessary water
and electrolytes.

A: oral rehydration salt (ORS)
                    OR
A: sodium chloride 0.9% (IV) Adults 1-2litres; Pediatrics 20mls/kg
                    OR
A: sodium lactate compound (ringer’s lactate)(IV) Adults 1-2litres; Pediatrics 20ml/kg
Remember to do reassessment after fluids resuscitations., If there is no electrolyte loss, give;
A: dextrose 5% (IV)
If the underlying disease condition is diagnosed, treat as per the specific condition in the guidelines.
Referral: Refer to a high center with expertise if there is no improvement.

 Note: Dehydration in Children refer to Plan A, B and C in IMCI guidelines

sections.title: Hyponatremia
sections.text:
Defined as serum sodium (Na+) levels less than 135mEq/L. It can be classified as: Mild hyponatremia (130-135 mEq/L),
Moderate hyponatremia (125 -129 mEq/L), Severe hyponatremia (< 125mEq/L).
Clinical Presentation
Clinical signs generally occur once levels are <125mEq/L. The following are symptoms related to hyponatremia:

     •    Nausea and vomiting                                              •     Loss of consciousness or coma
     •    Fatigue                                                          •     Cramps or muscle spasms
     •    Dizziness                                                        •     Irritability and restlessness
     •    Headache or confusion                                            •     Weakness
     •    Tremulousness or seizures                                        •     Thirst and anorexia

Investigations
Based on classification and patients’ clinical findings, the following investigations may be necessary:

     •    POC RBG                                                          •     Urine Osmolality
     •    Urine dipstick                                                   •     Thyroid profile
     •    Electrolytes                                                     •     CT brain (suspected cerebral
     •    Creatinine and Urea                                                    process)
     •    LFTs                                                             •     CXR       (suspected    pulmonary
     •    Serum Osmolality                                                       infection/edema – related to renal
     •    Urine Na+                                                              failure, CCF)

Non-Pharmacological Management
Nutritional measures adjusted to patients need
     •    Salt-containing foods
     •    Rehydration therapy
     •    Dietary modification

The goal of acute management is the treatment of serious complications and careful restoration of serum sodium concentration.
Management depends on the cause, severity and time course. Based on the duration of development, hyponatremia can be (i)
acute or (ii) chronic

      and clinical monitoring. If not available, refer the patient to a higher health facility with HDU/ ICU capabilities.

sections.title: Hypokalemia
sections.text:
It is defined as plasma potassium below 3.5mmol/l. It includes Weakness, constipation, paralysis, bradycardia and reduced
tendon reflexes.
Investigations
POC ECG, serum creatinine and urea, serum electrolytes, and/or bedside ultrasound
Additional investigations may be required based on the Clinical Presentation.
Non-Pharmacological Management
      •        Perform both primary and secondary assessments and provide the necessary interventions needed.
      •        Give oxygen if hypoxic or increased work of breathing
      •        Connect the patient to the monitor and obtain Vital signs
      •        Place IV access

Pharmacological Management
Mild hypokalemia (3.0-3.5mmol/l)
C: potassium chloride (PO) Adults 20-40mEq 8hourly (dissolved in 100-150mL water); Pediatrics 2mEq/kg 8hourly
diluted in oral fluids or food. In case of diarrhea, give ORS (5ml/kg/hr)
Moderate hypokalemia (2.5-2.9mmol/l)
C: potassium chloride (IV) Adults 10mEq/hour; Pediatrics 0.5mEq/kg/hour diluted in 25- 50mls of 0.9% sodium chloride or
DNS or 5% dextrose solutions via peripheral vein. Do not exceed 10mEq/hour.
Severe hypokalemia (<2.5mmol/l)
Both IV & oral replacement
C: potassium chloride (PO): Adults (28mmol K+) per hour if tolerated (dissolved in 100- 150mL water) diluted potassium;
Pediatrics (PO) 2mEq/kg 8hourly.
                    OR
C: potassium chloride (IV): Adults 20mEq in 100mL fluid over 1 hour via cubital fossa vein. Continue to measure
serum potassium every 1 to 2 hours until K+ > 2.8 mmol/L. Pediatrics 1mEq/kg/hour.
The calculated hourly dose is multiplied by 12.5ml volume for dilution with NS/DNS/D5%. Do not exceed 10mEq/hr

  Note: Magnesium should be checked. IF LOW, give Magnesium as follows:

Adults
A: magnesium sulphate 50% (IV) Adults: Initially give 4ml diluted to 10ml with 0.9% sodium chloride run over 20 minutes, then
potassium chloride infusion, then magnesium sulphate 50% (IV) 0.12ml/kg/day;
Paediatrics
A: magnesium sulphate 50% (IV) 0.1ml/kg/dose administered over 2hours
Hypokalemia in CARDIAC ARREST in Adults: KCl 10mEq IV over 5 min; the dose may be repeated once

sections.title: Hyperkalemia
sections.text:
It is defined when serum potassium levels are above 5.5 mEq/L. The most common cause is hemolysis from a blood draw.
Other causes include Renal failure, medications, and blood transfusions
Clinical Presentations
     •    Muscle weakness                                               •   Nausea and Vomiting
     •    Lethargy, fatigue                                             •   Difficulty breathing
     •    Paresthesias                                                  •   Palpitations, chest pain

Investigations
ECG, Blood gas analysis, creatinine, urea, serum electrolytes, toxicology screening
Management of hyperkalemia is focused on three (3) key areas:
     •    Stabilization of the cardiac membrane
     •    Intracellular potassium ions shifting

sections.title: Hypocalcemia
sections.text:
Hypocalcemia is defined as a total serum calcium concentration below 8.8 mg/dL (< 2.20 mmol/L) in the presence of normal
plasma protein concentrations, or as a serum ionized calcium concentration below 4.7 mg/dL (< 1.17 mmol/L). Reference

sections.title: Hypernatremia
sections.text:
Hypernatremia is defined as a plasma sodium concentration of >145mmol/L. Severe hypernatremia is a plasma
sodium value of >160 mmol/L. Hypernatremia can be due to loss of water, gain of sodium, or both. Loss of water
is the more common denominator. The main cause of hypernatremia is body water loss.
Clinical Presentation
Mild and chronic hypernatremia is usually asymptomatic. Severe acute hypernatremia causes CNS symptoms-
irritability, lethargy, seizure and coma
Investigations
    •    Urine specific gravity/osmolality                              •     Creatinine and BUN
    •    Serum electrolytes                                             •     Blood sugar

Non-Pharmacological Management
Encourage free water intake

Pharmacological Management
It depends on the severity of hypernatremia and the patient’s volume state.

sections.title: Anaesthesia
sections.text:
Anaesthesia is a state of controlled reversible loss of consciousness, usually accompanied by analgesia, muscle relaxation,
amnesia and areflexia. It is usually induced for the purpose of facilitating surgery and other therapeutic or diagnostic
procedures.

Anaesthesia may be achieved with either:

    •    Local anaesthesia -topical application/spray or                •    General anaesthesia
         infiltration of local anaesthetics                             •    A combination of         regional   and    general
    •    Regional anaesthesia alone e.g., spinal/epidural                    anaesthesia
         anaesthesia, arm block
    •    Regional anaesthesia with sedation

sections.title: Pre-anesthetic review and premedication
sections.text:
Pre-anesthetic review
    •   Patients MUST be reviewed in the pre-anesthetic outpatient clinic before any anesthetic intervention except for those
        admitted for emergency operations. The latter can be reviewed a few minutes before anesthesia or the night before
        the operation for elective inpatients.
    •   Done by reviewing surgical, medical and anesthesia-related records, performing focused anesthesia Assessment,
        identify anesthesia related risks and formulate anesthesia plan.
    •   Ultimate goals are: to optimize patient preparation, ensure safety and anticipate complications and put forward
        mitigation strategies

Pre-medications

Medicines that are administered before anaesthesia include:
Anxiolytics/amnesics

sections.title: General Anaesthesia
sections.text:
General anaesthetics are used for the induction of anaesthesia as boluses or for the maintenance of anaesthesia as
continuous infusions in Total Intravenous Anaesthesia (TIVA). Respiratory depression occurs following the induction of
General anaesthesia and ventilation should be supported as required. Administer at appropriate doses, after consideration of
patient factors, surgical factors and contraindications.

Intravenous anaesthetic agents (for induction and/or maintenance)

Pharmacological Management

B: ketamine (IV) 1–2mg/kg (For induction, however can be used for maintenance under TIVA, but contraindicated in those
who a significant rise in BP/IOP/ICP would constitute a serious hazard)
         OR
C: thiopental (IV) 3–5mg/kg for induction only.
[however not recommended for maintenance or repeated dose]
         OR
D: propofol (IV) 1.5–2.5mg/kg for induction of anaesthesia and 6–12m6-12mg/kg/hour infusion for maintenance in TIVA.
         OR
S: etomidate (IV) 0.3mg/kg (between 0.2–0.6mg/kg) for induction (cardiostable, it affects cortisol production)

Inhalational anaesthetic agents (for induction and/or maintenance)

B: isoflurane 1.2–2.5% in air, oxygen titrated to desired effect
          OR
S: sevoflurane 5–7% in air, oxygen titrated to desired effect.
Maintenance: 0.5–3% sevoflurane with or without the concomitant use of nitrous oxide.

   Note:
       •        Recommended to use Sevoflurane for induction only, then move to Isoflurane unless the condition recommends
                maintenance with Sevoflurane.
           •    Low-flow anesthesia is the best technique to conserve consumption of Sevoflurane
           •    Propofol is contraindicated for patients at risk of hypotension or in shock. Use IV ketamine infusion for maintenance
                of anaesthesia

sections.title: Neuromuscular Blocking Drugs (NMBD)
sections.text:
These are used to enhance intubation and to provide intraoperative muscle relaxation for surgery. It must not be used if difficult
intubation is anticipated.

Pharmacological Management

B: suxamethonium (IV) 1–2mg/kg for induction,
          OR
C: pancuronium (IV) 0.04–0.1mg/kg for induction /maintenance.
          OR
S: atracurium (IV) 0.4–0.5mg/kg over 60 seconds, followed by 0.08–0.1mg/kg 20– 45minutes after initial dose for maintenance
or infusion at 0.05–0.1 mg/kg/min (for patients with renal impairment)
          OR
S: rocuronium (IV) 0.6 -1 mg/kg can be used for induction if suxamethonium is contraindicated. In this case, the dose is
1.2mg/kg

Reversed by Sugammadex
 Note:
     •         Suxamethonium is contraindicated in patients with risk for developing hyperkalemia or with upper/lower motor neuron
               defect, prolonged chemical denervation, direct muscle trauma, tumour or inflammation, thermal trauma, disuse
               atrophy, severe infection
       •       Not recommended for infusion or maintenance of relaxation

Medicines for the reversal of neuromuscular blockade

B: neostigmine (IV) 50µg/kg
          AND
A: atropine (IV), 20µg/kg (maximum 1.2mg)
          OR
S: glycopyrrolate (IV)10 µg/kg
          OR
S: sugammadex (IV) 2–4mg/kg

sections.title: Locoregional Anesthesia (Local Anesthesia, Neuraxial anesthesia, Peripheral nerve block)
Local Anesthesia:
sections.text:
Temporary loss of sensation in a small area of the body to lessen pain and discomfort during medical, surgical and dental
procedures while the patient remains awake.
This can be in the form of topical application of Local Anesthetics (Cream- EMLA, Spray) or intramuscular infiltration.

sections.title: Topical Anaesthesia
sections.text:
Pharmacological Management

B: lidocaine cream (Topical) 2 to 5% -Apply at least 1 hour before and cover with an occlusive dressing.
          OR
B: lidocaine gel, topical, 2 g/100mL.
For numbing skin to aid clinical procedures like urethral catheterization (female 5–7 mL, male 10–15 mL).
          OR
B: lidocaine topical spray 2% and 10% solutions for topical anaesthesia of the airway (i.e., oropharynx and vocal cords), the
trachea, and nasal passages.
A: lidocaine (IM infiltration): Maximum 4.5mg/kg without vasoconstrictors (epinephrine (adrenaline)) or 7mg/kg with
vasoconstrictors
          OR
B: bupivacaine plain (site): 0.125% or 0.25%

sections.title: Neuraxial Anesthesia
sections.text:
This is the administration of a local anesthetic agent into the subarachnoid or epidural space to produce anesthesia, analgesia
or both. Encompasses epidural, Spinal anesthesia and caudal block.

sections.title: Epidural Anesthesia
sections.text:
•    Type of neuraxial anaesthesia of which a local anaesthetic (LA) is injected into the epidural space to anaesthetize
         the spinal nerve roots that traverse the space.
    •    Can serve for anaesthesia of abdominal, pelvic, and lower extremity procedures and, less commonly, thoracic
         procedures, but it is famously used for analgesia, especially for labor pain.

Pharmacological Management
A: lidocaine 1 to 2 %(epidurally)
          OR
B: bupivacaine 0.25 to 0.75% (epidurally)
Epidural Labour Analgesia

B: bupivacaine 0.1-0.25% with or without Fentanyl 25–50µg (epidurally) as an adjuvant.
         OR
B: bupivacaine 0.1% with fentanyl 2µg/ml at infusion rate of 012mls/hour (epidural infusion for analgesia)

sections.title: Spinal (Sub-arachnoid Block-SAB) Anesthesia;
sections.text:
•    In this type, LA agent is administered into the subarachnoid space and block spinal nerves
    •    Only preservative-free medicines should be used (risk of neurotoxicity).
    •    Larger doses cause block to spread higher, with risks of respiratory depression,
    •    Hypotension and loss of consciousness.
    •    In some selected procedures, you can combine spinal-epidural anaesthesia techniques to get both rapid anesthesia
         and later continue with post op analgesia.

B: bupivacaine 0.5% with or without dextrose (spinal use). Bupivacaine with dextrose-hyperbaric (heavy) allows the spread of
anesthetic block to be controlled by the patient/s positions during and shortly after injection.

sections.title: Caudal Anesthesia,
sections.text:
Type of epidural block where a LA is injected into the epidural space at the sacral hiatus, the lowest part of the spinal canal.
Mainly intended for analgesia in pediatrics.

Pharmacological Management
B: bupivacaine plain 0.25%, with or without Epinephrine for Caudal block. Dose: 0.5ml/kg- Perineal, 0.75ml/kg T10, 1ml/kg
lower thoracic.
          OR
D: ropivacaine 0.2% with or without Epinephrine for Caudal block. Target Dose: 0.5ml/kg- Perineal, 0.75ml/kg T10, 1ml/kg
lower thoracic.
   Note: For Caesarean deliveries: Lower doses are required due to physiologic changes of pregnancy: Bupivacaine 0,5%
   with dextrose, 1.8 mL (9 mg) with or without Fentanyl, 10 mcg (0.2 mL).

               neurological symptoms.
          •    A spinal haematoma can result in permanent paralysis unless decompressive surgery is performed within 8 hours of
               paralysis onset.
          •    Clopidogrel and platelet GPIIb/IIIa inhibitors have variable durations of effects on clotting after stopping these
               medications.
          •    Specialist advice should be sought before performing neuraxial blocks on patients receiving these medications.
          •    Patients on warfarin, practice of bridging anticoagulation (giving heparin after warfarin is stopped in preparation for
               surgery or invasive procedures. Practitioners should exercise careful judgment of competing risks related.
          •    Heparin may increase the risk of bleeding.
          •    Whatever practice is adopted the most important consideration is to ensure that adequate anticoagulation with warfarin
               is re-instituted once the risk of bleeding is over.

sections.title: Local Anesthesia Systemic Toxicity:
sections.text:
Pharmacological Management
Stop injection, follow the ABC approach, and ventilate with 100% oxygen. Seizure suppression with
D: midazolam 3-5mg
           OR
A: diazepam, IV, 5-10 mg.
If seizure persists, then
C: thiopental 1-2 mg/kg and or add diazepam. If worse, paralyse and intubate.
      •    S: Lipid emulsion (20%), IV, 1.5 mL/kg over 1 minute, then continuous infusion 0.25ml/kg per minute.
      •    Repeat bolus 1–2 times for persistent cardiovascular collapse.
      •    Double the infusion rate to 0.5 ml/kg/minute if BP remains low.
      •    Continue infusion for at least 10 minutes after cardiovascular stability is attained.
      •    Recommended upper limit: approximately 10ml/kg lipid emulsion over the first 30 minutes
      •    For cardiovascular instability, use IV fluids, inotropes and for cardiac arrest, initiate CPR.

sections.title: Anesthesia related Acute hypotension:
sections.text:
Treat the cause of hypotension, ensure appropriate fluids are given to correct hypovolemia.
     •     The medicines given below all require significant dilution before administration.
     •     Adrenergic and dopaminergic agents, e.g.:
     •     B: ephedrine (IV) 3–5mg as a single dose and then further boluses as required to a maximum of 30mg.
     •     Increases heart rate and contractility, and vasoconstrictor.
     •     Repeated administration can result in tolerance and tachyphylaxis.
     •     C: phenylephrine (IV) 50–100mcg, single dose and then 60–180mcg/minute.
     •     High doses may cause significant reflexes. Bradycardia: Treat this by discontinuing the phenylephrine only.

 Alternatively;
 A: epinephrine (adrenaline)/epinephrine (IV) (diluted to 10mcg/ml) give boluses of 5-10mcg may be needed to mitigate
 unresponsiveness to treatment.

sections.title: High spinal or total spinal anesthesia:
sections.text:
A high neuraxial block is a sensorimotor block that has reached a spinal segmental level higher than that required to achieve
surgical anaesthesia (sensory level T3 and above). Local anesthetic agent spreads too high in the spinal cord, blocking cardio
accelerator nerves and respiratory muscles, causing difficulty in breathing, severe hypotension and cardiac dysfunction.
     •    Anticipate and reassure the patient.
     •    Declare emergency and call for help. Position the head elevated to slow further spread.
     •    Ensure the wedge is placed properly.
     •    Use ABC approach, give Oxygen 100% by face mask or intubate (rapid sequence) with a hypnotic and muscle
          relaxant and ventilate if apneic.
     •    Give rapid fluid infusion and add vasopressors- ephedrine, phenylephrine or double-diluted epinephrine
          (adrenaline)/baby epinephrine (adrenaline) (10mcg/ml).
     •    If hypotension persists, consider vasopressor infusion.

Pharmacological Management
A: atropine (IV) 0.5mg bolus for bradycardia
          AND/OR
A: sodium chloride 0.9% /sodium lactate (IV) 500mls or 1000mls bolus

Precautions in Heart Failure and Pre eclamptic patients.

sections.title: Anesthesia-related acute Hypertension:
sections.text:
This can be triggered during intubation, especially in patients prehypertensive, such as in pre-eclampsia, known hypertensive
but uncontrolled hypertension. It can occur at induction of anaesthesia or post-operatively. ALWAYS establish the cause (e.g.,
light anaesthesia or inadequate pain relief) and treat as appropriate.

C: labetalol (IV) 5–10mg IV over 2 minutes.
Repeated at intervals of at least 5 minutes to a maximum of 200mg. Duration of action 50 minutes. Vasodilates and slows
heart rate.

Postoperative Nausea and Vomiting:
    •   Patients identified preoperatively as medium or high risk for PONV should be considered for prophylactic antiemetics.
    •   Prophylactic antiemetics are also required if postoperative vomiting is potentially dangerous, e.g., after jaw wiring,
        open eye surgery, oesophageal surgery.
    •   High-risk patients should receive antiemetics from ≥ 1 class.
    •   Adequate IV hydration is associated with less PONV and always treat hypotension if present
