sections.title: Malignant Hyperthermia:
sections.text:
•    Discontinue the anesthetic with risk to trigger- Inhalation and suxamethonium.
      •    Declare emergency, inform surgeon and call for help. Cool the patient and treat hyperkalemia as per protocol.
           Monitor ETCO2 and manage arrhythmia.

sections.title: Anesthesia in Diabetic Patient
sections.text:
Perioperative Hyperglycemia is associated with increased risk of infection, medical complications and death. The following
shall be considered;
     •    Ideally, the elective patient should have a preoperative glycated haemoglobin less than 9% or a fasting blood glucose
          level of 10 mmol/l or random blood glucose of 13 mmol/l.
     •    Screen for nephropathy, cardiac disease, retinopathy and neuropathy and inform the surgical team.
     •    If on oral hypoglycemic therapy and well controlled, and surgery is minor, omit therapy on the morning of surgery
          and resume therapy when eating normally.
     •    If on insulin, adjust depending on the type of surgery and expected fasting period as follows:

Minor surgery (duration < 3hours)
Insulin: in the morning, intermediate–acting insulin, 1/2 to 2/3 of the total daily dose.
     •     If blood glucose is above 20 mmol/l, give a small dose of short–acting insulin.
     •     In the evening, give intermediate–acting insulin, 1/3 of the daily dose. Fluid: 5% dextrose (IV), volume according to
           age.

Blood glucose monitoring: every 1–2 hours, target values between 10–14 mmol/l.

Major surgery (duration > 3hours) involving general anesthesia and therefore a period of fasting.
Insulin and fluid: infusion solution containing 5% glucose and 20 mmol/l potassium chloride (maintenance volume)
     •    Insulin infusion rate 0.05 IU/kg/hour.
     •    Blood glucose monitoring: every 1–2 hours; values between 6–14 mmol/l, if < 5 mmol/l reduce infusion rate, continue
          infusion therapy intraoperatively.
     •    Post operatively: give 5–10% dextrose (IV) 1 Litre + 20ml potassium chloride + 2/3 of total daily dose of insulin over
          8hours and repeat to maintain infusion therapy until food intake is re–established.

sections.title: Anesthesia in Hypertensive Patients
sections.text:
Monitor BP, scan monitors for HR, ECG rhythm, EtCO2, and temperature. Provided the patient is adequately oxygenated &
ventilated, deepen the anesthetic.
Examine patient:
     •    Pupils (high ICP).                                      •    Bladder distension.
     •    Diaphoresis       &      flushing     (carcinoid,       •    Hot (thyroid storm, malignant hyperthermia,
          pheochromocytoma, hyperthyroidism).                          serotonin syndrome).
     •    Rigidity (malignant hyperthermia, serotonin
          syndrome).
Examine drugs & equipment:
     •    Potential drug error                                    •    Tourniquet (pain)
     •    Possible TIVA or circuit disconnect (awareness)         •    Equipment error (falsely high reading)

Pharmacological Management

B: hydralazine (IV) 5-20mg (max 30mg) slow IV push every 20minutes
          OR
C: labetalol (IV) 5-20mg every10min (max total 300mg)
          OR
S: esmolol (IV) 0.5mg/kg over 1minute; start infusion at 50mcg/kg/min
          OR
S: nitroglycerin (IV) 50-100mcg; start infusion at 10mcg/min.

Treat the underlying cause, i.e., pain.

sections.title: Anesthesia in Asthmatic Patients
sections.text:
Considerations;
Risk of perioperative respiratory complications:
     •    Bronchospasm, mucous plugging, pneumothorax, atelectasis, pneumonia.
     •    Possible pulmonary hypertension & RV failure.

Need for preoperative optimization:
    •    Treatment of bronchospasm, infection, and atelectasis.
    •    Avoidance of triggers & exacerbating factors
    •    Avoid general anesthesia, endotracheal intubation, histamine-releasing medications, and light anesthesia.

Pharmacological Management
    •  Continue usual inhalers pre-operatively
    •  Stress dose steroids if recent high-dose steroid use.
    •  For Severe Asthma Exacerbation Treatment Options, refer to the Respiratory Diseases Condition chapter.

Anesthetics
B: ketamine (bronchodilator effect)
         OR
D: propofol (bronchodilator effect)

If intubation & ventilation:
      •    Use permissive hypercapnia.                                  •     Use prolonged expiratory time (e.g. I: E ratios
      •    Use low respiratory rates: start at 10-12                          1:3, 1:4, or even 1:5).
           breaths/minute but may need lower rates.                     •     Tidal volume 6-8cc/kg.
                                                                        •     FiO2 to achieve PaO2>60mm Hg

sections.title: Anesthesia in Sickle Cell Patients
sections.text:
•    Avoid precipitants of sickle cell crisis:
     •    Optimize perioperative pain control.
     •    Optimization (in consultation with hematology).

Risk factors for acute pain crises:
Procedural risk for complications:
     •    Low: minor surgery (e.g., inguinal hernia & extremity surgery).
     •    Intermediate: intra-abdominal operations (e.g., cholecystectomy).
     •    High: intracranial & intrathoracic procedures, hip surgery.

sections.title: Pediatric Anesthesia
sections.text:
Special anatomical, physiological and Pharmacological considerations in the pediatric group (different from adults):

     •    Larger head relative to the body-neck flection/obstruction
     •    Small mouth and large tongue proportion-obstruction
     •    Large head, little hair, prone to heat loss
     •    Breath mainly by nose, small and easy to obstruct
     •    Larynx is more anterior (at C3/4, while adults' C6)
     •    Short neck/Short trachea, little ETT movement-tube out
     •    Small airways-increased airway resistance and obstruction from secretions
     •    Narrowest part-cricoid ring in adult vocal cords. May lead to airway edema, difficult-Intubation.

Pre-anesthetic review and preparations
    •    Prenatal history-term or preterm delivery, what is the growth milestone. Any history of respiratory tract infections and
         the last episode.
    •    Airway assessment and cardiovascular examination are mandatory.
    •    Get or estimate body weight for drug calculations.
    •    Strict fasting guidelines with emphasis on solids up to six hours preop and pediatric patients to be first in the operating
         list.

Intraoperative considerations
      •    Premedication are vital to enhance smooth separation from parents. If IV line is in place IV induction should be
           considered.
      •    Otherwise, gas induction and then IV access with top up IV medications.
      •    Strict temperature management throughout and tight calculated IV fluids.
      •    For neonates and premature children, avoid opioid analgesics to prevent respiratory complications.

 Postoperative Care:
     •   Extubate when fully awake. For prolonged anesthesia, measure the sugar level and assess for opioid or
         benzodiazepine overdose
     •   Keep the patient warm

sections.title: Obstetric Anaesthesia
sections.text:
General anaesthesia (GA)

Preparation: Prevent aspiration pneumonitis (Refer to premedication section).
    •    Antibiotic prophylaxis: before skin incision as guided by guidelines.
    •    In view of potential difficult airway, ALL equipment for difficult airway including supraglottic airway devices (SGAs),
         and video laryngoscopes when available in addition to routine airway equipment. Have small-sized ETT 6.0 and 6.5
         cuffed with a stylet.

 Note: Applying left lateral displacement to prevent aortocaval syndrome is mandatory

 Monitoring:
     •    Routine; Noninvasive blood pressure (NIBP), ECG, SPO2.
     •    When available, consider Bispectral index (BIS) and neuromuscular blockage monitoring due to increased risk of
          awareness.
 Induction agents
 Hypnotics: hemodynamically stable

 D: propofol (IV) 1-2mg/kg,
 If hemodynamically unstable;
 B: ketamine (IV) 1-1.5mg/kg;
         OR
 D: propofol (IV) low dose 0.5-1mg/kg, with ketamine
         OR
 S: etomidate (IV) 0.3-0.5mg/kg;

Analgesia: Multimodal analgesia Opioids combined with non-steroidal analgesics and or IV paracetamol.
Opioids: Same dosages as in normal general anesthesia, except they should be administered after delivery of the baby to
avoid neonatal bradycardia and respiratory depression

Intubation: Perform rapid sequence intubation (RSI) with cricoid pressure using appropriate drugs and dosage (see section
for RSI).

Maintenance of anaesthesia:

Volatile anaesthetics:
B: isoflurane avoiding minimum alveolar concentration (MAC) higher than 1;
           AND
S: sevoflurane avoiding a minimum alveolar concentration (MAC) higher than 1.
           OR
Total intravenous anaesthesia (TIVA) using propofol or Ketamine infusion with muscle relaxant, depending on availability.

Maintenance Analgesia:

Multimodal, but opioids are given after delivery of the baby
Uterotonics – Administered after cord clamp:

A: oxytocin (IM) 10IU
         OR
A: oxytocin (IV) 10IU slow infusion.

  Note:
      •     Other uterotonics as appropriate, depending on the risk for haemorrhage.
      •     Recovery- Extubate when fully awake and maintaining airway reflexes.

Spinal anaesthesia (SA)

Single-shot spinal anaesthesia

B: bupivacaine heavy 0.5% (Intrathecal) alone 7.5-10mg
         OR
B: bupivacaine heavy 0.5% (Intrathecal) 7.5-10mg with opioids 20-25mcg fentanyl or 100-200mcg preservative free morphine.

Combined Spinal-Epidural anaesthesia (CSE)

When surgery is anticipated to last the duration of a single shot SA and an epidural kit is available, CSE allows surgical
anaesthesia and avoids conversion to GA.

Epidural anaesthesia

In selected obstetric conditions or conversion of neuraxial labour analgesia into surgical anaesthesia.

B: bupivacaine (Intrathecal) 10-15mls bolus
         OR
D: ropivacaine (Intrathecal) 10-15mls bolus (with or without opioids)

Pain management after caesarean delivery:
    •   Multimodal analgesia with systemic opioids, NSAIDs, and paracetamol.
    •   Peripheral nerve blocks (tranversus abdominis plane block, quadratus lumborum blocks), depending on expertise.

sections.title: Sedation
sections.text:
This procedural sedation and analgesia are commonly used in emergency units, radiological /diagnostic units, dentistry and
for certain endoscopic and gynaecological procedures.

Pharmacological Management
Minimal Sedation/Anxiolysis (no analgesic effect is required)

D: midazolam (IV) 0.05mg/kg (In a 60 kg patient, give boluses of 1 mg every minute; may require up to 5mg)
         OR
A: diazepam (IV) 0.1mg/kg (In a 60kg patient, give boluses of 2mg every minute; may require up to 10mg)

Medicines for moderate sedation & analgesia
If analgesia is required, one of the above is usually combined with an opiate. However, ketamine has analgesic activity and
can be used on its own or combined with a benzodiazepine.

B: ketamine (IV) 0.5mg/kg. Repeat doses of 0.5mg/kg as required, every 5-10minutes
         OR
C: morphine (IV) 0.1mg /kg in increments of 2mg every 5minutes
         OR
S: fentanyl (IV) 0.25µg/kg
         OR
S: dexmedetomidine (IV) 1mcg/kg bolus over 10 minutes, then 0.2-0.7µg/kg per hour infusion

Alternative medicines

D: propofol (IV) 0.5mg/kg. Repeated as 0.25mg/kg boluses every 5minutes as required
         OR
S: etomidate (IV) 0.1mg/kg. Repeat doses of 0.05 mg/kg (IV) every 5minutes, as required. But it is more likely to cause
myoclonus

Medicines for Deep Sedation & Analgesia:

This is usually achieved with either higher doses of medications used for moderate sedation, or by combining an opiate, a
benzodiazepine, and either Propofol or Etomidate. When agents are combined, lower doses may be adequate.

Supplemental Analgesia: Simple analgesics can be given before or after the procedure:

A: paracetamol (IV/PO): 1g 4-6 hourly when required to a maximum of 4g per 24hours.
          OR
A: diclofenac (IM) 75mg stat or 0.5mg/kg pediatric,
          OR
A: ibuprofen (PO) 400mg 8hourly with meals after the procedure.

                                                                     more)
Medicines for short–term sedation (less than 24 hours)

         OR                                                          D: midazolam (IV) 0.2mg/kg/hour.
D: propofol (IV) 0.5mg/kg/hour.

Due to high fat solubility, midazolam also becomes ‘long             to wean) as midazolam 0.2 mg/kg/hour) but more difficult
acting’ after infusions of more than 24 hours                        to titrate.

Supplemental analgesia

C: morphine (IV) 0.1–0.2mg/kg/hour.
         OR
S: fentanyl (IV) 1 µg/kg/hour (also becomes long acting after prolonged infusion due to fat solubility)

sections.title: Pain Management (Acute and Chronic Pain Management)
sections.text:
Pain is an unpleasant sensory and emotional experience associated with actual or potential tissue damage. The relationship
between pain (subjective) and actual or potential tissue damage (objective) is influenced by socio-cultural context as well as
the nervous system.

Perioperative Analgesia:
Multimodal approach; IM/ IV analgesics and/or a central neuraxial or locoregional anaesthetic block may be used. The
analgesic effect of these techniques may extend into the early postoperative period. However, it is best to assess pain
frequently to determine additional demand of analgesia.

Non-Opioid Analgesics                                                         OR

  Note:
       •   There are various medical conditions associated with severe acute pain e.g., myocardial infarction, renal colic,
           sickle-cell crisis and intra-articular haemorrhage due to haemophilia.
       •   The analgesic treatment for these conditions is the same as for patients with acute postoperative pain.
       •   Patients should be monitored for respiratory and cardiovascular depression when IV opioids are provided.
       •   Patients already on opioids for chronic pain, who experience an acute painful event, may be opioid tolerant and
           require higher IV opioid boluses to control their pain.

Chronic Pain Management

Chronic Non-Cancer Pain: A biopsychosocial assessment is necessary for effective pain management. Look out for the
etiology and perpetuating factors and manage accordingly. Note that there may be overlap between different aetiologies, and
condition specific pain management is paramount.

Pharmacological Management

Paracetamol, ibuprofen and tramadol may be used alone or in combination according to the severity of the pain.

Mild/moderate pain:
A: paracetamol (PO) 1 g 4-6hourly when required. Maximum daily dose: 4g in 24 hours.
         OR
A: ibuprofen (PO) 400mg 8hourly with meals. May be used in combination with paracetamol or opioids.

For high-risk patients or patients with peptic ulcers, add a proton pump inhibitor

C: lansoprazole (PO) 30mg once a day.

Severe pain:

B: tramadol, oral, 50–100mg 4-6hourly.
          OR
C: morphine syrup (PO).
Starting dose: 10-15mg (maximum 0.2 mg/kg) 4 hourly. Elderly or frail patients: 2.5–5mg (PO) (maximum 0.1 mg/kg) 4hourly.
Increase dose by 50% every 24 hours if pain control is inadequate.

sections.title: Critical Care
sections.text:
The goal is to guide the management of critically ill patients and perioperative care, emergency stabilization, and continuous
ICU support. The Core Principles of Critical Care include;
    •    Early recognition of deterioration (ABCDE).
    •    Support failing organs: respiration, circulation, consciousness.
    •    Prioritize oxygen, fluids, monitoring, and referral.

Table 2.4 Summary of Key Conditions and Initial Management
 Condition                                Key Initial Management
 Sepsis/Septic Shock, hypovolemic shock   Fluids (30ml/kg), antibiotics within 1 hour, monitor BP, urine
                                          Vasopressors/Inotropes and definitive source control.
 Cardiogenic Shock                               Inotropes.
 Haemorrhagic Shock                              Oxygen, Fluids (ie RL/0.9%-NS), Tranexamic acid, Vasopressors, Blood
                                                 and blood products.
 Respiratory Distress/Failure                    High-flow oxygen, sit the patient up, consider assisted ventilation

 Status Epilepticus                              Maintain and secure ABC, Anti-convulsant, check glucose &
                                                 temperature.
 Hypotension/Shock                               IV fluids, identify cause, use vasopressors if trained
 Unconscious Patient                             Airway protection, GCS, glucose check, avoid aspiration
 Post-op Monitoring                              Observe for bleeding, hypoxia, pain, delirium, and infection
 Anaphylactic Shock                              Epinephrine (adrenaline) IV/IM, Steroids, Anti-histamines,            plus
                                                 supportive care and specific antidote if poison/toxin is known.
 DKA/HHS                                         Fluids (ie RL/0.9%-NS), Insulin, treat any trigger, ABG and check serum
                                                 electrolytes (i.e., do not start Insulin without knowing K+).
 Acute kidney injury                             Look for the cause, maintain minimal fluid intake, and may need urgent
                                                 referral to a nephrologist (refer to a chapter for acute kidney injury)

Referral: Refer to Higher Level (Triage/Red Flags) urgently if:
    •    SpO₂ < 90% despite oxygen therapy
    •    SBP < 90 mmHg after fluids
    •    GCS < 8 or declining
    •    Oliguria/anuria
    •    Persistent seizures
    •    Uncontrolled pain or bleeding

sections.title: Indications for High Dependency Unit (HDU) admission
sections.text:
High Dependency Unit (HDUs) is an intermediate, step-down or step-up care unit. This is a specially staffed and equipped
section of a hospital, usually located close to the ICU, that provides a level of care intermediate between intensive care and
the general ward.

Acute Respiratory Support
    •   Mild to moderate hypoxia: SpO₂ < 90%                       Metabolic and neurological Compromise
    •   Need of high flow oxygen, Non-Invasive                         •   Severe sepsis, diabetic ketoacidosis, epilepsy or
        ventilation (NIV)                                                  meningitis
    •   Increased work of breathing or respiratory                     •   Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) ≤ 15
        fatigue, COPD or pneumonia                                     •   Severe electrolyte/metabolic disturbances
                                                                       •   Seizures
Cardiovascular Monitoring
    •   Systolic BP < 90 mmHg requiring fluid                      Single Organ Failure
        resuscitation                                                  •   Oliguria/anuria despite fluids

        arrhythmia

Postoperative Care

sections.title: Intensive Care Unit (ICU) Daily Assessment (FASTHUG BID)
sections.text:
FASTHUG BID is a widely used mnemonic in critical care to ensure comprehensive daily assessment and management of
ICU patients. It's an evolution of the original FASTHUG, expanded to cover more domains of ICU care.

See Table 2.5 Below

Table 2.5 FASTHUG BID Mnemonic in ICU Care
 Letter      Focus Area                Key Considerations
 F            Feeding                          Is the patient receiving adequate nutrition (enteral or parenteral)?
 A            Analgesia                        Is pain well-controlled? Are opioids or other analgesics needed or being
                                               reassessed?
 S            Sedation                         Is sedation needed? Can it be lightened or stopped? Daily sedation
                                               breaks if possible.
 T            Thromboprophylaxis               Is the patient on DVT prophylaxis (e.g., heparin, compression devices)?
 H            Head of bed elevation            Keep HOB elevated 30–45° to prevent aspiration and ventilator-
                                               associated pneumonia.
 U            Ulcer prophylaxis                Stress ulcer prophylaxis for patients at risk (e.g., on ventilation,
                                               coagulopathy).
 G            Glycemic control                 Keep blood glucose in target range (typically 140–180 mg/dL or 7.8–10
                                               mmol/L).

     •   B- Bowel care -Is the patient passing stool? Prevent ileus or constipation.
     •   I- Indwelling devices -Review lines, catheters, and tubes daily. Remove if no longer needed.
     •   D- De-escalation of therapy -Can antibiotics, ventilation, or other interventions be reduced or stopped?

ICU Discharge Criteria

Patients may be discharged from the ICU when intensive monitoring or organ support is no longer required, and they can be
safely managed in a general ward or step-down unit. Discharge Considerations;
     •   Prioritize discharge if ICU resources are needed for a more critically ill patient and the current patient is stable.
     •   Ensure proper documentation and communication with the receiving team.

sections.title: Iron Deficiency Anaemia
sections.text:
A lack of iron in the body (mainly due to nutritional deficiency, chronic blood loss, malabsorption and hookworm infestations
and increased demand such as during pregnancy).

Risks groups
    •   Pediatric population
    •   Pregnant women
    •   Patients with chronic or recurrent bleeding
    •   Patients on chronic use of proton pump inhibitors
    •   Gastrointestinal surgical resections.

Clinical Presentation
Fatigue, palpitation, dizziness, glossitis, koilonychias (spoon-shaped nails), and pica.

Investigations
    •    Full blood picture (FBP)
    •    Peripheral smear
    •    Iron studies- serum iron levels, total iron binding capacity, serum ferritin.
    •    Stool analysis for hookworm ova and occult blood. If stool for occult blood is positive, do an
         Oesophagoduodenoscopy (OGD) to confirm upper gastrointestinal bleeding.

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  To prevent iron deficiency;
    •  Eat a variety of iron-rich foods like meat, eggs, legumes (dried beans, lentils, peas), spinach and dark green leafy
       vegetables, iron fortified breads and cereals, nuts and seeds.
    •  To help in iron absorption from the diet
    •  Avoid drinking tea/coffee with meals
    •  Increase intake of Vitamin-C rich foods (e.g., citrus fruit, broccoli, cauliflower, guavas, tomatoes, bell peppers and
       strawberries) with meals to maintain iron in its reduced state.

 Pharmacological Management
 Treat the underlying cause of iron deficiency anaemia.
 Adults
 A: ferrous sulfate (PO) 200mg 24hrly for 3months.
 Children
 A: ferrous sulphate (PO) 5mg/kg 24hrly for 3 months. Continue for 3 months after the normal hemoglobin has been achieved.
          OR
 B: blood transfusion (is only indicated if anaemia is life-threatening; e.g., anaemia in failure, hypoxia.)
          OR
 D: iron sucrose (IV) 200mg in 100ml 0.9% sodium chloride running for 15 minutes once a day, three times a week for 2
 weeks.

  Note
      •     Parenteral iron is indicated in patients who cannot tolerate or are refractory to oral iron.
      •     Total cumulative dose = number of 100mg ampoules for Hb increase
      •     Divide the total cumulative dose in 200mg doses, given 24hourly

 Table 3.1: Number of 100mg/ampoules of iron sucrose needed for Hb increase based on body weight.

 Increase in Hb required (g/dl) i.e Target Hb minus Actual Hb
                                                                                 1g      2g     3g     4g    5g    6g    7g
 Body weight (Kg)                                         40                      6       7      8      9    10    11    12
                                                          45                      6       7      8      9    10    11    12
                                                          50                      6       7      9     10    11    12    13
                                                          55                      6       8      9     10    12    13    14
                                                          60                      6       8      9     11    13    14     16
                                                          65                      7       8     10     11    13    14     16
                                                          70                      7       8     10     12    13    15     17
                                                          75                      7       9     10     12    14    16     18
                                                          80                      7       9     11     13    15    17     18

                                                          95                      7      10     12     14    16    19     21
                                                         100                      7      10     12     15    17    19     22

    •    Duration of treatment may extend to 4 weeks based on the total cumulative dose required.
    •    Monitor blood counts and clinical assessment monthly.

 Note: Formulations of iron combined with other nutritional supplements (vitamins, 0.4mg-5mg folic acid, zinc and amino
 acids) are recommended to enhance absorption of iron and correct combined nutritional deficiencies.

sections.title: Megaloblastic Anemia
sections.text:
This is a condition whereby the bone marrow usually produces large, structurally abnormal, immature red blood cells
(megaloblasts), often due to inadequate intake or malabsorption of vitamin B12 or folate.

Clinical Presentation
Pallor, depression, hair loss, pins and needles, numbness in hands or feet, tremors and palsies, mildly jaundiced (lemon yellow
tint), beefy tongue, darkening of palms and ataxic gait.

Investigations
    •    FBC-Low Hb, sometimes pancytopenia, raised                      •    Serum folate level,
         mcv but maybe low or normal if coexisting with                  •    TSH
         iron deficiency (combined deficiency anaemia)                   •    Reticulocyte count
    •    Peripheral smear                                                •    Bone marrow aspiration may be indicated
    •    Serum vitamin B12,

 Pharmacological Management
 Vitamin (B12 deficiency anaemia) and other macrocytic anemias without neurological involvement
 C: hydroxocobalamin (IM) initially 1mg 3times a week for 2weeks
         THEN
 C: hydroxocobalamin (IM) 1mg every 3months.
 Review the patient’s blood counts and clinical assessment every 3months.

 Pernicious Anaemia (B12 deficiency) with neurological symptoms and signs

 C: hydroxocobalamin (IM) initially 1mg on alternate days until no further improvement (maximum reversal or neuro-
 psychiatric signs and symptoms are achieved) then 1mg every 2-3months
          OR
 C: methylcobalamin (PO) 500µgm 8hourly for 3 months
          AND
 A: folic acid (PO) 5mg 24hourly for at least 3 months. This must be started simultaneously with the injection of vitamin B12
          AND
 A: ferrous sulphate (PO) 200mg 8hourly for at least 3months

sections.title: Haemolytic Anaemia
sections.text:
Haemolytic anaemia results from an increase in the rate of red cell destruction in the intravascular or in the reticuloendothelial
system in some pathological disorders

Clinical Presentation
Pallor, jaundice, splenomegaly, Anaemia, Reticulocytosis, indirect hyperbilirubinemia, and haemoglobinuria

Investigations
    •    FBP                                                               •    Bilirubin (direct and indirect)
    •    Peripheral blood smear                                            •    Coombs test (Direct and Indirect)
    •    Reticulocyte count                                                •    LDH
    •    Haemoglobinuria                                                   •    Haptoglobin

Non- Pharmacological Management
Splenectomy may be considered in those who fail to respond to Pharmacological Management.

Pharmacological Management

A: prednisolone (PO) 1-1.5mg/kg/day for 1-3 weeks until Hb > 10g/dl
         AND/OR
S: cyclophosphamide (IV) 50mg/kg/day for 4days

If no response;
A: folic acid (PO) 5mg 24hourly should be given for 1to 3months.
           OR
B: blood transfusion if anaemia is severe
           OR
S*: High dose human immunoglobulin G (IV) 400mg/kg/day for 5days

sections.title: Sickle Cell Disease (SCD)
sections.text:
Clinical Presentation
Displays a wide spectrum of clinical manifestations with onset from 6 months of age, typically presenting with acute onset of
unexplained illness, accompanied by pain and swelling of different parts of the body, fever, anaemia, jaundice, dyspnea,
hepato-splenomegaly and neurological impairment with loss of vision.

Investigations
    •    Sickling test, Point-of-care rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs),
    •    High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC),
    •    Hemoglobin electrophoresis, Isoelectric focusing (IEF)

Other ancillary laboratory investigations useful in the detection and monitoring of the disease include:
    •    FBP                                                             •     ECG and ECHO
    •    Peripheral Smear                                                •     Spirometry
    •    Reticulocyte count,                                             •     Extended Blood grouping CXR,
    •    LDH, Bilirubin Direct                                           •     Abdominal USS
    •    Total liver and renal profile,                                  •     Transcranial Doppler USS,

 Note: Confirmatory test should be done to all patients with positive screening tests and those with negative screening
 test results but have Clinical Presentation suggestive of SCD.

Screening
From the age of 10 years, screen for renal disease (proteinuria by urine dipstick) and retinopathy annually
Annual screening for risk of stroke by transcranial Doppler from the age of 2years to 16years.

Pharmacological Management
Supportive therapy

A: folic acid (PO) 5mg 24hourly
           AND
A: phenoxy methyl penicillin (PO) 125mg for children younger than 3years;

A: phenoxy methyl penicillin (PO) 250mg for children 3 years and older, 12hourly until 5years of age in all children with SCA
for prophylaxis against Pneumococcal Infection.

Immunisation against pneumococcal infection

A: pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV-13) from two months of age, 3 doses 8 weeks apart (i.e at age 2months, 4 months
and 6 months), and a booster dose between 12-15 months.
If the child has not previously received this vaccine, then at least one dose should be given between 6-18 years.
S: pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV-23) - at 2 years, then after every 5 years for life.

Table 3.2 Analgesia for General Pain Relief

   Severity             Management
   Mild                 Reassurance, hot packs, reposition, massage, distraction (stories, play)
                        Child: A: paracetamol (PO) 15mg/kg 6hourly
                        Adult: A: paracetamol (PO) 1g 6hourly
   Moderate             As for mild pain, PLUS
                        Child: A: ibuprofen (PO) 5mg/kg 8hourly
                        Adult: A: ibuprofen (PO) 400mg 8hourly
   Severe               As for moderate pain PLUS
                        Child: C: morphine (PO) 0.5mg/kg 3–4 hourly as needed
                        Adult: C: morphine (PO) 5–10mg, 3–4 hourly as needed
                        If unable to take orally, administer paracetamol (IV) 1g 6-8hourly and morphine 0.1mg/kg 8-12hourly
                        If morphine is not available, tramadol may be used.
                        B: tramadol (PO) 50-100mg 6hourly as needed

Hydration: Encourage oral fluids first; it should be used whenever possible. Give IV fluids, preferably normal saline, if the
patient is unable to drink well, has severe pain, or abdominal symptoms.

   Body weight (kg)                       Fluids (ml/kg/day)
   <10 kg                                 150ml/kg/day
   11 – 20kg                              75ml/kg/day for every kilogram above 10kg
                                          ADDED to 1500ml for the first 10kg of weight
   > 20kg                                 30ml/kg for every kilogram above 20kg
                                          ADDED to 225Oml for the first 20kg of weight
   Divide the total daily volume by 24 hours to obtain hourly fluid rate

Disease Modifying Therapy

Principle of Dosage Initiation and Monitoring:

D: hydroxyurea (PO) 15 mg/kg/day 24hourly; (5–10 mg/kg/day if patient has chronic kidney disease).
         OR
D: hydroxyurea (PO) 20mg/kg/day, starting dosage for infants and children.

Increase the dose by 2.5–5 mg/kg/day every 3 months. The maximum tolerated dose (MTD) should not exceed 30mg/kg/day.

If haematologic toxicity occurs;
     •   Discontinue hydroxyurea until counts recover, usually 1-2 weeks,
     •   Reinitiate hydroxyurea at a dose of 2.5mg/kg/day less than the dose given before onset of cytopenias to achieve the
         maximum tolerable therapeutic dose,
     •   Do FBP according to the initiation schedule.

 Note:
     •     Clinical response to treatment with hydroxyurea may take 3-6months. A 6month trial on MTD is required before
           considering discontinuation due to treatment failure.
      •    Hydroxyurea should be stopped at least three months prior to conception in both males and females
      •    Hydroxyurea should be discontinued in all pregnant women
      •    Hydroxyurea should be discontinued in all breastfeeding women

Chronic Transfusion Program

Regular scheduled blood transfusions, including both simple and exchange (manual or automated).

D: Chronic (Top-Up) Blood Transfusion:
Scheduled, long-term red cell transfusion program aims to prevent complications in SCD by maintaining the target Hb and
reducing HbS level to 30%.
Potential risks include iron overload and alloimmunization; regular ferritin monitoring, chelation, and extended phenotype-
matched, leukodepleted blood are essential.

S: Exchange Blood Transfusion
Can be manual or automated by use of an Aphaeretic machine. Indicated in severe SCD patients with
    •   Abnormal TCD
    •   Cerebrovascular Accidents (CVAs)
    •   Recurrent Acute Chest Syndrome (ACS) major surgery
    •   Multi-organ failure, including Systemic Marrow Fat Embolism (SMFE)
    •   Multiple pregnancies
    •   Prevention of recurrent stroke.
    •   SCD undergoing a Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplant.

Relative Indications for Exchange Blood Transfusion
    •     Intractable or very frequent severe crises
    •     Major priapism unresponsive to other therapy.

   Note:
     • Because the cardiovascular system adjusts to the chronic anaemia, blood transfusion is not routinely indicated in
         steady state SCD simply for the reason that haemoglobin level is below 8-10g/dl.
     • Packed red cell transfusion is preferred to minimize the risk of fluid overload.

Allogeneic Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation

SCD in pregnancy
   •    Stop hydroxyurea 3 months before conception
   •    Educate the patient about the risks associated with pregnancy in SCD.
   •    Determine the haemoglobinopathy status of the partner.
   •    Document pre-pregnancy baseline results, if any.
   •    Refer the patient to a high-risk antenatal clinic for proper follow-up
   •    Prescribe routine prenatal vitamins, see under Obstetrics and Gynaecology chapter
   •    Prophylactic blood transfusion is not recommended.
   •    Vaginal delivery is preferred unless there is an indication for cesarean section.
   •    Prescribe prophylaxis for venous thromboembolism (VTE) for patients with additional risk factors for VTE e.g. history
        of VTE. See details under the coagulation disorders section 3.5
   •    Monitor hydration status, warmth, and give analgesia as needed after delivery.
   •    Assess and manage neonatal opioid dependency and withdrawal in all infants with a history of in utero opioid
        exposure.

Pharmacological Management.

A: acetylsalicylic acid (PO) 75mg 24hourly, starting from the second trimester to reduce the risk of pre-eclampsia.

Iron Overload in SCD
Excessive iron deposition in organs, including the liver, heart, pancreas, and endocrine glands, leading to fibrosis, organ
dysfunction, and failure caused by Chronic Transfusions:
Each unit of transfused blood contains approximately 200–250 mg of iron and the body lacks a physiological mechanism to
excrete excess iron.

Investigations
      •    Serum Ferritin
      •    ALT, AST, GGT
      •    MRI to assess for Liver Iron Concentration LIC

Pharmacological Management

Iron Chelation:

C: deferiprone (PO) 25mg/kg 8hrly until serum ferritin falls to safe levels
          OR
D: deferoxamine (IV/SC) 25-50mg/kg/day over 8-24 hours, 5 days per week

Check - Ferritin levels and LFTs 3 months, to monitor response, CBC weekly, stop if severe agranulocytosis develops.
Continue if - patient remains transfusion dependent, ferritin still above 1000ng/Ml, in heavily transfused patients, and
elevated MRI Liver/heart iron.
De-escalate or stop if ferritin falls to <500ng/Ml, transfusions have stopped, MRI liver/heart iron is reduced

SCD Emergency Conditions:

Acute chest syndrome
    •   Life-threatening – admit the patient in a high dependency unit or ICU,
    •   Diagnostic criteria – respiratory distress (fast breathing, SPO2<95% on air) and/or pleuritic pain, cough, fever,
        tachycardia, infiltrates on CXR,
    •   Investigations – arterial blood gases, creatinine, electrolytes, ALT, FBP, malaria test, blood and urine culture and
        sensitivity, CRP, CXR, HPLC,
    •   Management – Give supplemental oxygen to maintain SPO2>95%, analgesia for pain relief, fluids per hydration
        protocol, broad-spectrum antibiotics while awaiting culture and sensitivity results, top up blood transfusion or
        exchange transfusion if expertise available.

Acute anaemia
    •   Haemoglobin < 5g/dl or recent acute drop in Hb >2g/dl below steady state.
    •   Causes – infection, splenic sequestration, haemolytic crisis and aplastic crisis.
    •   Investigations – do FBP, reticulocyte count, creatinine, bilirubin, ALT, LDH, malaria test, urine and blood culture and
        sensitivity, blood grouping and cross-matching,
    •   Management – immediately transfuse packed red cells 10mls/kg over 4hours, repeat transfusion as needed as per
        transfusion protocol, treat the underlying cause, document the size of the liver and spleen.

Stroke
    •    See management details under the central nervous system chapter,
    •    Exchange transfusion or top-up transfusion to prevent recurrent stroke.

sections.title: G6PD Deficiency
sections.text:
G6PD is an inherited X-linked recessive genetic disorder; haemolysis results from oxidative damage to RBCs due to loss of
protective effect of the enzyme G6PD.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Usually asymptomatic but liable to haemolysis (acute anaemia) if infection, incriminated drugs (e.g., sulphonamides,
          chloroquine, primaquine or proguanil). or foods (e.g., fava beans) are taken.
     •    Pallor,
     •    Jaundice and
     •    Dark urine (Coca-colored urine)

Investigations
    •    FBP, peripheral smear, reticulocyte count,
    •    Methaemoglobin reduction (G6PD) test.

Pharmacological Management

A: folic acid (PO) 5mg 24hourly for 1-3 months.
           AND
D: Transfusion of packed red blood cells in severe anaemia. Give 10ml/kg body weight. Then assess the level of haemoglobin
and Clinical Presentation.

sections.title: Aplastic Anaemia (Bone Marrow Failure)
sections.text:
Aplastic anaemia is defined as pancytopenia resulting from aplasia of the bone marrow. it can be inherited (Fanconi anaemia)
or acquired (idiopathic, chemical, or drug-induced). It is one of the haematological emergencies.

Clinical Presentation
Vary with severity but include; Anaemia, easy bruising/bleeding, recurrent infection, Splenomegaly is not a feature.

Diagnostic Criteria
Pancytopenia, Bone marrow hypocellularity of < 30% hematopoietic cells.

Investigations
    •    FBP, peripheral smear, reticulocyte count,
    •    Viral screening (HIV, Hepatitis B, and C),
    •    Bone marrow aspiration and trephine biopsy.

Pharmacological Management

Supportive treatment
B: blood transfusion (preferred irradiated, leukodepleted) when Hb<7g/dl
          OR
S: platelet transfusion if bleeding or if platelet count is <10 X109/l. See dosage under the blood transfusion section 3.6
          AND
Prophylactic antibiotics, hygiene, isolation of the patient, and use of masks to prevent neutropenic sepsis in patients with ANC
of less than 0.5 X 109/l.

  Note: Culture and sensitivity in patients with neutropenic sepsis. Refer to management of neutropenic sepsis under
  malignant diseases chapter.

Definitive treatment
Allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation is indicated in patients younger than 45 years. Immunosuppressive
Therapy.

S: anti-thymocyte globulin (ATG) (IV) 40mg/kg 24hourly for 4-10 days.
          AND
S: cyclosporine (PO) 2-10mg/kg 12hourly for 6-24 months
          AND
S: eltrombopag (PO):
     •    Children <5 years: 2.5 mg/kg 24 hourly (every 24 hours)
     •    Children 6–11 years: 75 mg 24 hourly
     •    Adolescents ≥12 years: 150 mg 24 hourly
Duration of therapy: 6 months

For patients who develop cyclosporine toxicity (nephrotoxicity, hypertension, gingival hypertrophy and hirsutism), the following
drugs may be used, although the response rate is low.

D: methylprednisolone (PO) 5-10mg/kg for 3–14days
         OR
S: cyclophosphamide (IV) 45mg/kg /day for 4days.
         OR
S: danazol (PO) 5mg/kg 24hourly for 6months.

  Note
      •     Give supportive therapy and refer patients to higher health facility with adequate expertise and facilities.
      •     Monitor blood counts bi-monthly for outpatients, and as needed for admitted patients.

sections.title: Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS)
sections.text:
Pre-malignant condition, primarily a disease of older people.

Investigations
similar to aplastic anaemia, plus analysis of 5q deletion.

Pharmacological Management
B: blood transfusion for symptomatic treatment
          AND
S: azacitidine (SC) 75mg/m2 24hourly for 7 days, repeat after every 28days.

sections.title: Hereditary Bleeding Disorders
sections.text: Hereditary bleeding disorders include haemophilia A and B, Von Willebrand disease

sections.title: Haemophilia
sections.text:
Haemophilia is an inherited, X-linked lifelong bleeding disorder that affects males almost exclusively.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Spontaneous muscle and joint bleeding without injury,
     •    Prolonged bleeding after injury,
     •    Epistaxis and easy bruising.
     •    Complication includes arthropathy and disability.

Haemophilia A (Factor VIII deficiency)
Is the most common of the hereditary clotting factor deficiencies and are caused by a deficiency of factor VIII.

Haemophilia B (Factor IX deficiency)
It is caused by a deficiency of clotting factor IX, Presentation as in Haemophilia A, this is less common, 20%.

Classification of Haemophilia
Haemophilia is classified as mild, moderate, or severe according to the levels of circulating factor VIII or IX and indicates the
expected frequency of bleeding.

Table 3.3: Classification of Haemophilia
   Classification       Haemophilia     A          Haemophilia B             Clinical features
                        Factor    VIII             Factor IX level
                        level
   Severe               <1% of normal              ≤ 1% of normal        •   Spontaneous haemorrhage
                        ≤ 0.01 U/ml                ≤ 0.01U/ml            •   Frequent spontaneous haemarthrosis
   Moderate              2-5%of     normal                           •       Haemorrhage secondary to trauma or surgery
                         0.01-0.05 U/ml                              •       Occasional                   spontaneous
                                                                             haemarthrosis

   Mild                  5-40%of                   5-40% of normal       • Haemorrhage post trauma or surgery
                         normal                                          • Rare spontaneous

Investigations
    •    Prolonged aPTT but normal PT and platelet counts
    •    Confirm by factor VIII or IX assay

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Avoid I.M injections and use small-gauge needles if necessary
    •  Inform the patient and parents thoroughly on the problem, and provide means of alerting other
       medical/pharmaceutical personnel
    •  Genetic counselling
    •  For Acute Bleeding episodes (RICE): Rest, Ice/cold pack 5 minutes on, 10 min off, Compression, and Elevate the
       joint.

For haemarthrosis – AVOID incising or aspiration of the affected joint. Treat by replacing the specific factor e.g. factor 8 or 9
concentrate if available or FFP (10-15ml/kg), joint support and tabs Paracetamol for pain.

Pharmacological Management
Avoid use of NSAIDs, instead use paracetamol

Haemophilia A (Factor VIII Deficiency) no Inhibitor
Dose depends on bleeding severity                                    Haemophilia B (Factor IX deficiency), no inhibitor
                                                                     Dose depends on bleeding severity
Minor bleed:
S: coagulation factor VIII (IV) 20–40IU/kg.                          Minor bleed:
                                                                     S: coagulation factor IX (IV) 20-50IU/kg
Major bleed:
S: coagulation factor VIII (IV) 50–100 IU/kg 12hourly for 3-         Major bleed:
5 days or until bleeding stops, Expected response: 1IU/kg            S: coagulation Factor IX (IV) 100IU/kg
= 2% rise in factor VIII level. Half-life Factor VIII: 8–
24hours

Expected response: 1IU/kg= 1.5 rise in the factor IX level Half-life Factor IX: 16–24 hours

D: fresh frozen plasma (FFP) can be used where factor concentrate is unavailable. Average dose 10-15mls/kg.

  Note:
      •    If there is no response to appropriate replacement therapy tests for inhibitors (an inhibitor is formed when one
           develops antibodies against factor concentrates)
      •    Detection of inhibitor is by aPTT mix study and confirmed by the Bethesda assay (BU)

Factor VIII Inhibitor Management Options
    •    High dose factor concentrate infusion
    •    Use by-pass agent like FEIBA (Factor Eight Inhibitor By-passing Agent)
    •    Immune tolerance induction therapy (ITI)
    •    In case of emergency surgery, consider plasmapheresis
    •    Adjuvant antifibrinolytics agents e.g., Tranexamic acid, can be used with either of the above.
 Note:
     •     All patients suspected of haemophilia A or B should be referred to a higher facility with adequate expertise or
           consult the haematology Unit.
      •    Children with severe haemophilia are recommended to be on low-dose prophylaxis of factor concentrate
      •    Male circumcision should be done at a hospital where factor concentrate is available. Concentrate should be given
           before and after the procedure.

sections.title: Von Willebrand Disease (VWD)
sections.text:
Von Willebrand Disease is an inherited disease due to a deficiency of vWF. It is the commonest bleeding disorder in the
population, especially in women.

Clinical Presentation
History of easy bruising, Menorrhagia, Gum bleeding, Joint bleeding in severe cases

Investigations
    •    Confirmatory test: VWF level assay.
    •    PT, aPTT, and platelet count are normal except in severe cases.

Pharmacological Management

C: etamsylate (PO) 500mg 8hourly until the bleeding stops
         OR
C: tranexamic acid (PO) 500mg 8hourly until bleeding is stopped.

If no response

S: desmopressin (IV) 0.3µg/kg IV stat. Max. Dose20µg.

 Note:
     •     Patient unresponsive to DDVAP may be treated with virus-inactivated vWF containing FVIII concentrate.
     •     Never give Etamsylate or Tranexamic acid to patients bleeding per urethral

sections.title: Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC)
sections.text:
Clinical Presentation
     •    Usually are related to the underlying disorder.
     •    Bleeding manifestation,
     •    Extensive organ dysfunction,
     •    Shock, renal cortical ischemia, coma, delirium and focal neurological symptoms.

Rapid and appropriate treatment of the underlying disorder, including;

Non- Pharmacological Management
    •   Surgical debridement of necrotic tissues,
    •   Evacuation of dead fetus; Platelets transfusion for thrombocytopenia,
    •   Fresh frozen plasma (FFP) for coagulation factor depletion.
    •   Monitor prothrombin time (PT), international normalized ratio (INR), activated partial thromboplastin (aPTT), platelet
        count and fibrinogen
Pharmacological Management
    •  Antibiotics for infection,
    •  Chemotherapy for malignant causes,

  Note: If the patient is not bleeding Platelets concentrate is contraindicated. If DIC is severe enough to cause multiorgan
  dysfunction, management in an intensive care unit is required.

sections.title: Idiopathic Thrombocytopenic Purpura (ITP)
sections.text:
Clinical Presentation
     •    Long history of Purpura, menorrhagia, epistaxis, and gingival haemorrhage.
     •    Intracerebral haemorrhage occurs infrequently but is the most common cause of death
     •    Overt bleeding is rare unless thrombocytopenia is severe (less than 10 X109/L).

  Note: A palpable spleen strongly suggests that ITP is NOT the cause for thrombocytopenia.

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Patients with platelet counts over 50 X109/L usually do not have spontaneous bleeding and may undergo an invasive
       procedure.
    •  Emergency treatment of acute bleeding caused by severe thrombocytopenia needs immediate platelet transfusion.

Pharmacological Management

A: prednisolone (PO) 1mg/kg 24hourly for 3-6 weeks, then taper 10mg weekly (for all patients with platelet counts below 30
X109/l)
         OR
B: dexamethasone (IV) 40mg in 500ml 0.9% sodium chloride running for 4 hours once a day for 4 days.

If no response;

S: human Immunoglobulin G (IV) 0.4g/kg 24hourly for 5 days
        OR
S: human Immunoglobulin G (IV) 1g/kg 24hourly for 2 days followed by immediately platelets transfusion

sections.title: Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia (HIT)
sections.text:
Immune-mediated prothrombotic complication of heparin causing a platelet fall (≥50% from baseline), occurring typically 5–10
days after heparin exposure, with high risk of venous/arterial thrombosis.

Clinical Presentation
     •    4Ts score -Thrombocytopenia, Timing, Thrombosis, and other causes
     •    Low (0–3) HIT unlikely → consider other causes
     •    Intermediate/High (≥4): Treat as HIT.

Investigations
    •    FBP,                                                          •    PTT,
    •    peripheral smear,                                             •    INR
    •    PT,                                                           •    PF4-ELISA/functional assay as confirmatory
                                                                            test.
Non-Pharmacological Management

Avoid platelet transfusions unless life-threatening bleeding.

Pharmacological Management
      Start a non-heparin anticoagulant (use DOACs                        Use the non-heparin anticoagulant until platelet
       dosing on section 3.3.1).                                            recovery and at least the above durations.
      Duration of Non-Heparin Anticoagulation in HIT:                     Transition to oral anticoagulant (warfarin or
      HIT without thrombosis treatment should be                           DOAC) only after platelets ≥150 ×10⁹/L,
       continued for 4 weeks                                                overlapping if warfarin.
      HIT with thrombosis (HIT-T) treatment should be
       continued for 3 months

sections.title: Coagulation Disorders
sections.text:
Venous thromboembolism (VTE) is a common disorder that comprises deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism
(PE). In most cases, pulmonary embolism arises from proximal deep vein thrombosis i.e., popliteal, femoral or iliac veins in at
least 90%.

sections.title: Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT)
sections.text:
Clinical Presentation
     •    Leg pain, tenderness and swelling.                               •    Discoloration,   venous       distention   and
     •    A palpable cord representing thrombosed                               prominence of superficial veins and cyanosis.
          vessels.                                                         •    The clinical diagnosis of DVT is highly
                                                                                nonspecific.

Table 3.4: Wells Score for clinical prediction of DVT
 Clinical Feature                                                                              Score
     Active cancer (treatment ongoing, within 6 months, or palliative)                            +1
     Paralysis, paresis, or recent plaster immobilization of lower extremities                    +1
     Recently bedridden for ≥3 days or major surgery within 12 weeks                              +1
     Localized tenderness along distribution of deep venous system                                +1
     Entire leg swollen                                                                           +1
     Calf swelling ≥3 cm compared to asymptomatic leg (measured 10 cm below tibial
                                                                                                   +1
     tuberosity)
     Pitting edema confined to the symptomatic leg                                                 +1
     Collateral superficial veins (non-varicose)                                                   +1
     Previously documented DVT                                                                     +1
     Alternative diagnosis at least as likely as DVT                                               –2

Investigations
    •    PT, PTT and INR
    •    D-dimer,
    •    Doppler USS,
    •    CT or MRI Venography

Pharmacological Management

Start anticoagulation promptly if imaging delays and bleeding risk is acceptable. Long term anticoagulation is required to
prevent the frequency of symptomatic extension of thrombosis and/or recurrent venous thromboembolic events.
Unfractionated Heparin (UFH) or Low Molecular Weight Heparin (LMWH) is started, followed by Direct Oral Anticoagulation
without bridging. If Warfarin is started with initial unfractionated heparin or Low Molecular weight Heparinin therapy, bridge for
5days.

C: warfarin (PO) 5mg 24hourly for 5days, then adjust the dose according to INR levels for 3-6 months
          AND
D: low molecular weight heparin (SC) 1mg/kg 24hourly for 5days
          OR
C: unfractionated heparin (IV) by 75units/kg followed by continuous infusion of 18units/kg/hrs.

Adolescents or children: loading dose 75units/kg then 15–25 Units /kg/hr by IV infusion or 250units/kg 12hourly by SC injection.
S: rivaroxaban (PO) 15mg 12hourly for 21days, then rivaroxaban (PO) 20mg 24hourly for the remaining duration of treatment.
          OR
S: apixaban (PO) 10mg 12hrly for 7 days, then 5mg apixaban (PO) 12hrly for the remaining duration of treatment.

Pregnant women

Warfarin is teratogenic; low molecular weight heparin is recommended during pregnancy.

D: low molecular weight heparin (SC) 1mg/kg 12hourly for the whole duration of treatment.

sections.title: Pulmonary Embolism (PE)
sections.text: Refer to Cardiovascular Diseases Conditions, Chapter 20.

sections.title: Blood Transfusion
sections.text:
Currently, the following blood components are available for transfusion: packed red blood cells, Fresh Frozen Plasma, single-
unit platelets (plasma-rich) and whole blood units.

         i.     Whole blood: One unit contains 450mls of blood. Indications: Open heart surgery, and in the absence of PRBCs in
                patients with acute blood loss and hypovolaemia.
         ii.    D: Packed red blood cells (PRBCs); One unit increases haemoglobin (Hb) level by approximately 1g/dl in adult,
                whereas in children, a dose of 10-15mls/kg will increase the Hb by about 3g/dl.
                     •    Indications: acute blood loss, exchange transfusion, cardiac patients with Hb level <8g/dl, chronic
                          symptomatic anaemia with Hb <5g/dl, preoperative patients with Hb level <8g/dl, pre-radiotherapy patients
                          with Hb level <10g/dl, pre and post chemotherapy patients with Hb <9g/dl, and patients admitted to ICU
                          with Hb <7g/dl.
         iii.   D: Platelets; Dosage: 50mls per 10kg i.e., 5-6 RDP units in adults. In infants < 10kg, the dose is 5mls/kg, one adult
                therapeutic dose increases platelet counts by approximately 20-40 X109/L.
                     •    Indications include, Therapeutic: thrombocytopenia of platelet counts< 50X109/L with clinical evidence of
                          bleeding. Prophylactic in patients with platelet counts of: <10 X109/L, <20X109/L with additional risk factor
                          of bleeding, <50X109/L and planned for minor surgery, <100X109/L with multiple injuries, or microvascular
                          bleeding, or planned for major surgery. Also, in massive transfusion to maintain a platelet count of
                          >50X109/L.
                     •    Contraindications: Absolutely contraindicated in heparin-induced thrombotic thrombocytopenia (HITT) and
                          thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP). Relatively contraindicated in idiopathic thrombocytopenia
                          (ITP) unless a life-threatening bleeding is anticipated.

         i.v D: Fresh frozen plasma (FFP)
             Dosage: 10-20ml/kg, approximately 4-6 units for adult, this will raise a minimum of 30% of plasma clotting factors.
                 •    Indications: haemophilia if factor concentrates not available, patients with significant coagulopathy eg DIC,
                      Vitamin K deficiency and massive transfusion, thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) or haemolytic
                      uremic syndrome (HUS) as top up or exchange plasma transfusion, scoline apnoea, haemorrhagic disease
                      of the newborn.

Types of blood transfusion

    i.          Acute simple/episodic transfusion
                Used in the management of symptomatic patients with anaemia or bleeding tendencies.

   ii.          Chronic/top-up transfusion
                Used as a prophylactic to prevent complications, e.g. In patients with sickle cell anaemia (SCA)

  iii.          Exchange blood transfusion
                Indications: Severe hyperbilirubinemia (per nomogram), hemolytic disease, or failed intensive phototherapy. In SCD,
                exchange is indicated in patients with severe disease, those undergoing a major surgery and as a preparatory
                procedure before Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplant.

 i.v            Massive blood transfusion
                Transfusion of blood volume to the patient equivalent to his/her total blood volume in less than 24 hours, or 10 units
                or more in 24 hours. Administer in parallel a 1:1:1 ratio of 6 Units of RBCs, 6 Units of FFP and 6 Units of Platelets.
                The target is to achieve 1:1:1 ratio over 6 hours. Aim the PT, PTT <1.5x control mean, fibrinogen >1 g/L, target
                platelet > 100x109/L if pts has CNS trauma, eye and > 50x109/L for other type of injuries.

Plasma Derived Medicinal Products (PDMPs) available from commercial outlets
            •   Haemosolvate factors VIII and IX used in management of haemophilia
            •   Immunoglobulins used in immune-mediated conditions
            •   Albumin used in management of hypovolaemia, hypoalbuminaemia and in therapeutic plasma exchange.
