sections.title: Mpox
sections.text:
Mpox, previously known as monkeypox, is a viral illness caused by the monkeypox virus, a species of the genus Orthopoxvirus.
There are two distinct clades of the virus: clade I (with subclades Ia and Ib) and clade II (with subclades IIa and IIb).

Clinical Presentation
Mpox causes signs and symptoms which usually begin within a week but can start 1–21days after exposure. Symptoms
typically last 2–4 weeks but may last longer in someone with a weakened immune system. They include acute onset of fever
(>38.5°C) and chills, headache, sore throat, myalgia (muscle pain/body aches), back pain, profound weakness, or fatigue,
acute      skin rash, mucosal lesions or lymphadenopathy (swollen lymph nodes).
     •     The skin rash may include single or multiple lesions in the ano-genital region or elsewhere on the body.
     •     Mucosal lesions may include single or multiple oral, conjunctival, urethral, penile, vaginal, or anorectal lesions.
     •     Ano-rectal lesions can also manifest as ano-rectal inflammation (proctitis), pain and/or bleeding

Case Definitions

Suspect: A suspect case of Mpox can present with either of the following spectrum of symptoms.
Acute onset of fever (>38.5°C), headache, myalgia (muscle pain/body aches), back pain, profound weakness, or fatigue
OR
A person presenting with an unexplained acute skin rash, mucosal lesions or lymphadenopathy (swollen lymph nodes). Ano-
rectal lesions can also manifest as ano-rectal inflammation (proctitis), pain and/or bleeding

Probable: A suspected case with one or more of the following:
    •   Has an epidemiological link to a probable or confirmed case of Mpox in the 21 days before symptom onset?
    •   Has had multiple and/or casual sexual partners in the 21 days before symptom onset
    •   Has a positive test result for orthopoxviral infection (e.g., OPXV-specific PCR without MPXV-specific PCR or
        sequencing).
Confirmed: A person with laboratory confirmed MPXV infection by detection of unique sequences of viral DNA by real-time
polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and/or sequencing.

Transmission
Mpox spreads from person to person mainly through close contact with someone who has Mpox, including members of a
household. Close contact includes skin-to-skin (such as touching or sex) and mouth-to-mouth or mouth-to-skin contact (such
as kissing), and it can also include being face-to-face with someone who has Mpox (such as talking or breathing close to one
another, which can generate infectious respiratory particles). People can also contract Mpox from contaminated objects such
as clothing or linen, through needle injuries in health care, or in community settings such as tattoo parlours. During pregnancy
or birth, the virus may be passed to the baby. Contracting Mpox during pregnancy can be dangerous for the fetus or newborn
infant and can lead to loss of the pregnancy, stillbirth, death of the newborn, or complications for the parent.

Non-Pharmacological Management
All Cases
     •    Oral hydration and adequate nutrition (refer to Chapter 10)
     •    Skin care:
               o   Gentle washing of lesions with soap and water
               o   Keep lesions clean and dry
               o   Avoid scratching
               o   Apply moist dressings (e.g., Vaseline gauze)
               o   Refer to Chapter 13 for detailed skin care management and prevention of secondary infections
     • Monitor for secondary bacterial infections and manage promptly
     • Oxygen therapy if hypoxic
     • Advanced supportive care as needed, including nutritional support and wound care (refer to Chapters 10 and 13)
     • Infection prevention and control measures, including isolation and avoidance of close contact until lesions have
          healed completely
Severe/Complicated Cases (Admit if indicated)
    •     Intravenous hydration using 0.9% Normal Saline or Ringer’s Lactate, with monitoring for fluid overload
    •     Oxygen therapy if indicated
    •     Nutritional support
    •     Wound care and management of extensive skin lesions
    •     Monitoring and management of complications

Pharmacological Management
 Clinical Indication   Medicine(s) and Dosage
 Fever and Mild Pain   A: paracetamol 500 mg–1 g PO every 6–8 hours PRN (maximum 4 g/24 hours)
 Moderate Pain         A: ibuprofen 400 mg PO every 8 hours PRN (if no contraindications)
                             OR
                       Escalate analgesia according to the Pain Management Section in these Guidelines
 Severe Pain           B: tramadol 50–100 mg PO/IV every 6–8 hours PRN (maximum 400 mg/day)
                             OR
                       C: morphine 2.5–10 mg PO every 4 hours PRN
                             OR
                       C: morphine 2.5–5 mg IV every 4 hours PRN, titrated according to response
 Pruritus (Itching)    A: chlorpheniramine 4 mg PO every 6–8 hours PRN
 Secondary Bacterial   Treat according to site of infection, culture and antimicrobial susceptibility results, and
 Infection             relevant treatment guidelines.

  Note:
     •     Continue ART without interruption in people living with HIV.
     •     Initiate ART within 7 days of Mpox diagnosis in newly diagnosed HIV infection or after prolonged interruption.
     •     HIV testing should be offered to all suspected and confirmed Mpox cases.
     •     No routine antiviral therapy is currently recommended for Mpox.
     •     Refer to the Pain Management chapter for analgesic escalation.

Management considerations for severe/complicated disease

    •     Continue supportive treatment.
    •     Escalate analgesia according to the Pain Management Section in these Guidelines
    •     Treat confirmed secondary bacterial infections appropriately.
    •     No routine antiviral therapy for Mpox is currently recommended.

Mpox is treated with supportive care for symptoms such as pain and fever, with close attention to nutrition, hydration, skin
care, prevention of secondary infections and treatment of co-infections, including HIV if present. Individuals with HIV and Mpox
should continue taking their antiretroviral therapy (ART). ART should be initiated within 7 days of diagnosis of HIV.
Getting an Mpox vaccine can help prevent infection (pre-exposure prophylaxis). It is recommended for people at high-risk of
getting Mpox, especially during an outbreak. The vaccine can also be administered after a person has been in contact with
someone who has Mpox (post-exposure prophylaxis). In these cases, the vaccine should be given less than 4 days after
contact with someone who has Mpox. The vaccine can be given for up to 14 days if the person has not developed symptoms.

Public Health Control Measures
         •      Isolate at home (if mild and per healthcare provider guidance) or in hospital (if severe or high-risk transmission
                concerns) for the full infectious period — from onset of symptoms until all lesions have crusted, scabs have
                fallen off, and new skin has formed (typically 2–4 weeks).
         •      Cover all lesions with clean, dry bandages/clothing when around others. Wear a well-fitting medical mask
                  (surgical or respirator) when in the presence of others. Avoid close physical contact, including sexual activity,
                  until fully recovered and cleared by a healthcare provider.
          •       Advise the public to take a break from sexual activity with new or multiple partners during periods of increased
                  transmission to reduce risk.
          •       Those with close contact (household, sexual, healthcare, or prolonged face to face) with a confirmed/probable
                  case should self-monitor for signs/symptoms (fever, rash, headache, muscle aches, lymphadenopathy, etc.)
                  for 21 days after last exposure. During this period, avoid sexual activity, close physical contact, and high-risk
                  settings; report symptoms immediately for testing and isolation if needed.
          •       Use appropriate PPE when caring for patients: gloves, gown, eye protection (goggles/face shield), and
                  respirator (N95 or equivalent). Follow strict protocols for lesion swabbing (use sterile technique), safe handling
                  of sharps/needles, waste management, and environmental cleaning. Train staff on donning/doffing PPE,
                  airborne and contact precautions (droplet if respiratory symptoms present).

Additional measures (as applicable):
    • Promote hand hygiene, respiratory etiquette, and disinfection of frequently touched surfaces.
    • Conduct contact tracing and risk assessment for close contacts; consider post-exposure prophylaxis (e.g., vaccine)
         for high-risk contacts per national/WHO guidance (if vaccine available).
    • Engage communities in awareness: symptoms recognition, early care-seeking, avoiding self-medication, and
         reducing stigma.
    • Notify suspected/confirmed cases within 24 hours via IDSR; line list cases and link to lab results (PCR preferred)

sections.title: Influenza
sections.text:
Influenza is an acute respiratory viral infection caused by influenza viruses and readily spread from person to person, via
infectious respiratory particles (IRP), which are transmitted through the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes. There
are four types of influenza viruses: types A, B, C and D. Seasonal influenza A and B viruses circulate among humans
worldwide. However, a novel influenza A virus’s subtypes of animal origin (zoonotic influenza), such as avian influenza A virus
and swine influenza A virus can sporadically affect humans and are known to cause pandemics.
     •    Influenza A viruses are further classified into subtypes according to the combinations of the proteins H for
          Hemagglutinin and N for Neuraminidase on the surface of the virus (e.g., H1N1, H5N1, H3N2, etc.)
     •    Influenza B viruses are not classified into subtypes but can be subclassified into two lineages. Currently circulating
          influenza type B viruses belong to either the B/Yamagata or B/Victoria lineages.

Clinical Presentation
Clinical diagnosis of influenza is challenging as the signs and symptoms of the disease can be non-specific (many respiratory
pathogens can cause a similar illness) and can vary depending on virus type as well as patient host characteristics and other
factors. Most people with non-severe influenza illness recover from the fever and other symptoms within a week, without
requiring medical attention. Typically ranges from 2 to 7 days, though it can extend to 10 days for some subtypes (e.g., H5N1).
Symptoms: fever, sudden onset of cough, headache, muscle and joint pain, severe malaise, sore throat, rhinorrhea, chills and
sweating

Signs: elevated body temperature, pharyngeal erythema, nasal congestion or discharge, cervical lymphadenopathy, lung
wheezing or crackles if complications like pneumonia develop, tachycardia and general appearance of malaise or fatigue

Complications: septicemia, septic shock, severe pneumonia, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), multi-organ
failure, exacerbation of chronic medical conditions or even death.

Case Definitions
Suspected case: Any person presenting with unexplained acute lower respiratory illness with fever (>38 ºC) and cough, sore
throat, shortness of breath or difficulty breathing AND at least one of the following exposures within the 7 days prior to
     •    Infected animals (e.g., poultry, swine, or wild birds) or their environments (e.g., live animal markets, farms, or
          slaughterhouses).
     •    A confirmed human case of zoonotic influenza.

Probable Case: A suspected case with:
    •   A positive laboratory test for influenza A, but the subtype is not identified or is inconclusive (e.g., influenza A positive
        but not H1N1, H3N2, or other common human subtypes).
    •   Epidemiological evidence strongly suggesting zoonotic exposure (e.g., direct contact with infected animals or their
        products).
    •   No definitive confirmation of a novel influenza A subtype.

Confirmed Case: A suspected or probable case with:
Laboratory confirmation of infection with a novel influenza A virus of animal origin, such as:
    •    Detection of a specific novel influenza A subtype (e.g., H5N1, H7N9, H3N2v) by reverse transcription-polymerase
         chain reaction (RT-PCR) or other nucleic acid amplification tests.
    •    Virus isolation or sequencing confirming a novel influenza A virus not typically found in humans.
    •    Significant rise in subtype-specific antibodies (e.g., via serologic testing like hemagglutination inhibition or
         microneutralization assays).
    •    Laboratory testing must be conducted by a recognized public health laboratory, such as a WHO Collaborating Centre
         or a national reference laboratory.

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Encourage adequate rest to support recovery.
    •  Ensure sufficient fluid intake to prevent dehydration.
    •  Some severe and critical cases will need oxygen, mechanical ventilation (invasive or non-invasive) and/ or
       vasopressor therapy.
    •  Monitor for worsening symptoms (shortness of breath, persistent high fever, chest pain)

Pharmacological Management
A: paracetamol 500 mg – 1 g PO every 6–8 hours PRN for fever/pain (max 4 g/24h)
          OR
A: ibuprofen 400 mg PO every 8 hours PRN for fever and body aches (avoid in peptic ulcer disease, renal impairment, or
bleeding risk)

For nasal congestion:
B: ephedrine 60 mg PO every 6–8 hours PRN (maximum 240 mg/day; avoid in hypertension, heart disease)

For runny nose/itching/sneezing:
A: chlorpheniramine 4 mg PO every 6–8 hours PRN
          OR
C: loratadine 10 mg PO OD

For dry cough
A: dextromethorphan 15–30 mg PO every 6–8 hours PRN (antitussive cough suppressants)

Antibiotics only if bacterial superinfection is suspected (e.g., secondary pneumonia). Use per culture/sensitivity results or
empirically as per pneumonia guidelines

A: amoxicillin 500 mg PO TDS for 5–7 days
          OR
B: azithromycin 500 mg PO OD for 3–5 days
High-Risk or Severe Influenza (Admit if indicated):

Non-Pharmacological Management
     • Oxygen therapy if SpO₂ <94% (target ≥90–92%)
     • IV hydration if unable to take oral: 0.9% Normal Saline or Ringer’s Lactate (cautious titration, monitor fluid balance)
     • Monitor closely for complications
Pharmacological Management
A: paracetamol 500 mg – 1 g PO every 6–8 hours PRN for fever/pain (max 4 g/24h)
          OR
A: ibuprofen 400 mg PO every 8 hours PRN for fever and body aches (avoid in peptic ulcer disease, renal impairment, or
bleeding risk)

Stronger analgesia if required per pain ladder
Antibiotics for confirmed or suspected bacterial superinfection (Refer Chapter 9)

 Note:
     •     Asthma or COPD exacerbation: Refer to Chapter 9 for specific management (e.g., bronchodilators, inhaled
           corticosteroids, oxygen)
      •    Heart failure: Refer to Chapter 20 for specific management (avoid fluid overload, use diuretics cautiously)
      •    Children: Avoid aspirin entirely due to risk of Reye’s syndrome. Use Paracetamol or Ibuprofen at weight-based
           doses.
      •    No routine antiviral is recommended

Public Health Control Measures
    •   Notify the public health authorities immediately (within 24 hours) through IDSR
    •   Conduct contact tracing and follow-up for all identified contacts.
    •   Initiate a line listing of suspected and confirmed cases and ensure laboratory results are linked with cases
     •    Conduct case identification and perform Rapid Diagnostic Testing (RDT) and send specimens for confirmatory testing
          using RT-PCR at the designated Laboratories
     •    Conduct syndromic surveillance to identify community clusters and monitor disease trends.
     •    Implement genomic surveillance to detect emerging variants.
     •    Strengthen Infection Prevention and Control (IPC) measures in both health facility settings and community
          environments.
     •    Promote and implement social and behavioral interventions, such as physical distancing and proper cough and
          sneeze etiquette, especially during periods of high transmission
     •    Increase public and community awareness through health education on symptoms, modes of transmission, and
          prevention measures.

sections.title: Viral Keratoconjunctivitis (VKC)
sections.text:
It is a viral eye infection accounting for over 80% of cases of epidemic keratoconjunctivitis (EKC)/Red eye with more than 75%
attributed specifically to adenovirus infection. Epidemic keratoconjunctivitis (EKC) is an eye condition primarily characterized
by dilation of the conjunctival blood vessels (hyperemia), conjunctival edema (chemosis), and ocular discharge. It may be
unilateral but usually bilateral.

Adenovirus serotypes Ad 5, 8, 11, 13, 19, and 37 are frequently implicated in outbreaks of EKC and are known to cause severe
conjunctivitis. Adenoviruses are highly resilient, capable of surviving on inanimate surfaces for up to 30 days, which contributes
significantly to their potential for widespread transmission.

The incubation period for adenoviral EKC ranges from 2 to 14 days, with most individuals developing signs and symptoms
within 5 to 6 days’ post-exposure. Importantly, viral shedding can occur in asymptomatic individuals, and infected persons may
remain contagious for 10 to 14 days after symptom onset, posing a substantial risk for community and healthcare-associated
transmission.

Clinical Presentation
A typical case of VKC is presented by:
     •    Conjunctival injection (redness).                              •   Acute onset of unilateral or bilateral red eyes.
     •    Follicular conjunctivitis (small, raised bumps on              •   Watery or mucoid discharge.
          the conjunctiva).                                              •   Foreign body sensation, burning, or itching.
     •    Preauricular lymphadenopathy (swollen lymph                    •   Photophobia (sensitivity to light) in cases with
          nodes near the ear).                                               corneal involvement (keratitis).
     •    Corneal       involvement      (e.g.,     subepithelial        •   Possible      associated     upper      respiratory
          infiltrates or epithelial keratitis) in severe cases.              symptoms (e.g., sore throat, fever) due to
     •    Pseudo membrane formation in epidemic                              systemic viral infection.
          keratoconjunctivitis (EKC), a severe adenoviral
          form.
Transmission
Epidemic viral keratoconjunctivitis/Red eye is very contagious and mostly spread from human to human or inanimate objects
to human through hand-to-eye contact by hands or objects that are contaminated with the virus. Other ways include contact
with: Infectious tears, Eye discharge, Fecal matter, Respiratory discharge and large respiratory tract droplets.

Case definitions
Suspected Case: Any person presenting with acute red eye with watery discharge and without an alternative diagnosis (e.g.,
bacterial conjunctivitis or allergy) OR with history of exposure to a confirmed case or outbreak setting (e.g., schools, hospitals)
within 7-14 days.

Probable Case: A suspected case with clinical signs like follicular conjunctivitis or preauricular lymphadenopathy with
epidemiological link (e.g., contact with a confirmed case).

Confirmed Case: A suspected or probable case with a laboratory confirmation (e.g., positive PCR or immunochromatography
for adenovirus).

Differential Diagnosis
The above case definitions distinguish VKC from:
     •   Bacterial conjunctivitis which presents with purulent discharge without follicular response.
     •   Allergic conjunctivitis which presents with itching, seasonal, without lymphadenopathy.
     •   Herpes simplex virus (HSV) which present with keratitis (dendritic corneal lesions, unilateral).

Complications
    •    Persistent corneal infiltrates or secondary bacterial infections may require additional treatments, such as antibiotics
         for superinfections.
    •    Severe cases with vision-threatening complications need urgent ophthalmology referral.
 Note:
      •    Treatment is nonspecific, mainly is supportive and symptoms relief, preventing complications, and limiting spread,
           as there is no specific antiviral cure for most cases. Most cases resolve in 1-3 weeks without specific treatment.
      •    Topical Antihistamines or Decongestants: For itching or redness. Use cautiously to avoid rebound redness.
      •    Topical NSAIDs: In cases with significant discomfort or photophobia, such as ketorolac drops, but only under
           medical supervision.
      •    Oral Analgesics: Over-the-counter pain relievers
Non-Pharmacological Management
Supportive Care
    •    Cold Compresses: Reduce swelling and soothe irritation.
    •    Hygiene: Strict handwashing and avoiding touching eyes to prevent secondary infections and transmission.
    •    Avoid Contact Lenses: Discontinue use until symptoms resolve to prevent worsening or bacterial superinfection.

Pharmacological Management
Children > 6 years and adults
A: paracetamol (PO) 1g 8hourly (Pediatric 10–15mg/kg/dose 8hourly) when required, for 3-5days
         AND
C: oxymetazoline 0.025% eye drops, instill 1–2drops 6hourly for a maximum of 7days.
 Note:
      •    Antibiotics are ineffective for viral causes and only used if bacterial superinfection is confirmed.
      •    Always consult an eye care specialist for persistent symptoms, vision changes, or severe pain.
      •    Viral conjunctivitis is very contagious so report immediately using the electronic IDSR system, alert patients and
           members of the family
      •    For more information refer to chapter 14

Prevention
Preventive measures are essential to reduce the spread of epidemic keratoconjunctivitis. These include:
     •    Frequent handwashing with soap and clean running water. Using antiseptics, such as alcohol-based hand
          sanitizers, when soap and water are not available
     •    Avoiding touching or rubbing the eyes, especially with unwashed hands
     •    Self-isolation - Avoid school, work, or public places for 7-14 days or until symptoms resolve to prevent spread
     •    Avoid sharing personal items, such as towels, washcloths, eye makeup, pillows, eye drops, or contact lenses.
     •    Regularly clean high-touch surfaces (e.g., doorknobs, phones) with disinfectants effective against adenovirus (e.g.,
          bleach solutions).
     •    Wash bedding, towels and clothing in hot water to kill the virus.
     •    Practicing proper cough and sneeze etiquette, such as covering the mouth and nose with a tissue or elbow and
          washing hands afterward
     •    Discontinue contact lens use during outbreaks or if symptoms appear
     •    Ensure proper lens cleaning and storage to avoid contamination.
     •    Stay away from individuals with active VKC symptoms (red eyes, discharge).
     •    Use protective eyewear in high-risk settings (e.g., healthcare facilities during outbreaks).

sections.title: Human African Trypanosomiasis (HAT), (Sleeping Sickness)
sections.text:
Human African Trypanosomiasis (HAT), also known as sleeping sickness, is a vector-borne parasitic disease caused by
Trypanosoma brucei parasites, transmitted by tsetse flies (Glossina species). It occurs in two forms: Trypanosoma brucei
gambiense (chronic, West and Central Africa) and Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense (acute, East and Southern Africa). The
disease is endemic in sub-Saharan Africa and is nearly 100% fatal if untreated.

Clinical Presentation
Symptoms and signs
HAT progresses in two stages: Stage one, No CNS involvement (CSF: ≤5 white blood cells/µL, no trypanosomes) and stage
two, CNS involvement (CSF: >5 white blood cells/µL, trypanosomes detected, or elevated protein).

Haemolymphatic Stage (Stage 1):
Early phase after infection, when parasites multiply in blood and lymphatic system. Symptoms are non-specific, often leading
to misdiagnosis
     •   Symptoms: Fever (intermittent), Headache, Joint and muscle pain, Fatigue, Swollen lymph nodes (notably
         Winterbottom’s sign: posterior cervical lymph node enlargement in T.b. gambiense), Skin rash or chancre at bite site
         (more common in T.b. rhodesiense), Itching and/or Anaemia

Meningoencephalitis Stage (Stage 2):
Parasites invade the central nervous system (CNS). T.b. rhodesiense progresses rapidly (weeks to months), while T.b.
gambiense may take months to years
    •    Symptoms: Sleep disturbances (daytime sleepiness, nighttime insomnia, hence "sleeping sickness"), Confusion,
         irritability, or personality changes, Tremors, motor weakness, or difficulty walking, Seizures and Coma (if untreated)
Case Definitions
Suspected Case: Any person living in or visiting an endemic area with:
    •    Clinical symptoms (e.g., fever, lymphadenopathy, neurological signs).
    •    History of tsetse fly exposure.

Probable Case: Suspected case with positive serological tests (e.g., Card Agglutination Test for Trypanosomiasis, CATT) for
T.b. gambiense or clinical/epidemiological suspicion for T.b. rhodesiense.

Confirmed Case: Suspected case with laboratory confirmation of trypanosomes in blood, lymph node aspirate or
cerebrospinal fluid OR positive serology with clinical signs and CSF abnormalities (e.g., increased white blood cells or protein)
for stage 2.

Pharmacological Management
Treatment depends on the parasite type and disease stage.

Trypanosoma brucei gambiense: Stage 1:
D: pentamidine 4 mg/kg (IM/ IV) 24 hourly for 7 days, Maximum 300 mg per dose. Well-tolerated, effective for early stage.

Trypanosoma brucei gambiense: Stage 2:
D: fexinidazole: Oral treatment (given 24hourly for up to 10 days),
effective for both stages but preferred for stage 2 in adults and children >6 years (weight ≥20 kg). Simpler administration than
older regimens.
 Body Weight                     Days 1-4                        Days 5-10
 20 – 35 kg                      1200mg/day                      600mg/day
 35 – 50 kg                      1200mg/day                      1200mg/day
 ³ 50kg (Most Adults             1800mg/day
           OR
Nifurtimox-Eflornithine Combination Therapy (NECT): Eflornithine (IV, 7 days) + nifurtimox (oral, 10 days). Used when
fexinidazole is contraindicated.
S: nifurtimox (PO) 15 mg/kg/day, given 8hourly for 10days
           AND
S: eflornithine (IV) 400 mg/kg/day, given 12hourly for 7days (weight based, same dose in adults & children)
           OR
S: melarsoprol (IV) 2.2 mg/kg 24hourly for 10 days,
Reserved for fexinidazole/NECT failures. Requires hospitalization due to high risk of encephalopathic reaction

Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense: Stage 1
S: suramin (IV): Test dose: 100–200mg 24hourly, then: 20 mg/kg IV on days 1, 3, 7, 14, and 21 (Maximum 1 g per dose)
     •   Same dosing for adults and children
     •   Renal function monitoring required.

Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense: Stage 2:
S: Melarsoprol (IV) 2.2 mg/kg 24hourly for 10 days,
Follow-Up
Patients require follow-up for 18–24 months (CSF analysis every 6 months) to confirm cure, as relapses can occur).

sections.title: Leishmaniasis
sections.text:
Leishmaniasis is a parasitic disease caused by protozoans of the genus Leishmania, transmitted primarily by the bite of
infected female phlebotomine sandflies. It presents in three main forms cutaneous, mucocutaneous, and visceral.
     •    Visceral leishmaniasis (VL), also known as kala-azar, is fatal if left untreated in over 95% of cases. It is characterized
          by irregular bouts of fever, weight loss, enlargement of the spleen and liver, and anaemia. Most cases occur in Brazil,
          east Africa and India.
     •    Cutaneous leishmaniasis (CL) is the most common form and causes skin lesions, mainly ulcers, on exposed parts
          of the body. These can leave life-long scars and cause serious disability or stigma. About 95% of CL cases occur in
          the Americas, the Mediterranean basin, the Middle East and central Asia. Mucocutaneous leishmaniasis (MCL) leads
          to partial or total destruction of mucous membranes of the nose, mouth and throat. Over 90% of mucocutaneous
          leishmaniasis cases occur in Bolivia, Brazil, Ethiopia and Peru.

Case Definitions
Suspected Case:
    •   CL: Presence of characteristic skin lesions in a person from an endemic area, persisting for weeks to months, with
        or without a history of sandfly exposure.
    •   MCL: Mucosal lesions (nasal, oral, or pharyngeal) with or without a history of CL, in an endemic area.
    •   VL: Prolonged fever (>2 weeks), weight loss, and splenomegaly in a person from an endemic area or with travel
        history to such areas.

Probable Case: Suspected case with epidemiological link (e.g., travel to endemic area) and positive serology (e.g., rK39 rapid
test for VL) or suggestive histopathology.

Confirmed Case:
    •   CL/MCL: Demonstration of Leishmania parasites in tissue samples (e.g., skin biopsy, smear, or culture) or positive
        PCR.
    •   VL: Parasites identified in bone marrow, spleen, or lymph node aspirates, or positive PCR or serology (e.g., direct
        agglutination test, rK39) in the presence of clinical signs.
    •   PKDL: Clinical signs with parasitological or molecular confirmation, often in a patient with a history of VL.

Pharmacological Management
The treatment of leishmaniasis depends on several factors including type of disease, concomitant pathologies, parasite
species and geographic location. Leishmaniasis is a treatable and curable disease, which requires an immunocompetent
system because medicines will not get rid of the parasite from the body, thus the risk of relapse if immunosuppression occurs.
All patients diagnosed with visceral leishmaniasis require prompt and complete treatment.

Visceral leishmaniasis caused by L. donovani in East Africa
S: liposomal amphotericin B(IV):3–5mg/kg 24hourly by infusion given over 6–10days to a maximum 30 mg/kg
          OR
S: amphotericin B deoxycholate (IV):0.75–1mg/kg 24hourly by infusion, or on alternate days, for 15–20doses

Post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis in East Africa
S: liposomal amphotericin B: 2.5mg/kg 24hourly by infusion for 20 days, when indicated

Recommended treatment regimens for cutaneous leishmaniasis, Local therapy, all species

S: paromomycin 15% topical ointment apply 12 hourly (BD) to the lesion(s) for 20 days.
         AND
S: methylbenzethonium chloride 12% ointment apply 12 hourly (BD) to the lesion(s) for 20 days.

            AND/OR
S: thermotherapy Localized heat therapy (50 °C for 30 seconds) — 1–3 sessions (spaced as needed).
            AND/OR
S: sodium stibogluconate injection 100 mg/mL (intralesional). Inject directly into the lesion until complete blanching is achieved;
repeat once weekly for 3–6 weeks or until clinical healing occurs.
            OR
S: meglumine antimoniate infiltrate 1–5 ml per session into the base and edges of each lesion every 3–7 days for a total of 1–
5 infiltrations. (Inject until the lesion blanches; volume depends on lesion size.)

Systemic depending on the confirmed species the following treatment can be executed:
S: miltefosine (PO): 2.5 mg/kg 24hourly for 28days
          OR
S: amphotericin B deoxycholate (IV): 0.7mg/kg 24hourly, by infusion, for 25–30 days
          OR
S: liposomal amphotericin B(IV): 2–3mg/kg 24hourly, by infusion, up to 20–40 mg/kg total dose
(For patients who cannot tolerate Amphotericin B deoxycholate)

Relapse treatment:
S: amphotericin B deoxycholate (IV), as above
         OR
S: liposomal amphotericin B(IV): 3 mg/kg per day, by infusion, up to 20–40 mg/kg total dose may be considered

Recommended treatment regimens for mucocutaneous leishmaniasis All species
S: amphotericin B deoxycholate (IV): 0.7–1mg/kg by infusion every other day up to 25–45doses
         OR
S: liposomal Amphotericin B(IV): 2–3 mg/kg daily by infusion up to a total dose of 40–60 mg/kg

Complications
   •    Treat anemia, malnutrition, and secondary infections.
   •    Monitor for toxicity (e.g., nephrotoxicity with amphotericin, hepatotoxicity with antimonial).

Special Populations:
    •    Pregnancy: Avoid miltefosine (teratogenic); liposomal amphotericin B is preferred.
    •    HIV Co-infection: Requires higher doses and longer treatment (e.g., liposomal amphotericin B, 40 mg/kg total dose).
         Secondary prophylaxis may be needed to prevent relapse.
    •    Children: Adjust doses by weight; liposomal amphotericin B is safe and preferred.

sections.title: Snake Bites
sections.text:
A snakebite can be life-threatening if the snake is venomous. Less than 10% of 3500 snake species are venomous and they
include different species of Cobras, Mambas and Adders which are endemic in Tanzania. Clinical Presentation of a snakebite
varies depending on the type of envenomation a snake causes. The severity of the symptoms depends on the amount of
venom the snake injects into the victim. Some snakebites (10-30%) can be considered as dry bites where no venom is injected.
As a late appearance if symptoms after a snakebite is possible up to 24 hours a close monitoring needs to be conducted in
this time frame.
Types of Envenomation are:
      •    Neurotoxic Envenomation: in non-spitting cobras, mambas and sea snakes
      •    Hemotoxic Envenomation: in vipers, boomslang and Vine Snake
      •    Cytotoxic Envenomation: in Puffadder, Gaboon Adder, Night Adder, Stiletto Snake and Spitting Cobras
      •    Mixed Cytotoxic and Hemotoxic Envenomation: in Spitting Cobras and Puff Adder
A snakebite should be considered in any patient, presenting with severe pain or swelling of a limb or in any unexplained illness
presenting with bleeding or abnormal neurological signs. Some cobras spit venom into the eyes of victims causing pain and
inflammation.

Clinical Presentation

Table 4.5 Clinical Presentation & Severity of a snakebite

 Mild envenomation                      Fang marks (+), mild local reaction, no systemic reaction
 Moderate Envenomation                  Fang marks (+), moderate local reaction + systemic reaction, non-life- threatening
 Severe Envenomation                    Fang marks (+), moderate – severe local reaction, severe systemic life-
                                        threatening reaction

Neurotoxic Envenomation: Progressive Weakness
    •   Severe Envenomation: profuse sweating, excessive salivation and > 2 other neurological signs from the 5P and 5S
        (Pain, Paresthesia, Ptosis, Pupillary abnormalities, Descending Paralysis; Swallowing difficulties, Slurred Speech,
        Sweating, abnormal Secretion and abnormal Salivation)
    •   Life Threatening Envenomation: Shortness of breath due to weakness; Inability to swallow saliva, generalized severe
        weakness, Bradycardia < 50 bpm; Apnea, Hypotension and Fasciculations, Bulbar paralysis.

Hemotoxic Envenomation:
   •   Severe Envenomation: Unstoppable bleeding from fang marks / bite marks, Bleeding from older wounds, Dizziness,
       Fainting
   •   Life Threatening Envenomation: Systemic Bleeding, bruising of more than one limb, abnormal WBC20 Test,
       Increasing Anemia, Laboratory evidence of clotting abnormality, Shock, black urine.

Cytotoxic Envenomation:
    •    Severe Envenomation: Swelling Extending 10cm or more per hour; Swelling reaches wrist or ankle within one hour;
         Swelling reaches knee or elbow within 4 hours; Increasing swelling in the face, throat or genitals.
    •    Life Threatening Envenomation: Swelling Exceeding 15cm or more per hour; Progressive Swelling of a whole limb
         within 8 hours; Unexplained shortness of breath, Abnormal WBC20 Test, Compartment Syndrome.
Investigation:
    •    No specific investigations
    •    Mandatory for every snakebite: Assessment with detailed patients’ history
    •    The whole blood clotting test after 20 minutes (WBC20 Test).
    •    Enzyme linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA)
Supportive Investigations
    •    Vital signs: Including RR, BP, HR, GCS, ECG                  •    Muscle Destruction: Serum Amylase and CK &
    •    Electrocardiogram      (ECG):     ST-Depression,                  CK-MB should be monitored.
         Bradycardia, AV-Block can be observed. Monitor               •    Prothrombin Time, (PT), activated partial
         for real cardiac ischemia due to stress.                          thromboplastin time (aPTT) and INR. Prolonged
    •    Hemogram:         Presence     of    neutrophilic                 time in hemotoxic bites.
         leukocytosis signifies the systemic presence of              •    Arterial blood gas analysis for all patients with
         an envenomation.                                                  systemic or respiratory symptoms.
         Thrombocytopenia may be present in viper                     •    Urine examination: Can reveal hematuria,
         envenomation.                                                     kidney injury proteinuria, myoglobinuria or
    •    Kidney Function Tests: Serum Creatinine and                       hemoglobinuria.
         Urine Output monitoring

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Reassure the patient and try to calm the patient                     never delay treatment with Polyvalent Snake
       down.                                                                Antivenom.
    •  Immobilize the extremity where the patient was                  •    Every snakebite is a medical emergency unless
       bitten to reduce the spread and absorption of                        you can certainly identify a harmless snake.
       venom, Use a Splint or Pressure Immobilization                       Every snakebite should be assessed in a
       Bandage.                                                             hospital.
    •  Elevate the bitten limb if there is a moderate-                 •    Supportive Treatments may be required and
       severe swelling.                                                     include intubation & ventilation in neurotoxic
    •  Clean the bite site with sterile swabs and do a                      snakebite patients, wound debridement in

                                                                            transfusion in hemotoxic snakebite cases.

Symptoms might last for days and require permanent monitoring.
   •   Do endotracheal intubation +/- elective tracheotomy if respiratory distress due to weakness occurs.
   •   Monitor the patient closely for a minimum time of 24 hours after the snakebite. Symptoms can appear late, and
       envenomation can progress rapidly.

Surgical Intervention:
    •     Dead tissue should be removed from the wound.
    •     If there are signs of compartment syndrome a surgical intervention is required. Incisions to relieve pressure in the
          limb might be required.
    •     Skin grafting, if there is an extensive necrosis present.
    •     Tracheotomy if paralysis of muscles involved in swallowing occurs.

Pharmacological Management
Fluid resuscitation for patients in shock

A: sodium chloride 0.9% (IV) 10-20ml/kg. Repeat the dose after 30 minutes if shock is still present. Use Vasopressors if the
shock is persistent. Keep monitoring the Fluid intake and output.

If criteria of Polyvalent Snake Antivenom administration are present (see table 4.6 below), give Antivenom.

A: snake venom antiserum are potent polyvalent immunoglobulins prepared to control venom of poisonous snakes) using
indications shown below. Polyvalent means, that the Antivenom is effective against envenomation from various snake species
Antivenom preparation.

Dilute antivenom in 500 mls of 0.9% Sodium Chloride (Normal saline) and give intravenously in a slow continuous infusion.
over 20-40 minutes and monitor closely for anaphylaxis or other serious adverse reactions.

                                  confirmed evidence of coagulopathy

                                  Inability to swallow saliva; Progressive Weakness causing loss of consciousness or
 Neurotoxic                       respiratory distress; > 2 of the following symptoms: Profuse sweating, increasing salivation,
                                  Paresthesia, Ptosis, Pain, Pupillary abnormalities, Paralysis, Slurred speech, abnormal
                                  secretion; Bradycardia;
                                  Apnea; Hypotension and Fasciculations
 Mixed Hemotoxic & Cytotoxic Positive WBC20-Test, Increasing Anemia, Bleeding from older wounds, Laboratory
                             confirmed evidence of coagulopathy with signs of Cytotoxic envenomation.

If there is no improvement of the patient within 2 hours after the initial dose of Polyvalent Snake Antivenom give a repetitive
dose of Polyvalent Snake Antivenom. Dosage depends on the grade of envenomation and severity of the symptoms.
For mild degree of envenomation give 5 vials (50 ml)
For moderate degree of envenomation give 5–10 vials (50–100 ml)
Fore severe degree of envenomation gives 10–20 vials (100–200 ml)

  Note:
      •      Polyvalent snake antivenom should always be used as directed on the packing list. Effectiveness against certain
             species of snakes and the recommended dosage vary.
       •     Polyvalent Snake Antivenom should not be administered 48 hours after the snakebite. In some severe
             envenomation Polyvalent Snake Antivenom might be effective up to 72 hours after the bite.

Severe Snake Envenomation or Where Polyvalent Snake Antivenom is Unavailable
 Clinical Indication            Management
 Tetanus Prophylaxis                    A: anti-tetanus prophylaxis according to national immunization and wound
                                        management guidelines.
 Neurotoxic Envenomation (Cobra         B: neostigmine IV 1.5–2 mg initial dose, followed by 0.01 mg/kg every 30 minutes
 Bite)                                  as clinically indicated
                                                 AND
                                        A: atropine IV 0.6 mg initial dose, followed by 0.05 mg/kg every 30 minutes as
                                        clinically indicated.

 Clinical Indication                  Management
 Neurotoxic Envenomation              A: atropine IV 0.6 mg initial dose, followed by 0.05 mg/kg every 30 minutes as
 (Mamba Bite)                         clinically indicated
                                              AND
                                      A: paracetamol 1 g PO/IV every 8 hours for 24 hours in adults
                                               OR
                                      A: paracetamol 15 mg/kg PO/IV every 8 hours for 24 hours in children.

For Mamba Bite
    •  A tourniquet or, preferably, a pressure immobilization bandage may be applied where appropriate and by trained
       personnel while arranging urgent transfer for definitive care.
    •  Continuous monitoring of respiratory function is essential.
    •  Provide ventilatory support if respiratory paralysis develops.

  Note:
      •     These measures are adjunctive and do not replace administration of Polyvalent Snake Antivenom when
            indicated and available.
       •    Patients with neurotoxic envenomation should be managed in a facility capable of airway management and
            respiratory support.
       •    Frequent reassessment of neurological status, respiratory effort, and oxygen saturation is required.

Adverse reaction due to Polyvalent Snake Antivenom

In case of Polyvalent Snake Antivenom administration mild anaphylaxis can occur in around 20-30% of the cases and severe
anaphylaxis can occur in around 5-10% of the cases. Other than that, serum sickness, a late reaction to the Polyvalent Snake
Antivenom can occur 7-21 days after the administration. Anaphylaxis is treated with Epinephrine (adrenaline) (IM).
A: epinephrine (adrenaline) (IM) dose of 1:1000 (Repeat after 3-5 minutes if no improvement)
     •    Children < 6 years old: 150mcg IM (0,15ml)
     •    Children 6-12 years old: 300mcg IM (0,3ml)
     •    Children > 12 years old & Adults 500mcg IM (0,5ml)
          AND
A: chlorpheniramine (PO) (be ready if allergic reaction occurs). Dosage as below
     •    Children under 6years: 4mg 8hourly as needed
     •    6–12 years: 8mg 12hourly as needed.
     •    >12 years and older 12mg 12hourly as needed
  Note:
       •   If itching/rash, restlessness, cough, respiratory distress or hypotension develops stop Polyvalent Snake
           Antivenom and give:
           A: epinephrine (adrenaline) (SC) 0.01 ml/kg of 1/1000 or 0.1 ml/kg of 1/10,000 solution
                     AND
           A: chlorpheniramine (IM/ IV/SC) 250 micrograms/kg.
       •   When the patient is stable restart the Polyvalent Snake Antivenom infusion.
       •   Antivenom can be given every two hours until the patient’s condition improves, or the progression of the
           symptoms has stopped.
       •   Blood transfusion may be required if HB drops < 7mg/dl.
       •   Serum sickness usually occurs within 7-21 days and is treated with Steroids.
       •   Response of abnormal neurological signs to antivenom is more variable and depends on type of venom.

sections.title: Venom Ophthalmia
sections.text:
Spitting Cobras, like the Black-necked Spitting Cobra, the Ashe’s Spitting Cobra and the Red Spitting Cobra can spit the
venom into the eyes or onto the skin of a patient. Venom on intact skin can just be washed with water. Venom which was spilt
into the eyes of a patient can cause severe complications including blindness.

Clinical Presentation
Symptoms of venom ophthalmia include: Photophobia, Burning, Watering, Redness, Extreme Pain, Blurred Vision or
Blindness.

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  The victim should be advised not to rub their eyes.
    •  Victim should be advised to wash the eyes with clean water.
    •  Ensure the venom doesn’t enter the mouth of the victim.
    •  The victim should be instructed to open and close the eyes under water.
    •  Assess the patient under the slit lamp and check for corneal erosions.
Pharmacological Management

When Corneal Erosion is Present
 Clinical Indication          Management
 Prevention of Secondary      A: chloramphenicol 1% eye ointment, apply 1–1.5 cm ribbon into affected eye(s) 3–4
 Infection                    times daily until healed and for an additional 48 hours
                                     OR
                              A: oxytetracycline 1% eye ointment, apply 1–1.5 cm ribbon 2–4 times daily for 5–7
                              days
                                     OR
                              A: erythromycin 0.5% eye ointment, apply 1–1.5 cm ribbon 4 times daily for 3–5 days
 Pain and Photophobia         S: homatropine 2% eye drops, 1 drop twice daily for 2–3 days
                                     OR
                              D: cyclopentolate 1% eye drops, 1 drop twice daily for 2–3 days
 Systemic Analgesia           A: paracetamol 500 mg–1 g PO every 6–8 hours PRN (maximum 4 g/day)
                                     OR
                              A: ibuprofen 400 mg PO every 8 hours PRN (if no contraindications)
 Lubrication                  C: hydroxypropyl methylcellulose 0.3% 1–2 drops as needed

When No Corneal Erosion is Present
 Clinical Indication          Management
 Prophylaxis and Symptom      A: chloramphenicol 1% eye ointment, apply 1–1.5 cm ribbon 3–4 times daily for 48
 Relief                       hours
                                     OR
                              A: oxytetracycline 1% eye ointment, apply 1–1.5 cm ribbon 2–4 times daily for 48 hours
 Pain Relief (if required)    A: paracetamol 500 mg–1 g PO every 6–8 hours PRN
 Lubrication                  C: hydroxypropyl methylcellulose 0.3% 1–2 drops as needed

 Note:
     •     No Polyvalent Snake Antivenom is required for venom ophthalmia.
     •     Venom ophthalmia is a form of envenoming which can present with visual symptoms only and can lead to
           blindness if left untreated.
      •    Encourage the patient not to rub the eye.
      •    Routine use of topical corticosteroids is not recommended.
      •    Routine eye patching is not recommended.
      •    Patients with persistent pain, visual impairment, corneal ulceration, or non-healing epithelial defects should be
           referred urgently for ophthalmological assessment.
      •    Re-examine patients daily when corneal erosion is present until epithelial healing is complete.

sections.title: Lymphatic Filariasis
sections.text:
Lymphatic filariasis is a parasitic disease caused by thread-like filarial worms (Wuchereria bancrofti, Brugia malayi, and Brugia
timori) transmitted through mosquito bites. The parasites lodge in the lymphatic system, causing damage that leads to
abnormal enlargement of body parts and disability.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Acute episodes of fever with painful swelling of lymph nodes, typically in the groin or armpit
     •    Swelling of limbs (lymphoedema) or genitals (hydrocele in men, swelling of vulva in women)
     •    Chronic manifestations include elephantiasis (extreme swelling and thickening of skin), particularly affecting legs,
          arms, breasts, or genitalia
     •    Chyluria (passage of lymphatic fluid in urine, giving it a milky appearance)
     •    May be asymptomatic for years despite active infection

Case Definition

Suspected case: Any person presenting with chronic lymphoedema of limbs, hydrocele, or other signs of lymphatic
obstruction in endemic areas.

Confirmed case: A suspected case with microfilariae detected in blood smear or positive circulating filarial antigen test.

Laboratory Investigation
    •   Specimen: Thick blood smear collected at night (10 PM - 2 AM when microfilariae are most abundant in peripheral
        blood)
    •   Diagnostic test: Microscopic examination of Giemsa-stained thick blood smear to detect microfilariae
    •   Rapid diagnostic test: Immunochromatographic test (ICT) for circulating filarial antigen detection (can be done any
        time of day)
    •   Alternative: PCR for detection of filarial DNA

Prevention
    •   Sleep under insecticide-treated bed nets (ITNs) to prevent mosquito bites
    •   Use mosquito repellents on exposed skin
    •   Eliminate mosquito breeding sites by clearing stagnant water around homes
    •   Participate in mass drug administration (MDA) programs when implemented in endemic areas
    •   Wear protective clothing (long sleeves and trousers) during peak mosquito biting times

Pharmacological Management
Mass Drug Administration (MDA) for endemic communities:
A: ivermectin (PO) 150-200 mcg/kg as a single dose
         AND
A: albendazole (PO) 400mg as a single dose

Individual Treatment for confirmed cases:
Adults:
A: diethylcarbamazine (DEC) (PO) 6mg/kg 24hourly for 12days
          OR
A: ivermectin (PO) 200 mcg/kg as a single dose, repeated every 6-12 months
          AND
A: albendazole (PO) 400 mg as a single dose
Children:
A: diethylcarbamazine (PO) 6mg/kg 24hourly for 12 days
          OR
A: ivermectin (PO) 150-200mcg/kg as a single dose

 Note:
 Diethylcarbamazine should not be used in areas co-endemic with Onchocerca volvulus (river blindness) due to risk of
 severe adverse reactions.
 A: albendazole (PO) 400mg (for children >2 years) or 200mg (for children <2 years) as a single dose

Management of Chronic Complications for lymphoedema:
   •   Daily washing of affected limbs with soap and                     •   Use of appropriate footwear to prevent injury
       clean water                                                           and secondary infections
   •   Elevation of affected limbs when resting                          •   Treat secondary bacterial and fungal infections
   •   Exercise and movement to promote lymph flow                           promptly with antibiotics and antifungals

For hydrocele:
     •   Refer for surgical correction if severe or causing disability
 Note: For all notifiable diseases public health control measures will be regularly provided and updated by the Ministry of
 Health in collaboration with local authorities and relevant stakeholders

chapters.intro:
Notifiable Diseases, conditions and events usually pose a great public health threat, with a potential of international spread.
 They require immediate notification by health personnel (clinical, laboratory, environmental, etc.), to health authorities, as
 required by the International Health Regulations (IHR 2005). Notification is mandatory, to ensure prompt and effective
 response, to avoid further spread and to prevent deaths.
  Note:
      •     Immediately notify the Public Health Authorities using the electronic reporting system for priority diseases, i.e., the
            electronic Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response (e- IDSR) System
       •    Ensure that the disease, condition or event is recorded in the Health Facility e-IDSR reporting booklet
       •    Manage patients on site, in an isolation ward/room or an established isolation Centre
       •    Use Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) before attending a suspected patient
       •    Strictly apply principles of IPC during patient management and waste disposal

chapters.title: Malaria

sections.title: Asymptomatic Malaria Case
sections.text:
Asymptomatic malaria case can be found during Active Case Detection (ACD) by health workers in the community and in
households. Therefore, all patients with parasitemia are considered “malaria cases”, regardless of whether clinical symptoms
are present or not.

sections.title: Uncomplicated Malaria
sections.text:
Uncomplicated malaria is defined as symptomatic malaria without signs of severity or evidence (clinical or laboratory) of vital
organ dysfunction.

Clinical Presentation
Fever, Headache, Joint pains, Malaise, Vomiting, Diarrhoea, Body ache, body weakness, Poor appetite, Pallor, enlarged
spleen

Investigations
The recommended investigations are: Quality malaria microscopy or quality malaria Rapid Diagnostic Tests (mRDT)
   Note
       • It is compulsory to test and confirm all suspected malaria patients. Give antimalarial only to those who test
            positive.
       • In cases where non-response to malaria treatment (treatment failure) is suspected in patients who initially tested
            positive, microscopy is the recommended laboratory procedure as mRDTs are not recommended because
            parasite antigens persist up to 4 weeks after parasitaemia has cleared.

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Continue with feeding and fluid intake
    •  Followed up immediately if the condition worsens or on the fourth day if symptoms persist.

Pharmacological Management
Drug of choice for treatment of uncomplicated malaria is:
A: artemether + lumefantrine (PO) 20mg+120mg

Common fixed dose (FDC) formulations of Artemether +Lumefantrine (ALU):
     •   Artemether 20mg+Lumefantrine120mg; 6, 12, 18 and 24 tablets blister
     •   Artemether 80mg+Lumefantrine 480mg; 6 tablets blister
Dispersible tablets: Fixed formulation for children

Treatment of Malaria using ACT plus Primaquine.
To reduce transmissibility of treated malaria infection in a very low transmission area. A single low dose of 0.25mg/kg
primaquine with ACT is given to malaria patients.

The addition of a low single dose of Primaquine (0.25mg/kg maximum of 15mg in adults) to ACTs should be given to all eligible
patients because it affects the transmissibility of mature gametocytes of P. falciparum by minimizing further transmission of
the disease.

Formulation: Primaquine is available in the formulation of tablets 7.5 mg and 15 mg.
Dosage:

A: primaquine single 0.25mg/kg/dose (Table 5.5) should be given to all qualified patients with parasitological confirmed malaria
Indications
Primaquine should be given on the first day of treatment in addition to an ACT, preferably under Directly Observed Therapy
(DOT).

Contraindications
Not recommended in pregnant women, women in the first 6 months of breastfeeding and children less than 6 months of age.

Haemolytic Anemia, especially in G6PD individuals, is the major adverse event reported. Although, single low dose of
Primaquine is considered to be safe.

5.2.2: Malaria Chemoprevention medicine in Elimination Area.
Intermittent preventive treatment of malaria in pregnancy (IPTp) with Sulfadoxine +Pyrimethamine (SP) is recommended for

in Malaria Case Based Surveillance (mCBS).

The Medicine of choice for IPTp is SP. It is recommended at each scheduled antenatal care visit. The first IPTp-SP dose
should be administered as early as possible during the 2nd trimester of pregnancy and repeated at four weekly intervals until
the time of delivery

5.2.3: Chemoprophylaxis options for special risk groups
The term chemoprophylaxis is used to describe the administration of an antimalarial drug or drug combination in such a way
that blood levels are maintained above the inhibitory level of survival of the local strains of parasite for the whole of the period
at risk and, in the case of travelers, for an appropriate period afterwards in order to kill emerging liver forms. The recommended

5.2.4: Malaria chemoprophylaxis in sickle cell disease
Sickle cell disease (SCD) is an inherited condition where the sickle cell gene responsible for the production of abnormal
haemoglobin S is inherited from both parents.
In areas where malaria is common, SCD patients have low risk or malaria infection. However, when they do get malaria, it is
associated with high risk of morbidity and mortality.

It is recommended to give routine malaria prevention medicines (chemoprophylaxis) to individuals with SCD in areas where
malaria is endemic. This helps to reduce SCD crises and all other related complications.
The recommended chemoprophylaxis in Tanzania is:
C: atovaquone + proguanil: daily administration according to body weight
          OR
C: dihydroartemisinin + piperaquine (FDC) (PO): monthly administration according to body weight

Due to available safe and effective pharmacological action every SCD patient who require protection must receive a suitable
chemoprevention treatment.

Patients with high fever (38.50C and above) should be given appropriate dose of anti-pyretic medicine like paracetamol or

sections.title: Severe Malaria
sections.text:
In a patient with P. falciparum asexual parasitaemia and no other obvious cause of symptoms the presence of one or more of
features listed below classify the patient as suffering from severe malaria.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Prostration/extreme weakness                                •    Jaundice
     •    Impaired consciousness                                      •    Circulatory collapse/shock
     •    Change of behavior                                          •    Vomiting everything
     •    Convulsions                                                 •    Inability to drink or breast feed
     •    Respiratory distress (due to lactic acidosis                •    Bleeding tendency/DIC
          and/or pulmonary oedema)

Investigations
In severe malaria, blood slide (BS) is a recommended malaria test as it quantifies parasitemia. In severe ill patients receiving
injectable antimalarial, serial BS investigations monitors level of parasitemia to verify malaria recovery, or if clinical condition
is not improving to rule out another serious condition.
     •    Blood film for malaria parasites                                 •    Full blood cell count and differential white cell
     •    Blood glucose estimation in patients with altered                     count for additional diagnosis of other infectious
          consciousness                                                         diseases
     •    Haematocrit and/or haemoglobin estimation                        •    Blood gases, pH and anion gap– to diagnose
     •    Lumbar puncture to exclude meningitis (if                             acidosis
          facilities for LP assessment are available)                      •    Radiological investigation: Chest X–ray; look for
     •    Serum creatinine or urea– to assess Kidney                            pulmonary oedema or lobar consolidation
          function                                                         •    Blood culture and sensitivity where feasible
     •    Electrolytes– for early detection of acute renal
          failure
Non-Pharmacological Management
A rapid assessment must be conducted including airway, breathing, circulation, coma, convulsion, and dehydration status.

Referral: If effective management of severe malaria and supportive care for complications is not possible, patients should be
given pre-referral treatment and referred immediately to an appropriate facility for continued treatment.

Pharmacological Management
A: artesunate (IV/IM) 2.4 mg/kg in body weight on admission (time =0hour), then at 12hours and 24 hours for a minimum of
3doses in 24 hours regardless of patient’s recovery.
Children weighing less than 20 kg: 3mg/kg/dose (or higher). at 0, 12 and 24 hours

Complete artesunate injection treatment by giving a complete course (3days) of artemether-lumefantrine (ALU) or other ACT.
Consider broad spectrum antibiotic in case of septicemia.

Step 1: The powder for injection should be diluted with 1ml of sodium bicarbonate 5% solution (provided in each box) and
shaken vigorously 2–3 minutes for better dissolving until the solution becomes clear.
Step 2: For slow intravenous infusion (3–4minutes), add 5ml of dextrose 5% or Sodium chloride 0.9%, to obtain artesunate
concentration of 10mg/ml. For deep intra–muscular injection, add 2ml of dextrose 5% or Sodium chloride 0.9% to obtain

A: artemether (IM) 3.2mg/kg loading dose stat (0hour) then 1.6mg/kg (24hours and 48hours).

Injectable Artemether is to be used when Artesunate is contraindicated (in case of allergy, medicine interaction or non-
response) or when Artesunate is not available.

Management of complications
To reduce the unacceptably high mortality of severe malaria, patients require intensive care. Clinical observations should be
made as frequently as possible. Airway maintenance, nurse on side, fanning if hyperpyrexia is present, fluid balance review:

Coma (cerebral malaria): maintain airway, nurse on side, and exclude other causes of coma (e.g. hypoglycemia, bacterial
meningitis); avoid giving corticosteroids.
Dehydration: Correct dehydration appropriately

Hyperpyrexia: fanning, paracetamol if patient can swallow
Convulsions: maintain airways;
Adult
A: diazepam (IV) 0.15mg/ kg (maximum 10 mg) slow bolus IV injection.
Children
C: diazepam (rectal) 0.5–1.0 mg/ kg1.
If convulsions persist after 10 minutes repeat rectal diazepam treatment as above. Should convulsions continue despite a
second dose, give a further dose of rectal diazepam
          OR
A: phenobarbitone (IM/IV) 20 mg/ kg after another 10 minutes.
Hypoglycemia: remains a major problem in the management of severe malaria especially in young children and pregnant
women. It should be deliberately looked for and treated accordingly. Urgent and repeated blood glucose screening.
In children:
B: dextrose 10% (IV) 5 ml/kg
           OR
B: dextrose 25% (IV) 2.5ml/kg as bolus;
If 50%dextrose solution is available, it should be diluted to make 25% by adding an equal volume of water for injection or
normal saline.
In adults:
B: dextrose 10% (IV) 125ml
           OR
B: dextrose 25% (IV) 50ml as bolus.
Where dextrose is not available, sugar-water solution should be prepared by mixing 20g of sugar (4–level teaspoons) with
200ml of clean water. 50ml of this solution is given ORALLY or by nasogastric tube if semiconscious/unconscious.

Severe anaemia: Refer to haematology chapter 3
Acute pulmonary oedema: Refer to respiratory diseases conditions chapter 9
Acute renal failure: Refer to cardiovascular disease condition chapter 20
Shock: Refer to emergency and critical care chapter 1

sections.title: Management of Malaria in Special Groups
Malaria in Pregnancy
sections.text:
The effects of malaria in pregnancy are related to the malaria endemicity, with abortion more common in areas of low
endemicity and intrauterine growth retardation more common in areas of high endemicity.

sections.title: Uncomplicated Malaria in Pregnancy
sections.text:
In high-transmission areas (moderate to high immunity); malaria is usually asymptomatic in pregnancy or is associated with
only mild, non-specific symptoms. (See section 5.1 above)

Pharmacological Management
Artemether/Lumefantrine (ALU) is the recommended treatment of choice of a confirmed uncomplicated malaria to pregnant
women in all trimesters. See table 5.1 above

sections.title: Severe Malaria in Pregnancy
sections.text:
In low-transmission areas (low malaria immunity); women in the second and third trimesters of pregnancy are more likely to
develop severe malaria than other adults, often complicated by pulmonary oedema and hypoglycaemia.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Pulmonary oedema                                               •    Low blood sugar
     •    High fever                                                     •    Haemolytic anaemia
     •    Hyper parasitemia                                              •    Cerebral malaria

Pharmacological Management
A: Artesunate is the drug of choice for treatment of severe malaria in all trimesters. Refer table 5.10 for dosage

sections.title: Intermittent Preventive Treatment in Pregnancy (IPTp)
sections.text:
Malaria parasites can easily accumulate and multiply in the placenta leading to placenta malaria infections, resulting to
complications such as maternal anaemia, low birth weight, premature delivery, congenital infection and/or perinatal death.

The medicine of choice for IPTp
A: sulfadoxine + pyrimethamine (PO) 500mg +25mg as a fixed dose combination
     •   The dose is 3 tablets once
     •   A minimum of 3 doses in entire pregnancy period
     •   The first dose should be administered from 14 weeks of pregnancy onwards
     •   Each dose should be given at least 4 weeks apart
     •   The last dose can be administered up to the time of delivery, without safety concerns

sections.title: Management of Malaria in Neonates
sections.text:
Neonatal malaria is defined as symptoms attributable to malaria with evidence of ring forms of malaria parasite in the blood of
an infant within the first twenty-eight days (4 weeks) of life. Congenital malaria is defined as symptoms attributable to malaria
with evidence of ring forms of malaria parasite in the blood of an infant within the first seven days (1 week) of life. The signs
and symptoms resemble those seen in the new-born with septicemia

Clinical Presentation
     •    Fever                                                           •   Seizures
     •    Lethargy                                                        •   Jaundice
     •    Unable to breastfeed                                            •   Pallor
     •    Vomiting                                                        •   Hepatosplenomegaly
     •    Irritability
     •    Respiratory distress
     •    Laboratory findings will include the presence of malaria parasites.

Investigations
    •    Full blood picture
    •    blood sugar
    •    blood culture and sensitivity, blood smear for malaria parasite, serum electrolytes
    •    CSF for analysis

Management of neonatal malaria
Neonatal malaria should always be considered as severe malaria. Neonates with suspected malaria should be admitted to
hospital immediately as they can deteriorate quickly and die at home

Pharmacological Management
A: artesunate (IV/IM) is recommended treatment of choice for neonates.
         OR
A: artemether (IM) can be used as an alternative if Artesunate is not available
See table 5.10 and table 5.11 above for dosage

Broad spectrum antibiotic as majority of severe malaria accompanied with septicemia. Refer septicemia treatment section.

Nursing care and monitoring
    •   Monitor vital signs (PR, RR & Temperature)
    •   Monitor input/output
    •   Check BS for malaria parasite daily
    •   Ensure feeding
    •   Advise on use of Long-lasting insecticidal nets(LLINs)

sections.title: Management of Malaria in HIV and AIDS Patients
sections.text:
If malaria is diagnosed, depending on classification of the malaria diagnosis, a full treatment with antimalarial should be given
according to the malaria classification.
However, it should be noted that, clearance of parasitaemia may not necessarily be accompanied by clearance of symptoms
(fever) due to the presence of other underlying opportunistic infections. HIV and AIDS infected adults with low CD4 cell counts
may be more susceptible to treatment failure of anti-malaria drugs.

 Note:
 In suspected cerebral malaria in a HIV and AIDS patient, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination to rule out other life-
 threatening conditions such as bacterial and cryptococcal meningitis

chapters.intro:
Malaria case definition
A malaria case is a person with malaria infection, confirmed by microscopy or mRDT, regardless of whether fever and other
clinical symptoms are present.

chapters.title: Management Of Hiv And Aids

sections.title: Management of Adult and Adolescent Living with HIV with Antiretroviral Therapy
sections.text:
•     All individuals confirmed to have HIV infection are eligible for ART, regardless of CD4 count, WHO clinical stage, or
          any other criteria, provided that the individual is willing and ready to initiate ART and adhere to follow-up visits.
    •     ART should be initiated within 7days (same-day initiation), except when there is an increased risk of IRIS. RoC with
          advanced HIV disease should be closely screened for opportunistic infections (OIs) and may need ART initiation
          delay to prevent life threatening immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS).
    •     Goal of Combination antiretroviral therapy is to achieve; Undetectable viral load(<50copies/ml), restoration and/or
          preservation of immunologic function by attainment of CD4 recovery to normal thresholds ≥500 cells/mm³, reduction
          of HIV-related morbidity and mortality, improvement of survival and quality of life and prevention of new HIV infection
          (Undetectable=Untransmissible).

Initiating ART for Adult and Adolescent 15 years and above
ART should be initiated (to all adult and adolescents who are HIV infected) by qualified Health Care Providers in both facility
and community settings after a comprehensive medical history and physical examination, irrespective of CD4 count and WHO
clinical staging.

sections.title: Prevention of vertical transmission of HIV, Syphilis and Hepatitis B
sections.text:
The PMTCT program aims to eliminate vertical transmission of HIV, Syphilis, and Hepatitis B by using effective interventions
such as antenatal screening, treatment, and vaccination. The risks of vertical transmission without intervention are significant,
and multiple risk factors increase the chance of a mother transmitting HIV, Syphilis and Hepatitis B virus to her child. The goal
is to achieve aMTCT rate of less than 4% for HIV, less than 50cases of congenital syphilis per 100,000 live births, and less
than 0.1% prevalence of HBsAg among children.

Four elements of a comprehensive approach
 1. Primary prevention of HIV, Syphilis and HBV infections among women of childbearing age and their partners
 2. Prevention of unintended pregnancies amongst women living with HIV and HBV and linkage with other Sexual
      Reproductive Health services including STIs
 3. Prevention of vertical transmission of HIV, Syphilis and HBV from infected women to their infants
 4. Provision of treatment, care and support to women infected with HIV, Syphilis and HBV and their partners, infants, and
      families.

sections.title: HIV, Syphilis and Hepatitis B Testing and Counselling for Pregnant and Breast-feeding women
sections.text:
All pregnant women and their partners should be counselled and tested for HIV (unless known to be HIV positive), Syphilis
and Hepatitis B during their first ANC visit. If a client is diagnosed positive for any of the diseases i.e., HIV or Syphilis or
Hepatitis B manage the client accordingly.

High risk exposed infants: these are the infants with increased risk of transmission, it includes infants whose mother is one of
the following:
     •    Diagnosed with HIV during pregnancy or breastfeeding period
     •    Known to be living with HIV but not on ART
     •    Started on ART with less than four weeks before delivery.
     •    On ART with high viral load (≥50copies per ml of blood)

Low risk exposed infants: these are the infants whose mothers are already on ART and have achieved viral load of
<50copies/ml (obtained at least 4weeks apart or within 4weeks prior to delivery)

Low risk status can change to high risk and vice versa upon availability of HVL test results. For ARV prophylaxis and the
management of HIV exposed infants refer to Chapter IV on immediate post-delivery care.

Care for HIV-exposed infants
    •    Prophylaxis for Low-risk HIV Exposed Infants: Administer NVP syrup immediately after birth (preferably within
         72hours) and continue until 6weeks of age.
    •    Nevirapine prophylaxis should not be initiated for infants presenting after 4weeks of age.

sections.title: Care for Syphilis-exposed infants
sections.text:
All infants born to mothers with Syphilis infection should:
      •    Carefully be assessed for manifestations of congenital syphilis.
      •    Ensure proper treatment to infants diagnosed with congenital syphilis (Refer section 5.8.2.1 for management of
           Congenital Syphilis in National Guideline for Management of HIV, STIs and Hepatitis)

sections.title: Care for Hepatitis B-exposed infants
sections.text:
All infants born to mothers with HBV infection should receive.
      •    A birth dose of HBV monovalent vaccine within 24hours post delivery
      •    If available, a single dose of 100 IU HBIG intramuscularly should be given together with HBV
           vaccine birth dose. This should be given to all exposed infants born to mothers with high Hepatitis
           B DNA viral load (More than 200,000 IU/ML) preferably within 12 hours.’
      •    Subsequent 3doses of HBV vaccine during immunization schedule at 6, 10 and 14weeks of age
      •    Verify if:
                           o    Mother with high HBV DNA viral load (>200,000IU/ml) is on Tenofovir
                                prophylaxis.
                           o    Mother with HIV/HBV coinfection is on Tenofovir based regimen.

sections.title: Cotrimoxazole Preventive therapy
sections.text:
All HIV-exposed infants should begin cotrimoxazole Preventive Therapy (PT) at the age of six weeks until the end of HIV
exposure. Cotrimoxazole should continue up to seven days after being confirmed HIV negative.

sections.title: Maternal HIV Care and Treatment
sections.text:
PBFW living with HIV should be started on lifelong ART at the time of diagnosis. The recommended first line regimen is once
a day fixed dose regimen of Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) +Lamivudine (3TC) + Dolutegravir (DTG). Alternatively,
Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) +Lamivudine (3TC) + Efavirenz (EFV400mg) may be an option for use on events of or
DTG side effects and adverse events.
Before ART initiation, health care provider should discuss health benefits of lifelong ART, including ART impact in preventing
mother to child transmission of HIV. A client should understand and comprehend all possible side effects of ARVs. For clients
on 2nd and 3rd line ART regimens should continue with their current regimens.

A combination of a Protease Inhibitor (PI) and at least one new NRTI not previously used in first-line therapy are recommended
for second-line treatment for adults and adolescents PLHIV aged 15 and above, as shown in Table 6.3. Lamivudine (3TC) or
Emtricitabine (FTC) should be continued in subsequent regimens as it lowers viral fitness and increases susceptibility to AZT.

      •    RoC who received a PI-based regimen as their first line of treatment can be switched to a DTG-based regimen as

sections.title: Third-line Antiretroviral Therapy
sections.text:
RoC failing second line may have substantial NRTI and NNRTI-associated resistance mutations (RAMs), limiting their usage
in the third line regimen. Third-line regimens should include at least two, preferably three, effective drugs, constructed using
second-generation formulations of preceding antiretrovirals with low or no cross-resistance. These second-generation drugs
have a greater genetic barrier to resistance, and their efficacy is rarely jeopardized by RAMs associated with first-generation
formulations.

Third line ARVs recommended regimens include:
     •    Integrase Strand Transfer Inhibitors (INSTIs): Dolutegravir (DTG) and Raltegravir (RAL)
     •    Second generation PI: Boosted Darunavir (DRV/r)
     •    Susceptible NRTI after Genotypic Antiretroviral Resistance Testing and
     •    Recycled Lamivudine or Emtricitabine regardless of presence and level of RAMs selected by
          these ARVs

sections.title: Changing Antiretroviral Therapy
sections.text:
There are multiple reasons that may prompt the need to change antiretroviral therapy. These can be grouped into two major
categories:
    •     ARV specific adverse events (toxicity)
    •     Treatment failure
When changing treatment due to toxicity, Change or substitute only the ARV suspected to be causing the toxicity on the other
hand If changing due to treatment failure, the following should be observed;
    •     It is never recommended to switch to monotherapy
    •     Change at least two ARVs, preferably change all three ARVs (Do NOT retain the backbone)
    •     When making ARV selection, opt for drugs that haven't been previously used and don't have cross-resistance,
          overlapping toxicities, or drug-drug interactions
    •     Lamivudine has the advantage of reducing HIV viral fitness and increasing susceptibility to AZT and therefore should
          be retained when changing the failing regimen

sections.title: Changing ART due to Treatment Failure
sections.text:
Treatment failure can have categorized due to
    •   Virological failure
    •   Immunological failure
    •   Clinical failure

immunological and clinical failure for the decision to switch ART regimens
