sections.title: Initial management of Acute Ischemic Stroke
sections.text:
Acute ischemic stroke (AIS) is a leading cause of adult disability in the developed world. In AIS, thrombus impairs cerebral
blood flow, resulting in brain tissue infarction. Collateral blood flow gives rise to an area of hypo perfused tissue (ischemic
penumbra) that is at risk of infarction if hypoperfusion persists. Prompt reopening of an occluded blood vessel to re-establish
blood flow to the ischemic area (reperfusion) in eligible patients, can rescue the ischemic penumbra from death and spare the
patient from serious long-term disabilities.

Clinical Presentation
      •    Severe headache
      •    Focal neurological deficits
      •    decreased level of consciousness that may progress to coma
      •    seizures
      •    symptom progression over minutes or hours

Prehospital and lower-level health facilities
     •   Provide initial airway management and                                  facilitate initiation of treatment in the fastest
         hemodynamic stabilization                                              achievable onset-to-treatment time
     •   Exclude stroke mimics like hypoglycemia                            •   Consider prompt referral to a centre that can
     •   International stroke guidelines recommend                              handle stroke patients including rapid
         rapid identification of all fibrinolytic-eligible and                  neuroimaging         and      administration   of
         mechanical thrombectomy-eligible patients to                           reperfusion therapy.

Referral hospital and specialized centres
     •    Provide initial stabilization of the patient as per                   hours from last-known-well (LKW) state,
          ABCDE protocol                                                        perform brain MRI to identify diffusion-positive,
     •    Perform        rapid      careful     neurological                    FLAIR-negative lesions to aid selecting those
          examination.                                                          who can benefit from IV alteplase
     •    Order emergency brain imaging evaluation                              administration.
          before initiating any stroke specific treatments.                 •   In potential candidates for mechanical
     •    Screen for reperfusion eligible patients and                          thrombectomy, consider imaging of the
          initiate appropriate treatment protocol.                              extracranial carotid and vertebral arteries, in
     •    In patients with AIS who awake with stroke                            addition to the intracranial circulation, to
          symptoms or have unclear time of onset > 4.5                          provide useful information on patient eligibility
                                                                                and endovascular procedural planning.
  Note: Reperfusion criteria, all must be met
        •  Clinical diagnosis of an ischaemic stroke causing a measurable deficit
        •  The patient should be 18years or older
        •  Onset of stroke or last known well (LKW) state <4.5hours
        •  No increased bleeding risk contraindications
        •  Blood pressure controlled to <185/105mmHg target.
        •  Non-contrast brain CT has excluded intracranial hemorrhage and/or

Non-Pharmacological Management
     •  Oxygenation—support airway, maintain O2                                 lowered (Permissive Hypertension) in the first
        saturation >94%                                                         24 hours
     •  Monitor BP, if elevated, initiate BP lowering                       •   Monitor body temperature and initiate
        treatment to target BP<185/110 mmHg                                     treatment when >38°C
     •  For patients non eligible for fibrinolysis with                     •   In    immobile     stroke   patients    without
        extreme BP elevation SBP>220 or DBP> 120                                contraindications, offer compressive stockings,
        mmHg, should be lowered by 15% over the first                           or pneumatic compression devices for DVT
        24hrs                                                                   prophylaxis.
     •  For patients who are non-eligible for fibrinolysis                  •   Start on enteral diet (PO/NGT) after evaluation
        with moderate BP elevation SBP up to 220 or                             of swallowing
        DBP up to 120 mmHg BP should not be

Pharmacological Management
A: acetylsalicylic acid (PO) 325mg 24hourly for 4weeks
          AND
C: labetalol (IV) 10-20mg infusion 1-2min, repeated until target BP is attained.
          AND
D: paracetamol (IV) 1g 8hourly for 3-5days then when required.

 Note: For those treated with alteplase, acetylsalicylic acid administration should be delayed for 24 hours

Patients with an acute high-risk TIA or Minor Ischaemic stroke of non-cardioembolic origin (NIHSS 0-4) not at high bleeding
risk start Dual Antiplatelet Treatment (DAPT)
A: acetylsalicylic acid ASA (PO) 150mg STAT then 75mg daily
           AND
D: clopidogrel 300-600 mg stat then 75mg daily for 21 days
           OR
A: acetylsalicylic acid 300mg STAT then 75mg daily
           AND
S: ticagrelor 180mg stat then 90mg daily for 21days

Patients not meeting DAPT criteria initiate single antiplatelet
A: acetylsalicylic acid 150mg STAT then 75mg daily for 21 days
          OR
D: clopidogrel 300 to 600mg STAT then 75mg daily for 21 days

Patients with atrial fibrillation
C: warfarin (PO) 5mg daily for 21 days before 28 days after cardioversion
          OR
S: rivaroxaban (PO) 20mg od for 30days
          OR
S: apixaban (PO) 5mg 12hourly for 30 days

Patients with Confirmed Intracranial atherosclerosis initiate DAPT within 24Hrs of stroke onset or as soon as intracranial
atherosclerosis is confirmed.
A: acetylsalicylic acid 300mg
          AND
D: clopidogrel 600mg STAT continue A: acetylsalicylic acid 150mg AND D: clopidogrel 75mg daily for 90 days followed by A:
acetylsalicylic acid 75mg monotherapy lifelong
B: atorvastatin (PO) 40mg – 80mg daily for 180days
          OR
S: rosuvastatin (PO) 20mg - 40mg daily for 180 days

For seizure control
C: phenytoin (IV) 15mg/kg loading dose over 30min, then 100mg 8hourly for 28days.
           OR
S: levetiracetam (PO/IV) 500mg 12hourly for 14-28days

Initiate statins in eligible patients and continue statins in patients already taking statins at the time of onset of AIS.

Reperfusion treatment:
In patients qualified for intravenous thrombolysis, benefit of therapy is time dependent, and treatment should be initiated as
quickly as possible with a target door to needle time <60 minutes.
Admit the patient to an ICU or designated stroke unit for monitoring and initiate,

S: alteplase (IV) 0.9mg/kg maximum dose 90mg (given over 60minutes with initial 10% of dose given as bolus over 1 minute)
          OR
S: tenecteplase (IV) 0.25mg/kg maximum dose 25mg (given as a single bolus over 5 seconds)
Important precautions:
       •   Be prepared to treat potential emergent adverse effects, including bleeding complications and angioedema in
           patients undergoing fibrinolytic therapy.
       •   Maintain BP at <180/105mmHg for at least 24 hours following Alteplase infusion.
       •   Obtain a follow-up CT or MRI scan at 24 h after IV alteplase before starting anticoagulants or antiplatelet agents.

For management of intracranial hemorrhage complication within 24 hours following thrombolysis:
     •   Stop alteplase, obtain an emergent non contrast head CT.
     •   Obtain hematology and neurosurgery consultations
     •   Provide supportive care and initiate

C: tranexamic acid (IV) 1g infused over 10 minutes.
         AND
D: cryoprecipitate (includes factor VIII): 10 U infused over 10–30 min

In case of angioedema following Alteplase infusion, stop alteplase and provide airway support as required. Give
D: methylprednisolone (IV) 125mg
          AND
A: chlorpheniramine (IV) 10mg stat

If there is further increase in angioedema, administer
A: epinephrine (adrenaline) (S/C) (0.1%) 0.3 mL or by nebulizer 0.5 mL stat

Endovascular Treatment

Mechanical thrombectomy
Consider for selected patients who present between 6 and 24 hours of LKW with an anterior-circulation large-vessel occlusion
(ICA or proximal MCA) and meet other specified eligibility criteria based on expert assessment, clinical judgement, and
availability of required resources.

Surgical management of AIS
     •    Consider decompressive craniectomy in patients ≤60 years of age who deteriorate neurologically within 48
          hours from brain swelling associated with unilateral MCA infarctions despite appropriate medical therapy.
     •    Consider external ventricular drainage (EVD) in the treatment of obstructive hydrocephalus following cerebellar
          infarction.
     •    Emergency carotid end arterectomy (CEA) in the acute stage is not well established hence not recommended in
          initial management of AIS.

sections.title: Management of Epilepsy
sections.text:
Epilepsy is a common neurological disorder characterised by recurring seizures. About two-thirds of people with active
epilepsy have their epilepsy controlled satisfactorily with anti-seizure medication (ASM). Other treatment approaches may
include surgery and neuromodulation. Optimal management is required to improve patient’s health outcomes and minimise
detrimental impacts on social, educational, and occupational activities.

Clinical Presentation
Recurrent seizures

Investigations
      •    Serum electrolytes, random blood glucose                        •    Brain CT scan
      •    Serum antiseizure medication levels                             •    Brain MRI with epilepsy protocol
      •    Electroencephalogram (EEG)

Classification of epileptic syndromes
Classify epileptic seizures and epilepsy syndromes in all patients using a multi-axial diagnostic scheme (refer to ILAE
classification) as failure to classify the epilepsy syndrome correctly can lead to inappropriate treatment and persistence of
seizures.

Pharmacological Management
     •  Utilize a single ASM (monotherapy) and increase dose until seizures are controlled or side effects cannot be
        tolerated.
     •  If the initial treatment is unsuccessful, initiate alternative monotherapy with different medication before resorting to
        drug combinations.
     •  Combination therapy (adjunctive or 'add-on' therapy) should only be considered when attempts at monotherapy
        with ASM s have not resulted in seizure freedom.
     •  If trials of combination therapy do not bring about worthwhile benefits, revert treatment to the
        initial monotherapy regimen that has proved most acceptable to the patient and consider referral
        for expert evaluation.

For management of status epilepticus—refer to emergency and critical care chapter 1

Focal seizures
First Line:
A: carbamazepine (PO) 10-20mg/kg 12hourly for 28days
          OR
S: lamotrigine (PO) 1-5mg/kg 12hourly for 28days

Second line:
S: levetiracetam (PO) 10mg/kg 12hourly for 28days
Add-on treatment: gabapentin or sodium valproate as adjunctive treatment if first-line treatments are ineffective or not
tolerated.

Generalised tonic–clonic (GTC) seizures
C: sodium valproate (PO) 10-15mg/kg 12hourly for 28days
          OR
S: lamotrigine (PO) 1-5mg/kg 12hourly for 28days

Add on treatment: offer levetiracetam as adjunctive treatment if first-line treatments are ineffective or not tolerated.

Absence seizures
First Line:
C: sodium valproate (PO) 10-15mg/kg 12hourly for 28days

 Note: DO NOT offer carbamazepine, phenytoin or pregabalin for absence seizures.

Myoclonic seizures
First Line:
C: sodium valproate (PO) 10-15mg/kg 12hourly for 28days

Second line:
S: levetiracetam (PO) 10mg/kg 12hourly for 28days

Lenox Gastaut syndrome (LGS)
First Line:
C: sodium valproate (PO) 10-15mg/kg 12hourly for 28days

Second line:
S: lamotrigine (PO) 1-5mg/kg 12hourly as adjunctive treatment

 Note: DO NOT offer carbamazepine or pregabalin.

Idiopathic generalised epilepsy (IGE)                                 Juvenile Myoclonic epilepsy (JME)
First Line:                                                           First line:
C: sodium valproate (PO) 10-15mg/kg 12hourly for                      C: sodium valproate (PO) 10-15mg/kg 12hourly for
28days                                                                28days Second line:

Second line:                                                          S: lamotrigine (PO) 1-5mg/kg 12hourly for 28days
S: lamotrigine (PO) 1-5mg/kg 12hourly for 28days                                 OR
                                                                      S: levetiracetam (PO) 10mg/kg 12hourly for 28days

Childhood absence epilepsy
First Line:
C: sodium valproate (PO) 10-15mg/kg 12hourly for 28days

Second line:
S: lamotrigine (PO) 1-5mg/kg 12hourly for 28days
Add-on treatment: consider clonazepam, levetiracetam if first-line treatments are ineffective or not tolerated.

Management of epilepsy in pregnancy
The use of antiseizure medication (ASMs) is associated with increased baseline risk of fetal malformations during pregnancy.
Prescribe Folic acid to all women of childbearing age and girls on ASMs preconception. Attempt to decrease Pharmacological
Management to monotherapy and utilize the lowest possible effective dose of drugs that have shown minimal risk of maternal
and fetal neural tube defects
S: lamotrigine (PO) 1-5mg/kg 12hourly for 28days
           OR
S: levetiracetam (PO) 10mg/kg 12hourly for 28days
           AND
A: folic acid (PO) 5mg 24hourly for 120-180days
In women who have not had a seizure for at least 2years, attempt complete withdrawal of ASMs.

Surgical Management of Epilepsy:
     •    Resective Surgery                                               •    Lesionectomy
     •    Corpus Callosotom                                               •    Hemispherectomy/HemispHemisphorotomy
     •    Vagus Nerve Stimulation                                         •    Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS)

The choice of Neurosurgical intervention depends on Indication seizure trigger factor and Location.

Non-Pharmacological Management
     •  Consider ketogenic diet—based on specialist assessment and expert opinion
     •  Refer all medically refractory seizures for expert neurosurgical evaluation for epilepsy surgeries
     •  Consider evaluation for Vagus Nerve Stimulation (VNS) as an adjunctive treatment in reducing the frequency of
        seizures in adults who are refractory to AEDs but who are not suitable for resective surgery

sections.title: Parkinson’s Disease and other movement disorders
sections.text:
Parkinson’s disease (PD) is a common chronic, progressive, neurodegenerative disorder in geriatric population, characterized
by the loss of dopaminergic neurons from the substantia nigra that subsequently results in the loss of control of voluntary
movement over time

Clinical Presentation
      •    Motor symptoms: Resting Tremors, bradykinesia, rigidity, akinesia postural instability
      •    Non motor symptoms: drooling, dementia, depression, orthostatic hypotension

Diagnosis
     •    Clinical based and brain MRI to rule out atypical Parkinson disease mimics e.g. vascular parkinsonism,
          neuroferritinopathies, Wilsons disease, Neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation (NBIA) based on United
          Kingdom Parkinson’s Disease Society Brain Bank (UKPDSBB) criteria
     •    Atypical parkinsonism consists of dementia with Lewy bodies, corticobasal syndrome, progressive supranuclear
          palsy and multiple system atrophy

Surgical Management.
     •    Deep brain Stimulation (DBS)
     •    Implanting electrodes in specific areas of the brain to regulate brain activity and reduce symptoms
     •    It’s minimally invasive, reversible and adjustable.

Non-Pharmacological Management
Provide physiotherapy, occupational, speech and language therapies

Pharmacological Management

Motor symptoms
First line:
D: levodopa+ carbidopa (FDC) (PO) 100/25mg 8 hourly (escalate dose based on individual response) to be taken 30-45
minutes before meals

Give adjunctive treatment for motor symptoms: MAO-B or COMT inhibitors or Dopamine agonist in persistent motor symptoms
despite adequate tolerable doses of Levodopa+ carbidopa FDC treatment.

S: selegiline (PO) 2.5-5mg 24hourly (maximum dose 10mg/day)
           OR
S: entacapone (PO) 200mg with each dose of levodopa carbidopa

Non-motor symptoms Drooling:
S: glycopyrrolate (PO) 0.5-1mg 8hourly for 28days

Orthostatic hypotension: Look for offending medication (diuretics, alpha antagonist for prostatism, antihypertensive,
Amitriptyline, Levodopa) consider Levodopa dose reduction and give

D: fludrocortisone (PO) 0.1mg 24hourly for 28days
          AND
S: midodrine 2.5 to 10mg 8hrly

Depression: Individualize therapy, consider
S: fluoxetine (PO) 20mg 24hourly (maximum 60mg/day) for 28days
          OR
A: amitriptyline (PO) 50mg 24hourly for 28-84 days (May unmask dementia and orthostatic hypotension caution in the elderly)
Impulse control disorders: Consider modification of dopaminergic drug dosages.

Figure 8.1 Summary of Management of Parkinson’s Disease

sections.title: Pediatric Hydrocephalus
sections.text:
Pediatric hydrocephalus (HDC) is a common surgically correctable neurological problem in children with estimated incidence
of 1 in every 500 children. HDC can result from various congenital and acquired causes including aqueductal stenosis, Chiari
malformations, intraventricular hemorrhage, trauma, tumors, and infection. There are effective surgical interventions that can
preserve and improve quality of life in patients with HDC.

Clinical Presentation
Abnormal increase in head size, Seizure, Delayed/regressed developmental milestones, Headache and impaired vision

Investigations
      •    Cranial Ultrasound
      •    Non contrast head CT scan
      •    MRI brain scan

Surgical Management:
     •    Endoscopic third ventriculostomy with choroid plexus coagulation (ETV+CPC) as first line option in cases with clear
          obstruction to CSF flow.
     •    Insertion of ventriculoperitoneal shunt (VP shunt) where ETV+CPC is not available, has failed, or is contraindicated.
          Other alternative CSF shunts include ventriculoarterial (VA) or ventriculopleural shunts, as well as ventriculo-
          subgaleal shunting.

Non-Pharmacological Management
     •  Physiotherapy
     •  Educational therapy
     •  Screening for other congenital anomaly

Pharmacological Management
Management of associated seizures:

A: phenobarbitone (PO) 5mg/kg 12hourly for 4weeks
         OR
C: sodium valproate (PO) 10-15mg/kg 12hourly for 4weeks

On surgical procedure
C: cefazolin30mg/kg (maximum 2gm) 30 minutes before incision
       AND/OR
S: vancomycin (IV) or intrathecal 15 – 20 mg per/Kg 8 or 12 hourly

sections.title: Management of Pediatric CSF Shunt Infections
sections.text:
Clinical Presentation
CSF leak, purulence, skin erosion, Fever, meningismus, erythema, exposed or protruding hardware

Lab investigations
FBP, CRP, CSF analysis, C/S, Blood C/S

Non-Pharmacological Management
     •  Physical therapy
     •  Change position regularly
     •  Monitor fever and feeding surgical options
     •  Insert External ventricular drain (EVD) as interim measure for intracranial pressure monitoring and therapeutic
        diversion of CSF in the setting where an infected internal shunt device has been removed +/- intrathecal antibiotics
        e.g., Vancomycin
     •  ETV and serial irrigation with intrathecal (intravericular) antibiotics.

Pharmacological Management
Initiate empirical antibiotic treatment
C: amoxicillin + clavulanic acid (FDC) (IV) child <3months 30mg/kg 12hourly 3months and older 20-30mg/kg 8hrly (Max 3G
daily) for 2weeks
           OR
D: ceftriaxone+ sulbactam (FDC) (IV) 100mg/kg 12hourly for 14days
           AND
B: metronidazole (IV) 7.5mg/kg/day 8hourly for 14days

Alternative regimen based on C/S results
S: piperacillin+ tazobactam (FDC) (IV) 300mg/kg/day (of piperacillin component) divided in 4doses per day
         OR
S: meropenem (IV )10mg/kg 8 hourly, (may increase up to 40mg/kg) for 10-14days Shift to organism’s specific regimen after
CSF/hardware culture results

For confirmed Staph spp. infections add
S: vancomycin (IV) 10mg/kg 6hourly for 2weeks or more.
          OR
C: cefazolin30mg/kg (maximum 2gm) 30 minutes before incision
          AND
S: vancomycin (intrathecal) 15 – 20 mg per/Kg stat

sections.title: Congenital Spina Bifida
sections.text:
Spina Bifida (SB) is one of the commonest complex congenital birth defects in developing countries. Children with SB are
faced with multiple medical and psychosocial issues that require a comprehensive multidisciplinary care plan.

Clinical Presentation
Swelling on the back, CSF leak, Lower limb weakness, Lower limb deformities, Lower limb paralysis

Investigations
Prenatal diagnosis
      •    Ultrasound in second trimester of pregnancy
      •    Amniotic fluid analysis
Postnatal diagnosis
      •    Cranial Ultrasound—evaluate for associated hydrocephalus
      •    Neuraxial MRI (Brain and Spine) -is indicated in complex cases to plan surgical management and evaluate for
           associated defects—Hydrocephalus, chiari malformations, tethered cord
      •    Neural axis CT scan (Brain and Spine)
      •    Preoperative screening echocardiogram (ECHO)

Surgical management of Spina Bifida
Refer for expert neurosurgical evaluation for surgical closure of the spinal defect and subsequent evaluation for the need to
treat associated hydrocephalus

Surgical procedure
     •    Closure of the Spina bifida cystica defect/deformity
     •    +/- ETV + Choroid plexus Cauterization
     •    +/- CSF Shunting (e.g., Ventriculo Peritoneal Shunt, Ventriculo Subgaleal shunt, Ventriculo Atrial Shunting)

Non-Pharmacological Management
Neuro rehabilitation, Orthotics when necessary.

Pharmacological Management
Initiate antibiotics in children with open infected spinal bifida lesions
B: ceftriaxone (IV) 100mg/kg 12hourly for 2 weeks
           OR
B: amoxicillin + clavulanic acid (FDC) (PO) 15mg/kg 8hourly for 2weeks
           OR
C: amoxicillin + clavulanic acid (FDC) (IV)15mg/kg 8hourly for 2weeks
           AND
A: metronidazole (PO) 7.5mg/kg/day 8hourly for 2weeks
           OR
B: metronidazole (IV) 7.5mg/kg/day 8hourly for 2weeks

Supportive and preventive and measures
    •    Provide routine screenings and testing for specific secondary conditions (HDC, skeletal limb deformities, UTIs) to
         minimize medical complication rates and help control cost of care.

          o Provide lower limb orthoses (splints, calipers)
          o Provide a wheelchair for ambulation
    •    Track and counsel women about recurrence risk and prescribe 5mg of folic acid beginning at least one month
         (preferably 3 months) before another conception and continue through the first 3 months of pregnancy.
    •    Encourage women of childbearing age to consume food fortified with folic acid and other macronutrients:

 Note: Tanzania passed a policy for the mandatory fortification of commercial wheat and maize flour in 2011, Wheat flour is
      fortified with folic acid, iron, vitamin B12, zinc, thiamin, riboflavin, niacin, and vitamin A, while maize flour is fortified
      with folic acid, iron, and vitamin B12

sections.title: Trigeminal Neuralgia
sections.text:
Trigeminal neuralgia (TN) is a syndrome characterized by chronic paroxysmal brief episodes of unilateral electric shock-like
pains, in one or more divisions of the trigeminal nerve. TN is often mistaken as a dental problem leading to delayed correct
diagnosis and appropriate treatment. The diagnosis is based on the characteristic clinical picture.

Clinical Presentation
Unilateral recurrent sudden intense and sharp shock like brief pains in one or more division of trigeminal nerve, jaw, teeth,
gums, cheek pain exacerbated by cutaneous stimuli, e.g., chewing, brushing or touching the face

Investigations
    •    RBG, CBC ESR
    •    CT scan to exclude structural bond or brain pathologies
    •    MRI to assess the trigeminal nerve root entry zone (REZ)

Surgical management
Refer all patient with poor response to conservative management for expert Neurosurgical evaluation for microvascular
decompression (MVD), a surgical procedure undertaken to identify, isolate and separate a vascular loop abutting the trigeminal
nerve at the root entry zone (REZ).

Non-Pharmacological Management
Refer to a neurosurgeon for procedures that involve controlled trigeminal ganglion ablation to alleviate pain
    •     Radiofrequency ablation                                       •    Glycerol rhizolysis
    •     Gasserian ganglion balloon compression                        •    Stereotactic radiosurgery rhizotomy
          rhizotomy

Pharmacological Management
First line treatment:
A: carbamazepine (PO) 200mg 12hourly for 28-84days (Doses up to 300mg/day-2000mg /day)
            OR
Second line treatment
S: lamotrigine (PO) 25-600mg /d for 28-84days weeks

sections.title: Bell’s Palsy
sections.text:
Bell's palsy, also referred to as idiopathic facial nerve palsy is unilateral paralysis of all the muscles of facial expression of
suspected viral etiology. Inflammation and edema of the facial nerve likely play a role in pathogenesis. Reactivation of herpes
simplex virus (HSV) is also thought to play an etiologic role. Most patients recover within a few weeks or months.

Clinical Presentation                                                 Investigations
     •    Unilateral facial paralysis (sudden onset)                      •    HIV testing
     •    Inability to close the eye (Bells’ phenomena)                   •    RBG
                                                                          •    otoscopic exam

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Provide facial muscle massage and exercises
    •  Provide eye patch for ocular protection during sleep.
    •  Refer for ophthalmological evaluation in severe cases

Pharmacological Management

A: prednisolone (PO) 60mg 24hourly for 5 days, then taper down to 50mg 24hourly for next 5days.
         AND
B: acyclovir (PO/IV)800mg 4-8hourly for 7-14days.

sections.title: Spinal Cord and Peripheral Nerve Disorders
Acute Transverse Myelitis (TM)
sections.text:
Acute onset, usually postinfectious, rapidly progressive neurologic syndrome caused by focal inflammation of the spinal
cord. Thoracic spinal cord level is the most commonly involved.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Rapid progressive bilateral lower limb                         •    Numbness and paresthesis
          weakness                                                       •    Bladder and bowel incontinence
     •    Backache and neuropathic pain

Investigations
    •    FBP, serum electrolytes                                         •    Brain MRI—may be required to exclude
    •    CSF analysis                                                         multiple sclerosis
    •    Emergency MRI or CT/myelogram to rule out a
         compressive lesion.

Perform baseline severity score such as American Spinal Injury Association (ASIA) impairment score to assist in clinical
management decisions and monitor improvement.

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Monitor respiratory function, support ventilation                 •    Provide rehabilitation--exercises to assist
       where required                                                         ambulation
    •  Catheterize bladder and offer stool softeners to                  •    Offer assisted ambulation devices—e.g., high
       aid bowel emptying                                                     back wheelchairs
    •  Provide manual position changes 2hourly to
       avoid pressure sores

Pharmacological Management
Give high-dose steroids
D: methylprednisolone (IV) 500-1000mg/day for 3–5days

Consider cyclophosphamide in refractory cases (under the direction of an oncologist)
S: cyclophosphamide (IV) 800-1000mg/m2 pulse dose.

Long term management
Manage generalized pain with
A: diclofenac (IM) 75mg 12hourly for 3-5days
          OR
B: tramadol (PO) 50mg 8hourly for 7-14days.

Manage neuropathic pain with
D: pregabalin (PO) 75mg 12hourly (maximum dose 300mg) for 2-4weeks

Manage spasticity with
S: baclofen (PO) 10mg 8hourly, (maximum dose 120mg/day) for 2weeks
          OR
S: tizanidine (PO) 2mg 8hourly, (maximum dose 36mg/day) for 2weeks

sections.title: Guillan Barre Syndrome
sections.text:
Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS) is potentially fatal, immune-mediated acute-onset ascending sensorimotor neuropathy usually
triggered by infections. Timely recognition, diagnosis, and prompt referral to a centre equipped to provide ventilatory support
is essential to improve mortality and minimize long term morbidity.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Rapid ascending bilateral lower limb weakness
     •    Little or no sensory deficits                                  •    Cardiac arrhythmias
     •    Evolving respiratory distress                                  •    Facial or bulbar palsy.

Investigations
    •    FBP, serum electrolytes
    •    CSF analysis-albumin cytologic dissociation (↑ protein without pleocytosis)
    •    Emergency MRI to exclude acute spina cord inflammation or compression

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Provide rehabilitation-exercises to assist ambulation
    •  Assisted ambulation devices e.g., high back wheelchairs

Pharmacological Management
Admit to ICU and provide ventilatory support to all patients with evolving respiratory distress or severe autonomic
cardiovascular dysfunction
S: human immunoglobulin G (IV) 0.4g/kg 24hourly for 5days (started within 14days of disease onset)

For severe cases, consider
S: plasma exchange 200-250ml plasma/kg body weight for 5sessions (started within 28days of disease onset)

Monitor respiratory function-patient is deemed at risk of respiratory failure if the vital capacity is
<20ml/kg, the maximum inspiratory pressure is <30cmH2O or the maximum expiratory pressure is
<40cmH2O

sections.title: Peripheral Neuropathy
sections.text:
Peripheral neuropathies encompass disorders of peripheral nerve cells and fibers which manifest secondary to a wide range
of pathologies that can affect motor, sensory, and autonomic fibers. Peripheral neuropathies can be classified as
mononeuropathies, multifocal neuropathies, and poly- neuropathies. Further sub classifications categorize peripheral
neuropathies as axonal, demyelinating, or mixed types, which is essential for treatment and management purposes.
Clinical Presentation
     •    Numbness and paresthesis,
                                                                       •     Loss of coordination
     •    Neuropathic pain
                                                                       •     Orthostatic hypotension
     •    Extremities weakness,
                                                                       •     Cold, pale feet

    •  Offer support on cessation to patients with alcohol-induced neuropathy

Pharmacological Management

    •  Ensure glucose control in diabetic neuropathy, alcohol cessation in alcoholic neuropathy and correction of vitamin
       or mineral deficiencies in nutrition related peripheral neuropathies.
    •  For drug related neuropathies, stop the offending medicine and give a suitable substitute. e.g., substitute stavudine

sections.title: Multiple Sclerosis (MS)
sections.text:
Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an inflammatory demyelinating disease of the central nervous system. It is classified into different
types based on disease course, including relapsing remitting MS, Secondary progressive MS, Primary progressive MS and
Progressive relapsing MS

Clinical Presentation
     •    Unilateral, painful vision loss with impaired color perception (Optic neuritis)
     •    Subacute limb weakness
     •    Electric shock sensation on neck flexion (Lhermitte’s sign)
     •    Bladder/ bowel dysfunction
     •    Diplopia, nystagmus, vertigo ataxia dysarthria
     •    Memory or concentration impairment
     •    The clinical course of MS can be relapsing remitting (The commonest type). Primary progressive or secondary
          progressive.

Investigations
    •    MRI brain, Spine
    •    CSF analysis
    •    Visual Evoked potential (VEP)

  Note: Treatment aims at treating acute relapses, modify disease course, relieve symptoms and rehabilitate. Medical
  management along with multidisciplinary team: physiotherapy, occupational therapy, psychology/psychiatry, ophthalmology
  and other specialties are required to holistically treat these patients

Pharmacological Management
Acute relapse give High dose corticosteroids
D: methylprednisolone (IV) 1000 mg/day 24hourly for 5 days

Plasma exchange is considered for severe relapse, refractory to steroid
Modify disease course

Induction phase
S: rituximab (IV) 1000mg two weeks apart for one months

Maintenance phase
S: rituximab (IV) 1000mg every 6 months

Symptomatic management in MS: constipation (high fiber diet, laxatives) Depression (Antidepressants’) erectile dysfunction
(PDE5 inhibitors)

sections.title: Neuromyelitis Optica Spectrum Disorder (NMOSD)
sections.text:
Neuromyelitis optica Spectrum Disorder (NMOSD) is CNS demyelinating disease that primarily affects the optic nerves and
spinal cord leading to severe neurological symptoms

Clinical Presentation
     •    Optic neuritis, acute myelitis
     •    Area postrema syndrome: episodes of unexplained hiccups or nausea and vomiting
     •    Acute brainstem syndrome
     •    Symptomatic narcolepsy or acute diencephalic clinical syndrome with typical diencephalic MRI lesions
     •    Symptomatic cerebral syndrome with NMO type brain lesions.
     •    Diagnosis is made when Aquaporin 4 IgG positive (Preferably cell-based test + at least one core clinical characteristic
          Exclusion of any alternative diagnosis

                                                  OR
    •    In case of unknown Aquaporin 4 IgG status, at least 2 core clinical characteristics with
    •    A) at least one core characteristic being optic neuritis, acute myelitis with longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis
         (LETM) or area postrema syndrome
    •    B) dissemination in space
    •    C) fulfillment of other MRI characteristic of NMO
    •    E) exclusion of alternative diagnosis

Investigations
    •    Serum AQP4-IgG antibody test will be positive. A cell-based assay is recommended.
    •    MRI brain and spine, CSF
    •    VEP

Pharmacological Management:
Medical management along with multidisciplinary treatment with physiotherapy, occupational therapy, psychology/psychiatry,
and other specialties

In Acute attacks give High dose corticosteroids
D: methylprednisolone 1000mg (IV) daily for five days
Plasma exchange (PLEX)for refractory to high dose corticosteroid

Relapse prevention
Long term immunotherapy is essential to reduce relapse
S: azathioprine 1-2 mg/kg/day (PO)
          OR
S: mycophenolate mofetil 1000mg 12hourly
          OR
S: rituximab (RTX) 375mg/m2 weekly for 4 weeks or Rituximab 1000mg (IV) every after 6 months

sections.title: Myelin Oligodendrocyte Glycoprotein (MOG) Antibody Associated Disease (MOGAD)
sections.text:
MOGAD is a rare CNS demyelinating syndrome defined by antibodies against myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein. It overlaps
clinically with NMOSD and MS but has distinct features

Clinical Presentation
     •    Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM)
     •    Optic neuritis
     •    Transverse myelitis
     •    Autoimmune encephalitis

Investigations:
    •    Serum anti MOG IgG will be positive
    •    MRI brain spine
    •    CSF examination

Pharmacological Management:
Acute attacks, High dose corticosteroids
D: methylprednisolone (IV) 1000mg/day daily for five days require a slow taper of steroids to prevent relapse

Maintenance: Many MOGAD cases are monophasic, relapsing cases are managed with
S: mycophenolate mofetil (O) 1000mg 12hrly
          OR
S: rituximab (IV) 375 mg/m2 weekly for 4 weeks
          OR
S: rituximab (IV) 1000mg every 6 months
          OR
S: azathioprine or Methotrexate may also be used in doses similar to NMO

sections.title: Tension Type Headache
sections.text:
Overview: Tension type headache (TTH) is the most common primary headache disorder, usually mild-to-moderate and self-
limited

Clinical Presentation
Bilateral pressing, tightening non pulsating pain, Photophobia or phonophobia may occur

Investigation:
Clinical, CT/MRI once there are red flags Neurological deficits, papilloedema on fundoscopy

Pharmacological Management:
First line
A: paracetamol (PO) 10-15mg/kg 8hrly for 5-7days
           OR
A: ibuprofen (PO) 10mg/kg 8hrly 5-7days
           OR
A: naproxen (PO) 5-7mg/kg 8hrly 5-7days

Prevention: For frequent or chronic TTH >15days per month
A: amitriptyline (PO) 10-75mg at bed time three months reviewed subject to response

sections.title: Migraine
sections.text:
Migraine is a primary headache characterized by moderate to severe, often unilateral, throbbing pain, aggravated by
movement associated with nausea, photo/phonophobia, aura-visual or sensory symptoms before headache.

Clinical Presentation
Throbbing headache usually unilateral, photo-phono-phobia, nausea, vomiting

Investigation
Mainly clinical; CT /MRI brain scan

Pharmacological Management
First line
Mild attack
A: paracetamol (PO) 10-15mg/kg 8hrly for 5-7days
           OR
A: ibuprofen (PO) 10mg/kg 8hrly for 5-7days

Moderate to severe attacks
S: sumatriptan 0.1-0.3mg/kg stat then repeat after 2hrs if migraine persist
          OR
C: ergotamine tartarate (combined with caffeine) (PO) 1-2mg at the start of the symptoms then 2mg hourly if the symptom
persists; do not exceed 6mg in a day

Prophylaxis: consider if 2 or more attacks per week or significant disability
First line preventives

A: propranolol (PO) 40-240mg per day for 90days
          OR
A: amitriptyline (PO) 10-75mg nocte for three months
          OR
S: verapamil (PO) 80mg daily titrate by 80mg 3days (240-480mg)

Non- Pharmacological Management
Lifestyle: trigger avoidance, sleep, hydration and meals.
Behavioral therapy

sections.title: Trigeminal Autonomic Cephalalgias (TACs)
sections.text:
This group includes Cluster headache, paroxysmal hemicrania, SUNCT/SUNA, and hemicrania continua. They share
unilateral severe pain with ipsilateral autonomic symptoms.

sections.title: Cluster headache:
sections.text:
Clinical Presentation
Excruciating unilateral orbital/temporal pain, often with conjunctival injection, lacrimation, nasal congestion and agitation.
Attack lasts 15-180minutes, occurs in clusters weeks-months separated by remission.

Pharmacological Management:
Acute:
A: oxygen 12-15L/min ,100% Inhaled via mask
         OR
S: sumatriptan (SC) 0.1-0.3mg/kg stat.

Preventive
S: verapamil (PO) 360-480mg/day for 90-180days (High dose)

sections.title: Paroxysmal Hemicrania
sections.text:
Clinical Presentation:
Multiple daily attacks of severe unilateral headache with autonomic signs. Attacks are shorter than cluster

Pharmacological Management:
A: piroxicam 20-40(PO) mg daily leads to complete remission (Diagnostic) for five to seven days

Hemicrania continua: continuous unilateral headache with superimposed exacerbations and autonomic features
A: piroxicam (PO) 20-40mg daily for five to seven days

sections.title: Short Lasting Unilateral Neuralgiform headache with Conjunctival injection and Tearing (SUNCT AND SUNA)
sections.text:
Clinical: Very short (<1min), frequent attacks with lacrimation and flushing

Pharmacological Management:
S: lamotrigine (PO) 25-50mg/day initial three weeks titrate to 100-200mg twice a day for three to six weeks
          OR
D: gabapentin (PO) 100-300mg nocte initial 5 days titrate to 450-900 twice a day if symptoms persist

sections.title: New Daily Persistent Headache (NDPH)
sections.text:
Clinical Presentation:
Daily headache without relief, features of tension or migraine, no neurological deficit, may recall trigger -infection or stress

Investigation
MRI brain, CSF

Non-Pharmacological Management:
Trial of sleep hygiene, stress reduction and standard headache therapy

Pharmacological Management
A: amitriptyline (PO) 10-75mg nocte for three to six months
          OR
D: gabapentin (PO) 100-300 mg nocte initial five days titrate to 450-900 twice a day if symptoms persist

sections.title: Cervicogenic Headache
sections.text:
Headache caused by disorder of the cervical spine

Clinical Presentation:
Unilateral occipital or frontotemporal headache provoked by neck movement or sustained posture, radiates to the eye or
forehead. Limited range of neck movement Cervical spine tenderness or muscle spasm

Investigations
MRI/CT cervical spine

Non-Pharmacological Management:
Physical therapy focused on cervical mobilization, posture correction and relieve of muscle spasm

Pharmacological Management
A: Ibuprofen (PO) 800mg 8hrly for five to seven days
          OR
D: diclofenac (PO) 50mg + paracetamol 325mg + chlorzoxazone250mg (PO) 8hrly for five to seven days
          OR
S: triamcinolone+ lidocaine Injection (Cervical epidural or facet blocks)
          OR
S: radiofrequency ablation

sections.title: Mild Cognitive Impairment
sections.text:
Denotes cognitive decline greater than expected for age but without significant impairment of daily function

Clinical Presentation
Subtle memory lapses, word finding difficult or planning problem but retain independence in basic needs

Investigation
    •    Neuropsychological testing (MMSE/MOCA)                         •       CSF amyloid Beta 42 (CSFAB42)
    •    Blood tests CBC, B12, TSH                                      •       PET Scan (Amyloid Tau FDG)

Pharmacological Management
    •   Non pharmacological                                                 •    Pharmacological Management for reversible
    •   Control of vascular risk factors Hypertension,                           causes: depression, vitamin B deficiency,
        diabetes, smoking.                                                       hypothyroidism
    •   Health life style -aerobic exercise, cognitive
        engagement, sleep

sections.title: Alzheimer’s Disease (AD)
sections.text:
Clinical Presentation
     •    Insidious onset, progressive memory impairment – language, visuospatial skills and executive function
     •    Poor recall, disorientation, aphasia, or apraxia

Clinical investigation
Neuropsychological test, MRI PET scan, CSF biomarkers (Beta amyloid, Tau)

Pharmacological Management
Table 8.5 Treatment of Alzheimer’s Disease
 Disease stage       Medicine                                      Initial Dose        Maintenance Dose
 Mild to Moderate    S: donepezil                                  5mg 24 hourly       10mg 24 hourly (after 4-6weeks)

 Moderate Severe       S: memantine                                5mg 24 hourly       20mg 24 hourly (5mg increase every
                                                                                       week)
 Advanced              S: memantine + donepezil (FDC)              7mg/10mg            28mg/10mg
                                                                                       (Increment of 7mg at intervals of
                                                                                       ≥1week)

sections.title: Vascular Dementia
sections.text:
Cognitive impairment attributed to cerebrovascular disease abrupt or insidious focal signs weakness, gait disturbance
Executive dysfunction, slowed thinking

Investigation:
MRI/CT head scan, Carotid duplex

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Vascular risk factor control
    •  Rehabilitation
    •  Cognitive training

Pharmacological Management
No demential specific drugs
A: acetylsalicylic acid (PO) 75mg every 24 hours for 90 days
          AND
S: donepezil (PO) 5mg every 24 hours for 90 days

Treat Hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemias

sections.title: Frontotemporal dementia (FTD)
sections.text:
Clinical Presentation
     •    Onset before age 65yrs behavioral variant- personality changes, disinhibition, apathy, compulsive behavior
     •    Later Progressive aphasia language impairment Semantic or nonfluent

Investigation:
    •    Neuropsychometry
    •    MRI brain

Non-Pharmacological Management:
Speech therapy for aphasia, social support

Pharmacological Management
D: citalopram (PO) 10-20 mg 24 hourly

sections.title: HIV Associated Neurocognitive Disorders (HAND)
sections.text:
Clinical Presentation:
Cognitive slowing, memory and concentration impairment, motor slowing and coordination deficits

Investigation
    •    Neuropsychological testing
    •    MRI brain
    •    HIV viral load, CD4 cell count, CSFHIV RNA
    •    Vitamin B12, TSH, ACTH stimulation test

Pharmacological Management
Treat with ARV as per HIV/AIDS guideline and as per blood test results.

sections.title: Lewy Body Dementia (DLB)
sections.text:
Clinical Presentation
Dementia, visual hallucinations sleep disorder, parkinsonism, extrapyramidal features rigidity, bradykinesia

Investigation
MRI, DATscan (DaT SPECT)

Pharmacological Management:
Psychotic features if present
S: clozapine (PO) 6.5mg-12.5 24 hourly (increase in 3-5 days

For Parkinsonism
D: levodopa + carbidopa (PO) 125mg 24 hourly for three to 6 months

For REM sleep
D: clonazepam (PO) 0,5mg at bedtime for years

sections.title: Motor Neuron Disease (Includes ALS)
sections.text:
Characterized by degeneration of motor neurons both central and peripheral

Clinical Presentation
     •    Progressive painless weakness, asymmetric, muscle atrophy, fasciculations, spasticity and brisk reflexes
     •    Bulbar involvement-dysarthria, dysphagia. Preserved sensory function

Investigations
NCV, EMG, MRI Spine/brain, Pulmonary function test

Non-Pharmacological
    •   Non-invasive ventilation (BiPAP)
    •   Gastrostomy
    •   Multidisciplinary support (Physical therapy, speech, palliative care

Pharmacological Management
S: edaravone (IV) 60mg 24 hourly for 14 days followed by 14 days drug free. then 60mg 24 hourly for 10 days week-days only
         OR
S: edaravone (PO) 105mg (5ml) orally 24-hourly same schedule as the IV route above

sections.title: Myasthenia Gravis (MG)
sections.text:
Postsynaptic autoimmune disease with antibodies directed towards acetylcholine receptors

Clinical Presentation
     •    Fluctuating muscle weakness worsening with repetitive use improves with rest
     •    Ocular symptoms ptosis, diplopia, bulbar sing.
     •    Normal reflexes and sensation

Investigations
    •    Icepack test (placing a pack of ice on a closed              •    Repetitive nerve stimulation 2 or 3 Hz
         eyelid for one minute) look for improved ptosis              •    Single fibre electromyography jitter
         /diplopia                                                    •    Chest imaging CXR/CT/MRI -thymoma
    •    Serum acetylcholine receptor antibodies MUSK
         antibodies

Pharmacological Management:

Lifelong treatment
S: pyridostigmine (PO) 60mg 3-4 times daily, Maintenance 60mg every 3hrs up to 1500 in divided dose
           AND
A: prednisolone (PO) 5mg 24Hourly titrated to the need

Generalized or refractory MG
S: azathioprine (PO) 1-2mg/kg/day orally, maintenance dose 2-3mg/kg/day max dose should not exceed 3mg/kg/day
          OR
S: cyclosporin (PO) 3-5mg/kg/d 12 hourly
          OR
S: mycophenolate Mofetil (PO) 500mg 12hrly escalate to 1000mg 12 hourly for eleven to twenty-four months

sections.title: Lambert-Eaton Myasthenic Syndrome (LEMS)
sections.text:
LEMS is a presynaptic autoimmune disease with antibodies directed against voltage gated calcium channels that impair
acetylcholine release at neuromuscular junction,

Clinical Presentation
     •    Proximal leg and pelvic weakness that improve with repeated use
     •    Autonomic symptoms (Dry mouth, impotence, orthostatic hypotension
     •    Often associated with small cell lung cancer

Investigations
    •    EMG
    •    Serum P/Q type calcium channel antibodies
    •    Chest imaging

Pharmacological Management
S: 3,4-diaminopyridine (PO) 5mg 8hourly, increase by 5mg every 3-4 days max dose 80mg/day no single dose >20mg for 90
to 180 days subject to review

sections.title: Inflammatory myopathies
sections.text:
Include polymyopathies, dermatomyositis and inclusion body myositis

Clinical Presentation
Symmetric proximal muscle weakness, gradual onset

Investigations
    •    Serum CK
    •    EMG
    •    Muscle biopsy

Pharmacological Management:
D: methylprednisolone (IV) 1000mg infusion for three days
         OR
S: methotrexate (PO) 15mg every 24 hours for two months

sections.title: Toxic Myopathies
sections.text:
Commonly caused by drugs (e.g., statins, steroids, colchicine) or toxins

Clinical Presentation
Muscle pain insidious onset after starting treatment/offending agent

Investigation:
CK, Creatinine, electrolytes, TSH

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Discontinue the offending agent
    •  Rehydration
    •  Treat metabolic abnormalities identified - hypothyroidism

sections.title: Infectious Myopathies
sections.text:
Viral (e.g., influenza, HIV, Coxsackie) or bacterial infection

Clinical Presentation
Muscle pain, fever, abscess

Investigation:
CK, CBC

Non-Pharmacological Management
Abscess drainage, rehydration

Pharmacological Management
For HIV and other underlying infections treat accordingly as per HIV/AIDS guidelines and as these guidelines.

sections.title: Inherited Myopathies
sections.text:
Muscular dystrophies (e.g., Duchene, Becker) and congenital myopathies

Clinical Presentation
Progressive weakness early onset, calf pseudohypertrophy

Investigation
CK, EMG, Muscle biopsy.

Non-pharmacological
Occupational therapy, braces/orthoses

Pharmacological Management
No cure- mainly supportive
Corticosteroids (Duchenne)

sections.title: Insomnia
sections.text:
Clinical Presentation.
Sleep onset: Trouble falling asleep; Sleep maintenance Multiple or prolonged awakenings, non-restorative sleep

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Sleep hygiene: fixed awakening and sleeping                         •   Minimize caffeine
       time,                                                               •   Light therapy
    •  Limit day time naps,                                                •   Behavioral techniques
    •  reduce alcohol and smoking near bed time,

Pharmacological Management
D: eszopiclone 1mg before bedtime for five to seven days not more than 28 days
          OR
A: amitriptyline 12.5mg – 25mg at night

sections.title: Obstructive Sleep Apnoea (OSA)
sections.text:
This is discussed under Respiratory Chapter 9. Episode of upper airway collapse during sleep

Clinical Presentation: snoring, gasping daytime sleepiness

Investigation
Polysomnography, ECG, ECHO, Lung function test

Non-Pharmacological Management
Weight control, quit smoking, reduce alcohol
CPAP (Apnoea-hypopnoea index >5 in symptomatic or >15 asymptomatic) or Bi-level positive airway pressure (BiPAP)

sections.title: Restless Legs Syndrome (RLS)
sections.text:
Clinical Presentation
Urge to move the legs, unpleasant sensation can be bilateral at time involve the arms, worse at night or period of immobility
relieved by movement

Investigations:
CBC, Ferritin level, Creatinine,

Pharmacological Management
IF Ferritin <50ng/mL
A: ferrous sulphate 200mg daily for 90 days

Moderate to severe RLS
D: gabapentin (PO) 300mg nocte
         OR
D: pregabalin (PO) 75mg nocte for six months to one year

 Note: Treat coexisting conditions (Renal failure, diabetes, neuropathy)

sections.title: Narcolepsy
sections.text:
Clinical Presentation
Excessive (irresistible) day time sleep (Cataplexy, sleep paralysis, hypnagogic or hypnopompic hallucinations)

Investigations
Polysomnography - sleep latency, CSF – low hypocretin 1

Pharmacological Management
Sleepiness:
S: methylphenidate (PO) 10-60mg in three divided dose per day for three to six months

sections.title: Parasomnias
sections.text:
Clinical Presentation
Disruptive sleep related phenomena. Non-REM parasomnia: confusional arousals, sleepwalking, night terrors
REM parasomnias nightmares, sleep behaviors disorder-acting out dreams

Investigations:
CBC, RBG, TSH, EEG

Pharmacological Management
D: clonazepam (PO) 1mg (nocte reduces motor activity but doesn’t reestablish sleep atonia)

 Note: Treat OSA if present especially when using BDZ that can worsen breathing

sections.title: Functional Neurological Disorders (FND)
sections.text: Conversion disorders – refer to Mental Health section

sections.title: Charcot-Marie-Tooth Disease (CMT)
sections.text:
A group of inherited peripheral neuropathies

Clinical Presentation
Adolescent onset distal weakness-foot drop, sensory loss in stocking-glove pattern, pes cavus and hammer toes.
Diminished or absent reflexes

Investigation
    •    Nerve conduction velocity NCV,
    •    Genetic testing

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Stretching exercises
    •  Mobility aids
    •  Evaluation for bladder function

Pharmacological Management
There No cure, only supportive

S: baclofen (PO) 10mg for three to six months
          OR
S: tizanidine (PO) 4mg daily for three to six months

sections.title: Inherited Ataxias
sections.text:
•   Include Friederich’s ataxia
     •   Progressive cerebella dysfunction gait, trunk ataxia, dysarthria nystagmus

Investigation:
    •    MRI brain/spine
    •    Spinal cord/cerebellar degeneration

Treatment
Supportive

sections.title: Dystonia
sections.text:
Dystonia is defined by involuntary maintained contraction of agonist and antagonist muscles yielding abnormal posturing,
twisting and repetitive movements, or tremulous and can be initiated or worsened by attempted movement. Primary dystonia
(torsion dystonia) is the sole neurological sign and other causes of dystonia such as acquired or neurodegenerative process
have been ruled out.
Secondary dystonia is caused by environmental insult and other identified causes such as head injury, drug side effect or
neurological diseases such as Wilsons disease, Parkinson disease. Its disabling and painful condition.
Onset infancy or childhood, early or late adult, craniofacial, oromandibular trunk or limb, Acute, static or progressive course.

Investigation:
    •    CBC, Basic Metabolic Panel, LFT, Lipid panel, ESR, ANA, Cu, Ceruloplasmin, Metabolic testing
    •    Genetic testing
    •    Imaging: MRI brain with heme sensitive sequences
    •    MRI cervical spine

Pharmacological Management
Treat underlying etiology

For Focal or Segmental dystonia:
S: botulinum toxin A injections under EMG guidance.
Dose range 2.5 to 15 units depending on the site as per Botox Injection Protocol

Oromandibular dystonia: Muscles: Masseter, Temporalis, Media/lateral pterygoids and digastric
S: botulinum toxin A injection 15-50 units per side
Lingual (tongue) dystonia

Muscle: Genioglossus
Dose: Botox 5-15units per site
Technique: Submental approach to genioglossus or direct into the tongue body
Precaution: high risk of dysphagia and or dysarthria

Cervical: Sternocleidomastoid, splenius capitis, Trapezius, Levator scapulae and Scalenes
Dose SCM 15050units; Splenius Capitis 25-100units
Technique: injections guided by direction of head deviation (torticollis, retrocollis)
Precaution: Neck injections pose a risk for dysphagia

Spasticity (Upper and or Lower extremity):
Dose: Muscles: Upper Biceps 50-200units; Flexor carpi radialis/ulnaris 25-50 units
Lower limbs: Gastrocn- soleus (100-400units); Adductors (75-300units
Mid-belly approach under EMG guidance
Precautions: Excessive weakness in antagonist muscle may lead to functional loss

sections.title: Essential Tremor
sections.text:
Clinical Presentation
involuntary, rhythmic tremor on the hands, head (yes-yes; no-no motion), voice or legs. Worsen with action e.g. Writing.

Investigation:
Clinical diagnosis excluding Parkinson’s disease

Pharmacological Management
A: Propranolol (PO) 20mg – 40mg Q24H titrated to maximum effective dose,

sections.title: Respiratory Tract Infections
sections.text:
A respiratory tract infection is an infectious disease caused by viral, bacterial or other microbial pathogens affecting the upper
or lower respiratory system, including the airways and lungs.
For management of COVID 19 and Pulmonary TB please refer to chapters 4 and 7 respectively.

sections.title: Pneumonia
sections.text:
Pneumonia is an infection of the lung parenchyma characterized by inflammation and consolidation of the alveoli, most
commonly caused by bacterial, viral, or fungal pathogens.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Fever (typically>380C)                                           •   Respiratory distress
     •    Dry or productive cough                                          •   Reduced oxygen saturation/Hypoxemia
     •    Central cyanosis                                                 •   Chest pain and tachypnoea

     •     For patients with pneumonia treatment should be instituted when they have FEVER, COUGH AND CXR with
           findings suggestive of pneumonia.
      •    Consider alternative diagnosis when a patient is not responding.
      •    Pulmonary embolism should be investigated carefully for patient with shortness of breath and not responding to
           treatment of pneumonia

Investigations
    •    ABG

    •    CHEST X-ray-PA/LATERAL
    •    Bronchoscopy (Consider if immunosuppression, critically ill, fail to respond, suspected TB or PCP or poor response
    •    CT Scan: if patient is not improving, suspicion of fungal or alternative diagnosis

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Oxygen therapy when required
    •  Supportive care

       o Ensure that the child receives daily maintenance fluid appropriate for the child’s age but avoid over-hydration

Pharmacological Management
Non-severe pneumonia
A: amoxicillin (PO) 25mg/kg 8hourly for 5days
         AND
A: paracetamol (PO) 15mg/kg 6-8hourly for 5days (if fever present)
         OR
A: paracetamol (supp) 10–15mg/kg 6-8hourly for 5days (if fever present)
         OR
A: ibuprofen (PO) 10mg/kg 6-8hourly for 5days (if fever present)

Give the first dose at the clinic and teach the mother how to give the other doses at home. Encourage breasting and feeding.

Severe Pneumonia
A: benzylpenicillin (IV/IM) 50000 units/kg 6hourly for at least 3days
         THEN
A: amoxicillin (PO) 40 mg/kg 8hourly for 7days.

Alternatively

A: ampicillin (IV/IM) 50 mg/kg 6hourly for 5days
         AND
A: gentamicin (IV/IM) 7.5 mg/kg 24hourly for 5days
         THEN
A: amoxicillin (PO) 40 mg/kg 8hourly for 7days.
   Note
       •     For children above 5 years, atypical pneumonia should be considered e.g., mycoplasma
       •     Consider alternative diagnosis after three visit /not responding, refer patient to a pediatrician

sections.title: Pneumonia in Adults (Community Acquired Pneumonia)
sections.text:
CAP refers to a pneumonia that is acquired outside hospital commonly caused by Streptococcus
pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis, atypical bacteria (i.e, Chlamydia pneumoniae, Mycoplasma
pneumoniae, Legionella species) and viral respiratory pathogens (i.e rhinovirus, Corona virus and influenza

Clinical Presentation
     •    Fever                                                            •    Reduced oxygen saturation/Hypoxemia
     •    Cough dry or productive with/without purulent                    •    Increased tactile fremitus, bronchial breath
          sputum,                                                               sounds may be present if consolidation has
     •    Dyspnea,                                                              occurred.
     •    Pleuritic chest pain                                             •    Decreased tactile fremitus and dullness on chest
     •    Tachypnea                                                             percussion
     •    Crepitation/Rales heard over the involved lobe
          or segment

Investigations
    •    FBC (look for increased WBC, neutrophilia),
    •    CRP/ESR (increased)
    •    ABG (look for pH, bicarbonate, PaO2),
    •    RBG, Serology for HIV
    •    Sputum culture and sensitivity (are indicated for inpatients and those with severe disease
    •    Blood culture (are not recommended for ambulatory patients
    •    CHEST X-ray-PA/LATERAL (look for one or more focal pulmonary infiltrates, consolidation, tap effusion>5cm),
    •    Bronchoscopy (Consider if immunosuppression, critically ill, fail to respond, suspected TB or PCP other alternative
         diagnosis)
    •    CT-CHEST: if patient is not improving.

  Note: Do not use CT chest to diagnose pneumonia

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Stop smoking if previously smoking
    •  Vaccination when indicated, in specialized centre for patient >65yrs and below 5years and those with chronic lung
       diseases.

sections.title: Hospital Acquired Pneumonia/Nosocomial Pneumonia
sections.text:
This is defined as pneumonia that occurs two days (48hrs) or more after hospitalization but that was not incubating at the time
of hospital admission.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Fever
     •    Increase in respiratory rate
     •    Shortness of breath
Pharmacological Management
Empirical treatment until bacteriology available
C: ciprofloxacin (IV) 400mg 12hourly for 7days
          OR
D: ceftriaxone + sulbactam (FDC) (IV) 1.5g 12hourly for 7days

  Note: In specialized unit management of CAP/HAP can be changed with supportive culture and sensitivity done, this may
  necessitate use of other broader spectrum antibiotics 48-72hours until the results are obtained

sections.title: Acute Laryngo-Tracheobronchitis
sections.text:
Laryngo-tracheobronchitis (croup) is acute inflammation of the larynx, trachea and bronchi which occurs in young children
(usually between 6 months to 3 years of age). It arises as a result of narrowing of the airway in the region of the larynx. The
most common cause is viral infection (particularly parainfluenza viruses) but may also be due to bacterial infection. The
obstruction is due to inflammation and oedema.

Clinical Presentation
     •    The symptoms include paroxysmal “barking” cough, inspiratory stridor, fever, wheezing, hoarseness of voice and
          tachypnoea
     •    Such symptoms usually occur at night
     •    Respiratory failure and pneumonia are potentially fatal complications.

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Prevent asphyxiation                                              •    Humidification of inhaled air
    •  Treat inflammatory oedema                                         •    Hospitalization may be necessary

 Note
     •     No stridor at rest, give no antibiotics
     •     Stridor at rest or chest in-drawing or fast breathing Refer Immediately to hospital

Mild Croup                                                          Severe Croup
    •   Only stridor when upset, no moderate/severe                     •   Likely bacterial origin
        ARI                                                             •   Stridor in a calm child at rest
    •   Likely of viral origin                                          •   Chest in drawing
    •   Home care – steam inhalation                                    •   Antibiotics are NOT effective and should not be
    •   Antibiotics NOT required                                            given

Pharmacological Management
Admit to hospital, give Oxygen therapy to all patients with chest in-drawing (using nasal prongs only, DO NOT use
nasopharyngeal or nasal catheter) until the lower chest wall in drawing is no longer present

D: dexamethasone (PO) 0.6mg/kg 24hourly in 1–2 divided doses
         AND
A: epinephrine (adrenaline) (inhalation) 400mcg/kg 2hourly if effective; repeat after 30min if necessary.

sections.title: Laryngeal Diphtheria
sections.text:
Is an infection caused by Corynebacterium diphtheria; it is directly transmitted from person to person by droplets. Children
between 1–5 years of age are most susceptible although non-immune adults are also at risk. Diphtheria is characterized by
grayish-white membrane, composed of dead cells, fibrin, leucocytes and red blood cells as a result of inflammation due to
multiplying bacteria.

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Isolate the child                                                 •    Avoid oxygen unless there is incipient airway
    •  Gently examine the child’s throat – can cause                          obstruction
       airway obstruction if not carefully done.                         •    May need tracheostomy if there is incipient
    •  NGT for feeding if unable to swallow: Confirm                          airway obstruction: Worsening stridor, oxygen
       NGT position with X-ray.                                               desaturation

Pharmacological Management:
A: phenoxymethylpenicillin (PO) 250mg 6hourly for 14days
          OR
A: erythromycin (PO) 125–250mg 6hourly for 14days
          OR
B: azithromycin (PO) 500mg 24hourly for 3days
          OR
A: benzylpenicillin (IV) 25,000–50,000units/kg to a max. of 1.2MU 12hourly until the patient can take oral medicine
          AND
A: diphtheria antitoxin (IM or slow IV) dose depends upon the site and severity of infection:
First give a test dose of 0.1ml of 1 in 10 dilution of antitoxin in 0.9% Sodium Chloride intradermal to detect hypersensitivity. It
should be given immediately because delay can lead to increased mortality
The dose should be administered intravenously over 60minutes in order to inactivate toxin rapidly
      •    20,000–40,000 units for pharyngeal/laryngeal disease of <48 hours’ duration,
      •    40,000–60,000 units for nasopharyngeal disease
      •    80,000–120,000 units for >3days of illness or diffuse neck swelling "bull-neck"

sections.title: Whooping Cough
sections.text:
It is a highly infectious childhood disease caused by Bordetella pertussis. It is most severe in young infants who have not yet
been immunized.

Clinical Presentation
Paroxysmal cough associated with a whoop, Fever, Nasal discharge.

Non-Pharmacological Management
      •    Place the child head down and prone, or on the side, to prevent any inhaling of vomitus and to aid expectoration of
           secretions.
      •    Care for the airway but avoid, as far as possible, any procedure that could trigger coughing, such as application of
           suction, throat examination
      •    Do not give cough suppressants, sedatives, mucolytic agents or anti-histamines.
      •    If the child has fever (>38.50C) give paracetamol.
      •    Encourage breastfeeding or oral fluids
      •    Whooping cough is preventable by immunization with pertussis vaccine contained in DPT- Hep B-Hib vaccine at
           week 6, 10 and 14.
      •    Give oxygen to children who have spells of apnoea or cyanosis, or severe paroxysms of coughing.
      •    Use nasal prongs, not a nasopharyngeal catheter or nasal catheter which can provoke coughing.
Pharmacological Management
A: erythromycin (PO) 12.5 mg/kg 6hourly for 10days.
This does not shorten the illness but reduces the period of infectiousness
If there is fever

In Children older than age 2 months:
A: trimethoprim + sulfamethoxazole (FDC) (PO) 8mg+40mg/kg 12hourly for 7-14days

sections.title: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP)
sections.text:
Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP) is a potentially life-threatening fungal lung infection caused by Pneumocystis
jirovecii (formerly known as Pneumocystis carinii). It predominantly affects individuals with compromised immune systems. It
is a common Opportunistic infection in HIV.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Cough dry/productive                                             •    Scattered crackles and wheeze may be present,
     •    Exertional dyspnoea                                                   or rarely signs of focal consolidation
     •    Fever                                                            •    Pulse oximetry may show low SaO2
     •    Tachypnoea                                                       •    Extra-pulmonary disease may manifest as
     •    Chest pain                                                            hepatosplenomegaly,        lymphadenopathy or
                                                                                ocular disease
Investigations:
    •    Elevated LDH                                                      •    CT-CHEST: More sensitive, shows perihilar and
    •    ABG: Hypoxemia, increased alveolar-arterial                            midzone Ground Glass Pattern, Septal
         oxygen tension gradient                                                thickening     (Crazy       paving      pattern),
    •    Serum Beta-D-glucan levels                                             pneumatoceles. Rarely consolidations.
    •    Chest X-ray: may appear normal in 10-30% of                       •    Gallium scanning is highly sensitive but with low
         cases. Predominantly perihilar distributed Fine                        and variable specificity.
         reticular    interstitial  changes,       small                   •    Sputum/BAL (PCR or DFA staining): Detect
         pneumatoceles.                                                         Pneumocystis jirovecii

Non pharmacological and Supportive Therapy
    •   Maintain and monitor hydration                                     •    Nutrition support
    •   Antipyretic if there is fever                                      •    Oxygen therapy
    •   Continue therapy for bacterial pneumonia
Pharmacological Therapy
A: sulfamethoxazole + trimethoprim (Cotrimoxazole) (PO) 1920mg 8hourly for 21 days
In severe cases: cotrimoxazole (IV) 15–20mgTMP/75-100mgSMX/kg/day, 6-8hourly, may switch to oral after clinical
improvement.
            OR
If allergic to sulphur
D: trimethoprim (PO) 12- 15mg/kg/day
            AND
S: dapsone (PO) 100mg/day for 21 days
            OR
S: clindamycin (PO) 450mg 6hourly or 600 mg 8hourly
            AND
A: primaquine 30 mg 24 hourly daily for 21 days.

Adjuvant therapy with steroids may also be beneficial in severe cases. (PaO₂ <70 mmHg or A–a gradient >35 mmHg)

        THEN
A: prednisolone (PO) 40 mg 24 hourly day 6 -10
        THEN
