sections.title: Pulmonary Aspergillosis
sections.text:
Pulmonary aspergillosis is a spectrum of lung diseases caused by Aspergillus spp., most commonly Aspergillus fumigatus.
Manifestations vary depending on host immunity and underlying lung disease.

sections.title: Allergic Bronchopulmonary Aspergillosis (ABPA)
sections.text:
Occurs in patients with underlying chronic airway disease especially asthma or bronchiectasis. Caused by a hypersensitivity
reaction to Aspergillus

Clinical Presentation: Recurrent wheeze, cough, mucus plugs

Investigations
    •    Elevated total IgE (>1000 IU/mL)
    •    Positive Aspergillus-specific IgE/IgG
    •    CXR/CT: bronchiectasis, mucus plugging

Pharmacological Management
B: prednisolone (PO) 0.5 mg/kg/day (20–40 mg/day) for 3–6 months (taper slowly over weeks/months)
          AND
D: itraconazole (PO) 200mg 12-24hourly for 6-12months

sections.title: Chronic Pulmonary Aspergillosis (CPA)
sections.text:
Patients with underlying lung disease (e.g., Healed TB, COPD, sarcoidosis): e.g., aspergilloma

Clinical Presentation
Cough, hemoptysis, weight loss, fatigue. Symptoms >3 months

Investigations
    •    Cavity on imaging ± fungal ball
    •    Positive Aspergillus IgG

Exclude active TB or malignancy

Pharmacological Management
D: itraconazole (PO) 200mg 12-24hourly for 6-12months
Surgical resection or embolization for severe disease

sections.title: Invasive Pulmonary Aspergillosis (IPA): Severely immunocompromised (e.g., neutropenia, transplant)
sections.text:
Clinical Presentation
Fever, pleuritic pain, cough, hemoptysis, rapidly progressive symptoms

Investigations
    •    Imaging: Halo sign, air crescent sign on CT
    •    Serum/BAL galactomannan or beta-D-glucan
    •    Culture or biopsy confirmation

Pharmacological Management
S: liposomal Amphotericin B (IV) 0.7–1 mg/kg/day for 6–12 weeks or until improvement

  Note: Itraconazole requires acidic gastric environment for absorption; monitor LFTs. Liposomal Amphotericin B should be
  reserved for azole failures.

sections.title: Aspiration Syndromes
sections.text:
Aspiration syndromes are pulmonary conditions caused by inhalation of gastric contents, oropharyngeal secretions, or foreign
material into the lower respiratory tract, resulting in chemical lung injury, infection, or airway obstruction.

Types
1. Aspiration Pneumonitis
   Acute chemical lung injury following aspiration of sterile gastric contents.
2. Aspiration Pneumonia
   Infective process caused by aspiration of colonized oropharyngeal secretions.
3. Foreign Body Aspiration
   Mechanical airway obstruction by inhaled solid or liquid material. It is a medical emergency.

Risk Factor
    •    Reduced consciousness (alcohol intoxication,                    •    Gastro-oesophageal reflux
         anesthesia, seizures)                                           •    Elderly, debilitated patients
    •    Neurological disease such as stroke, dysphagia

Clinical Features
    •    Cough, choking                                                  •    Crackles or wheeze
    •    Dyspnoea, tachypnoea                                            •    Hypoxia
    •    Fever (more common in pneumonia)

Investigations
    •    Chest X-ray
    •    Full blood count (if infection suspected)
    •    Bronchoscopy (suspected foreign body aspiration)

    Note: Normal chest X-ray does not exclude foreign body aspiration; persistent clinical suspicion (sudden cough,
    unilateral wheeze, or unexplained respiratory symptoms) warrants early referral for bronchoscopy and specialist
    evaluation.

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •    Airway Protection: If the patient is choking, use the Heimlich maneuver. For unconscious patients, turn them on their
         side and clear the airway.
    •    Positioning: Place the patient in a Fowler’s or Trendelenburg position to prevent further aspiration and aid drainage.
    •    Suctioning: Immediately suction the oropharynx to remove material.
    •    Respiratory Support: Administer supplemental oxygen to maintain oxygen saturation. Intubation may be necessary
         in compromised airway reflexes or severe hypoxia.
    •    Chest Physiotherapy: May be considered after stabilization to aid secretion clearance in patients with retained
         secretions or reduced cough effort.

Pharmacological Management

Aspiration Pneumonitis
        Supportive care only
        Antibiotics NOT routinely indicated
        Bronchodilators may be used if bronchospasm or wheezing is present:

B: salbutamol 5mg nebulization, 6hourly (PRN depending on clinical response).
          OR
S: ipratropium 0.5mg nebulization, 6hourly (PRN depending on clinical response).
Observe closely for 24–48 hours

a) Mild–Moderate Aspiration Pneumonia
Adults:
B: amoxicillin + clavulanic acid (PO) 625 mg 8-12hourly for 5-7days.
        OR
C: amoxicillin + clavulanic acid (IV) 1.2g 8-12hourly for 5-7days.

Pediatrics:
B: amoxicillin + clavulanic acid (PO) 20–45 mg/kg/day in 2–3 divided doses (amoxicillin component) for 5-7days.

b) Severe Aspiration Pneumonia
Obtain sputum (and blood where indicated) for culture and sensitivity before starting antibiotics whenever possible, while
initiating empiric broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy with anaerobic coverage without delaying treatment.
Adults:
B: ceftriaxone (IV) 2 g 24hourly for 7-10days.
            AND
A: metronidazole: 500 mg IV/PO 8hourly for 7-10days.
            OR
S: piperacillin + tazobactam (IV) 4.5g 6-8hourly for 7-10days.
            OR
S: meropenem (IV) 1g 8hourly for 7-10days.

Pediatrics:
B: ceftriaxone (IV) 50–75 mg/kg/day 24hourly for 7-10days.
          AND
A: metronidazole (PO/IV) 7.5 mg/kg/dose 8hourly for 7-10days.
          OR
S: piperacillin + tazobactam (IV) 80 mg/kg/dose (piperacillin component) 6-8hourly for 7-10days.
          OR
S: meropenem (IV) 20-40mg/kg 8hourly for 7-10days.

In Penicillin Allergy
Adults
S: clindamycin (IV) 600mg 8 hourly OR (PO) 300–450 mg PO 6-8hourly for 7-10days.
Pediatrics
S: clindamycin (IV) 10–20 mg/kg/dose 8hourly for 7-10days.

c) Foreign Body Aspiration
       Urgent bronchoscopy                                                Ventilatory support if required
       Supportive oxygen therapy                                          Antibiotics only if secondary infection present

Complications
       Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS)                         Empyema
       Lung abscess                                                       Sepsis and Septic shock

Referral Criteria
    • Severe respiratory distress                                      •    Suspected foreign body aspiration
    • Hypoxia not responding to oxygen                                 •    Failure to improve after 48–72 hours

Prevention
    • Head elevation ≥30°                                              •    Avoid oral feeding in reduced consciousness
    • Swallowing assessment in high-risk patients                      •    Improved oral hygiene

sections.title: Obstructive Lung Diseases
sections.text: It’s a chronic airway disease which result in airway flow limitation can be either reversible or irreversible

sections.title: Asthma
sections.text:
Asthma is chronic inflammatory disorder of the airways, characterized by variable respiratory symptoms such as wheezing,
shortness of breath, chest tightness, and cough, along with variable expiratory airflow limitation.

Clinical Presentation
Asthma is likely when there are
         Typical intermittent symptoms that vary over time in frequency and severity
         History of atopy,
         Family history of asthma,
         Environmental/ occupational exposures,
         Response to asthma therapy.

Investigations
Diagnosis of asthma is based on clinical assessment supported by Lung Function Test that demonstrates variable airflow
obstruction in adults and children >5 years. Peak Flow Meter should be used when Spirometry is not available.
Other investigations include, CXR, FBP, ESR, S. IGE.

 Note:
          Diagnosing asthma in children under 5 can be challenging
          The presence of frequent asthma-like symptoms (e.g., wheezing, cough, difficulty breathing) and improvement with
           asthma medication are key indicators.

Asthma Management

sections.title: Management of Chronic Asthma
sections.text:
Asthma management should be an ongoing process of assessing, treating and reviewing the patient’s response.

Non-Pharmacological Management
The following factors should be addressed:
         Adherence to medications
         Correct inhaler technique should be demonstrated and checked regularly
         Avoidance of triggers and other factors that could worsen asthma including: Exposure to Environmental Tobacco
          Smoke, Polluted environment (both indoors and outdoors) and Medications such as aspirin or NSAIDs, Avoid non-
          selective β-blockers,
         Management of other medical conditions likely to affect asthma control such as cardiac disease, allergic rhinitis,
          obesity, Sleep Apnea and GERD.

Pharmacological Management
Anti-asthma drugs can be classified as controllers (required for maintenance treatment) and relievers (required for quick relief,
rescue drugs). Inhalers are the cornerstone of asthma therapy.
Controller medicines
        Inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) e.g. Beclometasone, budesonide, fluticasone
        Long acting β2 agonists (LABA) e.g., formoterol, salmeterol: Inhalation 100mcg, 200mcg
        Combined ICS-LABA: e.g., C: budesonide-formoterol (inhaler), C: Beclometasone-formoterol (inhaler),

           OR
Long-acting muscarinic antagonist (LAMA)

Reliever medicines

There are two treatment approaches as follows
a) Low-dose ICS–formoterol taken as needed when symptoms occur, with or without maintenances ICS-Formoterol depending

sections.title: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD)
sections.text:
Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) is a diverse lung condition marked by persistent airflow limitation and
respiratory symptoms of shortness of breath, cough, and exacerbations; resulting from structural abnormalities in the airways
(Bronchitis) or in the alveoli (Emphysema). It is usually caused by significant exposure to noxious particles or gases.

Risk Factors for COPD
                                                                    2. Occupational exposure
1. Indoor and outdoor air pollution                                        Coal miners
         Exposure from burning wood                                       Tunnel Workers
         Exposure to biofuel                                              Hard-rock miners
         Heating in poorly vented dwellings                               Concrete manufacture
                                                                           Livestock farming (i.e., to pesticides)

3. Cigarette smoking                                                5. Childhood Asthma
4. Use of domestic solid fuel                                       6. Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency

Clinical Presentation
         Shortness of breath                                               Coarse early inspiratory crackles.
         Cough, sometimes caused by the production of                      Use of accessory muscles
          mucus                                                             Pursed-lip breathing
         Wheezing                                                          Signs of cor pulmonale. (Raised JVP, peripheral
         Slow and prolonged expiration                                      oedema, hepatomegaly etc.)
         Chest wall hyperinflation,                                        Cyanosis
         Limited diaphragmatic motion on auscultation,                     Asterixis
         Distant breath sounds, and heart sounds

Investigations
        FBP (Raised hematocrit: men>52% and                                Sputum culture and sensitivity
         women >47)                                                         Sputum cytology (if the cough is persistent)
        ESR /CRP/Procalcitonin                                             Chest CT scan: Detailed disease assessment
        Lung function Test (Spirometry): For Diagnosis,                     and surgical planning when indicated.
         Assessment of severity and follow-up                               Bronchoscopy (to exclude foreign body
        Serum alpha-1 antitrypsin levels as indicated                       aspiration, tuberculosis, tumours, and other
        Chest radiography: Exclusion of other respiratory                   chronic diseases in patients with worsening
         conditions with similar presentation as well as                     symptoms, BAL for C/S)
         complications.

Non-Pharmacological Management
      Smoking cessation                                                     physiotherapy and avoid indoor and outdoor
      Remove from hazardous environment                                     pollutants)
      Prompt treatment of infective exacerbations                          Nutrition support
      Controlled oxygen therapy                                            Ventilatory support in specialized center
      Physiotherapy                                                        Lung volume reduction surgery
      Pulmonary Rehabilitation (consist of education,
       lifestyle modification, regular physical activities,

Pharmacological Management
Pharmacological therapy has 3 major goals: Reduce symptoms, reduce frequency and severity of exacerbations and improve
health status and exercise tolerance. It is guided by disease severity (GOLD stage), symptom burden, and exacerbation history.

1. Bronchodilators
a) Short-acting bronchodilators (for symptom relief)
Short-acting β2-agonists (SABA):

A: salbutamol inhalation. 100–200mcg 4–6 hourly. (inhaler)
         OR
B: salbutamol nebulizer 2.5mg 4–6hourly.

Short-acting anticholinergics (SAMA):
S: ipratropium inhalation 20–80mcg, 6–8hourly 20–40mcg 6hourly (inhaler)
          OR
S: ipratropium nebulization 0.5mg 6–8hourly

b) Long-acting bronchodilators (maintenance therapy)
Long-acting β2-agonists (LABA) inhalers:
C: formoterol 6 mcg 12hourly.
         OR
C: salmeterol 25 mcg 2 inhalations 12hourly

Long-acting muscarinic antagonists (LAMA):
S: tiotropium inhaler 18Mcg1 inhalation 24hourly

LABA+LAMA combinations provide enhanced bronchodilation and are preferred in moderate to severe disease.

2. Inhaled Corticosteroids (ICS)
        Used in combination with LABA or LABA/LAMA in patients with:
        Frequent exacerbations
        High eosinophil counts (>300 cells/µL)
ICS+LABA:
C: budesonide +formoterol combination: 200/6mcg. 1 inhalation 12hourly

 Note: ICS monotherapy is not recommended.

3. Triple Therapy
S: (ICS + LABA + LAMA) inhalation
For patients with persistent symptoms or exacerbations despite dual therapy.

4. Macrolides
B: azithromycin 500mg (PO) 24 hourly for 3 days
Prolonged macrolide use may be indicated in selected patients with frequent exacerbations despite optimal inhaler therapy
(antibacterial effects; Immune-modulatory and anti-inflammatory effects). Refer to specialist for evaluation.

5. Mucolytics
N-acetylcysteine, Carbocysteine): Reduces overproduction and hypersecretion, increases elimination.
C: n-acetylcysteine (PO) Tablets/Effervescent tablets- 600mg 24hourly.
         OR
C: n-acetylcysteine Inhaled solution: 10%/20% solution. 2- 4 ml nebulization 6 -8hourly.
(Pre-medication with Salbutamol nebulizer is advised to reduce risk of bronchospasm)

6. Vaccinations (Supportive)
Influenza, pneumococcal, and COVID-19 vaccines are essential to reduce risk of infection-triggered exacerbations.

sections.title: COPD Exacerbations
sections.text:
COPD exacerbation is a worsening or “flares up” of COPD symptoms, particularly dyspnoea, cough and/or sputum production,
that is acute in onset and leads to a change in medication." commonly caused by infection in the lungs but in some cases the
cause is unknown.

Triggers:
Infectious causes: ~70–80% (viral or bacterial respiratory infections)
Non-infectious causes: air pollution, poor adherence to therapy, pulmonary embolism, or comorbidities (e.g., heart failure,
gastro oesophageal reflux disease (GERD)

Clinical Presentation
Worsening cough, Change in sputum color, consistency, volume, Increase in dyspnea, Wheezing.

Investigations

        Sputum C/s
        FBP
        CRP, ESR, Pro-Calcitonin

sections.title: Suppurative Lung Diseases
sections.text:
A group of respiratory disorders characterized by chronic infection and pus formation in the airways and/or lung parenchyma,
leading to persistent inflammation, tissue destruction, and structural abnormalities.

Common Types: Bronchiectasis, Lung abscess, Empyema, Necrotizing Pneumonia

sections.title: Bronchiectasis
sections.text:
A chronic lung condition characterized by permanent, abnormal dilation of the bronchi due to chronic infection, inflammation,
and/or impaired mucociliary clearance.
It is a common complication/sequalae of Pulmonary Tuberculosis (Post TB Lung Disease).

Etiology (Causes):
Category                                 Examples
Post-infectious:                         Severe pneumonia, tuberculosis, measles
Congenital:                              Cystic fibrosis (CF), primary ciliary dyskinesia
Immune disorders:                        Common variable immunodeficiency (CVID), HIV
Obstruction:                             Tumors, foreign bodies
Idiopathic:                              No identifiable cause in ~30–50% of cases

Clinical Presentation
         Chronic productive cough (often with purulent
          sputum)
         Recurrent respiratory infections                                        Digital clubbing (in advanced cases)
         Hemoptysis                                                              Exacerbations are characterized by worsening of
         Dyspnea                                                                  symptoms and change in Sputum volume and
         Wheezing                                                                 quality
         Fatigue

        High-resolution CT (HRCT) scan of chest: Gold                             obstructive pattern
         standard                                                                 Immunoglobulin levels, sweat chloride test,
        Sputum culture and microscopy                                             ciliary function tests: Based on suspected cause

sections.title: Lung Abscess
sections.text:
A lung abscess is a localized collection of pus in the lung parenchyma caused by suppurative necrosis of lung tissue, resulting
in cavity formation, usually with an air-fluid level.

Etiology (Causes):
a) Primary Lung Abscess (Most common): Aspiration of oropharyngeal contents

Risk factors:
        Altered consciousness (e.g., alcohol, seizures, anesthesia), poor dentition, stroke
        Anaerobic bacteria are most common (e.g., Peptostreptococcus, Bacteroides, Fusobacterium)
b) Secondary Lung Abscess
        Post-obstructive (tumor, foreign body)
        Septic emboli (e.g., endocarditis)
        Immunosuppression
        Bronchiectasis, necrotizing pneumonia (e.g., Staph. aureus, Klebsiella)
        Direct extension from infection (e.g., empyema)

Clinical Presentation
         Fever, chills, night sweats
         Cough with foul-smelling, purulent sputum
         Hemoptysis (may occur)
         Pleuritic chest pain
         Weight loss, fatigue
         Clubbing (in chronic cases)

Investigations:
  Test                             Findings
 Chest X-ray                       Thick-walled cavity with air-fluid level
 CT Chest                          Better definition of cavity, rule out underlying mass or empyema
 Sputum culture                    Identify causative organisms (anaerobes, aerobes)
 Blood cultures                    Especially if febrile or septic
 Bronchoscopy                      If atypical features, no response to treatment, or suspicion of obstruction

Non-Pharmacological Management
a) Supportive Care
        Chest physiotherapy, hydration, nutrition
        Monitor inflammatory markers (e.g., CRP, WBC)
b) Drainage (If needed)
Percutaneous catheter drainage if:
        Large abscess
        Poor response to antibiotics
        Risk of rupture
c) Surgery
        Reserved for complications (e.g., massive hemoptysis, rupture, non-resolving abscess)
        Lobectomy may be needed in severe or recurrent cases

Pharmacological Management
Antibiotics (Mainstay of Treatment)
B: ampicillin + cloxacillin (FDC)(IV) 500–1000mg 8hourly for 7days then (PO) 8hourly for 3– 6 weeks (children 50mg/kg/dose)
          AND
B: metronidazole (IV) 500mg 8hourly for 7days then (PO) 400mg 8hourly for 4–6weeks (children 7.5mg/kg)

 Note:
 The duration of antibiotics therapy depends on the clinical and radiographic response of the patient, but completely healing,
 with radiographic normalization can be seen after two months. Refer patient to specialized unit if large cavity size (i.e., >6cm
 in diameter), persistent fever.

         OR
S: clindamycin (IV) 600mg 8hourly for 7days and then (PO) 300mg 8hourly for 4-6weeks
         OR
S: piperacillin + tazobactam (FDC) (IV) 4.5g 6hourly for 4-6weeks
         OR
S: meropenem (IV) 1g 8hourly for 4-6 weeks

sections.title: Interstitial Lung Diseases (ILDs)
sections.text:
Interstitial Lung Diseases (ILDs), also known as diffuse parenchymal lung diseases, are a heterogeneous group of disorders
characterized by inflammation and/or fibrosis of the lung interstitium, alveolar epithelium and small airways.

Examples of Common Interstitial Lung Diseases (ILDs)
 Category                              Examples
 Occupational and Environmental ILDs   • Silicosis
                                       • Coal workers' pneumoconiosis
                                       • Chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis (e.g., due to mould or agricultural
                                       exposure)
 Post-Infectious ILDs                  • Post-tuberculosis fibrotic lung disease
                                       • Post-COVID-19 fibrotic lung disease
                                       • HIV-associated interstitial lung disease
 Inflammatory/Autoimmune ILDs          • Sarcoidosis
                                       • Connective tissue disease-associated ILD (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis, systemic
                                       lupus erythematosus, systemic sclerosis)
 Idiopathic ILDs                       • Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF)
                                       • Non-specific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP)
Clinical Presentation:
Progressive dyspnea, Dry cough,

Investigations
        Full blood count (FBC).                                             Chest X -Ray: Reticular or nodular interstitial
        Autoimmune screen (ANA, RF, anti-CCP if                              patterns.
         connective-tissue disease suspected.                                High-resolution CT (HRCT): key investigation;
        ESR/CRP.                                                             identifies fibrosis, ground-glass opacities,
        Arterial blood gases (ABG) – assess hypoxemia.                       honeycombing
        Pulmonary function tests, Spirometry, DLCO,
         Six-Minute Walk Test
         and distribution of disease.

Non-pharmacological Management
      Smoking cessation                                                     Vaccinations (influenza, pneumococcal)
      Oxygen therapy if hypoxemic                                           Lung      transplantation:    Considered         in
      Pulmonary rehabilitation                                               advanced/refractory cases for eligible patients.

Pharmacological Management
Anti-fibrotic agents
Indicated for Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) and selected cases of progressive fibrosing ILD.
S: pirfenidone (PO) 200mg 8hourly, double the dose on week 2. Maintenance 800mg 8hourly.

 Note:
          Immunosuppressants for Connective Tissue - ILDs: Refer to Rheumatology chapter
          Corticosteroids/ immunosuppressants in inflammatory ILDs: Refer Sarcoidosis

sections.title: Sarcoidosis
sections.text:
Sarcoidosis is a multisystem granulomatous disease of unknown cause characterized by the formation of non-caseating
granulomas in affected organs, most commonly the lungs and lymphatic system.

Investigations
        Chest X-ray: Stages 0–IV (Bilateral hilar                           Pulmonary Function Tests: Restrictive pattern,
         lymphadenopathy, infiltrates, fibrosis)                              reduced DLCO
        High-Resolution CT (HRCT): Detailed lung                            Serum ACE: Elevated in ~60% (nonspecific)
         parenchyma assessment                                               Calcium: Hypercalcemia or hypercalciuria
                                                                             Tissue biopsy: non-caseating granulomas.

Pharmacological Management
First-line: Oral corticosteroids
A: prednisolone (PO): 0.5–1 mg/kg/day
Typical dose: 20–40 mg daily: 4–6 weeks, then reassess for clinical/radiological response. Gradual taper over 6–12 months
depending on response and severity.

Steroid-sparing agents:
S: methotrexate (PO) 10–25 mg weekly
          OR
S: azathioprine (PO) 1–2 mg/kg/day
          OR
S: hydroxychloroquine (PO) 200-400mg 24hourly (esp. for skin or hypercalcemia)

sections.title: Coal Workers’ Pneumoconiosis (CWP)
sections.text:
A chronic occupational lung disease caused by inhalation of coal mine dust, leading to lung fibrosis. It is preventable but
progressive if exposure continues.

Clinical Presentation
         Often asymptomatic in early stages
         Chronic cough, exertional dyspnea
         Sputum production, wheeze (esp. with coexisting COPD)
         Late-stage: hypoxemia, cor-pulmonale, respiratory failure
         High risk for TB and COPD
         Caplan's syndrome: CWP + rheumatoid arthritis

Investigations
        Chest X-ray: Small nodules (simple); large masses (PMF)
        HRCT: More sensitive—shows centrilobular nodules, fibrosis
        PFTs:

         o Normal or restrictive pattern
         o ↓ DLCO in advanced disease
    •    Occupational history: Critical for diagnosis

Non-Pharmacological Management
      No curative treatment
      Prevention: Eliminate exposure (dust control, PPE)
      Smoking cessation
      Vaccinations: Influenza, pneumococcus
      Pulmonary rehabilitation

Pharmacological Management
Symptom management
      Bronchodilators (if airflow limitation): See COPD section
      Oxygen therapy (if hypoxemic)

sections.title: Silicosis
sections.text:
Silicosis is a pneumoconiosis caused by inhalation of crystalline silica dust, leading to chronic lung inflammation and
progressive pulmonary fibrosis.

Clinical Presentation
         Chronic cough, exertional dyspnea
         Often asymptomatic early on
         Can progress to respiratory failure
         Crackles, cyanosis, and clubbing in advanced cases
         ↑ Risk of tuberculosis, lung cancer, and autoimmune diseases (e.g., scleroderma)

Complications
       Progressive Massive Fibrosis (PMF)
       Chronic respiratory failure
       Pulmonary hypertension
       Tuberculosis and atypical mycobacterial infections

Investigations
        Chest X-ray:
         -Small, rounded opacities (nodules) in upper lobes
         -"Eggshell calcification" of hilar lymph nodes

    •    HRCT chest
    •    Pulmonary function tests (PFTs): Restrictive or mixed pattern; ↓ DLCO
    •    TB screening recommended due to high risk

Non-Pharmacological Management
No cure – prevention is key

Prevention: Workplace control: wet drilling, ventilation, appropriate PPE

Health surveillance
periodic chest imaging, lung function testing
         Remove from exposure
         Supportive care:
          - Smoking cessation
          - Pulmonary Rehabilitation

    •       TB prophylaxis or treatment if indicated
    •       Lung transplant in advanced disease

Pharmacological Management
      Oxygen therapy
      Bronchodilators if obstruction present

sections.title: Lung Cancer
sections.text:
Malignant neoplasm originating from lung parenchyma or bronchial epithelium. is the leading cause of cancer-related death
worldwide. Main categories include Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer (NSCLC) and Small Cell Lung Cancer (SCLC).

Risk Factors
       Active and passive (second and third hand) cigarette smoking
       Occupational exposure (asbestos, silica, radon)
       Biomass smoke exposure (prolonged indoor cooking using firewood or charcoal in poorly ventilated environments)
       Air pollution
       Family history of cancer
       Chronic lung disease (COPD, pulmonary fibrosis)
       HIV infection and immunosuppression

  Note:
             Smoking in all forms (cigarettes, cigars, pipes, shisha ) accounts for 90% of lung cancer cases and is a major
              preventable risk factor; smoking cessation should be strongly advised for all patients.
             People living with HIV have an increased risk of lung cancer. Persistent respiratory symptoms in HIV-positive patients
              should prompt early imaging and specialist evaluation.

Clinical Presentation
         Persistent or worsening cough                                        Recurrent chest infections
         Hemoptysis                                                           Clubbing
         Dyspnea                                                              Lymphadenopathy
         Chest pain                                                           Pleural effusion
         Weight loss, anorexia                                                Features of metastasis (neurological deficits,
         Hoarseness or wheeze                                                  bone pain)

 Note: Symptoms and signs of lung cancer may mimic pulmonary TB, Patients with persistent or atypical features should be
 referred early for chest CT imaging and specialist evaluation to avoid delayed diagnosis.

Investigations
Initial Investigations                                                 Confirmatory Tests
          Chest X-ray                                                        CT scan of chest
          Full blood count                                                   Bronchoscopy with biopsy
          Liver function tests                                               CT-guided needle biopsy
          Tumor markers: CEA                                                 Sputum cytology

Management
  Category                 Management Measures
  General Measures         • Provide smoking cessation counselling
                           • Administer oxygen therapy in hypoxic patients
                           • Ensure adequate nutritional support
                           • Provide analgesia and symptomatic management
                           • Offer psychosocial support
  Specific Treatment       • Refer to Malignancies chapter 22
  Palliative Management • Provide pain management, including opioids where indicated
                        • Manage dyspnoea appropriately
                        • Perform drainage of pleural effusion when indicated
                        • Initiate end-of-life care planning

Referral Criteria
        Suspicious chest X-ray or hemoptysis
        Persistent cough >3 weeks in high-risk patient
        Unexplained weight loss with respiratory symptoms
        Confirmed malignancy for oncology evaluation

Prevention
       Smoking cessation
       Occupational safety measures

sections.title: Pulmonary Vascular Diseases (PVDS) and Cor Pulmonale
sections.text:
Pulmonary Vascular Diseases (PVDs) encompasses a group of disorders that affect the blood vessels within the lungs. These
disorders disrupt normal pulmonary blood flow, potentially leading to impaired gas exchange and right ventricular overload or
failure (Cor Pulmonale).

The major types are Pulmonary embolism, Pulmonary Hypertension, Pulmonary veno-occlusive disease, Pulmonary Arterio-
Venous Malformation etc.

sections.title: Pulmonary Embolism
sections.text: Refer cardiovascular disease conditions chapter 20

sections.title: Pulmonary Hypertension
sections.text:
Pulmonary Hypertension is defined as a mean pulmonary artery pressure (mPAP) ≥ 20 mmHg at rest, as measured by right
heart catheterization.
Classification (WHO Groups):
         Group 1 – Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension (PAH): Idiopathic, heritable, drug-induced, connective tissue disease, HIV,
          portal hypertension, congenital heart disease.
         Group 2 – PH due to Left Heart Disease
         Group 3 – PH due to lung diseases and/or Hypoxia: COPD, ILD, sleep apnea, high altitude.
         Group 4 – Chronic Thromboembolic PH (CTEPH)
         Group 5 – PH with Unclear Multifactorial Mechanisms: Hematologic, systemic, or metabolic disorders.

Clinical Presentation
         Exertional dyspnea                                                 Right ventricular heave
         Fatigue                                                            Jugular venous distension (JVD)
         Chest pain                                                         Hepatomegaly, ascites
         Syncope or presyncope                                              Peripheral edema
         Peripheral edema                                                   Tricuspid regurgitation murmur
         Loud P2

Investigations
Initial Testing
         ECG: right heart strain
         Chest X-ray: enlarged pulmonary arteries
         Echocardiography: RV function and estimate pulmonary pressures

Definitive Diagnosis
         Right heart catheterization (gold standard): confirms elevated mPAP ≥ 20 mmHg

Additional Evaluation
       V/Q scan or CTPA: to rule out CTEPH
       PFTs, ABG: for lung diseases
       Autoimmune panel, HIV testing, LFTs: to identify causes

Non-Pharmacological Management
      Oxygen therapy as indicated
      Exercise and supportive care

Pharmacological Management
      Diuretics (for fluid overload)
      Anticoagulation (especially in CTEPH)

Group-specific Treatments:
Group 1 (PAH):
Initial therapy:
Phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors (PDEi)

S: sildenafil (PO) 20 mg 8hourly
(Use the IV formulation if available for critically ill patients)

If inadequate response or intermediate risk, add Endothelin Receptor Antagonist (ERA)
S: bosentan (PO) 62.5 mg 12hourly
Early oral combination therapy (PDEi + ERA) in stage 2 or advanced disease

Calcium channel blockers (if Vaso reactive):
B: amlodipine (PO) 2.5mg - 10mg 24hourly
           OR
A: nifedipine Slow Release (PO) 30mg - 120 mg 12hourly
           OR
D: diltiazem 120 - 240 mg 24hourly

Group 2: Treat underlying heart failure or valvular disease
Group 3: Optimize treatment of lung disease and provide oxygen as required.
Group 4 (CTEPH):
             •    Lifelong anticoagulation
             •    Medical therapy including anticoagulation (could be lifelong), Pulmonary endarterectomy (surgical)
Group 5: Treat underlying disorder

sections.title: Cor Pulmonale
sections.text:
Cor Pulmonale is right ventricular (RV) enlargement and/or failure due to pulmonary hypertension (PH) caused by diseases of
the lung, chest wall, or pulmonary vasculature.
Excludes RV failure due to left heart disease or congenital heart disease.

Clinical Presentation
         Progressive exertional dyspnea                                     Ascites
         Fatigue, chest discomfort                                          Peripheral edema
         Swelling of legs                                                   Loud P2
         Abdominal distension                                               RV heave
         Raised JVP                                                         Tricuspid regurgitation murmur
         Hepatomegaly

Investigations
  Test                            Findings
  ECG                             Right axis deviation, RV hypertrophy
  Chest X-ray                     Enlarged pulmonary arteries, right heart border
  Echocardiogram                  RV enlargement, raised pulmonary pressures, TR
  ABG                             Hypoxemia ± hypercapnia
  PFTs                            Obstructive or restrictive pattern depending on underlying disease
  BNP/NT-pro BNP                  May be elevated if RV dysfunction present
  Right heart catheterization     Confirms PH and RV pressure status

Non-Pharmacological Management
      Optimize COPD, ILD, or other pulmonary disease treatment
      Smoking cessation
      Long-term oxygen therapy (LTOT) if PaO₂ < 55 mmHg (or < 60 mmHg with polycythemia/cor pulmonale)

Pharmacological Management
Give Diuretics:
        Furosemide, spironolactone for volume overload
        Use cautiously to avoid reducing preload too much

Pulmonary Vasodilators:
       Consider specific PH therapy (e.g., sildenafil, Bosentan) only if Group 1 PH or CTEPH

Others:
       Non-invasive ventilation (CPAP or BiPAP) in sleep-disordered breathing
       Anticoagulation if CTEPH or high risk of VTE

sections.title: Pleural Effusion
sections.text:
Pleural effusion, is collection of fluid abnormally present in the pleural space, usually resulting from excess fluid production
and/or decreased lymphatic absorption, is rarely a primary disease process but is usually secondary to other diseases.

Clinical Presentation
         Progressive dyspnea                                                Pleural friction rub
         Cough                                                              When pleural fluid >300ml
         Pleuritic chest pain                                                >Dullness to percussion
         Extrapulmonary symptoms that mimic features of                      >Decreased tactile fremitus
          congestive heart failure (CHF) etc.                                 >Asymmetrical chest expansion
         Night sweats, fever, hemoptysis, and weight loss                    >Displacement of the trachea and mediastinum
          should suggest tuberculosis (TB)                                    toward the side of the effusion- observed with
         Hemoptysis also raises the possibility of                           effusions larger than 1000 mL
          malignancy, other endotracheal or endobronchial                     >Diminished or inaudible breath sounds
          pathology, or pulmonary infarction

Investigations
        CXR
        Full blood picture
        Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR)
        Point of care bed side USS
        Pleural fluid analysis:
         >Gross appearance:
         >Biochemistry: Glucose, PH, LDH, Protein: Use Light’s Criteria to differentiate between transudative and exudative
         pleural effusions
         >Microbiology: Gram Stain, Gene Xpert, pleural fluid culture

        Other Tests as per indication                                       Rheumatoid Factor (if indicated)
         of suspected diagnosis                                              Autoimmune profile or single marker (ANA,
         Pleural Fluid                                                        ACE etc.)
         >ADA (High sensitivity and                                          Renal function (creatinine and BUN)
         specificity in TB pleuritis)                                        Liver function and liver enzymes (Albumin,
         >Cytology                                                            bilirubin total, direct, PT, PTT, INR ALT, AST,
         (Malignancy/autoimmune)                                              GGT, ALP)
         >Amylase (Pancreatitis)                                             ECHO
         >Triglycerides and cholesterol                                      ECG
                                                                             CT-Scan Chest with contrast
         >Bilirubin
                                                                             Thoracoscopy
        Tumor markers as indicated (e.g., CA-15, CEA,                       Image-guided (i.e., CT- or US-guided)
         CA-125etc).                                                          pleural biopsy

Management
      Serial Thoracentesis- for non-complicated pleural effusion.
      Chest Tube Drainage-Hemothorax, Empyema, Complicated para-pneumonic effusion, Post-trauma, Malignant
      Fibrinolytic Therapy-use of Streptokinase and Alteplase, indicated for patients with empyema and complicated
       loculated pleural effusions.
      Thoracoscopy and video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS: For patient with fibrinopurulent pleural infections and
       loculated effusion.
      Pleurodesis (pleural sclerosis) – Various agents can be used to sclerose the pleural space:
       >Povidone-iodine 20mls of 10% mixed with 80–100 mL of 0.9% NaCl,
       >Talk Slurry or Poudrage: via thoracoscope
       >Doxycycline, bleomycin sulfate,
      Thoracotomy, Decortication, and Open Drainage- Main salvage procedure after unsuccessful thoracoscopy.

Indication for thoracostomy/decortication
        Patients with organized empyemas who cannot tolerate thoracotomy or have trapped lungs can undergo rib resection
         with open drainage
        Chronic empyema with bronchopleural fistulas or chronic empyema that are not amenable to surgery
        Critical ill and toxic patients with associated mediastinitis or bronchopleural fistulas who require mediastinal drainage
         or fistula closure.

For Malignant Effusions
Chest tube drainage, radiation, chemotherapy, surgical pleurectomy, pleuroperitoneal shunt, pleurodesis or decortication and
indwelling pleural catheter.

 Note
     •    Emergent thoracentesis and/or chest tube placement is necessary in patients with pleural effusion causing imminent
          or ongoing respiratory compromise or hemodynamic instability.
      •   Refer to specialist/specialist review: Unexplained or recurrent effusion, malignant pleural effusion, Empyema
          thoracic, Loculated effusion.

sections.title: Obstructive Sleep Apnea Syndrome (OSA)
sections.text:
Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is a sleep-related breathing disorder characterized by recurrent episodes of complete (apnea)
or partial (hypopnea) upper airway collapse during sleep, leading to reduced or absent airflow despite ongoing respiratory effort,
often associated with oxygen desaturation and/or arousals from sleep.

Clinical Presentation
         Daytime sleepiness                           Trouble       concentrating;                   female)
         Restless sleep                                mood changes such as                          Crowded oropharynx
         Loud snoring                                  irritability, anxiety and                      (e.g., enlarged tonsils),
         Morning headaches;                            depression;                                    nasal septum deviation
         Insomnia;                                     Forgetfulness; Increased                      Cranio-facial
         Decreased sex drive;                          heart rate and/or blood                        abnormalities:
         Unexplained weight gain;                      pressure;                                      Retrognathia /
         Increased        urination                   Obesity                                        Micrognathia, Midface
          and/or nocturia.                             Large neck                                     hypoplasia
         Heartburn or gastro                           circumference (>43cm in                       Elevated BP
          esophageal reflux                             male, >40.5cm in
          disease

Investigations
        Use STOP-BANG questionnaire and EPWORTH Sleepiness Scale for screening.
        Polysomnography (PSG): Gold standard. Measures apnea–hypopnea index (AHI).

Non-Pharmacological Management
a) General & Lifestyle Measures                                            Avoid supine position (positional OSA)
         Weight loss: Most effective non-device therapy                   Smoking cessation
         Avoid alcohol and sedatives: Reduce airway
          collapsibility
b) Positive Airway Pressure (PAP) Therapy: The mainstay of OSA treatment, moderate to severe cases: CPAP/ APAP/ BiPAP
depending on tolerance and comorbidity.
c) Oral Appliances: Mandibular advancement devices (MADs)
d) Behavioral & Adjunctive Therapies: e.g., Cognitive behavioral therapy
e) Surgical Option: Considered when anatomic obstruction is identified and PAP is not tolerated: Refer to ENT chapter 15
         UPPP (Uvulopalatopharyngoplasty): Removes/repositions tissue at soft palate
         Tonsillectomy/adenoidectomy: Especially in children

Pharmacological Management
Limited role in OSA.

sections.title: Respiratory Failure and ARDS
sections.text:
Respiratory failure is a life-threatening condition in which the respiratory system fails to maintain adequate gas exchange,
resulting in hypoxemia, hypercapnia, or both.

Types of Respiratory Failure:
 Type                        Description                     Key Feature
 Type I (Hypoxemic)             Failure of oxygenation       PaO₂ < 60 mmHg (on room air)
 Type II (Hypercapnic)          Failure of ventilation       PaCO₂ > 45 mmHg

Causes:
 Type of Respiratory Failure Common Causes
                                • Pneumonia
                                • Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS)
Type I (Hypoxemic)              • Pulmonary embolism
                                • Pulmonary oedema (cardiogenic or non-cardiogenic)
                                • Interstitial lung disease
                                • Acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)
                                • Neuromuscular disorders (e.g., myasthenia gravis, Guillain–Barré syndrome)
Type II (Hypercapnic)           • Central nervous system depression (e.g., drugs, stroke)
                                • Obesity hypoventilation syndrome
                                • Chest wall disorders (e.g., kyphoscoliosis)

Clinical Presentation
         Dyspnea, tachypnea
         Cyanosis (Type I)
         Headache, confusion, asterixis (Type II – due to hypercapnia)
         Accessory muscle use, nasal flaring
         Signs of underlying cause (e.g., wheeze, crepitations, fever)

Investigations
        Arterial blood gas (ABG)
         •    ↓PaO₂ in Type I
         •    ↑PaCO₂ ± ↓PaO₂ in Type II

    •    Chest X-ray / CT chest: Identify underlying pathology
    •    Pulmonary function tests, if chronic cause suspected
    •    ECG, Echocardiogram: If cardiogenic causes suspected
    •    Labs: CBC, electrolytes, renal/liver function, infection markers

Non-Pharmacological Management
 Component          Management
 General Measures        • Identify and treat the underlying cause
                         • Monitor oxygenation and ventilation (SpO₂, arterial blood gases [ABG])
                         • Provide supportive care including fluids, antipyretics, and deep vein thrombosis (DVT) prophylaxis
 Oxygen Therapy          Type I Respiratory Failure (Hypoxemic):
                         • Administer supplemental oxygen to maintain SpO₂ ≥ 92%
                         Type II Respiratory Failure (Hypercapnic):
                         • Use oxygen cautiously to avoid worsening hypercapnia
                         • Target oxygen saturation according to clinical condition and ABG findings
 Ventilatory Support     • Non-invasive ventilation (NIV) indicated in selected patients, e.g., chronic obstructive pulmonary
                          disease (COPD) and obesity hypoventilation syndrome (OHS)
                         • Invasive mechanical ventilation for worsening hypoxia, hypercapnia, respiratory fatigue, or failure
                         of NIV
                         • High-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) may be used in selected cases of Type I respiratory failure

Pharmacological Management
Specific Treatments
a) COPD exacerbation: bronchodilators, steroids, NIV
b) Pneumonia: antibiotics
c) ARDS: lung-protective ventilation, prone positioning
d) Neuromuscular causes: IVIG/plasmapheresis + ventilatory support

sections.title: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS)
sections.text:
A severe inflammatory lung condition characterized by acute onset of hypoxemic respiratory failure with bilateral pulmonary
infiltrates, not fully explained by cardiac failure or fluid overload.

Based on the Berlin Criteria:
       Timing: Within 1 week of a known clinical insult or new/worsening respiratory symptoms
       Chest imaging: Bilateral opacities not fully explained by effusions, collapse, or nodules
       Origin of edema: Not primarily cardiac
       Oxygenation (on PEEP ≥5 cm H₂O):

   Severity                   PaO₂/FiO₂ Ratio
   Mild ARDS                  200–300 mmHg
   Moderate ARDS              100–200 mmHg
   Severe ARDS                <100 mmHg

Common Causes:
     Direct lung injury: Pneumonia (bacterial, viral including COVID-19), aspiration, inhalation injury, drowning
     Indirect lung injury: Sepsis, pancreatitis, trauma, massive transfusion, drug overdose

Clinical Presentation
         Acute dyspnea, tachypnea
         Hypoxia refractory to oxygen therapy
         Diffuse crackles on auscultation

Investigations:
        ABG: Respiratory alkalosis on ABG (early), later progressing to hypoxemia and hypercapnia
        Chest X-ray/CT: Bilateral infiltrates (ground-glass opacities or consolidation)
        Echocardiography: To rule out cardiogenic pulmonary edema
        Labs: To identify underlying cause and for monitoring (e.g., cultures, procalcitonin, inflammatory markers)

Non pharmacological
       Refer to higher facility for intensive care.
       Admit to ICU
       Treat underlying cause (e.g., sepsis, pneumonia)
       Lung-protective mechanical ventilation:
        >Low tidal volume (6 mL/kg predicted body weight)
        >Plateau pressure <30 cm H₂O
        >Adequate PEEP to prevent alveolar collapse
       Prone positioning: Especially in moderate–severe ARDS
       Neuromuscular blockade: In select cases of severe ARDS
       Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation (ECMO): For refractory hypoxemia despite optimal ventilation

Pharmacological Management
Conservative fluid management once hemodynamically stable

Adjunctive Therapies (selected cases):
        Inhaled nitric oxide (short-term benefit)
        Corticosteroids in selected cases: e.g. COVID-19 ARDS: B: Dexamethasone (IV) 6mg 24hourly.
        Protease inhibitors e.g.
         S: ulinastatin (IV) 200,000 to 600,000 IU/day, in 2-3 divided doses. Use restricted to ICU, under specialist supervision.

sections.title: Amoebiasis
sections.text:
Amoebiasis is an infection caused by the protozoa organism Entamoeba histolytica, which can cause colitis and other extra-
intestinal manifestations. The infection is primarily acquired through ingestion of contaminated food and water and occasionally
can be acquired through oral-anal sexual practices.

Clinical Presentation
         Bloody diarrhea                                                       Peritonitis in severe forms
         Crampy abdominal pain                                                 Evidence of motile trophozoites or cysts on saline
         Fever                                                                  wet mount from a stool specimen
         Weight loss

Pharmacological Management
Because metronidazole and tinidazole do not kill all cysts in the bowel, a two-step approach is necessary for complete
eradication:
Tissue Agents (Active Infection): Used to kill invading parasites and treat symptoms.

A: metronidazole (PO) 400–800mg 8hourly for 7-10days
          OR
B: tinidazole (PO) 2g 24 hourly for 3-5days due to shorter duration
          AND
C: diloxanide furoate (PO) 500 mg 8hourly for 10days
Luminal Agents (Cyst Eradication): Essential to kill cysts and prevent relapse, even if symptoms are gone.

sections.title: Amoebic Liver Abscess
sections.text:
It is the most frequent extra-intestinal manifestation of Entamoeba histolytica infection which results from the invasion of the
portal venous system from the colon leading to inflammation and subsequently abscess formation particularly involving the right
lobe of the liver.

Clinical Presentation
         High grade fever, 39°C                                                Positive imaging evidence of liver abscess
         Right upper quadrant pain,                                            Serological evidence of E. histolytica antibodies
         Tender and enlarged liver                                              or antigens

Pharmacological Management
B: metronidazole (IV) 800mg 8hourly for 10days.
          OR
B: tinidazole (PO) Adults: 2g 24 hourly for 3days

 Note
          Metronidazole and Tinidazole should not be given in the first trimester of pregnancy due to potential teratogenic
           effects.
          Should not be taken with alcohol due to disulfiram-like effects

Surgery:
Consider therapeutic aspiration of amebic liver abscess in the following situations: (1) high risk of abscess rupture, as defined
by cavity size greater than 5 cm; (2) left lobe liver abscess, which is associated with higher mortality and frequency of peritoneal
leak or rupture into the pericardium; (3) failure to observe a clinical medical response to therapy within 5-7 days; and (4) cannot
differentiate from a pyogenic liver abscess.

sections.title: Giardiasis
sections.text:
It is the infestation of the upper small intestine caused by the flagellate protozoan Giardia lamblia (or G. intestinalis), cytopathic
effects of which leads to malabsorption and diarrhea. It is more common in immune compromised individuals and is acquired
through ingestion of contaminated water

Clinical Presentation
         Crampy abdominal pain
         Chronic diarrhoea
         Steatorrhea
         Weight loss

Investigations
        Evidence of Giardia intestinalis trophozoites or cysts on serial 3 samples of stool examination
        Serological evidence of G. Intestinalis trophozoites antigen or antibody
        Evidence of G. Intestinalis in duodenal aspirates or biopsy specimen.

Pharmacological Management
A: metronidazole (PO) 400–800mg 8hourly for 5days
          OR
B: tinidazole (PO) 2g 24 hourly for 3days

For refractory cases:
D: nitazoxanide (PO) 500mg 12 hourly for 3 days

sections.title: Ascariasis
sections.text:
It is a small intestinal infestation caused by Ascaris lumbricoides which leads to malnutrition, iron deficiency anaemia, impaired
growth and cognition in susceptible hosts. It is most common infestation in children, and it is acquired through ingestion of
contaminated food and water.

Clinical Presentation
         Chronic Diarrhea                                                       Chronic Cough (Loffler’s syndrome)
         Steatorrhea                                                            Intestinal obstruction
         Malnutrition                                                           Obstructive jaundice

Investigations
Stool examination: evidence of ova or worms on wet mount

Pharmacological Management
A: mebendazole (PO) 500mg stat or 100mg 12hourly for 3days.
         OR
A: albendazole (PO) 400mg stat

sections.title: Ancylostomiasis
sections.text:
It is a hookworm disease caused by infestation of the small intestine with Ancylostoma duodenale or Necator americanus
leading to anaemia and malnutrition.

Clinical Presentation
         Abdominal pains                                                        Chronic cough (Loffler’s syndrome) PLUS
         Chronic diarrhea                                                       Evidence of ova or worms on wet mount stool
         Melena stool                                                            examination
         Weight loss                                                            Anaemia

Pharmacological Management
A: mebendazole (PO) 500mg stat or 100mg 12hourly for 3days.
          OR
A: albendazole (PO) 400mg stat
 Note
 If persistent, give second course after 4 weeks. Iron replacement and nutritional supplementation (protein and vitamins) should
 be part of the management strategy. Albendazole is contraindicated in the first trimester of pregnancy

sections.title: Strongyloidiasis
sections.text:
Small intestinal infestation caused by Strongyloides stercoralis usually asymptomatic in immune competent adult but can lead
to life-threatening infestation and disseminated strongyloidiasis in an immune-compromised host associated with high mortality
rates
Clinical Presentation
           Pruritic papulo–vesicular rash at the site of                     Colicky abdominal pains
            penetration or urticarial rash involving the                      Chronic diarrhea and passage of mucus
            perennial region extending to the buttocks, thighs                Weight loss
            and abdomen                                                       Hyper-infection syndrome
           Chronic cough
Investigations
Evidence of rhabditiform larva in wet mount stool examination with Serological evidence (ELISA) for anti-strongyloides antibody

Pharmacological Management
A: albendazole (PO) 400mg 12hourly for 3days (Repeat after 4 weeks if still positive stool findings)
         OR
A: ivermectin (PO) 200 µg /kg 24hourly for 2days
 Note: Give treatment for 10 days in case of disseminated/super infestation

sections.title: Taeniasis
sections.text:
Is a tapeworm disease acquired from eating raw or not-well cooked food? Can be due to Taenia saginata (beef tapeworm),
Taenia solium (pork tapeworm), Diphyllobothrium latum (fish tapeworm) and Hymenolepsis nana (faecal oral contamination
from human and dogs) leading to chronic malnutrition (Taeniasis) or multi-organ dissemination and dysfunction (Cysticercosis)

Clinical Presentation
         Taeniasis                                     Loss of or increased                         Pruritus ani
         Colicky abdominal pain                         appetite                                     Hyperexcitability
         Body Weakness                                 Constipation or diarrhea

Investigations
Evidence of characteristic ova, proglottids or scolex in the wet mount stool examination

Cysticercosis - The cysticerci are most often located in subcutaneous and intermuscular tissues, followed by the eye and then
the brain. The CNS is involved in 60-90% of patients i.e., Neurocystercosis which may manifest as:

Convulsions and/or seizures:
       Intracranial hypertension: headache, nausea,                            Behavioral changes and learning disabilities
        vomiting, vertigo, and papilledema.                                      more      marked     in    children    and
       Personality and mental status changes                                    immunocompromised adults. PLUS
        (Neuropsychiatric changes)                                              Head CT scan OR Brain MRI

  Note: Refer the patient to high centers for further investigation and expertise.

Pharmacological Management
Taeniasis
A: praziquantel (PO) 5–10mg/kg stat

Cysticercosis (NCC)
A: praziquantel (PO) 50mg/kg 24hourly for 21days
         OR
A: albendazole (PO) 15mg/kg 24hourly for 30days.
         AND
B: dexamethasone (IV) 4mg 12hourly can be given up to 7days.
         AND
A: carbamazepine (PO) initially 200 mg 12-24hourly, increased slowly to 0.8–1.2 g 24hourly in divided doses (for seizures refer
to CNS chapter)
  Note: Hydrocephalus should be treated with surgical shutting. Ocular manifestation cysticercosis, should be referred to eye
  specialist

sections.title: Echinococcosis
sections.text:
It is a canine tape worm Echinococcus granulosus which is transmitted by dogs, sheep and horses. Human infestation is through
contamination of food or water causing visceral cysts (Hydatid Cyst Disease) particularly in the liver and lungs and is usually
asymptomatic in susceptible host.

Clinical Presentation
         Upper abdominal discomfort and pain, poor appetite,
         Upper abdominal mass swelling with enlarged liver.
         Cough with features of acute hypersensitivity reaction. (for ruptured cysts)
         Portal hypertension, biliary obstruction or Budd-Chiari syndrome (for complicated cases)

Investigations
        Echinococcus serology
        LFT, RFT, FBC
        Abdominal Ultrasound
        Abdominal CT scan or MRI

Pharmacological Management
A: albendazole (PO) 400mg 12hourly for 3months
         OR
A: mebendazole (PO) 500mg 12hourly for 3months

Referral: For symptomatic/ complicated cases refer to higher centers with management and expertise.
        PAIR (puncture, aspiration, injection, and re-aspiration) is a percutaneous treatment alternative to surgery
        Surgical treatment: either radical pericystectomy or conservative deroofing

sections.title: Schistosomiasis
sections.text:
Parasitic disease caused by blood flukes (trematodes) of the genus Schistosoma. Common species found in Tanzania are
S. haematobium responsible for urogenital schistosomiasis and S. mansoni responsible for intestinal schistosomiasis as a result
of immune mediated reaction which leads to progressive inflammation and fibrosis of the urinary bladder or portal venous
system respectively.

Clinical Presentation
Schistosoma mansoni
         Swimmer’s itch or katayama fevers in acute                          Hepatomegaly
          infection phase.                                                    Portal hypertension with bleeding
         Colicky abdominal pains                                              esophageal varices
         Diarrhoea and dysentery                                             Decompensated liver disease
         Anemia

Schistosoma hematobium
        Dysuria and terminal hematuria                                       Glomerulonephritis and amyloidosis
        Hematospermia                                                        Bladder carcinoma
        Obstructive     uropathy       (hydronephrosis,                      Chronic kidney failure
         hydroureters)

Investigations
Laboratory evidence characteristic eggs in urine, (S. Hematobium) or in stool (S. mansoni, S. japonicum) examined by kato
katz thick smear procedure or PCR assays of both urine and stool samples.

Pharmacological Management
A: praziquantel (PO) 40mg/kg stat or in 2 divided doses (repeat every 6 months for continues exposure)

sections.title: Typhoid and Paratyphoid
sections.text:
It is an acute systemic disease resulting from infection by Salmonella typhi and S. paratyphi, serovar group A and B respectively.
Infection is acquired through ingestion of contaminated food and water.

Clinical Presentation
         Fever, severe headache, abdominal and muscle pains (myalgia)
         Delirium, obtundation, intestinal hemorrhage, bowel perforation,
         Sequela neuropsychiatric complications

Investigations
        Laboratory evidence of positive cultures from bone marrow aspirates; blood or stool done within 1 week of acute
         infection OR
        Salmonella stool antigen test
        Indirect fluorescent Vi antibody, ELISA for immunoglobulin M (IgM) and IgG antibodies to S. Typhi polysaccharide.

Pharmacological Management
Uncomplicated typhoid fever
A: ciprofloxacin (PO) 500mg 12 hourly for 10-14days
          OR
B: azithromycin (PO) Adult 500mg 24hourly for 7days
          OR
A: cefixime 400mg (PO) 24hourly for 7-14days

For complicated typhoid fever
C: ciprofloxacin (IV) 200-400 mg 12hourly daily 7days
          OR
B: ceftriaxone (IV) 1-2gm 24hourly 4-7days
  Note: Definitive treatment of typhoid (enteric fever) is based on susceptibility. For patients with severe or complicated disease
  (e.g., systemic toxicity, depressed consciousness, prolonged fever, organ system dysfunction or other features that prompt
  hospitalization), initial therapy with a parenteral agent is appropriate.

sections.title: Shigellosis
sections.text:
Shigella organisms are a group of gram-negative, facultative intracellular bacteria pathogens. They are grouped into 4 species:
Shigella dysenteriae, Shigella flexneri, Shigella boydii, and Shigella sonnei, also known as groups A, B, C, and D respectively.
Shigellosis is spread by means of fecal- oral, by ingestion by ingestion of contaminated food or water and leads to bacillary
dysentery.

Clinical Presentation
         Acute abdominal cramping, high-grade fever,                         Hemolytic      uremic     syndrome    (HUS),
          emesis and large-volume watery diarrhea                              microangiopathic        hemolytic    anemia,
         Tenesmus, urgency, fecal incontinence, mucoid                        thrombocytopenia, and renal failure
          bloody diarrhea                                                     Profound dehydration and hypoglycemia
         Severe headache, lethargy, meningismus,
          delirium, and convulsions
Investigations
         Laboratory evidence of microscopic isolation of the bacteria from stool or rectal swabs specimens
         Stool culture for suspected cases in early course of infection
         An enzyme immunoassay (ELISA) for shiga toxin detection in stool for S. dysenteriae type I

Pharmacological Management
A: ciprofloxacin (PO) 500mg 12hourly for 5days
          OR
A: erythromycin (PO) 500mg 6hourly for 5days.

sections.title: Cholera
sections.text: For diagnostic criteria, investigations, prevention and treatment refer to chapter under notifiable diseases chapter 4.

sections.title: Peptic Ulcer Disease
sections.text:
Refers to acid related peptic ulceration involving the lower esophagus; stomach and duodenum as a result of active
inflammation induced by acid –pepsin leading to disruption of the mucosal integrity causing local defect or excavation

sections.title: Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
sections.text:
It is a disorder resulting from gastric acid-pepsin activity and other gastric contents reflux into the esophagus due to incompetent
barriers at the gastroesophageal junction leading to active inflammation of the distal third of the esophagus (prolonged contact
with acid can evolve to stricture)

Clinical Presentation
         Heartburn and regurgitation are cardinal                            Chronic cough, laryngitis, pharyngitis
          symptoms.                                                           Chronic bronchitis, asthma, COPD, pneumonia,
         Odynophagia, dysphagia, weight loss and                              chronic sinusitis and dental decay
          bleeding

Investigations
        Endoscopic evidence mucosal ulceration
        Histological evidence of chronic active inflammation
        Positive finding with a gold standard 24-hours esophageal pH testing.

Pharmacological Management
Non-erosive, symptomatic
A: omeprazole (PO) 20mg 24hourly for 8weeks
         OR
S: esomeprazole (PO) 20mg-40mg 24hourly for 8weeks.

Erosive esophagitis
C: pantoprazole (PO) 40mg 24hourly for 8-16weeks

For refractory cases acid suppression therapy may require continuation up to 6 months. Lifestyle modification and avoidance
of triggers is important including avoidance of smoking, alcohol and NSAID use.

Referral: Refer to next level center with adequate expertise and facility for refractory cases or cases with alarming symptoms
(red flags) such as bleeding, anemia, early satiety, progressive dysphagia or odynophagia, unexplained weight loss, recurrent
vomiting or family history of gastrointestinal (GI) cancers, age ≥ 40 years.

sections.title: Gastroduodenal Ulcers (PUD)
sections.text:
This is a disorder resulting from breakdown of mucosal defense mechanisms against hydrochloric acid and proteolytic enzymes,
most commonly secondary to H. Pylori infection or NSAID use.

Clinical Presentation
         Burning epigastric abdominal pains, usually                         Hematemesis or melena stools
          relived by antacids.                                                Weight loss
         Anorexia, early satiety, bloating,

Investigations
        Endoscopic evidence of gastric or duodenal mucosal ulceration
        Risk stratification using Glasgow-Blatchford score

Pharmacological Management
A: omeprazole (PO) 20mg 24hourly for 8weeks
          OR
C: pantoprazole (PO) 40mg 24hourly for 8weeks
          OR
S: esomeprazole (PO) 20mg 24hourly for 8weeks
          AND
A: antiacid liquid mixture (PO) 10-15ml 12hourly to 8hourly for 7-14days

For bleeding PUD: refer to higher centers
C: pantoprazole (IV) 80mg stat then 40mg 12hourly for 2-3days, then (PO) as above if bleeding stops
         OR
S: esomeprazole (IV) 40mg 12hourly for 2-3days, then (PO) as above if bleeding stops
         OR
C: pantoprazole (IV) 80mg bolus followed by continuous infusion of 8mg/hour for 72 hours

sections.title: Helicobacter Pylori Related Peptic Ulcer Disease
sections.text:
Helicobacter pylori is a ubiquitous organism that is present in about 50% of the global population. Chronic infection with H pylori
causes atrophic and even metaplastic changes in the stomach, and it has a known association with peptic ulcer disease. The
most common route of H pylori infection is either oral-to-oral or fecal-to-oral contact.

Clinical Presentation
         Heartburn and regurgitation are cardinal                             Chronic cough, laryngitis, pharyngitis
          symptoms.                                                            Chronic bronchitis, asthma, COPD, pneumonia,
         Odynophagia, dysphagia, weight loss and                               chronic sinusitis and dental decay
          bleeding

Investigations
        Positive stool antigen test (Stop PPI 2 weeks                         Positive urease test on endoscopic biopsy
         before testing)                                                        sample
        Positive urease breath test                                           Identification of the pathogen by histopathology
                                                                                examination

Pharmacological Management
Triple therapy is indicated for complete eradication of the organism
First-Line Therapy
 Regimen                        Medicine, Dose & Frequency                                                      Duration
 Triple Therapy                 A: omeprazole (PO) 20 mg 12-hourly
                                       OR
                                C: pantoprazole (PO) 40 mg 12-hourly
                                       OR
                                S: esomeprazole (PO) 40 mg 12-hourly
                                                                                                                14 days
                                       AND
                                A: amoxicillin (PO) 1000 mg 12-hourly
                                       AND
                                A: metronidazole (PO) 400 mg 12-hourly
                                        OR
                                B: tinidazole (PO) 500 mg 12-hourly
                                A: PPI (as above) 12-hourly
                                       AND
                                A: amoxicillin (PO) 1000 mg 12-hourly
                                       AND
 Concomitant Therapy            A: metronidazole (PO) 400 mg 12-hourly                                          14 days
                                        OR
                                B: tinidazole (PO) 500 mg 12-hourly
                                       AND
                                C: clarithromycin (PO) 500 mg 12-hourly

Second-Line Therapy
 Regimen                       Medicine, Dose & Frequency                                                       Duration
                               A: PPI (as above) 12-hourly
                                       AND
                               D: bismuth subsalicylate (PO) 525 mg 6-hourly
                                       AND
 Bismuth-based                 A: metronidazole (PO) 400 mg 12-hourly                                           14 days
 Quadruple Therapy                      OR
                               B: tinidazole (PO) 500 mg 12-hourly
                                       AND
                               A: doxycycline (PO) 100 mg 12-hourly
                               A: PPI (as above) 12-hourly
                                       AND
                               D: bismuth subsalicylate (PO) 525 mg 6-hourly
 Alternative Quadruple
                                       AND                                                                      14 days
 Therapy
                               D: nitazoxanide (PO) 500 mg 8-hourly
                                       AND
                               A: doxycycline (PO) 100 mg 12-hourly

Treatment failure
H. pylori treatment failure is defined as the positive stool antigen test or urease breath test 5 weeks after the last dose of
eradication therapy. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) should be performed after (two) treatment failures. This is
associated with higher eradication rates compared with individuals without AST. After treatment failure, the treatment should
be individualized following the culture and sensitivity of the gastric biopsy or PCR.

sections.title: Non-ulcer Dyspepsia (Functional Dyspepsia, Indigestion)
sections.text:
It is a chronic recurrent dyspeptic disorder characterized by upper abdominal symptoms, discomfort, pain, fullness, early satiety,
bloating, burning epigastric pain syndrome and post prandial distress syndrome without any organic, systemic or metabolic
disease to explain its presence.

Clinical Presentation
         Dyspeptic symptoms present for last 3 months and onset at least months prior to diagnosis
         Bothersome abdominal discomfort post prandial fullness.
         Early satiety
         Epigastric pains
         Epigastric burning

Investigations
Lack of evidence of structural disease by upper endoscopic examination.

Non-Pharmacological Management
Non-Pharmacological Management of functional dyspepsia (FD) focuses on dietary adjustments, lifestyle modifications, and
stress reduction to alleviate symptoms like epigastric pain, burning, and early satiety. Key strategies include eating smaller,
frequent meals, reducing fat and caffeine intake, avoiding trigger foods (spicy, acidic), and utilizing stress-reduction techniques
like cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), yoga, or meditation.

a) Dietary Modifications:
           Meal Frequency: Eat smaller, more frequent meals rather than three large ones to reduce the burden on the
            stomach.
           Trigger Foods: Avoid foods that trigger symptoms, such as high-fat foods, alcohol, caffeine (coffee, tea),
            carbonated beverages, spicy foods, citrus fruits, and certain vegetables like broccoli or onions.
           Diet Composition: Adopt a diet rich in, or similar to, the Mediterranean diet, focusing on fresh foods while reducing
            processed items.
           Texture Modification: If necessary, ensure a portion of daily meals consists of soft or liquid foods.
           Fiber Reduction: Reduce fiber-enriched foods, particularly those containing inulin.

b) Lifestyle Changes:
            Stress Management: Implement relaxation techniques, such as yoga, meditation, or, specifically, cognitive
             behavioral therapy (CBT), which has shown significant promise in managing symptoms.
            Eating Habits: Chew food thoroughly and eat slowly.
            Habit Adjustments: Smoking cessation and avoidance of NSAIDs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) are
             recommended.

c) Other Therapies:
           Herbal Remedies: Some herbal teas (ginger, chamomile, peppermint) or preparations like STW-5 (Iberis amara)
            may provide relief,
           Acupuncture/Electrical Stimulation: These may be used for symptom management,

d) Psychotherapy:
          Psychological therapies, particularly CBT, are considered effective in treating FD by addressing the gut-brain
           interaction,

These approaches, often used alongside reassurance from a healthcare provider, can help manage symptoms effectively,

Pharmacological Management
H. pylori eradication (see under H. pylori)
A: omeprazole (PO) 20mg 24hourly for 4-8weeks
           OR
C: pantoprazole (PO) 40mg 24hourly for 4-8weeks
           OR
S: esomeprazole (PO) 40mg 24hourly for 4-8weeks
           AND
B: metoclopramide (PO) 10mg 8hourly when required (bloating and nausea symptoms, delayed gastric emptying)
           OR
D: domperidone (PO) 10mg 8hourly when required to alleviate bloating and nausea   symptoms, delayed gastric emptying.
           AND
A: amitriptyline (PO) 25mg at bedtime when required for refractory cases

 Note: Presence of alarm features (see list above under GERD) warrant OGD.

sections.title: Gastritis
sections.text:
This is an inflammatory mucosal response to injury from variety of agents and mechanisms including infections, drugs, alcohol,
acute stress, radiation, allergy, acid and bile, ischemia or direct trauma. The inflammation may involve the entire stomach
(pangastritis) or a region of the stomach (antral gastritis) while the severity of inflammation may be erosive or non-erosive.

Clinical Presentation
         Nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, belching, and bloating
         Acute abdominal pain or abdominal discomfort
         Fever, chills, and hiccups also may be present
Investigations
         Endoscopic evidence of gastric mucosal inflammation
         Histologic evidence of chronic active inflammation of biopsy specimen.

Non-Pharmacological Management
      Reduce the use of drugs known to cause gastritis (e.g., NSAIDs, alcohol)
      Stop smoking

Pharmacological Management
Triple therapy for H. pylori eradication if confirmed present.
Administer fluids and electrolytes as required, particularly if the patient is vomiting.

C: pantoprazole (IV) 40mg 6hourly 2-3days
         OR
S: esomeprazole (IV) 40mg 12hourly 2-3days
         AND
B: metoclopramide (IM) 10mg 12hourly when required (for cases presenting with intractable vomiting) in order to relieve
symptoms.
Switch to oral PPI once patient can tolerate oral intake. Referral
Refer to next level service with adequate expertise and facilities for complicated case with alarm features (anemia, vomiting
blood and weight loss, see complete list under GERD above).

sections.title: Gastrointestinal (GI) Bleeding
sections.text:
Intraluminal blood loss anywhere from the oropharynx to the anus. Classification: upper = above the ligament of Treitz; lower =
below the ligament of Treitz “Severe” GIB: defined as having associated shock, orthostatic hypotension, fall in hematocrit by
6% (or decrease in Hb by 2 g/dL), or requiring transfusion ≥2U PRBCs. Requires hospitalization.

sections.title: Upper GI Bleeding (UGIB)
sections.text:
PUD caused by Helicobacter pylori infection or NSAID use is the most common cause of nonvariceal UGI bleeding.
