sections.title: Biliary Tract Diseases
sections.text:
Cholestasis is a pathologic state of reduced bile formation or flow which can be hepatocellular (Intrahepatic), where an
impairment of bile formation occurs or ductular (extra hepatic), where impedance to bile flow occurs after it is formed.
Intrahepatic causes of cholestasis include viral hepatitis, alcohol, primary biliary cirrhosis, drug toxicity, Hodgkin’s lymphoma
and pregnancy. Extrahepatic causes include choledocholithiasis, carcinoma, and ascariasis of the biliary tree.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Jaundice,
     •    Dark urine,
     •    Pale stools, and
     •    Generalized body itching/pruritis.

Investigations
    •    Laboratory evidence of elevated serum levels of total bilirubin, direct bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, gamma-glutamyl
         transferase, and transaminases. WITH
    •    Supporting radiological evidence of dilated intra or extra hepatic biliary radicles.

Pharmacological Management
Definitive treatment, identify and treat specific cause
Supportive treatment:
S: cholestyramine (PO) 4–16g/day
          OR
S: ursodeoxycholic acid (PO) 20–30 mg/kg/day
  Note: Surgical intervention is indicated for extra hepatic cholestasis.

sections.title: Cholelithiasis
sections.text:
Cholelithiasis involves the presence of gallstones which are concretions that form in the biliary tract, usually in the gallbladder.
Choledocholithiasis refers to the presence of one or more gallstones in the common bile duct (CBD). Treatment of gallstones
depends on the stage of disease.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Asymptomatic in majority of patients.                             •    Physical exam: afebrile, and/or RUQ tenderness
     •    Biliary pain (episodic RUQ or epigastric pain),                        or epigastric pain
          pain radiating to scapula;                                        •    Nonspecific symptoms (e.g., indigestion,
     •    Pain precipitated by fatty foods; nausea                               dyspepsia, belching, or bloating)

Investigations
    •    Full Blood count                                                   •    MRI with MRCP
    •    Liver function panel                                               •    Scintigraphy (HIDA) scans
    •    Pancreatic enzymes (Amylase, Lipase)                               •    Endoscopic                      retrograde
    •    Abdominal radiography (upright and supine) – to                         cholangiopancreatography (ERCP)
         exclude other causes of abdominal pain                             •    Percutaneous transhepatic cholangiography
    •    Ultrasonography                                                         (PTC)
    •    CT scan –superior for demonstrating stones in
         the distal CBD
Complications
    •    Cholecystitis                                                      •    Cholecystenteric fistula stone erodes through
    •    Choledocholithiasis leading to cholangitis or                           gallbladder into bowel
         gallstone pancreatitis                                             •    Gallstone ileus: SBO (usually at term ileum) due
    •    Mirizzi syndrome                                                        to stone in intestine that passed through fistula
                                                                            •    Gallbladder carcinoma

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Asymptomatic gallstones – Expectant management
    •  Symptomatic gallstones – definitive surgical intervention (cholecystectomy)

Pharmacological Management
A: paracetamol (PO) 1g 8hourly for 5days
          OR
A: ibuprofen (PO) 400mg 4-6hourly for 3-5days
          OR
B: tramadol (PO) 50mg 12hourly for 3-5days
          AND
S: ursodeoxycholic acid 8-10mg/kg/day divided once to three times up to 6months
  Note: Cholecystectomy (open or laparoscopic) for asymptomatic gallstones may be indicated in the following:
      •   Those with large (>2 cm) gallstones
      •   Nonfunctional or calcified (porcelain) gallbladder on imaging studies and at high risk of gallbladder carcinoma
      •   Those with spinal cord injuries or sensory neuropathies affecting the abdomen
      •   Sickle cell anemia patients- difficult to distinguish between painful crisis and cholecystitis
      •   Cholecystectomy, Endoscopic, sphincterotomy, Extracorporeal shockwave lithotripsy

sections.title: Choledocholithiasis
sections.text:
Gallstone lodged in common bile duct (CBD). Occurs in some of patients with gallbladder stones; can form de novo in CBD.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Asymptomatic                                                   •    Jaundice,
     •    RUQ pain,                                                      •    Pruritus,
     •    Epigastric pain due to obstruction of bile flow                •    Nausea.
          which leads to increase in CBD pressure,

Investigations
    •    LFT                                                             •    Abdominal (RUQ) Ultrasound
    •    Amylase                                                         •    ERCP, if ERCP unavailable or unsuccessful
    •    Lipase.                                                         •    EUS/MRCP

Non-Pharmacological Management
ERCP & papillotomy w/ stone extraction (± lithotripsy) Cholecystectomy typically within 6 weeks unless contraindication

Pharmacological Management
S: cholestyramine (PO) 4-8g 12hourly when required for itching.

Complications
Cholangitis, cholecystitis, pancreatitis, stricture

sections.title: Cholecystitis
sections.text:
Cholecystitis is inflammation of the gallbladder that occurs most commonly because of an obstruction of the cystic duct by
gallstones (stone impaction in cystic duct leads to inflammation behind obstruction causing GB swelling and secondary infection
of biliary fluid).

Acalculous cholecystitis: Occurs in critically ill. GB stasis and ischemia (without cholelithiasis) leading to
necroinflammation.
Clinical Presentation
     •    RUQ/epigastric pain, radiating to right                         •    RUQ tenderness, Murphy’s sign, palpable
          shoulder/back, nausea, vomiting, fever                               gallbladder, jaundice
     •    Signs of peritoneal irritation may be present                   •    The absence of physical findings does not rule
     •    Patients with acalculous cholecystitis may                           out the diagnosis of cholecystitis
          present with fever and sepsis alone

Investigations
    •    FBP, LFT, amylase, lipase                                       •    Computed tomography (CT)
    •    Ultrasonography RUQ ultrasound: high                            •    Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
         Sensitivity and specificity for stones but need                 •    Hepatobiliary scintigraphy (HIDA)
         specific signs of cholecystitis: GB wall                        •    Endoscopic retrograde
         thickening >4 mm, pericholecystic fluid and a                        cholangiopancreatography (ERCP)
         sonographic Murphy’s sign
    •    Radiography

Pharmacological Management
In acute cholecystitis, the initial treatment includes bowel                  OR
rest, IV hydration, and correction of electrolyte                   C: ciprofloxacin (IV) 200-400mg 12hourly for 7-10days
abnormalities                                                                 AND
A: paracetamol (PO) 1g 8hourly daily ORD: paracetamol               B: metronidazole (IV) 500mg 8hourly for 7-10days
(IV) 1g 8 hourly daily (for analgesia cases)
          AND                                                       In cases of uncomplicated cholecystitis, outpatient
B: metoclopramide (IV/PO) 10mg 12hourly daily (for                  treatment may be appropriate.
intractable vomiting)                                               A: ciprofloxacin (PO) 500mg 12hourly for 7days
          AND                                                                 AND
S: piperacillin + tazobactam FDC (IV) 4.5g 6-8 hourly 7-10          A: metronidazole (PO) 400mg 12hourly for 7days
days (for severe/complicated
          OR
B: ceftriaxone (IV) 1-2gm 24hourly for 7-10days
   Note
        •     Laparoscopic cholecystectomy (standard of care for surgical treatment of cholecystitis) others include ERCP.
        •     Endoscopic ultrasound-guided transmural cholecystostomy, Endoscopic gallbladder drainage.
        •     Percutaneous cholecystostomy

sections.title: Cholangitis
sections.text:
Bile duct (BD) obstruction leads to infection proximal to the obstruction, etiologies include BD stone, malignant (biliary,
pancreatic) or benign stricture, infection with fluke (Clonorchis sinensis, Opisthorchis viverrini)

Clinical Presentations
     •    Charcot’s triad: RUQ pains, jaundice, fever/chills; present in three quarter of patients
     •    Reynolds’ pentad: Charcot’s triad + shock and altered mental status; present in 15% of patients

Investigations
    •    Ultrasound, RUQ USS often demonstrates dilation
    •    FBP, LFT, amylase, lipase
    •    Blood cultures
    •    ERCP; percutaneous transhepatic cholangiogram if ERCP unsuccessful

Pharmacological Management
B: ceftriaxone (IV) 1-2g 24hourly for 7-10days
          OR
S: piperacillin+ tazobactam FDC (IV) 4.5g 6-8hourly for 7-10days (for severe/complicated cases)
          OR
S: meropenem (IV) 1g 8 hourly for 7-10days

           AND
B: metronidazole (IV) 500mg 8hourly for 7-10days
Alternatively
C: ciprofloxacin (IV) 200-400mg 12hourly for 7-10days
AND
B: metronidazole (IV) 500mg 8hourly for 7-10days

 Note
     •     About 80% respond to conservative treatment and antibiotics then, 20% require urgent biliary decompression via
           ERCP (papillotomy, stone extraction and/or stent insertion)
      •    If sphincterotomy cannot be performed (larger stones), decompression by biliary stent or nasobiliary catheter can be
           done; otherwise, percutaneous trans hepatic biliary drainage or surgery

sections.title: Bleeding in Pregnancy
sections.text:
Bleeding during pregnancy is common, especially during the first trimester. Bleeding can sometimes be a sign of something
serious, therefore it is important to know the possible causes and take adequate measures.

sections.title: Abortion
sections.text:
It is a spontaneous loss of a fetus before it is viable (has the potential to survive outside the womb). The World Health
Organization (WHO) defines it as expulsion or extraction of an embryo or fetus weighing 500gm or less, approximately at or
less than 24 weeks of gestation. In Tanzania abortion is defined as loss of pregnancy before 28 weeks of gestation. Clinical
features will depend on the types of abortion.

sections.title: Threatened Abortion
sections.text:
Clinical Presentation
     •    Mild vaginal bleeding
     •    Mild/no lower abdominal pain
     •    Cervix is closed on digital examination

Investigation
    •    Check Hb level
    •    Blood group and Rh type
    •    Pelvic ultrasound
    •    Beta-HCG levels (where available)

Management of threatened abortion in Dispensary & Health Centre
    •    Adequate bed rest at home
    •    Avoid strenuous activities and sexual intercourse until all the symptoms have subsided
    •    Schedule a follow up within 7 days
    •    Tell the woman to come immediately if;
           o    Bleeding becomes heavy
           o    Experiences offensive discharge
           o    Severe abdominal pain
Referral
Refer to higher-level health facility with adequate expertise and diagnostics if:
    •    Bleeding recurs
    •    Experiences fever
    •    Experiences offensive discharge
    •    Experience severe abdominal pain

In higher level health facilities:
         •    Take thorough history and perform investigations to establish the causes
         •    Perform ultrasound to confirm pregnancy, gestational age, fetal viability and potential causes of abortion.
         •    Admit the patient and manage appropriately
         •    Encourage bed rest
         •    For unexplained recurrent miscarriage (3 consecutive abortions) or PRL due to luteal phase defect manage with

Pharmacological Management
S: dydrogesterone (PO) 40mg stat then 10mg 12 hourly until the bleeding stops for threatened abortion
         OR
S: dydrogesterone (PO) 10mg 24 hourly from conception up to 20 weeks for luteal phase defect.

Additional when needed
S: estradiol (PO) 2mg 12hourly until bleeding stops, then 2mg 24 hourly until 14 to 16 weeks

sections.title: Inevitable Abortion
sections.text:
Abortion is said to be inevitable when it is not possible for the pregnancy to continue and the cervix is dilated, but all the products
of conception are in situ.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Moderate or severe per vaginal bleeding
     •    Moderate or severe lower abdominal pain
     •    Membranes may be intact or ruptured with leakage of liquor
     •    The uterine fundal height may correspond with gestational age
     •    The cervix is dilated

Management of inevitable abortion in Dispensary & Health Centre (B-EMONC facilities)
Apply Danger, Response, Airway, Breathing, Circulation and Deformity and Exposure (DRABCDE) principles of resuscitation

Pharmacological Management
A: sodium lactate compound (ringer’s lactate)(IV)
         OR
A: sodium chloride 0.9% (IV) depending of amount of blood loss.
     •   Perform Manual Vacuum Aspiration (MVA) if gestation age is below 12 weeks or medical regimen with misoprostol
     •   Manage as incomplete abortion if after augmentation some products of conception remain in the uterus
     •   Manage as complete abortion if all products of conception are expelled

Referral: Refer to hospital if MVA is not possible and/or bleeding is persisting or severe to necessitate blood transfusion.

Management of Inevitable Abortion at the Hospital

Pharmacological Management
Apply Danger, Response, Airway, Breathing, Circulation and Deformity and Exposure principles of resuscitation
And subsequently Obtain blood samples for Hb, grouping and cross–matching

Give
A: sodium lactate compound (ringer’s lactate)(IV)
         OR
A: sodium chloride 0.9% aim at replacing 3 times the amount of estimated blood loss and Give blood transfusion if indicated.

If gestational age is 12 weeks or below: Perform surgical evacuation (MVA) OR Medical evacuation with misoprostol

If GA is 13-17: augment with
A: oxytocin 20IU in 500mls RL/NS at 40 - 60 drops/minute.
If augmentation with oxytocin is not possible,
give
A: misoprostol (SL/Bu) 400μg every 3-4 hours until expulsion.

If GA is 18-24: augment with
A: oxytocin 20IU in 500mls RL/NS at 40 - 60 drops/minute.
If augmentation with Oxytocin is not possible,
give
A: misoprostol (SL/Bu) 400μg every 3-4 hours until expulsion.

If GA is 25-27: augment with
A: oxytocin 20IU in 500mls RL/NS at 40 - 60 drops/minute.
If augmentation with oxytocin is not possible,
give
A: misoprostol (SL/Bu) 200μg every 3-4 hours until expulsion.
Manage as an incomplete abortion if, after augmentation, some products of conception remain in the uterus; otherwise, manage
as a complete abortion if all products of conception have been expelled.

sections.title: Incomplete Abortion
sections.text:
Abortion is said to be incomplete when after expulsion some of the products of conception get retained in the uterine cavity.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Severe Cramping lower abdominal pain
     •    moderate to severe PV bleeding
     •    Fundus smaller than dates
     •    The cervix is dilated and products of conception may be felt on or through the cervix on digital examination

Management of incomplete abortion at dispensary & health center (B-EMONC facilities)
   •   Apply Airway, Breathing, Circulation and Dehydration principles of resuscitation
   •   Check hemoglobin level

Pharmacological Management
A: sodium lactate compound (ringer’s lactate)(IV)
         OR
A: sodium chloride 0.9% depending on amount of blood loss

If feasible Perform digital evacuation of products of conception to minimize the PV bleeding also Perform medical (Misoprostol)
or surgical evacuation (MVA)

If gestation age (GA) is 12 weeks or below
Medical evacuation regime is
A: misoprostol 600μg buccal or 400μg sublingual (Repeated dose may be given after 3-4 hours to achieve complete expulsion).

If gestation age (GA) is above 12 weeks
Managed at a CEmONC facility (refer if non-CEmONC), Medical evacuation with
A: misoprostol 400μg sublingual /buccal for GA of 13-26 weeks and 200μg for GA of 26-27 weeks. (Repeated dose may be
given after 3-4 hours to achieve complete expulsion).

If Misoprostol is unavailable and the client is experiencing severe bleeding, a skilled and experienced providers should perform
Dilation and Evacuation (D&E) using forceps (do not use sharp curettage). Assess for infection and provide antibiotics
depending on the client’s status.

After evacuation give:
A: amoxicillin (PO) 500mg 8hourly for 5 - 7 days
          OR
B: amoxicillin + clavulanic acid (FDC) (PO) 625mg 12-hourly for 5 - 7 days
          AND
A: metronidazole (PO) 400mg 8-hourly, for 5 to 7 days
          AND
A: paracetamol (PO) 1gm 8-hourly for 3 - 5 days
          OR
A: ibuprofen (PO) 400mg 12-8hourly depending on severity of pain for 3 - 5 days.
          AND
A: ferrous sulfate + folic acid (FDC) (PO) 1 tab 24hourly for 4 weeks if anemic

Referral: Resuscitate the patient and refer to hospital level with an escort of a nurse or clinician if bleeding continues

Management of incomplete abortion at the Hospital level.
If patient is in shock,
     •    Shout for help, mobilize resources                                    replacing 3times the amount of estimated blood
     •    Apply ABCD principles of resuscitation                                loss
     •    Obtain blood for HB, grouping and cross–                         •    Digital evacuation of products of conception if
          matching                                                              feasible to minimize the PV bleeding
     •    Blood transfusion if indicated                                   •    MVA if gestation age is below 12 weeks
     •    Give If sodium lactate compound (ringer’s                        •    Evacuate uterus in theatre with sharp curette
          lactate)(IV) OR 0.9% sodium chloride aim at                           under general anesthesia if pregnancy was more
                                                                                than 12 weeks

Pharmacological Management
Pre-procedure prophylactic antibiotics
B: azithromycin (PO) 500mg stat
          OR
A: doxycycline (PO) 200mg stat 30 minutes prior to procedure.

After evacuation give antibiotics if indicated:
A: amoxicillin (PO) 500mg 8-hourly for 5 - 7 days
          OR
B: amoxicillin + clavulanic acid (PO) 625mg 12-hourly for 5 - 7 days
          AND
A: metronidazole (PO) 400mg 8hourly, for 5 to 7 days
          AND
A: paracetamol (PO) 1gm 8hourly for 3 - 5 days
          OR
A: ibuprofen (PO) 400mg 12-8 hourly (depending on severity pain) for 3 to 5 days.
          AND
A: ferrous sulfate + folic acid (FDC) (PO) 1 tab 24hourly for 4 weeks (if anemic)

Patient education.
     •   Counsel and educate the patient on possible reasons for abortion and future fertility
     •   Provide family planning counseling and give appropriate contraceptive method before the patient leaves the facility
         premises.
     •   Provide linkage to other reproductive and non-reproductive health services depending on patient needs

sections.title: Complete abortion
sections.text:
Abortion is said to be complete when the Products of conception are completely expelled

Clinical Presentation
          •   Minimal or no PV bleeding                                        •    The patient may be in Shock due to severe
          •   Uterus smaller than dates and often well                              bleeding
              contracted.                                                      •    Pharmacological Management
          •   Cervix may or may not be closed

Give hematinic if required also Give antibiotics If indicated
A: amoxicillin (PO) 500mg 8hourly for 5 - 7 days
         OR
B: amoxicillin + clavulanic acid (FDC) (PO) 625mg 12hourly for 5 - 7 days
         AND
A: metronidazole (PO) 400mg 8hourly for 5 - 7 days.

If patient is in shock;
     •    Shout for help and mobilize resources                           •    Insert an indwelling urethral catheter
     •    Apply ABCD principles of resuscitation                          •    Give ampicillin (IV) 1g and metronidazole (IV)
     •    Give A: sodium lactate compound (ringer’s                            500mg stat
          lactate)(IV) OR sodium chloride 0.9% (IV) 3 liters              •    Obtain blood for HB,
          or more in the first hour

Referral: Resuscitate the patient and refer to hospital with an escort of a nurse or clinician
Management in a hospital
         •   If patient is stable continue as above;
         •   If patient is in shock, perform as above and give blood transfusion if indicated

Patient Education
Provide counseling, education and FP services as in income plate abortion above

sections.title: Septic Abortion
sections.text:
Abortion is said to be septic when it is complicated by infections.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Moderate to severe Abdominal pain following                      •   May be in shock
          abortion                                                         •   Tender uterus with        or   without   rebound
     •    Fever may be present                                                 tenderness
     •    Foul smelling PV discharge which may be mixed                    •   Cervix is usually open
          with blood.
Management of septic abortion at the dispensary & health center
     •    Apply ABCD principles of resuscitation                           •   Insert an indwelling urethral catheter
     •    Give A: sodium lactate compound (ringer’s                        •   Obtain blood for Hb or FBC
          lactate)(IV) OR sodium chloride (IV) 0.9% in case                •   Perform Ultrasound if feasible
          of hypotension or shock. Avoid IV fluid in case of
          chronic anemia.

Pharmacological Management
Stabilize the client and start intravenous antibiotics immediately following one of the options below:

First line:
B: metronidazole (IV) 500mg 8-hourly for 24 - 48 hours
            AND
B: ceftriaxone (IV) 2gm 24hourly for 24 - 48 hours
            OR
C: amoxicillin + clavulanic acid (FDC) (IV) 1.2gm 12hourly for 24 - 48 hours
            AND
A: gentamicin 80mg (IV) 12hourly for 3-5 days

Second line:
B: metronidazole 500mg (IV) 8 hourly for 3 to 5 days then (PO) 400mg up to 10 days
          AND
C: ciprofloxacin (IV) 200mg to 400mg 12hourly for 3 to 5 days
          OR
D: ceftriaxone + sulbactam 1.5gm 24hourly for 3 to 5 days
Provide necessary pain medication.

Managed at a CEmONC facility as she may need laparotomy or blood transfusion (refer if non-CEmONC).
If products of conception are retained, evacuate as soon as possible

Referral: Resuscitate and immediately refer the patient to hospital with an escort of a nurse.
Management at the Hospital:
    •    Full Blood Count (FBC)
    •    Draw Blood for culture and susceptibility testing
    •    Check abdominal pelvic ultrasound as appropriate
    •    IV RL/NS depending on individual patient needs
    •    Give blood transfusion if indicated
    •    Evacuate the uterus with Dilatation and evacuation using atraumatic forceps (NOT SHARP CURETTAGE)

Give antibiotics and antipain as described above if indicated and when the patient is stable continue with;

A: metronidazole (PO) 400mg 8hourly for 7days
         AND
B: amoxicillin+ clavulanic acid (FDC) (PO) 625mg 12hourly for 7days
         AND
A: paracetamol (PO) 1g 8 hourly for 3 to 5 days

Patient Education
Counsel educate and provide appropriate contraceptive methods as per CPAC package

sections.title: Molar Pregnancy
sections.text:
A molar pregnancy is a gestational trophoblastic disease which grows into a mass in the uterus that has swollen chorionic villi.
These villi grow in clusters that resemble bunches of grapes. Once diagnosed it should be treated right away.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Vaginal bleeding                                                     •   Vaginal discharge of tissue that resemble grapes
     •    Uterus that is bigger than gestational age.                          •   Heavy PV bleeding when the mole abort
     •    Exaggerated pregnancy symptoms (Severe                                   spontaneously
          nausea and vomiting)
Management of Molar pregnancy at the dispensary and Health centers
     •    Apply Airway, Breathing, Circulation and Dehydration principles of resuscitation
     •    Check hemoglobin level
     •    If the patient is actively bleeding, catheterize, Establish Iv line and Give IV RL/NS 2lts at a rapid rate

Referral: Resuscitate and refer the patient to higher level facility with a nurse escort for appropriate management

Management of molar pregnancy at the Hospital
   •   Apply Airway, Breathing, Circulation and                            •    Infuse sodium lactate compound (ringer’s
       Dehydration principles of resuscitation                                  lactate)(IV) OR 0.9% sodium chloride (IV) as
   •   If the patient is patient is actively bleeding or in                     needed
       shock shout for help and mobilize resources                         •    Initiate blood transfusion if indicated
   •   Cheek HB, Blood grouping and Cross matching                         •    Perform suction curettage in operating theatre-
   •   Perform quantitative serum Beta Human                                    take endometrial sample for histopathology
       Chorionic Gonadotropin (bHCG)                                       •    Perform other investigations as appropriate
   •   Check abdominal pelvic Ultrasound to confirm                             (chest X ray, RFT, LFT, Chemistry panel)
       the diagnosis (Snowstorm appearance)

Follow up for Molar pregnancy after Molar Evacuation
     •  Check weekly bHCG until when it becomes normal (5-10mIU/ml) for 3 weeks consecutively
     •  Then check monthly bHCG and pelvic ultrasound for 12 months
     •  Advice the patient to use effective contraception during follow up as per guideline (preferably COCs)

sections.title: Missed Abortion
sections.text:
This happens when a Fetus less than 24weeks die in utero, but it’s not expelled out

Clinical Presentation
     •    History of amenorrhea                                            •    Uterine size smaller than dates
     •    Regression of the pregnancy symptoms                             •    Mild of no PV bleeding

Management of a missed abortion at the dispensary and Health center

Referral: Refer to higher level health facility with adequate expertise and diagnostics/equipment

Management of missed abortion at the hospital
Investigations
    •    Abdominal pelvic ultrasound
    •    Full blood count, Blood Grouping and cross matching
    •    Clotting indices (PT, APTT, INR)

Pharmacological Management
If the GA is less than 10 weeks (Including blighted ovum/anembryonic pregnancy)
C: mifepristone (PO) 200μg wait for 24 – 48 hours
          THEN
A: misoprostol (BU/SL/P) 800μg stat

If the GA is 10 -12 weeks
C: mifepristone (PO) 200μg wait for 24 – 48 hours
          THEN
A: misoprostol (BU/SL/PV) 800μg every 3 hours until expulsion

Alternatives for GA of 12 weeks or less perform MVA. (If cervical ripening is necessary, give
A: Misoprostol (Bu/SL/PV) 400μg 1-3 hours before the procedure).
If the GA is 13-17 weeks
C: mifepristone (PO) 200μg wait for 24 – 48 hours
          THEN
A: misoprostol (BU/SL/PV) 400μg every 3 hours until expulsion

If the GA is 18-24 weeks
C: mifepristone (PO) 200μg wait for 24–48 hours
          THEN
A: misoprostol (BU/SL/PV) 400μg 3hourly until expulsion

If the GA is 25-27 weeks
C: mifepristone (PO) 200μg wait for 24 – 48 hours
          THEN
A: Misoprostol (BU/SL/PV) 200μg 3hourly until expulsion
   Note Avoid misoprostol in case of previous uterine scar

Patient education.

sections.title: Ectopic Pregnancy
sections.text:
Ectopic pregnancy (EP) is defined as a pregnancy in which the implantation of the embryo occurs outside the uterine cavity,
most frequently in one of the two fallopian tubes or, rarely, in the abdominal cavity.

sections.title: Un-ruptured Ectopic Pregnancy
sections.text:
Clinical Presentation
     •    History of amenorrhea
     •    PV Sport bleeding in early pregnancy
     •    Unilateral Abdominopelvic pain. Unilateral(localized) abdominal tenderness

Management of Un-ruptured ectopic pregnancy
Referral: Patients should be referred to higher level facilities with equipment and expertise
At higher level facilities un-ruptured EP may be managed surgically or pharmacologically depending GA and available expertise

Pharmacological Management
S: methotrexate (IV) 50mg/M2 single dose (Maximum dose of 100mg in 24 hours)
           OR
S: methotrexate (PO) 1mg/Kg 24 hourly (Maximum dose of 100mg) for 5 days (in case IV methotrexate is not available)
           AND
S: folinic acid 0.1 mg/kg for 5 days

Perform weekly pelvic ultrasound to ensure regression of Gestation sac
Note: Laparoscopic procedure can be done in facility with expertise's and clear indications

 Note: Contraindications of methotrexate include a ruptured ectopic, ectopic mass greater than 3.5 cm, fetal cardiac
 activity, high level hCG value (10,000 IU), breastfeeding and immunodeficiency

sections.title: Ruptured Ectopic Pregnancy
sections.text:
Clinical Presentation
     •    History of amenorrhea
     •    Acute generalized abdominal-pelvic pain
     •    Hypotension
     •    Fast and weak pulse
     •    Abdominal distension and tenderness with rebound tenderness

Management of ruptured ectopic at the dispensary and Health Center (B-MONC facilities)
   •   Apply ABCD principles of resuscitation
   •   Perform abdominal pelvic ultrasound if available
   •   Check Hb
   •   Start sodium lactate compound (ringer’s lactate)(IV) OR 0.9% sodium chloride (IV) infuse at a rate of 500mls per hour

Referral: Ectopic pregnancy is an obstetric emergency, resuscitate and refer the patient immediately, with an escort by skilled
attendant.

Management of Ectopic pregnancy at the Hospital (C-EMONC facilities)

Investigations
    •    Abdominal pelvic/Transvaginal ultrasonography
    •    FBP or Hb level
    •    Grouping and cross-matching

Pharmacological Management
A: sodium lactate compound (ringer’s lactate)(IV)
         OR
A: sodium chloride 0.9% (IV) depending on amount of blood loss

Blood transfusion if indicated depending on the blood loss

Pre operative antibiotics
B: cefazolin (I/V) 1.5gm stat,
         OR
A: ampicillin (I/V) 2gm stat,
         AND
B: metronidazole (I/V) 500mg stat

Perform Emergency laparotomy

sections.title: Antepartum Hemorrhage
sections.text:
It is the bleeding from the birth canal after the 28th week of gestation but before the onset of labor. The main forms are placenta
previa and abruption placenta. Other rare cause may include VASA previa, heavy show and gynecological malignancies
(cervical cancer)

sections.title: Placenta Previa
sections.text:
It is an obstetric complication in which the placenta embeds itself partially or wholly in the lower segment of the uterus. It is an
obstetric emergency which should be managed in a facility offering CEMONC services

Clinical Presentation
Sudden onset of bright red fresh painless bleeding after 28weeks of gestation

Non- Pharmacological Management
    •   If partial Placenta Previa and asymptomatic –                       •    If ˃34weeks and no PV bleeding or contraction,
        Bed rest at home and follow up every 2 weeks                             expectant management
    •   If complete placenta previa then                                         •    Deliver by Cesarean section preferably at
        •    Admit for close monitoring and observation                               37–38 weeks of gestation
        •    Perform ultrasound to localize the placenta                         •    Deliver by caesarean section by C/S any
        •    Perform FBP, Coagulation tests, Blood                                    time in case of onset of labor or severe PV
             grouping and cross matching. Keep at least                               bleeding
             2 units of blood ready in the bank for
             transfusion in case of acute bleeding                          •    Partial or marginal placenta previa: Carefully
        •    Consider Blood transfusion if indicated                             perform amniotomy for vaginal delivery if the
                                                                                 head is engaged.
        •    Avoid vaginal digital examination

Pharmacological Management

A: nifedipine (PO) 20mg 8hourly until labor symptoms subside (consider blood pressure monitoring due to risk of
hypotension).
          AND
D: dexamethasone (PO) 6mg 12hourly for 48 hours if pregnancy is ˂34weeks for fetal lung maturation
          AND
A: magnesium sulfate as per protocol for protection of birth asphyxia and Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy complications
(Refer to eclampsia section).

sections.title: Placental Abruption
sections.text:
It is PV bleeding due to premature separation of a normally situated placenta in pregnancy after 28 weeks of gestation.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Vaginal bleeding of dark colored blood or clots. Sometimes bleeding can be concealed
     •    Abdominal pain is moderate to severe but may be absent in revealed AP
     •    The uterus may be enlarged and very tender or persistent-tetanic like contractions
     •    Fetal demise or fetal distress may be present

Management of Placenta Abruption at Dispensary and Health center.
   •   Apply the ABCD principles of resuscitation
   •   Insert large bore cannula IV line, start rapid infusion with RL/NS
   •   Insert Urethral catheter

Refer: resuscitate and refer immediately to the hospital with an escort of a skilled health attendant

Management of Placenta Abruption at the hospital Investigations
   •   Ultrasound: Fetal wellbeing, placenta localization and evidence of retro placental clot
   •   Full blood count and cross–match
   •   Renal function test, Liver function test and electrolytes
   •   Fibrinogen tests if available, D-dimer, PT, PTT, INR

 Note: The diagnosis of placental abruption is mainly clinical

Maternal resuscitation
    •   Apply the ABCD principles of resuscitation                          •    If Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation: Give
    •   Insert two (2) large bore IV lines and give Normal                       fresh frozen Plasma 1 Unit/hour, give whole
        Saline/Ringers Lactate. Replete crystalloids at                          blood 2–4 units
        ratio of 1 unit of blood loss: 3 unit of crystalloids               •    Monitor blood pressure, pulse, bleeding, hourly,
    •   Blood Transfusion is usually necessary                                   full blood count, clotting profile every 2 hours
    •   Give oxygen supplementation at a flow of 6L/min
    •   Insert a urinary catheter to monitor input/output

Obstetrical Management
    •    If the fetus is alive and viable: emergency Caesarean section
    •    If the fetus is dead: Normal vaginal delivery is preferable if no contraindication for vaginal delivery (e.g. uterine scar)
    •    Perform artificial rupture of membrane,

Pharmacological Management
If no spontaneous labor: induce with
A: oxytocin infusion 5IU in 500 ml sodium chloride 0.9% beginning with 10 drops/min increase the rate after every 20min until
optimal contractions are achieved.

     •    Do active management of third stage of labor and uterine massage
     •    Emergency Caesarean section should be considered if:
          > Worsening of maternal condition
          > Failure/Non progressing vaginal delivery

Prophylactic antibiotics
A: ampicillin (IV) 2g stat.
         OR
B: cefazolin 1g stat
         AND
B: metronidazole (IV) 500mg stat.
         OR
C: amoxicillin + clavulanic acid (FDC) (IV) 1.2g stat.
         AND
B: metronidazole (IV) 500mg stat.

sections.title: Obstructed Labor
sections.text:
Also known as labor dystocia, is when despite adequate uterine contractions the baby does not exit the pelvis during due to
being physically blocked. Obstructed may commonly be caused by; big baby, narrow maternal pelvis, malpresentation and
malposition.

Clinical Presentations
     •    Prolonged labor (˃8hours of active labor)                         •    Fetal distress
     •    Delayed second stage of labor (˃1hour)                            •    Severe molding (3+)

Management of obstructed labour at B-EMONC facilities
   •   Insert IV line with and start RL/ DNS infusion 2L                    •    Maternal dehydration (neglected obstructed
   •   Insert urethral catheter                                                  labour)
   •   Check Hb                                                             •    Bundle’s ring (sign of neglected obstructed
   •   Severe caput succedaneum                                                  labour)
                                                                            •    Encourage the patient to lay in left lateral position

Management of Obstructed labour at the C-EMONC facilities
   •   Optimize hydration by RL/NS 2lt before                               •    Perform emergency caesarean section.
       caesarean section                                                    •    Keep catheter for 3 or more days depending on
   •   Ensure the patient is catheterized,                                       assessment
   •   Perform FBP/Hb estimation

Pharmacological Management
                                                                                OR
A: sodium lactate compound (ringer’s lactate)(IV)/sodium               C: amoxicillin + clavulanic acid (FDC) (IV) 1.2g within
chloride (IV) 0.9% to ensure adequate hydration.                       30min before CS, continue 1.2gm 12 hourly for 3days.
          AND                                                                   AND
A: ampicillin (IV) 2g within 30m before CS, continue 1g                B: metronidazole (IV) 500mg within 30min before CS,
8hourly for 3days.                                                     continue 500mg 8hourly for 3days.
          OR                                                                    AND
B: ceftriaxone (IV) 1g stat within 30min before CS,                    A: gentamicin (IV) 80mg 12 hourly for 3-5 days
continue 1g 24hourly for 3days.

sections.title: Postpartum Hemorrhage (PPH)
sections.text:
It is abnormal uterine bleeding following delivery through 6 weeks (42 days). It is sub classified in to Primary and Secondary
PPH

sections.title: Primary Postpartum Haemorrhage
sections.text:
It is typically loss of more than 500 ml of blood from the genital tract after vaginal delivery or more than 1000 ml after Caesarean
section in the first 24 hours. OR it is any amount of blood loss after delivery that would result in hemodynamic instability.

Management of PPH at Dispensary and Health center
   •   Insert 2 large bore cannula IV line, start rapid                     •    Ensure no retained placental tissues
       infusion with sodium lactate compound (ringer’s                      •    Clamp or ligate bleeding perineal tears if any.
       lactate)or sodium chloride                                           •    Massage the uterus
   •   Start oxytocin (IV) 20IU in 500mls NS at a rate for                  •    Insert Urethral catheter
       20drops per minute

Referral: If bleeding continues, immediately refer the patient to the hospital with an escort of a skilled health attendant. Maintain
IV infusion during transfer.

Management of PPH at the hospital- at a comprehensive obstruction facility
   •   Shout for help and mobilize resources
   •   Obtain blood samples for Hb, blood grouping and cross matching
   •   Insert 2 large bore cannulas and start infusing compound sodium chloride or sodium chloride (IV) rapidly
   •   Blood Transfusion depending on amount of blood loss

Non-Pharmacological Management
Perform maneuvers like balloon tamponade, TAH, Iliac artery ligation, B-Lych suture including surgical interventions depending
on patient condition and available expertise.

Minimal invasive interventional radiology procedure
Uterine artery embolization for retractable hemorrhage PPH, when conventional medical and surgical measures fail, uterine
artery embolization (UAE) offers a life-saving, uterus-sparing alternative. Minimally invasive alternative to hysterectomy in
higher centers.

Pharmacological Management
Provide the “clinical care bundle- first response bundle for PPH”:
Start
A: oxytocin (IV) 20IU in 500mls sodium lactate compound (ringer’s lactate)or 0.9% sodium chloride (IV) titrate at 20 drops per
minute
          OR
A: misoprostol (PO) 1000mcg or per rectal
          AND
C: tranexamic acid (IV) 1gm bolus diluted in 20cc to give over 10 minutes. Repeat after 30 minutes if bleeding is still on-going
Prevention of PPH –Active management of Third Stage of Labour (AMSTL)
Ensure no remaining second twin

A: oxytocin (IM)10IU stat
          AND
(In High-risk women as per guidelines)
A: misoprostol (PO) 600mcg - 1200mcg stat
          OR
B: carbetocin 100mcg stat as 3rd line management after other interventions

Controlled cord traction (CCT) is recommended for vaginal births. Sustained uterine massage is not recommended as an
intervention to prevent PPH in women who have received prophylactic oxytocin.

Prevention of PPH in Cesarean section
Cord traction is the recommended method for the removal of the placenta in Cesarean section

A: oxytocin (IV/IM) 10IU (is the recommended uterotonic drug for the prevention of PPH plus MOTIVE bundle as per PPH
guidelines when indicated)
         OR
B: carbetocin (IV/IM) 100mcg stat as 3rd line management per guideline

sections.title: Prelabour Rupture of Membranes (PROM)
sections.text:
It is the rupture of membranes (breakage of the amniotic sac) before the onset of labor. If rupture occurs before 37weeks it is
called preterm prelabour rupture of membranes (PPROM). Prolonged PROM is a case of premature rupture of membranes in
which more than 24 hours have passed between the rupture and the onset of labour. Prolonged PROM for more than 18 hours
is a risk of ascending infection which can lead to chorioamnionitis (infection of chorion, amnion and amniotic fluid.

Clinical Presentation
Leakage of watery fluid per vagina confirmed by performing a sterile speculum examination.

Management of PROM at the dispensary and health center
Give the following antibiotics for prophylaxis against chorioamnionitis
A: erythromycin (PO) 500mg 8hourly for 7days
          AND
A: metronidazole (PO) 400mg 8hourly for 7days

Referral: Refer to the hospital for further evaluation and management

Management of PROM at the hospital
Investigations
    •    Ultrasound for fetal well-being, amount of liquor and gestation age.
    •    Perform a sterile speculum examination to confirm leakage
    •    Perform HVS for culture and susceptibility testing
    •    Urinalysis, screen for other infections

Pharmacological Management
If PROM at term: Delivery within 24 hours
Assess Bishop’s Score and Induce Labour accordingly with
A: misoprostol (PO) 25mcg 8hourly (Max 3doses) if unfavorable cervix.
          OR
A: oxytocin (IV) 5IU in 500ml of D5% titrate beginning with 10dpm if favorable cervix
Monitor FHR vigilantly during the process of IOL. Deliver by C/S if vaginal delivery is contraindicated, fetal distress or failed
induction of labour.

For Preterm PROM:
If no sign of infection, wait for foetal maturity and give
B: dexamethasone (IM) 6mg 12hourly for 48 hours if pregnancy is ˂34weeks for fetal lung maturation
           AND
A: magnesium sulfate for birth asphyxia and HIE complications protection as per protocol
           AND
A: nifedipine (PO) 20mg 8hourly for tocolysis (Consider blood pressure with risk of hypotension)
Monitor for infection (FBP, CRP, Pulse, Fever) and fetal wellbeing (fetal movement, FHR, obstetric ultrasound)

Administer prophylactic antibiotics
A: ampicillin (IV) 2gm stat
          THEN
A: erythromycin (PO) 500mg 8hourly for 7-10 days
          OR
B: amoxicillin + clavulanic acid (FDC) (PO) 625mg 8hourly for 7-10 days
          AND
A: metronidazole (PO) 400mg 8hourly 7-10 days.

Deliver irrespective of gestation age in case of infection

If there are signs of infections-pyrexia, foul smelling liquor (chorioamnionitis)
B: metronidazole (I/V) 500mg 8hourly for 24 hours
           THEN
A: metronidazole (PO) 400mg 8hourly for 5-7 days
           AND
B: ampicillin (I/V) 1gm 8hourly for 5-7 days
           OR
C: amoxicillin + clavulanic acid (FDC) (IV) 1.2g 12hourly for 5-7days
           OR
D: ceftriaxone + sulbactam (FDC) (IV) 1.5g 12hourly for 5-7 days

sections.title: Antenatal Care
sections.text:
The aim of the antenatal care is to provide a positive pregnancy experience that allows a positive transition to birth and
motherhood. Basic laboratory testing during antenatal care visits are as follows:
First visit:
Investigations
      •      Full blood count / Hemoglobin level                          •    Blood glucose by Oral glucose tolerance test or
      •      Blood grouping and Rhesus typing, (Indirect                       HbA1c or random blood sugar (RBG)
             coombs test for Rh-Negative mothers)                         •    Urine analysis
      •      Hepatitis B surface antigen screening (HBsAg)                •    Stool analysis
      •      Rapid plasma regains (RPR)/VDRL (For Positive                •    HIV (with partner as well)
             results, TPHA is recommended)                                •    Obstetric ultrasound (if available).
      •      Malaria rapid diagnostic test (MRDT) or Blood
             smear for malaria

Subsequent visits:
    •   Full blood count / Hemoglobin level                                 •    Obstetric ultrasound depending on Clinician’s
    •   Malaria rapid diagnostic test (MRDT) or Blood                            opinion/decision.
        smear for malaria                                                   •    HIV (with partner as well) after 3months from last
    •   Urine analysis                                                           test

sections.title: Anemia in Pregnancy
sections.text:
It is hemoglobin levels less than 11 g/dl in pregnancy. Mild anemia– hemoglobin: 8–11g/dl; Severe anemia– hemoglobin<7g/dl.
Iron deficiency anemia during pregnancy has been associated with an increased risk of low birth weight, preterm delivery and
perinatal mortality.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Tiredness, weakness, palpitations and dyspnea                     •    Intermittent claudication     (ache,      cramp,
     •    Exercise intolerance                                                   numbness or sense of fatigue)
     •    Pallor of skin and mucous membranes
     •    Dizziness, faintness, headache

  Note: Some patients with anemia in pregnancy may be asymptomatic

Investigations
    •    Full blood count and blood cross-match - red cell                  •    Stool and urine analysis
         morphology                                                         •    HIV test
    •    Red      blood     cell    electrophoresis     if                  •    MCA-PSV Doppler (For suspected fetal anemia)
         haemoglobinopathies suspected
    •    Blood smear for malaria

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Iron rich diet (fish, eggs, fruits and vegetables etc.)
    •  Prevent and early treatment of malaria
    •  Investigate and treat associated worm infestations

Pharmacological Management
Prophylaxis in Antenatal Care
A: ferrous sulfate (PO) 200mg 24hourly (60mg elemental iron and 0.4mg folic acid per day).
          OR
A: multiple micronutrient supplement (MMS) (PO) 1 tab/cap 24 hourly (Target is to give 60 mg of elemental Iron per day)

If Hb is <7g/dl in 1st and second trimester give:
A: ferrous sulphate + folic acid (FDC) (PO) 1 tab 12hourly for 4 weeks.
          OR
A: multiple micronutrient supplement (MMS) (PO) 1 tab/cap 24 hourly or 12hourly (Target is to give 90- 120 mg of elemental
Iron per day).

If HB is ˂7g/dl in 3rd trimester or in case of signs for severe anemia (features of heart failure)

Refer/admit the patient for blood transfusion at least 2 units of Packed RBCs

Continue with ferrous and folic acid, or multiple micronutrient supplementation (MMS) 1 tab/cap 12 hourly (Target is to give 90
120 mg of elemental Iron per day) as above after blood transfusion

  Note: Women at high risk for neural tube defect should receive high dose of folic acid (5mg 24hourly starting 3 months
  before pregnancy to 12 weeks of pregnancy. After 12 weeks, normal dose of 400mcg resumes).

sections.title: Hypertensive Disorders in Pregnancy
sections.text:
Hypertension is blood pressure (BP) 140/90 mmHg or greater, measured on two occasions at least four hours apart or elevated
systolic BP >30mmHg, or diastolic BP 15mmHg from the baseline.

sections.title: Chronic Hypertension
sections.text:
This is hypertension that is present at the booking visit or before 20 weeks or if the woman is already hypertensive before
conception. Most women with chronic hypertension are asymptomatic. New onset chronic hypertension should have further
evaluation to find underlying cause e.g., renal artery stenosis, chronic renal disease, Cushing syndrome etc.

Pharmacological Management
A: methyldopa (PO) 250–500mg 8hourly
          AND
A: nifedipine (PO) 20mg 12hourly

For eclampsia prophylaxis, consider adding:
A: acetylsalicylic acid 75 mg 24hourly
          AND
C: calcium + vitamin D 1 tab/1 cap 24hourly

sections.title: Pregnancy induced hypertension (gestational hypertension)
sections.text:
Gestational hypertension or pregnancy-induced hypertension (PIH) is the development of new hypertension in a pregnant
woman after 20 weeks of gestation without the presence of protein in the urine or other signs of preeclampsia. Usually
disappears within 12 weeks postpartum.

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Adequate rest at home and avoid strenuous activities
    •  Eat a normal balanced diet and plenty of oral fluids
    •  Schedule antenatal visits every 2 weeks up to 32 weeks and every week thereafter
    •  Recommend to deliver in the hospital and should be delivered at 37 completed weeks of gestation

Pharmacological Management
For mild hypertension 140–159 mmHg systolic and/or 90–109 mmHg diastolic.
A: methyldopa (PO) 250–500mg 8hourly
          OR
A: nifedipine (PO) 20mg 12hourly
          OR
C: labetalol (PO) 100mg 12hourly a day
          AND
(When indicated consider adding)

A: acetylsalicylic acid 75 mg 24 hourly
          AND
C: calcium + vitamin D 1 tab/1 cap 24 hourly

sections.title: Severe hypertension
sections.text:
Severe hypertension is Blood Pressure (BP) of 160/110 mmHg or higher. Admit the patient to hospital
A: methyldopa (PO) 500mg 8hourly
          AND
B: hydralazine 10mg (slow IV) stat (over 4-5 minutes); recheck the BP after 20 minutes if DBP is more/equal to 110mmHg give
another dose of hydralazine (IV slowly) 5–10mg.
          AND
A: nifedipine (PO) 20mg 12hourly
          OR
C: labetalol (PO)100mg 12hourly

Referral: Refer to the next level facility in case there is no improvement

sections.title: Pre-eclampsia
sections.text:
Is diagnosed when blood pressure is ≥ 140/90 mmHg after 20 weeks of pregnancy plus proteinuria of 300 mg per 24 hours or
>2+ on urine dipstick. Or elevation of BP in pregnancy with features of end organ damage (eg pulmonary edema, renal or liver
damage).
Diagnostic Criteria
     •   Most patients are asymptomatic, but symptoms may include headaches, dizziness, blurred vision, and epigastric pain.
     •   Blood pressure of ≥ 140/90 mmHg
     •   Proteinuria (≥ 300mg per 24 hours)
     •   Generalized edema may be present (not a necessary criteria)

Investigations
    •    Urine for Proteinuria (qualitative/quantitative 24-hour urine collection)
    •    Obstetric Ultrasound and biophysical profile
    •    Urea, creatinine, electrolytes, liver function test and uric acid
    •    FBP and clotting profile
    •    Fundoscopy

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Pregnancy < 37 weeks of gestation
    •  Hospitalization and close monitoring
    •  Bed rest
    •  Monitoring BP, urine output, proteinuria, fetal movement and fetal heart beats (every day)
    •  Pregnancy >37 weeks of gestation: admit and deliver accordingly.

Pre-eclampsia with Severe Features:
This is diagnosed when BP ≥ 160/110 mmHg (especially diastolic ≥110 mmHg), or BP of≥140/90mmHg with features of end
organ damage e. g severe headache, epigastric pain, blurring of vision +/_vomiting, pulmonary oedema, renal or liver damage,
features of hemolysis and low platelets.

Pharmacological Management
B: Hydralazine (IV) 5mg in 10ml sterile water over 4minutes’ initial dose. Followed by boluses 5–10mg as needed every 20
minutes until when the diastolic BP is less than 110mmHg)
           AND
A: methyldopa (PO) 500mg 8 hourly
           AND
A: nifedipine (PO) 20mg 8 hourly until BP is stabilized (Dosage should be monitored due to risk of Hypotension)
           OR
(if hypertension is refractory to hydralazine)

C: labetalol (IV bolus)10–20mg stat repeat each 10–20 minutes, with doubling doses not exceeding 80mg in any single dose
for maximum total cumulative dose of 300 mg.

Antenatal corticosteroids
B: dexamethasone (I.M) 6mg 12hourly for 48hours if the pregnancy is less than 34 weeks’ gestation and preterm delivery is
anticipated, to enhance fetal lung maturation.

Prophylaxis for Seizures
A: magnesium sulfate (IV) 1g hourly in 250 mililitre of Compound Ringers Lactate
         OR
A: magnesium sulfate (IV) 5g of 50% magnesium sulfate 4 hourly or alternate buttocks for 24 hours if GA is ≤34 weeks or until
24 hours post-delivery if GA is≥34 weeks (Refer to eclampsia section)

Obstetrical Management
If at term deliver immediately when stable, preferably vaginal delivery

sections.title: HELLP syndrome
sections.text:
It is a life-threatening complication of pre-eclampsia characterized by Haemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes and Low Platelets

Diagnostic criteria
Haemolysis
    •   Abnormal peripheral smear
    •   Total bilirubin > 1.2 mg/dL
    •   Lactic dehydrogenase > 600 U

Elevated Liver Functions
    •   Serum glutamic oxaloacetic transaminase > 70 U/L
    •   Lactic dehydrogenase > 600 U/L

Low Platelets
   •    Platelets < 1,000,000/mm3

Management of HELLP syndrome
The management is the same as for severe pre-eclampsia

sections.title: Eclampsia
sections.text:
Eclampsia is a condition peculiar to pregnancy and post-partum periods, characterized by elevated BP and tonic-clonic
convulsions which are not caused by epilepsy, severe malaria, meningitis, hypoglycemia or other causes of convulsions.
Majority (50%) occur preterm. Eclampsia may occur without prior elevation of BP.
Diagnostic Criteria
    •     Signs of severe pre-eclampsia (BP >160/110mm Hg)
    •     Loss of consciousness
    •     Tonic-clonic seizures, coma

Investigations
    •    Full blood count and crossmatch                                 •    Blood sugar estimation to exclude hypoglycemia.
    •    Clotting profile                                                •    Liver enzymes tests
    •    Ultrasound for GA and fetal viability                           •    Lamber puncture may be indicated to exclude
    •    Blood smear to exclude malaria                                       meningitis
    •    Urea and creatinine + electrolytes                              •    24h urine collection for proteinuria

Pharmacological Management
Manage with antihypertensives as in pre-eclampsia with severe features and magnesium sulfate (IV)

Loading dose: magnesium sulfate (IV) 4g of 20% slowly over 5minutes.

If having A: 50% magnesium sulfate, dilute it to make it A:20% magnesium sulfate by Drawing 8mls of 50% magnesium
sulfate by adding 12mls water for injection.
                   OR
     •    Draw 10mls (5gms) of 50% magnesium sulfate into each syringe 1ml of A: 2% lidocaine in each syringe then give
          deep IM into each buttock. Continue with maintenance dose until 24hours post-delivery or since the last episode of
          convulsion:
                   OR
     •    With magnesium sulfate infusion 1g per hour (in 200–300 ml of Ringer’s Lactate),
                   OR
     •    Magnesium sulfate 5g undiluted 50% of magnesium sulfate injection (add 1ml of lidocaine 2%) apply deep intra-
          muscular (IM) injection into each buttock every 4hrs for about 24 hours after delivery or the last seizure whichever
          come last.

If having 10% (W/V) A: magnesium sulfate Loading dose 4 gm = 4 ampules given direct I/V slowly for 30 minutes,
Maintenance dose 8gm = 8 Ampules in 500mls of R/L or N/S to run for 8 hours then repeat until 24 hours to make total of 3
doses in 24 hours.

 Note: The magnesium sulfate infusion should only be given if patellar reflexes are present, respiration rate is ≥ 12 per minute,
 and urine output is >100mls in 4 hours.

If convulsions recur within 15 minutes give;
A: magnesium sulfate 2g. Draw 4mls of 50% of magnesium sulfate (2gm), add 6mls of water for injection to make it 10mls of
20% magnesium sulfate then give IV slowly over 5 minutes.

If having 10% (W/V) magnesium sulfate
A: magnesium sulfate 2 gm = 2 ampules given direct I/V slowly for 30 minutes

Features of Magnesium Sulphate toxicity
    •   Respiratory depression (˂16cycles/min
    •   Reduced urine output(˂30mls/hour)
    •   Loss of deep tendon reflexes

In case of magnesium sulphate toxicity
     •   Stop magnesium sulphate administration
     •   Measure serum Magnesium level for monitoring progress if available
A: calcium gluconate (IV) 1g slow bolus in 2 to 3 minutes

Obstetrical management
Patients with eclampsia should be delivered within 12hours after the onset of seizures, even if the fetus is premature. Expectant
management is contraindicated. If not in labour, and no contraindications, induce labour with misoprostol according to uterotonic
and induction of labor protocols/guideline 50µg (PO), 4hourly or 25µg vaginally and repeat 6-8 hourly up to a total of four doses
maximum as per uterotonic guideline.
     •    If failure of induction or contraindication to vaginal delivery, immediate Caesarean section is indicated
     •    Recommend delivery at facility with neonatal care unit and prepare resuscitation for the new born as per protocol.

Prevention of pre-eclampsia and eclampsia
    •   Ensure effective antenatal care
    •   Calcium supplementation at doses of 1.5–2.0g elemental calcium/day for those at high risk of developing pre-
        eclampsia.
    •   Low-dose acetylsalicylic acid (aspirin, 75 mg) is recommended for the prevention of pre- eclampsia in women at high
        risk of developing pre-eclampsia.

sections.title: antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) in Pregnancy
sections.text:
It is an autoimmune disease characterized by the presence in maternal circulation of one or more auto antibodies against
membrane phospholipids. It is an acquired condition. Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) is characterized by venous or arterial
thrombosis and/or an adverse pregnancy outcome. APS occurs either as a primary condition or in the setting of an underlying
disease, usually systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).

Clinical Presentation
     •    Recurrent pregnancy adverse outcome e.g. (miscarriages) recurrent miscarriage, intrauterine growth restriction, early
          severe pre-eclampsia and preterm birth.
     •    Unexplained venous thrombosis (DVT) or arterial thrombosis (Stoke) or myocardial infarction
     •    Thrombocytopenia (common finding but among the clinical classification criteria)

Classification with APS requires one clinical and one laboratory manifestation:
Clinical manifestations
     •    A documented episode of arterial, venous, or small vessel thrombosis
     •    1 or more unexplained deaths of a morphologically normal fetus ≥ 10-week GA
     •    3 or more unexplained consecutive spontaneous abortions before the 10th weeks of GA with anatomic, hormonal or
          chromosomal causes excluded
     •    Eclampsia or severe pre-eclampsia according to standard definitions, or recognized features of placental insufficiency

Laboratory:
    •    Anti-cardiolipin IgG and/or IgM measured on 2 or more occasions, not less than 12 weeks apart;
    •    Anti-β2 glycoprotein I IgG and/or IgM measured on 2 or more occasions, not less than 12 weeks apart
    •    Lupus anticoagulant detected on 2 occasions not less than 12 weeks apart.

Pharmacological Management
A: acetylsalicylic acid (PO) 75-100mg 24hourly beginning as soon as the pregnancy is confirmed throughout pregnancy
          AND
C: unfractionated heparin (SC) 5000–10000 units 12hourly
          OR
D: low molecular weight heparin (SC) 30–40mg 24hourly

Patients with Thrombosis such as stroke or pulmonary embolism need therapeutic anticoagulation.
C: unfractionated heparin (SC) 5,000 bolus and subsequent 15,000–20,000 doses at 12hourly
intervals
          OR
D: low molecular weight heparin (SC) 1mg/kg 12hour
 Note: Warfarin should be avoided in pregnancy due to the risk of teratogenicity. The aPTT needs to be checked and is best
 done midway between the 12hourly doses, 24hourly. A target of 1.5-2.5 times the control should be aimed

Referral: Refer immediately to a level where expertise and monitoring for treatment through laboratory testing is available

sections.title: Deep Vein Thrombosis in Pregnancy
sections.text:
Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and acute pulmonary embolism (PE) are two manifestations of venous thromboembolism (VTE.
The risk of VTE is increased in pregnancy by about five times because of a more hyper-coagulable state. VTE contributes to
significant maternal morbidity and mortality. The mainstay of therapy for DVT is anticoagulation, provided there is no
contraindication.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Pain on the affected limb
     •    Swelling or redness of the calf or thigh
     •    Homan’s sign (pain in the calf in response to dorsiflexion of the foot)

Investigations
    •    Venous doppler ultrasound/Compression duplex ultrasound (CDUS)
    •    Venography (CT MRI)
    •    Fibrin degradation product (FDP) or D-dimer

Prevention of DVT
    •   Early passive and active ambulation in women undergoing major obstetric surgery
    •   Compressive stockings in women ≥100kg undergoing obstetric surgery
    •   LMWH prophylaxis 5000IU within 1-hour post-surgery to at risk women.
    •   For patient with swollen leg, elevation of leg plus elastic compression stocking help to reduce oedema

Pharmacological Management
C: unfractionated heparin (SC) 5,000 units bolus and subsequent 15,000–20,000 units doses at 12hourly intervals (under
supervision of a specialist)
          OR
D: low molecular weight heparin (SC) 1mg/kg 12hourly
          OR
C: warfarin (PO) 5mg 24hourly (in delivered women) consider bridging warfarin with Heparin for 5days as it takes longer to act.
Warfarin to be continued up to 6 weeks postpartum and continue with management as per DVT protocols

Minimally invasive interventional radiological procedure
    •   Catheter directed thrombolysis/thrombectomy
    •   Inferior Vena Cava filter placement

  Note:
  Check PTT every 4hours and PTT should be maintained at 1.5–2.5 X control. Once steady state has been achieved measure
  PTT levels daily. Change heparin to SC route after 5–10days

Referral: Immediate referral to a hospital with expertise and monitoring of the treatment through laboratory testing is
recommended [Refer to cardiovascular management protocol]

sections.title: Pulmonary Embolism in Pregnancy
sections.text:
It is a blockage, usually a blood clot that prevents oxygen from reaching the tissues of the lungs; it can be life-threatening

Diagnostic Criteria
    •   Acute onset of shortness of breath (dyspnea)                       •    Tachypnea
    •   Pleuritic chest pain                                               •    Diminished oxygen saturation
    •   Cough and/or hemoptysis                                            •    Diminished breath sounds
    •   Low grade fever

Investigations
    •    Venous Doppler ultrasound/Compression duplex                      •    CT scan,
         ultrasound (CDUS)                                                 •    MRI
    •    Pulmonary angiography                                             •    D-dimer
    •    Electrocardiogram (ECG)                                           •    Bleeding indices (PT, aPTT, INR)
    •    ECHO
    •    Chest X-ray (CXR) performed

Non-Pharmacological Management
Respiratory support and Oxygen supplementation

Pharmacological Management

C: unfractionated heparin (UFH) is the treatment of choice Loading dose 150 U/kg (or minimum of 5000 U) followed by Initial
infusion 15–25 U/kg/hour (or minimum of 1000U/hourly)
          OR
D: low molecular weight heparin (SC) 1mg/kg 12hourly
Referral
Immediate referral to a health facility where expertise and monitoring of the treatment through laboratory tests is available is
recommended. [Refer to cardiovascular management protocol]

sections.title: Vomiting in Pregnancy and Hyperemesis Gravidarum
sections.text:
It is excessive nausea and vomiting in early pregnancy requiring hospital admission and rehydration.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Weight loss                                                       •    Dehydration
     •    Excessive nausea and vomiting typically in early                  •    Altered general status (fast pulse, restlessness)
          pregnancy
Investigations
     •    Full blood count                                                  •    Thyroid function tests
     •    Blood for urea, electrolytes and serum creatinine                 •    Obstetric ultrasound to exclude            multiple
     •    Urinalysis, micro urine and culture, ketonuria                         pregnancy and GTD
     •    Liver function tests                                              •    Helicobacter pylori stool antigen test

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Nil per oral (nothing by mouth) for 24–48 hrs.                       •    Emotional support
    •  Input/output monitoring for 24–48 hrs.                               •    Rest and Lifestyle adjustment
    •  Monitor electrolytes for 24hrs                                       •    Ensure adequate hydration
    •  Counselling and Reassurance                                          •    Frequent small carbohydrate meal

Pharmacological Management
A: sodium lactate compound (ringer’s lactate)with 5% dextrose
         AND
A: sodium chloride 0.9% according to daily needs and severity.
         AND
C: thiamine (vitamin B1) (IV)100mg 24hourly mix in intravenous rehydration solution
         AND
B: metoclopramide (IM) 5–10 mg 8hourly till vomiting stops.
         OR
A: promethazine (IM) 12.5 mg 12hourly a day
         OR
B: pyridoxine + doxylamine (FDC) (PO) 10mg/10mg 8hourly till vomiting stops
         OR
D: ondansetron (IV) 4mg stat then depending on severity of condition
Referral: Depends on the status of the patient, refer to a hospital if vomiting is intractable and if there is a need for high volume
replacement.

sections.title: Heartburn in Pregnancy
sections.text:
Heartburn (also called acid indigestion or acid reflux) is a burning sensation that often extends from the bottom of the breastbone
to the lower throat. It is caused by some of the hormonal and physical changes in pregnant women. exclude peptic ulcer disease
and enteric fever (Helicobacter pylori stool antigen test, stool for occult blood, and stool salmonella typhi testare indicated in
severe form)

Non-Pharmacological Management

Pregnant women should avoid:
    •    Food and beverages that cause gastrointestinal distress
    •    Tobacco and alcohol
    •    Do not eat big meals, instead eat several small meals throughout the day
    •    Drinking large quantities of fluids during meals
    •    Do not eat close to bedtime, they should give themselves 2–3 hours to digest food before they lie down
    •    Sleep propped up with several pillows or a wedge.
Pharmacological Management
A: compound magnesium trisilicate (PO) as needed until when the heartburn subsides.
         OR
A: omeprazole (PO) 20–40mg 24hourly
         OR
C: pantoprazole (PO) 40mg 24hourly

sections.title: Other Medical Disorders in Pregnancy and Gynecology
sections.text:
Other medical disorders in pregnancy/other gynecological disorders include diabetes mellitus, glucose intolerance, malaria,
HIV/AIDs complications, Pelvic Inflammatory Diseases (PID) etc. All these complications are discussed under specific disease
chapters.

sections.title: Hyperglycemia in Pregnancy
sections.text:
Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM) is any degree of glucose intolerance first recognized in pregnancy. Diabetes in pregnancy
refers to those with pre-existing diabetes, whether diagnosed or not.

Screening at first antenatal visit
Perform screening in all women at the first antenatal clinic attendance if they have:
   • BMI > 25 kg/m2                                               • family history of DM
   • previous history of GDM                                      • known impaired glucose tolerance/ impaired fasting
                                                                     glucose
   • previous big baby                                            • grand multipara
   • poor obstetric history                                          glycosuria.

Women in early pregnancy with levels of HbA1c≥6.5% or blood glucose levels fasting ≥7.0 mmol/l or two hours 75g OGTT
≥11.1 mmol/l which are diagnostic of diabetes should be treated as having diabetes in pregnancy. Women with HbA1c 6.0–
6.4%, fasting glucose 5.1– 6.9 mmol/l (92-125 mg/dl) or two-hour glucose 8.6–11.0 mmol/l (153-199 mg/dl) should be assessed
to determine the need for immediate home glucose monitoring and, if the diagnosis remains unclear, assessed for gestational
diabetes by 75 g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) at 24–28 weeks.

Screening later in Pregnancy
    •   All women with risk factors (see above) should have a 75gm OGTT at 16–20 weeks
    •   A fasting plasma glucose at 16–20 weeks is recommended in low-risk women OR where 75gm OGTT is not practically
        feasible.

Diagnostic criteria for Hyperglycemia in pregnancy
 Category                            Test                                    Plasma Glucose Level
                                         Fasting plasma glucose              ≥ 7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dL)

 Diabetes in Pregnancy (Overt            2-hour plasma glucose (75 g         ≥ 11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL)
 Diabetes)                               OGTT)
                                         Random plasma glucose               ≥ 11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL) in the presence of
                                                                             symptoms
                                         Fasting plasma glucose              5.1–6.9 mmol/L (92–125 mg/dL)

 Gestational Diabetes Mellitus           1-hour plasma glucose (75 g         ≥ 10.0 mmol/L (180 mg/dL)
 (GDM)                                   OGTT)
                                         2-hour plasma glucose (75 g         8.5–11.0 mmol/L (153–199 mg/dL)
                                         OGTT)

 Note: All women during pregnancy should not miss an opportunity to be screened for diabetes mellitus and be counselled
 on appropriate nutritional practice during pregnancy.

Non-Pharmacological Managements
All women intending to become pregnant should:
     •  Be encouraged to achieve excellent glycemic control using glucose monitoring of both
     •  Fasting and postprandial values
     •  Be prescribed high-dose (5mg) pre-pregnancy folate supplementation, continuing up to 12 weeks’ gestation
     •  Have an eye exam and be informed of the risk of developing and/or progression of diabetic retinopathy
     •  Have a kidney assessment (random urine albumin/creatinine ratio and serum creatinine) and referred if urine protein
        ≥ 1g.

A combined health-care team (obstetrician, diabetologist or internist, diabetes educator, pediatrician/neonatologist) is required.
Review SMBG, blood pressure and urine protein and ketones by dipstick at each visit and eye examination in each trimester.
Target glycaemia:
    •     Pre-prandial blood glucose 3.5–5.5mmol/L
    •     Postprandial blood glucose 5–7.5mmol/L

Lifestyle management is the preferred means of managing gestational diabetes.
        •   Diet is based on the principles of optimal nutrition and controlled weight gain. A carbohydrate-controlled meal plan
            that promotes adequate nutrition with appropriate weight gain, normoglycemia, and the absence of ketosis. Diet
            and nutrition therapy should be the first line of treatment offered together with other services.
        •   Exercise can be helpful in lowering BG levels: the most acceptable form of exercise for most women are walking
            in their normal daily routine OR a planned 30mins/day brisk walking.

Glucose-lowering therapy should be considered in addition to diet + exercise where fasting or two hours glucose levels are
above target, for example, where two or more values per fortnight are:
        •    fasting or pre-prandial ≥5.5 mmol/L, or two hours postprandial ≥7 mmol/L at ≤35 weeks
        •    fasting or pre-prandial ≥5.5 mmol/L, or two hours postprandial ≥8 mmol/L at >35 weeks
        •    any postprandial values are >9 mmol/L.

When pharmacologic treatment of gestational diabetes is indicated, insulin and oral medications are equivalent in efficacy, and
either can be an appropriate first-line therapy.

Insulin should be considered as the ﬁrst-line treatment in women with GDM who are at high risk of failing on oral anti-diabetic
drug therapy, including some of the following factors:
        •    Diagnosis of diabetes <20 weeks of gestation                     •   1-hour postprandial glucose >140 mg/dL (7.8
        •    Need for pharmacologic therapy >30 weeks                             mmol/dl)
        •    Fasting plasma glucose levels >110 mg/dL                         •   Pregnancy weight gain >12 kg
             (6.1mmol/dl)

Pharmacological Management
A: metformin 500mg 12hourly, maximum 2000mg in 2–3 doses
         OR
A: glibenclamide 2.5mg 24hourly to a maximum of 10mg daily

  Note
  Oral hypoglycemics (except for metformin and glibenclamide) are contraindicated in pregnancy

  Insulin
  The rapid-acting insulin analogs (lispro and aspart) lower postprandial blood glucose and decrease the risk of nocturnal
  hypoglycemia. Patients on lispro and aspart prior to conception may continue them during pregnancy. Patients on regular
  insulin may be switched to lispro or aspart if 1–hour postprandial blood glucose levels are above target and/or the patient
  is also experiencing pre-meal or nocturnal hypoglycemia.
Postnatal Follow Up
         •   Women with gestational diabetes should be screened at 6–12 weeks postnatal to ensure return to normal glucose
             tolerance. Thereafter, a 1–2 yearly follow up is recommended.
         •   Metformin AND glibenclamide may be used even if a woman is breastfeeding.
         •   Encourage women to breastfeed.
         •   If retinopathy, check eyes 1 year postpartum

Family planning – this should be based on the medical eligibility criteria (category 1 for all the methods, unless when has
vascular changes – COC and DMPA category 3)

Breastfeeding – Women should be supported to breastfeed. It helps with postpartum weight loss, prevention of hypoglycemia
and incidence of childhood obesity.

Infections – They have ↑ risk for genitourinary, uterine, surgical site infections. Mastitis breast abscess - because large-sized
neonates do not suckle well. Should have a high index of suspicion for early identification and management of infections.

sections.title: Pelvic congestion syndrome/pelvic chronic pain
sections.text:
A chronic condition caused by venous insufficiency of the ovarian and pelvic veins.

Clinical condition
         •  Typically affects women of childbearing age, especially multiparous women.
         •  Presents with non-cyclic pelvic pain, often worsened by: prolonged standing, menstruation, sexual intercourse
            (dyspareunia), and post-coital ache

Minimally invasive interventional radiology procedure
Ovarian vein embolization
Ideal candidates:
        •   Chronic pelvic pain >6 months
        •   Dilated ovarian/pelvic veins on imaging (US/MRI/CT)
        •   Negative work-up for other causes (gynecologic, urologic, GI)
Diagnosis aided by:
       •    Transvaginal Doppler US: Dilated veins >5 mm, reversed/slow flow
       •    MR or CT venography
       •    Venography during procedure is gold standard

sections.title: Stimulation of Labour and Myometrial Relaxation
sections.text:
Myometrium stimulants should be used with great care before delivery especially in porous women. Use in obstructed labour
should be avoided

Oxytocics are indicated for: –
       •    Augmentation of labour                                                •    Uterine stimulation after delivery for
       •    Induction of labour                                                        management of PPH due to uterine atony
       •    Active management of third stage of labour.

Induction of Labour Indications/Contraindications
        •   The indication for induction must be documented, and discussion should include reason for induction, method of
            induction, and risks, including failure to achieve labour and possible increased risk of Caesarean section.
        •   If induction of labour is unsuccessful, the indication and method of induction should be re- evaluated.

Pre-induction assessment
       •    Health care providers should assess the cervix (using the bishop score) to determine the likelihood of success
            and to select the appropriate method of induction.
       •    The bishop score should be documented.
       •    Care providers need to consider that induction of women with an unfavorable cervix is associated with a higher
            failure rate and increased rate of operative deliveries.

Post-dates induction
       •    Women should be offered induction of labour between 41+0 and 42+0 weeks as this intervention may reduce
            perinatal mortality and meconium aspiration syndrome without increasing the Caesarean section rate
       •    Women who chose to delay induction >41+0 weeks should undergo twice-weekly assessment for fetal wellbeing

Options for Cervical Ripening/Induction: Unfavorable Cervix
       •    Intracervical Foley catheters are acceptable agents that are safe both in the setting of a vaginal birth after
            Caesarean section and in the outpatient setting
       •    Double lumen catheters may be considered a second-line alternative

Pharmacological Treatment
A: misoprostol (PO) 25µg 2hourly for 24hours or Misoprostol (PV) 25µg 6hourly for 24hours can be considered a safe and
