effective agent for labour induction with intact membranes and on an inpatient basis.

 Note:
     •        Misoprostol should not be used in the setting of vaginal birth after Caesarean section due to the increased risk of
              uterine rupture.
      •       Oxytocin should be started no earlier than 4hours after the last dose of misoprostol.
Options for induction with a favorable cervix
         •     Amniotomy should be reserved for women with a favorable cervix. Care should be given in the case of unengaged
               presentation because there is a risk of cord prolapse.
         •     After amniotomy, oxytocin should be commenced early in order to establish labour. • In the setting of ruptured
               membranes at term, oxytocin should be considered before expectant management.
         •     Women positive for group B streptococcus (GBS) should be started on oxytocin as early as possible after ruptured
               membranes in order to establish labour within 24 hours.
         •     Both high- and low-dose oxytocin may be considered within a hospital protocol.
         •     Because of the various concentrations, oxytocin infusion rates should always be recorded in mU/min rather than
               mL/hr.
         •     Oxytocin induction maybe considered in the hospital setting of vaginal birth after Caesarean section.
         •     For induction of labour use: Oxytocin IV, the dose will depend on parity
Primigravida
A: oxytocin (IV) 5IU in 500mls of 0.9% sodium chloride the initial dose should be 8-10drops/Minute, the titration may be gradually
increased at intervals not shorter than 20 minutes and increments of not more than 5drops/minute, until a contraction pattern
similar to that of normal labour is established. The recommended maximum rate is 40d/m.

Multiparous
A: oxytocin (IV) start with low dose (e.g., 2.5IU in 500mls of fluid titrate as above. Regulate the dose according to response.)
  Note
          •   Induction of labour with uterotonic drugs requires vigilant monitoring
          •   Induction of labour should only be attempted at hospitals with capacity to perform Caesarea section
Augmentation of Labour
If labour progress is not optimum labour augmentation is necessary. Can be achieved by:
A: oxytocin as above
            OR
Artificial rupture of membranes (ARM) and oxytocin. If membranes are already ruptured and no labour progress the steps
above should be followed; rule out obstruction before augmenting labour with oxytocin.

Myometrial stimulation after delivery

A: oxytocin (IM) 10IU after delivery of the infant; when no response give oxytocin (IV infusion) 20 units in 500mls of NS
running at 10–20 drops per minute.

After delivery consider maintaining myometrium contractility by the use of MOTIVE bundle as per uterotonic guideline

Myometrium relaxation (Tocolysis)
It is done to relax the uterus in order to:
       •   Relieve fetal distress immediately prior to                    •    Stop uterine contractions in premature labour
           Caesarian section                                              •    Perform external cephalic version
       •   Prevent uterine rupture

Pharmacological Management
A: nifedipine (PO) 20 mg stat, followed by 10–20mg 6–8hourly
          OR
A: salbutamol (PO) 4mg stat, when required (maximum daily dose 3
 Note
       •    β -stimulants should never be used if the patient had an antepartum hemorrhage
       •    β -stimulants are contra-indicated for cardiac disease and severe anemia in pregnancy

sections.title: Trial of Labor after Cesarean (TOLAC)/Vaginal Birth after Cesarean (VBAC).
sections.text:
Trial of Labor after Cesarean (TOLAC) is the planned attempt to deliver vaginally in a woman with a history of one prior cesarean
delivery. A successful TOLAC is referred to as Vaginal Birth after Cesarean (VBAC).

Eligibility Criteria for TOLAC
Single prior low-transverse cesarean scar, Singleton pregnancy, Cephalic presentation, Term gestation (≥37 weeks), Clinically
adequate pelvis, No contraindications to vaginal birth, Efw less than 3.5kgs

Contraindications to TOLAC
Prior classical (vertical) or T-shaped uterine incision, History of uterine rupture, Prior extensive uterine surgery (e.g.,
myomectomy involving the endometrial cavity), Placenta previa or other contraindications to labor ≥2 previous cesarean
deliveries with no prior vaginal delivery, Patient declines VBAC after counseling

Intrapartum Management of TOLAC

1. Pre-labor Counseling
          •   Discuss risks and benefits of VBAC vs. elective repeat cesarean delivery (ERCD)
          •   Highlight ~70–75% success rate of TOLAC in appropriate candidates
          •   Uterine rupture risk: 0.5–0.9% with one prior low-transverse scar
2. Timing of Delivery
          •   Await spontaneous labor up to 41 weeks in the absence of maternal/fetal complications
          •   Mechanical induction (e.g., Foley catheter) may be considered after 41-week
              Misoprostol is contraindicated due to high rupture risk
3. Labor Monitoring
          •   Continuous electronic fetal monitoring (EFM) is recommended
          •   Close monitoring of uterine activity(contractions) you can use CTG if available
          •   Early recognition of signs of uterine rupture: fetal bradycardia, loss of station, sudden abdominal pain
4. Labor Augmentation
          •   Low-dose oxytocin augmentation may be used with caution if labor stalls after spontaneous onset
          •   Avoid high-dose protocols
5. Preparation for Emergency Cesarean
          •   Ensure immediate surgical and anesthesia backup
          •   Informed consent and blood availability
6. Potential Complications
          •   Uterine rupture, Scar dehiscence, Postpartum hemorrhage, Birth asphyxia or neonatal encephalopathy

 Note: Risk of uterine rupture is higher with induced labor and with shorter underdeliver intervals (<18 months)

Postpartum Follow-Up
         •   Monitor for signs of hemorrhage and uterine tenderness
         •   Discuss outcome of delivery and implications for future pregnancies
         •   Emphasize importance of early ANC attendance in subsequent pregnancies
         •   Consider family planning counseling
         •   Advise hospital delivery in future pregnancies, preferably by 36–37 weeks to avoid unmonitored labor at home
Key Evidence Summary
TOLAC should be offered in Hospitals with readiness to offer emergency cesarean delivery, with access to surgical and
neonatal support. VBAC has a high success rate, especially with a previous vaginal delivery.

sections.title: Rhesus Incompatibility
sections.text:
Incompatibility between an infant’s blood type and that of its mother, resulting in destruction of the infant’s red blood cells
(hemolytic anemia) during pregnancy and after birth by antibodies from its mother’s blood circulation.

Investigations
    •    Maternal Blood group+ Rhesus factor
    •    Paternal blood group+ Rhesus factor
    •    Infant Cord blood at delivery for grouping, FBC, Coombs test to detect maternal antibodies and Total Bilirubin

Prevention of Rhesus isoimmunization
If the mother is Rhesus negative give
C: recombinant Monoclonal anti D immunoglobulin 300 microgram (IM) within 72 hours of delivery

Antepartum
C: recombinant monoclonal anti D immunoglobulin 300 microgram (IM) at 28-32weeks of gestation

Abortion in Rhesus negative mother give
C: recombinant monoclonal anti D immunoglobulin 300 microgram (IM) within 72hours of abortion

 Note: For the management of other medical conditions in pregnancy e.g. Malaria, Peripartum cardiomyopathy, Diabetes
 and Renal disease in pregnancy refer to specific chapters in this guideline.

sections.title: Mastitis
sections.text:
It is the inflammation of the breast usually associated with breastfeeding mostly caused by Staphylococcus                  aureus,
Streptococcus pyogenes

Clinical Presentation
Fever, headache, breast pain, body malaise, burning sensation, swelling, Redness, hard lump with tenderness, warmth, acute
lymphadenitis in armpit, no nipple retraction.

Non-pharmacological Treatment
       •   Increase breastfeeding, warm compression,
       •   Emptying breastfeed by using pump to reduce pressure
       •   Elevate the breast/Breast support by using pump
       •   Elevate the breast by using breast support

Pharmacological Management

Mild form, Oral antibiotics and Antipain                               Severe form, Admission and parenteral antibiotics/antipain
B: amoxicillin + clavulanic acid (FDC)(PO) 625mg 12hourly              B: amoxicillin + clavulanic acid (FDC) (IV)1.2gm 12 hourly
for 5-7days                                                            for 2-5 days then Oral
          OR                                                                     AND
C: flucloxacillin + amoxicillin (FDC) (PO) 500mg 12hourly              B: metronidazole (IV) 500mg 8 hourly for 2-5 days then
for 5-7days                                                            Oral
          AND                                                                    AND
A: ibuprofen (PO) 400mg 8hourly for 5days                              D: paracetamol (IV) 1gm 8 hourly for 1-2 days then Oral
          OR                                                                     OR
A: paracetamol (PO) 500–1000mg 8hourly for 5days                       A: diclofenac (75mg) (I/M or I/V) for 1-2 days then Oral

sections.title: Puerperal Sepsis
sections.text:
It is the infection of the uterus, surrounding tissues and lower genital parts within 6 weeks postpartum manifesting as postpartum
metritis, postpartum endometritis parametritis, peritonitis or septicaemia. Commonly caused by Anaerobes, Aerobes, MRSA

Clinical Presentation
          •   Fever (Hyper and Hypothermia),                                 •     Incisional site discharge,
          •   Lower abdominal pain,                                          •    subcutaneous hematoma,
          •   headache,                                                      •    Temperature raises
          •   body malaise,                                                  •    Low, Tachycardia,
          •   backache,                                                      •    Tenderness,
          •   foul smelling vaginal discharge,                               •    involuted uterus,
          •   diarrhea,                                                      •    Surgical site infection,
          •   infected perineal tear with redness,                           •    redness, wound discharge

Investigations
         •   Full blood picture/HB and Cross Matching
         •   Check LFT, RFT, Electrolytes
         •   Blood culture in case of suspected septicaemia
         •   Abdominal pelvic ultrasound
         •   Urinalysis

Management of Puerperal sepsis at Dispensary and Health Center

Pharmacological Management
Establish IV line and give
A: compound sodium lactate
          AND
A: sodium chloride 0.9% 2l then continue as required
          AND
B: amoxicillin + Clavulanic acid (FDC) (PO) 625 12hourly for 5days
          AND
A: metronidazole (PO) 400mg 8hourly for 5days
          AND
A: gentamicin (IV) 80mg 12hourly for 24-48hours.

Referral: resuscitate and refer immediately to hospital for further investigations and management.

Management of puerperal sepsis at the hospital
Note: Start with Triple therapy
Mild form: - (Two oral antibiotics and I/V Gentamicin)

Severe form: - commonly presents with Hypotension, Tachycardia HR->100/min, Temp >38, Peritonitis, Shock, Organ failure,
abscesses, RPOC, fluid in the pouch of douglas, hydronephrosis, altered mental status, and rebound tenderness
         •   Blood transfusion in anemic
         •   Continue with the above antibiotic for 5-7 days:

When to do Surgical interventions/Laparotomy: -
Presence of RPOC-Evacuation, generalized peritonitis, abscess, no improvement after 48 hours on proposed conservative
management, use physical examination and ultrasound to detect fluid in the peritoneal cavity, Consider Drainage to monitor
progress

Note: Culdocentesis and Paracentesis are not recommended, use physical examination and Ultrasound to detect fluid in
the peritoneal cavity or abscess

Pharmacological Management

B: metronidazole (IV) 500mg 8hourly for 5-7days
          AND
D: ceftriaxone + sulbactam (FDC) (IV) 1.5g 12hourly for 5-7 days
          OR
C: amoxicillin + clavulanic acid (FDC) (IV) 1.2gm 12hourly for 5-7 days

Consider Culture and Sensitivity to align with AMR/MDR, adjust drugs depending on the susceptibility test results or if not
available and there is no improvement after 3 days of treatment with above antibiotics switch to

S: piperacillin + tazobactam (FDC) (IV) 4.5g 6-8hourly for 5-7days
         OR
S: imipenem + cilastatin (FDC) (IV) 1g 8hourly for 5 - 7 days

Prevent Puerperal infections by
Observation of aseptic technique when performing all obstetric procedures including Pelvic examinations during labour.
Administration of prophylactic parenteral antibiotics within 30 minutes before performing a Caesarean section or manual
removal of Placenta, PROM more than 8 hours, PPH patients, avoid unnecessary cauterization
B: metronidazole (IV) 500mg stat
          AND
A: ampicillin (IV) 2g stat
          OR
C: cefazolin 1g stat
          OR
C: amoxicillin + clavulanic acid (FDC)(IV) 1.2g stat
          OR
D: ceftriaxone + sulbactam (FDC) (IV)1.5g stat

sections.title: Abnormal Uterine Bleeding (AUB)
sections.text:
It is the uterine bleeding in perimenopausal periods or abnormally heavy and or prolonged menstrual bleeding. Abnormal
uterine bleeding (AUB) is a common condition affecting women that has significant social and economic impact.

The causes of AUB are classified and summarized into an Acronym; PALM-COEIN
        •   P-Polyps                                               •   O-Ovulatory dysfunction
        •   A-Adenomyosis                                          •   E-endometrial causes
        •   L-Leiomyoma                                            •   I-Iatrogenic
        •   M-Malignancy                                           •   N-Not yet Classified
        •   C-Coagulopathy

Clinical Presentation
Polyps
Abnormal vaginal discharge, Pelvic pain, Pelvic/Vaginal heaviness, Uterine bleeding, Tenderness, Mass felt per abdomen,
Mass protruding through the cervix, Bulky-soft uterus
Adenomyosis
Heavy menses, prolongation of menses, painful menses, premenstrual pain, intermenstrual bleeding, pain during sexual
intercourse, bloating, Bulky uterus with softness, tenderness on touch

Leiomyoma
Heavy and/or prolongation of menses, painful menses, Abdominal mass with irregular margins and distension, Bulky uterus
with softness or firm,
Malignancy
      •  Presentation depends on type of malignancy                     •    Foul smelling bloody or mucoid vaginal
      •  Abnormal intermenstrual or postmenopausal                           discharge
         contact bleeding (cervical cancer)                             •    Weight loss, loss of appetite, early satiety

Note: Refer to specific gynecological malignancy

Coagulopathy
      •    History of bleeding tendencies       ∙
      •    Heavy and or prolonged menstruation
      •    Easy bruises, puncture site, petechial hemorrhage, fresh/non clotting bleeding
Anovulatory dysfunction
      •    Irregular bleeding, often heavy      ∙
      •    Infertility or subfertility
      •    Heavy/prolongation of menses, common on age extremity (Young and elderly), periods of amenorrhea, painful
           menses
Endometrial causes
      •    Heavy or prolonged menstruation
      •    Irregular menstruation associated with endometrial hyperplasia
      •    Common in advanced age, diabetic, obesity and low/null parity women
Investigations
      •    Investigate according to the possible cause of                 •    Examination under anaesthesia and biopsy in
           AUB basing on clinical suspicion                                    case of malignancy
      •    A complete blood count (CBC)                                   •    Cervical and vaginal swab
      •    Pregnancy test in reproductive age to exclude                  •    Abdominal pelvic Ultrasound, CT scan, MRI,
           pregnancy                                                           Xray as indicated
      •    LFT, RFT, Electrolytes
      •    Hysteroscopy, Cystoscopy, Proctoscopy in case of suspected malignancy

Pharmacological Management

Treatment will depend on the causative factor.
        •     Biopsy in case of suspected malignancy
        •     Specific Tumor markers in certain suspected malignancies e.g., ovarian tumors.
        •     Testing for coagulation disorders should be considered only in women who have a history of heavy menstrual
              bleeding beginning at menarche or who have a personal or family history of abnormal bleeding

C: tranexamic acid (PO) 500 –1000mg 6–8hourly as required until the bleeding is controlled
          OR
A: ethinylestradiol 30mcg+ Levonorgestrel 150mcg (PO) Useful for anovulatory bleeding.
          OR
A: medroxyprogesterone acetate (PO) 5–10mg 24hourly for 10–14days initially and repeated for 10days each month thereafter
          OR
C: norethisterone (PO) 5mg 24hourly for 10days. Then 5mg 12hourly from days (5 of cycle to 19) 19 to 26 of the two subsequent
cycles, should be given to prevent recurrence of the condition.
          OR
S. dydrogesterone 10mg to 20mg from 5th day for 14 days for 3 cycles.

 Note: In severe form, Combination of Tranexamic acid and Progesterone (Norethisterone or dydrogesterone) is recommended.

B: levonorgestrel intrauterine system (LNG-IUS)

GnRH analogs (pre-surgery or for temporary shrinkage),
S: leuprolide (GnRH agonist) 3.75 mg IM every 4 weeks (limit to 6 months pre-surgery).

Surgical management
AUB due to organic causes may be amenable to surgical intervention. The decision regarding the approach and the timing for
surgical intervention should depend on final diagnosis, expertise and other resources. Evacuation (D&C) is contraindicated
unless specific for diagnostic biopsy like endometrial polyp/hyperplasia following risk of endometrial synechiae (Asherman
syndrome)

Minimally invasive interventional radiology procedure
Uterine fibroid embolization

Referral: Immediately refer to the next level facility with capable for appropriate evaluation and management is recommend

sections.title: Dysmenorrhea
sections.text:
It is a painful menstruation preventing normal activities and requires medication. There are 2 types of dysmenorrhea:

Primary (no organic cause). Typically, pain occurs on the first day of menses, usually about the time the flow begins, improves
with age, shortly after menarche.

Secondary (pathological cause) e.g., usually the pain is due to other underlying causes involving reproductive organs e.g.,
PID, endometriosis, etc. late on-set (72 hours and more) of menstrual cycle, low back pain

Pharmacological Treatment
A: ibuprofen (PO) 200–600mg 8hourly (maximum 2.4 g/day)
           OR
A: acetylsalicylic acid (PO) 300–600mg 4hourly
           OR
C: diclofenac (PO) 50–100mg 8–12hourly
           OR
B: mefenamic acid (PO) 500mg 8hourly
           AND
A: hyoscine butyl bromide (PO) 20mg 8hourly for 5days
           AND
C: norethisterone 5mg (PO) 24 hourly to start on 5th day of cycle for 14 days for 3 cycles, 10mg 24 hourly to start on day 5 of
cycle for 14 days for patient not responding well on small dose
           OR
S: dydrogesterone 10mg (PO) 24 hourly to start on 5th day of cycle for 14 days for 3 cycles, 20mg 24 hourly to start on day 5
of cycle for 14 days for patient not responding well on small dose.

sections.title: Endometriosis
sections.text:
It is the presence of endometrial glands and stroma in locations other than the uterine endometrium and musculature. The
common locations of endometriosis include the pelvis, small intestines, bowels, appendix, anterior abdominal wall and incision
scars

Clinical Presentation
          •   Chronic pelvic pain, lower back pain and rectal pain
          •   Dysmenorrhea
          •   Dyspareunia
          •   Dysfunctional uterine bleeding
          •   Infertility
Management of Endometriosis Dispensary and Health center

Pharmacological Management
A: ibuprofen (PO) 200–400mg 8hourly (maximum 2.4 g/day)
          OR
A: acetylsalicylic (PO) acid 300–600mg 4hourly
          OR
A: diclofenac (PO) 50–100mg 8–12hourly
          OR
B: mefenamic acid (PO) 500mg 8hourly
          OR
A: hyoscine butyl bromide (PO) 20mg 8hourly for 5days

Referral: Refer the patient with endometriosis to hospital for further investigations and management.

Management of endometriosis at Hospital level

Investigations
         •   Abdominal pelvic/transvaginal ultrasound                         •   MRI
         •   CT scan                                                          •   Laparoscopy

Pharmacological Management
A: ethinylestradiol 30mcg + levonorgestrel 150mcg (PO) 1 tab 24hourly for 3months, skip brown tablets (ferrous fumarate) if
not anemic
          OR
A: medroxyprogesterone acetate (IM) 300mg monthly for 6months.
          OR
S: danazol (PO) 200-400mg 12hourly depending on the severity, Consider the androgenic effect on long duration use
Continue with management to maintain amenorrhea.
          OR
S: goserelin (IM) 3.6mg monthly for 3 to 6 months
          OR
S: leuprolide acetate 3.75mg IM/SC monthly for 3-6months

sections.title: Short term Contraceptive Methods
sections.text:
Short-term hormonal contraceptives
Before initiating hormonal contraceptives:
          •     Check blood pressure
          •     Perform vaginal examination (to check normal size of uterus)
          •     Check for contraindications like deep vein thrombosis
Follow up:
          •     Instruct women to always inform the doctor or nurse that they are on contraceptives while attending clinic or
                hospital.
          •     Women on oral contraceptives need regular physical check-ups including blood pressure measurement every
                six months
          •     Need to withdraw Contraceptives in:
                     o    Pregnancy
                     o    Severe headaches especially associated with visual disturbances
                     o    Numbness or paresis of extremities
                     o    Unexplained chest pain or shortness of breath
                     o    Severe leg pains etc.
                     o    Deep vein thrombosis.

The recommended short-term hormonal contraceptives are:
A: ethinylestradiol 30mcg + norgestrel 300mcg (FDC) (PO) 24hourly
          OR
A: ethinylestradiol 30mcg + levonorgestrel 150mcg (FDC) (PO) 24hourly
          OR
A: ethinylestradiol 30mcg + desogestrell 150mcg (FDC) (PO) 24hourly
          OR
A: medroxyprogesterone acetate (IM) 150mg every three months
          OR
A: levonorgestrel (PO).30mcg 24hourly

 Note
     •     Take the first pill on the 5th day of menstruation and then continue every day without any interruptions
     •     Check blood sugar and hypertension after every 6 months
     •     Avoid use in women with severe hypertension and women without proven fertility

Post-coital contraception
The method is applicable mostly after rape and unprotected sexual intercourse where pregnancy is not desired. Within 3 days
(72 hours) of unprotected sexual intercourse, give:

A: levonorgestrel (PO) 1.5mg stat
         OR
A: levonorgestrel (PO) 0.75mg 12hourly. 2 doses
         OR
B: copper T 380A Intrauterine Contraception Device (IUCD) may also be used.

 Note: Emergency contraception should not be used as a routine method of contraception. Clients should be advised to
 use regular effective contraceptive methods of their choice.

Barrier methods (condoms)
    •    Male Condoms
    •    Female Condoms
    •    Correct use of both male and female condoms is required with every act of sexual intercourse for greatest
         effectiveness.

  Note: Condoms are the only contraceptives that can protect against both pregnancy and STIs

sections.title: Long-term Contraceptive methods
sections.text:
Implant Contraceptives
Implants are contraindicated to:
         •    Severe hypertension                                                 •    Sickle cell anaemia
         •    Thromboembolism                                                     •    Genital bleeding
         •    Active liver disease                                                •    Severe headaches

Pharmacological Management
A: etonogestrel 68mg in single silastic capsule with applicator is implanted in the left upper arm with local anesthesia. Is effective
for 3 years
          OR
A: levonorgestrel 75mg in two silastic capsules implanted subdermal in the left upper arm with local anesthesia. Is effective for
5 years and is recommended for women who have completed their family or are not ready for sterilization or those not able to
take estrogen-containing contraceptives.

 Note: Implants may be inserted during the immediate postpartum period, or after 4 weeks postpartum

Intrauterine Contraceptive Device
It is the device containing copper or Levonorgestrel that is inserted in the uterus to prevent pregnancy

B: CuT380A Intrauterine Contraception Device (IUCD) may also be used

It can be inserted during the immediate postpartum period, within 48hours postpartum or after 4 weeks postpartum

The contraindication to postpartum IUD includes
     •   Active postpartum haemorrhage
     •   Puerperal sepsis/chorioamnionitis, active PID
     •   Allergy to copper
     •   Period within 48 hours and 4 weeks
B: levonorgestrel releasing intrauterine device as optional for Copper T IUCD

 Note: Use the WHO Medical eligibility criteria (MEC) wheel on providing FP methods

sections.title: Permanent (surgical) Contraceptive Methods
sections.text:
The available permanent contraceptive options include;
    •    Bilateral tubal ligation (female sterilization) for women who will not want more children
    •    Laparoscopic BTL
    •    Vasectomy for men who will not want more children to be linked to urologist/surgeon

sections.title: Infertility
sections.text:
Infertility is a condition of the reproductive system defined by the failure to achieve a clinical pregnancy after 12 months or more
of regular unprotected sexual intercourse.
A detailed history taking, and physical examination are invaluable for the diagnosis for causes of infertility

Investigation: Not every fertility test will be done for every case.

Women:
For women, fertility testing may include basic gynaecological examination
    •   VDRL tests                                                      •        Hysteroscopy-for unexplained irregularity of
    •   Urine routine and microscopic                                            menses (AUB/oligomenorrhea/amenorrhea)
    •   Cervical mucus examination                                      •        Diagnostic laparoscopy- This test is only done
    •   Abdominal pelvic/Transvaginal USS                                        when symptoms point to possible endometriosis,
    •   HSG (hysterosalpingogram)for tubal patency                               as part of treatment for blocked fallopian tubes,
    •   Saline Infusion Sonohysterography (SIS) for                              or in some cases of unexplained infertility.
        tubal patency with use of ultrasound                            •        Hormonal profile- FSH, LH, TSH, AMH, T3 & T4,
                                                                                 Testosterone,     prolactin,    estradiol    and
                                                                                 progesterone.

Men:
Perform the following
     •   Semen analysis                                                     •    Scrotal ultrasound to exclude obstructive causes
     •   VDRL tests                                                              (Varicose veins)
     •   Hormonal profile-FSH, Testosterone,             but                •    Consider sperm donation when indicated under
         sometimes also LH, estradiol, or prolactin                              Assisted Reproductive Therapy

Treatment will depend on the underlying cause

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Weight reduction in obese clients.
    •  Educate the couple on the importance of having regular sexual intercourse during the fertile window
    •  Try to avoid smoking/excessive drinking
    •  Counsel regarding age-related fertility decline

Pharmacological Management
Ovulation stimulation;
C: clomiphene citrate (PO) 50mg 24hourly for 5days from the 2nd–5th day of menstruation. (Maximum 6 cycles)

For patients not responding on clomiphene citrate, consider
S: tamoxifen (PO) 20mg 24hourly for 5 days from 2nd day to 5th day of menstruation

 Note: Do follicular tracking uss start on day 10 for 28 days cycle, for longer cycles (e.g., 32 days), start around Day 12, For
 shorter cycles (e.g., 24 days), start around Day 8 and Serum progesterone as indicated

sections.title: Polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS)
sections.text:
A: metformin (PO) 500mg 24 hourly is used for PCOS treatment, alone or along with other fertility drugs. Dose adjustment
depends on indication
          AND
S: letrozole (PO) 2.5–5 mg 24 hourly for 5 days starting day 2–5 of the cycle

sections.title: Hyperprolactinemia
sections.text:
C: bromocriptine (PO) 2.5–5mg 24hourly until the prolactin level is within the normal range
         OR
S: cabergoline (PO) 0.25–0.5mg once or twice weekly initially then the dose is gradually increased monthly until prolactin levels
normalize. Doses of less than 3mg per week are usually enough to achieve this goal

sections.title: Hirsutism
sections.text:
C: spironolactone (PO) 25mg 24hourly in case of hyperandrogen
         AND
S: dydrogesterone (PO) 10mg 24hourly for 14 days starting on day 11 of menstrual cycle

Minimally invasive interventional radiology procedure
For Women: -Therapeutic Fallopian Tube Recanalization
For Men: -Varicocele embolization

Advanced reproductive therapy (ART) and special cases (IUI, IVF/ICSIS)
Should be done by trained fertility specialist at a facility well equipped with embryology and andrology laboratory. ART will follow
proper indication, inclusion criteria, pre-treatment diagnostic workup, lifestyle management, advice on 1st line treatment options
available

Ovulation induction:
C: clomiphene citrate or S: letrozole, or S: tamoxifen as described above
         AND
S: menotropin 75 IU (I.V) on alternate days 3rd day, tailored treatment to patient with risk of ovarian sensitivity such as age and
BMI
Subsequent dose should be reduced or increased aiming for 2 to maximally 3 dominant follicles

Monitoring:
Usually done on day 12 to 14 of cycle but earlier (around day 10) if concern for multiple follicular development
Assess endometrial thickness (ET), follicle size and number, decide the need for serum E2, serum progesterone, and serum
LH measurement
Repeat assessment as indicated until leading follicle ≥18mm and ET≥7mm
Assess mid-luteal phase progesterone unless ovulation was well established in previous cycles

S: human chorionic gonadotrophins, 5,000 unit on day 9 to 12 of cycle depending on length of cycle, perform urinary hCG when
leading follicle ≥18mm and ET ≥7mm unless spontaneous LH surge detected.

Insemination: Do a single insemination 24-36 hours after LH surge

Number of cycles: Offer 3-4 cycles of IUI provided adequate response to ovarian stimulation and suitable post-wash sperm
quality

IVF and ICSI are done with treatment protocols, this guideline highlights the steps and medications used

Indications
     •   Bilateral tubal blockage
     •   Severe Endometriosis                                               •    Poor ovarian reserve
     •   Unexplained infertility (After failed expectant                    •    Failed other infertility treatment
         management or failed IUI)

STEPS INVOLVED IN IVF/ICSI

I. Controlled Ovarian Stimulation Long protocol treatment (Using GnRH –agonist)
S: goserelin Acetate 3.6 mg (SC)
          OR
S: leuprolide Acetate 3.75mg (IM)

Short protocol treatment (Using GnRH – antagonist)
S: cetrorelix acetate 0.25 mg (SC)

Soft stimulation (Low dose FSH menotropin 10IU/KG/24 hours: FSH plus LH
S: lutropin hormone 10 IU/KG/24 hours in combination with clomiphene citrate, or letrozole as per protocol

II. Egg retrieval (Ultrasound–guided Ovum Pick-up) done in theater at 36 hours after the time of trigger with hCG. The WHO
Safety Checklist should be observed as in any other surgical procedures.
The Embryologist should immediately examine the aspirated fluid under microscope in theater to look for oocyte before
transferring to the IVF Lab

III. Fertilization and Embryo culture are done few hours after the egg retrieval using the culture media and incubator in a
tightly controlled IVF laboratory.
The embryologist should monitor the process of fertilization, embryos development and grading them according to how the
develop at each stage
The husband/partner should produce the sample on the day of the egg retrieval. The sperm sample is best produced by
masturbation. It is recommended that the husband/partner should abstain from intercourse (No ejaculation) for two days before
the egg retrieval in order to give a good sperm sample.

IV. Embryo Transfer done under trans abdominal Ultrasound and the patient should be advised to have a full bladder before
the procedure. The fertility specialist and Embryologist should discuss with the patient/couple on the number of embryos to be
transferred at once, based on the specific patient circumstances, age of the woman and quality & number of the embryos
available.
It should be noted that transferring more than one embryo carries the risks of multiple pregnancies (twins or triplets) which are
serious. As globally most of ART units are moving towards single embryo transfer, it is recommended to consider transferring
of single or two embryos

V. Luteal Phase Support achieved by supplementation of progesterone 400mg per vagina twice a day from the day of egg
retrieval and continued depending on indications

VI. Pregnancy test Serum beta-hCG should be tested 10-12 days after the embryo transfer. If the test is positive, repeat it
two days later to check the rise of beta- hCG. In case of rise of beta-hCG, booking for a date of the first ultrasound scan should
be done for six weeks later.
In case of negative pregnancy test, the patient/couple should be given a follow up appointment with a fertility specialist to
discuss the cycle and further management

Surgeries under Infertility cases should be done under specialist care with consideration for fertility sparing
modalities:
    •    Tubal surgery for Tubal blockage under laparoscopic or open surgery approach
    •    Myomectomy for uterine fibroids under laparoscopic or open surgery approach
    •    Ovarian drilling is a possible surgical treatment for PCOS–related infertility under laparoscopic or open surgery
         approach

Referral: Refer all patients with infertility to a gynecologist/super-specialist under infertility and ART

chapters.title: Sexually Transmitted Infections

sections.title: STIs/RTIs Management Approaches
sections.text:
Management of STIs/RTIs can be done in either of the following approaches:
   •   Aetiological laboratory approach: By identification of causative agents through laboratory methods and sensitivity
       pattern to the medicine to used, followed by disease- specific treatment.

    •     Aetiological clinical approach: By targeting disease treatment based on suspected causative agents diagnosed
          clinically. This is not appropriate at any health facility because of its demands on the clinical acumen of the service
          provider and the danger of incorrect diagnosis and, hence, insufficient treatment.

    •     Syndromic approach: This identifies clinical syndromes (symptoms and signs) followed by syndrome-specific
          treatment that targets causative agents which cause the syndrome.

Management of STIs/RTIs using Aetiological Laboratory Approach
It identifies causative agents through laboratory methods, followed by disease-specific treatment. This is the best approach to
be used at a Health Facility (HF) which has a Laboratory capable of doing the Laboratory Investigation and producing timely
result(s) so as to enable the clinician to prescribe medicine (s) according to the causative agent(s) and sensitivity pattern.

sections.title: Chlamydia
sections.text:
A common sexually transmitted infection caused by Chlamydia trachomatis, often asymptomatic but associated with significant
reproductive complications if untreated.

Clinical Presentation
     • Often asymptomatic, especially in women.
     • When symptomatic, may present as:
          o Urethral discharge, dysuria, urethral itching (men).
          o Vaginal discharge, burning urination, lower abdominal pain, dyspareunia (women).
          o Rectal pain, discharge, or bleeding (rectal infection).
          o Pharyngitis (rare, oropharyngeal infection).
Investigations
    •    Preferred: Nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) from urine or swabs (urethral, cervical, rectal, or oropharyngeal
         sites).
    •    If NAAT unavailable: Gram stain (limited sensitivity), culture, or ELISA where available.
    •    In resource-limited settings, syndromic management based on symptoms is recommended.

Pharmacological Management
Non-pregnant adults and adolescents                                  Pregnant and breastfeeding women
A: doxycycline (PO) 100mg 12hourly for 7 days                        A: azithromycin (PO) 1g single dose
          OR                                                                   OR
A: azithromycin (PO) 1g single dose                                  A: amoxicillin (PO) 500mg 8hourly for 7 days
                                                                               OR
                                                                     A: erythromycin (PO) 500mg 6hourly for 7 days
  Note:
      •     Counsel patients on sexual abstinence until treatment completion and consistent condom use.
      •     Partner notification and treatment are essential to prevent reinfection and reduce transmission.
      •     Follow-up is recommended if symptoms persist or reinfection is suspected.
      •     Test-of-cure is generally not required except in pregnancy, persistent symptoms, or suspected treatment failure.

sections.title: Gonorrhea
sections.text:
A sexually transmitted infection caused by the bacterium Neisseria gonorrhoeae, affecting the urogenital tract, rectum, pharynx,
and eyes.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Men: Urethral discharge, burning or painful                       •    Both sexes: Rectal pain/discharge (if anorectal
          urination,     itchy     urethra,   increased                          infection),    pharyngitis      (if   oropharyngeal
          frequency/urgency.                                                     infection), conjunctivitis (rare but severe).
     •    Women: Vaginal        discharge,      dysuria,                    •    Complications: Pelvic inflammatory disease
          intermenstrual bleeding, lower abdominal pain,                         (PID), epididymo-orchitis, infertility, disseminated
          dyspareunia.                                                           gonococcal infection.

Investigations
    •    Nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) from                      •  Culture     and      sensitivity: Essential for
         urine, urethral, cervical, rectal, or pharyngeal                      antimicrobial resistance surveillance and in
         swabs (high sensitivity and specificity).                             cases of treatment failure.
Other options (where available):                                       Syndromic approach:
    •    Gram       stain: Gram-negative        intracellular              •   If laboratory testing is unavailable, manage
         diplococci (especially in symptomatic men).                           based on clinical syndrome (urethral/vaginal
                                                                               discharge, PID, etc.).

Pharmacological Management
First-line regimen for uncomplicated genital, anorectal, and           If doxycycline contraindicated or not available,
oropharyngeal gonorrhea (adults and adolescents):                      A: azithromycin 1g PO) single dose

A: ceftriaxone (IM) 500 mg single dose                                 Alternative Regimens
If >150 kg body weight, consider 1g IM single dose                     A: gentamicin (IM) 240mg single dose
          AND                                                                    AND
A: doxycycline (PO) 100 mg 12hourly for 7 days (if                     A: azithromycin (PO) 2g single dose
chlamydia not excluded)                                                          OR
                                                                       A: cefixime (PO) 800mg single dose

Table 12.1 Special considerations and partner management
 Condition/Aspect           Management
                               Ceftriaxone is recommended and considered safe. Avoid Doxycycline; use Azithromycin if
 Pregnancy
                               chlamydia coinfection is suspected.
 Neonatal Conjunctivitis       B: ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg IM/IV as a single dose (maximum 125 mg).
                               Treat all sexual partners within the last 60 days. Advise abstinence until treatment is completed and
 Partner Management
                               symptoms have resolved in both patient and partners. Promote and provide condoms.
 Follow-up                     • Test-of-cure: Recommended for pharyngeal infection, persistent symptoms, or alternative
                                   regimens.
                               • Re-testing: Re-screen at 3 months due to high risk of reinfection.

sections.title: Syphilis
sections.text:
A chronic sexually transmitted infection caused by the bacterium Treponema pallidum. It progresses in stages and can involve
multiple organ systems if untreated.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Primary syphilis: Painless genital, anal, or oral ulcer (chancre) and non-tender lymphadenopathy.
     •    Secondary syphilis: Generalized non-itchy rash (often on palms/soles), mucous patches, condylomata, fever, malaise,
          lymphadenopathy.
     •    Latent syphilis: Asymptomatic; detected by serology.
     •    Tertiary syphilis: Rare; gummatous lesions, cardiovascular or neurologic disease.
     •    Congenital syphilis: Stillbirth, neonatal death, or multisystem disease in infants.
     •    Neurosyphilis, ocular syphilis, otosyphilis: Can occur at any stage; present with neurological, visual, or auditory
          symptoms.

Investigations

Serologic testing:
    •    Non-treponemal: RPR, VDRL (for screening and monitoring).
    •    Treponemal: TPPA, FTA-ABS, EIA (for confirmation).
Direct detection: Darkfield microscopy or NAAT from ulcer exudate/tissue (if available).
CSF examination: For neurologic, ocular, or otic symptoms (cell count, protein, VDRL).
HIV testing: Recommended for all patients with syphilis.

Pharmacological Management
Early Syphilis (Primary, secondary, or early latent <2 years)
A: benzathine benzylpenicillin (IM) 2.4MU single dose

Late Latent Syphilis or Syphilis of Unknown Duration
A: benzathine benzylpenicillin (IM) 2.4MU once weekly for 3 consecutive weeks (Do not exceed 14 days between doses)
Syphilis in Pregnancy
   •     Benzathine benzylpenicillin is the only proven regimen to prevent congenital syphilis
   •     Desensitization and penicillin treatment are recommended for allergic pregnant women.

Neurosyphilis, Ocular Syphilis, Otosyphilis
A: benzylpenicillin (IV) 18–24 million units per 24hours, administered as 3–4 million units every 4 hours or continuous infusion
for 10–14 days.

For patients with penicillin allergy, the approach prioritizes confirming the allergy (e.g., via skin testing, as many reported
allergies are not true IgE-mediated reactions) and considering penicillin desensitization.

When desensitization is not feasible
A: ceftriaxone 1–2 g daily (intramuscularly or intravenously) for 10–14 days can be used.

Table 12.2: Adjunctive Therapy, Partner Management, and Follow-Up
 Component       Recommendation
Adjunctive          Corticosteroids may be considered in severe ocular or otic syphilis (consult specialist). Monitor for
Therapy             Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction (acute febrile reaction occurring within 24 hours of initiating therapy).
Partner             Notify, test, and treat all sexual partners exposed within the infectious period (past 3–12 months,
Management          depending on stage). Partner treatment is essential to prevent reinfection and further transmission.
                    Conduct clinical and serological follow-up at 6, 12, and 24 months after therapy. Monitor non-treponemal
Follow-Up           titres (RPR/VDRL) to assess treatment response. Repeat CSF examination at 6-month intervals if initial
                    abnormalities are present (in neurosyphilis).

sections.title: Mycoplasma genitalium
sections.text:
A sexually transmitted bacterium that causes non-gonococcal urethritis (NGU) and is associated with cervicitis and pelvic
inflammatory disease (PID). It is notable for high antimicrobial resistance, especially to macrolides.

Clinical Presentation
Urethritis, cervicitis; often asymptomatic.

Investigations:
NAAT specific for M. genitalium (if available).

Pharmacological Management
A: doxycycline (PO) 100mg 12hourly for 7 days
                  THEN
A: azithromycin (PO) 1g 24hourly, then 500mg 24hourly for 3days.

Resistance testing is recommended where possible.

sections.title: Ectoparasites
sections.text:
Parasites that live on the surface of the host (skin or hair) rather than inside the body. They commonly infest humans and can
cause irritation, skin disease, and transmit infections. Ectoparasites are transmitted through close contact, poor hygiene,
overcrowding, or contaminated clothing/bedding.

Clinical Presentation
Intense itching, visible lice or mites, excoriations.

Investigations
Clinical diagnosis by inspection.

Pharmacological Management
D: permethrin 5% w/v cream/lotion apply topically 12 hourly for 7days
         OR
D: malathion 0.5% lotion applied topically 12 hourly for 7days.

Treat close contacts; wash clothing and bedding.

sections.title: Trichomoniasis
sections.text:
A sexually transmitted infection caused by the protozoan parasite Trichomonas vaginalis. It commonly affects the urogenital
tract and is often asymptomatic, especially in men.

Clinical Presentation
Frothy, yellow-green vaginal discharge, vulvar itching, dysuria.

Investigations
Wet mount microscopy, culture, NAAT.

Pharmacological Management
A: metronidazole (PO) 2g single dose
         OR
A: metronidazole (PO) 400mg 12hourly for 7 days.

Treat sexual partners simultaneously.

sections.title: Lymphogranuloma Venereum (LGV)
sections.text:
A sexually transmitted infection caused by invasive strains (L1, L2, L3) of Chlamydia trachomatis. It is characterized by transient
genital lesions followed by painful lymphadenopathy or proctocolitis.

Clinical Presentation
Painful inguinal buboes, genital ulcers, rectal pain and discharge.

Investigations
NAAT for C. trachomatis serovars L1-L3, PCR.

Pharmacological Management
A: doxycycline (PO) 100mg 12hourly for 21 days.

Surgical drainage of buboes if necessary.

sections.title: Genital Herpes (Herpes Simplex Virus type 2)
sections.text:
A sexually transmitted viral infection caused mainly by Herpes simplex virus type 2, though Herpes simplex virus type 1 can
also cause genital disease.

Clinical Presentation
Painful vesicles and ulcers on genitalia, dysuria, systemic symptoms.

Investigations
PCR, viral culture, serology.

Pharmacological Management
B: acyclovir (PO) 400mg 8hourly daily for 7 days (initial episode).
Suppressive therapy or episodic treatment for recurrences.

sections.title: Anogenital Warts (Human Papillomavirus - HPV)
sections.text:
Anogenital warts are caused by infection with Human papillomavirus, most commonly types 6 and 11 (low-risk types). They
present as benign proliferative lesions affecting the anogenital region.

Clinical Presentation
Flesh-colored, cauliflower-like growths on genital or anal skin.

Investigations
Clinical diagnosis; biopsy if uncertain.

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Cryotherapy,
    •  Surgical removal, or laser therapy for extensive lesions.

Pharmacological Management
D: podophyllin 10-25% Solution/Gel/0.15% Cream: Apply to genital warts 12hourly for 3 days, followed by 4 days without
treatment, if no resolution repeat a weekly cycle for up to 4–5 weeks.
Management of STIs/RTIs using Syndromic Approach
This approach is recommended if the HF is not able to conduct appropriate Laboratory Investigation(s) and producing timely
result(s) to enable the clinician to prescribe the medicine in accordance with causative agent(s).
Syndromic management of STIs is based on the diagnosis of defined symptoms and easily recognizable clinical signs. Each
syndrome can be caused by several different causative agents.

For each syndrome, a well-defined standard treatment which has been proven to be effective against most endemic causative
agents for the syndrome are used.
Syndromic approach of managing STIs/RTIs entails the service provider to follow laid down steps in a flow chart which guides
him/her in making rational management decisions for treating the client. These are therefore known as treatment flow-charts.
They may also be known as treatment algorithms, treatment protocols or treatment decision trees.

They guide the provider through a series of decisions and actions that need to be made. Each decision or action is enclosed in
a box, with one or two routes leading out of it to another box, with another decision or action. Upon learning a patient’s symptoms
and signs, the service provider turns to the flow chart for the relevant syndrome and works through the decisions and
suggestions it guides to manage the client accordingly. Each flow chart is made up of a series of three steps. These are:
    •     The clinical problem (the patients presenting symptoms and signs),
    •     The decision that needs to be taken,
    •     The action that needs to be carried out.

sections.title: Urethral Discharge Syndrome (UDS)
sections.text:
UDS refers to the presence of abnormal secretions in the distal portion of the urethra Caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae and
Chlamydia trachomatis.

Clinical Presentation
Urethral discharge, Burning or painful micturition, Itchy urethra and increased frequency and urgency of micturition.

  Note
      •     Persistent or recurrent symptoms of urethritis may be due to drug resistance, poor compliance or re-infection.
            In some cases, there may be infection with Trichomonas vaginalis (TV).
       •    Male patients complaining of urethral discharge and/or dysuria should be examined for evidence of discharge.
            If none is seen per inspection, the urethra should be gently milked from the ventral part of the penis towards the
            meatus.
       •    Delayed or inadequate treatment may result into orchitis, epididymitis, urethral stricture and/or infertility.

Investigations
    •    Culture and Sensitivity                                           •    Quantitative or qualitative PCR
    •    Gram stain                                                        •    Genetic sequencing
    •    ELISA
Note: Management of UDS (see flow chart 12.1)

sections.title: Vaginal Discharge Syndrome (VDS)
sections.text:
VDS refers to change of colour, odour and/or amount of vaginal secretions caused by T. vaginalis, C. albicans, Bacterial
Vaginosis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Abnormal vaginal discharge,                                        •   Increased frequency and urgency of micturition
     •    Burning or painful micturition,                                        and/or painful coitus.
     •    Itchy vulva,
   Note
         •    A spontaneous complaint of abnormal vaginal discharge is most commonly due to a vaginal infection.
         •    T. vaginalis, C. albicans and Bacterial Vaginosis are the commonest causes of vaginal infection while
         •    Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis cause cervical infection.
         •    The clinical detection of cervical infection is difficult because a large proportion of women with gonococcal or
              chlamydia infections are asymptomatic.
         •    Vaginal discharge is therefore highly indicative of vaginal infection, but poorly predictive for cervical infection
         •    Due to the high prevalence of gonorrhea and chlamydia, all women presenting with VDS should receive
              treatment for both vaginal and cervical infections.
         •    Delayed or inadequate treatment of VDS may result to endometritis, salpingitis, oophoritis or ectopic pregnancy.
         •    Gonococcal or chlamydial cervical infection may be asymptomatic

Investigations
    •    Wet preparation                                                •   ELISA
    •    Gram stain                                                     •   Quantitative or qualitative PCR
    •    Culture and Sensitivity                                        •   NB starts simple to complex
    •    Fluorescent Microscopy
    •    Pap test (Papanicolau test)

Management of VDS (see flow chart 12.2)

sections.title: Lower Abdominal Pain Syndrome or Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID)
sections.text:
PID is defined as the inflammation of the uterus, fallopian tubes, ovaries and pelvic peritoneum. It is also known as lower
abdominal pain syndrome. It commonly occurs as a result of infection ascending from the cervix. It can also occur as a result
of trans-cervical procedure. Mainly caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis and Anaerobic bacteria

Clinical Presentation
Lower abdominal pain and tenderness, Painful micturition, Painful coitus, Abnormal vaginal discharge, Menometrorrhagia, fever
and sometimes nausea and vomiting.
   Note
          •    Delayed or inadequately treated PID may lead to chronic lower abdominal pain,
          •    Pelvic abscess,
          •    Ectopic pregnancy,
          •    Dysmenorrhea and infertility.

Investigations
         •   Wet preparation                                                •    Pap test (Papanicolaou’s test)
         •   Gram stain                                                     •    ELISA
         •   Culture and Sensitivity                                        •    Quantitative or qualitative PCR
         •   Fluorescent Microscopy

Management of PID (see flow chart 12.3)

In-Patient Management of PID

Pharmacological Management
All patients with PID who have fever or body temperature ≥ 380C should be admitted for closer care. The recommended in-
patient treatment options for PID are as follows:

Regimen 1:                                                         Regimen 2:
A: cefixime (PO) 400mg 12hourly for 7-14days                       B: ceftriaxone (IM) 1gm 24hourly for 5-7days
          AND                                                                AND
A: doxycycline (PO) 100mg 12hourly for 7-14days     OR             A: doxycycline (PO) 100mg 12hourly for 7-14days
          AND                                                                AND
A: metronidazole (PO) 400mg 8-12hourly for 7-14days                A: metronidazole, (PO) 400mg 8-12hourly 7-14days
          OR                                                                 OR
B: metronidazole (IV) 500mg 8-12hourly for 7-14days                B: metronidazole (IV) 500mg 8-12hourly 7-14day

          OR

Regimen 3
S: clindamycin (IV) 900mg 8hourly for 7-14days
         AND
A: gentamicin (IV) 1.5 mg/kg 6-8hourly 7-14days

   Note
       •       For all three regimens, therapy should be continued for two days after the patient has improved and then be
               followed by doxycycline (PO) 100 mg 12hourly for 14days.
          •    Patients taking metronidazole should be cautioned to avoid alcohol.
          •    Doxycycline is contraindicated in pregnancy.

sections.title: Painful Scrotal Swelling (PSS)
sections.text:
PSS is the inflammation of the epididymis and testis, often accompanied with scrotal pain, swelling and tenderness. It is also
known as epididymorchitis. Mainly caused by Neisseria gonorrhoea and Chlamydia trachomatis
Clinical Presentation
Scrotal pain, Scrotal swelling and tenderness, Scrotal oedema, Fever.

 Note: Among the common complications of painful scrotal swelling include infertility and scrotal abscess.

Investigations
    •    Gram stain
    •    Culture and Sensitivity
    •    ELISA
    •    Quantitative or qualitative PCR
    •    Genetic sequencing

Management of PSS (see flow chart 12.4)

sections.title: Ano-rectal Syndrome (ARS)
sections.text:
Defined as soreness, burning, itching or other irritation of the rectum together with redness in the area of anus. Sometimes it is
accompanied by diarrhea and it may occur as a toxic side effect of oral administration of certain broad-spectrum antibiotics
mainly caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis, Treponema pallidum, Herpes Simplex Virus, Shigella spp.,
or Entamoeba histolytic.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Purulent rectal discharge                                       •    Bloody stool (blood may be red, black, or tarry in
     •    Mucous rectal discharge                                              texture),
     •    Watery rectal discharge                                         •    Burning feeling,
     •    Soreness, burning, itching or other irritation of the           •    Change in bowel habits, constipation, diarrhea;
          rectum together with redness in the area of anus                •    Fecal incontinence (inability to control stools),
     •    There may also be ineffectual straining to                      •    Flatulence; pain, which may be severe, in the
          defecate (“tenesmus”), sometimes mistakenly                          abdomen, pelvis, or lower back
          described as “constipation” by patients.                        •    Urgent need to pass stool and watery diarrhea
     •    The anus and rectum may be intensely painful,                        including multiple episodes.
          with external and internal ulceration                           •    A proctoscopic examination (which should be
     •    Abdominal pain or cramping, abdominal swelling,                      done, if feasible) will reveal rectal pus, bleeding
          distention or bloating;                                              or ulceration

  Note
      •     Proctitis may be caused by Salmonella spp., Shigella spp., or Entamoeba histolytica as a part of gastroenteritis,
            which may manifest as diarrhoea with fever, anorexia, and abdominal cramps.
       •    Antibiotics that destroy normal intestinal bacteria and allow other bacteria to grow in their place may also cause
            proctitis.
       •    Herpes proctitis may be mistaken for the rectal manifestation of ulcerative colitis or Crohn’s disease.
       •    Proctitis typically causes painless bleeding or the passage of mucus (sometimes mistaken for diarrhoea) from the
            rectum.
       •    All cases of proctitis in MSM should be treated for gonorrhoea and chlamydia infections.
       •    Symptoms of diarrhoea, bloody stools, abdominal cramping, nausea, and/or bloating may indicate Giardia spp
            infection or amoebic dysentery.

Other non-STI causes of ARS include:
Anal fissure, Fecal impaction, Food intolerance, Gastroenteritis (bacterial and viral), Inflammatory bowel disease (includes
Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis), Neurological damage, and Perirectal or perianal abscess.
Other symptoms might occur with rectal discharge include gastrointestinal symptoms which vary depending on the underlying
disease, disorder or condition. These may include:
     •    Abdominal pain or cramping, abdominal swelling, distention or bloating; bloody stool (blood may be red, black, or tarry
          in texture), burning feeling, change in bowel habits, constipation, diarrhea; fecal incontinence (inability to control
          stools), flatulence; pain, which may be severe, in the abdomen, pelvis, or lower back, urgent need to pass stool and
          watery diarrhea including multiple episodes.
Investigations
    •    Wet preparation                                                  •    Treponema palladium particle        agglutination
    •    Gram stain                                                            (TPPA)
    •    Pap test (Papanicolaou’s test)                                   •    ELISA
    •    Culture and Sensitivity                                          •    Quantitative or qualitative PCR
    •    Rapid Plasma Reagin (RPR)                                        •    Genetic sequencing
                                                                          •    Fluorescent Microscopy

Management of ARS (see flow chart 12.5.)

sections.title: Oropharyngeal Syndrome
sections.text:
Oral sex can lead to oropharyngeal STIs (infections of mouth and throat). The causative agents include Human Papilloma Virus,
Herpes Simplex Virus, N. gonorrhoea, Chlamydia spp, Treponema pallidum

Clinical Presentation
Pharyngitis, History of unprotected oral sex

Investigations
    •    Wet preparation                                                  •    Treponema pallidum particle         agglutination
    •    Gram stain                                                            (TPPA)
    •    Pap test (Papanicolaou’s test)                                   •    ELISA
    •    Culture and Sensitivity                                          •    Quantitative or qualitative PCR
    •    Rapid Plasma Reagin (RPR)                                        •    Genetic sequencin
    •    Fluorescent Microscopy

Management of Oropharyngeal syndrome (see flow chart 12.6)

sections.title: Genital Ulcer Disease (GUD)
sections.text:
GUD is a loss of continuity of skin or mucous membrane producing one or more lesions in the genital area caused by Treponema
pallidum, Haemophilus ducreyi, Chlamydia trachomatis, Herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV), Klebsiella granulomatis

Clinical Presentation
Ulcer, Sore, Vesicle

Investigations
    •    Wet preparation                                                  •    ELISA
    •    Gram stain                                                       •    Quantitative or qualitative PCR
    •    Culture and Sensitivity                                          •    Genetic sequencing
    •    Fluorescent Microscopy
    •    Treponema palladium particle          agglutination
         (TPPA)
    •    Rapid Plasma Reagin (RPR)

Management of GUD (see flow chart 12.7)

sections.title: Neonatal Conjunctivitis (Ophthalmia Neonatorum)
sections.text:
Ophthalmia Neonatorum (ON) means inflammation of the conjunctiva of a newborn baby of less than 1 month of age.
Is a potentially sight threatening condition. If the baby is older, the cause is unlikely to be an STI. The main Causative agents
include Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis. Other non-STI causes of neonatal conjunctivitis include
Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus and Pseudomonas spp, Viral, chemical and physical
irritation.

Clinical Presentation
Reddish conjunctiva, Oedema/swelling of the eyelids, Purulent eye discharge

Prevention and control measures
    •   Screening of pregnant women,
    •   Early treatment of VDS in pregnant women
    •   Routine eye chemoprophylaxis in the newborn by providing
    •   A: 1% oxytetracycline eye ointment to all newborns.

 Note: Examine the neonate and exclude other congenital diseases

Management of Neonatal conjunctivitis (see flow chart 12.8)

sections.title: Inguinal Bubo (IB)
sections.text:
Inguinal and femoral bubos are localized enlargements of the lymph nodes in the groin area, which are painful and may be
fluctuant. They are frequently associated with lymphogranuloma venereum and chancroid. The main Causative agents include
Chlamydia trachomatis and Haemophilus ducreyi.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Localized enlargements of the lymph nodes in the groin area,
     •    Painful and may be fluctuant.
     •    Pain,
     •    Fever
     •    Tenderness.

 Note
     •     In many cases of chancroid an associated genital ulcer is visible, but occasionally may not be.
     •     Non-sexually transmitted local and systemic infections (e.g. infections of the lower limb) can also cause swelling
           of inguinal lymph nodes. These should therefore be ruled out.

Investigations
    •    Culture and Sensitivity
    •    ELISA
    •    Quantitative or qualitative PCR
    •    Direct Fluorescent Antibody (DFA)

Management of Inguinal BUBO (see flow chart 12.9)

sections.title: STI/RTI flow charts
sections.text:
Steps in using the flow charts:
    •     Start by asking the patient for his/her symptoms.
    •     Find the appropriate flow chart, stated in the clinical problem box with “Patient Complaints of.”
    •     The clinical problem box usually leads to an action box, which asks you to examine the patient and/or take the history.
    •     Next, move to the decision box. After taking the history and examining the patient you should have the necessary
          information to choose Yes or No accurately.
    •     Depending on your choice, there may be further decision boxes and action boxes.

  Note
  For the appropriate management of STIs/RTIs syndrome, drugs in the watch group (azithromycin, cefixime and ceftriaxone)
  are the standard recommended for use as a first line treatment for the most STIs/RTIs starting at the Dispensary level,
  therefore, should be used only for STIs/RTIs at Primary HFs)
