sections.title: Management of Other Common STI Conditions
Late Syphilis
sections.text:
This refers to Syphilis infection of more than 2years.

Pharmacological Management
A: benzathine benzylpenicillin (IM) 2.4MU once weekly for 3 consecutive weeks.
          AND
A: azithromycin (PO) 2g stat.

sections.title: Syphilis in Pregnancy
sections.text:
Pregnant women should be regarded as a separate group requiring close surveillance to detect possible re-infection after
treatment has been given. It is also important to treat the sexual partner(s).

Pharmacological Management
A: benzathine benzylpenicillin (IM) 2.4MU, as a single dose
In case of late syphilis 3 doses of benzathine benzylpenicillin should be provided.

sections.title: Congenital Syphilis
sections.text:
All infants born to sero-positive mothers should be treated with a single intramuscular dose of benzathine benzylpenicillin,
50000IU/kg whether the mothers were treated during pregnancy (with or without penicillin).

Pharmacological Management
Treatment regimens for early congenital syphilis (up to 2 years of age), and Infants with abnormal cerebrospinal fluid:
A: benzylpenicillin (IV) 100000–150000IU/kg/day administered as 50000IU/kg/dose 12hourly, for the first 7days and every
8hourly thereafter for a total of 10days

For congenital syphilis in children 2 or more years
A: benzylpenicillin (IV or IM) 200000 – 300000IU/kg/day administered as 50000IU/kg every 4–6hourly for 10–14days
          OR
A: erythromycin (PO) 7.5–12.5 mg/kg 6hourly for 30days.
As an alternative regimen for penicillin allergic patients, after the first month of life

sections.title: Syphilis and HIV Infection
sections.text:
All patients with syphilis should be encouraged to undergo testing for HIV because of the high frequency of dual infection and
its implications for clinical assessment and management.

sections.title: Genital Warts (Venereal Warts)
sections.text:
Human papilloma virus (HPV) is a common sexually transmitted pathogen. Genital warts are painless but may lead to serious
complications. The removal of the lesion does not mean cure of the infection. No treatment is completely satisfactory.
Recommended regimens for venereal warts are as follows:

Pharmacological Management
D: podophyllin 10–25% in compound tincture of benzoin, applied carefully to the warts, avoiding normal tissue. External genital
and perianal warts should be washed thoroughly 4–6 hourly after the application of podophyllin.

Podophyllin applied to warts on vaginal or anal epithelial surfaces should be allowed to dry before removing the speculum or
anoscope. Treatment should be repeated at weekly intervals.

Other treatment approaches Available at Referral level Health Facility
Cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen, solid carbon dioxide, or a cryoprobe. Repeat applications every 1-2 weeks OR
Electrosurgery OR Surgical removal

Vaginal Warts
Recommended regimens for treatment of vaginal warts are:
D: cryotherapy (with liquid nitrogen)
         OR
D: podophyllin 10–25% (allow to dry before removing speculum)

Cervical Warts
Treatment of cervical warts should not be started until the results from a cervical smear test are known

Meatal and Urethral Warts
D: Cryotherapy
         OR
D: podophyllin 10–25

chapters.intro:
Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) are generally acquired by sexual contact with a person who has an STI. The organisms
(bacteria, viruses or parasites) that cause sexually transmitted diseases may pass from person to person in blood, semen, or
vaginal and other bodily fluids. Reproductive tract infections (RTIs) occur in the genital tract and affect both women and men.
Some RTIs, such as syphilis and gonorrhea, are sexually transmitted, but many are not. In women, overgrowth of endogenous
microorganisms normally found in the vagina may cause RTIs (yeast infection, bacterial vaginosis).
Clinical Presentation
     •    Sores or bumps on the genitals or in the oral or                •    Unusual vaginal bleeding.
          rectal area.                                                    •    Pain during sex.
     •    Painful or burning urination.                                   •    Lower abdominal pain
     •    Discharge from the penis.                                       •    Genital ulcers, sores or blisters
     •    Vaginal discharge that is abnormal in colour,                   •    Swelling, lumps or ulcer in the
          odour, amount or consistency.                                        groin area
     •    Itching or irritation of the
     •    vulva or vagina.

sections.title: Bacterial Skin Infection
sections.text:
Staphylococci and streptococci cause most bacterial skin infections, ranging from common conditions such as impetigo and
cellulitis to severe multisystem disorders, including toxic shock syndrome.

sections.title: Impetigo
sections.text:
Impetigo is a contagious, superficial bacterial infection that is most frequently observed in children. It can be bullous or
nonbullous. The most common pathogen is Staphylococcus aureus.
Clinical Presentation:
     •    Polycyclic flaccid vesicles or bullae with clear yellow fluid
     •    May become pustules that enlarge and rapidly break down to form thick,
          adherent yellowish crusts
     •    May be associated with mild lymphadenopathy and fever

Investigations:
Skin swab for culture and sensitivity

Non-Pharmacological Management
   •   Regular hand washing                                      •     May keep away from school infected individuals
   •   Avoid sharing towels or clothes                           •     Remove crusts with soap, water or saline
   •   Avoid touching or scratching infected areas

Pharmacological Management
Limited Disease
A: gentian violet paint (topical) 12hourly for 5days
          OR
C: mupirocin ointment (topical) 12hourly for 7days
          OR
C: fusidic acid cream (topical) 12hourly for 7days

Extensive (Severe) Disease
B: cefalexin (PO) 250 to 500mg; paediatric 25-50 mg/kg 6hourly for 7days
          OR
A: erythromycin (PO): Adult 500mg; paediatric 25-50mg/kg 8hourly for 10days
          OR
B: amoxicillin + clavulanic acid 625mg (PO) 8hourly for 7days

sections.title: Bacterial Folliculitis
sections.text:
Folliculitis is an infection of the hair follicles commonly due to Staphylococcus aureus, and Gram-negative bacteria such as
Pseudomonas, Klebsiella, Enterobacter, and Proteus species

Clinical Presentation:
     •    Follicular pustules and inflamed, follicular papules   •     Pruritus is common
     •    Common areas include the scalp, face, upper            •     Tender lesions may be present.
          trunk, buttocks, and legs

Investigation:
    •    Skin swab for culture and sensitivity

Non-Pharmacological Management
   •   Wearing loose-fitting clothing                            •     Proper hygiene for the affected area
   •   Avoid scratching or shaving of the affected areas         •     Use clean razors and shaving technique to minimize
   •   Hair should be left to grow to at least 1 mm long.              trauma

Pharmacological Management
Refer to the management of impetigo

sections.title: Folliculitis Decalvans
sections.text:
Folliculitis Decalvans (FD) is a chronic and relapsing neutrophilic scarring alopecia that presents with alopecic patches,
pustules, and tufted hairs. The aetiology of FD remains uncertain, but it may represent an interaction between the infection by
S. aureus and the host.
Clinical Presentation:
      •     One or more areas of scarring alopecia on the scalp
      •     Multiple pustules on the scalp, particularly at the periphery of areas of
            alopecia
      •     Tufting of hair shafts
      •     Perifollicular scale extending onto the hair shaft

Investigations:
    •    Skin biopsy for histopathology
    •    Skin swab for culture and sensitivity

Pharmacological Management:
A: doxycycline (PO) 100mg 12hourly for 2-4weeks
          OR
S: clindamycin (PO) 300mg 12hourly for 3months
          AND
D: clobetasol propionate cream/ointment/gel (topical) 24hourly for not less than 16weeks
          OR
S: triamcinolone (intralesional) 10mg/ml monthly for 6-9 months

In recalcitrant cases
S: dapsone (PO) 100mg 24hourly for 6months
           OR
S: Isotretinoin (PO) 20-40mg 24hourly for 3 to 6 months

sections.title: Abscess
sections.text:
An abscess is a collection of pus within the dermis or subcutaneous tissue caused by Staphylococcus aureus.

Clinical Presentation:
     •    Painful, fluctuant, erythematous nodules filled with pus
     •    Spontaneous drainage of purulent material may occur
     •    Fever and chills are often absent

Surgical Treatment
    •    Incision and drainage
    •    If incision and drainage are not performed, apply hot compresses several times per day to the swelling until it breaks.

Pharmacological Management:
A: sulfamethoxazole + trimethoprim (cotrimoxazole) (PO) 480-960mg; paediatric 8-12 TMP mg/kg 12hourly for 5-7 days
         OR
B: cefalexin (PO) 250 to 500mg; paediatric 25-50 mg/kg 6hourly for 7days

sections.title: Erysipelas and Cellulitis
sections.text:
Cellulitis and erysipelas develop as a result of bacterial entry via breaches in the skin barrier. The most common causes of
cellulitis are beta-hemolytic streptococci, and S. aureus is a notable but less common cause.

Clinical Presentation:
     •    A prodrome of fever, chills and malaise                    •   Cellulitis involves the deeper dermis and
     •    Skin erythema, edematous and warm                              subcutaneous fat
     •    Petechiae and/or hemorrhage may be present                 •   Erysipelas involves the upper dermis and superficial
     •    Nearly always unilateral                                       lymphatics
     •    Lower extremities most common site

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Treatment of skin conditions and the point of microorganism entry
    •  Elevation of the affected part
    •  Bed rest

Pharmacological Management
A: weak potassium permanganate soaks, 1:40000 (0.025%) solution 12hourly for 3– 4days, with each session lasting for 15–
20minutes
           AND
A: silver sulfadiazine cream (topical) 12- 24hourly
           OR
C: mupirocin (topical) ointment 12hourly for 5–7days
           OR
C: fusidic acid (topical) cream 12hourly for 5–7days
           AND
A: phenoxymethylpenicillin (PO): adult 250–500mg; paediatric 25 mg/kg 6hourly for 5– 7days
           OR
B: cefalexin (PO) 250 to 500mg; paediatric 25-50 mg/kg 6hourly for 7days
           AND
A: ibuprofen 400mg (PO) 6hourly for 5days

 Note: Consider parenteral antibiotics if there are signs of toxicity such as fever >38oC, hypotension and tachycardia or if there
 are extensive erythema and high-risk neutropenia. BUT it should be guided by the results of culture and sensitivity

Referral: Refer if there are local or general signs of severity of developing necrotizing fasciitis.

sections.title: Paronychia
sections.text:
Paronychia is an inflammation affecting the lateral and proximal nail folds. It can be either acute or chronic. It often occurs after
injury or minor trauma and is caused by Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes, or by drugs (in acute cases), or
by repeated exposure to irritants or allergens (chronic cases).

Clinical Presentation
     •    Painful, erythematous, and swollen proximal and lateral nail folds
     •    A superficial abscess is frequently present.

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Keep hands dry
    •  Warm water or antiseptic soaks

Pharmacological Management

C: mupirocin (topical) ointment 12hourly for 7days                     ADD systemic therapies for severe disease
          OR
C: fusidic acid (topical) cream 12hourly for 7days                     B: cefalexin (PO) 250 to 500mg; paediatric 25-50 mg/kg
          AND                                                          6hourly for 7days
C: betamethasone valerate (topical) 12hourly for 14 days                         OR
          OR                                                           B: amoxicillin + clavulanic acid 625mg (PO) 8hourly for
S: tacrolimus ointment (topical) 12hourly for 14 days                  7days
                                                                                 OR
                                                                       S: clindamycin (PO) 300mg 12hourly for 14 days
                                                                                 AND
                                                                       D: itraconazole (PO) 200mg 24hourly for 14 days (for
                                                                       chronic diseases)

 Note: Acute paronychia with abscess is treated with incision and drainage

sections.title: Tinea Corporis
sections.text:
Tinea corporis is a superficial fungal infection (dermatophytosis) of the skin of the trunk and extremities, excluding the hair,
nails, palms, soles, and groin.

Clinical Presentation:
     •    Annular lesions with central clear
     •    Hair loss in areas of infection
     •    Associated with slight itching
     •    Fine scales may be present

Investigation
Skin scraping for KOH, Skin scraping for fungal culture.

Pharmacological Management
A: benzoic acid compound ointment (topical) 12hourly for 2-4 weeks.
          OR
A: clotrimazole cream (topical) apply 12hourly for 2-4 weeks
          OR
C: miconazole cream (topical) apply thinly 12hourly for 2-4 weeks
          OR
C: terbinafine cream (topical) 12hourly for 2-4 weeks
          OR
C: luliconazole cream (topical) 12hourly for 2-4 weeks

If extensive and refractory infections or for immunodeficient patient:
C: terbinafine (PO) 250mg; paediatric 62.5mg/ 10-20kg; 125mg/ 21-40 kg; 250mg/ above 40kg; 24hourly for 2-4 weeks
          OR
D: itraconazole (PO) 200mg; paediatrics 3-5mg/kg 24hourly for 2-4 weeks

sections.title: Tinea Capitis
sections.text:
It is a common superficial fungal infection (dermatophyte) of the scalp in children.
Clinical Presentation:
     •    Single or multiple patches with hair loss
     •    Fine scales may be present
     •    Associated with itching

Investigations:
Skin scraping for KOH, Skin scraping for fungal culture.

Pharmacological Management
A: griseofulvin (PO): Adult 500 mg; Paediatric 10-20mg/kg 24hourly for 4-6weeks
          OR
C: terbinafine (PO): Adult 250mg; paediatric 62.5mg/ 10-20kg; 125mg/ 21-40kg; 250mg/ above 41kg 24hourly for 4-6 weeks

sections.title: Tinea Pedis (Athlete’s Foot), Tinea Manuum and Tinea Cruris
sections.text:
Tinea Pedis is a common fungal infection of the toes, while Tinea Manuum affects the palms and interdigital spaces. Both Tinea
Pedis and Manuum are often the source of infection at other sites, especially the groin (Tinea Cruris).

Clinical Presentation
 Tinea Pedis                                                    Tinea Manuum                   Tinea Cruris
       •    Pruritic erosions or scales between the toes            •   Hyperkeratotic              •   Erythematous       or
            or                                                          eruption on the palm            hyperpigmented
       •    Diffuse scale on the plantar surface and side               or annular plaques              patch on groin
            of the foot or                                                                          •   Itching
       •    Vesicles and bullae on the plantar or sides of
            the feet

Investigations:
Skin scraping for KOH, Skin scraping for fungal culture.

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Frequent change of socks/footwear                   or              •    Keep the spaces between toes as dry as possible
       underwear.                                                               after bathing, always
    •  Use of cotton socks or underwear.

Pharmacological Management:
A: clotrimazole cream (topical) apply 12hourly for 2-4 weeks
          OR
C: miconazole cream (topical) apply thinly 12hourly for 2-4 weeks
          OR
C: terbinafine cream (topical) 12hourly for 2-4 weeks
          OR
C: luliconazole cream (topical) 12hourly for 2-4 weeks

If extensive and refractory infections

For Adults
C: terbinafine (PO) 250mg 24hourly for 2-4weeks

For paediatrics
10-20kg 62.5mg 24hourly for 2-4weeks;
21-40 kg 125mg 24hourly for 2-4weeks;
40 kg and above 250mg 24hourly for 2-4weeks

          OR

For Adults
D: itraconazole (PO) 200mg 24hourly for 2-4 weeks

For paediatrics
3-5mg/kg 24hourly for 2-4 weeks

sections.title: Tinea Unguium (Onychomycosis)
sections.text:
It is a chronic fungal infection of the toenails or fingernails. It is more common in adults than in children. Patients with diabetes,
advanced age, obesity, smoking, or peripheral neuropathy may be at a higher risk.
Clinical Presentation:
     •    White, yellow, or brown discoloration of the distal corner of the nail
     •    Subungual hyperkeratosis and onycholysis

Investigations:
KOH preparation, Fungal Culture and Sensitivity.

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Maintain foot hygiene
    •  Keep nails trimmed back
    •  Avoid occlusive shoes
    •  Wear flip flops/sandals in areas of high fungal density, e.g., communal showers

Pharmacological Management
A: fluconazole (PO) 150-300mg once weekly for 6–12 months
          OR
C: terbinafine (PO) 250mg; paediatric 62.5mg/ 10-20kg; 125mg/ 21-40 kg; 250mg/ above 40kg; 24hourly for 6-12 weeks
          OR
D: itraconazole (PO) 200mg, paediatrics 3-5mg/kg, 24hourly for 6-12 weeks

sections.title: Pityriasis Versicolor
sections.text:
It is a common fungal infection caused by yeast of the genus Malassezia.

Clinical Presentation:
     •    Hypo/hyperpigmented macules and confluent patches with fine scales
     •    Commonly occurs on the chest, back, arms, and occasionally the neck and face

Investigation
Skin scraping for KOH

Pharmacological Management
A: clotrimazole cream (topical) 12hourly for 4 weeks
          OR
C: miconazole nitrate cream (topical) 12hourly for 4 weeks
          OR
C: ketoconazole shampoo (topical) 3 times per week for 4weeks
          OR
C: luliconazole cream (topical) 12hourly for 4 weeks

If extensive and refractory or recurrent infections add:
A: fluconazole (PO) 300mg weekly for 2-4 weeks
          OR
D: itraconazole (PO) 200mg, paediatrics 3-5mg/kg, 24hourly for 2-4 weeks

sections.title: Intertrigo
sections.text:
It is a common inflammatory condition affecting skin folds. Usually triggered or aggravated by warm temperatures, friction,
moisture, maceration, and poor ventilation. Intertrigo is often worsened by infection, most commonly with Candida.

Clinical Presentation:
 •    Moist, erythematous, dyspigmented, homogenous patch
 •    Most occur in the groin, axillary area, inframammary area and umbilicus
 •    Associated with burning, tenderness, pruritus, and/or a malodorous discharge

Investigation:
Skin scraping for KOH

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Daily cleansing of intertriginous skin, followed by drying the affected area.
    •  Use of absorbent material or clothing, such as cotton, to separate the skin in folds.
    •  Weight loss in persons who are overweight or obese.

Pharmacological Management
A: clotrimazole cream (topical) 12hourly for 2-4 weeks
          OR
C: miconazole cream (topical) apply 12hourly for 2-4 weeks
          OR
C: ketoconazole cream (topical) apply 12hourly for 2-4 weeks
          AND
A: hydrocortisone cream/ointment (topical) 12hourly for 2-4 weeks

sections.title: Mycetoma (Madura Foot)
sections.text:
Mycetoma is a chronic disease usually of the foot, but any part of the body can be affected. Infection is most probably acquired
by traumatic inoculation of fungi (eumycetoma) or bacteria (actinomycetoma) into the subcutaneous tissue.

Clinical Presentation:
 •    Painless firm subcutaneous mass                               •   Sinus tracts
 •    Discharge containing macroscopic or microscopic grains        •   The foot is the most common site of infection,
                                                                        followed by the hand, trunk, and scalp

Investigations:
  •   Skin biopsy for histology
  •   X-Ray OR/AND CT scan
  •   Grains or tissue for culture and sensitivity

sections.title: Eumycetoma
sections.text:
Non-Pharmacological Management
Surgical Interventions

Pharmacological Management
D: itraconazole (PO) 200mg 12-hourly for 12 months

sections.title: Actinomycetoma
sections.text:
Pharmacological Management
A: sulfamethoxazole + Trimethoprim (PO) 480mg–960mg 12hourly for 5weeks
         AND
S: amikacin (IV) 7.5mg/kg 12hourly for 5 weeks
         OR
A: sulfamethoxazole + Trimethoprim (PO) 480mg–960 mg 12hourly for 5 weeks
         AND
S: dapsone (PO): adult 100mg 24hourly for 2–4months; Paediatric 25–50mg 24-hourly for 5 weeks

sections.title: Scabies
sections.text:
Scabies is an intensely pruritic and highly contagious infestation of the skin caused by the mite Sarcoptes scabies.

Clinical Presentation:
     •    Erythematous papules and vesicles, burrows, and intense pruritus worse at night
     •    Common sites include fingers, wrists, periumbilical skin, waist, genitalia and buttocks

Investigation
Skin scraping for KOH

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Treat all members of the household at the same time to prevent reinfection
    •  Wash and dry bedding and clothing using hot water and drying in direct sunlight
    •  Avoidance of skin-to-skin contact with the patient until at least eight hours after treatment

Pharmacological Management
A: benzyl benzoate emulsion (BBE), (25% for adults, 6.25% or 12.5% for children), apply for 3 consecutive nights and repeat
after 7 days
           OR
A: sulfur ointment/cream (topical) applied as BBE above
           OR
A: ivermectin (PO) 200mcg/kg stat then repeat after 1 or 2 week(s)
           AND
C: betamethasone valerate cream (topical) 12 hourly for 2 weeks
           AND
A: cetirizine (PO) 10mg 24hourly at night for 2 weeks
           OR
C: loratadine (PO) 10mg 24hourly at night for 2weeks

sections.title: Herpes Simplex
sections.text:
It is an acute viral infection caused by Herpes simplex virus hominis (types HSV1, HSV2 acquired by close contact with an
infected individual (Management refer to the STI chapter)

sections.title: Chicken Pox
sections.text:
It is a highly infectious disease caused by the Varicella zoster virus (VZV). Most often benign and self-limiting, chickenpox is
one of the most common childhood diseases.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Prodrome of fever, malaise, or pharyngitis                         •    Intense pruritus
     •    Followed by lesions that begin as macules that                     •    Occasional regional lymphadenopathy
          become papules, followed by vesicles

Pharmacological Management
B: acyclovir (PO) 800mg; paediatric 20mg/kg; 6hourly for 7 days
         AND
A: paracetamol (PO)1g; paediatric 10mg/kg; 8hourly for 3 days
         AND
A: calamine lotion (topical)l, apply over the whole body 12 hourly for 7 days

sections.title: Herpes Zoster (Shingles)
sections.text:
It is due to the resurgence or reactivation of the Varicella zoster virus infection, which also causes chickenpox.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Grouped vesicles overlying erythematous skin following a dermatomal distribution; typically, lesions do not cross the
          midline
     •    Severe burning pain

Pharmacological Management
B: acyclovir (PO) 800mg, paediatric 20 mg/kg 6hourly for 7–10days

For Secondary infection (bacterial), apply
Refer to the management of impetigo or cellulitis.

Post-Herpetic Neuralgia:
A: amitriptyline (PO) 25mg at night, may be increased to 150mg at night for 4 weeks
          OR
D: pregabalin (PO) 75-150mg 24 hourly or divided doses for 2-4weeks

sections.title: Molluscum Contagiosum
sections.text:
Molluscum contagiosum (MC) is a benign infection caused by a member of the Poxviridae family, namely molluscum
contagiosum virus (MCV). It infects only the skin and, rarely, the mucous membranes.

Clinical Presentation:
     •    Presents with normochromic or yellowish papule with central
          umbilication
     •    May be asymptomatic or accompanying with itching
     •    The most common areas include the trunk, axillae,
          antecubital and popliteal fossae, and crural folds.

Non-Pharmacological Management
Surgical procedures
C: Cryotherapy
     OR
D: curettage

Pharmacological Management
A: benzoyl peroxide (topical) 10% 24hourly for 4-8 weeks
           OR
S: tretinoin cream (topical) 0.5% at night for 4-8 week
           OR
S: imiquimod cream (topical) 3 times per week for 8-16 weeks

sections.title: Cutaneous Warts
sections.text:
Infections due to Human Papilloma Virus include: common warts, plane warts, plantar warts, and oral warts.

Clinical Presentation:
     •    Verrucous papules on the body, palms, soles, genital, and oral mucosa.
     •    Painful on applying pressure to warts on palms and soles.

Non-Pharmacological Management
C: cryotherapy
      OR
D: curettage
      OR
D: excision of large warts

Pharmacological Management
C: salicylic acid (topical) 20-40% at night for 4-8 weeks
           OR
S: tretinoin cream (topical) 0.5% at night for 4-8 weeks
           OR
C: silver nitrate pencil 3 times per week for 4 weeks for plantar, common warts.
           OR
S: imiquimod cream (topical) 3 times per week for 8-16 weeks

sections.title: Atopic Eczema (Dermatitis)
sections.text:
It is a chronic, itchy, inflammatory skin condition that affects both children and adults. AD is often linked to a personal or family
history of atopy, which includes eczema, asthma, and allergic rhinitis.

Clinical Presentation:
     •    Acute forms are weepy, chronic forms are           •       Chronic or relapsing course
          lichenified, scaly                                 •       Positive personal and/or family history of atopy
     •    Pruritus                                           •       Xerosis
     •    Eary age at onset

                                                                     Chronic AD: Lichenification and scaling
     Acute AD: Erythema on the cheek

Investigations
Serum IgE Level, FBP, Patch test, Prick Test

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Education on the condition                                •     Removing the exacerbating factors such as
    •  Maintaining skin hydration by reducing frequency of             irritants and allergens e.g., fragranced soaps,
       bathing                                                         rough wool clothing, perfumes, detergents
    •  Applying emollients or moisturizers immediately
       after bathing

Pharmacological Management
Mild Atopic Eczema
A: hydrocortisone cream/ointment (topical) 12 hourly (face/skin folds)
         OR/AND
C: betamethasone valerate cream/ointment (topical) 12 hourly (other body parts)
           OR
S: tacrolimus Ointment (face or skin folds) (topical) 12hourly

Moderate Atopic Eczema                                                Severe Atopic Eczema (e.g., erythroderma)
A: cetirizine (PO) 10mg 24hourly for 2 weeks                          A: prednisolone (PO) 0.5 -1mg/ kg 24hourly for 1-2weeks
           OR                                                         (short course)
C: loratadine (PO) 10mg 24hourly for 2weeks                                      AND
                                                                      S: methotrexate (PO) 7.5- 20mg, paediatric 0.2-0.5mg/kg
           AND
                                                                      weekly for >3 months
A: hydrocortisone cream/ointment (topical) 12 hourly                              OR
(face/skin folds)                                                     S: cyclosporine 3-5mg/kg/day up to 3months
           AND                                                                   AND
C: betamethasone valerate cream/ointment (topical)                    A: cetirizine (PO) 10mg 24hourly for 2 weeks
12hourly (other body parts)                                                      OR
           OR                                                         C: loratadine (PO) 10mg 24hourly for 2weeks
C: betamethasone dipropionate cream/ointment (topical)                           OR
12hourly                                                              S: desloratadine (PO) 5mg 24hourly for 2 weeks
           OR                                                                    AND
S: mometasone furoate cream/ointment (topical) 24hourly               S: phototherapy

 Note: Cyclosporine and methotrexate should be reserved for most severe cases in older children, adolescent and adults

Treatment of Infection in Atopic Eczema
 Type of infection      Clinical Presentation                               Treatment
 Impetigo               •    Polycyclic flaccid vesicles or bullae with     Refer to Treatment of Impetigo
                             clear yellow fluid
 Eczema Herpeticum      •    Disseminated non-grouped vesicular             B: acyclovir cream (topical) applied 4hourly for 7–
                             eruptions and pustules on erythematous         10days
                             lesions                                                   OR
                                                                            B: acyclovir (PO) 200mg 6hourly for 7–10days,
                                                                            (especially if severe)
 Dermatophyte            •    Depend on the type of Tinea                   Refer to section on fungal infection

sections.title: Contact Eczema (Dermatitis)
sections.text:
Contact dermatitis is a common inflammatory skin condition characterized by erythematous and pruritic skin lesions that occur
after contact with a foreign substance. There are two forms of contact dermatitis: irritant and allergic. Common allergens and
irritants include nickel, rubber, fragrances (Perfumes), topical antibiotics, water, soaps, cleansers, acids and alkalis.

Clinical Presentation:
     •    Well-demarcated, erythematous, vesicular and/or scaly patch
          or plaque
     •    Acute-blisters, weeping and oedema
     •    Chronic-lichenification, hyperkeratosis and fissuring
     •    Itching or painful, may be severe
     •    The distribution can be linear or localized                            Nickel allergy

Investigations:
Patch testing

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Avoid contact with the allergen or irritant
    •  Using moisturizers multiple times per day
    •  Avoid water, soap, oil, overheating, sweat, dust, and friction irritation, from doing further damage to the skin barrier

Pharmacological Management
C: betamethasone valerate cream/ointment (topical) 12hourly for 4weeks
          OR
S: tacrolimus Ointment (face or skin folds) (topical) 12hourly
          OR
(For moderate cases)
S: mometasone furoate cream/ointment (topical) 24hourly for 4weeks
          OR
(For severe cases)
D: clobetasol propionate cream/ointment (topical) 24hourly for 4weeks
  Note: A single application with occlusion at night is often more effective than multiple daytime applications.

sections.title: Seborrheic Eczema (Dermatitis)
sections.text:
It is a chronic, relapsing, and usually mild form of dermatitis confined to skin regions with high sebum production and the large
body folds. It is associated with the commensal yeast Malassezia.

Clinical Presentation:
     •    Erythematous patches or plaques with greasy-looking
     •    Distributed on areas rich in sebaceous glands, such as the scalp, ear, face, chest, back and the
          intertriginous area

Pharmacological Management
A: clotrimazole cream (topical) 12 hourly for 4-6weeks
          OR
C: miconazole cream (topical) 12 hourly for 4-6weeks
          OR
C: ketoconazole shampoo (topical) 3 times per week for not less than 3 months
          AND
A: hydrocortisone cream (topical) 12 hourly for 4-16weeks
          OR
C: betamethasone valerate cream/ointment 12hourly for 4-6 weeks
          OR
S: tacrolimus Ointment (topical) (face or skin folds) 12 hourly for 4-6 weeks

sections.title: Anaphylaxis
sections.text:
It is an acute and often life-threatening immunologic reaction, frequently heralded by scalp pruritus, diffuse erythema, urticaria,
or angioedema. Bronchospasm, laryngeal edema, hyperperistalsis, hypotension, and cardiac arrhythmia may occur. Antibiotics
(especially penicillin), other drugs, and radiographic contrast agents are the most common causes of serious anaphylactic
reactions.

Management: Refer to chapter on approach to patients with emergency conditions

sections.title: Psoriasis
sections.text:
Psoriasis is a common, chronic inflammatory skin condition that can present with various clinical forms. Types of psoriasis
include chronic plaque psoriasis, guttate psoriasis, erythrodermic psoriasis, and pustular psoriasis.

Clinical Presentation:
     •    Thick, silvery-white, scaly plaques mainly affecting the scalp, sacral region, and extensor surfaces of the body.
     •    Usually symmetrically distributed, with a chronic relapsing course.
     •    Can involve joints (psoriatic arthritis)

Investigations:
Skin biopsy

Non-Pharmacological Management
Phototherapy

Pharmacological Management
C: betamethasone valerate ointment (topical) 12hourly for not less than 12weeks.
           OR
C: betamethasone dipropionate and salicylic ointment (topical) 12hourly for not less than 4months
           OR
D: clobetasol propionate ointment (topical) 24hourly for not less than 4months (severe disease)
           OR
S: tacrolimus Ointment (topical) (face or skin folds) 12hourly for not less than 4 months
           AND
C: coal tar (topical) 5-10% in Vaseline in the morning for not less than 3 months
           AND
C: salicylic acid (topical) 5-10% in Vaseline to de-scale, apply at night for not less than 3 months

For severe or extensive disease:
         ADD
S: methotrexate (PO) 7.5-20mg with folic acid supplementation weekly for not less than 6 months
         OR
S: cyclosporine (PO) 3-5mg/kg/day up to 3months
         OR
S: adalimumab (SC) 80mg stat, then 40mg weekly for 6 weeks

 Note: Systemic steroids should not be used in psoriasis due to their rebound effect.

sections.title: Pityriasis Rosea
sections.text:
Pityriasis rosea (PR) is an acute, self-limiting exanthematous disease that primarily affects children and young adults aged
between 10 and 35 years. A large body of evidence supports the causal role of the endogenous systemic active human
herpesvirus (HHV)-6 and HHV-7 infections in PR pathogenesis.

Clinical Presentation:
     •    Prodromal symptoms such as mild fever, sore throat, headache and loss of appetite
     •    Begins with a "herald" or "mother" patch, a single round or oval lesion on the chest, neck, or back
     •    Secondary eruption consisting of smaller papulosquamous lesions along the cleavage lines of the skin in a distribution
          that resembles a “Christmas tree’’
     •    Pruritus is usually mild or absent

Pharmacological Management
A: hydrocortisone cream (topical) 12hourly for 4-16weeks
         OR
C: betamethasone valerate cream/ointment (topical) 12hourly for 4-6 weeks
       OR/AND
A: prednisolone (PO) 0.5 -1mg/kg 24hourly for 1-2weeks (short course)
         AND
B: acyclovir (PO) 400mg; pediatric 20mg/kg; 8hourly for 7 days

sections.title: Lichen Planus
sections.text:
Lichen planus (LP) is a chronic lichenoid inflammatory disorder of the skin, mucosa, and appendages. Viruses, drugs, and
contact allergens have been reported to be possibly associated with the development of LP.

Clinical Presentation:
     •    Pruritic, purple, polygonal, flat-topped papules or/and plaques
     •    Typical locations are the wrists, lower back, and ankles

Investigations:
    •    Skin biopsy
    •    Hepatitis C antibodies (patient with high risk)

Non-Pharmacological Management
S: Phototherapy

Pharmacological Management

C: betamethasone valerate ointment (topical) 12hrly for 2–4 weeks
           OR
D: clobetasol propionate ointment (topical) 24hourly daily for 2–4weeks
           AND
A: cetirizine (PO) 10mg 24hourly for 2 weeks
           OR
C: loratadine (PO) 10mg 24hourly for 2weeks
           OR
S: desloratadine (PO) 5mg 24hourly for 2 weeks

For extensive involvement:
A: prednisolone (PO) 0.5-1 mg/kg 24hourly for 3-4weeks then taper

For recalcitrant cases:
S: methotrexate (PO) 7.5-20mg weekly for not less than 6months with folic acid supplementation.

sections.title: Acne
sections.text:
Acne is a multifactorial disorder of the pilosebaceous unit. It is common among adolescents and young adults, but is not
restricted to these age groups. Acne variants include Post-Adolescent Acne, Acne Conglobata, Neonatal Acne, and Infantile
Acne.

Clinical Presentation:
 •    Open and closed comedones
 •    Papules, pustules, nodules and cyst
 •    Commonly affects the face, neck, chest, upper back
      and upper arms

Investigations
Laboratory tests and radiologic imaging are limited to patients who exhibit signs of associated diseases (Hyperandrogenism
and SAPHO syndrome) or acne fulminans.

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Avoid picking of acne lesions
    •  Avoid aggressive scrubbing of the skin
    •  Avoid underlying precipitating factors, e.g., stress, nuts, chocolate, overuse of ointments on skin, steroids,
       anticonvulsant drugs, etc.
    •  Use non-comedogenic moisturizers.
    •  Photodynamic therapy
    •  Laser therapy

sections.title: Cutaneous Drug Reactions:
sections.text:
It is a response to a medicinal product that is noxious and unintended. Up to 80% of Adverse drug reactions are dose-dependent
and predictable, while about 20% are independent of the administered dose and unpredictable.

Classification of adverse drug reactions:
 Type A: Predictable adverse reactions                        Type B: Unpredictable adverse reactions
 •   Over dosage (wrong dosage or defect in drug              •   Allergic reaction (drug allergy or hypersensitivity;
     metabolism)                                                  immunologic reaction to drug; requires previous exposure or
 •   Side effects (sleepiness from antihistamines)                cross-reaction)
 •   Indirect effects (antibiotics changing normal flora)     •   Pseudo allergic reaction (non-immunologic activation of mast
 •   Drug interactions (altered metabolism of drugs; most         cells).
     commonly involving the cytochrome P-450 enzymes)         •   Idiosyncratic reaction (unexplained reaction, not related to
                                                                  mechanism of action, without known or suspected
                                                                  immunologic mechanism).

  Note:80% of allergic and pseudo allergic drug reactions are caused by Beta-lactam antibiotics, aspirin, NSAIDs and
  sulfonamides

Non-life-threatening cutaneous adverse drug reactions may include fixed drug eruption (FDE), urticaria, exanthematous drug
eruptions, and lichenoid drug eruption, while life-threatening cutaneous adverse reactions include toxic epidermal necrolysis
(TEN), Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS), acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP), and drug reaction with
eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS).

sections.title: Fixed Drug Eruption (FDE)
sections.text:
It is a cutaneous drug reaction that recurs at the same site with repeated exposure to the agent.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Well-demarcated, round to oval, dusky red to brown/black macules that may develop into edematous plaques with or
          without vesiculation or blistering.
     •    Pruritus and a burning or stinging sensation are common.

Non-Pharmacological Management
Avoidance of a triggering drug

Pharmacological Management
A: hydrocortisone (IV) 200mg 12hourly for 24hours for 2-4 weeks
         OR
C: betamethasone valerate cream (topical) 12hourly for 2-4 weeks
         OR
D: clobetasol propionate cream/ointment (topical) 24hourly for 2- 4weeks

sections.title: Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS) and Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN)
sections.text:
They are rare and life-threatening mucocutaneous conditions caused by immune system activation, most commonly initiated
by certain drugs and their metabolites or infections. In SJS, <10% of BSA is affected by skin detachment, 10–30% is an overlap
area between SJS and TEN, and >30% is defined as TEN.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Prodromal symptoms with fever, malaise, sore throat, and arthralgia
     •    Early Lesions are ill-defined, erythematous, and coalescing macules
     •    Within days, blistering and detachment of the epidermis with light pressure (positive Nikolsky sign) occur
     •    All mucosal surfaces can be involved, including the buccal, oro/nasopharyngeal, and anogenital mucosa
     •    Eye involvement is common

Investigations

    •      Skin biopsy                             •    Creatinine                         •    Serum BUN
    •      FBP                                     •    Total protein                      •    Skin or blood culture and
    •      Serum electrolyte                       •    Serum albumin                           sensitivity
    •      Serum glucose

Non-Pharmacological Management

    •      Multi-disciplinary approach involving dermatologist,         •    Encourage high protein diet
           ophthalmologist, gynecologist and physician                  •    Avoid debridement and consider detached
    •      Withdrawal all suspected drugs                                    epidermis as natural biological dressing
    •      If SCORTEN is 0-1, admit into normal ward, if 2 or more      •    Fluid replacement with electrolyte solution
           admit to ICU                                                      2ml/kg/%BSA in the 1st 24 hours
    •      Keep warm at 28-300 C

Pharmacological Management
A: paracetamol (PO) 1g; paediatric 15 mg/kg, 6hourly, for 3 days (mild pain)
          OR
A: diclofenac (IM) 50-100mg stat (moderate pain)
          OR
C: morphine (IV) 0.1mg/kg stat (severe pain)
          AND
A: hydrocortisone (IV) 200mg 12hourly for 48hours
          OR
A: prednisolone (PO) 1-2mg/kg 24hourly for 5-7 days
          AND
S: cyclosporine (PO) 3-5mg/kg/day for 7-10 days

   Note:
       •     Antibiotics should only be given if there are signs of infection and should be guided culture results
       •     Systemic therapies (corticosteroids and cyclosporine), if employed, should be used within 24 to 48 hours of
             symptom onset

sections.title: Pellagra
sections.text:
It is a nutritional disorder caused by a deficiency of vitamin B3 (niacin) and/or tryptophan. It is characterized by four D's:
photosensitive dermatitis, diarrhoea, dementia, and, if not treated, death.

Clinical Presentation:
     •    Casal necklace: hyperpigmented scaling affecting the neck area
     •    Hyperpigmented scaly lesions on sun-exposed areas

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Topical emollients at least four times per day
    •  Encourage a high-protein diet

Pharmacological Management:
B: sunscreen (topical) SPF 30+ or above, applied at least twice a day, AM and Noon
          AND
A: hydrocortisone ointment (topical) 12-hourly (if mild disease, or on face) for 4 weeks
          OR
C: betamethasone valerate cream/ointment (topical) 12-hourly for other parts of the body for 4 weeks
          AND
C: nicotinamide (PO) 50-100mg; paediatric 5mg/kg in three divided doses, 24 hourly for 4 weeks

sections.title: Vitiligo
sections.text:
Vitiligo is an acquired disorder characterized by circumscribed depigmented macules and patches resulting from a progressive
loss of functional melanocytes. It is associated with other autoimmune diseases, such as autoimmune thyroid disease, adult-
onset insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus, and lupus erythematosus.

Clinical Presentation:
     •    Asymptomatic depigmented macules and
          patches
     •    Depigmented hairs are often present in lesional
          skin
     •    Affects more on the face and areas around the
          orifices, genitals, and hands

Investigations
Thyroid function test

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Avoiding Koebnerizing factors (friction, trauma)
    •  Moderate UV light exposure
    •  S: phototherapy (Disseminated Vitiligo)

Pharmacological Management
 Stabilization of the disease:                  Regimentation:
 A: prednisolone (PO) 10-20mg; paediatric 5-    C: betamethasone valerate ointment/cream 12hourly for 3-6 months
 10mg, 24hourly for 14 days                                                OR
             OR                                 S: mometasone furoate cream/ointment (topical) 24hourly for 3-6 months
 S: phototherapy (PUVA or NBUVB)                                           OR
 (Disseminated vitiligo)                        S: tacrolimus ointment (topical) 12hourly for 3-6 months (face, folds or
                                                mucous membrane)
                                                                           OR
                                                D: clobetasol cream/ointment (topical) 24hourly for 3-6 months
                                                                         OR/AND

sections.title: Melasma
sections.text:
Melasma is a common and chronic acquired disorder characterized by symmetric, hyperpigmented patches that typically occur
on the face. It is more common in females.

Clinical Presentation:
     •    Bilateral and symmetrical hyperpigmented
          macules or patches with an irregular border
     •    May affect the forehead, nose, cheeks, upper
          lip area, and chin

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Sun protection by wearing a wide-brimmed hat
    •  Camouflage if desired

Pharmacological Management
 S: tretinoin cream (topical) 24hourly (at night) for 3-6 months        Alternative Therapies:
                     AND                                                S: laser therapy’
 B: sunscreen SPF 30+ or above, applied at least twice a day, AM and           OR
 Noon                                                                   S: chemical Peels

sections.title: Oculocutaneous albinism
sections.text:
Oculocutaneous albinism (OCA) is a genetic disorder characterized by the complete or partial absence of melanin pigment in
the skin, hair, and eyes. Reduced skin pigmentation leads to photosensitivity and increased skin cancer risk.

Clinical Presentation:
     •    Ocular findings: Photophobia, reduced visual        •     Complete or partial absence of pigmentation on the
          acuity, strabismus, nystagmus, and lack of                skin, hair and eyes
          binocular vision.

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Avoiding UV exposure during the pick hours (10AM-            •   Skin examination at 6 months interval
       4PM)                                                         •   Wearing of sun-protective glasses
    •  Use of protecting clothing such as wide-brimmed              •   Genetic counselling to individuals and family on
       hats, shirts with a collar, long sleeves, long pants, and        the condition
       socks

Pharmacological Management
B: sunscreen SPF 30+ or above, applied at least twice a day, AM and Noon

Surgical Treatment:
    •    Cryotherapy of pre-malignant lesions (Actinic Keratosis)
    •    Wide excision of the malignant lesions

sections.title: Xeroderma Pigmentosum
sections.text:
A rare autosomal recessive disease with hyper photosensitivity, photophobia, early onset of freckling, and cutaneous
malignancies, associated with abnormal DNA repair.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Lentigens and freckles
     •    Multiple dry, scaly, mottled hyperpigmented
          and hypopigmented macules (Pigmentary
          changes)
     •    Extreme photophobia

Management
Refer to the management of oculocutaneous albinism.

sections.title: Pruritic Papular Eruption (PPE)
sections.text:
A skin condition characterized by itchy papular eruptions on the extensor area of the upper and lower limbs, which is associated
with HIV infection.

Clinical Presentation:
 •    Sever itchy papules more on the extensors
 •    Extensive excoriation with subsequent scarring
 •    Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation is often the
      most visible manifestation

Pharmacological Management
C: betamethasone valerate cream (topical) 12hourly for 3–4weeks
           OR
D: clobetasol propionate ointment (topical) 24hourly for 2–4weeks
           AND
A: cetirizine (PO) 10mg 12hourly for not less than 4weeks
           OR
C: loratadine (PO) 10mg 24hourly for not less than 4weeks

sections.title: Urticaria and Angioedema
sections.text:
Urticaria is the sudden development of transient wheals (superficial dermal swellings) and angioedema (deep dermal swellings)
or both. It can be acute or chronic, spontaneous or inducible. It can be induced by viral infections, bacterial infections, food
allergies, drug allergies, colds, heat, or tight clothing, among other factors.

Clinical Presentation:
     •    Wheals that come and go rapidly within 24 hours
     •    Wheals may be small or large, as well as single or multiple
     •    Wheals can co-exist with angioedema

Investigations:
    •    FBP                                                             •    Prick and Patch test
    •    CRP or ESR                                                      •    H. Pylori stool antigen
    •    TSH                                                             •    Stool for OVA

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Avoid precipitating factors, e.g., NSAIDs, food, spices
    •  Treatment of the underlying disorder

Pharmacological Management:
 Step One (monotherapy)                                            Step two
 A: cetirizine (PO)10mg 24 hourly for 2-4 weeks                    If step 1 does not control the symptoms increase the dose of
            OR                                                     antihistamine 1 in step 1 up to 4 folds or ADD
 C: loratadine (PO) 10mg 24 hourly for 2-4 weeks
            OR                                                     D: montelukast (PO) 10mg 24 hourly for 4-8 weeks
 S: desloratadine (PO) 5mg 24 hourly for 2-4 weeks

sections.title: Connective Tissue Diseases
sections.text:
They are autoimmune diseases of unknown aetiology that affect the skin,, blood vessels and internal organs. These diseases
include scleroderma, lupus erythematosus, and dermatomyositis or polymyositis.
For Clinical Presentation, investigation, and treatment, refer to the rheumatology chapter 26.

sections.title: Autoimmune Blistering Diseases
sections.text:
They are a group of disorders characterized by the formation of blisters on the skin and/or mucous membranes due to an
abnormal immune response that damages the skin's structural components. These include Pemphigus Vulgaris, Pemphigus
Foliaceous, Bullous Pemphigoid, Dermatitis Herpetiformis, Linear IgA Dermatoses, and Cicatricial Pemphigoid.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Tense or flaccid vesicles
          and bullae on the skin and
          mucus membranes
     •    Lesions     breaks     and
          leaving erosions
     •    Some are associated with
          itching
                                       Bullous Pemphigoid                           Linear IgA dermatosis

Investigations
    •    Skin      biopsy        for              •    Skin biopsy for direct                   •       Indirect
         histopathology                                immunofluorescence                               immunofluorescence
                                                                                                        assay
Pharmacological Management
C: betamethasone cream/ointment (topical) 12hourly for 4-8 weeks (limited diseases)
          OR
D: clobetasol propionate cream/ointment (topical) 24hourly for 4-8 weeks (limited disease)
         AND/OR
A: prednisolone (PO) 0.5-1mg/kg 24hourly for 2 months, then taper slowly to the lowest effective dose
          AND
S: methotrexate (PO) 10 – 15 mg weekly for not less than 4months with folic acid supplementation
          OR
S: mycophenolate mofetil (PO) 1g/day for not less than 4months
          OR
S: rituximab (IV) 375 mg/m2 weekly for 4 weeks

For Treatment of Dermatitis Herpetiformis
S: dapsone (PO)100mg 24hourly for not less than 2months

sections.title: Keloids and hypertrophic scars
sections.text:
Excessive connective tissue proliferation following an injury or spontaneously.

Clinical Presentation
Skin colored nodules or plaques within or extending beyond the scar line, commonly on the earlobes, Associated with pain and
itching.

Pharmacological Management
S: triamcinolone (intralesional) 2.5-5mg/ml monthly for 6-9 months
                    AND
D: clobetasol propionate ointment (topical) 24hourly for 6-9 months

Surgical and other treatment:
D: cryotherapy followed by Inj. Triamcinolone (intralesional) 2.5-5mg/ml monthly for 6-9 months
           OR
D: total excision or debulking of keloids followed by injection of Triamcinolone 20mg intraoperatively and postoperatively for 3
months.
           OR
S: radiotherapy (within 24 hours)
           OR
S: laser therapy

sections.title: Infantile Hemangioma
sections.text:
Benign vascular tumour which appears at birth as a mark and continues growing till 6-12 months, then starts involuting. May
be part of PHACE(S) syndrome or LUMBAR syndrome.

Clinical Presentation
     •    A patch of telangiectasias with surrounding pallor at birth
     •    80% of cases present as a single lesion only, 20% lesions are multiple
     •    Have a predilection for the head and neck, although they can occur anywhere in the skin, mucous membranes, or
          internal organs

Investigations
    •    FBG before initiating treatment and serially after
    •    ECG (ECHO)- Rule out cardiac insufficiency, cardiac or aortic anomaly
    •    Doppler USS- Evaluate the depth and size of infantile hemangioma

Pharmacological Management
A: propranolol (PO) 1mg/kg divided into 2 doses, given 12hourly for 6 months
         OR
S: bleomycin (intralesional injection) 0.3-0.5mg/kg monthly for 4-6 months
         OR
S: pulsed-dye laser therapy

sections.title: Cutaneous Cyst
sections.text:
Cysts are common cutaneous lesions that may cause cosmetic or health problems that evoke deep concern in patients and
their physicians. Common cutaneous cysts include milia and epidermoid cysts.

Treatment: Excision

sections.title: Skin Cancer
sections.text:
The most common skin cancers may be categorized into 2 major groups: melanoma and nonmelanoma skin cancers. The latter
group consists primarily of basal cell carcinomas and squamous cell carcinomas.
These tumors are rarely fatal, but are considered to be fast-growing tumors that, if neglected, may be locally and functionally
destructive. They are common in person living with albinism and xeroderma pigmentosum.
For more details, refer to the malignancies chapter 22.

sections.title: Skin Lightening Effects
sections.text:
Skin lightening (SL) is a practice where a person intentionally reduces the natural melanin pigmentation of their skin. The use
of cosmetic, non-medical skin depigmentation is common among darker-skinned individuals globally.
Skin-lightening (or "skin-bleaching") agents are vital tools in managing disorders of hyperpigmentation such as melasma and
post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation. However, some skin-lightening practices and ingredients can lead to various short- and
long-term complications.

Skin Lightening Agents:
    •    Hydroquinone                                                            •    Mercury salts
    •    Corticosteroids                                                         •    Caustic agents

Complications of Skin Lightening Agents:
   •    Contact Dermatitis                                                       •    Striae
   •    Exogenous Ochronosis                                                     •    Folliculitis
   •    Abnormal Skin Regimentation                                              •    Acne
   •    Hyperpigmentation of the finger joints or toes                           •    Tinea Corporis (Incognito)
   •    Nail discolorations                                                      •    Hypertrichosis
   •    Depression                                                               •    HPAA suppression
   •    Anxiety                                                                  •    Hyperglycemia
   •    Atrophy

Patient Management
     •   Early recognition of the use of skin-lightening agents
     •   Confirming the use of skin-lightening agents
     •   Patient counselling on cessation of use and potential local and systemic side effects of excessive use of skin lightening
         agents
     •   Specific management of complications, such as antifungal treatment of tinea, laser therapy for Ochronosis

sections.title: Major Blinding Eye Diseases
sections.text:
Eye diseases and refractive errors are conditions affecting the eye. Diseases of most important are those leading to blindness,
visual impairment (VI) or presenting with pain. Blindness is defined as a presenting visual acuity (VA) of less than 3/60 or central
visual field of less than 10º in the better eye. Visual impairment is categorized by WHO onto several categories depends on
VA. The definition of blindness/VI in children and infants is the same as that in adults though there are different methods for
testing vision in young children until when they are at preschool age when normal visual acuity chart can be used. The common
causes of blindness and visual impairment among adults are cataract, glaucoma, corneal blindness, diabetic retinopathy,
uncorrected refractive errors. There are other eye diseases that do not lead into blindness or visual impairment, these are also
addressed in this section. Given the asymptomatic nature of most eye diseases, it is advised that patients presenting to eye
clinic with whatever complaint must have basic eye examination of both eyes which entails (VA-Plain and PH, IOP, fundoscopy
and pupil exam) as a minimum.

sections.title: Cataract
sections.text:
Cataract is clouding of the lens which prevents clear vision and if not treated can lead to visual impairment and/or blindness.
Most of the time its due to ageing process (Senile Cataract) but can also result from trauma, inflammatory eye diseases or
systemic conditions. Children may be born with cataract (congenital) or develop cataract in the early ages of life (developmental
cataract).

Clinical Presentation
     •    Various degrees of progressive painless vision                    •    Conjunctiva and cornea are clear and the whole
          impairment unilateral or bilateral                                     iris can be seen clearly
     •    History of trauma with a sharp/blunt object for                   •    Obscured red reflex
          traumatic cataract                                                •    For Congenital Cataract, Squint and/or
     •    History of red eye for secondary cataract.                             nystagmus can be seen
     •    Initially glare and haloes around light
     •    Cloudiness in the lens seen as a white mark
          behind the pupil and iris seen with slit lamp
          microscope (Leukocoria)

   Note:
       •     Cataract may present in all age groups, blindness due to cataract is reversible but in children prognosis can be
             guarded depending on duration of the cataract.
        •    Currently, proven treatment is only by surgical removal of the cataractous lens and IOL Implantation
        •    IOL can range from Monofocal IOLs to premium IOLs such as Presbyopia-correcting IOL (Multifocal, EDOF and
             Accommodative IOLs) hence price of cataract surgery will vary depending on inserted IOL.
        •    Early treatment in children is mandatory
        •    White pupil in children may be a tumor in the eye, late referral may lead to permanent loss of vision, squint, loss
             of eye or loss of life
        •    No Cataract surgery should be done without Biometry for precise IOL power calculations

Investigations
    •    Visual acuity (Plain, PH and Corrected                             •    Slit Lamp Biomicroscopy
    •    B Scan if no fundal view                                           •    For some patients: ECG, Echo, BP, Blood sugars
    •    Pen torch eye exam for Cornea clarity and Pupil                         is recommended
         Exam-RAPD Check                                                    •    Refraction depending on the density of cataract
    •    Biometry: Keratometer, A Scan and IOL power                        •    S: Confocal microscopy, Corneal Tomography,
         Calculations                                                            Corneal Topography
    •    IOP Measurements                                                   •    Dilated Fundoscopy
    •    For elderly, Anaesthesiologists review is advised

For congenital cataract, the following additional investigations may be ordered with Pediatrician consultation
    •   ECG                                                         •    Chest X Ray
    •   Echocardiogram                                              •    Blood grouping and Cross- matching
    •   Hemoglobin                                                  •    TORCHES Profile
    •   Full blood picture                                          •    VDRL/PRP

Surgical Treatment
The only treatment available for Cataract is surgery. There are different cataract surgical procedures depending on the causes
of cataract, age of the patient and surgeons’ skills and equipment availability.
