sections.title: Glaucoma
sections.text:
Glaucoma is a syndrome characterized by optic nerve damage and peripheral visual field loss which may be associated with
raised intraocular pressure. The main classes of glaucoma are open angle glaucoma and angle closure glaucoma.
   Note:
        •    Glaucoma may be congenital, primary or secondary to ocular or systemic conditions
        •    By Far POAG is the commonest type of Glaucoma in adults
        •    AACG is a different entity and should be managed as ocular emergency
        •    Congenital Glaucoma can present with simple symptoms and needs high clinical acumen for diagnosis and
             treatment. So, they should be referred to center with capacity to manage congenital Glaucoma

sections.title: Primary Open Angle Glaucoma (POAG)
sections.text:
Clinical Presentation
     •    Painless loss of peripheral vision leading to absolute glaucoma as the end stage
     •    Affects mainly adults of 40 years of age and above
     •    Cornea and conjunctiva are clear
     •    Pupil in the affected eye does not react with direct light in advanced stage (RAPD +Ve)
     •    The optic nerve is always damaged, this can be seen through fundoscopy as enlarged CDR and NRR thinning
     •    One eye may be affected more than the other (Asymmetrical)
     •    First degree relatives of glaucoma patients are at 3x increased risk of developing Glaucoma and at younger age.

 Note
     •        Primary Open Angle Glaucoma does not have symptoms in early stages, hence routine intraocular pressure
              checkup and fundus examinations should be done in all people of 40 years and above by some qualified eye care
              personnel on annual basis.
      •       All suspected cases of glaucoma should be referred to qualified eye care personnel for confirmation of diagnosis,
              Investigations, commencement of treatment and follow up plan
      •       Medical and/or Laser treatment (SLT, MP-TSCPC) should precede Surgical treatment
      •       Refilling of antiglaucoma may be prescribed by a middle cadre eye worker but Biannual monitoring should be done
              at a centre where there is an Ophthalmologist
      •       For advanced and complicated Glaucoma, patients should be referred to a health facility where there are Glaucoma
              Specialists

Investigations
    •    Visual Acuity                                •    Tonometry                                •    Fundus Photography
    •    Pupil Exam                                   •    Gonioscopy                               •    Pachymetry
    •    Slit Lamp Biomicroscopy                      •    Refraction                               •    Optical Coherent
    •    Fundoscopy                                   •    Visual Field Analysis                         Tomography

Pharmacological Management
This is initiated after a diagnosis is reached by an ophthalmologist, refill of some medicines can be done by Assistant Medical
Officers in ophthalmology but with regular reviews at a health facility with eye specialist. Medical treatment should be lifelong
unless there are conditions necessitating other interventions
                                                                        ADD
D: timolol 0.25% or 0.5%, one drop in the affected eye,
                                                                        D: prostamide bimatoprost 0.03%, one drop, 24hourly in
instill 12hourly.
           OR                                                           the affected eye.
                                                                                  OR
D: betaxolol 0.25% or 0.5%, one drop in the affected eye,
                                                                        D: brimonidine tartrate 0.15–0.2%, one drop, 12hourly, in
instill 12hourly. Use lower strength in mild disease and
those at risk of complications.                                         the affected eye.
           OR                                                                     OR
                                                                        S: dorzolamide eye drop, one drop, 12hourly in the
D: latanoprost 0.005% one drop Nocte in the affected eye
                                                                        affected eye
In patients who comply to treatment and there is no good                          OR
response                                                                S: brinzolamide eye drop, one drop, 12hourly in the
                                                                        affected eye

  Note:
      •       These may be used as first-line in patients with contraindication of beta-blockers.
      •       They can be used as a second/third-line drug in patients on beta-blockers if the target IOP reduction has not
              been reached either as two drops or as FDC drops in a single bottle

In patients who are intolerant to prostaglandin analogue or are not responding
give:
D: brimonidine tartrate 0.15–0.2%, one drop, 12hourly, in the affected eye.
         OR
S: dorzolamide 20mg/mL, one drop, 8hourly in the affected eye
In special cases those with ACG give:
D: pilocarpine hydrochloride 2% or 4%, instill one drop in the affected eye 8 hourly.
 Note: Pilocarpine causes long-standing pupil constriction so it should not be used unless a patient is been prepared for
 some types glaucoma surgery or as an alternative topical treatment for patients who are contraindicated for Timolol use.
 Consult a specialist before using it.

In severe cases or while waiting for surgery, use:
D: acetazolamide (PO) 250mg - 500mg 6hourly

 Note:
     •        β-blockers are contraindicated to people who are known to have overt asthma as this group of medication may
              cause an acute asthmatic attack within a short time following instillation into the eye
         •    Brimonidine is contraindicated in children below 12years

Laser Treatment
     •       SLT may be indicated as initial treatment or in addition to or instead of eye drops or surgery to where it is available
     •       Laser trabeculoplasty (Argon Laser Trabeculoplasty, Selective Laser Trabeculoplasty) or limited
             cyclophotocoagulation or MP-TSCPC are different options among others

Surgical Treatment
It is done in all patients with poor compliance and when medical treatment is not useful. There are different surgical techniques
depending on the age of the patients, patients’ response to surgical treatment, surgeons’ surgical skills and availability of
equipment. It is recommended that all surgeries are done by Ophthalmologists after thorough assessment of the patients.
Angle Surgeries such as Goniotomy and MIGS should proceed Trab and/or tube surgeries. Adjuvant use of 5FU and MMC is
highly encouraged to prolong lifespan of the surgery.

sections.title: Acute Angle Closure Glaucoma (AACG)
sections.text:
This is also known as Congestive glaucoma and commonly affect people aged 40 years and above. It affects more females
than males and majority are hyperopia

Clinical Presentation
     •    Acute sudden onset of                      •    Shallow anterior chamber                  •    Firm or hard globe on
          painful red eye around the                 •    Fixed and semi-dilated                         digital palpation due to
          limbus                                          pupil                                          Severe            elevated
     •    Severe headache and                        •    Photophobia ++                                 intraocular pressure.
          cloudiness of the cornea                   •    Blepharospasm                             •    It may be asymptomatic if
          with decreased VA                                                                              IOP raises slowly (In
     •     Nausea/Vomiting                                                                               Chronic/Subacute cases)

Investigations
    •    Visual Acuity                                                      •    Fundoscopy when cornea clear up
    •    Tonometry                                                          •    Gonioscopy when cornea clear up
    •    Slit Lamp Biomicroscopy                                            •    Visual Field Analysis for chronic disease
Pharmacological Management
Institute therapy and then refer the patient to eye specialist at the Regional, Zonal or National Hospital for investigations and
proper management.
Try to achieve immediate IOP reduction
First-Line

D: acetazolamide (PO), 500mg immediately as a single                   D: pilocarpine hydrochloride 2% or 4%, instill one drop in
dose followed by 250mg 6hourly                                         the affected eye 8 hourly.
           AND                                                                   AND
D: timolol 0.25–0.5% eye drops, instill one drop 12hourly              A: ibuprofen 400mg (PO) 12hourly
in the affected eye                                                              OR
           AND                                                         A: paracetamol (PO) 1g 8hourly
Use the above combined treatment until you have achieved your target IOP reduction, then continue with only Timolol eye
drops for life unless patient has received surgical intervention and/or the trigger has been addressed and the IOP is reduced to
normal level and no optic nerve damage progression

Second-Line
If the above measures fail, use as a short-term treatment, give systemic osmotic agents:
C: mannitol 15–20% (IV)1.5–2mg/kg body weight to run slowly over 30–60minutes
          OR
D: paracentesis with a 30G needle for decreasing IOP
These medicines have diuretic effects, so they are only used as a single dose. They are also used in emergencies to prepare
patients with high intraocular pressure for surgery as they lower intraocular pressure rapidly.
Surgical Treatment
This is done at a centre with Eye Specialists and necessary diagnostic and treatment equipment. Surgical or Later Peripheral
Iridectomy will create a passage for the aqueous fluid from posterior chamber to the drainage angle.
Referral: Management of advanced angle closure glaucoma is done by eye specialist. All patients with Angle Closure
Glaucoma should be referred to eye specialist for other management modalities and continuity of care.
  Note:
      •      Acute Angle Closure Glaucoma is an Ophthalmological Emergency
      •      Immediately refer all patients with AACGto eye specialist after initial medical treatment to lower Intraocular pressure
      •      Patients who have had AACG should be monitored closely for relapse.
      •      Acetazolamide is a Sulfur containing medicine, do not use in patients allergic to Sulfur.
      •      Manage the associated pain and vomiting
      •      Look for any trigger and address it accordingly
       •     Educate patient and warn about relapse

sections.title: Childhood and Juvenile Glaucoma
sections.text:
It is a syndrome whereby the intraocular pressure is raised and cause abnormality of the eyeball and visual disturbances
including blindness if treatment is delayed. Presents from birth to 30 years.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Bigger than normal eye for age (buphthalmos)                   •    Cloudy cornea,
     •    Photophobia                                                    •    Mild Red conjunctiva though occasionally
     •    Tearing                                                        •    Decrease in visual acuity
     •    Blepharospasms

Investigations
For children, examination is done under General Anaesthesia (EUA)
     •    Tonometry                                                      •    Fundoscopy
     •    Cornea Diameters (H&V)                                         •    Gonioscopy depending on corneal visibility
     •    Slit lamp examination                                          •    Pachymetry

Surgical Treatment
Treatment for congenital glaucoma is usually surgery, which is done by either Pediatric Ophthalmologist or Glaucoma specialist.

Referral: Refer any child who has the above-mentioned signs to a specialist at the National Hospital or Zonal Referral Hospitals
where there is Paediatric Eye team. Even when you’re not sure of the diagnosis as it could be congenital glaucoma

 Note:
     •     Prophylaxis Laser (PI) is usually advised to the fellow eye to prevent attack
     •     First Degree screening by Gonioscopy is advised so as to capture them early
     •     For Juvenile Glaucoma (Age 16-30years) a secondary cause should be sought and addressed accordingly as
           most of the time Juvenile glaucoma is an aggressive form of Glaucoma hence prompt and proper management is
           highly advised.

sections.title: Secondary Glaucoma
sections.text:
This presents as a complication of other eye diseases such as uveitis, hypermature cataract, Pseudo exfoliation syndrome,
ACA abnormalities, ocular trauma and retinal diseases. It may also be due to prolonged use of steroids.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Poor vision in the affected eye associated with                •    New vessels on the iris if the cause is retinal
     •    High intraocular pressure                                           diseases
     •    Optic nerve damage                                             •    Shallow or normal depth Anterior Chamber

Investigations
    •    Visual Acuity                                                   •    Refraction
    •    Slit Lamp Biomicroscopy                                         •    Visual Field Analysis
    •    Fundoscopy                                                      •    Fundus Photography
    •    Tonometry                                                       •    Pachymetry test
    •    Gonioscopy                                                      •    Optical Coherent Tomograph

Pharmacological Management
Management of these patients depends on the cause, but it includes medical, surgical and laser. Institute these treatment as
you refer these patients: -
D: acetazolamide (PO) 500mg immediately stat followed by 250mg 6hourly
          AND
D: timolol 0.25–0.5% eye drops, instill one drop 12hourly in the affected eye.

Treatment of the preexisting eye disease is highly recommended.

Referral: Refer all patients suspected to have secondary glaucoma to a qualified eye specialist available at the Regional, Zonal
or National Hospital for proper assessment and definitive management.

sections.title: Ocular Trachoma
sections.text:
It has five grades according to WHO which are grouped into two (Active Trachoma and Cicatricial Trachoma). Active trachoma
usually happened in children below age of 9 years as is an acute conjunctivitis caused by infection with Chlamydia trachomatis
(bacteria). The Cicatricial trachoma (TS, TT and CO) is one of the commonest causes of corneal blindness worldwide. There
is an inward turning of the eye lashes which rub against the cornea and lead to corneal opacity which is the culprit for visual
impairment and/or blindness.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Purulent whitish discharge in active disease
     •    Photophobia in early stages or re- infection
     •    More than 5 Follicles in the upper tarsal plate seen as round and white nodules in active disease.
     •    In cicatricial stages, in-turned eyelashes rub on the cornea leading to corneal ulcers and eventually opacity if left
          untreated
     •    Loss of vision due to corneal scarring and opacification.

Clinical Stages according to World Health Organization

Active Disease
    •    Trachomatous Inflammation Follicular (TF) - Presence of at least 5 follicles on the upper tarsal plate
    •    Trachomatous Inflammation Intense (TI) – There is intense inflammation, the conjunctival blood vessels cannot be
         seen.

Cicatricial Disease
    •     Trachomatous Scarring (TS) – Presence of white scars in the upper tarsal plate
    •     Trachomatous Trichiasis (TT) – Presence of some eye lashes rubbing against the cornea
    •     Corneal Opacity (CO) – Presence of corneal opacity (scar) affecting the central cornea

Investigations
    •    Visual acuity                                                   •    Conjunctival swab for dipstick test and or PCR
    •    Refraction                                                      •    Lid eversion for follicles and tarsal conjunctiva
    •    Slit lamp bimicroscopy                                               scars

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Face washing and hygiene to prevent transmission of disease from one person to the other
    •  Environmental improvement/hygiene and sanitation
    •  Water availability and use of pit latrines

Pharmacological Management
A: oxytetracycline eye ointment 3% 24hourly for 6weeks
          OR
B: azithromycin (PO) 20mg/kg (Max 2g) stat- for treatment, preventive chemotherapy and in mass treatment campaign

  Note:
      •     Preventive chemotherapy in mass treatment campaign is conducted only once a year by NTD unit.
      •     Active disease in children should be treated aggressively to avoid later complications.
      •     TT should be managed by surgery timely before CO develops.

Surgery
For Trachomatous Trichiasis Surgical correction of entropion through BTRP. This procedure can be done at a Dispensary or
Health Centre and community level by a trained health worker.
For Corneal Opacities, the recommend treatment modality is Corneal Transplant in any form hence we are advocating for
Corneal banks establishment and tissue harvesting policies development to enable these patients to get appropriate care.

Referral: Refer all patients with recurrent TT or lower Eyelid TT to Oculoplastic Surgeon at Regional Referral or Zonal Referral
Hospital for proper assessment and surgical management.

sections.title: Diseases of the Retina and Posterior Segment
sections.text:
Main diseases of the retina that because blindness are Diabetic Retinopathy, Diabetic Macular Edema, Retinal Detachment,
Vitreous Hemorrhages, retinal vessels occlusions and Age-related Macular Degeneration.

sections.title: Diabetic Retinopathy
sections.text:
It is a chronic progressive sight-threatening disease of the retinal blood vessels associated with the prolonged hyperglycemia
and other conditions linked to diabetic mellitus such as hypertension. Its is a complication of long-standing diabetes mellitus in
the eyes
Clinical Presentation
      •    Initially asymptomatic
      •    Loss of vision in moderate and advanced stages, when there is severe NPDR or PDR presenting with vitreous/retinal
           haemorrhage, Tractional RD
      •    Diabetic cataract and anterior chamber new vessels in iris or angle

  Note:
      •     Regular and scheduled screening at Diabetic or Eye Clinic is recommended for early diagnosis for all DM patients
      •     All DM patients should be advised to visit eye clinic for checkup and DR Screening

Diabetic retinopathy is mainly grouped into three stages/presentations:
    •    Non-Proliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR)
    •    Diabetic macular Edema (DME)
    •    Proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR)

Investigations
    •    Visual acuity with and without pinhole                             •    Fluorescein Fundus Angiography (FFA)
    •    Tonometry                                                          •    S: Indocyanine green Angiography (ICGA)
    •    Dilated   fundoscopy      (Direct   or indirect                    •    Optical Coherence Tomography
         ophthalmoscopy with or without biomicroscopy)                      •    Gonioscopy
    •    Fundus photography                                                 •    Pupil Exam

Pharmacological Management
Dilate the pupils with combined
D: tropicamide 1% + phenylephrine 2.5% eye drops
          OR
D: tropicamide 1% with
          OR
D: cyclopentolate 1% eye drops to screen

Table14.2 below gives a summary of the Stages of Diabetic Retinopathy at Eye Clinic, treatment options and follow up schedule.
Treatment is done in consultation with Diabetologist/endocrinologist and Physician to ensure a good glycaemic and blood
pressure control

Consider Argon LASER in patients with severe Non-Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (NPDR) under the following
circumstances:
i. Older type 2 diabetics                                   v. Regular attendance to clinic for follow up is likely to be
ii. Difficult retinal view                                  poor
iii. Prior to cataract surgery                              vi. Difficult to examine patient due to other reasons.
iv. Only one eye situation where the first eye was lost due
to PDR

**Intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy administered on a monthly basis is effective in the management of PDR. Treatment frequency
should be individualized according to disease response, following a treat- and-extend protocol where appropriate
**Mild and moderate PDR should be treated with full scatter PRP (minimum 1200 shots in one sitting) or intravitreal anti-VEGF
injection whichever is available, accessible and affordable.

If both are available and affordable then anti-VEGF injection is the treatment of choice provided the patient:
i. Is able to come for follow up at regular intervals- every month for 3 months and then every 2 months for next 3 months and
    then 3monthly
ii. Can afford the injections which may total up to 6 injections in the first year
iii. Has no contraindications to the injections
If any one of the above does not apply, then the patient should have PRP done.

Treatment options for Diabetic Macular Edema (DME)
Management of DME depends on the clinical stage of DME and treatment options available at the facility where the patient has
been attended.
Primary tests are required to be performed in order to grade the DME. Macula OCT for all diabetic patients should be the
baseline test to determine presence or absence of DME. Macular thickness of equal or more than 400 microns should be
considered as DME. Those facilities without this tool, the clinical assessment will be the baseline test where the best corrected
visual acuity will be the key point for grading which will be matched with the clinical findings. Therefore, VA of less than 6/12
should be considered as DME case. It is important to exclude other causes of visual impairment before concluding the presence
of DME. Use of anti-VEGF has been found to be effective in the treatment of DME.

Table14.3: Treatment options for various grades of DME
 Grade                    Treatment option                                              Follow up period

                            a. VA is not improving
                            b. There is clinically persistent DME

                            i.        Grid LASER should be given for diffuse,
                                      Exudative or edematous macular edema
                            ii.       Focal LASER to areas of focal Exudative
                                      edema

Pharmacological Management
For glycemic control give antioxidant in non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy
D: multivitamin + carotenoids (PO) 24hourly to a maximum of 3months

For intravitreal anti Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor (VEGF) in Proliferative Disease
S: bevacizumab, 1.25mg per 0.05ml, intravitreal injection, stat.
          OR
S: ranibizumab, 0.5mg per 0.05ml, intravitreal injection stat.
          OR
S: aflibercept, 2mg per 0.05ml, intravitreal injection stat

Repeat after every month to a maximum of 3 months then 6 weekly to complete 6 injections. Re- assess on 3 monthly basis if
there are signs of disease progression, restart treatment, with close follow up.
          AND
S: triamcinolone acetonide, 0.05ml, intravitreal injection, stat. Repeat after 3months if necessary.

Surgical Treatment
    •    This is done in the Advanced proliferative stage                  •      The vitreous cavity may be filled with tamponade
    •    It involves removal of vitreous and or blood,                            liquid such as silicon oil or expansile gas like
         peeling of formed fibrovascular tissue and                               sulfur perfluoro propane or sulfur hexafluoride
         reattachment of retina if the retina is detached                         depending on the level of complication
    •    It is combined with retinal photocoagulation                      •      It may also be combined with Pharmacological
                                                                                  Management (Anti VEGF) mentioned above

Laser Treatment
Laser photocoagulation: Extent and type of this treatment depending on the stage of the disease
    •    Focal Laser
    •    Grid Laser
    •    Pan Retinal Photocoagulation for advanced disease

 Note:
     •     Ophthalmologists should work together with Physicians to holistically treat the diabetic patient.
     •     Poorly controlled diabetes mellitus and diabetic retinopathy can lead to blindness
     •     All patients with diabetes mellitus regardless of their eye conditions, should have a thorough eye examination by
           available eye care personnel or an eye specialist at least once a year.
      •    Dilated eye examination and direct viewing of the retina by an ophthalmologist or qualified eye care personnel is
           mandatory at initial diagnosis of Diabetes Mellitus and as per recommended schedule by the attending clinician.
      •    Urgent referral of all diabetic patients with sudden loss of vision to eye specialist is highly advised
      •    For detailed DR treatment refer to National DR Management guideline

sections.title: Retinal Detachment
sections.text:
Retinal detachment is a sight threatening condition with an incidence of approximately 1 in 10000. Three known forms of Retinal
detachment:
     •    Rhegmatogenous retinal detachments are often due to retinal tears associated with posterior vitreous detachment
          or trauma.
     •    Tractional retinal detachments can be seen in proliferative retinopathy due to diabetic disease, sickle cell and other
          disease processes leading to neovascularization of the retina.
     •    Serous/Exudative detachments are caused by a number of inflammatory, or exudative retinal disease processes
          such as sarcoidosis, medication toxicity, myeloma, or choroidal neoplasms.

Clinical Presentation
Sudden painless loss of vision with cuttens like complaints.

Investigations
    •    VA,
    •    B scan,
    •    Fundoscopy,
    •    OCT

Management
At Primary level once diagnosis of RD is suspected, referral should be done immediately to tertiary center with VRS for proper
management. Treatment options vary depends on type of RD.

Medical management for Serous RD. Any inflammatory disease or underlying mass should be identified and treated if possible
Surgical management is indicated for rhegmatogenous and tractional detachments. Surgical options are:
    •    Laser retinopexy is typically reserved for small, localized detachments
    •    Pneumatic retinopexy involves the injection of an intraocular gas bubble along with retinopexy using cryotherapy or
         laser
    •    Scleral buckles are silicone bands permanently placed around the outside of the globe under the extraocular rectus
         muscles to relieve any traction and support retinal tears
    •    Pars plana vitrectomy with appropriate vitrectomy probe

sections.title: Vitreous Hemorrhages
sections.text:
Vitreous Hemorrhage is a relatively common cause of acute vision loss, having an incidence of approximately 7 cases per
100,000.
The three most common causes include
     •   Proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR)
     •   Posterior vitreous detachment (PVD) with or without retinal tear
     •   Ocular trauma

Clinical Presentation
Sudden, painless visual loss or haze is a common presentation.

Investigations
    •    VA,
    •    Fundoscopy,
    •    B scan

Management
At Primary level if VH is suspected, refer urgently for proper management at tertiary level with information to minimize strenuous
activity, as an increase in blood pressure may disrupt the newly formed clot and cause new active bleeding. If history of using
of anticoagulation, advise to stop.
Intravitreal injection of anti-VEGF agents may be used to cause regression of neovascularization in proliferative retinopathies
such as AMD but not in DR.

Surgery
Pars plana vitrectomy is indicated for vitreous hemorrhage accompanied by retinal detachment or break seen on B-scan, non-
clearing vitreous hemorrhage

sections.title: Acute Retinal Vascular Occlusions
sections.text:
Acute retinal vascular occlusions are common causes of visual impairment. Two forms exist retinal artery occlusions (RAOs)
and retinal vein occlusions (RVOs). They are both associated with increased age and cardiovascular risk factors. These are
synonyms to CVA of the eye. Acute management of RAOs involves a multidisciplinary approach including neurologists with
stroke expertise, while RVO treatment is provided by ophthalmologists; optimization of systemic risk factors by patients’ primary
care providers is an important component of RAO and RVO management.

Clinical Presentation
Acute RAO results in acute monocular visual loss, with severity based on the size of the occluded vessel. attenuation of the
retinal arteries, segmentation of the retinal arterial blood columns with sometimes visible retinal arterial emboli, and acute retinal
ischemia, “cherry red spot”.
Acute RVO presents with sudden loss of vision with tomato paste fundus.

Investigations
    •    VA,                                         •    B scan,                                    •    Systemic       work      up
    •    Refraction,                                 •    Fundoscopy,                                     accordingly
    •    IOP,                                        •    OCT,
    •    Temporal artery palpation,                  •    FFA

Management
At primary level, if diagnosis is suspected. Decreasing of IOP should be considered through medical therapy.
Treatment at tertiary center with VRS can either be medical or surgical depending weather its ischaemic or hemorrhagic RVO.
AntiVEGF can be used.

sections.title: Papilloedema
sections.text:
Papilledema is a term that is exclusively used when a disc swelling is secondary to increased intracranial pressure (ICP). It
must be distinguished from optic disc swelling owing to other causes, which is simply termed "optic disc edema.

Clinical Presentation
Sudden Loss of Vision in patient with Hypertensive crisis usually associated with headache and increased ICP.

Investigations
    •    BP,                                                                •    Fundus autofluorescence,
    •    VA,                                                                •    Optical coherence tomography with enhanced
    •    Fundoscopy,                                                             depth imaging of the optic nerve head.
    •    Ultrasonography (B-scan),                                          •    CT Scan/MRI of the brain,
    •    Fluorescein angiography,

Pharmacological Management
Treat underlying cause by decreasing BP, Medication to lower ICP. Consult Physician for BP control Give
D: acetazolamide (PO) 500mg 12hourly for 5-7 days

If the patient is intolerant to acetazolamide, consider second line
A: furosemide (PO/IV) 20-40mg 24-12hourly

sections.title: Retinopathy of Prematurity
sections.text:
Retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) is primarily due to unmonitored supplemental oxygen. Major risk factors are Low birthweight
(<1500 grams), Gestational age of <30 weeks, High, unregulated oxygen at birth and/or fluctuations in oxygenation and Poor
postnatal growth

Prevention
Screenings of infants at risk with appropriate timing of exams and follow up is essential to identify infants in need of treatment
as per National RoP Guideline.

Diagnosis
Following pupillary dilation using eye drops, the retina is examined with an indirect ophthalmoscope. The peripheral portions of
the retina are pushed into view using scleral depression. International Classification of Retinopathy of Prematurity (ICROP3)
developed a diagnostic classification of ROP. These diagnostic classifications define ROP by location (zone), severity (stage)
and vascular characteristics in the posterior pole (normal, pre-plus, or plus disease).
Non-Pharmacological Management
Follow up interval and treatment will depend on classification of the disease as mentioned in the National RoP Guideline.
Treatment is mainly surgical:
     •    Cryotherapy to the avascular retina. This is mainly given to eyes with threshold RoP which is defined as defined as 5
          contiguous or 8 cumulative clock hours of stage 3 ROP in zone I or zone II with plus disease
     •    Argon and diode lasers to treat the avascular retina of threshold ROP.

Pharmacological Management
Anti-VEGF treatment for stage 3 ROP with plus disease in zone I (not zone II). Given as

S: bevacizumab intravitreal injection 0.2 mg monthly
          OR
S: ranibizumab intravitreal injection 0.2 mg monthly
          OR
S: aflibercept intravitreal injection 0.2mg monthly Follow up after treatment is crucial in these kids.

sections.title: Age Related Macular Degeneration (AMD)
sections.text:
It is a disease condition characterized by progressive macular changes that are associated with increase in age. There are two
types of AMD i.e., Wet AMD and Dry AMD.
Clinical Presentation
       •    Drusens around macula area (yellowish excrescence in the retina)
       •    Affects elderly over 60 years
       •    Poor central vision, characterized with scotomas and later can lead to blindness

Investigations
    •    Visual Acuity                            •   Optical        Coherence                    •    Fundus photography
    •    Refraction                                   Tomography                                  •    Fluorescein     Fundus
    •    Tonometry                                •   Fundoscopy through a                             angiography
                                                      well-dilated pupil,
Non-Pharmacological Management
S: Photodynamic therapy (PDT)

Pharmacological Management
This depends on types of AMD. Intravitreal injection is                        OR
recommended for Wet AMD                                              S: aflibercept, 2mg per 0.05ml, intravitreal injection stat

S: bevacizumab 1.25mg per 0.05ml stat                                Give Antioxidant in Dry AMD
          OR                                                         D: multivitamin + carotenoids, 1 tablet 24 hourly to a
S: ranibizumab 0.5mg per 0.05ml stat.                                maximum of 3 months

Surgical Treatment
Type of surgery depends on the presentation/ stage of the disease.

Referral: Refer patients with Age Related Macular Degeneration to Vitreo-retinal Surgeons for proper management

sections.title: Other Retina Conditions
sections.text:
Several other Retinal Conditions of importance exist such as Macular Hole and Inherited Conditions like Retinitis Pigmentosa
(RP)
     •   Macula Hole presents with acute loss of vision usually with positive Watzke-Allen test
     •   Retinitis Pigmentosa, usually present with night blindness and decreased peripheral vision at young age with
         characteristics bone spicule pigmentation on the retina.

Investigations
    •    VA,                                                              •    OCT
    •    Refraction,                                                      •    Electroretinogram (ERG)
    •    Fundoscopy                                                       •    Electrooculogram (EOG)
    •    B scan, Fundus photo

Management
   •   Macular Hole Surgery
   •   For RP, no proven treatment so far but treatments and strategies can help manage symptoms and improve quality of
       life. These include low vision aids, genetic counseling, and potential gene therapies for specific genetic mutate

sections.title: Refractive Errors and Optical surface disorders
sections.text:
These are eye conditions which presents with poor vision either at near or distance at any age. There are mainly 4 types of
refractive errors:
     •    Presbyopia,                                                  •    Astigmatism
     •    Myopia,                                                      •    Hyperopia.

  Note:
      •    Refractive errors are usually corrected by lenses and/or refractive surgery (Spectacles, contact lenses)
      •    A patient may have more than one type of refractive error.

sections.title: Presbyopia
sections.text:
This is a disorder of accommodation commonly occurring in older people commonly from age of 40 years

Clinical Presentation
     •    It usually starts after the age of 40 years
     •    The main complaint is difficulty in reading/writing or doing near works
     •    Inability to read in dim light
     •    Diagnosis is only through refraction.
     •    Attendance to heath facility is also a good opportunity for screening of glaucoma and diabetic retinopathy which are
          initially asymptomatic

Investigations
    •    Near Visual acuity                                              •    Near and distant Subjective refraction
    •    Colour vision test                                              •    In Children Wet/Cycloplegic Refraction should be
    •    Autorefraction                                                       done
    •    Tonometry                                                       •    Stereopsis test
    •    Near and distant Objective refraction                           •    Duochrome test
    •    Fundoscopy
Non-Pharmacological Management
    •    Convex lens (Plus lenses) spectacles for near vision.
    •    Contact Lenses can be used as well
    •    Refractive Surgery such as LASIK and SMILE

sections.title: Myopia (Short sightedness)
sections.text:
This is a condition whereby patient has difficulty seeing far objects.

Clinical Presentation
     •    It is common in young age between 5–25 years                   •    Blurry vision at distant
     •    The condition persists throughout life, though                 •    Frequently headaches especially at evening
          changes can happen                                             •    It is diagnosed through refraction.
     •    If not treated early, it may progress rapidly and
          lead to retinal complications
Investigations
     •    Distant Visual acuity                                          •    Fundoscopy
     •    Autorefraction                                                 •    Stereopsis test
     •    Near and distant Objective refraction                          •    Colour test
     •    Near and distant Subjective refraction                         •    Strabismus assessment in all children
     •    In Children Wet/Cycloplegic Refraction should be
          done
Non-Pharmacological Management
     •    Spectacles with Concave lens (Minus)for constant wear.
     •    Contact Lenses can be used as well
     •    Refractive Surgery such as LASIK and SMILE can be used

Pharmacological Management
To prevent progression of myopia low dose topical atropine 0.1mg/ml can be used for children aged 3–14 years with myopia
between – 0.50 DS and – 6.00 DS and a progression rate of 0.50 DS or more per year.

  Note:
      •     Secondary causes of Myopia should be ruled out and addressed accordingly
      •     For Children outdoors should be encouraged
      •     Low dose atropine can be used to control myopia progression as well

sections.title: Hypermetropia (Long sightedness)
sections.text:
This is a condition where patients have difficulty in seeing near objects. It is less manifested in children as they have a high
accommodative power.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Ocular strain
     •    Diagnosis in children should be reached after refraction through a dilated pupil (Cycloplegic refraction using
          cyclopentolate eye drop)

Investigations
    •    Distant Visual acuity                                           •    Fundoscopy
    •    Autorefraction                                                  •    Stereopsis test
    •    Near and distant Objective refraction                           •    Duochrome test
    •    Near and distant Subjective refraction                          •    Colour
    •    In Children Wet/Cycloplegic Refraction should be                •    Strabismus assessment in all children
         done

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Spectacles with Convex lens (Plus) spectacles for constant wear
    •  Contact Lenses can be used as well
    •  Refractive Surgery such as LASIK and SMILE can be used

  Note:
  Spectacles should be given to: -
      •    Children who have only significant hypermetropia (more than +3.00 Diopter of Sphere both eyes), all children who
           present with squint and have significant hypermetropia and children with anisometropia
      •    Elderly who presents with signs of ocular strain

sections.title: Astigmatism
sections.text:
This is a condition where the cornea and sometimes the lens have different radius of curvature in all meridians (different focus
in different planes). Some myopic and hyperopic patients may have astigmatism.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Poor vision at distance                                        •    Headache (sometimes) at the evening.
     •    Photophobia                                                    •    Diagnosis is reached through refraction

Clinical Presentation
     •    Visual acuity                                                  •    Fundoscopy
     •    Autorefraction                                                 •    Stereopsis test
     •    Near and distant Objective refraction                          •    Duochrome test
     •    Near and distant Subjective refraction                         •    Colour
     •    In Children Wet/Cycloplegic Refraction should be               •    Strabismus assessment in all children
          done

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Cylindrical lenses spectacles for constant wear. These can be plus or minus depends on refractive findings.
    •  Contact Lenses can be used as well
    •  Refractive Surgery such as LASIK and SMILE can be used
    •  Surgery (Limbal relaxation incisions) can be done

  Note:
      •     Reassessment for all types of refractive errors is done annually and change of lenses if there are significant
            differences and improvement with new correction.
       •    All children with rapid progression of refractive errors need to be seen by Paediatric Optometrist and Paediatric
            Ophthalmologist for further assessment

sections.title: Low Vision and Blindness
sections.text:
Low vision is a permanent visual impairment that cannot be corrected by medication, surgery, or standard spectacles and
interferes with daily activities. It is defined as visual acuity less than 6/18 but equal to or better than 3/60, or a visual field less
than 20 degrees in the better eye with the best possible correction.

Blindness defined as a presenting visual acuity of less than 3/60 in the better eye, or a visual field of less than 10 degrees
from the central fixation, even with the best possible spectacle correction.

Clinical Presentation
Inability to                                                                  •    Write at the same speed as peers
     •      Recognize people in the streets,                                  •    Play with friends.
     •      Read black boards,

Investigations
    •    Visual acuity                                                        •    Slit Lamp Biomicroscopy
    •    Refraction                                                           •    Fundoscopy
    •    Tonometry                                                            •    Low vision assessment
                                                                              •    Orthoptic Assessment
Non-Pharmacological Management
Mainly Rehabilitation
    •    Assessment of the patients’ visual function
    •    Accurate refraction and provision of spectacles if indicated
    •    Low vision devices such as optical devices (magnifiers, telescopes) or non-optical devices (reading stands and or
         reading slits) and white canes as per assessment results.
    •    Surgical intervention is indicated e.g., if a patient has cataract

Referral: All children with low vision should be referred to high level health facility for proper assessment and management by
a paediatric Eye Team

sections.title: Optical surface disorders
sections.text:
These are disorders affecting the cornea and lens to impact vision.
Keratoconus
This is bulging of the cornea due to thinning. It Causes Myopia and visual impairment. It is commonly in childhood especially
during puberty. Its cause is usually allergic conjunctivitis eye rubbing.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Bulging of the cornea,                   •    Vogt striae,                             •   History of VKC,
     •    Munson’s sign,                           •    Charleaux     sign      on               •   Corneal topography,
     •    Rizzuti’s sign,                               refraction,                              •   Keratometry
     •    Photophobia,                             •    Decreased Vision,
Non-Pharmacological Management
After thorough investigations to rule out and address risk factors,
     •    Corneal collagen cross-linking with riboflavin sensitizer, Corneal rings, Refractive laser surgery if all fail, Corneal
          transplantation can be considered.
     •    Specialty contact lenses can be used as indicated

sections.title: Painful Red Eyes
sections.text:
The eye conditions shown on Table 14.4 presents with an acute onset of red eyes: Ocular trauma, Corneal ulcer, Uveitis,
Conjunctivitis

Table 14.4: Summary on diagnosis of Red Eyes
 Disease Condition              Visual Acuity Affected Eye          Cornea              Pupil                Pain     Discharge
 Allergic/ viral Conjunctivitis Good          Both                  Clear               Normal               No       Watery/mucoid
 Bacterial Conjunctivitis       Good          Both                  Clear               Normal               No       Purulent
 Ophthalmia neonatorum          Poor +/-      One/both              Cloudy +/-          Normal +/-           Yes      Copious
                                                                                                                      Purulent
 Cornea ulcer                   Poor              One/ both         Gray spot           Normal               Yes      Watery/purulent
 Uveitis                        Poor              One/ both         Clear or            Small &              Yes      Watery
                                                                    cloudy              Irregular
 Acute glaucoma                 Poor              One               Cloudy              Mid dilated          Yes      Watery

sections.title: Ocular Trauma
sections.text:
These are eye injuries that result from blunt or sharp objects or from chemical substances injuring the eye. The management
of these injuries is guided by history from the patient and ocular findings by the clinicians. Classes of ocular trauma are as
follows: -

sections.title: Blunt Trauma/Non-Perforating Eye Injury/Foreign Body
sections.text:
Establish the cause to determine the type of injury and whether there is penetration.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Corneal abrasion/laceration with or without an imbedded foreign body.
     •    Eye lids may also be involved.
     •    Conjunctiva may be involved as well

Investigations
This is done after the first aid measures                                  •    Fundoscopy in blunt injury or embedded foreign
     •    Examine the injured eye with slit lamp or                             body
          magnifier and pen torch                                          •    B scan in embedded foreign body
     •    Fluorescein staining to reveal foreign body or                   •    CT Scan in suspected metal foreign body
          corneal laceration
 Non-Pharmacological Management
     •    Provide first aid measures to the patients as per presentation
     •    If no penetration, irrigate the eye with clean water or Ringers Lactate to reduce chemical substance in the eye
     •    Remove foreign body if visible with a cotton bud or surgical blade if shallow after topical application of an anaesthetic
          drop

Pharmacological Management
At the primary care:
Corneal Abrasion:
A: chloramphenicol eye ointment 1%, 8hourly to the injured eye until no fluorescein staining
          AND
S: Soft Contact Lenses is indicated for pain relief and quick recovery

Steps Guiding Management of Complicated Blunt Trauma
Complicated blunt trauma is a trauma where the vision is poor, patient’s experiences pain and there is hyphaema. It is best
managed by eye specialist as surgery may be required in the management.

Table 14.5: Steps guiding management of complicated blunt trauma
 Findings                                       Action to be taken
 No hyphaema, normal vision                     Observe
 Hyphaema, no pain                              Refer
 No hyphaema, normal vision, pain               Paracetamol, observe for 2 days, refer if pain persist
 Poor vision and pain                           Paracetamol, refer urgently
 Hyphaema, pain, poor vision                    Paracetamol, refer urgently

sections.title: Deep Corneal or Scleral Injuries (Penetrating)
sections.text:
These are corneal or scleral injuries caused by sharp objects.

Clinical Presentation
     •    History of injury with a sharp object such as knife or wire
     •    Swollen eye
     •    Eye discharge

Investigations
    •    Examine the injured eye with slit lamp or magnifier
    •    Fluorescein staining to reveal foreign body or corneal laceration
    •    Fundoscopy

Non-Pharmacological Management
Apply an eye shield or pad with no pressure and refer immediately while waiting for referral, use the following in the affected
eye.
Pharmacological Management
A: chloramphenicol 1% eye drop, 2 drops stat
          OR
A: chloramphenicol 1% ointment, stat
          OR
A: oxytetracycline eye ointment, stat
          AND
B: atropine 1%, 1–2 drops stat
          AND
A: tetanus vaccine (IM) 0.5ml stat as prophylaxis
          AND
A: paracetamol (PO)1gm 6-8 hourly to a maximum of 4 doses in 24hours, for 3days in adults, the dosage in children is 10–
15mg/kg 6-8hourly for 3days.

Referral indicated if
     •    Intraocular foreign body is suspected                             •    Conjunctival laceration requiring suturing (>1 cm)
     •    There is globe or intraocular penetration                         •    Laceration/perforation or diffuse damage to the
          evidenced by:                                                          cornea and sclera
          - Poor vision,                                                    •    Chemical and thermal injuries
          - Distorted pupil                                                 •    Damage to ocular adnexa including eyelids
          - Ocular contents of foreign body is seen                         •    Limited ocular movements
          - Circumferential subconjunctival hemorrhage
          - Hyphaema with or without raised intraocular
             pressure
Surgical Treatment
This is done by a well-trained eye specialist at the District, Regional, Zonal and National hospitals. It should be done within 48
hours of injury. Post-operative care should be monitored regularly for any signs of endophthalmitis.
  Note:
        •    Eye ointment should be applied very gently and in the lower fornix (behind the lower eyelid).
        •    Do not apply pressure on the eye in perforating injuries of the eyeball
        •    Delay in surgical management of the injury may cause irreversible blindness or may necessitate removal of an
             eye

Referral: Immediately refer the patient to a health facility with eye surgeon at the District, Regional, Zonal or National hospital
depending on the staff availability.

sections.title: Traumatic Optic neuropathy
sections.text:
Traumatic optic neuropathy (TON) is a condition in which acute injury to the optic nerve from direct or indirect trauma results in
vision loss. The most common cause of TON is indirect injury to the optic nerve, which is thought to be the result of transmitted
shock from an orbital impact to the intracanalicular portion of optic nerve.

Clinical Presentation
Patients with TON may have decreased visual acuity, decreased color vision, an afferent pupillary defect, and/or visual field
deficits.
Investigations
     •    CT scan of the brain and orbits.                            •  EOM tests,
     •    VA, Refraction,                                             •  Pupils’ exam
     •    IOP,
Management
Aside from observation, the two treatment options that can be considered include high-dose corticosteroids or surgical
decompression.
Erythropoietin (EPO) has shown promise as a potential treatment for TON.

  Note: Intervention within 48 hours or three days of injury may yield better outcomes Surgical decompression can be
  considered in cases of TON with evidence of optic nerve compression

sections.title: Chemical Injuries/Burn
sections.text:
This is an Ophthalmological emergency. It occurs when chemicals such as acid or alkali (e.g., household detergents, bleaching
agents), snake spit, insect bite, traditional eye medicine, cement or lime cause a damage to the eye.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Diagnosis relies mostly with patients’ history                    •    Loss of conjunctival blood vessels
     •    Patients may present with photophobia                             •    Traces of chemical substance such as cement or
     •    Inability to open eyes                                                 herbs and blisters or loss of eyelid skin in open
     •    Excessive tearing/watery eyes                                          flame injuries
     •    Cloudiness of cornea with blurred vision

Investigations
    •    Visual acuity
    •    Slit lamp biomicroscopy
    •    Fluorescein staining

Non-Pharmacological Management
If a patient gives you history of being in contact with the items mentioned above, the following should be done:
      •    Irrigate the eye with clean water or Ringer’s lactate continually for a minimum of 20–30 minutes to reduce chemical
           substances. Irrigate longer for severe alkali burn.
      •    Test the patients’ vision and examine the patient’s eye

Pharmacological Management
C: tetracaine 0.5% eye drops, instill 2 drops in the affected eye. Repeat irrigation if possible. Evert the eye lids and remove the
debris
          AND
A: chloramphenicol 1% eye ointment, apply 6hourly to prevent infection for 3days.
          OR
A: oxytetracycline eye ointment, apply 6hourly to prevent infection for 3 days.
          AND
A: paracetamol (PO)1gm 4–6hourly to a maximum of 4 doses in 24hours, for 3days in adults, the dosage in children is 10–
14mg/kg 4–6hourly for 3days

Referral: Refer all cases within 12hours to eye specialist at high level health facilities for more care

sections.title: Corneal Ulcer
sections.text:
This is a painful red eye condition resulting from a raw discontinuity to the corneal epithelium. It may be caused by infection
(bacterial, viral e.g., Herpes simplex virus and measles, fungal, trauma (physical or chemical) and nutritional (Vitamin A
deficiency). Systemic conditions can contribute to corneal ulcers as well.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Painful and red eye of acute onset                                •    Gray/white spot on the
     •    Excessive tearing                                                      cornea staining with
     •    Severe photophobia                                                     fluorescein
     •    Poor vision                                                       •    Hypopyon (Pus or white
                                                                                 cells in anterior chamber)
Investigations
    •    Visual acuity                                                      •    Fluorescein sodium drops or a drop of local
    •    Slit Lamp biomicroscope                                                 anesthetic on a fluorescein strip to assess the
    •    Corneal scrapping for Gram Stain and                                    pattern of the ulcer and measure the size of
    •    Corneal scrapping for Potassium Hydroxide                               corneal defect.
         staining

Pharmacological Management

While waiting for laboratory results,
give:
C: ciprofloxacin 0.3%, ophthalmic drops, instill 1–2drops 1–2hourly for 3days then reduce to 3–4hourly.
          OR
D: ofloxacin 0.3%, ophthalmic drops, instill 1 drop 1–2hourly for 3days then reduce to 3– 4hourly
          OR
S: moxifloxacin ophthalmic drops, instill 1 drop 1–2hourly for 3days then reduce to 3– 4hourly

Give antifungal, if fungal infection is suspected or confirmed
S: natamycin 5%, ophthalmic drops, instill 1 drop 1–2hourly for 3–4days (specialist use only). Then reduce to 1 drop 3-4hourly.
Continue for 14–21days until resolution of infection

          OR
S: econazole 2%, ophthalmic drops, instill 1 drop 1–2hourly for 3–4days (specialist use only). Then reduce to 1 drop 3–4hourly.
Continue for 14–21days until resolution of infection
          OR
S: chlorhexidine 0.2%, ophthalmic drops, instill 1 drop 1–2hourly for 3–4days (specialist use only). Then reduce to 1 drop 3–
4hourly. Continue for 14–21days until resolution of infection

Give antiviral if viral causes are suspected after the examination of the eye
C: acyclovir 3% eye ointment 5hourly a day until there is no corneal stain, then continue with treatment 8hourly a day for a
maximum of 10–14days

  Note: Treatment may be changed depending on corneal scrapping results

Referral: Refer to the next level of care where there is an eye specialist when there is hypopyon (white cells in anterior chamber)

sections.title: Herpes Simplex Keratitis
sections.text:
It is an inflammatory condition of the cornea caused by Herpes Simplex Virus. Usually present as dendric ulceration

Clinical Presentation
     •    Acute painful eye (usually unilateral)                           •    Reduced corneal sensation
     •    Blurring of vision                                               •    Dendritic corneal ulcer seen on staining with
                                                                                fluorescein

Investigations
    •    Visual acuity                                                     •    Fluorescein staining
    •    Slit lamp biomicroscopy                                           •    Corneal sensitivity test

Pharmacological Management
C: acyclovir 3%, ophthalmic ointment applied in the lower conjunctival sac, 4hourly. Continue for 3 days after ulcer has been
healed.
         AND
B: acyclovir, (PO), 400mg 8–4hourly a day for 7–10days depending on initial response as well as the extent of the ulcer.
  Note:
      •     Topical corticosteroids are contraindicated when corneal ulcer is suspected
      •     Use of contact Lenses should be avoided until complete healing
      •     Corneal Opacity as a sequela of corneal ulcer can result and leading to blurry vision

sections.title: Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus
sections.text:
Occurs when Varicella Zoster Virus reactivates in the trigeminal ganglion and passes down the ophthalmic division of the
trigeminal nerve

Clinical Presentation
     •    Presents with painful vesicular rash in the trigeminal V1 area–vesicles on the tip of the nose indicate nasociliary
          branch involvement and increases the risk of ocular involvement
     •    Some patients develop conjunctivitis, keratitis, uveitis, retinitis and cranial nerve involvement (oculomotor and optic
          nerves)
     •    Later, chronic ocular inflammation, loss of vision, post herpetic neuralgia
     •    All patients should be offered HIV testing

Investigations
    •     Visual acuity                                                    •    Fluorescein staining
    •     Slit lamp bimicroscopy                                           •    HIV Testing
    •     Corneal sensation test
Pharmacological Management
B: acyclovir (PO) 800mg 4hourly for 7–10days
          AND
A: amitriptyline (PO) 25mg at night for 3months.

 Note:
     •        Treatment should be initiated within 3 days of the onset of symptoms, except in HIV infected patients who should be
              treated if there are active skin lesions
         •    Management of Herpes Zoster is Multidisciplinary so consult physician for proper management of the patient.

Referral: Refer to eye specialist in case of: -
    •    Vesicles on the tip of the nose                                    •    Red eye (uveitis or keratitis)
    •    Fluorescein staining of the cornea shows corneal                   •    Cranial nerve palsies
         ulceration
    •    Decreased vision

sections.title: Uveitis
sections.text:
This is Inflammation of the uveal tissue (Iris, choroid and ciliary body) and its adjacent structures. Majority of the cases are
idiopathic whereby other cases are due to autoimmune diseases e.g. Rheumatoid Arthritis, Sarcoidosis, SLE ocular or systemic
infections e.g. Viral, Tuberculosis, Leprosy, and Syphilis.

Clinical Presentation
It has three main Clinical Presentations namely acute, chronic and acute on chronic. The commonest form is anterior uveitis.
In acute type, patients present with: -
     •    Painful red eye                                              •    Loss of vision
     •    Excessive tearing                                            •    Cells and flare in anterior chamber
     •    Severe photophobia                                           •    Irregular pupil with synechiae

Investigations
    •    Visual acuity                                                      •    Urinalysis
    •    Slit lamp biomicroscopic examination anterior                      •    FBC
         chamber                                                            •    ESR
    •    Tonometry                                                          •    Antinuclear Antibody
                                                                            •    VDRL
    •    B scan
                                                                            •    HIV Testing
     •       Chest X-Rays if Tuberculosis and Sarcoidosis are suspected.

Pharmacological Management
Treatment for uveitis is mainly steroids and specific treatment according to the cause. This should be initiated in a facility where
workup and close monitoring can be done.

Steroidal Anti-inflammatory medicines

D: dexamethasone 1% eye drops, 1–3hourly in the affected eye for 4-6weeks
         OR
D: prednisolone 0.5% or 1 % eye drops, 1–3hourly in the affected eye for 6weeks
         OR
D: betamethasone 1% eye drops, 1–3hourly in the affected eye for 4-6weeks
         AND
A: prednisolone (PO) 1mg/kg body weight, given in a tapering manner to maximum of 4–6 weeks
         OR
D: dexamethasone (PO) in tapering dosage for 2-4 weeks

In Cases which doesn’t resolve with above regime, addition of the following is recommended
S: triamcinolone (subtenon) 20mg stat, it can be repeated after 4 weeks if need arise.
           OR
S: methotrexate 20mg weekly (PO) in collaboration with an ocular oncologist
           AND
Pupil dilating eye drops
B: atropine eye drops or ointment 1% 12hourly in the affected eye
           OR
D: cyclopentolate 1 % eye drops, 1–2drops 8hourly in the affected eye.
Treatment for uveitis is to be continued for at least 4-6weeks
  Note
      •      Treatment of uveitis must involve various specialists such as oncologist, immunologist, physician
      •      Acute uveitis is a serious problem and the patient should be referred urgently for specialist treatment
      •      Recurrences may occur or acute disease may end up becoming a chronic uveitis
      •      If Uveitis is not managed appropriate blinding sequalae can result

sections.title: Conjunctivitis
sections.text:
This is an inflammation of the conjunctivae and one of the most common causes of red eyes. The cause of conjunctivitis may
be allergy, viral, or bacterial. Clinical features and treatment guideline depend on the type and cause of conjunctivitis.
  Note:
        •    If conjunctivitis is due to an infection, counsel on the importance of frequent hand washing, use separate linen,
             towels and wash towels and avoid direct contact with infected materials or individuals
        •    Contacts lenses should not be worn in patients with conjunctivitis until the condition has resolved

sections.title: Allergic Conjunctivitis Clinical Presentation
sections.text:
Different types of allergic conjunctivitis (AC) exist such as simple AC, Seasonal AC, Vernal Keratoconjunctivitis (VKC-common
in tropics), Atopic keratoconjunctivitis (AKC)

Clinical Presentation
     •    Itching of eyes,                                                  •    the eyes may be normal or slightly red,
     •    sand sensation,                                                   •    Conjunctival swelling in severe cases,
     •    photophobia,                                                      •    Limbal hyperpigmentation and papillae of the
     •    brownish of the eye,                                                   upper tarsal conjunctiva.
     •    eyelids hyperpigmentation                                         •    Normal iris, pupil and visual acuity.
     •    sometimes mucoid discharge                                        •    Corneal complications in very advanced stages

Investigations
    •    Visual acuity                                                      •    Skin Allergic test
    •    Slit lamp biomicroscopy                                            •    Ocular allergic test
    •    Full blood picture

Non-Pharmacological Management
Treatment of allergic conjunctivitis depends on the severity of the condition and age of the patient. In mild acute cases,
Avoid allergens, Cold water compresses for 10 minutes four times a day

Pharmacological Management

D: olopatadine eye drops 0.1/0.2% eye drops bid/od respectively for 2-4 weeks and titrate against presentation
           OR
C: cetirizine eye drops nocte 1-2 weeks
           OR
C: sodium cromoglycate 2% eye drops, instill 6hourly per day for at least a month. Use may be seasonal (1–3 months) or long-
term use.

Oral drugs can be added as needed such as
A: chlorpheniramine (PO) 0.1 mg/kg/dose 6–8hourly
           OR
A: cetirizine PO nocte 3-5 days in acute phase
  Note: Do not give antihistamine to children under 2 years of age as its effectiveness at this age group has not been proven.

Referral: Refer to eye specialist for further specialized care in case of the following:
    •    Moderate to severe allergic conjunctivitis
    •    No response after initial treatment
    •    Persons wearing contact lenses
    •    Children <2 years of age

At the specialized center, the following treatment may be added depending on the patient’s presentation especially in VKC.
Short term steroid eye drops (in severe cases with involvement of the cornea, apart from mast cell stabilizers,
give
D: dexamethasone eye drops 0.1%, 6hourly for a maximum of 14days.
          OR
D: prednisolone 0.5% eye drops, 6hourly for a maximum of 14days.
          OR
D: betamethasone eye drops 8hourly for a maximum of 14 days

In very severe form of allergic conjunctivitis such as VKC, give steroid injection
S: triamcinolone acetonide (subtenon) 20mg stat
          OR
D: methylprednisolone sodium acetate (subtenon) 20mg stat

sections.title: Viral Keratoconjunctivitis
sections.text:
The commonest causative organism is adenovirus. It may be unilateral but usually bilateral and involves the cornea and
conjunctiva as well. It is the commonest cause of red eye epidemics and is one of the notifiable national diseases.

Clinical Presentation
     •    It may be associated with upper respiratory tract                •    Normal visual acuity but may be blurry in cornea
          infection                                                             involvement
     •    Presents with morning crusting and watery eye                    •    Preauricular lymphadenopathy
          discharge                                                        •    It appears in epidemics so there will be history of

     •    Diffuse pink or red conjunctiva due to                           •    It is usually self-limiting, but the irritation and
          subconjunctival hemorrhages                                           discharge get worse on 3 – 5 days before getting
     •    Photophobia if the cornea is involved                                 better and symptoms can persist for 2–3 weeks.

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Advise on correct cleansing or rinsing of eyes with clean water
    •  Cold compresses for symptomatic relief
    •  Sunglass in severe photophobia

Pharmacological Management
Children > 6 years and adults
C: acyclovir eye drops, instill 1–2drops 6hourly for a maximum of 7days.
         AND
A: paracetamol (PO) Adult; 1g. Pediatric 10–15 mg/kg/dose 6hourly when required.

   Note:
       •     Viral conjunctivitis is very contagious so patients and members of the family should be alerted
       •     Assess for superimposed bacterial infection and treat accordingly
       •     Outbreaks usually happen in schools and other congregations

Referral: Refer all patients to a centre with eye specialist if there is
     •   No response after 5 days                                          •    Irregular pupil
     •   Unilateral red eye for more than one day                          •    Haziness of cornea
     •   Suspected herpes conjunctivitis                                   •    Persistent painful eye
     •   Loss of vision

sections.title: Bacterial Conjunctivitis
sections.text:
Purulent conjunctival inflammation caused by bacterial infection. Common bacteria are chlamydia trachomatis, gonorrhea (can
break intact cornea)

Clinical Presentation
     •    Mucopurulent discharge from one or both eyes                     •    Eyelids may be swollen
     •    Sore, gritty or scratch eyes and swollen lids                    •    Matting of eye lashes in
     •    Conjunctiva redness more                                              the morning with eyelids
          at the fornices                                                       stuck shut

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Educate patient on personal hygiene to prevent spread
    •  Educate patient correct application of ophthalmic ointment
       - To wash hands thoroughly before applying ophthalmic ointment
       - Not to share the ophthalmic ointment and drops
    •  Eye swabs for Gram stain and for culture and sensitivity may be needed to tailor down treatment.

Pharmacological Management
A: chloramphenicol 1%, ophthalmic ointment, applied 8hourly for 5days.
          OR
C: ciprofloxacin 0.3%, ophthalmic drops, instill 1drop, 4hourly for 2days. Then reduce frequency to 1 drop 6hourly for 5days
          OR
D: ofloxacin 0.3%, ophthalmic drops, instill 1 drop 4hourly for 2days. Then reduce the frequency to 1drop 6hourly for 5days
          OR
S: moxifloxacin ophthalmic drops, instill 1 drop 4hourly for 2days. Then reduce the frequency to 1drop 6hourly for 5days
          AND
A: paracetamol (PO) Adult 1g. Children 10–15 mg/kg/dose 6hourly when required.

Referral: Refer to eye specialist if no improvement after 5days of treatment if VA is still stable.

sections.title: Ophthalmia Neonatorum/Neonatal Conjunctivitis
sections.text:

from mother’s birth canal secretions. It is characterized by inflammation of the conjunctivae, sticky eyes to abundant purulent
discharge and eyelids oedema. Causative organisms are Neisseria Gonorrhea, Chlamydia spp and Staphylococcus spp.

Non-Pharmacological Management
Cleanse or wipe eyes of all newborn babies with a clean cloth, cotton wool or swab, taking care not to touch or injure the eye

Pharmacological Management

prevention is better than cure

sections.title: Structural Abnormalities of the Eye
sections.text:
These includes:
    •    Squint: eyes are aligned; one eye appears to be turned in or out, in children or in adult. Refer urgently all children
         who present with squint to Paediatric Eye Tertiary Centre
    •    Ocular swellings disease: The most common ocular swellings are Chalazion, Stye, Pre- septal/Orbital Cellulitis,
         pterygium and Squamous cell carcinoma of the conjunctiva.
    •    Eyelids abnormalities: eyelashes rubbing on cornea (trichiasis), in-turned eyelids (entropion), eyelids bent out too
         much (ectropion), drooping eyelids (ptosis), inability to close the eyes (lagophthalmos)

  Note: Abnormal tissues excised from eye patients should be subjected to pathology examination for proper diagnosis

sections.title: Squint/Strabismus
sections.text:
This is ocular misalignment. Usually, a common problem in children before 2 years of age but tends to resolve after that age. If
significant ocular misalignment is present, it definitely needs work up.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Esotropia,
     •    Exotropia,
     •    wide nasal bridge

Investigations
    •    Corneal light reflex,                                                  •     Refraction,
    •    Cover-uncover test,                                                    •     VA
    •    Double Maddox rod,

Management
Correct refractive errors if present with spectacles, Occlusion therapy either mechanical or pharmacological, If persist referral
to orthoptist and/or Paediatric ophthalmologist should be considered for squint surgery on EOM
after assessment. 37

sections.title: External Eye and Eye Lid diseases
sections.text:
Commonest Chalazion, Stye, Pterygium, Orbital/ Preseptal cellulitis, dacryocystitis and OSSN.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Depends on the condition but can be lid swelling (Chalazion, Stye, Pre septal), conjunctival swellings
          (Pterygium/OSSN), Proptosis in orbital cellulitis.
     •    Pre-septal and orbital cellulitis are associated with systemic symptoms as well and hence needs appropriate
          management.

Investigations
Usually, its clinical diagnosis

Management
Depends on the pathology
For Chalazion is usually incision and curettage, for Stye give antibiotics and analgesics for pain. Pre-septal and orbital cellulitis
usually strong antibiotics and analgesics.

sections.title: Orbital and Pre-Septal Cellulitis
sections.text:
Orbital cellulitis is an infection of the soft tissues of the orbit posterior to the orbital septum. It may be a continuum of preseptal
cellulitis, which is an infection of the soft tissue of the eyelids and periocular region anterior to the orbital septum. Orbital cellulitis
may result from an extension of an infection from the paranasal sinuses or other periorbital structures such as the face, globe,
or lacrimal sac, direct inoculation of the orbit from trauma or surgery or as a hematogenous spread from bacteremia
