sections.title: Eyelids abnormalities
sections.text:
Refers to Eyelashes rubbing on cornea (trichiasis), in-turned eyelids (entropion), eyelids bent out too much (ectropion), drooping
eyelids (ptosis), inability to close the eyes (lagophthalmos)
Rule out secondary causes and address appropriate, referral to secondary or tertiary center for appropriate management.
Pharmacological Management
C: oxymetazoline 0.1% drops 8hourly for 4-6 weeks.
Can be used for Ptosis management due to myasthenia gravis.

Surgical Treatment
Depending on the cause for Ptosis different surgeries can be performed such as Muller muscle–conjunctival resection, Levator
advancement or resection, Frontalis suspension

sections.title: Dacryocystitis
sections.text:
Dacryocystitis is inflammation of the lacrimal sac which typically occurs secondarily to obstruction within the nasolacrimal duct
and the resultant backup and stagnation of tears within the lacrimal sac. Three clinical forms for the disease exist: Congenital-
NLDO, Acute dacryocystitis usually requires systemic antibiotic therapy prior to intervention for the NLDO. Chronic
dacryocystitis typically presents with fewer inflammatory signs and requires surgical therapy for the underlying cause

Clinical Presentation
In acute dacryocystitis, the symptoms may occur over several hours to several days and include
     •    pain, erythema, and edema over the medial canthus and the area overlying the lacrimal sac at the inferomedial portion
          of the orbit. The redness can extend to involve the bridge of the nose. Purulent material can sometimes be expressed
          from the puncta and tearing may be present.

In chronic dacryocystitis,
     •    excessive tearing and mucus reflux (mucocele) are the most common symptoms. Changes in visual acuity may be
          present due to altered tear film dynamics.

Investigations
The diagnosis of dacryocystitis is generally made based on the patient’s history and physical exam. Crigler maneuver, or tear
duct massage, can be performed to express material for culture and gram stain. The fluorescein dye disappearance test (DDT),

Pharmacological Management
For congenital NLDO has up to a 90% chance of resolution by 1 year of age, so treatment is delayed until 2 years of age
meanwhile Crigler massages is advised.
Acute dacryocystitis should be treated with oral empirical antibiotics with gram-positive coverage

A: amoxicillin (PO) 500mg 8hourly for 7 days
          AND
A: ciprofloxacin (PO) 500mg 12hourly for 7 days
          OR
B: azithromycin (PO) 500mg 24hourly for 5 days

If No response within 48 hours give referral for further care. Once the acute inflammation/infection is controlled, the underlying
cause can then be addressed

For Chronic dacryocystitis. Patients who fail conservative treatment often undergo lacrimal probing, which is successful in 70%
of cases. If the dacryocystitis still persists, additional surgical interventions may be needed, such as stenting, balloon
dacryoplasty, and either external or endonasal DCR (Dacryocystorhinostomy Surgery)

sections.title: Retinoblastoma
sections.text:
It is the commonest childhood malignant tumor of the eyes. It is diagnosed between the first 1– 3 years of life. It has a lower
survival rate after diagnosis hence, monthly screening of all under-five children is important for timely referral and management
through RCH clinics.

Clinical Presentation
     •    White pupil reflex (leukocoria)                                 •    Ocular/periocular inflammation
     •    Squint                                                          •    Secondary glaucoma
     •    Rarely vitreous hemorrhage                                      •    In late stages proptosis and whole eye structure
     •    Hyphema/Hypopyon                                                     protrusion

Investigations
    •    Visual acuity                                                        •   Examination under anaesthesia
    •    Tonometry                                                            •   Histology of an enucleated eye in advanced
    •    Fundoscopy                                                               disease
    •    B Scan                                                               •   Cerebral Spinal Fluid analysis in advanced
    •    CT Scan of the head and orbits                                           disease

treatment modalities:

sections.title: Squamous Cell Carcinoma of Conjunctiva
sections.text:
Invasive squamous cell carcinoma of conjunctiva is the major and most common ocular malignancy of the eye in adults. The
tumor typically occurs on the bulbar conjunctiva, originating at the limbus, and often spreads onto the cornea, globe, orbit and
nasolacrimal system. The cancer is a slow growing tumor of middle-aged to elderly people. It is common in
immunocompromised individuals

Clinical Presentation
     •    It manifests usually as a fleshy vascularized mass at the limbus. (Temporal or nasally)
     •    In advanced stage, it may intrude the eyeball and extend to other ocular adnexa structures
     •    Definitive diagnosis is by histopathological assessment of excised tissue

Investigations
    •    Visual acuity                                                    •    Histology
    •    Slit lamp Biomicroscopy                                          •    PITC
    •    Tonometry                                                        •    DM Screening
    •    Fundoscopy

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Check for HIV status of the patient as recurrences occurs most frequently in HIV positive patients
    •  Close follow up of patients for at least the first 12 months postoperatively to look for residual or recurrent tumors

Pharmacological Management
S: 5-fluorouracil (5FU) 50mg/mL, on a sponge, for about 2.5minutes then wash off with sodium lactate compound (ringer’s
lactate)solution.
          OR
S: mitomycin C 0.2mg/mL, on a sponge, for about 2.5minutes then wash off with sodium lactate compound (ringer’s
lactate)solution.
          AND
C: dexamethasone + chloramphenicol eye drops, 0.1%–0.5 %, 6hourly, for 3–4weeks
          OR
C: dexamethasone + gentamicin eye drops, 0.1–0.3%, 6hourly, for 3–4 weeks (These are post operatively until the wound is
healed)
          THEN
S: 5-fluorouracil (5FU) 1% eye drops, 4times daily for 2–3weeks
          OR
S: cyclosporine 0.05% eye drops bid for 2-3 weeks

  Note:
      •     5-fluorouracil (5FU) is used after the excision wound has healed
      •     5FU eye drops may cause watery eye, discomfort or eye inflammation, manage accordingly

sections.title: Dry Eye Syndrome/Keratoconjunctivitis Sicca
sections.text:
It occurs when there is inadequate tear volume, poor quality tears or functional disorders of tear drainage.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Feelings of dryness, grittiness, burning and foreign body sensation, usually worse during the day
     •    Stringy discharge, redness and transient blurring of vision are also common. Exclude allergic conjunctivitis

Investigations
    •    Visual acuity                                                    •    Tear break up time
    •    Refraction                                                       •    Slit lamp biomicroscopy
    •    Fundoscopy                                                       •    Tear meniscus height (meniscometry)
    •    Schirmer tear Test

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Control symptoms and look for secondary                            •    Use humidifier in areas with low humidity
       causes for treatment such as MGDs.                                 •    Punctal plugins to decrease tear drainage
    •  Educate patients to avoid unprescribed eye                         •    Tear conserving interventions such as punctal
       medications which may worsen the dryness and                            plugs or nighttime masks/goggles
       control their environmental factors by e.g.,                       •    Bandage Contact Lenses can be used as well
       blinking frequently during visual attentive tasks                  •    Specialty contact lenses such as scleral lenses
       and the use of 20-20-20 rule avoid air
       conditioners directly on the face.

Pharmacological Management
C: hydroxypropyl methylcellulose 0.7%, ophthalmic drops, 1drop, 6hourly.
            OR
C: carboxymethylcellulose-0.5%w/v + glycerin-0.5%w/v eye drops 12hourly for 3months
            OR
S: cyclosporine 0.05%/0.09% eye drops 12hourly for 1-2months -increase tear production)
            OR
S: lifitegrast 5% ophthalmic solution 12hourly 1-2 months have shown to alleviate symptoms
            OR
S: autologous serum tears 12hourly for 1-2 months

 Note:
     •     Dry eye syndromes are a multifactorial disease and should be managed wholistically
     •     Rule out risk factors and address them accordingly such as MGDs, Blepharitis
     •     Menopause women are prone to dry eyes so advise them accordingly

sections.title: Endophthalmitis
sections.text:
It is an infection of the ocular cavity. It is an ophthalmic emergency that can cause blindness that may occur secondary to
bacteraemia (endogenous infection) or following penetrating eye injury or after intraocular surgery

Clinical Presentation
     •    Loss of vision, associated with pain in the                     •    Blood culture should be done to identify the
          affected eye                                                         source and how it can be treated (for
     •    Injected painful eye                                                 bacteraemia)
     •    Hypopyon                                                        •    In post injury or surgery, culture of specimens of
     •    Corneal oedema                                                       aqueous or vitreous humour should be done

Investigations
    •    Visual acuity                                                    •    B Scan
    •    Slit lamp biomicroscopy                                          •    Vitreous Tap for Gram stain, Culture and
    •    Tonometry                                                             sensitivity
    •    Refraction

Pharmacological Management
Start Topical antibiotics and oral antibiotics as well and refer immediately to an ophthalmologist for treatment
C: ciprofloxacin eye drops hourly                                                AND
          OR                                                          B: ceftriaxone (IV) 2g 24hourly for 7days
B: chloramphenicol eye drops hourly                                              OR
          OR                                                          D: ceftazidime (IVI) 2.25 mg/0.1 mL 24hourly
D: moxifloxacin eye drops hourly                                                 AND
          OR                                                          C: chloramphenicol (PO) 500mg 12hourly for 5-7 days
D: gentamicin Subconjunctival. 24hourly                                          OR
          AND/OR                                                      A: ciprofloxacin (PO) 750mg bid for 5-7 days
S: at this level tap for vitreous sampling should be done
and immediately Intravitreal Vancomycin                               If fungal is suspected:
1.0 mg/0.1 mL and Amikacin 400 μg/0.1 mL for Penicillin               S: Amphotericin B deoxycholate Intravitreal 5-10 μg/0.1
(PCN) allergic patients 24hourly for 5 days and assess                mL should be given

Note:

           asap.
     •     Adjust antibiotics accordingly to culture and sensitivity
     •     4th generation fluoroquinolones have better ocular penetration.
     •     Systemic ceftazidime, cefazolin, ciprofloxacin, gatifloxacin and moxifloxacin have been shown to penetrate the
           blood ocular barrier efficiently and can be used as adjunctive oral antibiotics.

sections.title: Visual Problems
sections.text:
Visual problems may be due to refractive errors, damage to the eye or optic nerve. This may be an indication of underlying
diseases such as diabetes or hypertension.

Investigations
    •    Assess ocular alignment
    •    Determine visual acuity accurately in both eyes                    •    Red Reflex Test
         by Snellen chart                                                        The patient looks past the examiners head
    •    If vision is diminished, (less than 6/12), perform                      focusing on a distant target.
         the following: -                                                        - With the ophthalmoscope at 0 (zero) the
    •    Pin hole test                                                             examiner keeps close to his eye and then
         - Make a hole of about 1mm wide in a piece of                             focuses the beam of light so that it falls on the
            dark/black paper – you can push a hole in a                            pupillary area of the cornea
            paper or card with a pen tip                                         - The examiner stands about 60cm away from
         - Ask the patient to look through this hole at the                      the patient.
         Snellen chart                                                           - In normal individuals, the examiner should be
         - If vision improves, this means that the patient                         able to see a red or pink colour (reflex) through
         has a refractive error                                                    the pupil which comes from the retina.

Significance of absent red reflex
If there is history of trauma or diabetes, the absence of a red reflex is probably due to:
      •    Retinal detachment
      •    A vitreous hemorrhage
      •    Mature cataract

If there are cataracts, one usually sees:
      •   Black shadows against the red reflex in immature cataract, or
      •   Absence of red reflex in mature cataracts

In a >50years of age with no history of trauma, diabetes or previous eye disease, an absent red reflex is often due to cataract
formation, especially with decreased visual acuity.

 Note: Associated diabetes or hypertension should be adequately managed with referral, as surgery can only be considered
 with appropriately managed systemic disease

sections.title: Onchocerciasis (River Blindness)
sections.text:
Onchocerciasis is a tissue parasitic infestation caused by a filarial worm, Onchocerca volvulus. The microfilariae invade
lymphatic system, subcutaneous and deep tissues producing acute inflammation and chronic inflammation at a later stage

Clinical Presentation
     •    Skin inflammation with papules
     •    Subcutaneous nodules
     •    Atypical skin lesions (scarred, saggy, hanging areas of skin, leopard skin)
     •    Skin nodules under the bony prominent areas
     •    Microfilaria in anterior chamber
     •    Scleritis and Keratitis leading to Impaired vision as well as blindness

Investigations
    •    Visual acuity
    •    Rapid diagnostic test (OV-16 - Onchocerciasis IgG)
    •    Skin snip for microscopic examination
    •    Slit lamp eye examination.
    •    B Scan

Pharmacological Management
Treatment is done in consultation with dermatologists and infectious disease specialists.
Apart from WHO recommended mass treatment campaign to community at risk with annual preventive chemotherapy which
polarize/paralyze the worm, treatment depends on individual patient presentation.

A: ivermectin (PO) 0.15mg/kg once every 12months for 12–15years
 Note:
      •   Patients with heavy ocular infestation require retreatment every 3 to 6 months.
      •   Treatment will only arrest progression of the clinical features but not reverse them.

sections.title: Circumscript otitis Externa (Furunculosis)
sections.text:
This is a localized infection of the hair follicle on the outer one-third of the external auditory canal. It is caused by Staphylococcus
aureus.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Ear pain that is severe and disproportional to the visible lesion
     •    Reduced hearing
     •    Localized swelling on the external auditory canal
     •    There may be a purulent discharge if the swelling ruptures

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •   Aural toilet if there is otorrhea (ear suctioning under direct vision).
    •   Aural toilet using a clean dry cotton cloth while at home.
    •   Instruct the patient to keep the ear dry and avoiding scratching

Pharmacological Management
Antibiotics are reserved for cases with systemic symptoms (e.g., fever, cellulitis) or microbiologically confirmed resistant infections.
Routine use is discouraged to prevent antimicrobial resistance

sections.title: Diffuse Otitis Externa (Swimmer’s ear)
sections.text:
This is an inflammation of the entire external auditory canal. It can be caused by bacteria, fungus or both.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Itchy, dry and scaly ear canal and painful ear
     •    There may be a water or purulent discharge, debris and reduced hearing
     •    Pain may become extreme when the ear canal becomes completely occluded with edematous skin and debris.

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •   Aural toilet at least once a week (ear suctioning under direct vision using microscope or endoscope).
    •   Instruct the patient to keep the ear dry and avoiding scratching.

sections.title: Necrotizing (Malignant) Otitis Externa
sections.text:
This is a life-threatening invasive infection that affects the external auditory canal leading to skull base osteomyelitis. It is common
to elderly diabetic patients and other immunosuppressive conditions. Most common causative organism is Pseudomonas
aeruginosa followed by Aspergillus. Controlling the underlying cause of immunosuppression is of paramount importance.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Nocturnal exquisite ear pain, discharge, fullness and hearing impairment.
     •    May present with facial nerve paralysis or other cranial nerves palsy.
     •    Oedema of the external auditory canal with or without presence of granulation tissues at the junction between the bony
          and cartilaginous parts of the inferior portion of external auditory canal
     •    Necrosis of external auditory canal
Non-Pharmacological Management
     •    Aural toilet at least three sessions per week (ear suctioning under direct vision using microscope or endoscope) until
          disease is controlled.
     •    Placement of an aural wick
     •    Instruct the patient to keep the ear dry and avoiding scratching

Investigations
    •    Culture and sensitivity of discharge and tissue.
    •    Erythrocyte Sedimentation rate
    •    C – reactive protein
    •    Full blood picture
    •    Glycosylated hemoglobin HbA1c / Fasting blood glucose
    •    HR CT Scan Temporal bone

Pharmacological Management
Antibiotics: Systemic antibiotics are essential due to the severity and osteomyelitis risk. Treatment should be guided by culture and
sensitivity result.

sections.title: Ear Keloid
sections.text:
This is abnormal proliferation of scar tissue that forms at the site of cutaneous injury and grows beyond the original margins of
the scar. Most common causes are ear piercing, trauma or surgical incisions.

Clinical Presentation
Swelling of the involved area of the ear, most commonly ear lobe

Non-Pharmacological Management
Use of pressure therapy e.g., pressure clips

Pharmacological Management
Intra-lesional steroid injection
S: triamcinolone acetonide (Intra-lesional) 40mg depending on the size of the lesion weekly for 4weeks before excision and
4weeks after excision

Surgical management
Total keloidectomy +/- Steroid injection. (should be done by expertise, involve dermatologist/plastics for best decision)

sections.title: Cerumen Impaction
sections.text:
Usually occurs following the use of cotton buds which hinder the natural movement of cerumen outwards

Clinical Presentation
     •    Reduced hearing                                                 •    Itching
     •    Ear pain                                                        •    Tinnitus
     •    Ear fullness

Pharmacological Management
A: hydrogen peroxide 3% ear drops2-4drops each ear 6-8hourly for 7days.

Non-Pharmacological Management
Remove using cerumen hook or suctioning under direct vision

sections.title: Foreign Body in the Ear
sections.text:
Usually happens in children. Common foreign bodies include beads, stones and seeds (bean, maize, orange). In adult’s foreign
bodies include cotton bud and insect

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Should be removed under direct visualization e.g., headlight, Otomicroscopy or endoscopy.
    •  An insect should be killed (by soaking the ear canal with normal saline or spirit) before removal

 Note: Do not attempt to remove ear foreign body if you don’t have proper instruments and expertise.

     •    History of trauma direct or indirect
     •    Ear bleeding +/-discharge

    •  For indirect trauma avoid ear drops and water in the ear
    •  For direct trauma aural toilet can be done then ear drops instilled

  Note: Patient should be educated on cleansing mechanism of the ear and not to use cotton bud.

sections.title: Otitis Media (Acute or Chronic)
sections.text:
It is an inflammation of the middle ear cavity. It is considered acute when the inflammation is of less than 2 weeks’ duration,
and chronic when the inflammation is of more than 2 weeks’ duration with tympanic membrane perforation.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Examine the pinna
     •    Using an otoscope carefully examine the external auditory canal and the tympanic membrane

sections.title: Acute Otitis Media
sections.text:
Clinical Presentation
     •    Previous upper respiratory tract infection                      •    Inflamed, bulged tympanic membrane
     •    Fever                                                           •    Painful ear
     •    Hearing often reduced                                           •    Restlessness

Non-Pharmacological Management
Acute otitis media should be treated with analgesics, antibiotics and/or Myringotomy to reduce pain and to obtain pus for culture
and sensitivity)

Pharmacological Management
Antibiotics should be avoided in mild cases to reduce resistance AND only indicated for severe cases (e.g., high fever, severe
pain, bilateral disease) or in children <2 years.

     •     Foul smelling ear discharge
     •     Mastoiditis

sections.title: Chronic Suppurative Otitis Media
sections.text:
This is a perforated tympanic membrane with persistent drainage from the middle ear for more than 2-6 weeks. Most common
causative organisms are Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus aureus, Proteus species, Klebsiella pneumonia, and
diphtheroid.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Discharge of pus from the ear
     •    Perforated tympanic membrane
     •    Reduced hearing

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Keep ear dry/avoid water into the ear
    •  Aural toilet – ear suctioning under direct vision (Otomicroscopy/endoscopy), removal of debris
    •  Ear wicking regularly, with a dry cotton wick at home

Pharmacological Management
Prefer topical over systemic antibiotics to reduce resistance. Systemic antibiotics are reserved for complications (e.g.,
mastoiditis)
C: ciprofloxacin ear drops, three drops 12 hourly for 14days
          OR
A: hydrogen peroxide 3%, 2–4 drops, 6–8-hourly for 14 days (adults and children)
          OR
D: ofloxacin ear drops: 2 to 4 drops each ear 6-8hourly for 14days
          AND
(If systemic complication)
A: ciprofloxacin (PO) 500mg 12hourly for 10days

For Children:
A: ciprofloxacin (PO) 10–20mg/kg 12hourly for 10days

Investigations
    •    Pure Tone Audiometry
    •    HR CT SCAN-Temporal Bone

Surgical treatment
S: Tympanoplasty +/-Mastoidectomy (Tympano-mastoidectomy)
S: Ossiculoplasty (Autologous or Prothesis)
 Note:
     •     Treatment of shorter than 10 days will result into treatment failure
     •     Avoid ototoxic drugs (gentamicin or neomycin)

sections.title: Mastoiditis with Sub-Periosteal Abscess
sections.text:
It is due to infection of the mastoid air cells in the middle ear, a complication of chronic suppurative otitis media. It presents as
a fluctuant painful swelling on the post auricular area. The overlying skin is also inflamed.

Non-Pharmacological Management
Aspirate the swelling before incision and drainage, and then refer for mastoidectomy at a zonal/national hospital

Pharmacological Management
C: ciprofloxacin ear drops, 3drops, 12hourly for 14days
          AND
Intravenous antibiotics are required due to the severity and risk of intracranial complications
B: ceftriaxone (IV) 1–2 g, 12-hourly for 7–14 days

For Children
B: ceftriaxone (IV) 50–100 mg/kg, 24-hourly for 7–14 days (children)
Investigations
     •    Culture &sensitivity
     •    CT SCAN-Temporal Bone

Surgical treatment
    •    Incision and drainage                                              •     Tympano-mastoidectomy
    •    Mastoidectomy/Drainage mastoidectomy                               •     Ossiculoplasty

  Note: Treatment shorter than 10days will result into treatment failure

sections.title: Otitis Media with Effusion (Glue Ear)
sections.text:
The presence of middle ear fluid without signs of acute infection. OME often occurs after acute otitis media (AOM) episodes,
but it also may occur as a result of Eustachian tube dysfunction in young children in the absence of a preceding AOM.

Clinical Presentation
It is often discovered by chance with: -
Little or no ear pain, Gradual loss of hearing, No ear discharge and Aural fullness.
Investigations
Tympanometry, Audiometry.

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Close follow-up                             •       Valsalva maneuver                     •     Encourage chewing

Pharmacological Management
B: ephedrine (0.5% and 1%) nasal drop, Adults and children above 12years: Instill 1 to 2 drops in each nostril, not more than
4 times a day for 3 to 5 days
           AND
D: fluticasone propionate (50mcg/spray) nasal spray. Adults and adolescents more than 12years:
2sprays in each nostril 24hourly as needed. Children 4 months-1years: 1spray in each nostril 24hourly as needed.
           OR
S: mometasone (nasal spray) Adults and adolescents from 12years: 2 sprays in each nostril 24hourly as needed.
Children 6-11years: 1spray in each nostril 24hourly as needed
  Note: Otitis media with effusion with hearing loss that does not improve after 3months should be referred to a specialist for
  myringotomy and grommets insertion.

Surgical treatment
Myringotomy + grommet insertion (microscopic/endoscopic)
+/- Adeno (tonsillectomy)

sections.title: Hearing Loss
sections.text:
A child with hearing loss should be detected and intervention started immediately after delivery. New born hearing screening is
done using an otoacoustic emission machine. Any child suspected of hearing loss (usually presenting with delayed speech
development) should be referred to a zonal/national hospital immediately since early intervention has a better outcome.

sections.title: Sensorineural Hearing Loss (SNHL)
sections.text:
Loss of hearing that results from defective function of cochlea or auditory pathway. It may be congenital or acquired.

Clinical Presentation
Hearing impairment as confirmed by hearing assessment tests.

Investigations
    •    Distraction Test/Free Field Test – for children                  •    Auditory Brainstem Response (ABR)
    •    Tympanometry                                                     •    CT-Scan/MRI for bone cochlea and auditory
    •    Pure Tone Audiometry                                                  nerve assessment for pre cochlea implantation
    •    Otoacoustic emission (OAE)

Non-Pharmacological Management
(Rehabilitation)                                                          •    Bone-anchored hearing Aid (BAHA)
    •     Avoiding exposure to noises                                     •    Cochlea Implantation (C.I), with interval
    •     Avoiding unnecessary use of ototoxic drugs                           programming/troubleshooting –for severe and
    •     Digital programmable hearing aid- for mild to                        profound SNHL.
          moderate SNHL                                                   •    Speech therapy
    •     Super power digital programmable hearing aid-                   •    Sign language/ lip reading
          for severe and profound SNHL

Pharmacological Management
C: calcium + vitamins 1 tablets 24hourly for not less than 3months

Surgical treatment
Cochlear implantation

sections.title: Sudden Sensorineural Hearing Loss
sections.text:
Clinical Presentation
     •    Hearing loss that is sensorineural in nature
     •    Hearing loss of at least 30 decibels (dB) over at least three consecutive test frequencies
     •    Hearing loss that occurs within a 72-hour period

Investigations
    •    Tuning Fork Test
    •    Tympanometry
    •    Pure Tone Audiometry

Pharmacological Management
Treat underlying cause if known
A: prednisolone (PO) 60mg 24hourly for 5days then taper down to 50mg 24hourly for next 5days.

For Children:
A: prednisolone (PO) 1mg/kg 24hourly for 5days then taper down by half for the next 5days.
          AND
C: calcium + vitamins 1tablet 24hourly for not less than 3months

sections.title: Otosclerosis
sections.text:
Otosclerosis is a bony overgrowth that involves the footplate of the stapes. As the overgrowth develops, the stapes can no
longer function as a piston, it becomes fixated. Conduction gradually becomes worse until a maximal conductive hearing loss
of 60 dB is reached.

Clinical Presentation
Hearing loss, Dizziness, Tinnitus.

Investigations
    •    Tympanometry
    •    Pure tone Audiometry (PTA)
    •    CT- Scan -of temporal bone

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Hearing aids (H/A)-Digital Programmable Hearing Aids
    •  Cochlea implantation

Surgical treatment
    •    Stapedectomy
    •    Cochlea Implantation
    •    Middle ear implant

sections.title: Peripheral Vertigo (Meniere’s disease and Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV)
sections.text:
Clinical Presentation
 Meniere’s disease                                         Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo( PPPV)
 Vertigo                                                   Vertigo
 Nausea                                                    Nausea
 Vomiting                                                  Vomiting

    •    Audiometry                                                    •    HINTS Examination
    •    Vestibular test                                               •    MRI Brain-to rule out cerebellopontine angle
    •    Video nystagmogram (vNG)                                           (CPA) tumours
    •    Video head impulse test (vHIT)

Non-Pharmacological Management (FOR BPPV)
    •  Epley maneuver
    •  Berbecure maneuver
    •  Vestiulr rehabilitation therapy
    •  Stabilometer
Pharmacological Management (FOR MENIERES)
B: intratympanic dexamethasone (IV) 4mg
          AND
D: betahistine (PO) 24-48mg 8 hourly for 14days. Maintenance dose 24mg 24hourly for 14 days

sections.title: Vestibular Neuritis /Vestibular Neuronitis and Labyrinthitis
sections.text:
Clinical Presentation
     •    Rapid onset severe vertigo, nausea, vomiting
     •    Spontaneous vestibular nystagmus 325
     •    Gait instability

Pharmacological Management
Symptomatic approach
A: promethazine (PO/IV) 12.5-25mg 8hourly
         AND
B: metoclopramide (PO/IV) 5 – 10mg 8hourly
         AND
C: diazepam (PO) 1- 5 mg 8-12hourly
         OR
D: betahistine (PO) 16-24mg 12hourly

sections.title: Vestibular Migraine
sections.text:
Clinical Presentation
     •    Dizziness/Vertigo
     •    Moderate to severe temporal headache
     •    Sensory amplification e.g., hyperaccusis

Investigations
    •    Audiometry                                                      •    Video head impulse test (vHIT)
    •    Vestibular test                                                 •    MRI Brain-to rule out cerebellopontine angle
    •    Video nystagmogram (vNG)                                             (CPA) tumours

Pharmacological Management
A: propranolol (PO) 40mg 12hourly for 14days
         OR
B: amlodipine (PO) 10mg 24hourly for 14days

sections.title: Tinnitus
sections.text:
Clinical Presentation
Perception of sound in proximity to the head in the absence of an external source

Non-Pharmacological Management
Tinnitus masking

Pharmacological Management
D: betahistine (PO) 48mg daily (16-24mg regime) preferably after meals for 2 months

For Children 5-12 years:
D: acetazolamide (PO) 250mg 24hourly 14days

sections.title: Glomus Tumours
sections.text:
Paragangliomas are rare neuroendocrine tumors that arise from the extra-adrenal autonomic paraganglia, small organs
consisting mainly of neuroendocrine cells that are derived from the embryonic neural crest and have the ability to secrete
catecholamines.

Clinical Presentation
Neck mass (at angle of mandible), Rising sun signs, Pulsatile tinnitus, Hearing loss(conductive).

Investigations
    •    Audiometry
    •    CT-angiogram
    •    MRI-Head & neck HRCT
    •    Scan-head & neck

Surgical treatment
Glomus Tumour excision, Embolization (MDT with Interventional radiologist and neurosurgeon)

sections.title: Vestibular Schwannomas
sections.text:
Also known as acoustic neuromas, acoustic schwannomas, acoustic neurinomas, or vestibular neurilemomas) are Schwann
cell-derived tumors that commonly arise from the vestibular portion of the eighth cranial nerve.

Clinical Presentation
Hearing loss, Tinnitus.

Investigations
    •    Audiometry                                                      •    Videonystagmography (VNG)
    •    MRI-brain (with gadolinium as contrast)                         •    Video Head Impulse Testing (vHIT)
    •    Auditory Brainstem Response (ABR)                               •    Acoustic Reflex Testing (ARTs)

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Observation/watchful waiting
    •  Radiotherapy

Surgical treatment
Tumour (schwanoma) excision

sections.title: Hereditary/Congenital Hearing loss
sections.text:
Refers to hearing impairment present at birth, while hereditary hearing loss is caused by genetic mutations that may present at
birth or later in childhood. Both may be sensorineural, conductive, or mixed in type.

Classification
 Type            Description
 Indication      Hearing loss occurs with other physical or systemic abnormalities (e.g., Waardenburg, Pendred, Usher
                 syndromes)
                 Hearing loss is isolated with no other clinical features (accounts for ~70% of genetic cases)
                 Autosomal recessive (most common), autosomal dominant, X-linked, or mitochondrial
Causes

    •    No babbling by 6 months                                               Hearing Screening
    •    Delayed speech by 12–18 months

sections.title: Acute Rhinitis
sections.text:
It is a viral inflammatory condition in the nasal mucous membrane, usually part of a more wide- spread infection of the upper
respiratory tract.

Non-Pharmacological Management
Bed rest& warm drinks

Pharmacological Management
B: ephedrine nasal drops (1% for adults and 0.5% for children) 1–2drops into each nostril 6hourly for not more than 5days

sections.title: Acute Non-Allergic Rhinitis
sections.text:
Clinical Presentation
     •    Nasal blockage
     •    Post nasal drip
     •    Erythematous turbinate

Pharmacological Management
A: prednisolone (PO), Adults: 60mg 24hourly for 5days then taper down to 50mg 24hourly for next 5days.
Children: 1mg/kg 24hourly for 5days then taper down by half for the next 5days.
          AND
B: ephedrine (0.5% and 1%) nasal drop, Adults and children above 12years: Instill 1- 2drops in each nostril, not more than
4times a day for 3-5days
          OR
C: oxymetazoline (0.05%) nasal drops/spray Dosage for adults and children above 6years: Instill 2 -3drops or sprays in each
nostril 12hourly for 3-5days
          AND
D: fluticasone propionate (50mcg/spray) nasal spray, Adults and adolescents more than 12years: 2sprays in each nostril 24
hourly as needed. children 4-11years: 1 spray in each nostril 24hourly as needed
          OR
S: mometasone nasal spray, Adults and adolescents from 12years: 1sprays in each nostril 24hourly as needed,
children 6-11 years: 1spray in each nostril 24hourly as needed

 Note: Oral drugs to reduce swelling of the mucous membrane, antihistamines and antibiotics are not indicated

sections.title: Allergic Rhinitis
sections.text:
It is an irritation of the nasal mucosa by an allergen in a previously sensitized individual. Common allergens include house dust
mites (mite’s feaces), pollens, cockroach antigen, animal dander, molds (in- door), birds feathers

Clinical Presentation
     •    Itchy nostrils, throat, eyes                                    •    Sneezing
     •    Watery nasal discharge                                          •    Post nasal drip
     •    Nasal congestion                                                •    Cough

Investigations
    •    Anterior rhinoscopy (rigid or fibreoptic nasolaryngoscopy) – watery nasal discharge, Turbinates congestion
    •    Total or specific IgE
    •    Skin prick Allergy test

Non-Pharmacological Management

sections.title: Rhinosporiodiosis
sections.text:
Chronic, granulomatous disease caused by Rhinosporidium seeberi, an aquatic protistan parasite. It primarily affects the nasal
mucosa and nasopharynx, but can also involve other mucous membranes and, rarely, the skin and internal organs.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Unilateral nasal obstruction
     •    Epistaxis
     •    Local Pruritus
     •    Rhinorrhea
     •    Pink or deep red polyp, strawberry like appearance, Bleeds easily on manipulation

Pharmacological Management
S: dapsone (PO), Adults: 100mg 24hourly for 6months. Children1-2mg/kg 24hourly, not to exceed 100mg 24hourly

Surgical treatment
Wide excision with wide area electro-coagulation of the lesion base

sections.title: Rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis
sections.text:
A potentially lethal invasive fungal infection which commonly affects the immunocompromised and diabetic patients and is most
commonly caused by genera Mucorales and include Rhizopus, Mucor and Rhizomucor.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Fever, Headache
     •    Nasal congestion, Purulent nasal discharge
     •    Facial numbness
     •    Eshar of nasal mucosa
     •    Proptosis, Blindness

Pharmacological Management
S: amphotericin B deoxycholate (IV)

Adults: Test dose of 1mg IV infused over 20-30 minutes.
Loading dose of 0.25-0.5mg/kg infused over 2-6hours.
Maintenance dose of 0.25-1mg/kg IV 24hourly for 3-6weeks.

Children: Test dose of 0.1mg/kg not to exceed 1mg: infused over 20-60minutes.
Loading dose of 0.25mg/kg infused over 2-6hours.
Maintenance dose of 0.25/kg 24hourly to ensure a total dose of 30-40mg/kg is given over 3-6weeks

Control underlying risk factors

Surgical treatment
Endoscopic debridement (FESS) of the necrotic tissue and Biopsy

 Note: High index of suspicion in patient with DKA and nasal symptoms above

sections.title: Congenital Choanal Atresia
sections.text:
A congenital blockage (bony, membranous, or mixed) of the posterior nasal opening, causing nasal obstruction. It may be
unilateral or bilateral. Neonates are obligate nasal breathers; therefore, complete bilateral choanal atresia is a medical
emergency requiring immediate oral airway support until surgical creation of a patent nasal airway. Early recognition and referral
are critical in bilateral cases. Always assess for associated anomalies (e.g., CHARGE syndrome).

Clinical Presentation
     •    Bilateral: Neonatal respiratory distress relieved               •      Thick nasal discharge on the defective nostril
          by crying, difficulty feeding, cyanosis.                        •      Failure to pass nasogastric tube
     •    Unilateral: Persistent unilateral nasal obstruction
          or discharge.
Investigation
     •    Primary level: Failure to pass a nasogastric tube through the nostril.
     •    Secondary level: Clinical assessment; refer.
     •    Tertiary level: Nasal endoscopy and CT scan Paranasal sinuses (PNS) for confirmation and surgical planning.

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Primary level: Maintain airway (oral airway or prone/lateral positioning), oxygen (oral) if needed, urgent referral.
    •  Secondary level: Supportive care (suction, feeding via orogastric tube), refer to tertiary immediately.
    •  Tertiary level: if suspected at tertiary facility, urgently follow the above approach and consult ENT on call immediately
       or refer.

Surgical treatment
(At a center with ENT surgeon)
Surgical correction preferably via endoscopic trans nasal approach (endoscopic stentless Cho anoplasty)

Postoperative care includes the following;
S: esomeprazole 1mg/kg once 4 weeks                                   C: oxymetazoline 0.05%/ephedrine nasal drops 8hly 5
        AND                                                           days),
A: sodium chloride saline drop (irrigation) 8 hourly for 4                    AND
weeks                                                                 D: dexamethasone + ciprofloxacin nasal drops
        AND                                                           (0.1%+0.3%), 3 drops/nostril 12 hourly)

Monthly follow-up nasoendoscopy for 3 months

 Note: Delaying unilateral choanal atresia repair until after 6 months of age may reduce the need for revision surgery as the
 child grows.

sections.title: Nasal Turbinate Hypertrophy
sections.text:
Turbinate hypertrophy is a complication of allergic rhinitis

Clinical Presentation
     •    Snoring
     •    Nasal obstruction
     •    Nasal irritation
     •    Enlarged inferior or middle turbinate on rhinoscopy

Pharmacological Management
As for Allergic Rhinitis

Surgical treatment
Partial submucosal Turbinectomy/Turbinoplasty – (open or endoscopic)

sections.title: Nasal Bone Fracture
sections.text:
Clinical Presentation
     •    History of nasal trauma
     •    Deviation of nose or septum
     •    Nasal bleeding
     •    Nasal obstruction

Pharmacological Management
Antibiotics & Analgesics) as for nasal septal abscess and hematoma

Surgical treatment
Closed reduction and alignment of nasal structures under LA or GA this should be done 1-2weeks if there is edema. Can be
done using nasal speculum or endoscopically.

Nasal Septal Deviation (Non-Traumatic)

Clinical Presentation
Nasal obstruction, Nasal dryness, +/_Epistaxis.

Surgical treatment
Septoplasty –open or Endoscopic

sections.title: Adenoid Hypertrophy
sections.text:
It is hypertrophy of the lymphoid tissues in the nasopharynx; presenting with stertor, mouth breathing, snoring sleep apnea and
sometimes otitis media with effusion. It is reported mainly in children although it can affect adults mainly with chronic nasal
allergies and immunosuppression.

Investigations
    •    Nasopharynx lateral view X-ray.
    •    Fiberoptic nasolaryngoscopy (gold standard)

Pharmacological Management
A: cetirizine (PO) 10mg 24 hourly for 4weeks. Children: 5mg 24 hourly for 4weeks
           AND
A: sodium chloride 0.9% nasal spray/drops 4hourly for 2weeks
           AND

Adenoidectomy/Adenotomy

It is the inflammation of the mucosal lining of the nose and paranasal sinuses of not more than 12 weeks’ duration. In sinusitis

sections.title: Chronic Rhinosinusitis
sections.text:
Can be caused by Bacterial or Fungal

Clinical Presentation
     •    Anterior and/or posterior nasal mucopurulent drainage
     •    Nasal obstruction/nasal blockage/congestion
     •    Facial pain, pressure and/or fullness
     •    Hyposmia or Anosmia
     •    Halitosis

Investigations
CT scan of paranasal sinuses (PNS)-gold standard-should be done after adequate medical treatment with persistent symptoms.

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Saline nasal wash
    •  Steaming with or without camphor, eucalyptus and menthol topical.

Pharmacological Management
as for acute sinusitis BUT should be for 4-6 weeks

Surgical treatment
Surgery if associated with complications e.g., obital/periobital abscess, pottys puffy tumour, Brain abscess and nasal polyposis
and Failure of disease resolution after adequate medical treatment.
Frontal Trephination OR Caldwell Luc operation OR Open ethmoidectomy OR Functional Endoscopic Sinus Surgery (FESS)

sections.title: Nasal Polyposis
sections.text:
This is mucosal change due to chronic mucosal inflammation. Ethmoidal polyp- This is a complication of allergic rhinitis or
chronic rhinosinusitis. Antrochoanal polyp benign tumor of the maxillary sinus that prolapse to the nasal cavity.

Clinical Presentation
     •    History of allergy or asthma                                   •    Snoring and mouth breathing
     •    Nasal congestion/blockage                                      •    Post nasal drip
     •    Nasal discharge

Investigations
    •    Direct nasal Endoscopy (DNE) or Fiber optic nasopharyngoscopy
    •    Serum Total/specific IgE
    •    CT-Scan of paranasal sinuses (CT-PNS)

Pharmacological Management
As for allergic rhinitis/acute rhinosinusitis

Surgical treatment
    •    Intranasal polypectomy
    •    Partial/Medial maxillectomy
    •    Functional Endoscopic Sinus surgery (FESS)

sections.title: Nose Bleeding (Epistaxis)
sections.text:
Nose bleeding is a condition which is common in adults. It may be due to a local cause in the nasal cavity (e.g., trauma, tumor,
foreign body, septal varices, or septal deviation); or a systemic cause (e.g., blood disorders, vascular disorders, renal failure,
hepatic failure, or use of anticoagulants (warfarin, heparin). Most cases of epistaxis are minor; do not require hospitalization.
Patients with significant nose bleeding do require hospitalization.

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Stabilize the patient: put an open intravenous line, do blood grouping and cross matching
    •  Put the patient in a sitting position and advise the patient to pinch the soft part of the nose gently for 5minutes
    •  Put on a gown, glasses, head light and sterile gloves and evacuate clots. Do a thorough head and neck examination
    •  Cauterize septal varisces (if any) using a silver nitrate pencil
    •  Do an anterior nasal packing by introducing into the nasal cavity as far posterior as possible sterile Vaseline gauzes
       (or iodine-soaked gauzes if not available) or special merocele pack, using a dissecting forceps (if bayonet forceps is
       not available)
    •  Put rolled dry gauze on the columella and plaster it

If the patient is still bleeding
      •    Perform a Flexible nasoendoscopy                                      •    Place a posterior nasal pack under general
      •    Do a posterior nasal packing using a Foley’s                               anaesthesia (GA)
           catheter introduced through the nasal cavity into                     •    Put dry gauze on the nose to prevent necrosis of
           the oropharynx, balloon it with normal saline up                           the columella and fix the catheter on the nose
           to 10–15cc while pulling it outward to impinge on                          with an umbilical clamp
           the posterior nasal choana, then do anterior                          •    Almost all of the nasal bleedings will be
           nasal packing as above.                                                    controlled by this way

sections.title: Foreign Bodies in the Nose
sections.text:
This situation usually occurs mostly in children.

Non-Pharmacological Management
Restrain the child before removal using a cerumen hook, if the child cannot be restrained sedation is advised

 Note: A unilateral foul-smelling nasal discharge in a child is due to a foreign body until proven otherwise

sections.title: Obstructive Sleep Apnea Syndrome (OSAS)
sections.text:
Disorder characterized by recurrent episodes of upper airway obstruction during sleep, resulting in interrupted ventilation,
intermittent hypoxia, and sleep fragmentation. The obstruction typically occurs at the level of the pharynx, often due to collapse
or anatomical narrowing involving ENT structures such as the adenoids, tonsils, nasal passages, soft palate, and base of
tongue.
In both children and adults, ENT-related anatomical factors contribute significantly to the pathophysiology of OSAS, and their
recognition is critical for effective treatment planning.
This section addresses only non-central sleep apnea. Central sleep apnea and non-Surgical treatment are discussed in the
Respiratory and CNS chapters. ENT specialists play a key role in the multidisciplinary management of OSAS.

Etiology and Risk Factors
In Children                                                            In Adults
     •    Adenoid and/or tonsillar hypertrophy (most                        •    Obesity (primary risk factor)
          common cause)                                                     •    Nasal obstruction (polyps, septal deviation,
     •    Nasal obstruction (e.g., allergic rhinitis, inferior                   turbinate hypertrophy)
          turbinate hypertrophy, deviated nasal septum)                     •    Redundant soft palate and uvula
     •    Pharyngo- Laryngomalacia                                          •    Tonsillar hypertrophy (less common)
     •    Craniofacial     anomalies      (e.g.,     midface                •    Macroglossia or retrognathia
          hypoplasia, Pierre Robin sequence)                                •    Alcohol or sedative use before bedtime
     •    Neuromuscular disorders

     •    Obesity (as a contributing factor)

Clinical Presentation
While symptoms vary with age, a high index of suspicion should be maintained for
     •    Loud habitual snoring                                       •    Poor concentration, irritability, or morning
     •    Witnessed apneas or gasping episodes during                      headaches
          sleep (this can be reported by bedpartner or                •    Nocturnal enuresis in children
          parent/caretaker)                                           •    Decreased quality of life and sexual dysfunction
     •    Daytime somnolence or hyperactivity (children)                   (adults)
     •    Mouth breathing and nasal speech
     •    Learning or behavioral difficulties (children)

Clinical assessment
     •    Detailed sleep history (snoring, witnessed apneas, sleep position, restlessness, daytime function)
     •    Examination of nasal patency, tonsillar size (Brodsky scale), adenoid facies, craniofacial features
     •    Screening tools: STOP-BANG (adults), Pediatric Sleep Questionnaire (children)

Investigations

    •   Flexible nasopharyngoscopy: to assess upper                            evaluate the site and severity of upper airway
        airway dynamics and obstruction                                        obstruction. In case where the above are

sections.title: Pharyngotonsillitis
sections.text:
Acute inflammation of the pharynx and/or tonsils, commonly viral; bacterial cases often due to Group A Streptococcus (GAS).
It is a frequent cause of outpatient visits in children aged 3–15 years.

sections.title: Laryngitis
sections.text:
Inflammatory condition of the larynx can be infectious or non-infectious, acute (3–7 days) or chronic (>3 weeks). Diagnosis is
often made by case history alone and treatment often targets symptoms.
     •   Acute viral laryngitis is commonest and self-limiting, often linked to upper respiratory infections.
     •   Bacterial laryngitis is less common but can be more severe.
     •   Clinical Presentation may differ between children and adults.
     •   Signs of infectious laryngitis include odynophagia, cough, fever, and respiratory distress.

sections.title: Acute Laryngitis
sections.text:
(Please refer Respiratory chapter for more specific details)
     •   Children are more prone to airway compromise with bacterial laryngitis—prompt recognition is critical.
     •   In adults, reflux and occupational overuse are more common contributors to chronic or recurrent acute laryngitis.
     •   Most cases (especially viral or traumatic) are self-limiting, requiring only supportive care.

sections.title: Laryngopharyngeal reflux disease (LPR) with/without Vocal cord nodules or Laryngeal polyp)
sections.text:
•    Occurs when gastric contents reach the larynx, affecting the glottis and vocal cords.
    •    It commonly presents with hoarseness, globus sensation, chronic throat clearing, and sometimes heartburn or
         regurgitation.
    •    Unlike gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), which involves the lower esophageal sphincter, LPR is linked to
         dysfunction of the upper esophageal sphincter.
    •    Proper evaluation and management require a coordinated interprofessional approach.

Investigations
Fiberoptic Nasolaryngoscopy
Non-Pharmacological Management
     •    Voice rest
     •    Lifestyle Modifications – First-Line
          - Weight loss (if overweight or obese), eat smaller, more frequent meals, avoid lying down within 3 hours after eating
          - Reduce or eliminate: Fatty, spicy, or acidic foods, Caffeinated and carbonated beverages, stop tobacco use and limit
            or avoid alcohol

    •    Requires gastroenterology and surgical consultation

sections.title: Recurrent Respiratory Papillomatosis (Laryngeal Papillomas)
sections.text:
It is the commonest benign laryngeal tumor of the larynx caused by Human papilloma virus (HPV), occurring in both children
and adults. It has a higher recurrence rate in children than in adults, among adults it may turn into a malignancy.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Hoarse voice, audible respiration (inspiratory stridor)
     •    Progressive difficulty in breathing
     •    Progressive inspiratory stridor
     •    On and off cough

Investigations
    •    Perform a thorough respiratory system examination
    •    Indirect laryngoscopy for papilloma croups on the larynx
    •    Rigid laryngoscopy (Endoscopy) OR Fiber optic Nasolaryngoscopy

Non-Pharmacological Management
If in distress, perform a tracheostomy first then refer

Referral: Refer the patient to the next facility with adequate expertise and facilities

Surgical treatment
    •    Microsurgical debridement is the mainstay, observe laryngeal mucosa and think of voice quality, avoid introducing
         anterior laryngeal web (Direct Laryngoscopy under GA+ microlaryngeal surgery(D/Scopy+MLS) Bronchoscopy is
         advised every time when doing Direct Laryngoscopy under GA
    •    Tracheostomy shall be avoided, if it has to be done, only short term

sections.title: Foreign Bodies in the Throat
sections.text:
If the foreign body is suspected to be in the hypopharynx, esophagus, trachea or bronchus
      •    Take a thorough history and do a thorough physical examination
      •    Do chest X ray to confirm your diagnosis (though some foreign bodies are radiolucent)

Refer to a next level hospital with facility for removal (never attempt if not trained)

Surgical treatment
    •    Oesophagoscopy for oesophageal foreign body (FB)
    •    Bronchoscopy for airway FB

sections.title: Subglottic Hemangioma
sections.text:
Congenital subglottic hemangiomas are vascular lesions that undergo a phase of rapid growth that is initiated during the first
few weeks to months of life. They may present as solitary lesions or as part of a segmental hemangioma syndrome.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Hoarseness of voice
     •    Inspiratory stridor
     •    Cough
     •    Cyanosis
     •    Concomitant cervical facial hemangioma

Pharmacological Management
A: prednisolone (PO) Children: 1mg/kg 24hourly for 5days then taper down by half for the next 5days.
         AND
A: propranolol (PO) for children: Starting dose of 0.6mg/kg 12hourly for 1week, then increase dose to 1.1mg/kg 12hourly for
2weeks; then Maintenance dose 1.7mg/kg 12hourly for at least 6months.

Surgical treatment
Tracheostomy if severe inspiratory stridor is present.

sections.title: Laryngomalacia
sections.text:
This is the most common congenital anomaly of the larynx, characterized by partial or complete collapse of supraglottic
structures on inspiration. This is the most common cause of noisy breathing in infancy. Gastroesophageal reflux disease
(GERD) has been implicated.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Inspiratory stridor relieved by lying prone
     •    Difficult breathing/dyspnoea
     •    Difficult feeding
     •    Chocking on feeding

Investigations
    •    Fiber optic nasolaryngoscopy when awake
    •    Direct laryngo-tracheo-bronchoscopy (DLTB)

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Sleep prone rather than supine
    •  Feeding modification
    •  Close observation of upper respiratory tract infections

Pharmacological Management
 Indication        Medicine                       Population     Dose            Frequency      Duration
                                                  Adults         20 mg
                       A: omeprazole (PO)                                        24 hourly      4–8 weeks (review response)
 Associated                                       Children       0.7–1 mg/kg
 Gastroesophageal             OR
 Reflux (common)                                  Adults         20–40 mg
                       S: esomeprazole (PO)                                      24 hourly      4–8 weeks
                                                  Children       10–20 mg

Surgical treatment
    •    Supraglottoplasty at any age for type III and IV, otherwise watchful waiting while on pharmacotherapy
    •    Tracheostomy for severe cases

sections.title: Vocal Cords Paralysis
sections.text:
It is due to total interruption of nerve impulse resulting in no movement of laryngeal muscles. Vocal cord paralysis is a sign of
disease and not a diagnosis by itself, vocal cord paralysis can be unilateral or bilateral.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Change in voice/hoarseness (for unilateral vocal                •    Stridor
          cord paralysis)                                                 •    Cough and aspiration
     •    Vocal fatigue                                                   •    History of neck surgery(thyroidectomy)
     •    Dyspnoea/upper airway obstruction                               •    Neck or mediastinal tumors

Investigation
    •    Fiber optic nasolaryngoscopy
    •    Direct laryngo-tracheo-bronchoscopy (DLTB)
    •    Video stroboscopy

Non-Pharmacological Management
Speech therapy

Surgical treatment
Depends on the severity and desired outcome.
    •    Tracheostomy                                                     •    Cordectomy
    •    Arytenoidectomy                                                  •    Thyroplasty type i& ii
    •    Vocal cord lateralation through endoscopy                        •    Injection of Teflon paste
    •    Endoscopic Anterior-posterior cricoid split                      •    Muscle or cartilage implant

sections.title: Infection of Thyroglossal Duct Cyst, Dermoid Cyst, Branchial Cleft Cysts
sections.text:
Clinical Presentation
     •    For Thyroglossal cyst- Midline upper neck mass which is cystic just below the hyoid bone. If infected my present with
          tenderness. My also present as discharging sinus
     •    For branchial cleft cysts mass or discharging sinus along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle.

Investigation
Neck USS

Pharmacological Management
B: amoxicillin + clavulanic Acid (FDC) (PO)
Adults: 625 mg – 1 g 12 hourly for 7–14 days
Children ≤ 3 months: 30 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses (12hourly) for 7–14 days
Children > 3 months: 25 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses (12hourly) for 7–14 days
Surgical treatment
  •    Thyroglossal duct cyst excision (Sistrunk procedure)
  •    Branchial cyst/fistula excision

sections.title: Subglottic Stenosis
sections.text:
Narrowing of airway below vocal cords and above first tracheal ring. Can be congenital or acquired (e.g., post-intubation,
trauma, infection).

Case Definition
 •    Subglottic lumen narrower than normal for age:
 •    Neonates: <4.0 mm
 •    Infants: <4.5 mm
 •    Adults: <13 mm

Pediatric Myer-Cotton Grading:
I: <50%, II: 51–70%, III: 71–99%, IV: complete obstruction

Clinical Presentation
Neonates/Infants
     •    Biphasic stridor, retractions, feeding difficulty
     •    Failed extubation or persistent croup

Older children/adults
    •     Progressive dyspnea, stridor, hoarseness
    •     Recurrent “asthma” or upper airway infections

Referral Criteria
    •    All suspected or confirmed cases, especially pediatric
    •    Adults with progressive airway symptoms or failed conservative care
    •    Facilities without endoscopic capability → refer early

Investigations
    •    Flexible nasolaryngoscopy (screening)                          •   CT neck (adults or high-grade cases)
    •    Direct     laryngoscopy,    Tracheoscopy             &         •   ABG/pulse oximetry for oxygenation
         bronchoscopy (DLTB) (gold standard)                            •   Screen for GERD if recurrent symptoms
    •    Neck/chest X-ray
Non-Pharmacological Management
    •    Oxygen and positioning support                                 •   Nutritional support and speech therapy
    •    Avoid repeated intubation/suctioning                           •   Early referral to ENT with airway expertise

Pharmacological Management
    •  Systemic steroids (short course for inflammation)
    •  PPI or H2 blockers for GERD-related inflammation (as recommended in LPRD section above)
    •  Antibiotics only if signs of infection (e.g., Amoxicillin + Clavulanic acid, Cefuroxime)

Surgical treatment
    •    Endoscopic (Grades I–II, selected III)
    •    Balloon dilation or laser excision
    •    Open surgery (Grades III–IV or failed endoscopy)
         - Laryngotracheal reconstruction (LTR)
         - Cricotracheal resection (CTR)
    •    Tracheostomy (temporary or definitive)

  Note:
      •      Avoid prolonged/repeated intubation in neonates.
      •      Recurrent “croup” or failed extubation → consider SGS.
      •      Rationalize steroid and antibiotic use.
      •      Multidisciplinary care improves outcomes.

sections.title: Deep Neck Spaces Infections
sections.text:
Clinical Presentation
     •    Truisms                                                          •    Difficult breathing
     •    Induration and swelling below the angle of                       •    Neck stiffness/torticollis
          mandible                                                         •    Neck swelling, mass, or lymphadenopathy
     •    Medial bulging of the pharyngeal wall                            •    Systemic toxicity with fever and rigors
     •    Difficult swallowing (dysphagia/odynophagia)

Investigations
    •    Full blood picture                                                •    Neck + Chest plain x-ray
    •    PCT (Serial test might help to monitor prognosis                  •    Neck + Chest CT scan (Post Op scans can help
         in serious cases)                                                      avoid re-drainage)
    •    Culture and sensitivity for aspirated contents

sections.title: Peritonsillar Abscess (Quincy)
sections.text:
Peritonsillar abscess is a collection of pus located between the capsule of the palatine tonsil and the pharyngeal muscles.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Severe sore throat (usually unilateral) with Fever
     •    "Hot potato" or muffled voice
     •    Pooling of saliva or drooling may be present
     •    Trismus, neck swelling and pain and may have ipsilateral ear pain
     •    Fatigue, irritability
     •    Swollen and/or fluctuant tonsil with deviation of the uvula to the opposite side

Pharmacological Management
Antibiotics: Indicated due to bacterial etiology (commonly group A Streptococcus or mixed anaerobic infections). Intravenous
antibiotics are preferred initially

    •    Drainage/quincy tonsillectomy
    •    Interval tonsillectomy

sections.title: Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibromas (JNA)
sections.text:
Are rare vascular tumors seen in adolescent males.

Clinical features
     •    Nasal bleeding
     •    Nasal blockage
     •    May present with eye protrusion

Investigation
CT-Scan (with contrast) PNS/Skull base-will show widening of sphenopalatine fissure and anterior bowing of posterior wall of
maxillary sinus.

  Note: Never take biopsy for suspected case of JNA

Surgical treatment
Embolization of internal maxillary artery THEN
Excision of Angiofibroma (Open or Endoscopic/modified Denkers operation)

sections.title: Salivary Gland Tumors
sections.text:
Salivary gland tumors include a heterogeneous group of lesions. Most salivary gland tumors are composed of more than one
cell type. Tumours may arise from major or minor salivary glands. (Parotid, Submandibular, Lingual and minor salivary gland
tumours)

Clinical Presentation
Painless progressive swelling of a given salivary gland.

Investigation
    •    Fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC)
    •    Do not take incisional biopsy unless lesion is ulcerative.

Surgical treatment
    •    Partial or Total parotidectomy-for parotid tumours
    •    Submandibular gland tumor excision-for submandibular gland
    •    Sub lingual gland tumor excision
         - Minor salivary gland tumors excision

sections.title: Parapharyngeal Tumours
sections.text:
Both benign and malignant tumors may arise from any of the structures contained in this space. Among parapharyngeal space
(PPS) tumors; 70-80% are benign, and 20-30% are malignant. Most PPS tumors are of salivary or neurogenic origin.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Sore throat                                                       •    Dysphonia
     •    Tonsillar/pharyngeal mass                                         •    Otalgia
     •    Neck/submandibular mass                                           •    Snoring

Investigation
    •    Fine neddle aspiration cytology (FNAC)
    •    CT SCAN-Neck & skull base
    •    MRI –Head and neck

Surgical treatment
Parapharyngeal tumour excision

sections.title: Cancer of the Larynx
sections.text:
It is the commonest ENT malignancy. Risk factors include cigarette smoking, alcohol intake, gastroesophageal reflux disease
and human papilloma virus.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Progressive hoarseness of voice
     •    Difficulty in breathing (inspiratory stridor)
     •    Hemoptysis

Referral: Refer the patient to the next facility with adequate expertise and facilities

Investigations
Rigid Laryngoscopy (endoscopy) or Fiberoptic nasolaryngoscopy(diagnostic)

Surgical treatment
    •    Direct Laryngoscopy +Biopsy under General Anaesthesia (GA)
    •    Tracheostomy
    •    Total/Partial laryngectomy +/- neck dissection

  Note: Any patient with progressive hoarseness of voice for more than two weeks should undergo laryngoscopy

sections.title: Sino-Nasal Malignancy
sections.text:
Is a malignancy of the nose and paranasal sinuses? Risk factors include wood dust (both soft and hard), wielding dust, lather
industry fumes, hydrocarbons fumes, and aflatoxin dust.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Nasal bleeding                                                    •    Cheek swelling
     •    Nasal discharge                                                   •    Proptosis
     •    Nasal obstruction                                                 •    Hearing loss
     •    Teeth loosening

Referral: Refer the patient to the next facility with adequate expertise and facilities

Investigations
    •    Biopsy-transnasal biopsy/Endoscopic
    •    CT-Scan –paranasal sinus (PNS)
    •    Chest x –ray
    •    Urinalysis-bence -Jones proteins

Surgical treatment
    •    Total Maxillectomy-Open OR
    •    Partial Maxillectomy-Open/Endoscopic

  Note: Refer patient for adjuvant chemo and radiotherapy

sections.title: Naso-Pharyngeal Malignancy
sections.text:
It is a malignancy which arises from the nasopharynx. Risk factors include genetic predisposition, Epstein Bar virus, smoked
and/or salted foods.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Cervical lymphadenopathy, usually bilateral
     •    Nose bleeding
     •    Nasal blockage
     •    Unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus or ear pain

Referral: Refer the patient to the next facility with adequate expertise and facilities

 Note: A patient presenting with cervical lymphadenopathy has nasopharyngeal carcinoma until proven otherwise

Investigations
    •    Biopsy-Transnasal/Endoscopic
    •    Fine needle aspiration cytology for neck mass
    •    CT-Scan-head and neck
    •    Chest x-ray
    •    Serology for Epstein Bar virus (EBV)

Non-Pharmacological Management
Radiotherapy

sections.title: Oropharyngeal Malignancy
sections.text:
Oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinomas arise in the soft palate, tonsils, base of tongue, pharyngeal wall, and vallecula.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Sore throat
     •    Throat pain/painful swallowing
     •    Voice change (“hot potato” voice)
     •    Difficulty in breathing
     •    Oropharyngeal mass/ulcer

Investigations
    •    Rigid endoscopy
    •    Flexible Nasoendoscopy
    •    Transoral biopsy
    •    Serology for HPV (human papilloma virus)
    •    CT-Scan or MRI -Head & Neck

Management
   •   Surgery: open or transoral
   •   Definitive Management: Refer Malignancy chapter.

sections.title: Hypo-Pharyngeal Malignancy
sections.text:
It is a malignancy which arises from the hypopharynx. Risk factors include cigarette smoking, alcohol intake and
gastroesophageal reflux disease.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Progressive dysphasia                                             •    Cervical lymphadenopathy
     •    Progressive odynophagia                                           •    Difficulty in breathing (inspiratory stridor)
     •    Hematemesis/hemoptysis                                            •    Excessive salivation/Pooling of saliva
     •    Ear pain (referred otalgia)

Referral: Refer the patient to the next facility with adequate expertise and facilities

Investigations
    •    Rigid Hypopharyngoscopy (endoscopy) or Fiber optic nasolaryngoscopy(diagnostic).
    •    CT-Scan-head and neck
    •    Chest x-ray

Surgical treatment
Direct Hypopharyngoscopy +Biopsy under general anesthesia (GA)

Definitive Management
Chemoradiotherapy depending on histological results –Refer to malignancies chapter 22

sections.title: Metastatic Lymphadenopathy and Neck Masses
sections.text:
Cervical lymph nodes are a common site of metastases for malignant tumors that originate at primary sites in the head and
neck. Primary lymphoma in neck nodes must be considered in any differential diagnosis. Sometimes the origin might be
unknown

Clinical Presentation
Neck mass unilateral or bilateral, Neck ulcer.

  Note:
       •    An adult patient with neck mass, should be approached with a presumption of malignancy until proven otherwise.
       •    Once the diagnosis of metastatic squamous cell carcinoma is made, a search for the primary tumor must be performed.
            The probable primary site can often be identified by history and physical examination; panendoscopy and directed imaging
            may be required.

Investigations
    •    Neck ultrasound                                                    •    Direct nasal endoscopy (DNE)
    •    Fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC)                             •    Fiber optic nasolaryngoscopy
    •    Panendoscopy of upper aerodigestive areas                          •    Rigid laryngoscopy (endoscopy)
         (nose and paranasal sinuses, nasopharynx,
         oropharynx,     larynx,     hypopharynx and
         Oesophagoscopy.

  Note: Do not treat patient with cervical lymphadenopathy as a case of TB adenitis until malignancy is ruled out and TB adenitis is
  proved.

Surgical treatment
Biopsy for histology from suspected site, Neck dissection: Radical or Modified Neck Dissection.

sections.title: Speech Disorders
sections.text:
Speech disorder refers to any condition that affects a person’s ability to produce sounds that create words. This includes
stuttering, apraxia, dysarthria can be caused by brain damage/stroke, muscle weakness, hearing loss, dementia etc.

Investigations
Audiometry, Otoacoustic emission (OAEs), Auditory Brainstem Response (ABR)

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Auditory verbal training-for post cochlea                            •    Hearing Aids
       implantation                                                         •    Cochlea implantation
    •  Speech therapy for        aphasia, stuttering,
       apraxia and dysarthria.

Surgical treatment
Posterior tympanotomy-for cochlea implantation.

chapters.intro:
Ear, Nose and Throat (ENT) is a specialty in medicine that deals with medical and surgical management of disorders affecting the
ear, nose, throat, head and the neck. Symptoms and diseases affecting this area are common and commonly lead to patients
seeking medical care.

chapters.title: Oral And Maxillofacial Conditions

sections.title: Eruption of Deciduous Teeth
sections.text:
Eruption of deciduous /primary teeth refers to the process where the first set of teeth emerge through the gingiva into the mouth.
This typically begins around five months of age and continues until the child is about two and a half years old. The following
conditions may associate with eruption process; eruption cysts, gingival cysts of the newborn and pre/natal teeth

Clinical Presentation
     •    Drooling
     •    Bulge gingiva
     •    Gingival soreness
     •    Mild fever; may not need treatment

  Note:
      •     Nylon teeth” is a myth/belief existing in some traditions. These are conditions associated with the eruption of
            deciduous/primary teeth.
       •    Pre/ Natal teeth if they are loose may be removed by dental personnel, but if they are firm should not be removed

sections.title: Shedding of Deciduous Teeth
sections.text:
Phenomenon where deciduous/primary teeth are replaced by permanent teeth. This process occurring between ages of 5–12
years as a normal physiological change. Deciduous teeth should be left to fall out themselves unless the teeth are carious or
there is any other indication. Parents should be counseled accordingly and be instructed to assist their children to loosen the
already mobile teeth.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Mixed dentition
     •    Loose deciduous teeth

Investigation
CBCT or OPG X-ray or/ and PA X-ray

Surgical treatment
Tooth extraction; when deciduous fail to exfoliate or permanent teeth erupt in wrong direction

Pharmacological Management
A: paracetamol (PO) 1g 8hourly for 3days
         AND
A: amoxicillin (PO) 250mg 8hourly for 5days (If necessary)

  Note: Recommended age for taking CBCT or OPG is above 6years

sections.title: Malocclusions
sections.text:
Malocclusion is any variation in the arrangement of teeth leading to abnormal occlusion to the extent that may be functionally
harmful or aesthetically objectionable.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Class I malocclusion: Diagnosed when there is any occlusal abnormality or individual tooth malocclusion in a case
          with normal arch relationship in anteroposterior plane.
     •    Class II malocclusion: Mesiobuccal cusp of upper first permanent molar occludes mesial to the buccal developmental
          groove of the lower first permanent molar
     •    Class III malocclusion: The upper first permanent molar occludes distal to the buccal developmental groove of the
          lower first permanent molar
     •    Skeletal malocclusions: These malocclusions are caused by defects in the underlying skeletal structure itself.

Investigation
CBCT or OPG X-ray

Non-Pharmacological Management
Preventive measures
     •    Parents counselling on avoiding oral habits to their child
     •    Caries control
     •    Release of abnormal frenal attachment
     •    Management of abnormal oral musculature and related habits

Non-surgical treatment
Interceptive orthodontics
Also known as early orthodontic treatment or Phase one orthodontics, is a proactive approach aimed at addressing dental and
jaw development issues in children, typically between the ages of 6 and 10 years, during the mixed dentition phase when both
primary and permanent teeth are present.
     •   Guide jaw and dental development to ensure proper alignment and function
     •   Create space for erupting permanent teeth, reducing the risk of crowding
     •   Correct harmful oral habits such as thumb sucking or tongue thrusting
     •   Assessing breathing pattern of the growing child such as mouth breather in a child with adenoids, guide ENT
         evaluations
     •   Address skeletal discrepancies that can affect facial aesthetics and function
     •   Space maintainers: Preserve space for permanent teeth if baby teeth are lost prematurely
     •   Palatal expanders: Widen the upper jaw to correct cross-bites and create space
     •   Partial braces or aligners: Address specific alignment issues in developing teeth

Definitive Orthodontics
Often referred to as "Phase II" or comprehensive orthodontic correction, is the full-scale alignment of permanent teeth and the
correction of bite relationships after early intervention (Phase I) or as a single-phase approach. Main goals include: Precise
alignment of all permanent teeth, Correction of bite issues (overbite, underbite, crossbite) and achieving proper jaw harmony
and long-term functional stability. This treatment should start when most permanent teeth (excluding wisdom teeth) are erupted
(around ages 10–14 years).
     •    Appliances Used; Fixed braces (metal/ceramic) or clear aligners (Invisalign)
     •    Treatment Duration; Generally, 12–30 months, often around 18–24 months, influenced by complexity

Retention Phase: After active treatment, patients wear retainers (fixed or removable) to maintain tooth position, retainer to be
worn both day and night during the first six month and another six months during the night only.

 Note: Fixed orthodontic treatment is a specialized procedure which shall be performed by Orthodontist for patient of all age
 groups. A Pedodontist (Pediatric Dentist) Shall provide fixed orthodontic treatment only to patient below twenty (20) years of
 age.

sections.title: Dental Caries
sections.text:
Dental caries is a chronic non communicable disease of the teeth that results in the localized dissolution and destruction of
calcified tissues. It is characterized by the demineralization of the inorganic portion and destruction of the organic substance of
the tooth.

                                                                                  Cement
