                                                    and indirect pulp capping     eugenol / Intermediate restorative
                                                    Note: Recall after 6–8 weeks  materials, then Cention N
                                                    to confirm tertiary dentine
                                                    formation, then place
                                                    permanent filling

   Note:
       •     For temporary restoration use Zinc oxide eugenol or Reinforced zinc oxide eugenol
       •     For permanent restoration of Class, I, II, V, and pit & fissure use Cention N, or Composite resin or High viscosity glass
             ionomer cement.
        •    For permanent restoration of Class III, IV use Cention N or Composite resin.

Pharmacological Management
Analgesics: for toothache
A: paracetamol (PO) 1gm 8hourly for 3days
          OR
A: ibuprofen (PO) 400mg 8hourly for at least 3days
          OR
C: diclofenac (PO) 50mg 8hourly for at least 3days
          OR
A: diclofenac (IM/IV) 75mg stat

sections.title: Endodontic treatment/ root canal treatment
sections.text:
Endodontic treatment or root canal treatment is a dental procedure used to repair and save a badly damaged or infected tooth.
It involves removing the infected or damaged pulp from tooth’s root canals, cleaning and disinfecting the area, and then filling
and sealing it. This procedure aims to eliminate infection and protect the tooth from future microbial invasion, ultimately saving
the tooth from extraction.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Symptomatic irreversible pulpitis                                •    Asymptomatic apical periodontitis
     •    Asymptomatic irreversible pulpitis                               •    Chronic apical abscess
     •    Pulp necrosis (with/ without fistula)                            •    Acute apical abscess
     •    Previously endodontically treated tooth                          •    Condensing osteitis
     •    Previously initiated therapy (pulpotomy         or
          pulpectomy)
     •    Symptomatic apical periodontitis

Non Pharmacological Management
    •   Administer local anesthesia if indicated                       •    Removing pulp tissues
    •   Isolation of offending tooth (use rubber dam)                  •    Cleaning and shaping the canals
    •   Prepare access cavity to access pulp chamber                   •    Obturation (filling and sealing the canals)
        and root canals                                                •    Restoration
 Note:
      •   Dental therapist and Assistant dental officer practicing in health center and district hospital shall perform
          endodontic treatment to anterior teeth only (Incisors & Canines) with single rooted canal
      •   Dental Surgeon (DDS) and Dental specialist shall perform endodontic treatment on all teeth.

Pharmacological Management
 Treatment Category      Management
                         B: sodium hypochlorite (NaOCl) 0.5%–8.25% As per procedure, During procedure.
 Root canal irrigants        AND
                         D: ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) As per procedure, During procedure.
                         B: calcium hydroxide with iodoform, As per protocol and indicated
 Root canal medicaments       OR
                         B: eugenol As per protocol and indicated
                         A: paracetamol (PO) 1 g 8 hourly 3 days
                              OR
 Analgesics              A: Ibuprofen (PO) 400 mg 8 hourly At least 3 days
                              OR
                         C: diclofenac (PO) 50 mg 8 hourly At least 3 days
                         A: amoxicillin (PO) 500 mg 8 hourly 5 days
 Systemic antibiotic          OR
                         A: erythromycin (PO) 500 mg 8 hourly 5 days
 Anti-infective          A: metronidazole (PO) 400 mg 8 hourly 7 days

Surgical treatment
Pulpotomy OR Partial pulpectomy OR Total pulpectomy OR Apexification AND Coronal restoration

  Note:
  Regarding coronal restoration; for grossly/ deep / extensive carious lesions, restore with the following procedure
       •    Sandwich technique
       •    Inlays and Onlays for vital tooth
       •    Post and core restoration for non-vital tooth
  In pathological teeth discoloration conditions like amelogenesis imperfecta, intrinsic discoloration (e.g. dental fluorosis) or
  other conditions restore the teeth by direct or indirect veneers technique.

sections.title: Tooth Wear (Attrition, Abrasion, Erosion, Abfraction)
sections.text:
Tooth wear is a progressive loss of tooth structure caused by mechanical or chemical processes
unrelated to caries or trauma.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Flat, worn occlusal or incisal surfaces (attrition)           •   Smooth, shallow lesions on facial surfaces from
     •    Cracking enamel on cervical area not caused by                    acids (erosion)
          poor brushing technique (abfraction)                          •   Tooth sensitivity
     •    Notches on cervical margins from brushing
          (abrasion)

Investigation
    •    CBCT
    •    OPG X-ray
    •     PA X-ray

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Educate on brushing technique and use of soft toothbrush
    •  Dietary counseling to avoid acidic foods and drinks
    •  Desensitizing toothpaste with active ingredients of potassium nitrate or stannous fluoride

Non-surgical treatment
    •   Professional application of 5% Sodium fluoride (NaF) varnish
    •   Use of occlusal splints for bruxism with decreased Occlusal vertical dimension (OVD) for 6 months and fabricate metal
        crown for at least 8 posterior teeth to raise OVD
    •   Composite filling or Glass ionomer cement for deep cervical abrasion

sections.title: Dentine Hypersensitivity (DHS)
sections.text:
Is a common dental condition affecting one or more teeth when exposed to certain stimuli. This pain occurs when the dentin
layer of the tooth becomes exposed and is triggered by thermal (hot or cold temperatures), osmotic (sweet), chemical (acidic
foods and drinks), and tactile (brushing, probing).

Clinical Presentation
Short, sharp, and sudden pain

Prevention
    •   Proper oral hygiene practice
    •   Avoid coarse toothpaste
    •   Avoid highly acidic food staff

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Proper oral hygiene practice
    •  Desensitizing toothpaste with active ingredients of potassium nitrate or stannous fluoride

Non-surgical treatment
    •   Professional application sodium fluoride (NaF)                  •   Crown fabrication (for bruxism)
        5% varnish                                                      •   Endodontic treatment (for severe form)
    •   Composite filling or Glass ionomer cement

sections.title: Pericoronitis
sections.text:
Inflammation of the soft tissues covering the crown of erupting tooth and occurs more commonly in association with the
mandibular third molar (wisdom) teeth.

Clinical Presentation
     •    High temperature                                              •   Signs of partial tooth eruption
     •    Discomfort in swallowing and chewing                          •   Bad smell (Foetor-ox oris)
     •    Well localized dull pain, swollen and tender gum              •   Trismus
          flap
Investigation
     •    CBCT
     •    OPG
     •    Periapical Dental X-ray

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Excision of the operculum/flap (flabectomy) under local anesthesia.
    •  Disimpaction of the third molar associated with the condition.
    •  Grinding or extraction of the opposing tooth.

Pharmacological Management
A: hydrogen peroxide mouthwash 3% (PO) 6hourly for 5days (Gurgle /rinse)
         AND
A: amoxicillin (PO) 500mg 6hourly for 5days
         AND
A: metronidazole (PO) 400mg 8hourly for 5days If severe (rare) refer to treatment of dental abscess section

sections.title: Tooth extraction/ exodontia
sections.text:
Is a dental procedure involving the removal of a tooth from its socket in the jaw bone

Clinical Presentation
     •    Severe tooth decay                                           •    Periapical abscess that does not respond to
     •    Advanced periodontal disease; leading to lose                     endodontic treatment
          and unstable teeth                                           •    Supernumerary teeth
     •    Impacted teeth                                               •    Failed root canal treatment
     •    Orthodontic treatment
     •    Tooth fracture; extending to the root or those that
          cannot be restored
Investigation
     •    PA X-ray or
     •    CBCT
     •    OPG X-ray
  Note: Tooth extraction can be done under Local anesthesia or/and Sedation or General anesthesia In children/ Adult
  lidocaine gel 2% and lidocaine spray 10% used before injecting anesthesia

sections.title: Impacted tooth/teeth
sections.text:
An impacted tooth is a tooth which is still completely or partially covered by mucosa and bone for more than 2 years following
its physiological eruption time. Although the prevalence varies from location to location and from tooth to tooth. Third molars
(wisdom teeth) are the most prevalent impacted teeth followed by maxillary canine teeth.

Table 16.3 Classifications of impacted teeth
 S/N     Type of Impaction                         Description
 1       Mesioangular                              Tooth is angled forward, toward the front of the mouth
 2       Distoangular                              Tooth is angled backward, toward the rear of the mouth
 3        Vertical                                 Tooth is upright but fails to erupt fully
 4        Horizontal                               Tooth is lying completely on its side
 5        Buccal or Lingual                        Tooth is tilted toward the cheek (buccal) or tongue (lingual) side

Clinical Presentation
     •    Unerupted tooth                                                 •    Periodontal pocket
     •    Recurrent pain                                                  •    Pericoronitis
     •    Swelling                                                        •    Trismus
     •    Bad arrangement of teeth

Investigations
    •    Periapical X-ray
    •    OPG
    •    CBCT
Non-Pharmacological Management
    •    There are four treatment options for impacted teeth: observation, intervention, relocation and extraction (Disimpaction)
         depending with the classification, symptoms, age and orthodontic needs.
    •    Relocation of impacted tooth/teeth
    •    Relocation (also called orthodontic exposure and traction) is a common and effective procedure used to bring an
         impacted tooth into alignment within the dental arch using orthodontic forces. This is especially common for impacted
         maxillary canines, but may also apply to premolars or incisors.

Disimpaction of impacted tooth/teeth
This is the surgical procedure for removing an impacted tooth that has failed to erupt into its normal position in the dental arch
due to physical barriers like bone, adjacent teeth, soft tissue or developmental anomalies.

Indications for Disimpaction
     •   Pain, pericoronitis (infection around impacted                   •    Development of cysts or tumors (e.g.,
         tooth)                                                                dentigerous cyst)
     •   Recurrent food impaction or decay of adjacent                    •    Functional or esthetic concerns (especially for
         tooth                                                                 anterior teeth)
     •   Periodontal damage to adjacent teeth                             •    Interference with prosthetic work or orthognathic
                                                                               surgery

 Note: Disimpaction can be performed under local anesthesia, sedation or general anesthesia depending with the age,
 severity (multiple impacted teeth, deeply impacted tooth located in close proximity with the vital structures).

Pharmacological Management
 Therapeutic Category    Management
                         A: hydrogen peroxide 3% mouthwash 3–4 times daily, As indicated
 Antiseptic mouthwash           OR
                         A: povidone iodine 0.5% mouthwash 3–4 times daily, As indicated
                                A: diclofenac (IM/IV) 75 mg stat
                                       THEN
                                A: paracetamol (PO) 1 g 8 hourly 3 days
 Analgesics                             OR
                                A: ibuprofen (PO) 400 mg 8 hourly 3 days
                                       OR
                                C: diclofenac (PO) 50 mg 8 hourly 3 days
                                A: amoxicillin (PO) 500 mg 8 hourly 5–7 days
 Systemic antibiotic                   OR
                                B: azithromycin (PO) 500 mg 24 hourly 3 days

 Anti-infective                 A: metronidazole (PO) 400 mg 8 hourly 5 days

sections.title: Bleeding socket
sections.text:
Can be defined as bleeding that continues beyond 8 to 12 hours after dental/tooth extraction. Local causes of bleeding include,
traumatic extraction, bleeding due to disturbing the primary blood clot by the patient through rinsing or inadequate compression
on the gauze. Systemic factors include platelet problems, coagulation disorders or excessive fibrinolysis, and inherited or
acquired problems (medication induced).

Clinical Presentation
     •    Bleeding that continues beyond 12 hours after extraction
     •    Development of a large hematoma or ecchymosis within the oral soft tissues;

Primary Bleeding Socket
    •    Active bleeding from the socket
    •    Patient may be dehydrated and pale if has lost significant amount of blood
    •    Features of decreased pulse rate and volume, hypotension also if patient has lost significant amount of blood

Secondary bleeding
    •   The socket may show features of infection or trauma

Investigations
Depending with the severity of bleeding, patient may need further investigations such as full blood picture, grouping and
compatibility testing and coagulation parameters

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  If the patient is using anticoagulants, discuss with physician for decision to stop or adjust anticoagulants
    •  Depending with the results of the investigations above, patient may be given blood transfusion
    •  Give local anesthesia (lidocaine 2% with epinephrine (adrenaline) 1 in 80,000 IU).
    •  Clear any clot available and examine the socket to identify source of bleeding. Suturing of the wound only when
       necessary (like significantly traumatized gingiva).
    •  Give proper instructions to follow (bite on gauze pack for 30 minutes, not to rinse or eat hot foods on that day at least
       for 12 hours and avoid disturbance to the wound).
Pharmacological Management
C: tranexamic acid (PO) or (IV) 500 mg 8hourly for the first 24hours
          AND
A: paracetamol (PO) 1g 8hourly for 3days
          OR
C: diclofenac (PO) 50mg 8hourly for 3days
          OR
A: ibuprofen (PO) 400mg 8hourly for 3days

sections.title: Infected Socket
sections.text:
A post extraction complication due to infection of the clot due to contamination (infected socket). The condition is painful and if
not managed well could lead to osteomyelitis.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Severe painful socket 2–4days after tooth                         •    Swollen gingiva around the socket
          extraction                                                        •    Sometimes there may be lymphadenopathy and
     •    Fever                                                                  trismus (inability to open the mouth)
     •    Necrotic blood clot in the socket

Investigations
Periapical X-ray of the socket may be necessary when there is limited improvement despite treatment.

Non-Pharmacological Management
Socket debridement under local anesthesia with lidocaine 2% and irrigate with hydrogen peroxide 3% followed with copious
amounts of normal saline. The procedure of irrigation is repeated the 2nd and 3rd day and where necessary can be extended
to the 4th day if pain persists.

Pharmacological Management
Patient is instructed to rinse with
A: hydrogen peroxide 3% mouthwash 3–4 times a day.
          OR
A: povidone iodine 0.5% solution 3–4 times a day.
          AND
A: amoxicillin (PO) 500mg 8hourly for 5–7days
          OR
B: azithromycin (PO) 500mg 24hourly for 3days
          AND
A: metronidazole (PO) 400mg 8hourly for 5days

sections.title: Dry Socket
sections.text:
This is a post extraction complication due to failure to form a clot (dry socket). The condition is very painful, and it differs from
an infected socket by lack of clotting and levels of severity of pain.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Severe pain 2–4 days’ post- extraction
     •    Pain exacerbated by entry of air on the site
     •    Socket devoid of clot
     •    Surrounded by inflamed gingiva

Non-Pharmacological Management
Immediately on diagnosing a communication the tooth should be checked to ensure that it has been completely extracted. The
treatment of OACs varies depending on the size of the opening access. Communications less than 2 mm in diameter can close
spontaneously. Communication larger than 2 mm, require surgical interventions. Techniques for surgical closure include
palatal rotational flaps, palatal transposition flaps, buccal advancement flaps, as well as a combination of buccal and palatal
flaps.

Pharmacological Management
A: metronidazole (PO) 400mg 8hourly for 5days
         AND
B: amoxicillin + clavulanic acid (FDC) (PO) 625mg 12hourly for 7days

sections.title: Edentulism
sections.text:
Is the partial or full loss of natural teeth and subsequent resorption of the alveolar bone.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Sunken facial appearance
     •    Difficulty chewing/ speaking

Investigations
    •    CBCT
    •    OPG X-ray
    •    Peri Apical Dental X-ray
    •    Diagnostic cast

Non-Pharmacological Management
Patient education on maintenance of prosthesis

Non-surgical treatment
    •   Impression for working cast development
    •   Design and fabricate dental prosthesis (partial or complete dentures)

   Note: Dental prosthesis can be partial or complete, and either removable or fixed

sections.title: Denture Stomatitis
sections.text:
An inflammatory condition of the oral mucosa beneath a denture, often due to poor hygiene, fungal infection, or trauma from ill-
fitting dentures.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Red, swollen mucosa beneath the denture
     •    Discomfort or burning sensation
     •    Sometimes asymptomatic

Investigations
Swab for Candida culture (if needed)

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Improve denture hygiene
    •  Instruct patient to remove denture at night

Non-surgical treatment
Professional denture cleaning

Pharmacological Management
A: nystatin oral suspension 100,000 units/mL (PO) rinse every 6hours daily for 7–14 days
          OR
C: miconazole oral gel 2% (topical) apply every 6hours daily after meals

sections.title: Flabby Ridge
sections.text:
Fibrous, mobile soft tissue commonly found in long-term denture wearers.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Unstable denture
     •    Discomfort under denture

Non-Pharmacological Management
Mucosal conditioning

Non-surgical treatment
    •   Modify impression technique (use mucostatic impression materials)
    •   Surgical correction if severe

sections.title: Combination Syndrome
sections.text:
Specific pattern of bone resorption in maxillary edentulous patients opposed by mandibular natural teeth.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Maxillary anterior ridge resorption
     •    Mandibular anterior teeth supra-eruption
     •    Posterior bone loss in mandible

Non-surgical treatment
    •   Balanced occlusion
    •   Fabricate overdenture
    •   Implant-supported denture

sections.title: Burning Mouth Syndrome Related to Prosthesis
sections.text:
Burning sensation in the oral cavity, often associated with denture use in the absence of visible mucosal changes.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Burning, tingling, or scalding pain
     •    Typically affects tongue, lips, palate

Non-Pharmacological Management
Psychosocial support

Non-surgical treatment
Denture adjustment

Pharmacological Management
D: clonazepam (PO)/(Topical)/(IV) 0.25mg - 1mg 8hourly at least for 14days
          OR
A: amitriptyline (PO) 25 – 50mg every night at bedtime at least for 7 days

sections.title: Epulis Fissuratum (Denture-Induced Hyperplasia)
sections.text:
Benign hyperplastic tissue reaction to chronic irritation from ill-fitting denture.

Clinical Presentation
Fold of excess tissue in the vestibule, Irritation or ulceration under denture

Non-surgical treatment
Denture adjustment

Surgical treatment
Surgical excision if lesion persists

Pharmacological Management
A: hydrogen peroxide 3% mouth wash 6hourly for at least for 7days
          OR
B: povidone Iodine (PO) 0.5% solution 8hourly at least for 7days
          OR
B: chlorhexidine gluconate (PO) 0.1% 12hourly at least for 7days
          AND
C: lidocaine + Chlorhexidine gluconate + Metronidazole gel (PO) 8hourly at least for 7days

sections.title: Gingivitis
sections.text:
Gingivitis is an inflammatory process limited to the mucosal epithelial tissue surrounding the cervical portion of the teeth and
the alveolar processes. Gingivitis has been classified by clinical appearance (e.g., ulcerative, hemorrhagic, necrotizing,
purulent), etiology (e.g., drug-induced, hormonal, nutritional, infectious, plaque-induced), and duration (acute, chronic).

sections.title: Chronic gingivitis
sections.text:
The most common type of gingivitis caused by the accumulation of microbial plaques in persons with inadequate oral hygiene.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Gingival redness
     •    Swollen and shiny gingival tissue
     •    Increased tendency of the gingival to bleed on gentle probing or spontaneously, during tooth brushing or even on
          touch and on biting bread and fruits.
     •    Bad breath from the mouth

Non-Pharmacological Management
Proper oral hygiene instruction and counselling.

Non-surgical treatment
Scaling to remove bacterial plaque and calculus with Hydrogen peroxide 3%.

Pharmacological Management
 Therapeutic Category             Management
 Analgesics                       A: paracetamol (PO) 1 g 8-hourly At least 3 days
                                          OR
                                  A: ibuprofen (PO) 400 mg 8-hourly At least 3 days
                                          OR
                                  C: diclofenac (PO) 50 mg 8-hourly At least 3 days
 Antiseptic mouthwash             A: hydrogen peroxide 3% (mouthwash) 6-hourly At least 7 days
                                         OR
                                  A: povidone iodine 0.5% (mouthwash) 8-hourly At least 7 days
                                         OR
                                  B: chlorhexidine gluconate 0.1% (mouthwash) 12-hourly At least 5 days
 Topical oral gel                 C: lidocaine + chlorhexidine gluconate + metronidazole gel (PO) 8-hourly At least 7 days

 Systemic antibiotic              A: amoxicillin (PO) 500 mg 8-hourly At least 7 days
                                         OR
                                  A: erythromycin (PO) 500 mg 8-hourly At least 7 days

sections.title: Acute Necrotizing Ulcerative Gingivitis (ANUG)
sections.text:
It is a painful and severe form of gingivitis, characterized by rapid destruction of gingival tissue, particularly in the interdental
papilla. The condition is often associated with poor oral hygiene, smoking, malnourished children, weakened immune system,
and individuals with debilitated diseases such as Diabetes and HIV/AIDS.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Painful swollen gingiva                                           •    Fever, malaise, and swollen regional lymph
     •    Bleeding gingiva                                                       nodes
     •    Halitosis                                                         •    In some patients (especially malnourished
     •    Gingival Ulcerations covered with Yellow-whitish                       children), ANUG may presents with extensive
          slough                                                                 destruction of the face and jaws in the severe
                                                                                 form known as Cancrum Oris

Non-Pharmacological Management
Proper oral hygiene instruction and counselling

Surgical treatment
Scaling to remove bacterial plaque and calculus with Hydrogen peroxide 3%, under local anesthesia

Pharmacological Management
 Therapeutic Category            Management
 Analgesics                      A: paracetamol (PO) 1 g 8-hourly At least 3 days
                                         OR
                                 A: ibuprofen (PO) 400 mg 8-hourly At least 3 days
                                         OR
                                 C: diclofenac (PO) 50 mg 8-hourly At least 3 days
 Antiseptic mouthwash            A: hydrogen peroxide 3% (mouthwash) 6-hourly At least 7 days
                                         OR
                                 A: povidone iodine 0.5% (mouthwash) 8-hourly At least 7 days
                                         OR
                                 B: chlorhexidine gluconate 0.1% (mouthwash) 12-hourly At least 5 days
 Topical oral gel                C: lidocaine + chlorhexidine gluconate + metronidazole gel (PO) 8-hourly At least 7 days

 Systemic antibiotic             A: amoxicillin (PO) 500 mg 8-hourly At least 7 days
                                        OR
                                 A: erythromycin (PO) 500 mg 8-hourly At least 7 days
 Anti-infective
                                 A: metronidazole (PO) 400 mg 8-hourly At least 7 days

sections.title: Gingival hyperplasia
sections.text:
A condition characterized by an excessive growth of gingiva. The condition can be localized (affecting a specific area) or
generalized (affecting the entire gumline).
This condition can be caused by medications (such as anticonvulsants, immunosuppressants, and calcium channel blockers),
Hormonal Changes (during puberty and pregnancy), and hereditary.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Puffy, swollen gingiva                                           •    Potential difficulty with chewing and speaking
     •    Gums that may partially or completely cover the                  •    Halitosis
          teeth
Non-Pharmacological Management
     •    Oral hygiene instruction and counselling
     •    Address the underlying cause (e.g. changing medications)

Surgical treatment
Gingivectomy
Pharmacological Management
 Therapeutic Category      Management
 Analgesics                A: paracetamol (PO) 1 g 8-hourly At least 3 days
                                   OR
                           A: ibuprofen (PO) 400 mg 8-hourly At least 3 days
                                   OR
                           C: diclofenac (PO) 50 mg 8-hourly At least 3 days
 Antiseptic mouthwash      A: hydrogen peroxide 3% (mouthwash) 6-hourly At least 7 days
                                   OR
                           A: povidone iodine 0.5% (mouthwash) 8-hourly At least 7 days
                                   OR
                           B: chlorhexidine gluconate 0.1% (mouthwash) 12-hourly At least 5 days
 Topical oral gel          C: lidocaine + chlorhexidine gluconate + metronidazole gel (PO) 8-hourly At least 7 days

 Systemic antibiotic             A: amoxicillin (PO) 500 mg 8-hourly At least 7 days
                                        OR
                                 A: erythromycin (PO) 500 mg 8-hourly At least 7 days

sections.title: Desquamative Gingivitis
sections.text:
Clinical term describing red, glazed, and peeling gingiva often linked to systemic conditions (e.g., lichen planus).

Clinical Presentation
Red and painful gingiva, Erosions and sloughing epithelium.

Investigations
Biopsy if needed for diagnosis

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Gentle brushing; use soft bristle tooth brush
    •  Avoid irritants (spicy food, alcohol)

Pharmacological Management
A: hydrogen peroxide 3% mouth wash 6hourly for at least for 5days
          OR
B: povidone Iodine (PO) 0.5% solution 8hourly at least for 5days
          OR
B: chlorhexidine gluconate (PO) 0.1% 12hourly at least for 5days
          AND
C: lidocaine + chlorhexidine gluconate + metronidazole gel (PO) 8hourly at least for 5days
          AND
C: triamcinolone (Topical) 0.5% 8hourly at least for 5 days

sections.title: Periodontitis
sections.text:
Defined as a microbially-associated, host-mediated inflammation that results in loss of periodontal attachment. This includes
destruction of the periodontal ligament and alveolar bone, often accompanied by pocket formation, gingival recession, or both.

sections.title: Periodontitis Levis
sections.text:
A periodontal disease characterized by the slow, progressive loss of the tooth-supporting tissues (periodontal ligament and
bone).

Clinical Presentation
     •    Halitosis                                                      •    Bleeding gingiva
     •    Inflamed gingiva                                               •    Gingival recession

Investigations
    •    CBCT
    •    OPG
    •    Periapical Dental X-ray

Non-Pharmacological Management
Proper oral hygiene instruction and counselling.

Surgical treatment
Scaling and root planning to remove bacterial plaque and calculus with hydrogen peroxide 3%

Pharmacological Management
 Therapeutic Category Management
                      A: hydrogen peroxide 3% mouthwash 6 hourly At least 7 days
                                OR
 Antiseptic mouthwash B: chlorhexidine gluconate 0.1% mouthwash 12 hourly At least 5 days
                                OR
                      B: povidone iodine 0.5% mouthwash 6 hourly At least 7 days
 Topical oral gel     C: lidocaine + chlorhexidine gluconate + metronidazole gel (PO) 8 hourly At least 7 days
                             A: amoxicillin (PO) 500 mg 8 hourly
 Systemic antibiotic                 OR
                             A: doxycycline (PO) 100 mg 12 hourly 5 days
 Anti-infective              A: metronidazole (PO) 400 mg 8 hourly 5 days

sections.title: Periodontitis Gravis
sections.text:
Also known as advanced periodontitis, is a severe form of gum disease where the supporting structures of the teeth are severely
damaged, leading to significant bone loss and potential tooth loss. It's characterized by deep pockets and loose or shifting
teeth.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Halitosis                                                      •    Gingival recession
     •    Malocclusion                                                   •    Pain when chewing
     •    Inflamed gingiva                                               •    Loose or shift teeth
     •    Bleeding gingiva

Investigation
CBCT, OPG X-ray , PA X-ray

Non-Pharmacological Management
Oral hygiene instruction and counselling.

Surgical treatment
    •    Scaling and root planning to remove bacterial plaque and calculus with hydrogen peroxide 3% (Under local
         anesthesia)
    •    Surgical procedure to repair damaged tissues (in advanced cases)
    •    S: Bone graft to restore lost bone (in advanced cases)

Pharmacological Management
 Therapeutic Category Management
 Analgesics           A: paracetamol (PO) 1 g 8 hourly At least 3 days
                             OR
                      A: ibuprofen (PO) 400 mg 8 hourly At least 3 days
                             OR
                      C: diclofenac (PO) 50 mg 8 hourly At least 3 days
 Antiseptic mouthwash A: hydrogen peroxide 3% mouthwash 6 hourly At least 7 days
                             OR
                      B: chlorhexidine gluconate 0.1% mouthwash 12 hourly At least 5 days
                             OR
                      A: povidone iodine 0.5% mouthwash 8 hourly At least 7 days
 Topical oral gel     C: lidocaine + chlorhexidine gluconate + metronidazole gel (PO) 8 hourly At least 7 days
 Systemic antibiotic        A: amoxicillin (PO) 500 mg 8 hourly 7 days
                                  OR
                            A: erythromycin (PO) 500 mg 8 hourly 7 days
                                  OR
                            A: doxycycline (PO) 100 mg 12 hourly 10 days
 Anti-infective             A: metronidazole (PO) 400 mg 8 hourly 7 days

sections.title: Peri-implantitis
sections.text:
Inflammation of the tissues around a dental implant with loss of supporting bone.

Clinical Presentation
Bleeding on probing, Pocket formation around implant, Suppuration, Radiographic bone loss

Non-Pharmacological Management
Oral hygiene instructions

Surgical treatment
Periodontal debridement

Pharmacological Management
 Therapeutic Category Management
                      A: paracetamol (PO) 1 g 8 hourly At least 3 days
                             OR
 Analgesics           A: ibuprofen (PO) 400 mg 8 hourly At least 3 days
                             OR
                      C: diclofenac (PO) 50 mg 8 hourly At least 3 days

sections.title: Dental Abscess (Odontogenic Abscess)
sections.text:
Is a localized collection of pus in the orofacial region secondary to dental caries, deep fillings or failed root canal treatment and
trauma to the jaws and supporting structures as a result of spread of polymicrobial infection.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Fever and chills                                                  •    Intraoral or extraoral Pus discharge
     •    Throbbing pain of the offending tooth                             •    Trismus (inability to open the mouth)
     •    Painful swelling around the orofacial area,                       •    Regional lymph nodes enlargement and tender
          submandibular and neck region

Investigation
    •    OPG or CBCT
    •    Pus swab for Gram stain, culture, and sensitivity.

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Incision and drainage of pus followed by irrigation with hydrogen peroxide 3% and copious amount of sterile saline
       (0.9% Sodium chloride)
    •  Dressing with dry or medicated gauze
    •  Extraction of offending tooth/teeth

Pharmacological Management
A: amoxicillin (PO) 500mg 8hourly for 5days
         AND
A: metronidazole (PO) 400mg 8hourly for 5days.

In severe cases,
B: amoxicillin+ clavulanic acid (FDC) (PO) 625mg 8hourly for 5days
         AND
A: metronidazole (PO) 400mg 8hourly for 5days.

If a patient is allergic to penicillin
A: erythromycin (PO) 500mg 8hourly for 5days

Where parenteral administration of antibiotics is necessary (especially when the patient cannot swallow and has life threatening
infection), consider the following
B: ceftriaxone (IV) 1gm 24 hourly for 5days
           AND
B: metronidazole (IV) 500 mg 8hourly for 5days
           AND
A: gentamicin (IV) 80mg 8hourly for 5days

   Note:
       •     Incision and drainage are mandatory in cases of deeper spaces involvement followed by a course of antibiotics.
             The practice of prescribing antibiotics to patients with abscess and denying referral for definitive care until pus
             has established or resolved has been found to lead to more problems for orofacial infections therefore early
             referral for definitive care is important
        •    Depending on the level of debilitation patient may need admission to the ward for supportive therapy and dressing
             twice per day.

sections.title: Ludwig’s Angina
sections.text:
This is a serious life-threatening generalized septic cellulitis of the fascia spaces found on the floor of the mouth and tongue. It
is an extension of infection from mandibular molar teeth into the floor of the mouth covering the submandibular, sublingual, and
submental spaces bilaterally.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Brawny induration                                                 •    Tissues may become gangrenous with a peculiar
     •    Tissues are swollen, board like, not pitted and no                     lifeless appearance on cutting
          fluctuance                                                        •    Three fascia spaces are involved bilaterally
     •    Respiratory distress                                                   (submandibular, submental, and sublingual)
     •    Dysphagia

Investigations
Routine investigations                                                 Specific investigations
    •     Blood Glucose (Fasting/Random)                                   •     OPG, CBCT, CT Scan
    •     Renal Function Tests                                             •     Chest X-ray
    •     Complete Blood Count (CBC)                                       •     Pus swab for Culture and sensitivity

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Incision and drainage are done (even in absence of pus) to relieve the pressure and allow irrigation
    •  Only when the airway distress is significant and there is evidence that it is not relieved by incision and drainage then
       tracheostomy is needed.
    •  Patient should be admitted for Supportive care During incision and drainage pus should be taken for culture and
       sensitivity. Offending tooth should be removed at the same sitting if the patient can open the mouth.

Pharmacological Management
B: ceftriaxone (IV) 1g 24hourly for 5days
          OR
B: amoxicillin + clavulanic acid (FDC) (PO) 625mg 12-8hourly for 5days
          AND
B: metronidazole (IV) 500mg 8hourly for 5days

If allergic to penicillin use
A: erythromycin (PO) 500mg 6hourly for 5days

Once the patient can swallow, replace IV medication with oral treatment.

 Note: For this condition and other life-threatening oral conditions consultation of available specialists (especially oral and
 maxillofacial surgeons) should go parallel with life saving measures.

sections.title: Osteomyelitis of the Jaw
sections.text:
Osteomyelitis of the jaw is a localized or diffuse infection and inflammation of the bone and bone marrow of the mandible or
maxilla, caused by bacterial invasion, often originating from a dental or periodontal infection, trauma, or surgical procedures.

Clinical Presentation
     •    In the initial stage there is no swelling                        •   Later as the bone undergoes necrosis the area
     •    Malaise and fever                                                    becomes very painful and swollen
     •    Enlargement of regional lymph nodes                              •   Pus ruptures through the periosteum and
     •    Teeth in the affected area become painful and                        discharged outside the skin surface through a
          loose.                                                               sinus
Investigations
     •    OPG                                                              •   CT-Scan
     •    CBCT                                                             •   Pus for culture and sensitivity

Non-Pharmacological Management
Treatment for osteomyelitis involves eliminating the source of infection and necrotic tissue, establishing drainage, restoring
blood supply, and controlling the infection with appropriate antimicrobial therapy.

Pharmacological Management
For acute osteomyelitis of the jaw                                   For chronic osteomyelitis of the jaw which sequestrectomy
S: clindamycin (PO) 150mg 12hourly for 5 days                        has been done
           AND                                                       A: metronidazole (PO) 400mg 8hourly for 5days
A: metronidazole (PO) 400mg 8hourly for 4-6weeks. If                          AND
culture is available treat according to results.                     S: clindamycin (PO) 300mg 8hourly for 5days

sections.title: Cervicofacial necrotizing fasciitis
sections.text:
Necrotizing fasciitis (NF) is a life-threatening polymicrobial soft tissue infection characterized by rapid and progressive
necrotizing process of the subcutaneous tissues, fats and fascial planes, with resulting skin gangrene and systemic toxicity.

Clinical Presentation
     •    Toothache or recent dental infection/extraction                  •   Crepitus (subcutaneous gas) may be felt on
     •    Severe pain out of proportion to clinical findings                   palpation
     •    Swelling and erythema of the face, neck, or                      •   Skin discoloration: dusky, violaceous, or gray
          submandibular area                                                   patches followed by skin breakdown
     •    Fever, malaise, chills, and trismus                              •   Rapid tissue necrosis

Investigations
Refer Ludwig’s angina

Non-Pharmacological Management
Meticulous surgical debridement, meticulous daily wound dressing, and hyperbaric oxygen therapy

Pharmacological Management
Refer Dental Abscess

sections.title: Oral Candidiasis
sections.text:
This is a fungal infection of the oral mucosa caused by Candida infection mainly Candida albicans.

Clinical Presentation
Features of candidiasis are divided according to the types as follows:

Pseudomembranous
    •  White creamy patches/plaque
    •  Cover any portion of mouth but more on tongue, palate, and buccal mucosa
    •  Sometimes may present as erythematous type whereby bright erythematous mucosal lesions with only scattered
       white patches/plaques

Hyperplastic
    •   White patches leukoplakia-like which are not easily rubbed-off.

Non-Pharmacological Management
Assess and correct the predisposing factor

Pharmacological Management
C: miconazole Oral gel 2% (PO) 2hourly

However, in chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis with immunosuppression, topical agents may not be effective. In such
instances systemic administration of fluconazole or itraconazole Is advised.

sections.title: Angular cheilitis (angular stomatitis)
sections.text:
Is a clinical entity characterized by erythema, rhagades, ulcerations, and crusting of one or both lip commissures and peri-labial
skin, responsible of an unpleasant and painful discomfort.
      •    The cause of Angular cheilitis is multifactorial and could range from local etiologies (Reduced or loss of vertical
           dimension of the jaws, Habitual lip licking or picking, Ill-fitting orthodontic appliances) to systemic ones (nutritional
           deficiencies, infection, chemicals).

Clinical Presentations
     •    Angular cheilitis can be either unilateral or bilateral
     •    Soreness, erythema, pain, pruritus, burning sensation and fissuring at the angles of the mouth
     •    Commonly associated with denture stomatitis s but may represent a nutritional deficiency or it may be related to
          orofacial granulomatosis or HIV infection

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Improve the vertical facial height by newer dentures or fillers
    •  Habit cessation,
    •  Proper fitting appliances

Pharmacological Management
When the condition is caused by fungal infection, the following topical formulas can be used
A: nystatin suspension (PO) 100,000IU (1 ml) mixture held in the mouth for at least 3minutes before swallowing, 6hourly
         OR
C: miconazole 2% oral gel apply 12 hourly for 7days

When the condition is caused by bacteria, the following can be used
C: lidocaine + chlorhexidine gluconate + metronidazole gel (PO) 8hourly at least for 7days
Where topical application has failed, or candida infection has been considered severe; use.
A: fluconazole (PO) 150mg 24hourly for 7days
          OR
D: itraconazole (PO) 200mg 24hourly for 7days

  Note: Candidiasis has several risk factors; it is recommended that for HIV/AIDS patients with candidiasis, refer to the
  Tanzania HIV/AIDS Guidelines.

sections.title: Herpes Simplex Virus
sections.text:
This is a viral infection commonly affecting the lips and perioral soft tissues presenting as papulovesicular lesions which
ultimately ulcerate. The primary infection affects mainly the gingiva and palate.

Clinical Presentation
     •    A prodromal of tingling, warmth or itching at the site usually precedes the occurrence
     •    About 12 hours later, redness appears followed by papules and then vesicles
     •    These vesicles then burst, weep, dry, scab and then heal
     •    The length of the cycle is variable 5–12days mean time being 7days

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  Adequate hydration
    •  Avoid salty and acidic drinks
    •  Cover lesions on the lips with Petroleum jelly and control any underlying cause

Pharmacological Management
This is an otherwise self-limiting condition but if persistent for 10days or recurrent infection use medication:

For Herpes Labialis
B: acyclovir cream applies 4hourly for 5days                           For oral facial lesions of herpes zoster treat with
                                                                       B: acyclovir (PO) 400–800mg 6hourly for 14days
For Herpes Stomatitis
B: acyclovir (PO) 200mg 6hourly for 7-10days                           Pain control by analgesics
         AND                                                           A: paracetamol (PO) 1g 8hourly for 7days
B: acyclovir cream 12hourly for 7-10days                                         OR
                                                                       C: diclofenac (PO) 50mg 8hourly for 7days
In immunocompromised patients                                                    OR
B: acyclovir (PO) 400mg 6hourly for 14days                             A: ibuprofen (PO) 400mg 8hourly for 7days

sections.title: Aphthous Ulceration
sections.text:
Aphthous or recurrent aphthous stomatitis (RAS) or recurrent aphthous ulceration (RAU) are painful recurrent mucous
membrane ulcerations. Usually affect the non-keratinized oral mucous membrane. (Buccal, labial, floor of the mouth, soft palate,
ventral surface of the tongue, and alveolar mucosa.

Clinical Presentation
Minor Aphthous Ulcers
     •    Sudden onset, small round or ovoid painful ulcers 2–4 mm in diameter, surrounded by an erythematous halo and
          some edema.
     •    Occurs in groups of only a few ulcers (i.e. 1–6) at a time.

Major Aphthous ulcers
    •   Painful ulcers on non-keratinized oral mucous membrane, they are large 1–3 cm edged ulcers, and several may be
        present simultaneously.

Herpetiform ulcers
    •     These occur in a group of multiple tiny ulcers (<1–3 mm) which can coalesce into larger irregular ulcers which heals
          within 7–10days.
Pharmacological Management
B: chlorhexidine gluconate 0.1% mouthwash used 8hourly                If systemic therapy is required;
for 5days                                                             A: prednisolone (PO) 20mg 8hourly for 3days then dose
          OR                                                          tapered to 10mg 8hourly for 2days then 5mg 8hourly for
A: povidone iodine 1% mouthwash 8hourly for 5days                     other 2 days.
          AND
C: triamcinolone acetonide cream 0.1% apply 12hourly for              Pain control by analgesics
5days                                                                 A: paracetamol (PO) 1g 8hourly for 3days
          OR                                                                    OR
D: dexamethasone oral paste apply 8hourly for 5 days                  C: diclofenac (PO) 50mg 8hourly for 3days

sections.title: Dental implants
sections.text:
Dental implant. Is an artificial tooth root made of compatible metal usually titanium implanted in the jaw bone to replace the
missing single or multiple missing teeth?

Indication for dental Implant(s)
     •   Replacement of a single missing tooth                             •    Support over denture
     •   Replacement of multiple missing teeth                             •    Retention of prosthesis in severely resorbed jaw
                                                                                bone

Further indication for edentulous patient
In a totally edentulous patient with good bone height and width
      •    Mandible 6 implants
      •    Maxillary 6 implants

In severe bone loss
     •   Maxillary 4 implants -tilted
     •   Mandible 4 implants -tilted

A number of 4-6 implants can be used to support a fixed prosthesis usually made of porcelain fused metal (PFM) or Zirconia.
In a compromised or very severely bone loss 2 implants will be used to provide support and retention of removable prosthesis.

Implant surgery procedure
Implant surgery can either be one stage or two stages surgery depending on the bone condition
    •    In aesthetic zone consider temporization
    •    Some bone modifications can be done during implant surgery before implant by using bone grafting materials for
         better outcome.
    •    Patient should well motivated to cooperate during and after implant surgery for maintenance.

Investigation
    •    P.A X-ray                                                         •    CBCT/ Medical CT scan
    •    OPG                                                               •    Cast Models

  Note: Proper review of medical history of patient is mandatory as it exclude medical condition which may interfere with
  implant success. e.g. DM and other medical conditions.

Surgical guide.
They are custom made for each patient. They are used as guides for drilling in the optimum locations implant placement then
removed after placement.

Study cast
Evaluate occlusal centric relation, including any premature occlusal contacts, the relationship of the edentulous area to the
adjacent natural teeth and opposing arches.

Intra-operatively, the following should be observed to have a successful Implant
     •   Assess anatomical variation of vital structures so that implant should not sit or touch vital structures.
     •   Maintain Sterility as interfere with Osseo-integration
Surgical technique
Adequate blood supply (proper incision design and flap reflection. Using sharp gradual series of drill sizes with copious amount
of irrigation by normal saline.

Pharmacological Management
Post implant insertion
A: hydrogen peroxide 3% 6hourly for at least for 5days
         OR
B: chlorhexidine gluconate 0.2% 12hourly at least for 5days
         AND
A: metronidazole (PO) 400mg 8hourly for 7days
         AND
A: amoxicillin (PO) 500mg 8hourly for 7days

sections.title: Traumatic Dental Injuries
sections.text:
It may result in loosening, displacement and or loss of teeth, fracture of teeth and or bone, lacerations, and bleeding. The
commonest causes are falls (in sports and play) at home or school and motor accidents. Most affected are upper incisors.

Clinical Presentation
 Type                Presentation
 Tooth Concussion Is an injury to supporting tissues of tooth, without displacement
 Sublaxation          Is the partial displacement, but is commonly used to describe loosening of a tooth without
                      displacement
 Intrusion            Is the displacement of tooth into its socket often accompanied by fracture of alveolar
                      Bone
 Luxation             Is the displacement of tooth laterally, labially or palatally
 Avulsion             Is the complete loss of tooth from the socket

Soft tissue Injuries Abrasion
Where friction between an object and the surface of the soft tissue causes a wound. This wound is usually superficial, denudes
the epithelium, and occasionally involves deeper layers.

Contusion/Bruising
Indicates that some amount of tissue disruption has occurred within the tissues, which resulted in subcutaneous or sub mucosal
hemorrhage without a break in the soft tissue surface.

Laceration
Is a tear in the epithelial and sub epithelial tissues. They often result from blunt or penetrating injuries due to motor traffic
crashes, assaults, falls, or sports injuries.

sections.title: Facial Bones Injuries
sections.text:
Types of Facial Bone Fractures Include:
    •    Nasal Bone Fractures.
    •    Mandibular Fractures: includes fractures of the body, angle, symphysis, Para symphysis, condyle, and ramus.
    •    Maxillary (Upper Jaw) Fractures: include Le Fort fractures: classified into three patterns based on fracture lines:
              o    Le Fort I: horizontal maxillary fracture (separates maxilla from the palate)
              o    Le Fort II: pyramidal fracture involving nasal bridge, maxilla, and orbital floor
              o    Le Fort III: craniofacial disjunction, separating the entire midface from the skull base.
    •    Zygomatic bone Fractures: Involves the zygomatic bone and/or its articulations with maxilla, frontal bone, temporal
         bone, and sphenoid.
    •    Orbital Fractures: involves either the rims or the walls of the orbit. Common types of wall fractures: orbital floor
         (blowout), medial wall, lateral wall, and roof fractures.
    •    Naso-Orbito-Ethmoid (NOE) Fractures: fractures involving the central upper face. They affect the nasal bones, medial
         orbital walls, and ethmoid bone, and often disrupt the medial canthal ligament and lacrimal system.
    •    Palatal Fractures: Fractures of the hard palate, often associated with maxillary fractures.

1. Initial Assessment & Emergency Management
Follow ATLS principles:
     •     Airway with cervical spine control,
     •     Breathing,
     •     Circulation,
     •     Disability,
     •     Exposure.

Facial fractures demand extra vigilance for airway compromise from bleeding, edema, or bone displacement. The airway can
quickly be secured using nasal/oral airway adjuncts, intubation, or emergency tracheostomy as needed.
A thorough history from the patient is required. In emergency setting, AMPLE mnemonic is used in trauma history to quickly
gather essential information about a patient's medical background during emergency assessment:

     •    A – Allergies: Identify any known drug or food allergies (especially to antibiotics, anesthetics, or latex).
     •    M – Medications: Current prescriptions, over-the-counter drugs, anticoagulants (e.g., warfarin, aspirin), steroids, or
          herbal supplements.
     •    P – Past medical history: Includes significant illnesses (e.g., diabetes, heart disease, seizures), surgeries, previous
          trauma, bleeding disorders.
     •    L – Last meal: Important for anesthesia planning (risk of aspiration); also relevant in surgical timing.
     •    E – Events/environment related to injury: Mechanism of injury (e.g., fall, assault, MVC), use of safety gear (seatbelt,
          helmet), loss of consciousness, alcohol/drug use, environmental exposures (e.g., smoke inhalation).

2. Imaging & Diagnosis
Dental CT (CBCT) or normal CT scans are the standard radiological investigation, especially with suspected midface or complex
fractures; Plain X-rays may be adequate for isolated nasal or mandibular injuries. In case of isolated mandibular fractures OPG
can suffice.

3. Fracture Management
a) Closed Reduction
It is reserved for non-displaced or minimally displaced fractures (e.g., nasal, condylar, pediatric, body of the mandible). Midface
bones (nasal and zygoma) closed reduction is best within 7–10 days in adults, sooner in children. For the mandibular fractures
closed reduction should be carried as soon as possible.
Maxillomandibular fixation (MMF)/intermaxillary fixation (IMF): Establishes occlusion, used in closed or open techniques for
mandible and midface stability. Duration typically 4–8 weeks, or shorter with rigid fixation. Use arch bars, interdental wires, or
bone screws; treatment Modalities

b) Open Reduction and Internal Fixation (ORIF):
Indicated for displaced, unstable, comminuted, or load-bearing fractures (mandible, Le Fort, ZMC). Aim is to achieve anatomical
reduction, occlusion restoration, facial contour.
Utilize titanium miniplates, reconstruction plates, 3D plates, lag screws, biodegradable implants as appropriate.
Choose incision and approach based on location (intraoral for symphysis/body; extraoral like Gillies for zygoma).

  Note: ORIF for fractures of the jaws and midface should be performed by a specialist Oral and Maxillofacial surgeon.

4. Management Principles

Nasal Fractures
    •    Evaluate for septal hematoma; drain within 24 hours.
    •    Closed reduction (manual or instruments) ideally within 5–7 days post-injury in adults, sooner in children.
    •    Use external splints for 7–10 days.

Mandibular Fractures
   •   Non displaced/minimally displaced (e.g. condylar neck): Closed treatment with MMF for 4–6 weeks.
   •   Displaced/body/angle fractures: ORIF with rigid plating; restore occlusion via intraoperative MMF first.
   •   Provide nutritional and oral hygiene support; instruct on MMF care.

Midface Fractures
Le Fort I–III
    •     Indicated for displaced fractures with instability, altered occlusion, or orbital involvement.
    •     ORIF of buttress and orbital rim; MMF for 4-6 weeks.

Zygomatico-Maxillary Complex (ZMC)
    •  Displacement: ORIF via Gillies, intraoral, or transconjunctival approaches.
    •  Fix plate at zygomaticomaxillary buttress and/or frontozygomatic suture.

Orbital Fractures
Symptomatic entrapment or large floor defects: ORIF with titanium mesh or porous polyethylene implants

5. Antibiotics & Infection Prevention and Analgesics
    •    Give prophylactic antibiotics for open fractures or fractures communicating with oral/nasal cavities
         B: amoxicillin (clavulanic acid) 625mg 12hrly for 5 days

    •    Optimal oral hygiene (chlorhexidine rinses, brushing) and nutritional support play key roles in infection reduction.
    •    For pain control: Start with strong analgesics (e. g Tramadol (PO), Pethidine (IV) (if admitted)) for first 24hrs to 36
         hours, then moderate analgesics (paracetamol (PO) or ibuprofen (PO)) until when the patient is free from pain.

6. Postoperative Care & Rehabilitation
     •   Use light pressure dressings to reduce edema; remove after 2–5 days.
     •   Monitor overnight for bleeding, airway issues, vomiting.
     •   Regular follow-ups: 5–7 days (sutures), every 2 weeks, and at 6–8 weeks for MMF removal if used.
     •   Gradually reintroduce diet from liquids to soft and then normal consistencies after removal of MMF.

7. Site-Specific Considerations
     •   Nasal fractures: Watch for septal hematomas—drain urgently to avoid deformity. Closed reduction within days yields
         favorable cosmetic results; remodeling may occur in children.
     •   Mandibular fractures: Favor ORIF for most load-bearing body and angle fractures; reserve closed reduction for
         minimally displaced, pediatric, condylar neck, comminuted, or atrophic cases.
     •   ZMC fractures: Surgery needed for displaced fractures—restore projection and orbital volume. Miniplates/screws via
         Gillies or similar approaches.
     •   Le Fort and midface: ORIF with MMF to restore buttresses and occlusion.
     •   Pediatric considerations: Prefer conservative treatment for nasal, condylar, and NOE fractures unless displaced.
         Surgical intervention (ORIF) indicated in displaced NOE type II–III. Growth concerns may necessitate revisional
         procedures later.
     •   Comminuted fractures in atrophic or edentulous mandibles: Consider reconstruction plate with load bearing
         properties.
     •   Patients with coagulation disorders: Coordinate with hematology; ensure optimized clotting profile preoperatively.

Pharmacological Management
Pain control by analgesics
A: paracetamol (PO) 1g 8hourly for 3days
          OR
C: diclofenac (PO) 50mg 8hourly for 3days
          OR
A: ibuprofen (PO) 400mg 8hourly for 3days

Prophylactic antibiotics are indicated in cases of suspected contamination or extensive damage
B: ampicillin + cloxacillin (FDC) (PO) 500mg 8hourly for 5days

sections.title: Tumours and Tumour-Like Conditions of Oral Cavity and Facial Region
Benign Odontogenic Tumors
sections.text:
Each tumour presents with different cardinal features clinically, radiologically and on histopathological diagnosis.
Ameloblastoma

Clinical Presentation
          •   Recognized between ages of 10 to 80                              •    Loosening of teeth, with roots resorption
              years80% form in the mandible and 70%                            •    Gradual facial asymmetry due to
              develop in the posterior molar region and                             enlargement and destruction of bone
              often involve the ramus                                          •    Ping pong and/or bone cracking effects
          •   Painless, slow growing tumor that may be
              solid or cystic

Investigations
Radiographically, the tumour presents with multilocular radiolucency, honeycomb, or soap bubble appearance.

 Note: Diagnostic confirmation of this tumour is through histopathology. Complete excision e.g. e.g. marginal resection,
 segmental resection plus bone grafting and partial or total resection of the jaw is the treatment of choice. Hence refer the
 patient to the center where there is oral and maxillofacial surgeon

sections.title: Calcifying odontogenic tumor
sections.text:
Clinical Presentation
          •   Most often found in the mandibular molar/premolar region, but 33% of cases are found in the maxilla
          •   It is associated with an unerupted or impacted tooth in 50% of cases

Investigations
         •   Radiographically these lesions can be radiolucent, but more characteristically are mixed lucent and opaque
             masses, exhibiting a snow-driven appearance

Non-Pharmacological Management
       •   Complete excision of the tumour with border of normal bone should be curative, but curettage or incomplete
           excision has high recurrence rates.

sections.title: Amelobastic Fibroma
sections.text:
Clinical Presentation
          •   Slower growing tumor than the simple ameloblastoma and does not infiltrate between bone trabeculae.
          •   Occurs during the first two decades of life
          •   75% of ameloblastic fibromas are found in the posterior mandible in the area of a developing tooth. It is benign
              and expansile, growing as a pushing front rather than invading surrounding tissues

Investigations
         •   Radiographically this lesion appears as a uniocular or bilocular radiolucency, most often in the posterior
             mandible.
         •   The radiographic appearance is identical to that of unicystic ameloblastoma, and both lesions should be
             differential diagnoses because they affect similar age groups and have similar clinical and radiographic
             appearances. Histologic examination differentiates the two.

Non-Pharmacological Management
       •   Enucleation and curettage and extraction of associated teeth is usually adequate for small tumours. For big
           tumours conservative resection may be required, where necessary to be followed with reconstruction.

sections.title: Adenomatoid odontogenic Tumors (AOT) Clinical Presentation.
sections.text:
•    Usually occur in the second and third decades
         •    Usually encountered incidentally
         •    It has a female predilection
         •    Two thirds of the cases occur in the anterior maxilla, one third occur in the anterior mandible, and it is never
              found posterior to the premolars
         •    Two thirds of the cases are associated with an impacted tooth (usually the cuspid) Present with mild swelling or
              in association with a clinically missing tooth

Investigations
Radiographically this lesion generally appears as a well-demarcated radiolucency. In 75% of cases, it is associated with an
unerupted tooth, usually the canine. It may contain radiopaque flecks, which represent calcified material.

Non-Pharmacological Management
Enucleation is curative and recurrence is almost unknown.

sections.title: Odontogenic Myxoma
sections.text:
Clinical Presentation
          •   Occurs mostly in the second to fourth decades of life
          •   Clinically indistinguishable from ameloblastoma, but on aspiration while ameloblastoma yields
          •   straw-colored or yellow fluid Odontogenic myxoma may not yield anything due to the thick mucoid clear
              contents of the tumour.
          •   The radiographic appearance; typically, it has honeycomb appearance, although
          •   It often appears quite like ameloblastoma e.g multilocular radiolucency

Investigations
OPG, CBCT, Tissue biopsy (Confirmation is through histopathology)

Non-Pharmacological Management
Wide surgical excision Similar approach to the treatment of ameloblastoma. It has a high recurrence rate if not completely
removed.

sections.title: Cemento-ossious lesions
sections.text:
These are groups of benign fibro-osseous lesions that affect the jawbones, particularly the tooth-bearing areas. These lesions
involve replacement of normal bone with fibrous tissue that contains varying amounts of mineralized material (bone, cementum,
or both).

Clinical Presentation
     •    Commonly occurring in the posterior region of the mandible,
     •    Occurs mainly in females of African origin aged between 40 and 50 years.

Three main types:
a) Periapical
b) Focal and
c) Florid.
     •     Periapical type is usually seen in the anterior mandible,
     •     Focal type is usually involving single teeth in the posterior mandible
     •     Florid type is seen all quadrants but mainly in the posterior part of the mandible.
     •     Generally symptomless and are incidentally diagnosed during routine radiographic examinations.

Investigations
Radiographically ranging from radioluscencies, mixed radioluscent-radioopaque, and completely radiopaque lesions.

Non-Pharmacological Management
    •  They are only treated when they produce symptoms, interfere with other dental treatments or when infected.
    •  When surgery is indicated, complete enucleation is necessary.

Pharmacological Management
Management is similar to chronic osteomyelitis above

sections.title: Odontoma (Compound and Complex)
sections.text:
This is a developmental malformation made up of enamel, dentin, cementum, and pulp (odontogenic tissues) and is considered a
hamartoma. It is the most common odontogenic tumours.
Clinical Presentation
     •    Normally discovered incidentally during routine dental examinations or radiographs
     •    Missing eruption of the permanent tooth
     •    They can occur anywhere in the jaws but mainly in the anterior maxilla (compound) and posterior mandible (complex).
     •    Vary in size but can grow to huge lesions

Investigation
  •    Periapical X-ray, OPG, CBCT
  •    Generally, the lesions appear radiopaque with compound type appears as a collection of tooth-like structures, whereas the
       complex type appears as a disorganized mass of dental tissues.

Management
Surgical (Enucleation)

sections.title: Pregnancy Tumours (also called pyogenic granuloma)
sections.text:
Clinical Presentation
  •    Not a true tumour, but rather a rapid over growth of tissue in response to local irritation.
  •    They most commonly appear after first trimester, grow rapidly, and typically regress after delivery.
  •    Found on the gingiva mainly in between the teeth. Occasionally can occur on the tongue, lips and palate.
  •    They are exophytic, lobulated, or smooth surfaced lesion with a red to purplish color and a soft, spongy texture and easily
       bleed

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •  Surgical intervention is often not required. However, pregnancy tumors can be removed during the second trimester if they
     interfere with occlusion, are painful, bleed excessively, or are excessively large. Lesions excised during pregnancy often
     recur.
  •  After delivery, pregnancy tumors typically recede spontaneously but excision may be necessary for those cases which
     persist.

 Note: Other non- odontogenic tumors are Osteomas, Myxomas, Chondromas, Central giant cell and Fibro-osteoma.

sections.title: Head and Neck Vascular lesions (Vascular anomalies)
sections.text:
These are a group of disorders involving abnormal development or growth of blood vessels (arteries, veins, capillaries) or
lymphatic vessels. Classified into two main groups hemangiomas and vascular malformations

Clinical Presentation
 S/N Feature                    Hemangioma                                  Vascular Malformation
 1      Time of                 Present at birth; most diagnosed by 1       Present at birth but often not diagnosed until second
        Presentation            year of age                                 decade
 2      Growth Pattern          Rapid growth up to 6–8 months, then         Slow growth throughout life; increases with
                                slows and involutes by 5–9 years            infection, trauma, or hormonal changes; does not
                                                                            involute
 3      Pathophysiology         Neoplastic growth with increased            Growth due to abnormal flow dynamics and
                                endothelial cell turnover                   recruitment of collateral vessels
 4      Osseous                 Rare                                        Common (~35%)
        Involvement
 5      Sex Distribution        Female-to-male ratio ≈ 5:1                  Female-to-male ratio ≈ 2:1
