        Characteristics                                                     high-flow (arterial or arteriovenous)

Investigations:
  •    US ultrasound,
  •    CDUS color Doppler ultrasound,
  •    MRI magnetic resonance imaging

Management
Currently, various medical and surgical options are available for the treatment of hemangiomas. In Tanzania we recommend
Intralesional bleomycin injections (IL-Bleo) under Ultrasound guidance as the management of choice of head and neck
hemangiomas.

Refer to the algorithm below.

sections.title: Oral squamous cell carcinoma
sections.text:
Clinical Presentation
  •    A sore in the mouth that does                                    •      Persistent white or red patch on the tongue,
       not heal (most common                                                   gums, tonsils, or lining of the mouth.
       symptom).                                                        •      Difficult moving jaw or tongue.
  •    Pain in the mouth.                                               •      Difficult chewing or swallowing.
  •    Persistent lump or thickening of                                 •      Enlarged cervical lymph nodes may be present
       mucosa in the cheek.
  Note: Take a tissue biopsy of the lesion and send for histopathology investigation or refer the patient as early as possible
  to a center where there is oral and maxillofacial surgeon and Histopathology unit.

Management
   •   Depending on the stage of tumor, management include; wide tumour excision (stage I, II, and III) and neck dissection
       followed by radiotherapy or chemotherapy.
   •   For stage IV tumor; depending with general condition of the patient, management may range from palliative
       chemotherapy or radiotherapy or radio-chemotherapy.

sections.title: Oral Kaposi’s Sarcoma
sections.text:
Oral Kaposi’s Sarcoma (OKS) is a malignant angioproliferative tumour of endothelial origin involving the oral cavity. It is
caused by infection with Human Herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8).
It commonly occurs in the context of advanced HIV-related immunodepression and may represent the first manifestation of
HIV infection.

Clinical Presentation
  •    slow- to fast-growing masses
  •    May appear as ecchymotic patches, nodular, and exophytic lesions presenting a color that can vary
       from dark reddish to purplish blue
  •    Most frequently affected intra-oral sites are the hard-palatal mucosa and the gingiva
  •    Size of the lesions varies from few millimeters to some centimeters and the growing of multiple
       lesions could lead to large, confluent masses involving an entire area of the oral cavity

Management.
Local surgery and highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) are considered keystones in the management of epidemic KS

  Note: For detailed management of KS please refer to the malignancy on chapter twenty-two

sections.title: Lymphomas
sections.text:
These are group of neoplasms of varying degrees of malignancy which are derived from B-cells of lymphoid tissues, the
lymphocytes and histiocytes in any of their developmental stages.
While lymphoma primarily affects lymph nodes, it can also occur in non-lymph node tissue (tonsils, parotid gland, thyroid gland,
tongue, paranasal sinuses, and nasal cavity), this is known as extra nodal lymphoma

Lymphoma is classified as Hodgkin lymphoma and non-Hodgkin lymphoma.
Both types of Lymphoma have similar symptoms which may include but not limited to painless swelling of lymph nodes, fever,
Night sweats, Unexplained weight loss, and fatigue

Burkitt’s lymphoma (African Jaw Lymphoma)
Burkitt lymphoma is an aggressive non-Hodgkin B-cell lymphoma characterized by rapid tumor growth, frequently affecting the
jaw, abdomen, or central nervous system associated with Epstein-Barr virus (EBV).
Three clinical subtypes: endemic, sporadic, and immunodeficiency-related. The endemic form, common in Africa, is linked to
malaria and EBV,

Clinical Presentation
  •    Confined almost exclusively to children between 2–14years of age.
  •    Rapidly growing tumor mass of the jaws, destroying the bone and causing teeth loosening with
       extension the maxillary, ethmoid and sphenoid sinuses as well as the orbit.
  •    Visceral organ involvement may occur.

sections.title: Malignant Salivary glands tumours
sections.text:
These are malignancies arising from major salivary glands (parotid gland, submandibular gland, sublingual gland) and minor
salivary glands of the upper aerodigestive tract.
The most common malignant salivary glands tumours include mucoepidermoid carcinoma (MEC), acinic cell carcinoma (ACC),
adenoid cystic carcinoma (AdCC), carcinoma ex-pleomorphic adenoma (CExPA), and adenocarcinoma.

Clinical Presentation.
  •    Asymptomatic, firm mass with occasional pain and facial paralysis
  •    Some presents with ulceration

Investigations
  •    Ultrasound is the first non-                                    •    Magnetic resonance imaging
       invasive option for evaluating                                       (MRI)
       major salivary gland tumors                                     •    Fine needle aspiration cytology
  •    Computerized tomography                                              (FNAC)
       (CT)                                                            •    Open tissue biopsy

Management
Mainstay treatment of salivary gland malignancies is surgery (wide tumour excision and neck dissection) followed by adjuvant
chemotherapy and/or radiotherapy.

  Note: Diagnostic confirmation is through histopathology; hence, it is emphasized to do early detection and referral to all
  patients suspected to have head and neck malignancies. (For detailed management of malignant tumors please refer to the
  malignancy on chapter twenty-two)

sections.title: Odontogenic and Non- Odontogenic Cysts
sections.text:
Odontogenic cysts
 •   A group of jaw cysts that are formed from tissues involved in odontogenesis (tooth development).
 •   Odontogenic cysts are closed sacs filled with fluid, and have a distinct membrane derived from rests
     of odontogenic epithelium.

Non-odontogenic jaw cysts
  •  A group of cysts arising from epithelial remnants of embryonic ducts left behind after embryonal facial and jaw
     development; they are located deep within the tissues in the region of former epithelial ridges, epithelial walls, and
     primary facial fissural and cleft structures.
  •  Some few examples of frequently encountered cysts in the orofacial region are:

sections.title: Dentigerous cyst
sections.text:
Dentigerous cysts, also called follicular cysts, are slow-growing benign and non-inflammatory odontogenic cysts that are
thought to be developmental in origin.

Clinical Presentation
  •    Uninfected dentigerous cysts are painless and non - tender on palpation.
  •    Larger cysts cause a marked, smooth, rounded expansion of the bone, which may be reduced to a thin layer of cortical
       plate.

Investigations
Radiographically, they usually present as a well-defined and unilocular radiolucency surrounding the crown of an unerupted or
impacted tooth within the mandible.

sections.title: Radicular (Apical) cyst
sections.text:
Radicular cyst is an inflammatory jaw cyst originating from epithelial remnants of the periodontal ligament because of
inflammation that is generally a consequence of pulp necrosis.
The resulting cyst commonly involves the apex of the affected tooth either by dental caries or trauma.

Investigations
  •    Take OPG or Skull X-ray, the cysts appear as rounded, radiolucent areas sharply demarcated from normal.
  •    Apical periodontal cysts are associated with the roots of dead teeth bone by a thin, radiopaque, limiting line of compact
       or cortical bone.

Non Pharmacological Management
Dental cystectomy under local or general anesthesia.

sections.title: Globulomaxillary cyst
sections.text:
The globulomaxillary cyst is a cyst that appears between a maxillary lateral incisor and the adjacent canine. It often causes the
roots of adjacent teeth to diverge.

Investigations
It exhibits as an "inverted pear-shaped radiolucency" on radiographs, or X-ray films.

Non-Pharmacological Management
Dental cystectomy under local or general anesthesia.

sections.title: Dermoid Cyst
sections.text:
Dermoid cysts are rare masses of the oral cavity derived from ectodermal elements. They are benign, slow-growing tumors that
are typically asymptomatic but cause complications of inflammation or dysphagia, dystonia, and airway encroachment due to
mass effects.

Clinical Presentation
  •    Massive swelling of the floor of the mouth, which had displaced the tongue cranially.
  •    Painless slowly growing cystic lesion in the sublingual and or submental spaces.
  •    A dentigerous cyst may be suspected where a tooth is missing from the arch without any history of
       previous extraction.

Non-Pharmacological Management
Enucleation through an external approach below the mandible or intraorally though an incision in the floor of the mouth.

sections.title: Ranula Cyst
sections.text:
A mucous extravasation cyst involving a sublingual gland and is a type of mucocele found on the floor of the mouth.

Clinical Presentation
  •    Translucent, blue, dome-shaped, fluctuant swelling in the tissues of the floor of the mouth.
  •    The swelling is not fixed, may not show blanching, and is non-painful unless it becomes secondarily infected.
  •    The usual location is lateral to the midline, which may be used to help distinguish it from a midline
       dermoid cyst.

Non-Pharmacological Management
Excision of sublingual salivary gland which is affected.

sections.title: Management of Oral Conditions during Pregnancy
sections.text:
The oral changes which are seen in pregnancy include gingivitis, gingival hyperplasia, pyogenic granuloma, and salivary
changes.
Gastric acid secretion and the reflux of the acid into the oral cavity leads to worsening of enamel erosion, increased caries risk,
increased tooth mobility and loss.

For the first trimester (1-12weeks)
During the first trimester, it is recommended that the patients be scheduled to assess their current dental health, to inform them
of the changes that they should expect during their pregnancies, and to discuss on how to avoid maternal dental problems that
may arise from these changes.

Recommendations
  •  Educate the patients about the maternal oral changes which occur during pregnancy. Emphasize strict oral hygiene
     instructions and thereby, plaque control.
  •  Limit dental treatment to a periodontal prophylaxis, normal filling, and emergency treatments only.
  •  Avoid routine radiographs.
  •  They should be used selectively and only whenever they are needed.

For the second trimester (13-24weeks)
  •    During the second trimester, the organogenesis is complete, and the risk to the fetus is low.
  •    The mother has also had time to adjust to her pregnancy, and the fetus has not grown to a potentially uncomfortable
       size that would make it difficult for the mother to remain still for long periods.

Recommendations
  •  Maintenance of oral hygiene and plaque control.
  •  It’s safe to perform scaling, polishing and curettage if necessary.
  •  Active oral diseases should be controlled.
  •  It’s safe to perform elective procedures i.e. Root canal, extraction, restorations.
  •  Avoid routine radiographs. Use selectively and when they are needed.

For the third trimester (25-40weeks)
The fetal growth continues and the focus of the concern now, is the risk to the upcoming birth process and the safety and
comfort of the pregnant woman. It is safe to perform a routine dental treatment in the early part of the 3rd trimester.

Recommendations
  •  Maintenance of oral hygiene and plaque control.
  •  It’s safe to perform scaling, polishing and curettage if necessary.
  •  Active oral diseases should be controlled.
  •  It’s safe to perform elective procedures.
  •  The radiograph use should be minimized.
  •  Procedures should not to be performed after mid time of the third trimester, unless it is emergency
     or life threatening condition

 Note: Pregnancy should not be considered as an absolute reason to deny required dental care. Pregnant patients must be
 educated about the importance of maintaining good oral hygiene, expected changes in the oral cavity and routine dental
 visits.

sections.title: Temporal Mandibular Disorder and Chronic Orofacial Pain
sections.text:
Temporomandibular disorders (TMD) are disorders of the jaw muscles, temporomandibular joints, and the nerves associated
with chronic facial pain.

sections.title: Temporomandibular Disorders (TMDs)
sections.text:
A collective term embracing several clinical problems that involve the masticatory musculature, the temporomandibular joint
and associated structures, or both.

Clinical Presentation
  •    Facial pain.
  •    Limitation of jaw motion.
  •    Clicking on the joint site
  •    Muscle tenderness and stiffness.
  •    Along with any number of associated symptoms in the head, face, and neck region.

Investigations
  •    Plain X-ray of involved joint/ joints.
  •    Panoramic X-ray
  •    CBCT or CT scan
  •    Diagnostic arthroscopy (Intervention Radiology)

Non-Pharmacological Management

Reassurance and counseling
Provide counseling to the patient on the natural history and course of temporomandibular disorders, the role of stress and
parafunctional habits such as clenching and grinding of the teeth, the frequency of the problem in the population, and the self-
limited nature of the disorder.

Heat application
Application of heat to the sides of the face with a heating pad, hot towel, or hot-water bottle. Vigorous treatment may be achieved
with ultrasound or short-wave diathermy heat treatments, which are widely available in physiotherapy units.

Fabrication of Intraoral Occlusal Orthotic Appliances
These devices are worn on the teeth like a retainer or a removable denture and are usually made of processed, hard acrylic.

Physiotherapy
Perform manual manipulation, massage, and ultrasonography, which are helpful in reconditioning and retraining the masticatory
and the other cranio-cervical muscles that are usually involved in temporomandibular disorders.

Arthrocentesis
Under Local anesthesia TMJ joint lavage is done through cutaneous needle puncture using 25 to 60ml of lactate Ringer Solution
with or without intraarticular injection.

Pharmacological Management
A: amitriptyline (PO) 25mg nocte for 1month.
          AND/OR
A: ibuprofen (PO) 400mg stat then 200mg 8hourly 7-14days
            OR
C: diclofenac sodium (PO) 50mg 8hourly for 7-14days
            OR
D: meloxicam (PO) 7.5-15mg 12hourly-24hourly for 7-14days

 Note: Consider concomitant use of gastro protective treatment in patients with preexistent history of peptic ulcers or when
 giving NSAIDs for a duration of 2 weeks or more

Intra articular injection
D: methylprednisolone (Intra articular) 40mg/ml per day repeat every after 2-12 weeks, maximum of 4injections per year for a
duration of 2years.
          OR
S: triamcinolone (Intra articular) and 40mg/ml per day repeat every after 2-12 weeks, maximum of 4injections per year for a
duration of 2years.
          OR
D: betamethasone (Intra articular) 12mg/ml 6mg/ml for small joints per day repeat every after 2-12 weeks, maximum of
4injections per year for a duration of 2years.
          AND
A: lidocaine 1% (Intra articular) 1-2mls.
          AND
S: hyaluronic acid (Intra articular)16mg once per week for 3 consecutive weeks

Supplements
S: glucosamine sulfate1500mg +chondroitin sulfate 1200mg (FDC) (PO) taken with meal once a day for 3-6months

Surgical management for advanced disease
  •   TMJ Arthroplasty
  •   Total joint replacement

sections.title: Temporomandibular Joint (TMJ) Dislocation.
sections.text:
TMJ dislocation occurs when the mandibular condyle moves out of its normal position in the glenoid fossa of the temporal bone,
typically anterior to the articular eminence. It can be unilateral or bilateral and is often painful and distressing for the patient.

Clinical Presentation
  •    Inability to close the mouth
  •    Pain in the preauricular area
  •    Difficulty speaking and swallowing
  •    Facial asymmetry (especially in unilateral dislocations)
  •    Mouth stuck in an open position
  •    Palpable depression in the preauricular area
  •    Condyle displaced anteriorly and inferiorly

Investigations
  •    Clinical diagnosis based on history and physical examination
  •    Plain X-rays (Panoramic or Lateral TMJ view): may help confirm dislocation

Management
 •   Acute Anterior TMJ Dislocation:
 •   Manual Reduction (Hippocratic technique)
 •   Patient seated with head supported
 •   Provider stands in front, places thumbs over the lower molars (with gauze padding) and fingers
     under the mandible
 •   Downward and posterior pressure applied to guide the condyle back into place
 •   Use sedation (e.g., midazolam, diazepam) or local anesthetic if needed to overcome muscle spasm

Post-reduction care
  •    Apply a soft bandage (Barton bandage) to limit mouth opening
  •    Advise soft diet for 1–2 weeks
  •    Avoid wide mouth opening (yawning, dental procedures)

  Note: for chronic TMJ dislocation, or unattended dislocation for more than two weeks, refer the patient to maxillofacial
  surgeon for surgical reduction.

sections.title: Chronic Orofacial Pain other than Temporomandibular Disorders
sections.text:
16.31.3.1Trigeminal Neuralgia
A sudden, usually unilateral, severe, brief, stabbing, recurrent pain in the distribution of one or more branches of the fifth cranial
nerve.
Clinical Presentation
  •    Episodes of severe, shooting, or stabbing pain                     •    Pain in areas supplied by the trigeminal nerve,
       that may feel like an electric shock.                                   including the cheek, jaw, teeth, gums, lips, or less
  •    Spontaneous attacks of pain triggered by things                         often the eye and forehead.
       such as touching the face, chewing, speaking, or                   •    Pain affecting one side of the face at a time
       brushing teeth.

sections.title: Persistent Idiopathic Orofacial Pain (a Typical Facial Pain, a Typical Odontalgia)
sections.text:
A persistent facial pain that does not have the characteristics of the cranial neuralgias and is not attributed to another disorder.

Clinical Presentation
  •    Poorly localized deep pain that does not follow                    •    There is a female preponderance in the third to
       anatomically defined patterns.                                          fourth decades.
  •    Patients may have had multiple dental treatments
       to try and remove the pain.

Investigation
  •    Thorough clinical history and examination
  •    Take radiographs of the dentition preferable OPG

Non-Pharmacological Management
Irreversible or invasive procedures should not be undertaken on teeth to try and relieve the pain if the clinical picture, vitality
testing or radiographic examination would not support the procedure.

Pharmacological Management
A: amitriptyline (PO) 25mg nocte 24hourly for 1month. (Dosage can be adjusted up to 75mg in 24hrs.)
          AND
A: carbamazepine (PO) 200mg 24hourly for 1month.Dosage can be adjusted up to 1200mg at the same frequency and duration.

sections.text: For details management of these two conditions, refer a chapter for disease of musculoskeletal system

sections.title: Management of Cleft Lip and Palate
sections.text:
A cleft lip is a birth defect where the upper lip fails to form completely, creating a gap that may extend into the nose. It can occur
on one side (unilateral) or both sides (bilateral) and may appear as a small notch or a wide opening.
A cleft palate occurs when the tissues that form the roof of the mouth (palate) do not fully come together during fetal
development. This results in an opening that can affect the hard palate (the bony front portion) and/or the soft palate (the soft
back portion) of the mouth. Cleft palates can occur with or without a cleft lip

chapters.intro:
These include diseases and disorders that affect the teeth, gums, and supporting structures of the mouth. They involve medical
disorders that affect the jaw (maxilla and mandible), face, and related structures, such as sinuses, salivary glands, muscles,
nerves, blood vessels and temporomandibular joint (TMJ). These conditions may be congenital, traumatic, infectious,
neoplastic, or degenerative in nature.
Before doing oral examination or any dental procedures, patients should gurgle with hydrogen peroxide 3% or povidone iodine
0.5% or chlorhexidine gluconate 0.1% to minimize infectious agent’s contamination between patient and oral health care
provider.

sections.title: Osteomyelitis
sections.text:
Osteomyelitis is an infection of the bone or bone marrow caused by pyogenic bacteria or mycobacteria or fungi. This condition
is most common in children under 12 years. Staphylococci aureus are the most frequent responsible organisms. In patients
with sickle cell disease Salmonella species become more common pathogens than in healthy hosts. Can be classified as acute
or chronic depending on duration of symptoms.

sections.title: Acute osteomyelitis
sections.text:
Clinical Presentation
  •    Fever, malaise severe pain at the site of infection, fatigue, irritability, restriction of movement (pseudo paralysis of limb
       in neonates) local edema, erythema, and tenderness
  •    A history of recent trauma, surgery, or infection of another organ If the infection is close to a joint there may be a
       ‘sympathetic’ effusion or concomitant septic arthritis.

   Note: Risk Factor: Poor social economic status, immunosuppression and malnutrition

Investigations

  •    Erythrocyte sedimentation Rate                                          case like Kingella kingae species
  •    C-Reactive protein                                                 •    Bone Scan using Technetium –99in acute
  •    Urinalysis                                                              infection

  •    Blood for culture and Sensitivity                                  •    Plain X – ray

       sensitivity                                                             shoulder, pelvic, spine
  •    Bone and or deep tissues for Culture and

  •  Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) for special case like Kingella kingae species

Surgical treatment
Surgical drainage and bone drilling or window recommended in all cases presenting with history lasting > 24 hours,

sections.title: Septic Arthritis
sections.text:
Inflammation of a synovial membrane with purulent effusion into the joint capsule, often due to bacterial infection, but can be
caused by fungi and mycobacteria species. If not treated within 24 to 48hours may cause irreversible joint erosion, septicemia
and can even be fatal.

Clinical Presentation
As for acute osteomyelitis however this time sign and symptoms will be localized around the affected joint (refers Kocher’s
criteria in standard text book for clinical diagnosis)

Pharmacological Management
Treat like acute osteomyelitis

Surgical drainage
  •   Open surgery – incision and drainage followed by meticulous irrigation
  •   Arthroscopic joint drainage, debridement and washout with copious amount of normal saline

sections.title: Gonococcal Arthritis
sections.text:
Pharmacological Management
A: benzylpenicillin (IV) 2.5–5 MU 6hourly for 7days
          AND
D: ceftriaxone + Sulbactam (IV) 1.5g 24hourly for 7days
           OR
S: cefepime (IV) 2g 12hourly for 7days
  Note
     •    Adjust treatment basing on culture and sensitivity results.
     •    Repeat serial CRP, FBP, ESR starting 48hrs after initiation of appropriate treatment until
          normalize

Surgical drainage
  •   Open surgery- i.e., incision, drainage and irrigation with copious amount of Saline
  •   Arthroscopic joint drainage, debridement and joint washout with copious amount of normal saline

sections.title: Fracture related infections (FRI)
sections.text:
This is a surgical site infection post-surgical treatment of fracture. It occurs more frequent in open fractures, can be early or late
infection and can occur in unhealed or healed fracture

Clinical Presentation of FRIs
  •    Pain                                                               •    Signs-sinus, effusion, wound
  •    Loss of ROM                                                             erythema
  •    Swelling                                                           •    X rays –periosteal reaction,
  •    Local warmth                                                            subchondral bone resorption

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •  Rest and splintage of affected                                       •    Addressing the predisposing
     joint for 48hrs                                                           condition
  •  Nutritional support                                                  •    Physiotherapy to improve
                                                                               range of motion of nearby joint

Pharmacological Management
Should be guided by results of culture and sensitivity, but initially broad-spectrum antibiotic.
C: amoxicillin + clavulanic acid (FDC)(IV)1.2g12hourly until the result for C/S are out then change accordingly.

Stage 1: Extensive surgical debridement, remove metal implant and replace with external fixation, traction or orthotics, use
antibiotic beads/ antibiotic impregnated bone cement to deliver high concentration of local antibiotics

Stage2: Revision surgery once CRP and other inflammatory marker become negative

sections.title: Tropical Pyomyositis
sections.text:
This is a condition whereby there is pyogenic infection of large muscle/muscles with extensive necrosis of the involved muscle.
This condition occurs more commonly in the tropics, affecting immunocompromised individual than normal individual. The cause
is uncertain since abscess multiple pockets explored early are sterile but later culture of the pus usually yields Staphylococcus
aureus.

Clinical Presentation
Fever and painful induration/fluctuation of one or more of the large muscles, mostly in the lower extremities

Investigations
  •    Complete blood count (CBC)                                        •   Ultrasound
  •    Erythrocyte sedimentation rate                                    •   Plain X-ray
       (ESR                                                              •   Muscle biopsy for culture and
  •    C–Reactive Protein test (CRP)                                         sensitivity

High level facilities treatment should be guided C/S results

          OR

          OR

          OR
S: clindamycin (IV) 600mg 8hourly for 7days
          OR
S: vancomycin (IV) 1g 12hourly for 7days

Surgical treatment
Incision and drainage and irrigation with copious amount of saline

sections.title: Heterotopic Ossification
sections.text:
Heterotopic ossification is defined as bone formation in non-osseous tissues. Usually occurs in trauma such as fractures and
surgical procedures, the exact cause remains unknown.

Clinical Presentation
  •    Pain and reduced ROM following trauma or post-surgical intervention.
  •    Swelling and tenderness, which can mimic a low – grade infection.
  •    Bone in soft tissue starts to appear on plain radiographs 4 to 6weeks after the trauma/surgery

Pharmacological Management
A: indomethacin (PO) 75-150mg per day in single daily dose or divided dose 12hrly
         OR
A: ibuprofen (PO) 200 – 400mg 8hourly

Post-surgical treatment
A: indomethacin (PO) 75mg to 150mg 24hourly for 6 weeks to prevent recurrence

Surgical treatment
  •   Surgery is delayed for 6 months after the initial trauma/surgery to allow the bone to mature and a
      distinct fibrous capsule to develop.
  •   Provide low dose radiotherapy Post surgery

sections.title: Tendinopathies
sections.text:
These are clinical syndrome characterized by chronic, localized tendon pain exacerbated by mechanical loading. Caused
mostly by tendon overuse and metabolic factors. Classified as Acute or Chronic.

Clinical Presentation
  •    Pain with palpation of the affected part
  •    Kinetic chain changes (muscle weakness, abnormal movement patterns or joint stiffness)
  •    Pain during tendon loading which may be also referred pain.
  •    Muscle spasm

Investigations
  •    MRI for tendinopathy involving deep tendon like around the shoulder joint
  •    Ultrasound scan (grey scale or colour Doppler USS)
  •    Plain X-ray

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •  Physiotherapy (active exercise, stretching)                      •    Reduction of aggravating activities
  •  Activity modification                                            •    Ice, heat (chronic tendinopathy)
  •  Correction of any biomechanical faults
  •  Joint mobilization and friction(massage).

Pharmacological Management
Pain management in acute state as needed

          OR

          OR

          OR
D: tramadol 37.5mg + paracetamol 325mg (PO) 8hourly for7-14days
          OR
A: paracetamol 500mg+ ibuprofen 400mg (PO) 8hourly for 7-14days

Topical analgesics can be added in combination with oral medications in cases of severe pain,
A: diclofenac gel applies 12hourly
          OR
S: ketoprofen gel apply12hourly

For patient with gastritis or peptic ulcer disease use Proton pump inhibitors in combination with above medications
A: omeprazole 20mg 24 hourly for 2 weeks or more
          OR
C: pantoprazole 40 mg 24 hourly for 2 weeks or more

Corticosteroid Therapy
A: prednisolone (PO) 40mg 24 hourly for 3 days then taper down over 2-4weeks
          OR

of 2years.
          OR

of 1-3 weeks between injections.
          OR

Surgery
When no improvement after 6 months of combined physiotherapy and medical treatment. Open surgery or arthroscopic surgery
surgical debridement, and or tendon transfer can be done.

sections.title: Osteoporosis and Brittle Bone Diseases
sections.text:
Disease which is characterized by low bone mass, microtextural disruption and skeletal fragility and it has no clinical
manifestation until there is a fracture. Contrary to Brittle bone disease which are inheritable with many different phenotypic
presentations, however medication for the treatment of these two diseases are more or less similar.

Clinical Presentation
  •    Bone pain
  •    Presence of fragility fracture (spine, hip, wrist, humerus, ribs and pelvis)
  •    Family history of osteoporotic fracture

Investigations
  •    Complete blood count
  •    Dual-energy X-ray Absorptiometry (DEXA) to measure spine and hip bone density as reference
       point
  •    Serum25-hydroxyvitaminD,
  •    Serum Calcium

Diagnostic criteria
Table 17.1 T-score chart based on the mineral density measurement by DEXA. Osteoporosis is diagnosed when a
person’s BMD is equal to or more than 2.5 standard deviations below this reference measurement.
 Status                                    Hip BMD
 Normal                                    T- score of-1 or above
 Osteopenia                                T-score lower than -1 and greater than-2.5
 Osteoporosis                              T-score of - 2.5 or lower
 Severe osteoporosis                       T-score of - 2.5 or lower, and presence of at least one fragility fracture

Non-Pharmacological Managements
  •  Fall prevention.
  •  Diet containing Calcium and vitamin D.
  •  Exercise

sections.title: Condition which may require Amputation.
sections.text:
Amputation is the surgical removal of part of a limb or extremity such as an arm, leg, foot, hand, toe, or finger. This is the
treatment of choice for diseased limbs and devastating extremity injuries for which attempts at salvage and reconstruction may
be lengthy, emotionally, and financially costly and have a less than satisfactory results.

Clinical indication
  •    Trauma most common reason                                         •   Metabolic disease
       for extremity amputation                                          •   Tumor
  •    Vascular disease                                                  •   Congenital anomalies
  •    Infection

Goals of amputation
 •    Preserve functional length                                         •   Prevention of symptomatic neuromas
 •    Prevention of adjacent joint contractures                          •   Early return of patient to work and recreation
 •    Preservation of useful sensibility
 •    Early prosthetic fitting

sections.title: Diabetic Foot Ulcers
sections.text:
A common surgical complication in diabetic patients. Ulcers can be secondarily infected by staphylococci, streptococci,
coliforms, and anaerobic bacteria which can lead to cellulitis, abscess formation, gangrene, and osteomyelitis.

Clinical Presentation
The three main factors that lead to tissue necrosis in the diabetic foot:-
  •    Neuropathy
  •    Infection
  •    Ischemia

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •  Metabolic control
  •  Relieve pressure: non-weight bearing mocking cessation is essential.
  •  Wound care
  •  Frequent (e.g., weekly) removal of excess keratin and allow efficient drainage of the lesion.

Pharmacological Management
D: ceftriaxone + sulbactam (IV) 12hourly for 7-10days
          AND
B: metronidazole (IV)500mg 8hourly for 7-10days

Change antibiotics depending on culture results
S: piperacillin + tazobactam (IV) 4.5g 6-8 hourly 7-14days (for severe/complicated cases)
         OR
S: meropenem (IV) 1g 8 hourly 7-14 days

Surgical treatment
  •   Surgical debridement
  •   Amputation depending Wagner’s classification

Table17:3 Wagener’s Classification for Diabetic Foot Ulcers

 GRADE1                                Superficial ulcer
 GRADE2                                Deep ulcer, no bony involvement or abscess
 GRADE3                                Abscess with bony involvement (as shown by X- ray)
 GRADE4                                Localized gangrene e.g. toe, heel etc
 GRADE5                                Extensive gangrene involving the whole foot
 Note: Grade1-3ulcers are termed non – gangrenous ulcers and Grade 4 and 5 ulcers are termed gangrenous ulcers

sections.title: Common Congenital Anomalies of Musculoskeletal System
Talipes equinovarus (congenital clubfoot)
sections.text:
Talipes equinovarus is one of the most common musculoskeletal birth defects affecting approx. 1/1,000 live births. If untreated
it causes long-term functional disability. The condition can vary in its degree of severity ranging from quite mild to very severe.
It may present with other defects such as spina bifida, arthrogryposis multiplex congenita, congenital myotonic dystrophy, or
diastrophic dysplasia.

Clinical Presentation

Birth deformities of the foot with
  •     Small foot and calf
  •     Cavus (tight intrinsic muscles)
  •     Adductus of forefoot (tight tibialis posterior)
  •     Varus (tight tendo Achilles, tibialis posterior, tibialis anterior)
  •     Equinus (tight tendoachilles)

Investigations
  •   Most clinical diagnosis
  •   Plain X-ray

Management
Non operative management – Ponseti method of serial manipulation and casting,
  •   The goal is to rotate foot laterally around a fixed talus.
  •   Order of correction follows acronym (CAVE) 1. Cavus 2. Adductus 3. Varus 4. Equinus.
  •   Heel cord tenotomy needed in at least 80-90% of children followed by Foot abduction orthosis
      (FAO) until the child is 4 years old.
  •   Non noncompliance to FAO is the biggest risk factor for deformity recurrence

sections.title: Rickets
sections.text:
Refers to softening and weakening of bones in children, usually due to vitamin D deficiency. Vitamin D promotes the body’s
absorption of calcium and phosphorus. Extreme or prolonged lack of vitamin D makes it difficult to maintain proper calcium and
phosphorus levels in bones, which can cause rickets.

Types of Rickets                                                    Differential diagnosis
  •   Nutritional rickets                                             •    Blounts disease
  •   Vitamin D dependent rickets                                     •    Hypophosphatemia
  •   Vitamin D Resistant Rickets                                     •    Metaphysealy dysplesia
      - Type I
      - Type II

  •    Congenital rickets

Clinical Presentation                                               Investigations
  •    Delayed growth                                                 •    Alkaline Phosphatase
  •    Bowlegs (varus deformity)                                      •    Serum Calcium
  •    Knock knees (valgus deformity)                                 •    Serum Phosphorus
  •    Windswept deformities                                          •    X rays of the deformed part
  •    Weakness and pain in the
       spine, pelvis and leg

Management
Vitamin D supplements
Surgical management
   •   Growth modulation like hemi epiphysiodesis
   •   Corrective osteotomies around the knee
   •   Gradual correction with TSF

sections.title: Physiological Bowing/Knocked Knees
sections.text:
Is considered bending of knees at an early age due to early walking and overweight below the age of 2 years

Diagnosis process
  •   Diagnosis is mainly by physical examination–obvious varus/valgus deformity and metaphysical
      widening.
  •   Blood tests to measure the levels of calcium and phosphate in the blood (Refer to table17.2)
  •   Bone X-rays to check for bone deformities.

Management
 •   First consultation: rule out if it’s physiological – bow legs at young age before the age of 3 years
     without signs of rickets
 •   If it is physiological then consider follow up every 6 months +/- vitamin D supplements
 •   At the age of 3 years if deformity more than 8 degrees consider Surgical treatment like – hemi
     epiphysiodesis at around the age of 3years if the deformity is due to Blount’s disease consider
     hemi epiphysiodesis/corrective osteotomy.

sections.title: General Management of Trauma and Injuries
sections.text:
Trauma may occur because of motor vehicle crashes, fights, falls, gunshots, sports, animal bites etc. and is associated with
head, musculoskeletal, visceral, and neurovascular injuries. The aim of managing trauma is to prevent further injuries and life-
threatening complications that may lead to increased morbidity and mortality. There is a systematic trauma protocol in place,
ABCDE protocol, emphasizing on the primary survey, resuscitation, secondary survey, and finally definitive care.

Clinical Presentation
  •    There is a history of trauma
  •    Level of consciousness
  •    ABCDE

sections.title: Timing and algorithms of Polytrauma Management.
sections.text:
Polytrauma patients are the ones with two or more significant system injuries, including life threatening injury (severe, moderate
head, chest, or abdomen injury).

The priorities in trauma care are treating the lethal injury first (damage control) then reassess and treat again having the
following objectives:                                                   The steps in management are:
   •    life salvage                                                      •    Primary survey
   •    limb salvage                                                      •    Resuscitation
   •                                                                      •    Secondary survey
   •    salvage of total function if                                      •    Definitive care
        possible

Figure18.1 Algorithm in managing a polytrauma patient

Massive transfusion protocol
Massive transfusion protocols are activated by a clinician in response to massive bleeding. Generally, this is activated after
transfusion of 4-10units. MTPs have a predefined ratio of RBCs, FFP/cryoprecipitate, and platelets units (random donor
platelets) in each pack (e.g., 1:1:1 or 2:1:1 ratio) for transfusion.

Figure 18.2: Clinical flowchart/infographic of a Massive Transfusion Protocol (MTP) used in emergency care for
patients with severe or life-threatening bleeding.

sections.title: Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI)
sections.text:
TBI is defined as an alteration in brain function, or other evidence of brain pathology, caused by an external force. TBI is a
leading cause of death and permanent disability worldwide. Primary brain injury occurs at time of trauma (e.g., cortical
contusions, brain lacerations, diffuse axonal injury) while secondary injury develops following the initial insult (brain edema,
hypoxemia, ischemia due to elevated intracranial pressure). TBI is often associated with ophthalmic, ENT, dental and
maxillofacial injuries.

Clinical Presentation
  •    History and/or clinical evidence of blunt or penetrating trauma to the head
  •    Transient or sustained alteration in level of consciousness s
  •    Other evidence of altered brain function i.e., seizures, amnesia, focal deficits

Clinical classification of TBI
  •     Perform the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) to assess clinical severity of TBI across care paths. (see
        below)
  •     Report each component of GCS; Eye, Verbal, and Mo tor response, e.g., E4V4M5, not just the total
        score.
  •     If a GCS component is untestable due to intubation, sedation, etc., record the reason.

Neurosurgical Interventions for TBI
  •   Refer for emergency neurosurgical evaluation all patients with epidural hematomas (EDH), subdural hematomas

sections.title: Spinal Cord Injury (SCI)
sections.text:
Acute spinal cord injury (SCI) refers to disturbances to patients normal sensory, motor, or autonomic function resulting from
trauma. Following the initial insult, up to 25% of spinal cord injuries is thought to occur not at the time of the initial trauma but
later during treatment or transport. SCI management, therefore, should be multidisciplinary incorporating appropriate
prehospital services, Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS) protocols, prompt neurosurgical interventions, and timely
rehabilitation.

sections.text:
Table 18.9: Classification of Thoracic Injuries
Injury to the chest/thorax are generally divided into blunt and penetrating can involve multiple areas of the chest/thorax including

                                                                • Clavicle fracture
                                                                • Sternal fracture

                                                                • Pneumomediastinum

Clinical Presentation:
Chest pain and shortness of breath, Difficulty in breathing, Dyspnea and tachypnea.

Investigations
  •    ABO Grouping and cross-matching
  •    FBP
  •    Blood Urea Nitrogen and Creatinine
  •    Electrolytes
  •    PT, PTT, INR
  •    Lactate levels and Blood Gases
  •    Fast USS, eFAST
  •    Chest X-ray and CT scan chest

Management
Resuscitation:
  •  Maintain ABCs.
  •  Maintain airway, stabilize the cervical spine
  •  Give oxygen, If O2 sat below 92%, If dyspneic, Low O2 saturation with reduced or absent air entry,
     suspect pneumothorax/hemothorax
  •  If tension pneumothorax is suspected, needle decompression is performed followed by chest tube
     insertion +UWSD
  •  IV Fluids:
     Give
     A: sodium chloride 0.9% or compound sodium lactate. (Adult 2000mls and Pediatrics 20ml/kg).

Give Blood
  •    If severe pallor, ongoing bleeding, Hb<5 and Hb<7 (with active bleeding in trauma)
  •    Adults 2units within 1hour and pediatric 20ml/kg 1hour (whole blood) or 10ml/kg (pRBC)
  •    If ongoing indication for blood, start massive transfusion in the following ratio: 1-unit pRBCs (20ml/kg in Pediatrics): 1-
       unit FFP (20mls/kg in Pediatrics): 1-unit PLT (20ml/kg in Pediatrics)

Pharmacological Management
Pain Management and Sedation
D: paracetamol (IV) 1g stat in Pediatrics 15mg/kg stat.

In Severe Pain
C: morphine (IM) 5-10mg stat
          OR
B: pethidine (IV) 50-100mg stat +/- Low dose ketamine for additional sedative effect (0.3mg/kg)

In contaminated wounds
B: ceftriaxone (IV) 1g stat
          AND
B: metronidazole (IV) 500mg stat

 Note
   •  Almost all penetrating injuries will need thoracic surgeon review and intervention with ICU
      admission.
   •  Mild blunt chest injuries can be admitted in the ward for monitoring before discharge

sections.title: Abdominal Trauma
sections.text:
Unrecognized abdominal injury remains a frequent cause of preventable death after trauma.
The initial evaluation in abdominal trauma patient must include the primary and secondary survey There are two basic
categories of abdominal trauma:
  •    Penetrating trauma where surgical consultation is important e.g. Gunshot, stabbing.
  •    Non-penetrating trauma e.g., compression, crush, seat belt, acceleration/deceleration injuries.

Investigations
  •    FAST/eFAST
  •    Pelvic X-ray FBP
  •    Diagnostic peritoneal lavage.
  •    Blood grouping and x-match
  •    Abdominal CT scan for stable patient
  •    CXR

Management
 •   Goal of acute management is to stabilize the patient and to determine need for urgent laparotomy
 •   An exploratory laparotomy may be the best definitive procedure if abdominal injury needs to be excluded

Absolute indications for surgery
  •   Hemodynamic instability
  •   CXR with free air
  •   Peritonitis or drainage of fecal contents
  •   Evisceration of bowels

Pharmacological Management
D: paracetamol (IV) 1g 8hourly for 24hours
         OR
C: morphine (IV) 10mg 6hourly for 24hours

sections.title: Soft Tissue Injuries
sections.text:
Clinical Presentation
  •    Pain only, traumatic swelling, bruises with intact skin, cuts, abrasions, puncture wounds or open wounds of varying
       size and severity
  •    Injury to internal organs must be recognized and referred, including subtle signs of organ damage, e.g.;-
         - blood in the urine – kidney or bladder damage
         - shock – internal bleeding
         - blood or serous drainage from the ear or nose – skull base fracture
  •    An injury causing a sprain or strain may be initially overlooked. Exclude fractures by performing appropriate X-rays

   Note:
     •   Closed injuries and fractures of long bones may be serious and damage blood vessels
     •   Contamination with dirt and soil complicates the outcome of treatment

Emergency management
 •   Immobilize injured limb after reduction by POP cast or splint
 •   Monitor vital signs
 •   Monitor the arterial pulse and capillary refill below an injury on the limb with swelling.

Wound care
 •   Surgical debridement of the wound
 •   Suture or splint when needed
 •   Avoid primary suture if the wound is infected:
      - Dirty or contaminated
      - Crushed
      - In need of debridement
      - Projectile inflicted
      - Caused by bites

Pharmacological Management
A: paracetamol (PO) 15mg/kg 6hourly in 24 hours
          OR
A: diclofenac (IM/IV) 75mg 12hourly (if can’t tolerate oral medication)
          AND
B: ceftriaxone 1g (IV) 12hourly 3days.
          AND
B: metronidazole (IV) 500mg 8hourly for 3days.
          AND
A: tetanus prophylaxis: 0.5mL Tetanus Vaccine and 1mL Tetanus immunoglobulin (Depending on the immunization protocol)

Topical medication
C: mupirocin gel 1.3% patch –apply one patch on the affected area 12hourly for 2weeks.

sections.title: Dislocations
sections.text:
A dislocation is complete and persistent separation of two or more bones that form a joint with part of the supporting joint
capsule and some of its ligaments are disrupted. Dislocations can be congenital or acquired. In subluxation, the bones in a joint
are partly out of position. Traumatic dislocations are orthopedic emergency.

Management
 •   It’s an orthopedic emergency
 •   Closed reduction, under conscious sedation or general anesthesia
 •   Open reduction if closed reduction fails
 •   Chronic dislocation
 •   Surgical open reduction and fixation of underlying cause

Recurrent dislocation:
Arthroscopic or open surgical stabilization of the joint

                                                                AND
                                         A: tetanus immunoglobulin (TIG) (IM) 250IU single dose or as above regime
                                         same for pediatric above 7years
                                                               Add:
                                         A: benzathine benzylpenicillin (IV) 2–4MU 4hourly for 3days (when suspicious
                                         with
                                         clostridium species)

 Surgical management
 NOTE: Type 1 – 2 in our setting can be       Debridement of the wound and the fracture site, removing all devitalized tissue
 managed by medical doctors /general          present, should happen within 6-24hours, repeat debridement every 24-48 hours
 surgeon with basic principles of trauma      as needed.

 Type 3A and 3B can be managed by             individualized.
 orthopedics alone, 3B requires plastics      Soft tissue coverage should happen within 72hours, or as guided by plastic

sections.title: Peripheral vascular injury
sections.text:
Injury to peripheral arteries, which can compromise viability of the limb and is life threatening. Accounts for approximately 80%
of all vascular injuries. It is a surgical emergency.
Causes:
   •     Penetrating injury (Gun short injuries, Open                    •    Dislocation of major joint, i.e knee joint
         fractures type IIIC)                                            •    Crush injuries
   •     High energy injuries, i.e motor cycle /vehicle
         accidents

Clinical Presentation
  •    Observed pulsatile bleeding                                     •    Signs of distal ischemia with comprehensive
  •    Arterial thrill (i.e, vibration) by manual palpation                 neurovascular assessment
  •    Bruit over or near the artery on auscultation                   •    Visible expanding hematoma

Investigations
  •    x-ray                                                           •    Ankle brachial index
  •    CT angiography                                                  •    Baseline investigations; CBC, blood grouping,
  •    CT scan                                                              renal function tests

Management
Multidisciplinary approach
 •      Cross match and prepare blood (4 to 8 units)
 •      Recanalization using Forgaty catheter
 •      Vascular repair, such as end to end anastomosis, segmental reconstruction/ replacement of entire
        segment

sections.title: Pelvic and acetabular fractures
sections.text:
Fractures of the pelvis typically resulting from high energy blunt trauma although fail and elderly patients may sustain injuries
from low energy mechanism, and the injuries ranges from benign to life threatening. Hemorrhage is the leading cause of death
overall.
Associated injuries
   •    Chest injury                                                    •    Urological injuries
   •    Long bone fractures                                             •    Head and abdominal injuries
   •    Spine fractures

Classified depending on the direction of force causing the injury
  •    Anterior-posterior compression
  •    Lateral compression
  •    Vertical shear

Clinical Presentation
  •    Pain                                                            •    Flank hematoma
  •    Shock                                                           •    Laceration of perineum
  •    Inability to bear weight.                                       •    Degloving injuries
  •    Limb length discrepancy with                                    •    Scrotal, labial or perineal
       possible rotation of one or both                                     hematomas
       extremities.

Investigations
  •    FBP, grouping Cross-matching
  •    Chemistry panel
  •    Radiography
        - Pelvic X- ray AP, and JUDET VIEWS
        - trauma series radiography whenever necessary (Cervical, Chest and Pelvis)
        - Abdominal pelvic USS
        - CT (contrast enhanced)
        - Pelvic angiography in case of persistent shock or suspected vascular injuries
        - Cystography
        - MRI
        - Retrograde urethrogram

Management
Start with ABCDE Trauma Protocol irrespective of the level of facility

Non-Pharmacological Management

At Community/dispensary level/health Centre level
  •   Immobilize pelvic fracture with Pelvic binder/ bed sheet
  •   Monitor vital signs.
  •   Monitorthearterialpulseandcapillaryrefillbelowaninjuryonthelimbwithswelling

Refer patients with pelvic fractures upon resuscitation. The referring professional should inform the destination hospital (by
phone) of the impending transfer and in non-emergencies a referral letter summarizing signs and symptoms and initial
management should be sent with the patient.

Definitive treatment at hospital level

Non-Operative treatment
  •  BLS/ATLS protocol
  •  Secure Air way with cervical spine control, ABCD (AMPLE protocol)
  •  Resuscitation
  •  DVT Prophylaxis

Give,
  •   A: diclofenac (IM/IV) 75mg stat, then continue with ibuprofen (PO) OR Paracetamol (PO) when
      required
  •   Pelvic binder/sheet
  •   Bed rest.
  •   Weight bearing as tolerated (for stable fractures)

Operative treatment.
 •    Anterior subcutaneous pelvic fixator (ANFIX)
 •    External fixator
 •    Pelvis reconstruction surgery with Plates and /or Screws
 •    Diverting colostomy (in open pelvic fractures)
 •    Acetabular reconstruction surgery for acetabular injuries

sections.title: Supracondylar Fracture
sections.text:
This fracture occurs just above the two condyles of the distal humerus, commonly seen between 5- 10 years. Can be extension
type (95%) or flexion type (5%). Further classified by Gartland as type I, II and III in order of severity of injury.

Clinical Presentation
  •    History of injury,                                                •   Bony crepitus,
  •    Swelling,                                                         •   Deformity,
  •    Subcutaneous ecchymosis,                                          •   Tenderness around the elbow,
  •    Pain,                                                             •   May include loss of sensation and loss of pulse to
  •    Limited range of motion,                                              the forearm if accompanied with nerve or vascular
                                                                             injury.

Investigation
  •    Plain x-ray (AP & amp; L)
  •    Doppler ultra sound if suspecting vascular injury
  •    CT scan for complex fractures
  •    CT angiography for complex fracture with vascular injury.

Management
Follow trauma management protocol for prehospital, primary facility and hospital

Table18.14 Definitive management
 Type                                            Management
 Gartland’s Type-I and Type-IIA                  - Closed manipulation and reduction under general anesthesia or deep
                                                 sedation.
                                                 - Maintenance of reduction with a plaster slab or arm cast and sling for three
                                                 weeks. Confirm reduction by X-ray. Start physiotherapy after three weeks
 Gartland’s Type-IIB and Type-III                Close reduction under image intensifier and percutaneous pinning with
                                                 Kirschner. Keep K wires for three weeks, start physiotherapy as soon as
                                                 pain permit
 Gatland type I to III with vascular injury or   Open reduction and internal fixation using ‘Kirschner Wires, keep K wires for
 open wound or failed close reduction            three weeks, start physiotherapy as soon as pain permit

  Note:
    •   Patients with gross swelling at the elbow, poor skin condition with contusion and blistering,
        vascular insufficiency should be kept on skin or skeletal traction before close definitive
        management unless they warrant emergency surgical intervention
    •   Skeletal traction: A Kirschner -wire is passed through the olecranon process and an overhead
        traction is applied

sections.title: Epiphysial injuries
sections.text:
Fractures involving the epiphyseal plate at the end of the long bone of a growing child. Classified by Salter Harris classification
into 5 types based on fracture line
Clinical Presentation
   •    History of injury,                                              •    Bony crepitus,
   •    Swelling,                                                       •    Deformity,
   •    Subcutaneous ecchymosis,                                        •    Tenderness around the affected joint,
   •    Pain,                                                           •    May include loss of sensation and loss of pulse
   •    Limited range of motion,                                             below the affected joint if accompanied with nerve
                                                                             or vascular injury.

Investigations
Plain radiography, CT Scan, MRI.

Table18.15: Definitive management
       Type                Fracture pattern or radiological image                                   Management
 Salter-Harris I     Fracture line through Physis only, can be minimally     Closed manipulation and reduction under general
                     or grossly displaced                                    anesthesia or deep sedation. Maintenance of
                                                                             reduction with a plaster slab or cast confirm reduction
                                                                             by X-ray
 Salter-Harris II    Fracture line through Physis + metaphysis with          Closed reduction and casting
                     triangular fragment extending to metaphyseal area                 OR
                     (Thurston-Holland sign)                                 Closed reduction and percutaneous screw or wire
                                                                             fixation
                                                                                       OR
                                                                             Screw for larger metaphyseal fragment
                                                                                       OR
                                                                             Wires crossing physis for smaller metaphyseal
                                                                             fragment
 Salter-Harris III   Fracture line through Physis + Epiphysis. CT scan       Closed reduction and casting
                     may be needed to evaluate articular displacement                  OR
                                                                             Close reduction under image intensifier/open
                                                                             reduction, screw fixation. Screw along width of
                                                                             epiphysis avoiding physis
 Salter-Harris IV    Fracture line through Epiphysis, physis, and            Close reduction under image intensifier/open
                     metaphysis                                              reduction to facilitate anatomical reduction of physis
                                                                             to minimize risk of physeal bar. Fixation best
                                                                             accomplished from epiphysis to epiphysis and/or
                                                                             metaphysis to metaphysis
