                     require comparison X-ray or CT scan or MRI

  Note
  Fracture of upper extremities and lower limb requires arm sling after reduction and protective walking with crutches,
  respectively. Immobilize for three to six weeks while assessing sign of healing by imaging.

sections.title: Compartment syndrome
sections.text:
Is condition which follow trauma/ repeated strenuous activities causing micro trauma resulting into elevation of the interstitial
pressure in a closed Osseo fascial compartment that results in microvascular compromise. Can be acute or chronic.

Clinical Presentation
  •    History of Trauma or repeated extensive exercises
  •    Severe pain at rest with any movement, especially passive stretching of the muscles.
  •    Pain out of proportion to original injury should raise suspicion.
  •    Paresthesia
  •    Late stage Pallor, Pulselessness and Poikilothermia

Investigations
  •    Urine myoglobin                                                 •    Complete Blood Count
  •    Urinalysis                                                      •    Coagulation studies
  •    X-ray                                                           •    Creatine phosphokinase (CPK)
  •    Ultrasound,                                                     •    Serum creatinine
  •    CT,                                                             •    Serum electrolyte
  •    MRI
  •    Measure compartment pressure (Using
       Tonometer/fiberoptic transducer /Simple
       needle/Wick Catheter/Slit catheter)

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •  Remove Bandages and casts
  •  Elevate the affected limb to the level of the heart
  •  Nutritional support
  •  Early rehabilitation to minimize complications

Pharmacological Management
  •  Facilitate renal clearance of myoglobin (aim urine output at 1 – 2 mL/kg/hr)
  •  Infuse intravenous fluids at 500 mL/hr. 0.9% sodium chloride or sodium lactate compound (ringer’s
     lactate)crystalloid solution
  •  Consider 22.4m Eq sodium bicarbonate to alkalinize urine
  •  Hemoglobin and myoglobin are more soluble in an alkaline solution.

Antibiotics
B: ampicillin + cloxacillin (FDC) (IV) 1–2g 8hourly for 3days
          OR
S: clindamycin (IV) 600mg 8hourly for 3days
          AND

Analgesics
A: diclofenac (IM/IV)75mg 12hourly 24-72hours
          OR
B: pethidine (IV)100mg 6hourly for 24-72hours
          OR
B: tramadol (IM/IV) 50-100mg 8hourly for 24-72hours
Change to oral medication as soon as a patient can tolerate

Prophylaxis medication
Anti-venoms for snake or insect bite and tetanus immunoglobulin and toxoid in case of animal bite or penetrating trauma

Surgical–fasciotomy
  •   Compartment pressures >30mmHg, is an indication for fasciotomy
  •   Perform single or two incisions are made to release intra-compartmental pressure depending on
      the site
  •   Wounds are often closed by skin grafting.

  Note
    •  Acute compartment syndrome is a surgical emergency which requires surgical
       management within 6-8hours, patient diagnosed in primary health care facilities should be
       referred immediately.
    •  The referring professional should inform the destination hospital (by phone) of the
       impending transfer.

sections.title: Diabetes Mellitus
sections.text:
Diabetes mellitus is a clinical syndrome characterized by persistently high blood glucose values due to deficiency or diminished
effectiveness of insulin.

Classification
Diabetes mellitus can be classified as follows:
  •    Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (T1DM) – due to autoimmune β-cell destruction
  •    Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM) – due to a progressive loss of β-cell insulin secretion frequently
       with underlying insulin resistance
  •    Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM) – diabetes diagnosed at any time of pregnancy that was not
       clearly overt diabetes prior to gestation
  •    Specific types of diabetes – due to other causes e.g., MODY, LADA, diseases of the exocrine
       pancreas, endocrinopathies and drugs or chemicals.

Clinical Presentation
  •    Main clinical features of diabetes are thirst, polydipsia, polyuria, tiredness, loss of weight, blurring of vision.
  •    Many people have no classical symptoms and may only present late with the symptoms related to complications e.g.,
       pruritus vulvae and balanitis due to infections, paresthesia or pain in the limbs, non-healing ulcers, and recurrent
       bacterial infections.

WHO diagnostic Criteria 2011
 •   Fasting plasma glucose level ≥ 7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dL)
 •   Plasma glucose≥ 11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL) two hours after a 75 g oral glucose load in a glucose tolerance test
 •   Symptoms of hyperglycemia and random plasma glucose ≥11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL)
 •   Glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) ≥ 6.5%.

 Note: HbA1c is not reliable in individuals with hemoglobinopathies (sickle cell anemia, thalassemia) other types of anemia and
 other conditions affecting red blood cell lifespan.

sections.title: Diabetes Mellitus in Pregnancy
sections.text:
Women in early pregnancy with levels of HbA1c≥6.5% or blood glucose levels fasting ≥7.0 mmol/l or two hours ≥11.1 mmol/l
which are diagnostic of diabetes should be treated as having pre-existing diabetes (type 1 or type2).

The diagnosis of gestational diabetes mellitus after 15weeks pregnancy should be based on any one of the following values:
  •    Fasting plasma glucose = 5.1-6.9 mmol/l (92 -125 mg/dl)
  •    1-h post 75g oral glucose load >=10.0 mmol/l (180 mg/dl) *
  •    2-h post 75g oral glucose load 8.5 – 11.0 mmol/l (153-199 mg/dl)

At risk screening
Early diagnosis and good control reduce the risk of costly complications and reduces the deterioration of islet function in T2DM.
The following people should therefore be screened with fasting blood glucose or HbA1c at least yearly when they visit health
facilities:
  •      Those aged ≥40 years
  •      Children and adults <40 years who are overweight or obese and who have two or more additional
         risk factors for diabetes
  •      Individuals with HbA1C 5.7-6.4%, FBG 5.6 to 6.9mmol/(IFG), 2hour post OGTT 75g BG 7.8 to 11mmol/l(IGT).
  •      People on long-term steroids or immunosuppressants
  •      Women with a history of gestational diabetes mellitus or polycystic ovary syndrome
  •      All pregnant women at the first antenatal visit if overweight, have had gestational diabetes, babies with birth weight >4
         kg, previous stillbirths or neonatal deaths. Screening should be repeated in the second trimester if negative.
  •      All women during the 2nd or 3rd trimester (for gestational diabetes

Non- Pharmacological Management
For people who have the above risk factors should be guided on diabetes preventive interventions as below.
  •    Dietary modification (see Nutrition chapter 24)
  •    Physical activity (see Nutrition chapter 24)
  •    Weight reduction
  •    Medication with metformin.

Goals of diabetes management
Table 19.1: Goals for Optimum Management of Diabetes
 Diet                          Advise same as for people without diabetes
 Body mass index               Therapeutic goal is 5–10% weight loss for people who are overweight or obese, but aim
                               for BMI<25 kg/m2
 Waist circumference             <102 cm for men, <88 cm for women
 Physical activity               At least 30 minutes of moderate physical activity on most days of the week (total ≥150
                                 minutes/week)

 Cigarette consumption           0 per day
 Alcohol consumption             Not more than 2 standard unit drinks (20 g) per day for men and 1 unit
                                 for women
 Blood glucose                   Non-pregnant: 4–6 mmol/L fasting; 6–8 mmol/L postprandial Pregnant: ≤5.0 mmol/L
 level                           fasting, ≤6.7 mmol/L postprandial

                                 Self-monitoring of blood glucose is essential to improve outcomes
 HbA1c                           Target ≤7%. Should be measured every three months until stable, thereafter at least twice
                                 a year. For healthy older adults <7.5%. Older adult with multiple coexisting chronic
                                 illnesses <8%
 Lipids                          Total cholesterol: <5.2 mmol/L HDL-C: ≥1.0 mmol/L, LDL-C: <2.6 mmol/L, Triglycerides:
                                 <1.7 mmol/L
 Blood pressure                  Target ≤130/80 mmHg
                                 For those with albuminuria/proteinuria, and high CV risk<130/80 mmHg

 Urine albumin                   Spot collection: <20 mg/L

                                 Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR): women: <3.5 mg/mmol; men: <2.5 mg/mmol

Table:19.2 Healthy Lifestyle Management for Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM)
 Component                            Details
 Dietary Control                      • Meet requirements for growth, development, physical activity, and maintain
                                       desirable body weight (weight reduction in overweight/obese patients).
                                      • Achieve and maintain near-normal blood glucose levels to prevent hypo- and
                                       hyperglycemia and reduce chronic complications.
                                      • Attain optimal lipid and blood pressure control to reduce macrovascular risk.
 Dietary Measures                     • Each meal should include a variety of foods from core groups: vegetables,
                                       fruits, whole grains, proteins (meat/legumes), and dairy.
                                      • Distribute food evenly throughout the day with small meals/snacks between
                                      main meals.
 Food Composition – Protein           • 15–20% of total energy intake (≈1 g/kg/day).
 Food Composition – Carbohydrates     • 45–60% of total energy.
                                      • Avoid <100 g/day (risk of ketosis).
                                      • Synchronize carbohydrate intake with insulin/oral hypoglycemic agents.
                                      • Prefer complex carbohydrates (whole grains, cereals, roots, tubers).
                                      • Avoid simple sugars, sugar-sweetened beverages, and honey.
                                      • Distribute into 3 meals with snacks rather than 1–2 large meals.
 Food Composition – Fats              • <30% of total energy intake.
                                      • Reduce to ≤20% in obese adults with diabetes.
 Salt Intake                          • Limit to <1 teaspoon per day.
 Physical Activity                    • Engage in aerobic exercise (e.g., brisk walking) and muscle-strengthening
                                       activities.
                                      • Benefits: improved glucose tolerance, energy expenditure, mood, BP, lipid
                                       profile, and mobility.
                                      • Adjust medication/food intake to prevent hypoglycemia.
 Smoking                              • Avoid completely.
 Alcohol Intake                       • Limit to ≤1 drink/day for women and ≤2 drinks/day for men.

Figure 19.1 Algorithm for the Glycemic Management of T2DM

Pharmacological Management
Oral hypoglycemics
  •    Review the blood glucose at follow-up clinic and adjust medicines as needed until blood glucose is controlled.
  •    If lifestyle measures on their own fail to achieve blood glucose control or blood glucose levels are
       persistently high (fasting >11 mmol/l or random >15 mmol/l) initiate:

A: metformin (PO) 500mg 12hourly with or after meals. Increase, as required, until a maximum of 2500mg in 2–3 divided doses.
            OR
A: glibenclamide (PO) 2.5–10mg 12hourly
(If Metformin is contraindicated)
            OR
A: glimepiride (PO) 1–4mg 12hourly
            OR
A: gliclazide (PO) 40–160mg 12hourly
    •   If the maximum dose of metformin does not result in adequate glycemic control, either one of the above sulphonylureas
        may be added, starting with the lower dose and increasing until control is achieved or the maximum dose is reached.
    •   If patient has established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, heart failure and chronic kidney disease add SGLT2
        inhibitors

S: dapagliflozin (PO) 10mg daily

Other medications that can be used as an add on therapy before insulin

Dipeptidyl Peptidase-4 Inhibitors (DPP4 inhibitors)
May be used as an add-on for patients who need modest additional glucose lowering. They are safe to combine with metformin,
thiazolidinedione, insulin, sulfonylurea add SGLT2 inhibitors.
S: sitagliptin (PO) 100mg once a day

Thiazolidinediones
They are commonly prescribed as third line therapy. They offer an advantage in the context of high risk for hypoglycemia,
severe insulin resistance (prediabetics), and coexisting nonalcoholic steatohepatitis
D: pioglitazone (PO) 15 - 30mg 24 hourly (max 45/day)

  Note
    •  Activity of sulphonylureas is prolonged in both hepatic and renal failure
    •  Metformin is contraindicated in those with severe renal, liver and cardiac failure.
    •  The lower dosage is appropriate when initiating treatment in elderly patients with uncertain meal schedules, or in
       patients with mild hyperglycemia
    •  Sulphonylureas are best taken 15 to 30 minutes before meals
    •  Pioglitazone should be avoided in patients with heart failure, history of fracture or high risk of fracture
    •  SGLT2 inhibitors have risk for developing euglycemic DKA

If a combination of medicines is still inadequate, then insulin should be added as detailed below in the section on insulin.

Management with Insulin Injection in Type 2 Diabetes
Insulin injections are in T2DM in the following conditions:
  •     Initial presentation with fasting blood glucose more             •    Organ failure: Renal, liver, heart
        than      13.9    mmol/random        blood   glucose                  etc.,
        >16.7mmol/l, HBA1C>10                                            •    Diabetes not well controlled with
  •     Presentation in hyperglycemic                                         diet or oral drugs
        emergency                                                        •    Latent autoimmune diabetes of
  •     Peri-operative period especially                                      adults (LADA)
        major or emergency surgery                                       •    Contraindications to oral drugs
  •     Other      medical      conditions
        requiring tight glycemic control

  Note: The maximum glucose lowering efficacy of oral drugs is usually evident by six months. Therefore, the efficacy of any
  added therapy must be assessed within six months and an alternative drug instituted in case of failure

Insulin injections should be initiated by a doctor able to fully instruct the patient in its use and how to manage acute changes in
plasma glucose. Insulin will be available at lower health facilities for management of stable patients who require prescription
refills. Refer to specialist for more than 24 hourly insulin doses.

Table 19.2: Types of Insulin as per WHO Essential Medicine List
  Type of Insulin                      Name                                           Basal or short acting
  Short acting                         A: Regular Insulin (human soluble)             Short acting
  Intermediate acting                  A: isophane Insulin                            Basal
  Pre mixed insulin                    D:biphasic human insulin regular NPH Basal + Short acting
                                       30/70
  Long-acting insulin                  D: Long-acting insulin (analogue)              Basal
Insulin as substitution therapy
Oral medicines are discontinued (except metformin if patient is obese, and SGLT2 inhibitors)
D: pre-mixed insulin is introduced at a dosage of 0.2 IU/kg body weight and this is split into:
   •    ⅔ in the morning and ⅓ in the evening, increase daily dose by 2 to 4 units every two to three days to achieve fasting
        plasma glucose target (3.9-7.2mmol/l) while avoiding hypoglycemia
   •    Inject 30 minutes before the morning and the evening meals for human insulin
   •    Inject 0 to 15minutes before meal for analog insulins.

Basal Bolus Regime:
A: Regular insulin (short acting), should be used as a pre-prandial insulin together with a basal insulin, if glycemic targets are
not meet despite adequately titrated basal insulin or when basal insulin dose >0.5units/kg/day.

Insulin as supplemental therapy
Oral medicines are continued (half or stop sulphonylureas dose, monitor blood glucose levels)

A: isophane insulin administered at night before 22:00h at a total daily dose of 0.1–0.2 IU/kg/day. if persistently elevated fasting
plasma glucose increase dose by 2 to 4 units every 2 to 3 days to achieve target fasting glucose

D: long-acting insulin (analogue): administered at 10units 24 hourly (morning or bedtime) or 0.1 to 0.2 units/kg 24 hourly.
Increase daily dose by 2 to 4 units every two to three days to achieve fasting plasma glucose target.

Self-monitoring in patients with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM)
Self-Monitoring Blood Glucose (SMBG) is usually recommended in the following patients:
  •    Patients on insulin and glucose lowering agents that can cause hypoglycemia (sulphonylureas)
  •    When monitoring hyperglycemia arising from illness
  •    With pregnancy and pre-pregnancy planning
  •    When changes in treatment, lifestyle or other conditions requires data on glycemic patterns
  •    When HbA1c estimations are unreliable (e.g. haemoglobinopathies).

sections.title: Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (Childhood diabetes)
sections.text:
Type 1 is caused by insulin deficiency following destruction of pancreatic beta cells. One fourth of the cases are diagnosed in
adults

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •  Nutrition (refer to nutrition chapter 24)                           •    Psychological support is important to cope with this
  •  Exercise requirements are as for children without                        chronic illness.
     diabetes                                                            •    Hypo-hyper glycemia education needs to be
                                                                              reinforce frequently.
Pharmacological Management

Step 1 Calculate total daily insulin need, generally 0.3 to 1unit/kg/day initially, after honeymoon period its between 0.7-
1.5units/kg/day. However individual patient needs should be considered.

Basal -bolus regime
  •    Basal insulin: Long acting(analogs) or NPH (intermediate acting)
  •    Bolus insulin: Regular(soluble) or Rapid acting (lispro, aspart, glulisine)
  •    Estimated dose is adjusted depending on the child’s response

Step 2 Calculate basal insulin
  •    Basal long-acting insulin analog: dose is 40%-50% the TDD, give 24 hourly in the evening
  •    Basal NPH: two thirds of TDD before breakfast, one third before dinner or at bedtime.

Step 3: Calculate bolus insulin dose
Usually, 50% of the total dose, the dose of insulin given depends on the anticipated carbohydrates, premeal BG as well as
exercise activity. Total premeal bolus is the sum of the dose calculated based on ICR plus dose adjusted to correct premeal
hyperglycemia. ICR (amount of carbohydrate (grams) covered by 1unit of insulin=450/TDD
Example
  •    if TDD is 45units, the I unit of rapid or short acting is estimated to cover 10gram , ICR 1:10, if patient is planned for
       40grams of carbs the bolus dose will be 40/10=4units
  •    If the setting is not ideal for this calculation, then the table below can be used for fixed doses and adjustments made
       according to the child’s response.

Table 19.3: Recommended Insulin Dosage
Time                 Type of insulin                             Proportion
Break-fast           Short acting or rapid acting                30% of total daily dose
Lunch                Short acting or rapid acting                20% of total daily dose
Supper               Short acting or rapid acting                10% of total daily dose
Bedtime              Long or intermediate acting                 40% -50%of total daily dose

  Note
    •  Diabetes in children is often misdiagnosed as some other condition – e.g. as pneumonia or asthma (labored
       breathing),
    •  Insulin should be given for life and the dose adjusted according to weight and glucose response
    •  Self-glucose monitoring by glucometer at home 3-4times/day
    •  Pre-mixed insulins not advised in children

Clinical monitoring of people with diabetes

Table 19.4: Clinical Monitoring of People with Diabetes
 Component                     Initial Visit                                     3-Month Visit              Annual Visit
 History & Diagnosis           • Full history and diagnosis                      • Relevant interval        • As per initial visit
                                                                                   history
 Physical Examination            • Height and weight                             • Weight                   • As per initial visit
                                 • Waist/hip circumference                       • Blood pressure
                                 • Blood pressure                                • Foot inspection
                                 • Detailed foot examination
                                 • Tooth inspection
                                 • Eye examination
 Eye Assessment                  • Visual acuity + fundoscopy                    —                          • As per initial visit
 Cardiovascular Assessment       • ECG                                           —                          • As per initial visit
 Biochemistry                    • Blood glucose                                 • Blood glucose            • As per initial visit
                                 • HbA1c                                         • Urine protein
                                 • Lipid profile (TC, HDLC, LDLC, TG)            • HbA1c every 6
                                 • Serum creatinine                                months
                                 • Urine: glucose, ketones, protein
 Education                       • Diabetes education                     • Reinforce education   • Reinforce as per
                                                                            advice                 initial visit
 Nutrition                   • Nutritional advice                         • Reinforce nutrition   • Reinforce as per
                                                                            advice                 initial visit
 Medication                  • Initiate if needed                         • Review and adjust     • Review as per
                                                                            therapy                initial visit
TC = Total Cholesterol; HDLC = High-Density Lipoprotein Cholesterol; LDLC = Low-Density Lipoprotein Cholesterol; TG =
Triglycerides

Surgery in diabetes General measures
Correct perioperative management depends on type of surgery (major or minor), type of diabetes and recent diabetes control.
A perioperative HBA1c, fasting or random blood glucose is recommended to assess glycemic control and identify undiagnosed
diabetes
  •    Surgery should be delayed if possible if HBA1C >9% or blood glucose fasting >10 mmol/l or random glucose > 13
       mmol/l.
  •    Screen for nephropathy, cardiac disease, retinopathy and neuropathy and inform surgical team.
  •    Optimal glycemic target in the perioperative period should be to maintain blood glucose levels between 7.8-10mmol/l

If diabetes is well controlled and surgery is minor:
   •   If on oral agent therapy, omit therapy on morning of surgery except SGLTS2 inhibitors which should be stopped 24 to
       72hour before surgery and resume therapy when eating normally
   •   For T1DM, continue with normal basal dose of insulin, the short acting or rapid acting insulins can be given as per
       correctional scale insulin.
   •   Decrease the dose of long-acting basal insulin by 20% to 25% the evening before surgery. If they routinely take basal
       insulin only in the morning, the reduced dose should instead be administered on the morning of surgery.
   •   In cases of intermediate-acting insulin such as neutral protamine Hagedorn (NPH), the usual dose is administered the
       evening prior and reduced by 50% on the morning of surgery.
   •   Patients using premixed insulin (NPH/regular 70/30) should preferably receive long-acting insulin the evening before
       surgery instead of their premixed formulation. Or reduce the premixed insulin dose by 50%
   •   Pre-prandial insulin should be stopped; subcutaneous correctional insulin is initiated with blood glucose monitoring every
       4 to 6 hours

Table 19.5: Correctional Insulin Scale
 BG           Premeal: Sensitive (BMI <25 or <50          Premeal: Average (BMI        Pre-meal:
 (mmol/l)     units/d)                                    25-30 or 50-90 units/d)      Resistant (BMI >30 or >90 units/d)
   7.2- 8.3   0 units                                     1 unit                       2units
  8.4-11.1    1 unit                                      2 units                      3units
 11.2-13.8    2 units                                     4 units                      6units
 13.9-16.0    3 units                                     6 units                      9units

If poor glycemic control or major surgery:
   •   Use continuous IV insulin infusion, start with half of the patient’s usual total daily dose (TDD usually 0.4 to 0.5 U/kg/day)
       or 1-5 units of regular insulin per hour.
   •   Monitor blood glucose before, during and after surgery as outlined below: aim for blood glucose levels of 7.8–10 mmol/l.
   •   Check potassium levels and start potassium infusion as per DKA protocol
   •   Infuse 0.9% NaCl with D5W IV at 50 mL/hr.

Insulin infusion protocol
  Blood glucose (mmol/l)                                        Initial rate of insulin (unit/hr.)
  10-12                                                         1
  12.1-14                                                       2
  14.1-17                                                       4
  >17                                                           5

Adjusting infusion rate according to blood sugar levels, if blood glucose (BG) is:
  •    < 4mmol/l: stop insulin infusion, administer D50% 50mls iv push stat, continue D 5%infusion at 50ml/hr, monitor blood
       glucose every 30min, restart insulin at half the initial rate when blood glucose >10mmol/l
  •    4.1-6mmol/stop insulin infusion, administer D50% 25mls, continue with D5% at 50ml/hr, monitor sugars every 30min,
       restart insulin infusion at half the initial rate when BG>10
  •    6.1-7.7 continue D5% infusion, decrease insulin infusion to half the initial rate
  •    7.8-10 Goal range, no changes, measure BG q1h if three BG are within range then BG q2h.
  •    10-15.1 if BG decreases or remains same on check no change in infusion rate, if BG increases on check increase
       infusion rate by 1unit/hr.
  •    15.2-20 if BG decreases or remains unchanged on check, maintain same rate of infusion, if BG is greater than last check
       increase infusion rate by 2units/hr.
  •    >20 increase rate by 2units per hour, consider bolus insulin

Continue the infusion until 60 minutes after the first meal. Long acting/intermediate acting insulins can be resumed 2 to 4 hours
before stopping the insulin infusion.

sections.title: Management of Diabetes during Religious Fasting
sections.text:
There are several types of fasting:
  •    Normal fast (the common fast): the person abstains from all foods but can take water for a limited time. Or abstain from
       food and water for a specific number of hours during the day.
  •    Total fast = total abstinence from both food and water. This should not go beyond a maximum of three days and is not
       recommended for those people taking insulin secretagogues or insulin.
  •    Partial fast = abstain from selected foods and drinks, or omit a certain meal each of the fasting days.

sections.title: Those with very poor glucose control should be discouraged from fasting
sections.text:
•    A total fast is not recommended for anyone with high risk. Adequate hydration is important even during the period of
       fasting.
  •    For those on insulin, a partial fast is preferred to total or normal forms of fasting.
  •    Self-blood glucose monitoring is mandatory for people with diabetes who elect to fast.
         - Once-a-day is adequate for patients on diet only or diet with metformin.
         - At least 3 times a day in patients on insulin secretagogues
         - More frequently if hyperglycemia is marked and the urine tested for ketones.
  •    Consider terminating the fast if frequent hypoglycemia or intercurrent infections.
  •    Vigorous activity should be avoided during period of fast.
  •    Ensure ready access to a healthcare provider during the period of fast.

sections.title: Management of normal fasting for people treated with oral hypoglycemic agents
sections.text:
•    Fasting is possible in this situation.
  •    Usual dietary advice should be followed at this time.
  •    Patients on metformin, alpha-glucosidase inhibitors and thiazolidinediones can continue taking the usual doses at the
       time of breaking the fast and before dawn (if they have another meal at that time).
  •    If on a second or third generation sulphonylureas (glibenclamide, gliclazide, glipizide, glimepiride), this should be taken
       at the time of breaking the fast and not before dawn.

sections.title: Management of normal fasting for T2DM patients on insulin
sections.text:
•    If on 24 hourly insulin before bed, this can be given as usual
  •    If on 12 hourly short- and intermediate-acting insulin:
          - Before the dawn meal, give the usual evening dose of short-acting insulin without any intermediate-acting insulin.
          - Before the evening meal give the usual morning dose of short-acting and intermediate-acting insulin.
  •    If on basal bolus regimen:
          - Usual doses of the short-acting insulin can be given before the dawn and evening meals, and usual doses of the
            intermediate-acting insulin can still be given at 10pm.
          - Regular SBGM is essential to ensure prevention of hypoglycemia
          - Titration of doses should occur according to SBGM results.
  •    Neither the insulin injection nor the breaking of the skin for SBGM will break the fast.

Management of other fasting types
Table 19.6: Types of Fasting and Recommended Diabetic Treatment
 Treatment regimen                                    Fasting regimen                    When to take antidiabetic agents
  Diet only                                            Total, normal of partial fast     Not applicable
  Metformin, Thiazolidinediones                        Normal or partial fast            With meals
  Insulin secretagogues Sulphonylureas                 Partial fast                      Before meals
  Daily intermediate or long-acting insulin            Partial fast                      Before first meal
  Multiple insulin doses using intermediate and short  Avoid fasting                     Not applicable
  acting insulin
  Long-acting plus bolus fast acting insulin           Avoid fasting or partial fast      Lantus am and analogue with meals

sections.title: Hyperglycemia in Pregnancy
sections.text:
Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM) is any degree of glucose intolerance first recognized in pregnancy. Diabetes in pregnancy
refers to those with pre-existing diabetes, whether diagnosed or not.

Screening at first antenatal visit
Perform screening in all women at the first antenatal clinic
attendance if they have:
   •   BMI > 30 kg/m2                                               •   Known impaired glucose tolerance (plasma
   •   Previous history of GDM                                          glucose 7.8-11mmol/l 2hrs after 75 OGTT)
   •   Previous big baby >4000g                                     •   Impaired fasting glucose (fasting plasma glucose
   •   Poor obstetric history                                           5.6-6.9mmol/l).
   •   family history of DM                                         •   Grand multipara
   •   Older maternal age>35                                        •   Glycosuria.
   •                                                                •   PCOS
Screening later in Pregnancy
   •   All women with risk factors (see above) should have a 75 g OGTT at 24–28 weeks. Or earlier as per the clinician.
   •   A fasting plasma glucose at 24–28 weeks is recommended in low-risk women

Non-Pharmacological Management
All diabetic women intending to become pregnant should:
   •    Be encouraged to achieve excellent glycemic control using glucose monitoring of both fasting and postprandial values
   •    Be prescribed high-dose (5mg) pre-pregnancy folate supplementation, continuing up to 12 weeks’ gestation
   •    Have an eye exam and be informed of the risk of developing and/or progression of diabetic retinopathy
   •    Have a kidney assessment (random urine albumin/creatinine ratio and serum creatinine) and referred if urine protein ≥
        1g.
   •    A combined health-care team (obstetrician, diabetologist or internist, diabetes educator, pediatrician/neonatologist) is
        required.
   •    Review SMBG, blood pressure and urine protein and ketones by dipstick at each visit and eye examination in each
        trimester.
   •    Target glycaemia:
           - Pre-prandial blood glucose 3.5–5.5mmol/L
           - Postprandial blood glucose 5–7.5mmol/L

  •    Lifestyle management is the preferred means of managing gestational diabetes.
         - Diet is based on the principles of optimal nutrition and controlled weight gain.
         - Exercise can be helpful in lowering BG levels: the most acceptable form of exercise for most women is walking in
            their normal daily routine.
  •    Glucose-lowering therapy should be considered in addition to diet where fasting or two hours glucose levels are above
       target, for example, where two or more values per fortnight are:
         - Fasting or pre-prandial ≥5.5 mmol/L, or two hours postprandial ≥7 mmol/L at ≤35 weeks
         - Fasting or pre-prandial ≥5.5 mmol/L, or two hours postprandial ≥8 mmol/L at >35 weeks
         - Any postprandial values are >9 mmol/L.
  •    When pharmacologic treatment of gestational diabetes is indicated, insulin and oral medications are equivalent in
       efficacy, and either can be an appropriate first-line therapy.

Pharmacological Management
A: metformin (PO) 500mg 12hourly, maximum 2000mg in 2–3 divided doses
         OR
A: glibenclamide (PO) 2.5mg 24hourly to a maximum of 10mg daily

  Note:
    •   Oral hypoglycemics (except for metformin and glibenclamide) are contraindicated in pregnancy
    •   Glibenclamide can cause hypoglycemia for the new born.

S: Insulin
Insulin dose should be tailored to achieve target BG levels, use of human insulins minimizes transplacental transfer of insulin
antibodies, but insulin analogs like lispro, aspart, glulisine and glargine have also been deemed safe for use in pregnancy.
Insulin regimes are as per adult insulin regimes.

Postnatal Follow Up
  •   Women with gestational diabetes should be screened at 6–12 weeks postnatal to ensure return to normal glucose
      tolerance. Thereafter, a 1–2 yearly follow up is recommended.
  •   Metformin, glibenclamide and insulin may be used even if a woman is breastfeeding. Encourage women to breastfeed.
  •   If retinopathy, check eyes 1 year postpartum

sections.title: Diabetes and HIV
sections.text:
The management of people with both diabetes and HIV need to consider the following:
  •   ARVs are associated with increased metabolic dysfunction, including insulin resistance, dyslipidemia and lipodystrophy
  •   Protease inhibitors (PIs) increase insulin resistance and reduce insulin secretion by interfering with GLUT–4 mediated
      glucose transport
  •   Standards of treatment and management of diabetes for patients with HIV are generally the same as those for diabetic
      patients without HIV and patients who acquire HIV may continue to be managed with the same drug therapy as before
  •   Sulfonylureas may not be effective in the face of severe insulin resistance. In case
  •   Glycemic control deteriorates, insulin should be initiated, rather than increasing dosage or number of oral medications
  •   People who are on ARTs need to be screened for diabetes at least once a year and especially if they have other CVD
      risk factors

sections.title: Diabetes and Tuberculosis
sections.text:
Diabetes and tuberculosis are interlinked as follows:
  •    People attending TB clinics should be screened for diabetes and those attending diabetes clinics should be screened
       for TB if presenting with symptoms.
  •    Diabetes may be associated with delayed sputum conversion (>60 days), higher probability of tuberculosis treatment
       failure, higher recurrence and relapse rates, higher overall mortality, higher rates of multi-drug resistance TB and more
       atypical presentation in hyperosmolar hyperglycemic nonketotic coma or ketoacidosis
  •    For both conditions, controlling blood sugar, being more physically active, avoiding chronic stress, getting enough sleep
       and maintaining ideal weight are recommended.

Review Drug Requirements
  •   Rifampicin is a potent hepatic enzyme-inducing agent, accelerates the metabolism of oral hypoglycemic agents and
      shortens the plasma half-life of sulphonylureas
  •   Isoniazid antagonizes sulphonylureas, impairs insulin release and action and leads to increased requirement of insulin
      and oral antidiabetic medication
  •   Therefore, people with diabetes may require an increase in dosage of antidiabetic medication if they develop
      tuberculosis.

Use Oral Antidiabetic Medicines Carefully in Tuberculosis
  •   People with diabetes mellitus and tuberculosis should be treated with insulin injection, or in case a diabetic with
      tuberculosis is on oral hypoglycemic agents, it may be necessary to switch to insulin.
  •   Tuberculosis affects both the liver and pancreas: oral antidiabetic drugs are contraindicated in hepatic disease, which is
      a common adverse effect of antituberculosis therapy.
  •   Metformin produces weight loss, particularly in high doses, and it is also an anorectic.
  •   Marked weight loss and higher insulin and caloric needs in tuberculosis are other important indications for reviewing oral
      antidiabetic therapy in diabetes mellitus.

sections.title: Hypoglycemia
sections.text:
Hypoglycemia is defined as blood glucose <3.9mmol/L.

Clinical Presentation
  •    Hunger
  •    Sweating                                                        •    Headache
  •    Trembling or shaking                                            •    Confusion
  •    Anxiety                                                         •    Lack of concentration
  •    Dizziness                                                       •    Weakness
  •    Lightheadedness                                                 •    Changes in behavior (e.g. irritability, tearfulness,
  •    Palpitation                                                          crying), paranesthesia.
  •    Numbness around the lips and fingers

Patients may also present with convulsions, seizures or coma due to delayed corrective action or impaired hypoglycemia
awareness where the patient loses the ability to detect the early symptoms of hypoglycemia due to repeated episodes of mild
hypoglycemia or long duration of diabetes leading to loss of adrenergic and glucagon response, with eventual loss of adrenergic
and neuroglycopenic symptoms.

Non-Pharmacological Management
For Conscious Patients, should be advised to
Quickly take a glass of a sugar-rich drink
          OR
Eat one table spoon of sugar or honey
          AND
Have a meal.

If symptoms persist after 5 minutes repeat the above.

Pharmacological Management
For unconscious Patients:
C: dextrose 50% (IV) (40-50ml) (not for pediatrics)
          OR
A: dextrose 10% (IV) (200–300ml).
Repeat if patient is not responsive or if after 15 minutes, the blood glucose is still below 4mmol/l. Followed by 8–10 % glucose
infusion.
Use
A: dextrose 5%if the higher concentrations are not available.
          OR
S: glucagon (IM or SC) 1mg stat adults, children/adolescents 0.02 -0.03mg/kg/dose may be repeated after 15min

Neonatal hyperinsulinemia hypoglycemia 1mg/dose (SC) stat, continuous IV infusion 1-20mcg/kg/hour. Refer to neonatal
chapter for diazoxide

 Note: If IV access is impossible, consider nasogastric tube or rectal glucose

On Recovery
 •   Give long-acting carbohydrate snack e.g. a piece of bread
 •   Identify the cause of hypoglycemia and correct it
 •   If hypoglycemia is a result of long acting sulphonylureas, insulin or alcohol, frequently monitor blood glucose (2hourly)
     and give IV dextrose infusion (5–10%) for 12– 24 hours
 •   If patient is not responding look for another cause or refer.

sections.title: Diabetic Ketoacidosis and Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic States
sections.text:
These are acute metabolic complications of diabetes mellitus that may lead to severe dehydration, altered level of
consciousness and electrolyte imbalance. The presence of acidosis, ketonemia and ketonuria in diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)
differentiates it from hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state (HHS).

Clinical Presentation
  •    Nausea/vomiting                                                  •    Abdominal pain
  •    Shortness of breath                                              •    Fever
  •    Obtundation/drowsiness                                           •    Altered mental function
  •    Thirst/polyuria                                                  •    Dehydration
  •    Fruity smelling breath                                           •    Lethargy
  •    Confusion                                                        •    Coma

  Note
    •  When you suspect DKA, confirm diagnosis immediately
    •  All patients with confirmed DKA should be admitted to hospital for close monitoring and appropriate management;
       severe cases require high-dependency or intensive care.

Table: 19.7: Diagnostic Criteria for DKA and HHS
Parameter                        Mild DKA        Moderate DKA               Severe DKA           HHS
 Blood Glucose                    >13.9          >13.9                       >13.9                >30
 Arterial PH                      7.25-7.3       7.00-7.24                   <7.00                >7.30
 Serum bicarbonate                15-18          10-15                       <10                  >18
 Urine ketones                    Positive       Positive                    Positive             Small
 Serum ketones                    Positive       Positive                    Positive             Small
 Serum osmolality                 Variable       Variable                    Variable             >320
 Alteration in sensorium          Alert          Alert/drowsy                Stupor/coma          Stupor/coma

Investigations
Apart from the ones in the table above, check serum electrolytes, urea and creatinine.

Non-Pharmacological Management
Management of DKA and HHS is similar.
  •  Frequent monitoring of patients
  •  Improvement of circulatory volume and tissue perfusion
  •  Careful search and management of the precipitating causes With proper treatment, the average time to resolution is
     between 10–18 hours for DKA and 9–11 hours for HHS.

Pharmacological Management
  •  Replacement of electrolyte losses (potassium)
  •  Administration of insulin

Fluid management protocol
The first step - infusion of isotonic saline to expand extracellular volume and stabilize cardiovascular status. Fluid replacement
alone results in:
  •     Improvement of hyperglycemia, reduce insulin resistance
  •     Lowering the plasma osmolality,
  •     Reducing vasoconstriction and improving perfusion,
  •     Restores renal perfusion
  •     Reduce insulin resistance by ↓ stress/counterregulatory hormone levels
  •     Both DKA and HHS patients have severe volume depletion -- estimated water deficit of 100mls/kg body weight
  •     Usual initial fluid → isotonic saline (0.9% NaCl)
  •     Optimal rate of fluid infusion depends on the clinical state of the patient. On average 15 to 20 ml/kg/hour (about 1000
        ml/hour) max. <50ml/kg in the first four hours.

When volume deficit is corrected adjust iv isotonic saline to 250 to 500ml/hr. if serum sodium is high switch to half saline.

Electrolyte management protocol
Almost all patients with DKA or HHS have a substantial potassium deficit.
  •    Acidosis –shift to extracellular
  •    Urinary losses related to the glucose osmotic diuresis
  •    Secondary hyperaldosteronism.
  •    Loss is high 3-10mEq/kg

Despite total body potassium deficit, concentration is usually normal or elevated due to
  •   Insulin deficiency and hyperosmolality
  •   Both result in potassium movement out of the cells
  •   Insulin treatment reverse distribution

Establish adequate kidney function urine output>50ml/hr. If Patient is oliguric give KCL when K <4 or ECG signs of hypokalemia
(U wave)

Table 19.8: Potassium Repletion in DKA and HHS
K+>5.2 mEq/L                  Do not give K+ initially, but check serum K+ with basic metabolic profile every 2 hours
K+<3.3 mEq/L                      Hold insulin and give K+ 20-30 mEq/hr until K+>3.3 mEq/L
K+ = 3.3-5.2 mEq/L                Give 20-30 mEq K+ in each L of IV fluid to maintain serum K+ 4-5 mEq/L

Insulin therapy management protocol
Continuous IV infusion of regular insulin is the treatment of choice
  •    Correct hypovolemic shock and hypokalemia if present, before starting insulin

Insulin therapy
  •    Lowers serum glucose concentration (↓ hepatic glucose production>> ↑ peripheral utilization)
  •    Diminishes ketone production (reducing both lipolysis and glucagon secretion)
  •    Augment ketone utilization.

Conventional Insulin Guidelines
Both HHS and moderate to severe DKA
  •   IV bolus of regular insulin (0.1 U/kg body weight) followed by a continuous infusion of regular insulin of 0.1 U/Kg/hour =
      7 U/hour in a 70 kg patient
  •   Alternatively, omit bolus dose →continuous IV infusion of regular insulin at a rate of 0.14 U/kg per hour (equivalent to
      10 U/hour in a 70 kg patient), Reduce rate to 0.05units/kg/hr when SBG<13.9mmol/l
  •   bolus insulin is a priming dose, saturates insulin receptors before continuous insulin, avoid lag time in achieving steady
      state insulin levels
         - In practice -100iu in 100mls of NS titrate in 5-7cc/h in the first 24hours
                          OR
         - 60iu in 60mls of NS titrate 6-7cc/hour in 24hours
  •   Insulin dosing is the same in DKA and HHS
  •   If plasma glucose does not decrease by 2.8-4.2mmol/l in the first hour, increase the infusion rate of insulin by 50% to
      100%
  •   Optimal rate of glucose declines 5.5mmol/l/hour
  •   Keep serum glucose. Between 8.3 to 11.1mmol/l until resolution of DKA
  •   It takes 12-24 hours to clear ketones from circulation after hyperglycemia is controlled

Resolution criteria
Venous ph.>7.3, serum bicarbonate >18mmol/serum glucose <11.1mmol/l
For children
Detailed management of DKA is presented in the algorithm for management of pediatric diabetic ketoacidosis in low resource
center below. Further details can also be found in chapter 1(Emergency Medicine)

Severity of DKA
  •    Mild: pH 7.2-7.3, bicarbonate 10 to 18mEq/l
  •    Moderate: pH 7.1 to7.2, bicarbonate 5 to 10mEq/L
  •    Severe: pH <7.1, bicarbonate <5mEq/l
        - Average fluid deficit is approximately 7% i.e. 70ml/kg(range 30 to 100ml/kg)
        - Give NS or RL 10ml/kg (mild DKA)-20ml/kg (moderate/severe DKA) as an I.V infusion over 20 to 30min.Give
           additional boluses, if necessary, based on the cardiovascular status. If glucose <13.9-16.7mmol/l change fluid to
           5%dexstrose.
        - Fluid Requirements = DEFICIT + 48 hours’ maintenance

Table: 19.9: Maintenance Fluid
 Age (years)                       Weight (kg)                     Maintenance fluid (ml/kg/day)
 <1                                3-9                             80
 1-5                               10-19                           70
 6-9                               20-29                           60
 10-14                             30-50                           50
 >15                               >50                             30
Electrolytes:
Sodium levels are generally low due to hyperglycemia; it should rise as hyperglycemia corrected. high levels may be due to
water loss.
Potassium: (Infusion rate 0.5mEq/kg/hr)
          o <3.5mEq/L add 40mEq/L of KCL to 1L saline, delay insulin therapy.
          o 3.5 to 4.5mEq/l add 40mEq/l of KCLto 1L saline when insulin therapy is started.
          o >4.5mEq/L-monitor every hour and begin potassium as above
Serum electrolytes should be monitored q2h initially, then 4 to 6 hourly later)

Insulin:
After the initial fluid bolus start insulin (rapid or regular) infusion at (0.05-0.1units/kg/hour.1ml of saline should contain 1unit of
insulin. If iv insulin is not available Sc insulin regime (0.1 unit’s/kg rapid acting every one to two hours, regular insulin every
three to four hrs.) can be used.

Cerebral injury
Monitor neurological status first 12 to 24, suspicious symptoms include changes in mental status, new or worsening headache,
recurrence of vomiting and age-inappropriate incontinence. Initiate treatment promptly with 0.5 to 1g/kg of mannitol if cerebral
injury is suspected. CT when stable.

sections.title: Diabetes and Cardiovascular Diseases
sections.text:
Diabetic patients are 2–4 times likely to develop cardiovascular diseases mainly due to atherosclerosis and hypertension.

The clinical spectrum of cardiovascular diseases includes:
  •    Coronary heart disease
  •    Angina (which may be silent)
  •    Acute coronary artery syndrome
  •    Congestive cardiac failure
  •    Sudden death
  •    Cerebral vascular accident (stroke, transient ischaemic attacks and dementia)
  •    Peripheral vascular disease (intermittent claudication, foot ulcer and gangrene).

Assessment (annual)
  •  ECG, Chest X-Ray, if with symptoms/signs of heart failure.
  •  Peripheral vascular disease evaluation includes doppler and angiography of lower limbs.

Pharmacological Management
Acute coronary syndrome
All adults with T2DM and recent acute coronary syndrome and/or coronary stent should receive dual anti-platelet therapy for
12 months after the event or procedure:

A: acetylsalicylic acid (PO) 75–100mg 24hourly
          AND
D: clopidogrel (PO) 75mg 24hourly

  Note:
    •   Acetylsalicylic acid is also indicated for primary prevention for people with T2DM >40years with family history of
        ischemic heart disease (IHD), cigarette smoking, obesity, proteinuria, or dyslipidemia.
    •   It is contraindicated in peptic/duodenal ulcer, dyspepsia, heartburn, malignant hypertension, hemorrhagic stroke.

Hyperlipidemia

Statin therapy results in a significant decrease in CVD morbidity and mortality in T2DM and are indicated in Type 2 diabetics >
40 years of age, or diabetes for > 10years

B: atorvastatin (PO) 10mg 24hourly. Dose may be increased to 80mg daily if required.
         OR
S: rosuvastatin (PO) 10mg 24hourly. Dose may be increased to 40mg daily if required

  •    Fenofibrate reduces incidence of retinopathy and need for laser surgery, peripheral neuropathy, and improvement in
       proteinuria, suggesting a more generalized effect on microvascular disease independent of dyslipidemia.
  •    Fibrates:
               o Should be used in mixed hyperlipidemias which have not responded adequately to diet or other therapy.
               o Are more effective in lowering triglycerides and increasing HDL, but less effective in lowering cholesterol.
               o Should be used with caution in combination with statins.
               o Can enhance the effects of warfarin and antidiabetic agents
               o Are contraindicated in patients taking Orlistat.

D: fenofibrate (PO) 67–267mg 24hourly

Hypertension
In people with T2DM, antihypertensive therapy with an angiotensin receptor blockers (ARB) or angiotensin-converting enzyme
inhibitors (ACEI) decreases the rate of progression of albuminuria, promotes regression to normal albuminuria and may reduce
the risk of decline in renal function.

Therefore:
BP-lowering therapy in people with diabetes should preferentially include an angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor (ACEI) or
angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB) e.g.
C: enalapril (PO) 10 – 40mg 24hourly, taken either as a single dose or two divided doses (enalapril (PO) 5 mg–10mg 12hourly)
          OR
C: lisinopril (PO) 5-10mg 24hourly

Alternatively
B: losartan (PO) initial dose 50mg stat. Maintenance dose; losartan (PO) 50–100mg 24 hourly in single or 2 divided doses.
          OR
S: candesartan (PO) 8-16mg 24hourly

  •    It is reasonable to target BP levels of <130/80 mmHg for people with diabetes.
  •    Combining an ARB and an ACEI is not recommended.
  •    If monotherapy does not sufficiently reduce blood pressure review management of hypertension in cardiac chapter 20
       to add other medications.

sections.title: Diabetic Peripheral Neuropathy
sections.text:
All patients should be screened for distal symmetric polyneuropathy starting at diagnosis of T2DM and at least annually
thereafter.

Clinical Presentation
  •    A combination of typical symptoms with typical signs as outlined in the table below, particularly symmetric distal sensory
       loss.
  •    Typical signs on examination in the absence of symptoms or with only presence of painless foot ulcer

Table 19.10: Clinical Features of Large Vs Small Nerve Fiber Neuropathy
 Component       Large Myelinated Nerve Fibers             Small Myelinated Nerve Fibers
 Function        • Pressure sensation                      • Nociception (pain)
                 • Vibration                               • Temperature sensation
                 • Proprioception (balance)                • Protective sensation
 Symptoms        • Numbness                                • Pain (burning)
                 • Tingling                                • Electric shock–like sensations
                 • Poor balance / unsteady gait            • Stabbing pain
 Clinical        • Ankle reflexes: reduced/absent          • Thermal (cold/hot) discrimination: reduced/absent
 Examination • Vibration perception: reduced/absent        • Pinprick sensation: decreased or absent
                 • 10 g monofilament: reduced/absent
                 • Proprioception: reduced/absent

Pharmacological Management
It is difficult to treat. Some of the drugs used include:
D: pregabalin (PO) 75-150mg (24hourly–12hourly) for 4weeks, increase based on response and tolerability max 600mg.
             OR
D: gabapentin (PO) 100-300mg (24hourly – 8hourly), increase dose as per response and tolerability max 3.6g
Tricyclic antidepressants may help
A: amitriptyline (PO) 25-75mg 24hourly
             OR
C: imipramine (PO) 100mg 24hourly

Gastroparesis
Due to autonomic neuropathy
B: metoclopramide (PO) 10mg 8hourly
         OR
D: domperidone (PO) 10mg 8hourly

Diabetic Foot:
Give foot care education and advice on appropriate footwear.

sections.title: Diabetic Nephropathy
sections.text:
It is one of the most important causes of chronic renal failure. Persistent microalbuminuria is both a marker for the development
of overt nephropathy and cardiovascular risk. Patients with microalbuminuria who progress to macroalbuminuria (>300 mg/24
h.) are likely to progress to end– stage renal disease over a period of years. Patients with diabetes and chronic kidney disease
(CKD) should be treated with a comprehensive strategy to reduce risks of kidney disease progression and cardiovascular
disease.

Non-Pharmacological Management
Patients with diabetes and CKD should be advised to Intensify management of modifiable risk factors that include :-
  •    Stop smoking.
  •    Treat urinary infection aggressively.
  •    Avoid drugs toxic to the kidney.
  •    Consume an individualized diet high in vegetables, fruits, whole grains, fiber, legumes, plant- based proteins,
       unsaturated fats, and nuts; and lower in processed meats, refined carbohydrates, and sweetened beverages
  •    Undertake moderate-intensity physical activity for a cumulative duration of at least 150 minutes per week, or to a level
       compatible with their cardiovascular and physical tolerance

Pharmacological Management
Renin–angiotensin system (RAS) inhibition is recommended for patients with albuminuria and hypertension
  •   Most patients with T2D, CKD, and eGFR => 30 ml/min per 1.73 m2 would benefit from treatment with both metformin
      and an SGLT2i.
  •   Patient preferences, comorbidities, eGFR, and cost should guide selection of additional drugs to manage glycemia,
      when needed, with glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1 RA) generally preferred.

A: metformin (PO) 500mg or 850mg (12hourly – 24 hourly); usual maintenance dose: 1g 12hourly

SGLT-2 Inhibitors
S: dapagliflozin (PO) 10mg 24hourly
           OR
DPP4 Inhibitors are also safe for use,
S: sitagliptin (PO) 100mg 24hourly:
eGFR 30-45 50mg 24hourly eGFR<30 25mg 24 hourly

If very poor sugar controls, then insulin should be initiated but with caution due to poor insulin clearance in CKD. Insulin regime
refers to previously outlined recommendation.
   •    Monitor serum creatinine and potassium annually and more frequently if there is evidence of renal impairment.
   •    Hyperkalemia associated with the use of an ACEI or ARB can often be managed by measures to reduce serum
        potassium levels rather than decreasing the dose or stopping the ACEI or ARB immediately
        > Avoid potassium-containing salt substitute or food products containing the salt substitute.
        > Avoid drugs that can impair kidney excretion of potassium: over-the-counter nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs,
        supplements, and herbal treatments
        > Avoid constipation by ensuring enough fluid intake and exercise.
        > Consider diuretics treatment to enhance the excretion of potassium in the kidneys especially when there is concomitant
        volume overload or hypertension.
        > Consider oral sodium bicarbonate especially in patients with CKD and metabolic acidosis.
   •    Metformin should not be used once the eGFR<30
   •    Treat blood pressure aggressively with target of <130/80 mmHg.
   •    Add diuretics if necessary (but in large doses inhibit insulin release

sections.title: Diabetic Retinopathy
sections.text:
It is one of the major causes of blindness. Poor glycemic control, nephropathy, hypertension and pregnancy, long duration of
diabetes are among the risk factors. It is preventable and its progression retarded by improved glycemic control and blood
pressure. Screening for early detection and laser therapy can prevent blindness

Screening for Diabetic Retinopathy
For all people with diabetes, yearly screening is necessary for early detection of ocular complications. The screening should
begin:
  •     Comprehensive eye examination in woman                         •   Five years after the diagnosis of diabetes for
        planning pregnancy, and during the first trimester,                individuals with Type 1 diabetes diagnosed after
        preferably at booking of antenatal clinic (ANC).                   puberty (around 14years).
        Further screening should be determined by the                  •   At puberty for individuals diagnosed with type 1
        degree of retinopathy detected at the initial                      diabetes before puberty
        appointment.                                                   •   At the time of diagnosis of diabetes for individuals
                                                                           with type 2 diabetes

For each of the scheduled screening visits, detailed patient’s assessment should include a complete ophthalmic examination
in the following steps:
   •    Take visual acuity (VA) without and with spectacles           •   Perform retinal evaluation by direct or indirect
   •    If VA less than 6/9 take VA with pin hole                         Ophthalmoscope or Fundus Photography
   •    Dilate the pupil by using the mydriatic agents                •   Identify retinal changes, document and if applicable
        (Tropicamide)                                                     grade the diabetic retinopathy and maculopathy as
   •    Identify presence of cataract or other causes of                  shown in Table 19.11
        media opacification.                                          •   Explain the results of screening to the patient and
                                                                          schedule rescreening (Table 19.11)

Table 19.11: Classification and Management of Diabetic Retinopathy
 Grade Features                                                                                      Outcome / Action
 R0      No disease                                                                                  Rescreen in 12 months
 R1      Mild background DR:                                                                         Rescreen in 12 months
         • Microaneurysms
         • Flame hemorrhages/exudates
         • >4 blot hemorrhages in one or both hemifields
         • Cotton wool spots
 R2      Moderate background DR:                                                                     Rescreen in 6 months
         • >4 blot hemorrhages in one hemifield
 R3      Severe non-proliferative (pre-proliferative) DR:                                            Refer to Eye Clinic
         • >4 blot hemorrhages in both hemifields
         • Intraretinal microvascular anomalies (IRMA)
         • Venous beading
 R4      Proliferative DR:                                                                           Refer to Eye Clinic
         • Neovascularization of the disc (NVD)
         • Neovascularization elsewhere (NVE)
         • Vitreous hemorrhage
         • Retinal detachment
 M0      No macular involvement                                                                      Rescreen in 12 months
 M1      Hard exudates within 1–2 disc diameters of fovea                                            Rescreen in 6 months
 M2      Blot hemorrhage or hard exudates within 1 disc diameter of fovea                            Refer to Eye Clinic
