         • Small pupil
         • Vitreous hemorrhage
         • Tractional retinal detachment
         • Corneal opacity

Key: R=Retinopathy; M=Maculopathy; P=Photocoagulation, U=Unclassified, At all times, remind patients to stop
smoking and intensify blood pressure, lipids and glycemic control.

sections.title: Thyroid Disorders
sections.text:
Thyroid disorders are conditions that affect the thyroid gland. There are specific kinds of thyroid disorders that includes
hypothyroidism, hyperthyroidism, goiter, thyroid nodules and thyroid cancer.

sections.title: Hypothyroidism
sections.text:
Hypothyroidism is a condition in which a person's thyroid hormone production is below normal. Common causes of the disease
are chronic autoimmune thyroiditis, post-surgery and post radioactive iodine. For neonatal hypothyroidism refer to neonatal
chapter.

Clinical Presentation
  •    Increased cholesterol levels,            •    Hair loss                                •    Constipation
  •    Depression                               •    Memory loss                              •    Hoarse voice
  •    Fatigue                                  •    Dry, rough skin

Investigations
  •    TSH should not typically be measured in seriously ill patients unless there is a strong suspicion of thyroid dysfunction.
       If TSH is elevated, it should be repeated together with free thyroxine (FT4) for confirmation.
  •    If TSH high, FT4 is low-overt hypothyroidism
  •    TSH high, normal Ft4-sublinical hypothyroidism

Indications for Treatment
All patients with overt hypothyroidism should be treated regardless of symptoms, unless the hypothyroidism is transient
(painless thyroiditis or subacute thyroiditis.
   •    TSH level persistently >10mU/L; treat all patients due to, increased likelihood of progression to overt disease and a
        higher risk of congestive heart failure, cardiovascular disease and mortality.
   •    TSH levels (4.5–10mU/L); consider, treatment in patients younger than 65 with increased cardiovascular risk (e.g.,
        previous cardiovascular disease, hypertension, documented diastolic dysfunction, atherosclerotic risk factors
        (dyslipidemia, diabetes mellitus, smoker), goiter, positive antithyroid peroxidase antibodies, evidence of autoimmune
        thyroiditis by ultrasound, pregnancy, or infertility), particularly when TSH level is persistently >7mU/L.
   •    Levothyroxine therapy could be considered also for symptomatic middle-aged patients for a short period of time. If a
        clear beneficial effect is observed, levothyroxine therapy could be maintained.
   •    Persistently mildly increased TSH levels (>4.5–10mU/L) with positive Thyroid Antibody and thyroid sonographic findings
        typical of autoimmune thyroiditis.

Pharmacological Management
Initial dose:
Clinical hypothyroidism
D: levothyroxine (PO) 1.6–1.8µg/kg ideal body weight 24hourly

Subclinical hypothyroidism
D: levothyroxine (PO) 1.1–1.2µg/kg is recommended 24hourly

  •    Take at least after 2hours fast, 30minutes before food intake. Alternatively, at bedtime (3 or more hours after the evening
       meal).
  •    When initiating therapy in young healthy adults with overt hypothyroidism, consider beginning treatment with full
       replacement doses
  •    Routine use of combined therapy with levothyroxine and triiodothyronine for hypothyroid patients is not recommended
  •    Assess TSH and adjust dosage when there are large changes in body weight, with aging, and with pregnancy.
  •    There is no convincing evidence to support routine use of thyroid extracts, L-T3 monotherapy, compounded thyroid
       hormones, iodine containing preparations, dietary supplementation, and over the counter preparations in the
       management of hypothyroidism.

Monitoring
 •    TSH monitoring 6–8weeks after any levothyroxine dose change, and yearly life–long monitoring once euthyroid is
      achieved (target TSH 0.2–4.0um/l). FT4 can be measured in early stages of treatment.
 •    In patients with central hypothyroidism, assessments of serum free T4 should guide therapy and targeted to exceed the
      mid normal range value for the assay being used.
 •    Wait for TSH equilibration–TSH equilibration requires eight to 12 weeks after any thyroxine dosage change. Once a
      stable dose is achieved–yearly TSH is sufficient.

In Pregnancy
When the elevation of the TSH level is confirmed, free T4 should be measured in order to classify the hypothyroidism as clinical
or overt (OH) and subclinical (SH).
   •   TSH > 2.5–4.0mU/L or with normal free T4: SH.
   •   TSH > 2.5 –4.0mU/L with low levels of free T4: OH.
   •   TSH =10.0mU/L, despite the level of free T4: OH

Women in reproductive period should be euthyroid before conceiving, as the hypothyroidism is associated with neural
development. Dose may be doubled during pregnancy and returned to normal dose after deliver

sections.title: Hyperthyroidism
sections.text:
Hyperthyroidism is a condition in which an overactive thyroid gland is producing an excessive amount of thyroid hormones that
circulate in the blood. Graves' disease, multinodular goiter (TMNG), inflammation of the thyroid gland (thyroiditis) and excessive
iodine intake are the most common cause of hyperthyroidism.

Clinical Presentation
  •    Tremors                                                           •    A rapid heart rate
  •    Excessive sweating                                                •    An enlarged thyroid gland
  •    Smooth velvety skin                                               •    Frequent bowel movements
  •    Fine hair

Investigations
  •    Baseline complete blood count, including white count with differential, and a liver profile (bilirubin and transaminases)
  •    Differential white blood cell count should be obtained during febrile illness and at the onset of pharyngitis in all patients
       taking antithyroid medication. Routine monitoring of white blood counts is not recommended
  •    Test for THS and T4
  •    When thyrotoxicosis is confirmed, if cause is not known request thyroid uptake scan

  Note: Management of hyperthyroidism depends on the cause

sections.title: Toxic Multinodular Goiter or Thyroid Antibody Positive
sections.text:
Patients with overtly Toxic multinodular goiter or Thyroid antibody are treated with either:

Non-Pharmacological Management
S: Radio iodine (131-I) therapy
         OR
S: Thyroidectomy

 Note: Long term, low-dose carbimazole should not be used for either condition except in some elderly

Surgery
  •   Patients with overt hyperthyroidism should be rendered euthyroid prior to the procedure with carbimazole pre-treatment
      (15–40mg daily, divided into 2–3doses a day for 4–8 weeks then a maintenance dose of 5–15mg, taken 24 hourly) with
      or without beta–adrenergic blockade (e.g. propranolol 1—40mg 6hourly). Preoperative iodine should not be used in this
      setting.
  •   Following thyroidectomy for Toxic multinodular goiter, it is suggested that serum calcium or intact parathyroid hormone
      levels be measured, and that calcitriol and oral calcium supplementation (maximum 1,200mg of calcium per day in two
      divided doses) be administered based on these results.
  •   Following surgery for Toxic multinodular goiter, thyroid hormone replacement should be started at a dose appropriate
      for the patient’s weight (0.8µg/lb. or 1.7µg/kg) and age, with elderly patients needing somewhat less. TSH should be
      measured every 1–2months until stable, and then annually.

Radioiodine
Radioactive iodine therapy should be used for retreatment of persistent or recurrent hyperthyroidism following inadequate
surgery for Toxic multinodular goiter or Thyroid antibody.

sections.title: Grave’s Hyperthyroidism
sections.text:
Pharmacological Management
 Medicine        Initial Therapy (4–6 weeks)          Maintenance Therapy (Gradual                Duration / Notes
                                                      reduction over 3–6 months)
 C: carbimazole      10–60 mg/day in 2–3 divided      5–10 mg/day                                 Continue for 12–18 months;
                     doses                                                                        taper or discontinue if TSH is
                                                                                                  normal

Beta Blockers are used for excessive sympathetic symptoms.
A: propranolol (PO) 40 to 120mg (24hourly or 12hourly)
         OR
B: atenolol (PO) 50–100mg 12hourly

Factors which favor use of antithyroid medicines
  •   High likelihood of remission (patients, especially females, with mild disease, small goiters, and negative or low-titer TSH-
      receptor antibody)
  •   Elderly or others with comorbidities increasing surgical risk or with limited life expectancy or unable to follow radiation
      safety regulations
  •   Previously operated or irradiated necks
  •   Moderate to severe active Graves’ ophthalmopathy

Radioactive Iodine
Potassium iodide (B) should be given in the immediate preoperative period as 5–7drops (0.25– 0.35 mL) Lugol’s solution (8
mg iodide/drop) or 1–2 drops (0.05–0.1 mL) saturated solution of potassium iodide (50 mg iodide/drop) three times daily mixed
in water or juice for 10 days before surgery

Factors which favor use of radioiodine
  •   Individuals with comorbidities increasing surgical risk
  •   Patients with previously operated or externally irradiated necks
  •   Lack of access to a high-volume thyroid surgeon
  •   Contraindications to antithyroid medicines use
  •   Females who are not pregnant and are not planning a pregnancy in the future (4–6months) following radioiodine therapy

Surgery
Consider the following factors
  •   Symptomatic compression or large goiters
  •   Low uptake of radioactive iodine
  •   Thyroid malignancy is documented or suspected or large non-functioning nodule
  •   Coexisting hyperparathyroidism requiring surgery
  •   Females planning a pregnancy in <4–6months
  •   Patients with moderate to severe active Graves’ ophthalmopathy
  •   If a patient with Grave’s disease becomes hyperthyroid after completing a course of carbimazole, consideration should
      be given to treatment with radioactive iodine or thyroidectomy. Low-dose carbimazole treatment for longer than 12–
      18months may be considered in patients not in remission who prefer this approach but evidence is that remission rate
      in adults is not improved by a course of medicines longer than 18 months
  •   Whenever possible, patients with Grave’s disease undergoing thyroidectomy should be rendered euthyroid with
      carbimazole.

sections.title: Thyroid Storm (Crisis)
sections.text:
Thyroid storm is one of the most life-threatening endocrine emergencies, resulting from exacerbation of manifestations of
thyrotoxicosis.

Triggers of thyroid storm include:
  •   Antithyroid withdraw                                              •    External beam radiation therapy.
  •   Acute infections                                                  •    It should be considered in very sick patients if they
  •   Thyroidal or nonthyroidal surgeries                                    present with recent history of thyrotoxicosis and a
  •   Iodinated contrast dyes                                                recent history of precipitating factor.

Patients with thyroid storm (tachycardia, arrhythmias, congestive heart failure, hypotension, hyperpyrexia, agitation, delirium,
psychosis, stupor and coma, as well as nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and hepatic failure) should receive a multimodal treatment
including:
   •    Beta-adrenergic blockade                                     •      Aggressive cooling with paracetamol and cooling
   •    Antithyroid medicine therapy                                        blankets
   •    Inorganic iodide                                             •      Volume resuscitation
   •    Corticosteroid therapy                                       •      Respiratory support
                                                                     •      Monitoring in an intensive care unit.

Thyroid storm is not a matter of thyroid levels increased beyond those of uncomplicated thyrotoxicosis, but the systemic
decompensation that occurs.

Table 19.12: Pharmacological Management
 Medicine            Dosing                                     Comments
 D: propylthiouracil 500–1000 mg (IV) loading dose,             • Blocks new thyroid hormone synthesis
                     then 250 mg every 4 hours                  • Inhibits peripheral conversion of T4 to T3
 C: carbimazole      40–60 mg (PO) 24 hourly                    • Blocks new thyroid hormone synthesis
 A: propranolol      60–80 mg (PO) every 4 hours                • Controls adrenergic symptoms
                                                                • Blocks T4 to T3 conversion at high doses
                                                                • Use caution and consider invasive monitoring in heart
                                                                failure
                                                                • Alternative: Esmolol infusion
 C: potassium           5 drops (0.25 mL ≈ 250 mg) (PO)         • Do NOT start until at least 1 hour after antithyroid drugs
 iodide (SSKI)          every 6 hours                           • Blocks thyroid hormone release
                                                                • Also reduces hormone synthesis
 A: hydrocortisone      300 mg (IV) loading dose, then 100      • May reduce T4 to T3 conversion
                        mg every 8 hours                        • Prevents relative adrenal insufficiency • Alternative:
                                                                Dexamethasone

 Note: In thyroid storm, propylthiouracil is preferred to carbimazole

sections.title: Cushing’s Syndrome
sections.text:
Cushing syndrome is a clinical condition resulting from prolonged exposure to excessive glucocorticoids from either
endogenous or exogenous sources. The most common cause of Cushing’s syndrome is from the administration of exogenous
sources.
Table:19.13 Classification of Cushing Syndrome
 Category                Subcategory / Cause                     Details
                         Pituitary adenoma (Cushing’s disease)   • Accounts for ~90–95% of ACTH-dependent cases
 ACTH-Dependent
                         Ectopic ACTH syndrome                   • Non-pituitary tumors producing ACTH
                         Adrenal adenoma                         • Autonomous cortisol secretion
 ACTH-Independent
                         Adrenal carcinoma                       • Malignant cortisol-secreting tumor
 Exogenous Causes        Glucocorticoid therapy                  • Most common overall cause of Cushing syndrome
 Pseudo-Cushing          Depression                              • Functional hypercortisolism without true Cushing
 States                                                          syndrome
                         Alcoholism                              • Reversible cortisol excess state
                         High cortisol secretion without typical • Biochemical hypercortisolism without clear clinical
 Other Conditions
                         features                                signs
                         Pregnancy                               • Physiological increase in cortisol levels

Clinical Presentation
The symptoms and signs of Cushing's syndrome result directly from chronic exposure to excess glucocorticoid. Establishing
the diagnosis is often difficult because none of the symptoms or signs are pathognomonic of the syndrome. An important clinical

clue to the presence of glucocorticoid excess is the simultaneous development and increasing severity of several of these
symptoms Common presenting symptoms include; -
   •   Central obesity
   •   Facial plethora
   •   Weakness of the proximal muscles
   •   Easily bruises and striae
   •   Hirsutism
   •   Glucose intolerance

Investigations
At least two first-line tests should be abnormal to establish the diagnosis of Cushing's syndrome
  •    The low-dose dexamethasone suppression tests                             - High dose dexamethasone suppression test
  •    24hrs urinary cortisol,                                           •    Pituitary CT - sensitivity of about 50% for identifying
  •    Late night salivary cortisol                                           microadenomas
  •    Differential Diagnostic Testing to established, the               •    MRI pituitary sensitivity up to 100%
       cause of Cushing’s syndrome                                       •    Adrenal ultrasonography/CT for suspected Adrenal
          - Morning serum ACTH                                                source

Table:19.14 Management of Cushing Syndrome
 Component                      Details
 General Considerations         • Without treatment, Cushing syndrome is often fatal.
                                • Mortality is commonly due to cardiovascular disease, hypertension, or infections.
                                • With appropriate therapy, symptoms improve within 2–12 months.
 Definitive Therapy (Preferred) Surgery according to source:
                                • Adrenal source → Adrenalectomy
                                • Pituitary source → Transsphenoidal resection
                                • Ectopic source → Tumor resection
 Pharmacological Management     S: metyrapone 30 mg/kg (PO), maximum 3,000 mg
                                • Administration: Usually given at midnight with a snack

sections.title: Prolactinoma
sections.text:
Are prolactin – secreting pituitary tumors
Classification
May present as Macroprolactinomas (<10mm) or Macroprolactinomas (>10mm)

Clinical Presentation
Symptoms are due to hyperprolactinemia which include galactorrhea, oligo/amenorrhea, infertility, reduced libido, impotence
and gynecomastia in male, headache and visual abnormality in large adenomas.

Investigations
Serum prolactin levels
  •    <100ng/ml possible prolactinoma 100-200ng/ml likely prolactinoma
  •    >200 ng/ml –diagnostic of prolactinoma

Pharmacological Management
Prolactinomas are unique among pituitary tumors in that first line treatment is medical not surgical. The mainstays of
management for prolactinomas are the dopamine agonist which are:

S: cabergoline (PO) 0.25-1mg (twice a week)
         OR
C: bromocriptine (PO) 2.5-20mg (24hourly or 12hourly)

sections.title: Diabetic Insipidus (DI)
sections.text:
DI is a disorder of water balance caused by non-osmotic renal loss of water leading to excretion of large volume of dilute urine

Classification
Central DI: Is caused by either complete or partial deficiency of antidiuretic hormone (ADH) secretion from the posterior pituitary
gland
Nephrogenic DI: Is caused by end organ unresponsiveness of the kidney to ADH
Dipsogenic DI: Is caused by excessive and inappropriate fluid intake due to a defective in thirsty mechanism

Clinical Presentation
Polyuria especially nocturnal

Investigations
  •    Polyuria and urine osmolality of <300 for a given plasma osmolality
  •    Volume depletion and orthostatic hypotension may be found
  •    Plasma Sodium may be normal or elevated

Pharmacological Management
In case of water deficit - water replacement. Treating of the underlying defect Central DI:
S: desmopressin (IV) 2-4 µg/day divided 12hourly
          OR
S: desmopressin (PO) Initial dose 0.05mg 12hourly; effective range: 0.1-1.2mg divided 8- 12hourly
          OR
S: desmopressin (Intranasal) 10-40µg (0.1-0.4mL) 24hourly, either as a single dose or divided into 2 or 3doses; usual dose is
20µg (0.2mL) 24hourly in 2divided doses

Nephrogenic DI: Treat the underlying cause
A: bendroflumethiazide (PO) 5mg 24hourly
         OR
D: hydrochlorothiazide 12.5- 25mg 24hourly)

sections.title: Pheochromocytoma
sections.text:
Pheochromocytoma are neuroendocrine tumors arising from catecholamine producing chromaffin cells of the adrenal medullar
but about 15–20% are extra-adrenal in origin

Clinical Presentation
The classic symptoms of pheochromocytoma are due to episodic release of excess catecholamines into circulation
(Norepinephrine and Epinephrine) which include; -
  •    Headaches
  •    Palpitations
  •    Anxiety and diaphoresis
  •    Hypertension which can be paroxysmal (∼48%) or persistent (∼29%).

Investigations
Table:19.15 Biochemical Tests Comparisons
  Test                                               Sensitivity (%)                     Specificity (%)
  Urine catecholamines                               83                                  88
  Urine total metanephrines                          76                                  94
  Urine catecholamines + metanephrines               90                                  98
  Urine VMA (vanillylmandelic acid)                  63                                  94
  Plasma catecholamines                              85                                  80
  Plasma metanephrines                               99                                  89

Tumor Localization
  •  Anatomic localization of a catecholamine-secreting tumor should be performed only after biochemical diagnosis has
     been confirmed
  •  Approximately 85% of catecholamine-secreting tumors are found in the adrenal glands, and 95% are found in the
     abdomen and pelvis
  •  Either CT or MRI are effective for localization of catecholamine-secreting tumors -sensitivity 89 vs 98% resp.

Table 19.16: Management of Pheochromocytoma
 Component                        Details
 Definitive Therapy               • Surgical resection of the tumor is the mainstay of treatment after confirmation of diagnosis
 Pre-operative Management         • Control effects of excess catecholamines to prevent perioperative complications
                                  • Use α-adrenergic blockade before surgery
 Non-selective α-blocker          • Initial dose:
                                  S: phenoxybenzamine 10 mg (PO) every 12 hours
                                  •Titrate to 20–40 mg every 8–12 hours
 Selective α-blocker              S: doxazosin 1–2 mg (PO) 24 hourly
 Additional Therapy               • Combined α + β blockade may be required (β-blocker added only after adequate α-blockade)

Table19.17: Causes of Adrenal Insufficiency
 Type                          Cause Category          Specific Causes
                               Autoimmune              • Autoimmune adrenalitis (most common)
                               Infections              • Tuberculosis
                                                       • HIV
                                                       • Fungal infections
                               Infiltrative diseases   • Metastatic cancer

                                                       • Amyloidosis
                                                       • Sarcoidosis
                               Genetic                 • Congenital adrenal hyperplasia
                                                       • Adrenoleukodystrophy
                               Vascular                • Adrenal hemorrhage (e.g., sepsis, anticoagulation)
                               Pituitary disorders     • Pituitary tumors
                                                       • Pituitary surgery
 Secondary
                                                       • Irradiation
                               Hormonal deficiency     • Isolated ACTH deficiency
                               Drug-induced            • Chronic glucocorticoid therapy → suppression of hypothalamic CRH
 Tertiary                      Hypothalamic causes     • Hypothalamic tumors
                                                       • Trauma

Table 19.18: Investigations for Adrenal Insufficiency
 Category               Test                                        Findings / Purpose
                        Serum electrolytes                          • Hyponatremia
                                                                    • Hyperkalemia (especially in primary adrenal insufficiency)
 Baseline Tests         Blood glucose                               • Hypoglycemia common
                        Complete blood count                        • May show anemia
                                                                    • Eosinophilia
                        Morning serum cortisol                      • Low levels suggest adrenal insufficiency
                        Plasma ACTH                                 • Elevated in primary
 Hormonal Assays                                                    • Low/normal in secondary/tertiary
                        Renin and aldosterone                       • High renin with low aldosterone (primary adrenal
                                                                    insufficiency)
                        Short Synacthen (ACTH stimulation)          • Failure of cortisol rise confirms diagnosis
 Dynamic Testing        test
                        Insulin tolerance test                      • Assesses secondary/tertiary causes (if safe to perform)
                        Adrenal CT/MRI                              • Detect infections, hemorrhage, tumors, calcification
 Imaging
                        Pituitary MRI                               • Indicated if secondary adrenal insufficiency suspected

                        Thyroid function tests                      • Assess for polyglandular autoimmune syndromes

                        HIV testing, TB screening                   • Performed when clinically indicated

Non Pharmacological Management
  •  Patient education: lifelong condition, recognition of adrenal crisis, emergency instructions.
  •  Lifestyle: balanced diet, adequate salt intake (especially in hot climates or during exercise).
  •  Medical alert identification: steroid card/bracelet.
  •  Vaccination & infection prevention: prompt treatment of infections.
  •  Stress management: patients must understand need for dose adjustment during illness, surgery, or trauma.

Pharmacological Management
Glucocorticoid Replacement
D: hydrocortisone: 15–25 mg/day orally in 2–3 divided doses (main dose in morning).
         OR
B: prednisolone (alternative): 3–5 mg/day orally 24 hourly.

Mineralocorticoid Replacement (not secondary/tertiary).
D: fludrocortisone: 50–200 µg/day orally 24 hourly.

Adrenal Crisis (Medical Emergency)
Causes
  •   Infection,
  •   Trauma,
  •   Surgery,
  •   Abrupt steroid withdrawal,
  •   Dehydration.

Clinical Presentation
Severe hypotension, shock, vomiting, abdominal pain, confusion, hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia.

Pharmacological Management
B: hydrocortisone (IV )100 mg bolus, then 200 mg/24h (continuous infusion or 50 mg every 6 hours).
A: sodium chloride 0.9% ± dextrose 5%. (IV) fluids: rapid

 Note: Correct electrolytes hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypercalcemia if present

sections.title: Disorder of Sexual Development (DSD)
sections.text:
DSD formerly known as intersex conditions are classified on the basis of genetics and the state of gonads. They may be caused
by virilization 64XX or under virilization 46XY. As well as (streak Ovary, Ovotestis, dysgenetic testis). The most common DSD
is Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (CAH).

Clinical Presentation
  •    Infant born with ambiguous or abnormal genitalia
  •    Infant with undescended testis, unilateral or bilateral
  •    Infant with hypospadias

Investigations
  •    Serum electrolytes
  •    Chromosomal analysis
  •    Karyotyping in a male looking male with undescended testis and/or hypospadias whether the genitalia appear normal
       or not
  •    Endocrine screening
  •    Anti-Müllerian Hormone (AMH)

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •  Counseling of the parents on
  •  The condition
  •  Naming of a child and
  •  Gender assignment

Pharmacological Management
Depends on type of the DSD it is either CAH or other forms of DSD (non-CAH DSD)
CAH DSD
Salt losing in crisis-
  •     Bolus normal saline (0.9% NaCl) and maintenance,
  •     Hypoglycemic 2-4 ml of 10% dextrose

Long-term treatment
D: hydrocortisone infants 2.5 to 5mg/dose, children 5-10mg 3times daily, adolescents &adults 15 to 30mg/day 2-3 divided
doses
Non-CAH DSD
D: testosterone 50-400mg monthly for 3cycles, then asses +/- D: testosterone cream

sections.title: Obesity (Adiposity Based Chronic Disease) in adults
sections.text:
Table19.19: Diagnosis and Assessment of Obesity
 Component                                 Assessment/Criteria
 Initial Screening                         Body Mass Index (BMI) = Weight (kg) ÷ Height² (m²); remains the first step
                                           for screening overweight/obesity.
 Assessment of Adiposity Distribution (for • Waist circumference: ≥94 cm in men, ≥80 cm in women indicates increased
 BMI ≥25 kg/m²)                            risk.
                                           • Waist-to-height ratio: >0.5 suggests central adiposity.
                                           • Waist-to-hip ratio: >0.90 in men, >0.85 in women indicates abdominal
                                           adiposity.
 Clinical Significance of Abdominal        Provides independent risk information beyond BMI and is strongly associated
 Adiposity                                 with cardiometabolic diseases and adiposity-related comorbidities.
 Clinical Staging of Adiposity             Stage 0: Adiposity without complications.
                                           Stage 1: Adiposity with mild/moderate complications (e.g., prediabetes, mild
                                           hypertension).
                                           Stage 2: Adiposity with severe complications (e.g., Type 2 Diabetes,
                                           advanced cardiovascular disease, Obstructive Sleep Apnea).
 Functional Assessment                     Evaluate:
                                           • Physical limitations
                                           • Sleep disorders (e.g., sleep apnea)
                                           • Mood disorders
                                           • Quality of life impact
 Component                                     Assessment/Criteria
 Laboratory Evaluation                         • Fasting blood glucose
                                               • HbA1c
                                               • Lipid profile (total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, triglycerides)
                                               • Liver function tests (for Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver
                                               disease)
                                               • Thyroid function tests (if secondary causes suspected)
 Medication Review                             Assess for medicines associated with weight gain:
                                               • Corticosteroids
                                               • Antipsychotics
                                               • Insulin
                                               • Certain antihypertensives
 Risk Stratification                           Assess for cardiometabolic risk factors:
                                               • Hypertension
                                               • Hyperlipidemia
                                               • Hyperglycemia
                                               • Elevated liver enzymes
                                               • Family history of premature cardiovascular disease
 Complications of Overweight/Obesity           Increased risk of:
                                               • Cardiovascular disease
                                               • Type 2 Diabetes
                                               • Pulmonary Embolism
                                               • Gallbladder disease
                                               • Colorectal Cancer
                                               • Osteoarthritis
                                               • Chronic back pain
                                               • Increased all-cause mortality
 Psychosocial Assessment                       Individuals living with obesity may experience stigma, shame, depression,
                                               and anxiety; psychosocial support should be considered.

Hospitals and health professionals as role models
  •   An overweight/obese health worker is less likely to counsel patients with obesity
  •   Provide healthy food choices for patients, employers, visitors, and communities, with pricing incentives
  •   Label drinks sold in hospital cafeterias as red, yellow, or green to shift consumption towards healthier beverages
  •   Prohibit fast food outlets in hospital premises

Table 19.20: Non-Pharmacological Management
 Component                                Recommendations
 Weight Loss Goal                         • Modest sustained weight loss of 3–5% improves triglycerides, blood glucose, HbA1c,
                                          and reduces risk of Type 2 Diabetes.
 Nutritional Management                   • Provide dietary counseling (refer to nutrition chapter).

 Tailored Physical Activity Program       • Start with 30 minutes of moderate-intensity activity 3–5 times/week.
                                          • Progress to ≥60 minutes on most days.
                                          • Include muscle-strengthening activities ≥2 days/week.
                                          • Physical activity equivalent to 60 minutes of brisk walking daily helps prevent weight
                                          regain.
 Behavioral Support                       • Identify triggers for overeating/inactivity and modify behaviors.
                                          • Encourage goal-setting.
                                          • Maintain food/activity records.
                                          • Promote consistent eating patterns.
                                          • Encourage family support.
 Structured Lifestyle Programs            • Participate in structured programs combining diet and exercise for ≥6 months.

 Weight Maintenance                       • Provide ongoing support (monthly or more frequent).
                                          • Encourage 200–300 minutes/week of physical activity.
                                          • Weekly weight monitoring.
                                          • Continue reduced-calorie diet.
 Bariatric surgery                        Consider for:
                                          • BMI ≥40 kg/m², or
                                          • BMI ≥35 kg/m² with comorbidities when lifestyle modification/pharmacotherapy fails.
 Medication Monitoring                    • Review and adjust antihypertensive and antidiabetic medications as weight loss
                                          progresses.

Table 19.21: Innovative Strategies for Obesity Prevention and Management
 Component                                Recommendations
 Primary Care Strengthening               • Use patient registries.
                                          • Implement electronic health records.
                                          • Promote multidisciplinary care teams.
 Digital Health Tools                     • Text messaging support
                                          • Remote monitoring (BP, glucose, smart scales)
                                          • Mobile applications
                                          • Telehealth support
 Healthy Healthcare Environments          • Provide healthy food choices with pricing incentives.
                                          • Use beverage labeling (red/yellow/green).
                                          • Restrict fast food outlets within hospital premises.

Table 19.22: Physical Activity Recommendations
 Component                           Details
 General Benefits                    • Physical fitness requires proper nutrition, moderate-to-vigorous activity, and
                                     adequate rest.
                                     • Improves insulin resistance, lowers HbA1c (~0.7% in Type 2 Diabetes),
                                     improves lipid profile, lowers blood pressure, and supports weight control.
 Types of Activities                 • Occupational: walking, lifting, farming.
                                     • Leisure: exercise, sports, gardening, dancing.
 Aerobic Activities                  • Improve body composition and cardiorespiratory fitness.
                                     • Examples: brisk walking, cycling, swimming, jogging, sports.
                                     • Moderate intensity: able to talk but not sing.
                                     • Vigorous intensity: only a few words before pausing for breath.
                                     • Recommended ≥30 minutes/day, ≥5 days/week.
 Muscle-Strengthening Activities     • Improve muscle mass, strength, and endurance.
                                     • Examples: push-ups, pull-ups, crunches, heavy gardening.
                                     • Perform ≥8 repetitions, ≥2 days/week.
 Stretching Activities               • Improve flexibility and range of motion.
                                     • Examples: neck flexion, arm rotations, trunk rotations.
 Coordination Activities             • Improve balance, agility, and proprioception (important for fall prevention in older
                                     adults).
                                     • Example: standing on one leg/toes.
 Improving Exercise Adoption         • Assess physical activity levels in all patients.
                                     • Provide brief advice on recommended activity levels during routine care.

Pharmacological Management
Indicated for BMI ≥30 kg/m², or ≥27 kg/m² with comorbidities, or if lifestyle changes fail to achieve ≥0.5 kg/week weight loss
after 3–6 months.

 Note: medications are used as an adjunct to diet and physical exercise

S: orlistat: 120 mg orally every 8 hours with meals containing fat, avoid if not having meals; reduces fat absorption by ~30%.

GLP-1 and GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonists are now strongly recommended for adiposity related chronic disease management
and their metabolic complications.

Continue pharmacotherapy beyond 12 weeks only if ≥5% initial body weight loss is achieved after three months.

sections.title: Prevention of Cardiovascular diseases
sections.text:
Cardiovascular disease (CVD) prevention is a coordinated set of actions, at the population level or targeted at an individual at
risk of developing cardiovascular disease, that are aimed at eliminating or minimizing the impact of CVDs and their related
disabilities.

Diagnostic/screening Criteria
Major risk factors for ischaemic cardiovascular and cerebrovascular disease are:
  •    Diabetes mellitus
  •    Hypertension                                                   •   Smoking
  •    Central obesity: waist circumference ≥ 94cm (men)              •   Age: Men >50 years, Women >60 years
       and ≥ 80cm (women)                                             •   Family history of early onset cardiovascular
  •    Dyslipidemia (fasting levels): Total cholesterol > 5               disease; Male relatives <55 years and Female
       mmol/L, or LDL> 3mmol/L, or HDL< 1 mmol/L in                       relatives <65 year
       men and < 1.2mmol/L in women

Estimation of total cardiovascular risk is important for prevention of CVD in an individual, should be adapted to his or her total
CV risk: the higher the risk, the more intense the management should be (See Table 20.1).

Table 20.1: Cardiovascular Disease Risk Classification and WHO Risk estimation
 Risk Category       Criteria
 Very High Risk      Subjects with any of the following:
                     • Documented Cardiovascular Disease (clinical or unequivocal on imaging), including:
                     - Previous Acute Myocardial Infarction
                     - Acute Coronary Syndrome
                     - Coronary revascularization or other arterial revascularization procedures
                     - Stroke
                     - Transient Ischemic Attack
                     - Aortic aneurysm
                     - Peripheral Artery Disease
                     • Unequivocal imaging evidence of CVD (e.g., plaque on coronary angiography or carotid ultrasound). Does
                     not include increased carotid intima-media thickness alone.
                     • Diabetes Mellitus with target organ damage (e.g., proteinuria) or major risk factors such as smoking, marked
                     hypercholesterolemia, or marked hypertension.
                     • Severe Chronic Kidney Disease (GFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m²).
                     • Calculated CVD risk score ≥10%.
 High Risk           Subjects with:
                     • Markedly elevated single risk factors:
                     - Cholesterol >8 mmol/L (>310 mg/dL), e.g., familial hypercholesterolemia
                     - Blood pressure ≥180/110 mmHg
                     • Most other patients with Diabetes Mellitus (except young people with type 1 DM without major risk factors).
                     • Moderate Chronic Kidney Disease (GFR 30–59 mL/min/1.73 m²).
                     • Calculated CVD risk score ≥5% and <10%.
 Moderate Risk       • Calculated CVD risk score ≥1% and <5% over 10 years.
                     • Many middle-aged individuals fall into this category.
 Low Risk            • Calculated CVD risk score <1%.

Non-pharmacological Treatment
Table 20.2: General measures for Lifestyle modification
 Risk Factor         Target Goal / Recommended Level
 Smoking             • No exposure to tobacco in any form.
 Diet                • Reduce dietary sodium intake to ≤2.4 g sodium/day (≈6 g sodium chloride/day).
                     • Diet low in saturated fats.
                     • Emphasize whole grains, vegetables, fruits, and fish.
                     • Limit alcohol intake to:
                     – Men: ≤2 units/day
                     – Women: ≤1 unit/day
                     • Alcohol consumption should not exceed 5 days/week.
                     • 1 unit of alcohol = 25 mL spirits, 125 mL wine, 340 mL beer/sorghum beer, or 60 mL sherry.
 Physical Activity   • At least 150 minutes/week of moderate-intensity aerobic exercise (e.g., 30 minutes/day for 5 days/week),
                                OR
                     • 75 minutes/week of vigorous-intensity aerobic exercise (e.g., 15 minutes/day for 5 days/week),
                                OR
                     • An equivalent combination of moderate and vigorous activity.
 Body Weight         • Maintain BMI 18.5–24.9 kg/m²

 Risk Factor         Target Goal / Recommended Level
 Waist               • Men: <94 cm
 Circumference       • Women: <80 cm
 Blood Pressure      • Target: <140/90 mmHg
 LDL-Cholesterol     Very high risk: <1.8 mmol/L (<70 mg/dL) or ≥50% reduction if baseline is 1.8–3.5 mmol/L.
 (Primary Lipid      High risk:<2.6 mmol/L (<100 mg/dL) or ≥50% reduction if baseline is 2.6–5.1 mmol/L.
 Target)             Low–moderate risk:<3.0 mmol/L (<115 mg/dL).
 HDL-Cholesterol     • No specific treatment target.
                     • Lower risk associated with:
                     – Men: >1.0 mmol/L (>40 mg/dL)
                     – Women: >1.2 mmol/L (>45 mg/dL)
 Triglycerides       • No specific treatment target.
                     • <1.7 mmol/L (<150 mg/dL) indicates lower risk.
                     • Higher levels warrant assessment of other risk factors.
 Diabetes Mellitus   • Target HbA1c: <7%

Recommended to repeat CV risk assessment every 5years, and more often for individuals with risks close to thresholds
mandating treatment.
For specific pharmacological treatment for hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia refer specific sections, respectively.

sections.title: Management of Dyslipidemias
sections.text:
Lowering blood cholesterol levels using statins is recommended to reduce the impact of cardiovascular morbidity and mortality

Clinical indication for lipid lowering medicine therapy
  •    Established atherosclerotic disease
  •    Ischemic heart disease
  •    Peripheral vascular disease
  •    Atherothrombotic stroke

  Note
  Lipid lowering medicines should be administered in this setting even if the level of cholesterol is normal
     •    Type 2 diabetics >40 years of age, or diabetes for >10 years,
     •    Existing cardiovascular disease,
     •    Chronic kidney disease (eGFR < 60mL/min).
     •    CV risks of more than >20% in 10years Such high-risk patients will benefit from lipid lowering (statin) therapy
          irrespective of their baseline LDL levels.

Pharmacological Management
B: atorvastatin (PO) 20mg to 80mg 24hourly
          OR
S: rosuvastatin (PO) 10mg-40mg 24hourly
          AND
D: fenofibrate (PO) 120mg /160mg /200mg 24hourly

  Note
    •  Criteria for initiating lipid lowering therapy are the same as for HIV uninfected patients. Fasting lipid levels should be
       done 3months after starting lopinavir/ritonavir and atazanavir/ritonavir.
    •  Patients at high risk (>20% risk of developing a CVS event in 10years) should switch to atazanavir/ritonavir and
       repeat the fasting lipid profile in 3 months.
    •  Concomitant use of Ezetimibe and Atorvastatin can lead to liver damage and rhabdomyolysis.
    •  Fenofibrate indicated Hypertriglyceridemia, in which statin alone is not enough to treat & lower the
       hypertriglyceridemia.

sections.title: Chronic Stable Coronary Artery Disease (CSCAD) / ISCHAEMIC Heart Disease (IHD)
sections.text:
Clinical history is characterized by chest pain due to myocardial ischemia usually inducible by exercise, emotion, or other stress
and reproducible, relieved by rest but may occur spontaneously and stable in nature, occurs in high-risk patient.

Non-Pharmacological Management
General Measures
  •   Lifestyle modification (refer to table 20.2).
  •   Annual control of lipids, glucose metabolism and creatinine are recommended in all patients with known IHD.
  •   A resting ECG is recommended in all patients at presentation and immediately after an episode of chest pain suspected
      to indicate clinical instability of CAD, Consider immediate referral.
  •   A resting transthoracic echocardiogram is recommended in some patients for:
      > exclusion of alternative causes of angina
      > regional wall motion abnormalities suggestive of CAD
      > measurement of LVEF for risk stratification purpose
      > evaluation of diastolic function.

Consider referral if no echocardiogram available or unavailability of skilled personnel to perform transthoracic.
  •   Stress ECG
  •   Stress Echocardiography; a) Physical (Exercise) Stress Echo; b) Dobutamine (Pharmacological) Stress Echo performed
      to Orthopedic related disorders pt who cannot walk on the Treadmill machine).

Pharmacological Management
A: acetylsalicylic acid soluble (PO) 75–150mg 24hourly
          OR
D: clopidogrel 75mg (PO) 24 hourly (in patients allergic to aspirin)
          AND
C: isosorbide dinitrate (PO) 20mg-40mg 12hourly

If nitrates cannot be tolerated, consider stepwise approach below.

Step 1: add ß-blocker if not contraindicated:

B: atenolol (PO) 12.5/25mg 24hourly
         OR
C: metoprolol succinate (SR) (PO) 25–200mg 24hourly
         OR
S: metoprolol tartrate (IV) 5mg 2min for max 3doses, then (PO) 50-100mg 12hourly
         OR
S: bisoprolol (PO) 2.5mg /10mg 24hourly

Step 2: Consider long-acting calcium channel blocker or I(f) current inhibitor, if a ß-blocker cannot be tolerated or
contraindicated.

D: diltiazem (PO) 60mg 6 to 8hourlydaily; if suspects Prinzmetal Angina.
           OR
S: verapamil (PO) 60mg -120mg 8hourly 24hourly
           OR
S: ivabradine (PO) 2.5mg /5mg 24hourly

Step 3: Add low inward sodium current blocker anti-anginal

S: ranolazine (PO) 375-1000 mg/kg 12hourly

  Note:
    •   All patients with chronic stable angina are high-risk for cardiovascular events, lipid lowering medicines should be
        initiated (See Section 20.2).
    •   Consider immediate referral to high level of care where there are adequate resources for case management.

Indications for Referral
  •    Angina or chest pain suspected to indicate clinical instability of CAD
  •    When diagnosis is in doubt/ failed medical therapy; no echocardiogram available or unavailability of skilled personnel to
       perform transthoracic echocardiogram.

Before referring to the high facility there is likelihood of clinical instability of stable CAD consider giving:

A: acetylsalicylic acid (PO) 300mg stat.
          AND
B: atorvastatin (PO) 80mg stat
          AND
D: clopidogrel (PO) 300mg stat

sections.title: Unstable Angina (UA)
sections.text:
Unstable angina is a medical emergency and if untreated can progress to Non-ST Elevation Myocardial Infarction (NSTEMI)
Diagnostic Criteria
Presents as chest pain or discomfort like stable angina but with the following additional characteristics:
  •   Angina at rest or minimal effort, occurring for the first time, particularly at rest and prolonged >10minutes, not relieved
      by sublingual nitrates.
  •   The pattern of angina accelerates and gets worse.
  •   The chest pain may be associated with ST segment depression or T wave inversion or normal ECG without rise in
      cardiac enzymes (biomarkers i.e. Total Creatinine, Creatine - MB and Troponin)

sections.title: Non-ST Elevation Myocardial Infarction (NSTEMI)
sections.text:
Non-ST Elevation Myocardial Infarction is a medical emergency characterized with chest pain that is increasing in frequency
and/or severity or occurring at rest, associated with elevated cardiac enzymes and ST segment depression or T wave inversion
or normal ECG.

Diagnostic Criteria
Presents with typical chest pain with the following additional characteristics.
  •     Electrocardiogram (ECG) may show ST segment depression or transient ST segment elevation, or normal ECG does
        not exclude the diagnosis (serial ECG is important).
  •     Raised Cardiac Biomarker’s – Total Creatine Kinase (Total-CK), Creatine Kinase - MB (CK- MB) and standard/highly
        sensitive Troponin I or T.
Non-Pharmacological Management
Both UA and NSTEMI are medical emergencies with the same pathophysiological progressive instability of CAD, which share
similar management approach.
Supportive Therapy
  •     Admit patient into high dependent ward/ICU/CCU for hemodynamic monitoring, bed rest in Fowler’s position and
        reassurance.
  •     Oxygen via nasal blog cannula or face mask if saturation < 92%.
  •     Establish Peripheral Intravenous line for intravenous fluid or drug administration.
  •     Hemodynamics blood pressure, heart rate and electrocardiogram rhythm monito
Pharmacological Management
Adjunctive therapy, Control cardiac pain.
C: glyceryl trinitrate (Nitroglycerin) sub–lingual/ spray 0.5mg (make sure patient has not taken phosphodiesterase–5 inhibitor).

For persistent pain and if oral therapy is insufficient.
S: glyceryl Trinitrate (Nitroglycerin) (IV), 1–2µg/kg/min titrated with chest pain over 8– 24hours.
           OR
C: morphine (IV)1–2mg/minute dilute 10mg up to 10mL with sodium chloride solution 0.9%. Total maximum dose10 mg, repeat
after 4hours if necessary
   Note: If pain is not responsive to this dose, it is suggestive for ongoing unresolved ischemia. This requires immediate
   referral to high level of care where resources available to manage Acute Coronary Syndrome or to exclude differential
   diagnosis.

Antiplatelet Therapy
A: acetylsalicylic acid (PO) 300mg stat then followed by 75mg/100mg 24hourly
           AND
D: clopidogrel (PO) 300mg /600mg start then followed by 75mg 24hourly
           OR
S: ticagrelor (PO) 180mg stat followed by 90mg 12 hourly
For first year following ACS event: 90 mg 12hourly. After 1year of maintenance: 60mg 12hourly.
           OR
S: prasugrel (PO) 60mg stat then followed by 10mg 24 hourly

Statin high dose
B: atorvastatin (PO) 80mg stat then 40mg 24hourly
          OR
S: rosuvastatin (PO) 10mg-40mg 24hourly

Anticoagulant
C: unfractionated Heparin (IV) 70–100U/Kg body weight 24hourly
         OR
D: low molecular weight heparin (SC) 1mg/kg body weight 12hourly

Beta blocker (ß –blockers)
In case of LV dysfunction
C: carvedilol initial dose (PO) 6.25mg 12hourly preferred, titrate the dose upward. Max. Dose 25mg 12hourly
          OR
In the settings of normal LV systolic function
B: atenolol 25–50mg (PO) 24hourly,
          OR
C: metoprolol succinate (SR) (PO) 25 – 200mg 24hourly.
          OR
S: metoprolol tartrate 5mg (IV) 2min for maximum of 3 doses, then (PO) 50-100mg 12hourly
          OR
S: bisoprolol (PO) 2.5mg – 10mg 24hourly
Angiotensin Converting Enzyme Inhibitors (ACEIs)
B: captopril (PO) 6.25mg–25mg 8hourly
          OR
C: enalapril (PO) 10mg 12 hourly
          OR
C: lisinopril (PO) 5mg /10mg 24hourly

If ACEI’S are not well tolerated, consider ARB’s
B: losartan (PO) 25mg/50mg 24hourly
          OR
S: candesartan (PO) 8mg/16mg 24hourly
          OR
S: telmisartan (PO) 40mg / 80mg 24hourly
          OR
S: irbesartan (PO) 150mg / 300mg 24hourly

Referral
High suspicion index of acute coronary syndrome immediate consider referral to high level of care where resources are available
to manage. In acute settings before referral from low to high level of care if available consider giving the following urgently:
C: glyceryl trinitrate (Nitroglycerin) sub-lingual 0.5mg spray prn for intolerable chest pain
          AND
A: acetylsalicylic acid (PO)300mg stat (chew)
          AND
D: clopidogrel (PO) 300mg/600mg stat
          AND
S: rosuvastatin (PO) 10mg-40mg stat (High dose)
          OR
B: atorvastatin (PO) 80mg stat (High dose)

sections.title: ST Elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI)
sections.text:
STEMI is a medical emergency caused by the complete or partial occlusion of a coronary artery and requires prompt
hospitalization and intensive care intervention management

Clinical Presentation
Severe chest pain with the following characteristics
  •    Site: retrosternal or epigastric, quality: crushing, constricting, or burning pain or discomfort.
  •    Radiation to the neck and/or down the inner part of the left arm.
  •    Duration: at least 20 minutes and often not responding to sublingual nitrates.
  •    Occurrence: at rest. May be associated with pulmonary oedema sweating, hypotension or hypertension, arrhythmias.

Diagnostic Criteria
Simple recognition triage: Two out of three points most likely point to STEMI diagnosis
  •   Symptoms - typical/atypical chest pain
  •   ECG – ST elevation in in two contiguous leads ≥0.1mV
  •   Raised cardiac biomarkers– Total Creatine Kinase (Total-CK), Creatine Kinase -MB (CK-MB) and Standard/Highly
      Sensitive Troponin I or T

Non-Pharmacological Management
Supportive therapy
  •   Consider cardio-pulmonary resuscitation, if necessary, before transfer (cardiac arrest– cardiopulmonary resuscitation).
  •   Oxygen 40% via facemask, if saturation < 92% or if in distress
  •   See section 20.4.2 above on supportive therapy for NSTEMI

Pharmacological Management
Adjunctive therapy Control cardiac pain
C: glyceryl trinitrate sub-lingual/ spray 0.5mg (make sure patient hasn’t taken phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor).

For persistent pain and if oral therapy is insufficient
S: glyceryl Trinitrate (IV) 1–2 µg/kg/min titrated with chest pain over 8–24 hours.
          OR
C: morphine (IV) 1–2 mg/minute dilute 10 mg up to 10 mL with sodium chloride solution 0.9%. Total maximum dose: 10 mg,
repeat after 4 hours if necessary.

Anti-platelets therapy
A: acetylsalicylic (PO) 300mg stat then followed by 75mg/100mg (PO) 24hourly
          AND
D: clopidogrel (PO) 300mg/600mg stat then followed by 75mg 24hourly
          OR
S: prasugrel (PO) 60mg stat, given after defining coronary anatomy prior to onset of PCI, then 10mg as maintenance dosage.
          OR
S: ticagrelor (PO) 180mg stat followed by 90mg 12hourly

Statin high dose
B: atorvastatin (PO) 80mg start then 40mg 24hourly
          OR
S: rosuvastatin (PO) 10mg-40mg 24hourly

Anticoagulant
C: unfractionated Heparin (IV) 70–100U/Kg 24hourly
         OR
D: low molecular weight heparin (SC) 1mg/kg 12hourly, Reduce dose in renal failure patient to 0.5mg/kg

Beta blocker (ß –blockers) In case of LV dysfunction
C: carvedilol (PO) initial dose 6.25mg 12hourly daily preferred, titrate dose upward to maximum dose 25mg hourly daily

In the settings of normal systolic function
B: atenolol (PO) 12.5mg or 25mg or 50mg 24hourly
          OR
C: metoprolol succinate (SR) (PO) 25 – 200mg 24hourly
          OR
S: metoprolol tartrate (IV) 5mg 2min for max 3doses, then (PO) 50-100 mg 12hourly
          OR
S: bisoprolol (PO) 2.5mg – 10mg 24hourly
          OR
S: verapamil SR (PO) 240 mg – 480 mg daily in 1-2 divided doses

 Note: Verapamil SR should be initiated from 7 days’ post myocardial infarction; any single dose should not exceed 240mg
 as secondary prevention of myocardial infarction.

Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme Inhibitors (ACEIs)
B: captopril (PO) 6.25mg or 12.5mg 8hourly
          OR
C: enalapril (PO) 10mg 12hourly
          OR
C: lisinopril (PO) 5mg-10mg 24hourly

If ACEI’S are not well tolerated, consider ARB’s
B: losartan (PO) 25mg/50mg 24hourly
          OR
S: candesartan (PO) 8mg/16mg 24hourly
          OR
S: telmisartan (PO) 40mg / 80mg 24hourly
          OR
S: irbesartan (PO) 150mg / 300mg 24hourly

Definitive management of STEMI – Reperfusion therapy (Myocardial reperfusion)
Myocardial reperfusion with rapid recanalization of infarct related artery is the key to success in the management of ST Elevation
Myocardial Infarction (STEMI). Timely reperfusion is crucial for minimization of infarct size and thereby for preservation of left
ventricular function and reduction in mortality in STEMI patients. The two main reperfusion strategies for STEMI patients are;
  •    Thrombolytic/Fibrinolytic therapy (preferably chest pain duration less 12 hrs.)
  •    Primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PPCI) (preferably less than 90 mins of Door to Needle Time)

Thrombolytic agents
S: streptokinase (IV) 1.5 million units diluted in 100 mL sodium chloride 0.9%, infused over 30–60minutes
          OR
S: alteplase (TPA) (IV) 15mg as bolus, 0.75mg/kg over 30min, then 0.5mg/kg over 60min
          OR
S: tenecteplase (same recanalization)0.25-0.5/mg/kg IV bolus

Absolute contraindication for Thrombolytics
  •   Previous allergy to streptokinase or used within the            •    Relative contraindication for Thrombolytics
      last year for streptokinase only.                               •    Refractory hypertension
  •   Stroke CVA within the last 3 months                             •    TIA in the preceding 6 months,
  •   History of recent major trauma                                  •    Subclavian central venous catheter
  •   Bleeding within the last month                                  •    Warfarin therapy
  •   Aneurysms                                                       •    Pregnancy
  •   Brain or spinal surgery or head injury within the               •    Traumatic resuscitation
      preceding month                                                 •    Recent retinal laser treatment
  •   Active bleeding or known bleeding disorder.

Referral is urgent for all suspected or diagnosed cases to high level care equipped with cardiac catheterization laboratory for
Coronary angiogram (CAG) followed by Percutaneous Coronary Intervention (PCI). In case of triple vessel or multivessel
disease, or left main disease consider Coronary artery bypass graft (CABG), especially in patients with diabetes mellitus, high
syntax score

sections.title: Hypertension
sections.text:
Hypertension is elevation of Blood Pressure SBP ≥ 140 mmHg and DBP ≥90 mmHg measured at least three separate
occasions. Hypertension is a major independent risk factor for the development of CAD, stroke, and renal failure.

Diagnostic Criteria
Blood Pressure should be measured on three separate occasions, a minimum of 2 days apart and/or taken over for a period of
two months. Minimum of 3 blood pressure readings must be taken at the first visit to confirm hypertension. Ambulatory Blood
Pressure monitoring should be done to exclude Masked or white coat hypertension and monitoring of Blood Pressure response
to anti-hypertensives.

Table 20.3: Classification of Hypertension and Confirmation of Diagnosis
 Class of Hypertension SBP (mmHg) DBP (mmHg) Confirmation of Diagnosis
 Grade 1                   140–159        90–99          Confirm after 3 months of lifestyle modification
 Grade 2                   160–179        100–109        Confirm during the same visit
 Grade 3                   ≥180           ≥110           Confirm during the same visit

Consider secondary hypertension with identifiable cause in young patients < 40 years or elderly patient > 60 years presenting
for first time with hypertension.

 Note
   •  Recommend an alternative contraceptive method for women using oestrogen containing oral contraceptive.
   •  Evidence of end organ damage, i.e. cardiomegaly, proteinuria or uremia, retinopathy or evidence of stroke, dictates
      immediate treatment.

Treatment goal of Hypertension
  •   In patients aged 18 - 59 years without major comorbidities, and in patients 60 years or older who have diabetes, chronic

  •   In patients aged 60 years or older who do not have diabetes or chronic kidney disease, the blood pressure goal level

sections.title: Resistant (Refractory) Hypertension
sections.text:
Hypertension that remains >140/90mmHg despite the use of 3 antihypertensive drugs in a rational combination at full doses
and including a diuretic i.e. thiazide. Consider all correctable causes of refractory hypertension before you refer.

sections.title: Hypertensive Urgency
sections.text:
Symptomatic severe hypertension SBP 180mmHg and/or DBP >110 mmHg without evidence of target organ damage, such as
pulmonary edema, cardiac ischemia, neurologic deficits, or acute renal failure.
 Note: All patients with hypertensive urgency should be treated in hospital

Pharmacological Management
The goal is to lower DBP to 100mmHg slowly over 48–72hours. This can be achieved with two or more oral agents preferably,
Refer to Figure 20.3.

sections.title: Hypertensive Emergency
sections.text:
A marked elevated systolic blood pressure SBP≥180mmHg and/or a diastolic DBP≥130mmHg associated with life threatening
situations (target end organ damage) one or more of the following:
   •    Unstable angina/myocardial infarction
   •    Hypertensive encephalopathy e.g. severe headache, visual disturbances, confusion, coma, or seizures which may result
        in cerebral haemorrhage
   •    Acute left ventricular failure with severe pulmonary oedema (extreme breathlessness at rest)
   •    Excessive circulating catecholamine: e.g. pheochromocytoma – rare cause of emergency; food or drug interaction with
        monoamine oxidase inhibitors
   •    Rapidly progressive renal failure
   •    Acute aortic dissection
   •    Eclampsia and severe pre-eclampsia

Pharmacological Management
C: labetalol (IV) 20–80mg bolus every 10 minutes or 0.5–2mg/min infusion stat 20 mg, then 20–80 mg every10 min as needed,
or stat with 0.5 mg/min infusion, then 1–2 mg/min (may be up to 4 mg/min) IV infusion up to 300 mg/d max.

sections.title: Heart Failure
sections.text:
Heart Failure is a clinical syndrome characterized by typical symptoms (e.g. breathlessness, ankle swelling and fatigue) that
may be accompanied by signs (e.g. elevated jugular venous pressure, pulmonary crackles and peripheral oedema) caused by
a structural and/or functional cardiac abnormality, resulting in a reduced cardiac output and/or elevated intracardiac pressures
at rest or during stress.

sections.title: Heart Failure in Pregnancy
sections.text:
Symptoms and signs of heart failure in a pregnant woman are an indication for urgent assessment to establish a diagnosis and
appropriate management. This is best accomplished through a multidisciplinary approach in which both cardiologists and
obstetricians need to participate in order to provide expert counselling and care in pursuit of safe motherhood, as well as to
exclude underlying cause of heart failure.

sections.title: Acute Heart Failure (AHF) or Decompensated Acute Heart Failure (ADHF)
sections.text:
AHF is defined as rapid or gradual onset of signs and symptoms of heart failure that results in urgent unplanned hospitalization
or Emergency Medicine Department visits. The clinical signs and symptoms are significantly life threatening if the above
features occur in patients with established diagnosis with structurally heart disease categorized as Acute Decompensated Heart
Failure (ADHF). The cause and immediate precipitating factor(s) of the AHF must be identified and treated to prevent further
damage to the heart.

Non-Pharmacological Management
Oxygen therapy and/or ventilatory support.
  •   Non-invasive positive pressure ventilation includes both CPAP and bi–level positive pressure ventilation (PPV)
  •   Mechanical ventilation

 Note: In AHF, oxygen should not be used routinely in non–hypoxemic patients, as it causes vasoconstriction and a reduction
 in cardiac output

Pharmacological Management
Recommendations for the management of patients with acute heart failure:

Diuretics: Diuretics are a cornerstone in the treatment of patients with AHF. In patients with new- onset AHF or those with
chronic, decompensated HF not receiving oral diuretics the initial recommended dose should be 20–40 mg intravenous
furosemide (or equivalent); for those on chronic diuretic therapy, initial intravenous dose should be at least equivalent to oral
dose. Diuretics should either be given as intermittent boluses or as a continuous infusion, and the dose and duration should be
adjusted according to patients’ symptoms and clinical status. Combination of loop diuretic with either thiazide-type diuretic or
spironolactone may be considered
Loop diuretic
A: furosemide (IV) 20–120mg 24hourly

Intravenous vasodilators should be considered for symptomatic relief in AHF with SBP >90 mmHg (and without symptomatic
hypotension). Symptoms and blood pressure should be monitored frequently during administration of intravenous vasodilators.
In patients with hypertensive AHF, intravenous vasodilators should be considered as initial therapy to improve symptoms and

sections.title: Chronic Heart Failure
sections.text:
Patients who have had HF as defined above for some times are often said to have ‘Chronic Heart Failure’. A treated patient
with symptoms and signs that have remained generally unchanged for at least 1 month is said to be ‘Stable chronic heart failure’

Diagnostic Criteria
The diagnosis of chronic heart failure requires the following features:
  •    Symptoms of heart failure, typically breathlessness or fatigue, at rest or during exertion
  •    Objective evidence of cardiac dysfunction preferably by Echocardiography (Systolic and/or Diastolic)
  •    A clinical response to treatment is supportive but not sufficient for diagnosis.

Hence diagnosis and management of CHF should be sought at referral centres where at least echocardiography assessment
can be performed.

Management of Systolic Heart Failure (LVEF< 45–50%) Goals of treatment
 •   Prevention of disease leading to cardiac dysfunction and heart failure e.g. hypertension, coronary artery disease, valve
     disease etc.
 •   To achieve maintenance or improvement in quality of life and improve survival

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •  Avoid excessive fluid intake in severe HF Limit fluid intake to 1–1.5 L/day if fluid overloaded despite diuretic therapy.
  •  Regular exercise within limits of symptoms and other lifestyle modification (refer to table 20.2).

  Note: Sexual counselling regarding the risk of pregnancy and the use of oral contraceptives and phosphodiesterase-5
  inhibitors (e.g. sildenafil) are not recommended in advanced HF, if used nitrates should be avoided <24–48hours of nitrate
  intakes.
