sections.title: Pulmonary Oedema
sections.text:
Diagnostic Criteria
Common cause of pulmonary oedema is cardiac/fluid overload, and the common causes include: -
  •   Systolic heart failure complicating fluid overload
  •   Renal failure complicating fluid overload- Iatrogenic fluid overload Other Cause of pulmonary oedema
  •   Increased capillary permeability acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS); many causes include Systemic sepsis–
      gram negative infection, pancreatitis, head injury, aspiration of gastric contents, amniotic embolus.

Non-Pharmacological Management
Initial management
   •     Maintain airway, bed rest in Fowler`s position except if hypotensive or comatose.
   •     Administer oxygen to keep PO2> 60 mmHg (O2 saturation > 90%)
   •     Correct base–acid & electrolyte disorders, determine and correct arrhythmias,

Pharmacological Management
Cardiac failure
A: furosemide (IV) 20mg–80mg may be repeated in 10–15 minutes, If symptoms persist,
          AND
C: morphine (IV) 1–3mg diluted form,
Inotropic support if hypotensive SBP <90mmHg,

S: dobutamine (IV) 2–20 µg/kg/min
Intravenous vasodilator nitroglycerine if SBP > 100mmHg

Non–cardiac (ARDS)
  •   Treat the underlying conditions                                 •    Inotropic support if SBP<90mmHg
  •   Ventilate with PEEP – if RF                                     •    Dialysis if renal failure

  Note
    •  All patients suspected with pulmonary oedema should be referred to high level of care where hospital resourced with
       high care dependent unit or intensive care unit.
    •  Patient should be stabilized first at low level of care before referral to the high level of care.

sections.title: Infective Endocarditis (IE)
sections.text:
The infective process of endocardial layer of the heart can involve native or prosthetic valve and congenital defects/shunts.
Alpha–haemolytic streptococci are the most common causes of native valve endocarditis but Staphylococcus aureus is more
likely if the disease is rapidly progressive with high fever or is related to a prosthetic valve (Staphylococcus epidermidis).

Diagnostic Criteria
Use Modified Dukes Criteria below and consult microbiologist where possible. Three sets of blood cultures should be taken
before starting treatment.

Modified Dukes Criteria Major Criteria
 •    Positive blood cultures of typical organism for IE from at least two separate blood cultures
 •    Evidence of endocardial involvement by echocardiogram (Trans–thoracic Echo/Trans– oesophageal Echo)

Minor Criteria
  •   Fever > 38ºC
  •   Presence of Rheumatic heart disease, congenital heart disease
  •   Vascular phenomena; Major arterial emboli, septic pulmonary infarcts, mycotic aneurysm, intracranial haemorrhage,
      conjunctival hemorrhage, Janeway lesions
  •   Immunological phenomena; glomerulonephritis, Osler`s nodes, Roth`s spots,
  •   Rheumatoid factor.
  •   Serologic evidence of active infective endocarditis or blood culture not meeting major criterion.

Definition of infective endocarditis according to the modified Duke criteria: Definitive diagnosis of IE

Pathological criteria: Microorganisms demonstrated by culture or on histological examination of a vegetation, a vegetation that
has embolized, or an intracardiac abscess specimen
         OR
Pathological lesions: vegetation or intracardiac abscess confirmed by histological examination showing active endocarditis.

Table 20.6: Diagnostic Criteria for Infective Endocarditis (IE)
  Diagnosis Category                                                     Criteria
 Definite IE (Clinical   • Two major criteria OR
 Criteria)               • One major criterion + three minor criteria OR
                         • Five minor criteria
 Possible IE             • One major criterion + one minor criterion OR
                         • Three minor criteria
 Rejected IE             • Firm alternative diagnosis OR
                         • Resolution of symptoms suggestive of IE with antibiotic therapy for ≤ 4 days OR
                         • No pathological evidence of IE at surgery or autopsy, with antibiotic therapy for ≤ 4 days OR
                         • Does not meet criteria for possible IE, as listed above

   Note
     •  Positive blood cultures remain the cornerstone of diagnosis and provide live bacteria for both identification and
        susceptibility testing.
     •  To improve yield of culturing bacteria at least three blood sample sets are taken at 30 minutes apart each containing
        10mL of blood and should be incubated in both aerobic and anaerobic atmospheres.
     •  Sampling should be obtained from a peripheral vein using a meticulous sterile technique.

Pharmacological Management
Empirical Treatment; Consider negative blood culture or if risk delaying treatment for blood culture outweigh the befit of starting
treatment early
Treatment for native valves:
A: benzylpenicillin G (IV) 18–24milllion Units/24hours 4hourly in equally divided dose 4– 6weeks
           OR
B: ceftriaxone (IV) 2g 24hourly 4–6weeks
           AND
B: cloxacillin (IV) 2g 6hourly 4–6 weeks
           AND
A: gentamicin (IV) 1–1.5mg/kg 8 hourly for at least 2weeks
           OR
If methicillin–resistant staphylococci anaerobes (MRSA)
S: vancomycin (IV) 30mg/kg 24 hourly in two equally divided dose, not to exceed 2gm in 24hours unless serum levels are
monitored 4–6weeks.

  Note: It is important to assay serum gentamicin levels every 3–4days. One–hour peak concentration should not exceed
  10mg/l and trough concentration (2–hour pre– dose)

Prosthetic valve empirical treatment
A: benzylpenicillin G (X–Pen) (IV) 18 –24 million Units 4 hourly for 24hours in equally divided dose 6 – 8 weeks
          OR
B: ceftriaxone (IV) 2g 24hourly >6 weeks
          AND
B: cloxacillin (IV) 2g 6 hourly >6 weeks
          AND
A: rifampicin 300 –600mg (IV) 8hourly >6 weeks
          AND
A: gentamicin 1mg/kg (IV) 8hourly 2 weeks.

  Note
    •  It is important to assay serum gentamicin levels every 3–4days. One–hour peak concentration should not exceed
       10mg/l and trough concentration (2–hour pre– dose) should be less than 2mg/L.
    •  Gentamicin in renal failure should be given based on CrCl.
    •  Patients with complicated IE should be evaluated and managed in high level of care or centre, with immediate surgical
       facilities and the presence of a multidisciplinary including an Infectious Disease specialist, a microbiologist,
       cardiologist, imaging specialists, and cardiac surgeons

Infective Endocarditis Prophylaxis
  •    Antibiotic prophylaxis should be considered for patients at highest risk for IE:
  •    Patients with any prosthetic valve, including a trans catheter valve, or those in whom any prosthetic material was used
       for cardiac valve repair.
  •    Patients with a previous episode of IE.
  •    Patients with Congenital Heart Disease (CHD):
               -Any type of cyanotic CHD.
               - Any type of CHD repaired with a prosthetic material, whether place surgically or by percutaneous techniques,
               up to 6 months after the procedure or lifelong if residual shunt or valvular regurgitation remains.

 Note: Antibiotic prophylaxis is not recommended in other forms of valvular or CHD.

Prophylaxis of Endocarditis Infective
  •   To reduce the risk of bacterial endocarditis, antibiotic prophylaxis should be given to patients undergoing dental
      procedures requiring manipulation of the gingival or periapical region of the teeth or perforation of the oral mucosa.
  •   Antibiotic prophylaxis is not recommended for,
  •   Respiratory tract procedures including bronchoscopy or laryngoscopy, or trans nasal or endotracheal intubation
  •   Gastrointestinal or urogenital procedures or Trans–oesophageal Echocardiogram, gastroscopy, colonoscopy,
      cystoscopy, vaginal or caesarean delivery.
  •   Skin and soft tissue procedures

Table 20.7 : Antibiotic Prophylaxis for Infective Endocarditis
 Situation                     Antibiotic                            Single dose 30–60 min before procedure
                                                                   Adult Dose                    Children Dose
 No allergy to penicillin or     A: amoxicillin          2 g PO/IV                       50 mg/kg PO/IV
 ampicillin                            OR
                                 A: ampicillin*
 Allergy to penicillin or        S: Clindamycin          600 mg PO/IV                         20 mg/kg PO/IV
 ampicillin

*Alternatively,
B: ceftriaxone (IV) 1g for adults or 50 mg/kg for children.
Cephalosporins should not be used in patients with anaphylaxis, angio–oedema, or urticaria after intake of penicillin or ampicillin
due to cross–sensitivity.

sections.title: Acute Rheumatic Fever
sections.text:
It is a non–suppurative sequela of a group A ß haemolytic streptococcal (GABHS) pharyngeal infection.

Diagnostic Criteria
See table 20.8 below

Definitive Diagnosis
  •    Two major criteria or
  •    One major criterion with two minor criteria, with evidence of antecedent streptococcal infection

Table 20.8: Jones Criteria for Acute Rheumatic Fever
      Major Criteria             Minor Criteria     Supporting Evidence of Recent Group A Streptococcal Infection
 • Carditis                 Clinical:               • Positive throat culture or rapid antigen detection test for Group a
 • Migratory polyarthritis  • Fever                 Streptococcus AND/OR
 • Sydenham’s chorea        •Arthralgia             • Elevated streptococcal antibody titres:
 • Erythema marginatum                                – Anti-streptolysin O (ASO)
                            Laboratory:               – Anti-deoxyribonuclease B (anti-DNase B)
                            • Elevated acute phase
                             reactants (e.g. CRP)
                            • Prolonged PR interval

Non–Pharmacological Management
Acute stage:
  •    Bed rest and supportive care until all evidence of active carditis has resolved
  •    Patient education.
  •    Intensive health education for prevention of sore throats.

Pharmacological Management
Treatment of acute attack for eradication of streptococci in throat: Regardless of the presence or absence of pharyngitis at the
time of diagnosis.

A: benzathine benzylpenicillin (IM) 1.2MU stat
Children > 5 years 0.3MU, 5–10 years 0.6 MU > 10 years 1.2 MU stat
         OR
A: phenoxymethylpenicillin (PO) 500mg 8-12 hourly 24 hourly for 10days
Children > 10years 500mg, 5–10 years 250mg, < 5years 125mg (PO) 8-12 hourly for 10 days

Patients allergic to penicillin
A: erythromycin (PO) 500mg or 40mg/kg 6hourly for 10days.

Treatment of Acute Arthritis and Carditis:
A: acetylsalicylic acid (PO) 25mg/kg 6hourly 24hourly as required.
Acetylsalicylic acid should be continued until fever, all signs of joint inflammation and the ESR have returned to normal and
then tapered gradually over 2 weeks. If symptoms recur, full doses should be restarted. *Dose should be reduced if tinnitus or
other toxic symptoms develop

In severe carditis with development of increasing heart failure or failure of response to aspirin,
Add
A: prednisolone (PO) 1–2mg/kg 24hourly for 3–4weeks

Then review and gradual reduction and discontinuation of prednisolone may be started after 3–4 weeks when there has been
a substantial reduction in clinical disease.

Heart failure should be managed in the usual way (see Heart Failure Section 20.9).
Treatment of Sydenham’s chorea:
B: haloperidol (PO) 1.5–3mg 8hourly for 24 hours as required (Adult). Paediatrics 50µg/kg for 24 hours in 2 divided doses.

Referral: Ideally all patients should be referred to high level of care a specialized hospital care, where surgery is contemplated

Antibiotic prophylaxis after rheumatic fever
Prophylaxis should be given to all patients with a history of acute rheumatic fever and to those with rheumatic heart valve
lesions. The optimum duration of prophylaxis should be up to at least 21years of age.

 Note: Specific situations requiring prophylaxis for longer periods (up to 30years as a guide):
   •    Definitive carditis in previous attacks
   •    High risk of exposure to streptococcal infection at home or work (crowded conditions, high exposure to children)

A: benzathine benzylpenicillin (IM) 2.4MU monthly or every three weeks*
Children <12yrs 1.2MU every 4 weeks or 3 weeks* up to 21–30yrs
          OR
A: phenoxymethylpenicillin (PO) 250mg 12hourly
Children <12yr 125–250mg 12hourly for 24hours up to 21–30years
          OR
A: erythromycin (PO) 250mg 12hourly for 24hours Adult
Children <12yr 125–250mg 12hourlyfor 24hours up to 21–30yrs*every 3week regimen is more effective

As a general recommendation patient with high index of suspicion for valvular heart disease should get access for evaluation

sections.title: Acute Pulmonary Embolism
sections.text:
Clinical Spectrum less than two weeks
  •     Sudden onset of dyspnoea often with unexplained anxiety (most common)
  •     Pleuritic chest pain and Haemoptysis
  •     Massive embolism: pleuritic chest pain, cyanosis, right heart failure and shock. Minor emboli or pulmonary infarction
        may herald massive embolism and must be treated vigorously
  •     About 90% of emboli are from proximal leg deep vein thromboses (DVTs) or pelvic vein thromboses. DVTs are at risk
        for dislodging and migrating to the lung circulation. Thus, termed as venous thromboembolism (VTE).

Diagnostic Criteria
Determination pre-test probability of PE, Use validated scoring system: Wells Score
  •   Score > 6.0–High clinical probability proceeds with imaging test to confirm PE and treat,
  •   Score 2.0 to 6.0–Moderate clinical probability; negative D–dimer, PE is excluded and D– dimer positive, obtain imaging
      tests to confirm based on result treat.
  •   Score < 2.0–Low clinical probability negative D–dimer, PE is excluded. Positive D–dimer obtain imaging tests to confirm
      or rule out and based on result treat

Alternatively
  •    Score > 4–PE likely, d–dimer positive proceeds with diagnostic imaging to confirm and treat PE.
  •    Score 4 or less–PE unlikely, consider d–dimer to rule out PE.

Table 20.8: Wells Score
 Variable                                                                          Score
 Clinically suspected DVT                                                          3.0 points
 alternative diagnosis is less likely than PE                                      3.0 points
 Tachycardia (heart rate > 100)                                                    1.5 points
 Immobilization (≥ 3d)/surgery in previous four weeks                              1.5 points
 History of DVT or PE                                                              1.5 points
 Hemoptysis                                                                        1.0 points
 Malignancy (with treatment within six months) or palliative                       1.0 points

  •    ECG – Not reliable test for diagnosis may be normal. However,
  •    Sinus tachycardia most common feature, acute right ventricular strain – i.e. right axis shift, S1Q3T3 occurs in small
       percentage of cases, may develop acute bundle branch block – right or left, may simulate right ventricular infarction,
       may develop arrhythmias – e.g. atrial fibrillation
  •    Arterial blood gases; not diagnostic, the pO2 decreased <60mmHg due ventilation/perfusion mismatch. pCO2
       decreased due to hyperventilation, pH increased but may decrease in shocked patient
  •    D–dimer test – very sensitive blood test, but not specific. A negative test d–dimer test excludes an embolus in majority
       of cases (best exclusive test to rule out PE when is negative)
  •    Chest X–ray – Not very reliable usually normal, diaphragm may be raised on affected area, atelectasis may occur,
       peripheral wedge–shaped shadow & plural effusion
  •    Cardiac Echocardiography: Useful in diagnosis, features suggestive or support
  •    Evidence of massive embolus acute right ventricular strain
  •    Computer Tomography Pulmonary Angiogram Scan (CTPA); Useful can demonstrate the presence and extent of
       proximal pulmonary emboli
  •    Ventilation/Perfusion Scan; Useful in stable patient to confirm the diagnosis. The presence of a perfusion defect with
       normal ventilation not corresponding to an x–ray abnormality is characteristic
  •    Pulmonary Angiography: Still gold standard investigation, may be necessary to establish
  •    Diagnosis and catheter-based embolectomy in the catheterization lab.

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •  Administer O2 – maintain pO2 > 60mmHg,
  •  Treat shock
  •  Correct electrolyte & acid base abnormalities and arrhythmias
  •  Ventilate if patient has a respiratory failure

Pharmacological Management
Anticoagulation
C: unfractionated heparin (UFH) (IV) 10,000units then maintenance infusion starts with 6,000U over 6 hours to keep PTT or
clotting time 2–3times above baseline. PTT should be performed 12hourly per lab instruction.
           OR
D: low molecular weight heparin (SC) 1mg/kg 12hourly for 24hours

Start warfarin after 24hours of heparin and continue post discharge for long–term. If the aetiology unknown may be for life, if
aetiology is established at least for six months. Maintain INR 2.0–3.0

Thrombolytic (Fibrinolysis)
Indicated in proximal massive pulmonary emboli and haemodynamically unstable if no contraindication exists
S: streptokinase (IV)250,000IU over 30minutes, then 100,000IU per hour for 24hours
          OR
S: alteplase (rtPA) (IV) 100mg over 2hours
          OR
S: tenecteplase 0.2-0.5mg/kg IV bolus

Referral: All cases suspected of pulmonary embolus should be referred to a high level of care – specialized hospital care with
HCDU/ICU

sections.title: Chronic Pulmonary Embolism
sections.text:
Chronic pulmonary embolism is mainly a consequence of incomplete resolution of acute pulmonary thromboembolism. Clinically
symptoms and signs may be preceded by Acute Pulmonary Embolism for more than 2weeks.

Pharmacological Management
Long-term oral anticoagulation

C: warfarin (PO) 2–10mg 24hourly
(Maintain INR 2.0–3.0 for warfarin use individuals.)
          OR
S: rivaroxaban (PO) 15-20mg 24hourly

Referral: All cases suspected of pulmonary embolism should be referred to a high level of care
IVC filter (IVC filters are a valuable tool for preventing PE in patients who cannot be managed with anticoagulation, but their
use should be carefully considered due to the increased risk of DVT and potential long-term complications. Their benefit is most
pronounced in the early period after placement, and filters should be removed when no longer indicated

sections.title: Cardiac Arrhythmias/ Dysrhythmias
sections.text:
Always exclude underlying structural cardiac disease in all patients with cardiac dysrhythmias as well as performing Holter
ECG monitoring aiding at detecting type of arrhythmia.

sections.title: Narrow QRS Complex Tachyarrhythmias (SVTs)
sections.text:
Definition Sustained (> 30 seconds) or non–sustained narrow QRS (≤ 0.1 seconds) tachycardias.

Atrial Fibrillation
Acute onset (< 48 hours)
  •     Assess clinically, e.g. heart failure, mitral stenosis, thyrotoxicosis, hypertension, age and other medical conditions.
  •     Consider anticoagulation with heparin or warfarin.
  •     Synchronized DC cardioversion is occasionally necessary in emergency especially haemodynamic instability or consider
        if is the first episode.

Non-acute/chronic (> 48 hours)
  •   As above, but not immediate DC cardioversion is indicated, unless in hypotensive emergency cases. Anticoagulation
      with oral warfarin 2-5mg orally once a day for at least a month, then perform elective cardioversion at specialized
      hospital. Atrial flutter
  •   P waves visible before QRS, commonly occurs, usually 2:1. (150 per minute). P waves, usually negative in Lead II
      precede QRS, blocked P in ST segment or hidden by QRS.
  •   Vagal stimulation with ECG may reveal blocked P waves.

sections.title: AV Junctional Re-Entry Tachycardias
sections.text:
•    Usually paroxysmal, often young with normal heart.
  •    AV nodal re-entry or WPW syndrome.
  •    P waves usually not visible (hidden by QRS).

Non-Pharmacological Management
Electrical Cardioversion. Synchronized DC cardioversion, 200 J, after sedation with:
A: diazepam (IV)10–20 mg stat

If flutter has been present longer than 48hours, defer cardioversion for 4weeks after anticoagulation with warfarin, unless severe
symptoms or heart failure requires urgent cardioversion.

Pharmacological Management
None is nearly as effective as DC cardioversion. Consider anticoagulants if Atrial flutter sustained.
Long term treatment: Recurrent atrial flutter is an indication for referral. Many can be cured by radiofrequency catheter ablation.

Atrial tachycardias
  •     Rare, often incessant P before QRS (often long PR) or hidden in T
  •     May cause heart failure (tachycardia cardiomyopathy).

Atrial fibrillation
With fast ventricular response without aberrant conduction.

Pharmacological Management
Anticoagulation
C: warfarin (PO) 2–10mg 24hourly (Maintain INR 2.0–3.0 for warfarin use individuals.)
          OR
S: rivaroxaban (PO)15-20mg 24hourly (in Non-valvular AF)

Control the ventricular rate with one of the following):
D: digoxin (IV) Initial dose: 0.25-0.5mg; then 0.25mg 4-6hourly to maximum of 1mg; Maintenance dose: 0.125-0.25mg 24hourly
          OR
D: digoxin (PO) 0.25mg daily; use only in heart failure).
          OR
B: atenolol (PO) 50–100mg 24hourly (contraindicated in asthmatics).
          OR
D: diltiazem (IV) initial dose: 15-20mg over 2minutes; may repeat in 15 minutes, Maintenance dose: 5-15mg hourly by
continuous IV infusion
          OR
S: verapamil (IV) 5 to 10 mg over 2minutes; may repeat in 30minutes DC cardioversion in selected cases, after 4weeks of
anticoagulation

Digoxin only controls rate at rest and is insufficient on its own. If used for long-term, combine with β – blocker:
D: digoxin (PO) 0.125-0.25mg 24hourly

In the elderly and patients with renal impairment: Adjust dosages according to trough levels within the therapeutic range. Do
levels only if the patient has been on the drug for at least 10 days.
          AND / OR
B: atenolol (PO) 50–100 mg 24hourly
          OR
S: bisoprolol (PO) 2.5mg – 10mg 24hourly
          OR
C: metoprolol (PO) 25mg -50mg 24hourly
          OR
S: sotalol (PO) 80mg – 160mg 12hourly

  Note: Avoid use of Digoxin in patients with Accessory pathway.

With fast ventricular response with Aberrant conduction (e.g.: Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, WPW)

Catheter ablation of the accessory pathway in symptomatic patients with preexisted AF, especially if the accessory pathway
has a short refractory period that allows rapid antegrade conduction.

Long – term: Continue warfarin anticoagulation long-term, unless contraindicated:
C: warfarin (PO) 5mg 24hourly
           OR
S: rivaroxaban (PO) maintenance dose; 15mg / 20mg 24hourly
           OR
Left atrial appendage occlusion (LAAO).
In poor HR control, frequent or severe symptoms for curative RFA

  Note
    •  INR monitoring in patients on warfarin. Maintain therapeutic Range INR 2–3: Stable patients check 3 monthly. If INR
       < 1.5 or > 3.5: do monthly monitoring.
    •  Left atrial appendage occlusion (LAAO) is indicated in Atrial Fibrillation patients who cannot tolerate long-term
       Anticoagulation or contraindicated to OACs (Oral anticoagulants) and have thrombo-embolic risk (CHA2DS2-VASc
       score ≥2), increased risk of bleeding (HASBLED score ≥ 3) and thrombo-embolic events despite adequate OAC
       after excluding other plausible causes (e.g. carotid disease).

sections.title: AV Junctional Re-Entry Tachycardias
sections.text:
Non-Pharmacological Management
Vagal maneuvers: Valsalva or carotid sinus massage. The patient should be supine and as relaxed as possible, to avoid
competing sympathetic reflex

Pharmacological Management
If vagal maneuvers fail:
S: adenosine (IV) 6mg over 1-3 seconds (maybe given IO) followed by rapid flush with 20mL NS, if no conversion within 1-
2minutes give 12mg, repeat a second time if necessary (30mg total).

If none of the above is effective, and patient is hypotensive, consider DC shock

Prevention of recurrent paroxysmal atrial fibrillation
Only in patients with severe symptoms despite the above measures:
S: amiodarone (PO) 200mg 8hourly for 1week, followed by 200mg 12hourly for one week and thereafter 200mg 24hourly.
Specialist initiated.

Precautions:
  •   Half dosage of warfarin and monitor INR closely if patient on warfarin, until stable
  •   Avoid concomitant digoxin use.

  Note: Verapamil and digoxin are contraindicated in WPW syndrome.

Long-term treatment: Teach the patient to perform vagal maneuver’s, Valsalva is the most effective. For infrequent, non–
incapacitating symptoms:
B: atenolol (PO) 50–100mg 24hourly (If asthmatic)
          OR
S: verapamil (PO) 80–120mg 8hourly for 24hours (Normal heart)

Referral: Refer to Cardiac specialized center for Mapping and Radiofrequency Ablation (RFA)

sections.title: Wide QRS (Ventricular) Tachyarrhythmias (VTs)
sections.text: Sustained (> 30 seconds) or non-sustained wide QRS (> 0.12 seconds) tachycardias

sections.title: Regular Wide QRS Tachycardias
sections.text:
These are ventricular tachycardias until proved otherwise. Regular wide QRS supraventricular tachycardias are uncommon.

Non-Pharmacological Management
Refer all cases after resuscitation and stabilization. Emergency DC cardioversion is mandatory with a full protocol of
Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation (CPR)
  •   If no cardiac arrest: DC cardioversion, 200J, after sedation with: Diazepam, I.V, 10–20mg If 200J fails, use 360J.
  •   If cardiac arrest: Defibrillate (not synchronized).

Pharmacological Management
DC cardioversion is first line therapy for regular wide QRS tachycardias. Medicines are needed if VT recurs after cardioversion
or if spontaneous termination/recurrence.

S: amiodarone (IV) 5mg/kg (150-300mg) infused over 30minutes then continue with maintenance dose to total dose of
1200mg/24hours
        OR
S: amiodarone (PO) 800 mg 24hourly for 7days, 600mg/day for 3days followed by a maintenance dose of 200–400mg/day

Amiodarone may cause serious long-term side effects due to long half-life. Therefore, patients require regular monitoring by
specialist.
A: lidocaine (IV) 50–100mg (1–2mg/kg) initially and at 5minute intervals if required to a total of 200–300mg,

Thereafter, for recurrent ventricular tachycardia only
A: lidocaine (IV)1–3mg/minute for 24–30hours. lidocaine will only terminate ± 30% of sustained ventricular tachycardias, and
may cause hypotension, heart block or convulsions.

  Note
    •  Never give verapamil IV to patients with a wide QRS tachycardia.
    •  For emergency treatment of ventricular tachycardia, DC cardioversion is first–line therapy, even if stable.

sections.title: Sustained (> 30 Sec) Irregular Wide QRS Tachycardias
sections.text:
They are usually due to atrial fibrillation with bundle branch block, or pre-excitation (WPW syndrome).

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •  If the QRS complexes have a pattern of typical right or left bundle branch block, with a rate
  •  < less than 170/minute, treat as for atrial fibrillation. See the section on atrial fibrillation.
  •  If the rate is > 170 per minute, and/or the complexes are atypical or variable, the likely diagnosis is WPW syndrome with
     atrial fibrillation, conducting via the bypass tract, DC conversion.

Referral: Refer patient to high care centre for further management including arrhythmia mapping and RFA

sections.title: Non-Sustained (< 30 Sec) Irregular Wide QRS Tachycardias
sections.text:
They are usually ventricular, commonly in acute myocardial infarction. In acute myocardial infarction, only treat non–sustained
ventricular tachycardia if causes significant haemodynamic compromise. Ensure the serum potassium level is above 4 mmol/L.

Pharmacological Management
Medicines are needed if VT recurs after cardioversion or if spontaneous termination/recurrence.

S: amiodarone (IV) 5 mg/kg (150-300mg) over 30minutes then continue with maintenance dose to total dose of 1200mg
for24hours
         OR
S: amiodarone (PO) 800mg 24hourly for 7days, followed by 600mg 24hourly for 3 days then a maintenance dose of 200–
400mg 24hourly

Only in a haemodynamically stable patient:
A: lidocaine (IV) 50–100mg (1–2mg/kg) initially and at 5minute intervals if required to a total of 200–300mg

Thereafter, for recurrent ventricular tachycardia only:
A: lidocaine (IV) 1–3mg/minute for 24–30hours
In the absence of acute ischemia or infarction, consider torsade’s de pointes.

sections.title: Torsade’s De Pointes Ventricular Tachycardia (VT)
sections.text:
Has a twisting pattern to the QRS complexes and a prolonged QT interval in sinus rhythm, it is usually due to a QT–prolonging
drug, ± hypokalemia.

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •  Cardioversion/defibrillation, as necessary.
  •  Torsade’s complicating bradycardia: temporary pacing

Pharmacological Management
Stop all QT-prolonging drugs. Correct serum potassium.

A: magnesium sulphate (IV) 2g over 5–10minutes

If recurrent episodes after initial dose of magnesium sulphate:
A: magnesium sulphate (IV) 2g over 24hours Torsade’s complicating bradycardia: temporary pacing.
          AND
A: epinephrine (adrenaline) infusion to raise heart rate to >100 per minute (if temporary pacing unavailable).

Referral: Refer all cases of wide QRS tachycardia, after resuscitation and stabilization for possible arrhythmia mapping and
RFA.

sections.title: Heart Block (Second and Third Degree)
sections.text:
Most cases occur in patients over 60 years and is idiopathic. Acute, reversible AV block commonly complicated by inferior
myocardial infarction, here temporary Pacemaker used as bridge therapy. The condition may also be induced by medicines,
metabolic and electrolyte derangements.

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •  Emergency cardio-pulmonary resuscitation.
  •  External pacemaker should be available in all secondary hospitals and must be preceded by appropriate analgesia.

Pharmacological Management
Analgesia if external pacemaker:
C: morphine (IM)10–15mg 3–6hourly

For Temporary treatment of complete AV block before referral for pacemaker:
A: atropine (IV) bolus 0.6–1.2mg every 3 – 5min (max 3mg) may be repeated until a temporary or permanent pacemaker is
inserted.
(Use in an Inferior Infarct patients, hypotension, and second-degree AV block).

For resuscitation of asystole:
A: epinephrine (adrenaline) (IV) 1:10000, slow 5mL (0.5mg)

Referral
  •   All cases with a heart rate below 40 beats/minute after resuscitation and stabilization to high level of care where
      permanent pacemaker implantation can be performed.
  •   All cases of second or third-degree AV block, whether myocardial infarct or other reversible cause is suspected, and
      whether the patient is thought to be symptomatic.

  Note: Complete Heart Block Is a Medical Emergency Refer Urgently

sections.title: Sinus Bradycardia & Sinus Arrest
sections.text:
This rhythm does not require treatment, unless they are causing symptoms, i.e. syncope, dizziness, tiredness, and poor effort
tolerance. Sinus bradycardia <50/minute or sinus arrest with slow escape rhythm, accompanied by hypotension, strongly
suggests a treatable underlying cause:
   •    Acute inferior myocardial infarct
   •    Hyperkalemia, especially if wide QRS and/or peaked T waves
   •    Drugs, especially combination of verapamil and ß –blocker or digoxin
   •    Hypothermia
   •    Hypoxia
Treat the cause. Consider atropine if inferior in

 Implantation [Temporary/Permanent Pacemaker Implantation (single or Dual chamber) depending on the underlying cause],
 prepare Vancomycin injection for sterilization of Permanent Pacemaker pouch.

sections.title: Aortic diseases and peripheral arterial diseases
Aortic Aneurysm
sections.text:
In clinical practice aortic root dilatation can be suspected in male adults when the aortic diameter is >40mm and at females at
>36mm.
Causes: hypertension, marfan syndrome, syphilis

Clinical Presentation
Shortness of breath, awareness of heartbeat, hoarseness of voice.

Investigations
  •    CXR-widening of mediastinum,
  •    Echocardiogram-in ascending aortic root and arch,
  •    CT-aortogram is the definitive diagnostic tool

Management
Consult specialist and refer to the high-level specialized hospital Management for AAA
  •   AAAs are usually treated with surgical repair in ruptured, symptomatic or appropriately sized aneurysms. When
      indicated, unruptured aneurysms can undergo elective repair Newer minimally invasive techniques extend aortic
      aneurysm treatment into an increasingly elderly population. Recommend elective repair for the patient at low or
      acceptable surgical risk with a fusiform AAA that is ≥5.5 cm in males and >5cm in females.
  •   If an AAA ruptures, emergency surgical repair is required. The primary repair methods are as follows:
  •   Open - This requires direct access to the aorta via a transperitoneal or retroperitoneal approach
  •   Endovascular - This involves gaining access to the lumen of the abdominal aorta, usually via the femoral vessels; an
      endograft, typically a polyester or Gore-Tex graft with a stent exoskeleton, is placed within the lumen of the AAA,
      extending distally into the iliac arteries

sections.title: Aortic Dissection
sections.text:
Aortic Dissection Is the life-threatening condition in which a tear develops in the inner layer(intima) of the aorta.

Causes and risk factors: Hypertension, marfan-syndrome, trauma, etc.

Clinical Presentation
severe chest pain (tearing or ripping in nature), fainting, sweating, vomiting, pulse deficits or differences in blood pressure
between arms

Classification:
  •    Stanford type A- involves the ascending aorta (may extend to the arch or descending aorta)- requires urgent surgery
  •    Stanford type B- involves only the descending aorta- may be managed medically unless complications arise

Investigations
  •    CXR- an abnormal aortic contour,
  •    Aortic knuckle double,
  •    CT-aortogram is crucial in diagnosing and assessing aortic dissection

Management
Consult specialist and refer to the high-level specialized hospital

20.17.3 Peripheral arterial disease (PAD)
Chronic peripheral arterial disease (PAD) may be asymptomatic, present with intermittent claudication, or manifest as critical
limb ischemia.
Intermittent claudication is one of the most common manifestations of peripheral arterial occlusive disease (PAOD) caused by
atherosclerosis. It is characterized by reproducible ischemic muscle pain that occurs during physical activity and is relieved by
a short period of rest. The pain results from inadequate blood flow to the affected limb.

sections.title: Varicose Veins and Venous Ulcers
sections.text:
Varicose veins and telangiectasia (spider veins) are dilated, elongated and tortuous superficial veins of lower limbs, the visible
surface manifestations of an underlying problem with reverse venous flow, which is also termed venous insufficiency syndrome.
Mild forms of venous insufficiency are merely uncomfortable, annoying, or cosmetically disfiguring, but severe venous disease
can produce serious systemic consequences and can lead to loss of life or limb.

Inspection may reveal the following findings:
   Signs and symptom                                        Inspection may reveal the following findings
   Leg heaviness- Venous claudication                       Ulceration
   Pain or tenderness along the course of a vein            Lipodermatosclerosis
   Pruritus                                                 Interdigital mycosis
   Burning sensations                                       Eczematous lesions
   Restless legs                                            Micro ulcers
   Edema                                                    Stasis dermatitis
   Skin changes                                             Prominent varicose veins
   Paresthesias                                             Scars from a prior surgical operation
                                                            Evidence of previous sclerosant injections
Investigations
  •    Doppler Ultrasound,
  •    Magnetic resonance venography (MRV)

Management
Conservative treatment with stockings and external compression is an acceptable alternative to surgery, but worsening
cutaneous findings or symptoms despite these measures usually warrant intervention.

The following are the modern techniques used to ablate varicosities:
  •    Sclerotherapy – The most widely used medical             •    Endovenous RF thermal ablation (performed by

       ((performed by vascular surgeon & interventional         •    Endovenous laser thermal ablation (performed by

Lymphedema
Lymphedema is an abnormal collection of protein-rich fluid in the interstitium resulting from obstruction of lymphatic drainage.

Clinical Presentation
  •    Chronic swelling of an extremity preceded                         •     Severe impairment of daily activities
       lymphedema                                                        •     Recurrent bacterial or fungal infections
  •    Primarily lower extremity involvement (80%) but                   •     Recurrent episodes of cellulitis, lymphangitis,
       can also involve the upper extremities, face,                           fissuring, ulcerations, and/or verrucous changes
       genitalia, and trunk
  •    Fevers, chills, and generalized weakness

Investigations
  •    Lymphoscintigraphy is the new criterion standard
       for evaluation of the lymphatic system                            •     CT angiography
  •    Doppler uss                                                       •     MRI Angiography

Management
The goals of lymphedema management are to restore limb function, reduce swelling and associated physical and psychological
morbidity, prevent recurrent infections and other complications, identify and treat the underlying cause in secondary
lymphedema, and promote weight management and regular physical activity to improve clinical outcomes and reduce disease
progression.

Non Pharmacological Management
Conservative measures for managing lymphedema include the following:
  •   Maintenance of appropriate hygiene and skin care           •   Avoiding trauma
  •   Use of complex physical therapy (first-line                •   Avoiding constrictive clothing
      treatment) and compression stockings                       •   Elevating affected limb
  •   Weight loss (if overweight)

Surgical treatment
Surgical treatment is indicated for selected patients with refractory lymphedema and is intended to reduce limb volume, improve
lymphatic drainage, and enhance function and quality of life. Surgery is palliative rather than curative and should be used as
an adjunct to, not a replacement for, ongoing conservative management, including compression therapy and skin care.

sections.title: Congenital Heart Disease (CHD)
sections.text:
These are structural abnormalities of the heart and intrathoracic blood vessels that occur during fetal development. It is the
most common type of birth defect. CHD is divided into non-cyanotic CHD and cyanotic CHD.

Clinical Presentation
  •    Failure to thrive                                                 •     Tachypnoea
  •    Interrupted breastfeeding                                         •     Cyanosis and digital clubbing
  •    Recurrent cough and difficulty in breathing                       •     Echocardiographic evidence of CHD

Critical cyanotic congenital heart disease (CCHD): Defined as lesions requiring surgery or catheter-based intervention in
the first year of life

Evaluation
Prenatal screening during a standard obstetric ultrasound examination
Pulse oximetry screening – recommended to done to all newborns when at least 24 hours of age. To be done in the right hand
and either foot. A positive screening result includes one of the following:
  •    Any Oxygen Saturation less than 90%                               •  Chest X-ray
  •    Oxygen Saturation less than 95% in both                           •  Electrocardiogram
       extremities, on 3 measures, each separated by 1                   •  Echocardiogram
       hour
  •    More than 3% absolute difference in oxygen
       saturation between the right hand and foot on 3
       measures, each separated by 1 hour

  Note: Appropriate referral to a facility with neonatal intensive care unit or cardiac care unit

Initial stabilization
   •     Inotropes to manage shock and hypotension
   •     Appropriate respiratory support – oxygen therapy and mechanical ventilation for severe cases

Pharmacological Management
If ductal-dependent CHD confirmed or if there is a strong suspicion but echocardiography not readily available:
D: prostaglandin E1 0.01 mcg/kg per minute (maximum dose 0.1 mcg/kg per minute

Other supporting management: PDA stent                                       Definitive management: Intracardiac repair (ICR)

chapters.title: Kidney And Urological Disorders

sections.title: Chronic Kidney Diseases (CKD)
sections.text:
It is structural or functional kidney damage present for >3 months, with or without a decreased glomerular filtration rate (GFR).
Early screening in high-risk groups [hypertension, Diabetes and glomerular diseases] is crucial in improving the outcome of
CKD. Once the cause and plan for care have been established, adults with early CKD stages 1-3 can be managed at the
primary care level. Patients with CKD stage 4 should be referred to a nephrologist whenever possible.

Common causes of CKD
  • Vascular: Hypertension, renal artery stenosis, vasculitis, etc.
  • Glomerular diseases; Diabetes, autoimmune diseases (e.g., lupus nephritis), chronic systemic infections (e.g., HIV, HBV,
    syphilis), drugs, neoplasia
  • Tubulointerstitial diseases; UTI, drug-induced interstitial nephritis (e.g. rifampicin, allopurinol, fluoroquinolones,
    sulphonamides, β-lactam antibiotics, proton pump inhibitors, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs)
  • Structural: Polycystic kidneys, renal masses, obstruction (stones, strictures)
  • Others; Congenital: Chronic kidney disease can be entirely asymptomatic until over 75% of kidney function is lost

Clinical Presentation
Clinical features depend on the stage of kidney disease. In advanced stage includes:
  •     Anorexia
  •     Malaise
  •     Vomiting
  •     Oliguria/anuria

Investigations
  •    Kidney function tests (serum creatinine and urea) -             •    Parathyroid hormone levels, Serum Phosphate,
       at diagnosis, check every month for 3 months. If                     and Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)
       active sediment/proteinuria, provider may check                 •    Urinalysis (Protein, red blood cells and cast cells),
       more frequently                                                      then quantify the amount of protein in urine by
  •    FBC (HB)                                                             Esbach test or Urine albumin-creatinine ratio or
  •    Serum electrolytes Potassium, Calcium Phosphate                      Urine protein-creatinine ratio
       and Sodium [CKD stage 3-5: Check monthly]                       •    Kidney-Ureter-Bladder (KUB) ultrasound
  •    Serum albumin                                                   •    CXR
  •    Total protein                                                   •    ECG
  •    Serum lipids (cholesterol / LDL/ HDL/ Triglyceride              •    Echocardiogram
  •    Serum bicarbonate levels (venous) [CKD stage 3-                 •    Other tests to be done as per the doctor's discretion
       5: Check monthly]                                                    and needs on the specific patient

  Note:
  Determine and address the underlying cause of CKD, especially when considering kidney transplantation.
    •   Treat reversible causes of kidney dysfunction.
    •   Prevent or slow the progression of kidney disease.
    •   Treat complications of kidney dysfunction.
    •   Identify and adequately prepare patients who may require kidney replacement therapy.

Hyperlipidemia and Referral to a Nephrologist (CKD)
Hyperlipidemia, when present as a co-existent risk factor in chronic kidney disease (CKD), should be managed according to
the relevant cardiovascular guidelines (see Chapter 20 Cardiovascular disease conditions).

Referral to a nephrologist is indicated in the following situations:
  •    Reduced kidney function: eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m² (CKD stage G3 or worse) or rapid decline in eGFR (>5 mL/min/1.73
       m² per year).
  •    Significant albuminuria/proteinuria: Persistent urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) ≥30 mg/g on at least two
       occasions, nephrotic-range proteinuria (>3.5 g/day), or nephrotic syndrome.
  •    Active urinary sediment or unexplained hematuria: Presence of red blood cell casts, dysmorphic red blood cells, or other
       active sediment.
  •    Suspected or confirmed secondary kidney disease: Including congenital anomalies, glomerulonephritis, and systemic
       diseases such as lupus nephritis or HIV-associated nephropathy.
  •    CKD complications: Refractory anemia, electrolyte disturbances (e.g., hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis), or bone
       mineral disorders not responding to initial therapy.
  •    Pediatric CKD: Any child diagnosed with CKD.
  •    Preparation for renal replacement therapy (RRT): Planning for dialysis access or kidney transplant evaluation.

sections.title: Diabetic Kidney Disease
sections.text:
Diabetic kidney disease (DKD) is a clinical diagnosis based on the presence of albuminuria, reduced estimated glomerular
filtration rate (eGFR), or both in patients with diabetes mellitus. It includes diabetic nephropathy, which classically presents with
microalbuminuria (30–300 mg/g or 3–30 mg/mmol) and diabetic retinopathy.

DKD typically develops after long-standing diabetes (usually >10 years in type 1 diabetes) but may be present at the time of
diagnosis in type 2 diabetes. It may also occur without retinopathy or without albuminuria, particularly in type 2 diabetes.
Alternative causes of kidney disease should be considered when atypical features are present.

Clinical Presentation
  •    Hypertension
  •    Diabetic retinopathy
  •    Edema
  •    Symptoms of advanced CKD (fatigue, pallor, bleeding tendency)
  •    Signs of peripheral neuropathy

Investigations
  •    Urinalysis: Dipstick testing for proteinuria and             •    Confirm elevated albuminuria in at least 2 of 3
       microscopic examination for casts (RBC casts,                     samples over 3–6 months
       WBC casts) and dysmorphic red blood cells                    •    Imaging: Kidney, ureter, and bladder (KUB)
  •    Albuminuria quantification: Spot urine albumin-to-                ultrasound to exclude obstruction or structural
       creatinine ratio (ACR) or 24-hour urine protein                   abnormalities
       collection                                                   •    Additional investigations may be performed based
                                                                         on clinical judgment and patient-specific needs

Referral to a Nephrologist for Kidney Biopsy
Kidney biopsy should be considered when the cause of kidney disease is unclear or atypical features are present, including:
  •   Albuminuria >300 mg/g within 5 years of onset of            •     Presence of systemic illness (e.g., Systemic Lupus
      type 1 diabetes                                                   Erythematosus)
  •   Active urinary sediment (RBC casts, dysmorphic              •     Rapid decline in eGFR (>5 mL/min/1.73 m² per

sections.text:
•   For adults and children with CKD and albuminuria (UACR ≥30 mg/g), target BP is <50th percentile (pediatric) or <120/80

sections.title: Fluid overload
sections.text:
Resistant fluid overload in CKD refers to persistent volume retention despite standard sodium restriction and diuretic therapy.
The management focuses on the following objectives; -
  •    Control fluid retention
  •    Prevent complications such as hypertension, edema, and heart failure
  •    Preserve kidney function and improve quality of life

Investigations
  •    Natriuretic Peptides (BNP, NT-proBNP)                           •   Hematocrit, Hemoglobin
  •    Creatinine, BUN, eGFR                                           •   Serum Albumin, Total Protein
  •    Serum/Urine Sodium, Potassium, Chloride                         •   Other tests to be done as per the doctor's discretion
  •    Serum Osmolality                                                    and needs on the specific patient

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •  Sodium restriction: Limit intake to <90 mmol/day (~5–6 g salt/day)/ one teaspoon per day
  •  Patient education: Emphasize adherence to fluid and salt restriction, medication compliance, and self-monitoring
     (weight, edema)
  •  Avoid nephrotoxic drugs and agents that worsen fluid retention (e.g., NSAIDs, certain calcium channel blockers)
  •  Adjust doses of antihypertensives and diuretics according to kidney function

Pharmacological Management
First-line Therapy: Loop Diuretics
A: furosemide (PO): Start 20–40 mg once or twice daily; titrate up to 200 mg/day
            OR
S: torsemide (PO) Start 10–20 mg 24 hourly; titrate up to 200 mg/d
           ADD
Thiazide or Thiazide-like Diuretics If diuresis is inadequate
D: hydrochlorothiazide (PO) 25-50 mg 12 hourly
           OR
S: metolazone (PO): 2.5–5 mg 24 hourly, given 30 minutes before loop diuretic. (Note: Monitor electrolytes closely due to the
risk of hypokalemia and hyponatremia.)

Monitoring
 •    Monitor blood pressure, serum electrolytes (potassium, sodium), and kidney function regularly
 •    Monitor for signs of volume overload or depletion

sections.title: Refractory Fluid Overload
sections.text:
When oral therapy is insufficient or rapid volume control is needed

Pharmacological Management
A: furosemide 20–40 mg IV bolus; 6–8 hourly (in severe cases, doses up to 600 -1500mg/ day )
Maximum single bolus dose:160–200 mg
Doses above 80 mg should be given by slow IV infusion (Infusion rate: ≤4 mg/min).
         OR
S: torsemide 10–20 mg IV 24 hourly. Longer half-life; titrate up to 100–200 mg/day as tolerated

Address contributing factors such as hypoalbuminemia, medication non-adherence, or heart failure

Adults
S: albumin solution (IV ) 20% or 25% , 0.5–1 g/kg/dose IV Maximum: generally should not exceed 2 g/kg/day
Children
S: albumin solution (IV ) 20% or 25% , 0.5–1 g/kg/dose IV administered over 30 minutes–2 hours, depending on indication and
clinical status.
May repeat doses every 24–48 hours depending on clinical response and volume status

Administer with
loop diuretics
A: furosemide 1–2 mg/kg IV) to enhance diuresis and prevent volume overload

Monitor: blood pressure, fluid balance, signs of volume overload (pulmonary edema, hypertension), electrolytes
Avoid: in patients with uncontrolled hypertension, congestive heart failure, or pulmonary edema

Use this formula for calculating doses depending on IV albumin concentration available at the facility

Referral: Refer to a nephrologist CKD patient if fluid overload is refractory to medical management or
if they have resistant hypertension, refractory fluid overload, rapid decline in kidney function, high risk of kidney failure, severe
albuminuria, serious electrolyte disturbances, or AKI superimposed on CKD or if dialysis is indicated.

  Note: Patients who might qualify for dialysis and transplantation or who have complications should be referred early to
  ensure improved outcome and survival on dialysis, i.e. as soon as GFR drops below 30 mL/min/1.73m2, or as soon as
  diagnosis is made/suspected

sections.title: Dialysis
sections.text:
Refer to the National guidelines for Dialysis services from Ministry of Health for detailed indications, procedures and
management of patients on dialysis (Hemodialysis or Peritoneal dialysis)

Dialysis is a medical treatment that performs the essential functions of the kidneys by removing waste products, excess fluids,
and electrolytes from the blood when the kidneys are no longer able to do so adequately. It is a form of renal replacement
therapy used in patients with advanced chronic kidney disease or acute kidney injury.

sections.title: CKD Associated Metabolic Acidosis
sections.text:
Defined as Serum bicarbonate < 22 mmol/L in a patient with chronic kidney disease

Clinical Presentation
  •    Fatigue, weakness, malaise                                     •    Growth retardation
  •    Deep,      rapid    breathing       (compensatory              •    Worsening protein catabolism, worsening CKD
       hyperventilation)                                                   progression
  •    Nausea, anorexia                                               •    Confusion,   arrhythmias   (rare in   chronic
  •    Muscle wasting, bone pain                                           compensated states)

Investigations
  •    ↓ Bicarbonate (<22 mmol/L)
  •    Metabolic acidosis (↓ HCO₃⁻, normal/compensatory ↓ CO₂)
  •    Elevated creatinine and urea (CKD evidence)
  •    May be elevated (hyperkaliemia common in CKD)
  •    Underlying CKD changes (proteinuria, low concentrating ability)
  •    Usually normal to mildly increased in CKD

Non-Pharmacological Management
 Intervention            Details
 Dietary modification    Increase intake of fruits and vegetables (if potassium allows)
 Protein management      Avoid excessive protein restriction; maintain adequate intake to reduce catabolism
 CKD control             Optimize blood pressure and glycaemic control
 Dialysis (advanced CKD) Consider if refractory metabolic acidosis in end-stage CKD
 Education               Advise adherence to CKD diet and medications

Pharmacological Management
D: sodium bicarbonate (PO) 650 mg 12 hourly
          OR
B: calcium carbonate (PO) 500 mg 12 hourly
  Note:
    •    Treatment targets and monitoring should be kept at sodium bicarbonate: 22–26 mmol/L
    •    Check serum bicarbonate levels regularly (e.g., every 2–4 weeks initially) to guide dose adjustments.
    •    Monitor serum calcium and electrolytes to avoid hypercalcemia (especially with calcium carbonate).
    •    Assess for symptom improvement and signs of volume overload.

sections.title: Hyperkalaemia
sections.text:
Defined as serum potassium ≥5.5 mmol/L

Severity Classification
  •    Mild: 5.5–6.0 mmol/L
  •    Moderate: 6.1–6.5 mmol/L
  •    Severe: >6.5 mmol/L or presence of ECG changes (e.g., peaked T waves, prolonged PR, widened QRS)

Clinical Presentation
  •    Ascending muscle weakness                                      •    Paralysis
  •    Muscle fasciculations                                          •    Cardiac conduction abnormalities and arrhythmias

Investigations
  •    Serum potassium: repeat at 0 hr, 1 hr, 3 hr as                 •    Serum bicarbonate, creatinine, full blood count
       clinically indicated                                           •    Blood glucose, lipid profile, uric acid
  •    ECG: monitor for changes such as decreased P
       wave amplitude, peaked T waves, prolonged PR
       interval, and widened QRS

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •  Restrict dietary potassium (avoid bananas, potatoes, green leafy vegetables)
  •  Discontinue or withhold potassium-elevating medications (e.g., RAAS inhibitors, NSAIDs, potassium-sparing diuretics

Pharmacological Management

Step 1: Stabilize Cardiac Membrane Indicated for serum K+ >6.5 mmol/L or ECG changes

sections.title: CKD Associated Anaemia
sections.text:
Patients with CKD present with anemia due to erythropoietin deficiency, iron deficiency due to low iron stores, and impaired
iron utilization due to inflammation. Other causes include shortened red blood cell lifespan due to Uremic toxins, nutritional
deficiencies, such as folate and vitamin B12, and blood loss due to frequent blood draws, gastrointestinal bleeding, or dialysis-
related blood loss further decreases red blood cell counts. [Refer to the national guidelines for dialysis]

Investigations
For anaemia patients with CKD stage 3-5
  •    Full blood count                                                     dehydrogenase (LDH), C-reactive protein (CRP),
  •    Reticulocyte count: Iron Studies:                                    Vitamin B12 and folate levels: Liver function tests
  •    Serum ferritin, Transferrin Saturation (TSAT)                   •    Serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP), serum free
  •    For Unexplained Anemia or Complex Cases:                             light chains, urinary Bence-Jones protein, Thyroid-
       Peripheral blood smear, Haptoglobin and lactate                      stimulating hormone (TSH)
                                                                       •    Stool analysis
Pharmacological Management
Hemodialysis patients: follow the National Dialysis guideline recommendations
Iron Therapy if: Ferritin <100 ng/mL and TSAT <30%, or Ferritin 100–300 ng/mL with TSAT <20–30%

A: ferrous sulfate (PO) 325 mg (65 mg elemental iron) 1–3 times daily
Intravenous (IV) iron is preferred if oral iron is ineffective, not tolerated, or rapid correction is needed.
D: iron sucrose 100–200 mg IV per dose, repeated weekly until iron repletion (typically 1–2 g total).

Erythropoiesis-Stimulating Agents (ESAs)
Non-Dialysis: adults and paediatric:

D: erythropoietin alfa 50 to 100 I.U/kg body weight, 3 times per week (IV) or (SC).
Avoid targeting hemoglobin >11 g/dL due to increased cardiovascular risks. Dose adjusted based on Hb response, aiming to
keep Hb generally between 10 and 11.5 g/dL

Hemodialysis: adults /paediatric
D: erythropoietin alfa 50 IU/kg three times per week intravenously (IV) if IV access is available.

Maintenance phase:
Adults: The total weekly dose ranges from 75 IU/kg to 300 IU/kg, adjusted to maintain hemoglobin between 10-12 g/dL.
Maximum doses should not exceed 150 IU/kg three times per week, or 240 IU/kg once weekly, or 480 IU/kg once every two
weeks
Children: Maintenance phase: Dose is adjusted to maintain hemoglobin between 9.5-11 g/dL. Children under 30 kg may require
higher maintenance doses than adults. Dose adjustments are made cautiously to avoid hemoglobin rises greater than 2 g/dL
over 4 weeks

S: darbepoetin alfa:
Older children (1–18 years) and adults: 0.45 mcg/kg IV or SC once weekly or 0.75 mcg/kg every two weeks.
Children
1–7 months 0.25 to 1.1 mcg/kg/week,

sections.title: Mineral Bone Disease (MBD)
sections.text:
Mineral and bone disorders (MBD) are common in CKD patients, including those on hemodialysis, and significantly increase
the risk of fractures and cardiovascular complications. New evidence shows that disrupted mineral metabolism, inflammation,
and hormonal imbalances like elevated FGF23 contribute to both bone disease and vascular calcification.

Clinical Presentation
  •    Bone pain, fractures                                                •     Soft tissue and vascular calcification
  •    Convulsions, tetany (due to hypocalcemia)                           •     Cardiovascular complications and         increased
  •                                                                              mortality

Investigations
For CKD Stage 3 and Below                                                  •     Vitamin D levels (25-hydroxyvitamin D)
  •    Serum calcium (corrected for albumin)                               •     Serum albumin (for calcium correction)
  •    Serum phosphate                                                     •     Lateral lumbar X-ray
  •    Intact parathyroid hormone (iPTH)                                   •     DEXA scan (bone mineral density)

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •  Dietary management: Low phosphate diet and adequate calcium intake
  •  Lifestyle modification encourages physical activity as tolerated

Pharmacological Management
Hyperphosphatemia -treatment
Adults
B: calcium carbonate (PO) 500–1500 mg per day 8hourly taken with meals
Children
B: calcium carbonate (PO) 500 mg per day 8hourly taken with meals
          OR
Adults:
S: calcium acetate (PO): 667 mg (2 tablets) 8hourly with meals
Children
S: calcium acetate (PO) 667mg (one tablet) 8 hourly with meals
          OR
Adults
S: sevelamer carbonate (PO) 800-1600mg per dose 8 hourly with meals
Children
S: sevelamer carbonate (PO) dose by body surface area (BSA) ≥0.75 to <1.2 m², the typical starting dose is 800 mg three times
daily with meals.
For children with BSA ≥1.2 m², the starting dose is often 1,600 mg three times daily with meals.

Monitoring and Follow-up
 •    Repeat serum calcium, phosphate, PTH, and vitamin D every 3–6 months depending on CKD stage and treatment
      status.
 •    Monitor for signs of vascular calcification clinically and by imaging as indicated.
 •    Adjust therapy based on trends rather than single values.

sections.text:
Hyponatraemia is defined as a serum sodium concentration <135 mmol/L.

sections.title: Haemodialysis (HD) Catheter Related Bloodstream Infection
sections.text:
Hemodialysis catheter care is a critical component in ensuring effective and safe dialysis treatment for patients with end-stage
renal disease. Proper catheter maintenance, including strict aseptic technique and meticulous site care, helps prevent infections
and mechanical complications that can significantly impact patient outcomes.

Principles of hemodialysis catheter care
  •    Strict aseptic technique and catheter care bundles to prevent infections:
  •    Use A:>0.5% chlorhexidine with alcohol for skin antisepsis
  •    Apply antimicrobial ointments D: mupirocin at exit site
  •    Dressings: Use sterile gauze or transparent semi permeable dressings; change gauze every 2 days and transparent
       dressings at least every 7 days unless contraindicated.

sections.title: Exit-site infection: Infection localized at the catheter exit site on the skin.
sections.text:
Infection localized at the catheter exit site on the skin

Clinical Presentation:
Redness, tenderness, crusting, and purulent discharge at the catheter exit site.

Investigation:
Culture from the drainage material at the exit site

Pharmacological Management:
Localized infection (without systemic symptoms)
C: mupirocin 2% ointment (topical) Apply to the affected exit site 8- 12 hourly daily for 5–10 days after cleaning the site.

If associated with surrounding cellulitis, purulent discharge, or failure of topical treatment
Use systemic antibiotics guided by suspected organism and culture results.
B: ampicillin + cloxacillin FDC (PO) 500mg 8 hourly for 7- 14 days
          OR
A: Ciprofloxacin (PO) 500 mg 12 hourly for 7–14 days
(if Gram-negative infection suspected)

sections.title: Tunnel infection: Infection along the subcutaneous tunnel through which the catheter passes.
sections.text:
Infection along the subcutaneous catheter tunnel,

Clinical Presentation:
Tenderness, erythema, swelling, or purulent discharge along the tunnel tract

Investigations
Clinically and by culture of tunnel site drainage

Pharmacological Management
Same as for catheter-related bloodstream infection

sections.title: Catheter-related bloodstream infection (CRBSI) : is a systemic infection originating from the catheter. . 536
sections.text:
A systemic bloodstream infection originating from an intravascular catheter, confirmed or strongly suspected when the catheter
is the source of bacteraemia.
Clinical Presentation:
Fever, chills, rigors, hypotension, or sepsis without another obvious source.

Investigations
  •    Obtain two sets of blood cultures (one from catheter hub, one peripheral or dialysis circuit
  •    Catheter tip cultures
  •    Full blood picture (FBP)
  •    Imaging and further investigations if metastatic infection suspected (e.g., echocardiogram for endocarditis)

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •  Immediate referral for sepsis management if the patient is in shock.
  •  Catheter removal; in non-response to appropriate antibiotic therapy or tunnel infection or metastatic infection (e.g.,
     endocarditis, osteomyelitis) or hemodynamic instability or severe sepsis

Pharmacological Management
All patients should have appropriate cultures (e.g. blood & site cultures) taken before starting therapy. Empirical treatment
should be guided by local antibiogram data and adjusted according to culture & sensitivity results to reduce antimicrobial
resistance.

Empirical Antibiotic Therapy (while waiting for Culture and sensitivity results)
Coverage: Both Gram-positive (especially Staphylococcus aureus, including MRSA) and Gram-negative organisms. Treatment
duration is 14-21 days

Adults
S: vancomycin (IV) in MRSA: Loading dose of 20 mg/kg over the last hour of dialysis, then maintenance doses of 500–1000
mg IV during the last hour of subsequent HD sessions, three times weekly
          OR
C: flucloxacillin (IV) in MSSA: 1-6 g/day divided into 3 doses and then oral therapy
          AND
D: ceftazidime (IV): a loading dose of 1 g IV after hemodialysis (HD) followed by 1 g after subsequent HD sessions

Children
S: vancomycin (IV) in MRSA: 10 mg/kg/dose, over the last hour of dialysis, then maintenance doses with consideration for
serum level monitoring
           OR
 C: flucloxacillin (IV) in MSSA: 25-50 mg/kg/day divided into 3 doses and then oral therapy
           AND
D: ceftazidime (IV):50 mg/kg every 48 hours,
           OR
B: ceftriaxone 1–2 g IV after dialysis, 3 times weekly. administered after dialysis on dialysis days
  Note:
     •    Give empirical treatment while waiting for culture results
     •    Antibiotics should then be tailored to bacteriological results
     •    If negative culture results continue with empirical treatment showing cl

sections.title: Acute Kidney Injury (AKI)
sections.text:
Acute kidney injury is a sudden decline in the glomerular filtration rate (GFR) resulting in elevation of serum blood urea,
creatinine and other waste products. Practically AKI is recognized when there is urine output of less than 0.5ml/kg/hour for >6
hours. Causes of AKI are classified as pre-renal, renal and post-renal causes and usually result in reversible kidney failure,
these causes include;

Table 21.15: Classification, Causes and Management of Acute Kidney Injury (AKI)
 Type of AKI     Description                Common Causes                          Management
 Pre-renal AKI Loss of effective blood      • Hypovolaemia (e.g. diarrhoea, burns, • Restore intravascular volume
                 flow to the kidneys        acute blood loss)                      • D: Intravenous fluids
                                            • Heart failure                        • Manage hypotension
                                            • Hepatic failure                      • Use inotropes where indicated
                                            • Hypotension                          • Treat underlying cause

 (Renal) AKI     kidney tissue              • Nephrotoxic medications              • Discontinue offending nephrotoxic
                                            • Rhabdomyolysis                       drugs
                                            • Tumour lysis syndrome                • Provide supportive management
 Post-renal      Occurs due to urinary      • Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH)   • Relieve obstruction
 AKI             tract obstruction          • Urinary stones                       • Urinary catheterization
                                            • Obstructed urinary catheters         • Nephrostomy where indicated
                                            • Bladder stones                       • Treat underlying cause

Clinical Presentation
Oedema, Oliguria/anuria, Convulsions in children

Investigations
Early disease (diagnosis of AKI)
  •    Serum creatinine: increase of ≥26.5 μmol/L (≥0.3 mg/dL) within 48 hours, or ≥50% increase within 7 days defines AKI
  •    Urine output <0.5 mL/kg/hour for more than 6 hours

Advanced disease
  •   Urine output <0.5 mL/kg/hour for more than 12 hours

Additional investigations

  •    Urinalysis (dipstick and microscopy)
  •    Serum electrolytes (potassium, chloride, bicarbonate, sodium, phosphate, and calcium)
  •    Arterial blood gases

  •   Uric acid
  •   Urine electrolytes – fractional excretion of sodium
  •   Chest X-ray
  •   ECG
  •   Kidney biopsy if the cause is not clinically obvious or if glomerular disease is strongly suspected
  •   Creatine kinase if rhabdomyolysis is suspected

Non-Pharmacological Management

     the patient has respiratory distress                              •    Provide adequate nutritional support with sufficient
  •  Stop intake of all salt- and potassium-containing                      energy and protein; consider enteral or parenteral

sections.title: Glomerular Diseases (GD)
sections.text:
Glomerular diseases include a broad array of clinicopathological syndromes which progress to glomerulosclerosis and
eventually end stage kidney disease. Glomerular disease may be a result of a primary condition of the kidney or may be
secondary to a systemic disorder.

Clinical Presentation
  •    Proteinuria
  •    Reduced GFR (and its effects)
  •    Haematuria
  •    Hypertension
  •    Oedema

sections.title: Glomerular disease - Nephritic syndrome
sections.text:
A non-infectious inflammatory process that involves the nephron. History and examination should exclude secondary causes.

Clinical Presentation
  •    Painless macroscopic turbid, bloody or brownish                   •    Hypertension encephalopathy with impaired level of
       urine                                                                  consciousness or convulsions
  •    Peripheral and facial oedema                                      •    Little or no urine excretion
  •    Difficulty in breathing

Investigations
  •    Serum Creatinine                                                  •    Complete blood count
  •    Blood urea nitrogen/Urea                                          •    Kidney biopsy and histology
  •    Urinalysis (Dipstick + microscopy)                                •    Others on tertiary hospital e.g. ANA, dsDNA, RF, ,
  •    confirm proteinuria by Urine albumin-creatinine                        complements, Syphilis tests (VDRL or RPR)
       ratio (UACR) or Urine protein-creatinine ratio
       (UPCR)
  •    Urine culture

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •  Give oxygen, and nurse in semi-Fowler's position if the patient has respiratory distress.
  •  Restrict intake of all salt
  •  Restrict potassium containing foods and fluids
  •  Restrict fluid intake to 10 mL/kg/day daily plus visible fluid losses

Pharmacological Management
Adults
Fluid overload
A: furosemide (IV bolus) 80mg If hypertension

If diastolic blood pressure is greater than 100mmHg or systolic blood pressure is above 150mmHg:
B: amlodipine (PO) 5mg stat before referral to higher facility
Continue with other medications as in hypertension section (caution contraindications)

  Note: The definitive treatment of nephritis depends on the cause – an assumption of acute post streptococcal nephritis or
  any other disease cannot be made without specific investigation, which may include kidney biopsy.

sections.title: Nephrotic syndrome
sections.text:
It is a kidney disorder characterized by urinary protein loss leading to generalized body swelling. It is severe proteinuria defined
as: Adults: 3.5 g/day,

Clinical Presentation
  •    Oedema
  •    Hypoalbuminemia
  •    Hyperlipidaemia
  Note:
     •    Diagnosis of nephrotic syndrome requires a kidney biopsy, however in children (1year-18 years) biopsy is indicated
          for children with steroid resistant nephrotic syndrome
     •    Children (1-18 years) should be given treatment with steroid, they should be referred for renal biopsy if there is no
          response.
Non-Pharmacological Management
  •  Adequate calories and adequate protein 1g/kg/d
  •  No added salt to limit fluid overload

Pharmacological Management
The management of glomerular disease depends on the type/cause of the disease and is individualized guided by a specialist
according to the histology results obtained after renal biopsy

  Note: Referral to nephrologist may include treatment using immunosuppressant such as prednisolone, mycophenolate
  mofetil, cyclophosphamide, angiotensin blockade .

sections.title: Transplant Donor Evaluation
sections.text:
General Principles
The evaluation of a living kidney donor aims to ensure donor safety, minimize risks, and support informed, voluntary decision-
making without undue pressure. The transplant program’s policies should guide the evaluation process. Both accepted and
excluded donors require appropriate follow-up care plans.

Clinical Assessment
  •    A thorough medical history and physical examination must be documented.
  •    Psychosocial evaluation is essential to assess mental health, social support, and the donor’s understanding of risks and
       benefits.

Eligibility Criteria
  •     Adults aged 21 years and above are eligible for living donation.
  •     Evaluation should be individualized, considering demographic and health profiles, with particular attention to long-term
        kidney health risks.

Investigations

Table 21.18: Pre-Donation Assessment for Living Kidney Donors
 S/N Domain                        Recommended Assessment
 1.    General Medical             Height, weight, BMI, blood pressure (measured on two separate occasions), baseline
       Assessment                  laboratory investigations including hematology, coagulation profile, electrolytes,
                                   fasting blood glucose, lipid profile, liver function tests, chest X-ray, and ECG.

                                   fitness, informed consent capacity, and adequacy of social support.
 3.    Surgical Suitability        Assessment of obesity, anticoagulation status, vascular anatomy including imaging
       Assessment                  (KUB and abdominal ultrasound), and urological assessment where indicated.

 5.    Cancer Screening            Age- and risk-appropriate cancer screening including imaging, colonoscopy,
                                   cystoscopy, and other relevant investigations. Prior treated malignancy is not an
                                   absolute contraindication but requires individualized assessment and waiting periods.
                                   PSA screening is recommended for men aged ≥50 years. Pap smear screening
                                   should follow national cervical cancer screening guidelines.
 6.    Pulmonary Assessment        Clinical history, physical examination, and additional investigations as indicated.
 7.    Cardiovascular Evaluation   ECG, echocardiography, stress testing (stress ECG or dobutamine stress
                                   echocardiography for donors >40 years or those with cardiovascular risk factors), and
                                   ambulatory blood pressure monitoring where indicated.
 8.    Peripheral Arterial Disease Clinical assessment, vascular imaging (CT renal angiogram with IVU), and surgical
       Assessment                  consultation where indicated.
 9.    Neurological Assessment     Evaluate history of stroke or transient ischemic attack (TIA); defer donation for at
                                   least 6 months after such events. Screen for intracranial aneurysms in high-risk
                                   conditions such as autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD).
 10.   Gastrointestinal/Liver      Clinical history and examination to exclude active gastrointestinal or liver disease;
       Assessment                  perform targeted investigations such as abdominal ultrasound and others as
                                   indicated.
 11.   Hematological Assessment Screen for thrombophilia and antiphospholipid antibodies in high-risk individuals.
                                   Anticoagulation therapy alone is not a contraindication.
 12.   Immunological               Document sensitizing events such as blood transfusions and pregnancies; perform
       Assessment                  HLA antibody testing.
 13.   Infection Screening         Screen for Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, HIV, CMV, VDRL, urine culture, and other
                                   regionally relevant infections.

Marginal or Expanded Criteria Living Donors (ECLDs)
Marginal or Expanded Criteria Living Donors (ECLDs) are living kidney donors who have one or more of the following risk
factors:
Table 21.19: Risk Factors
  S/N Risk Factor
  1      Age >60 years
  2      Body mass index (BMI) >30 kg/m²
  3      Controlled hypertension
  4      Mildly reduced kidney function (e.g., estimated glomerular filtration rate [eGFR] <80 mL/min)
  5      Impaired glucose tolerance
  6      History of smoking

sections.title: Transplant Candidate
sections.text:
All patients with CKD stage 4-5 should be informed of, educated about and considered for kidney transplantation regardless of
socioeconomic status, sex, or ethnicity. Pre-emptive transplantation referral should be 6-12 months before anticipated RRT
initiation. Active diseases should be controlled first before transplantation.

The following are not recommended for kidney alone transplant: -
  •     Multiple myeloma and AL amyloidosis
  •     Decompensated cirrhosis
  •     Severe irreversible obstructive or restrictive lung disease
  •     Severe uncorrectable and symptomatic cardiac disease
  •     Progressive central neurodegenerative disease

Kidney Transplant Candidate Assessment
All transplant candidates should undergo comprehensive evaluation as detailed outlined on the table 21.20 below

       Assessment               avoidance/cessation.

                                anatomy, evaluation of native kidneys in autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease,
                                and urological assessment where indicated.

 4     Cancer Screening         Perform age- and risk-appropriate cancer screening before transplantation and continue
                                screening after transplantation. This may include imaging, cystoscopy, colonoscopy,
                                and other investigations for high-risk individuals. Patients with cured malignancy should
                                not be automatically excluded; waiting period depends on type of malignancy.
