sections.title: Transplant Recipient
sections.text:
This section will cover the management of kidney transplant recipients (KTRs). It includes initial and maintenance
immunosuppression, monitoring and management of special conditions. Enhanced investigations and treatment in this group
is paramount to ensure kidney graft survival.

sections.title: Induction Therapy
sections.text:
Induction immunosuppression is used to reduce the risk of early acute graft rejection after kidney transplantation. The two main
classes of induction agents are:

Interleukin-2 receptor antagonists (IL-2RA) example Basiliximab and Lymphocyte-depleting agents Example: Rabbit
Antithymocyte Globulin (rATG)
Rabbit Antithymocyte Globulin (rATG) is preferred over horse ATG and is the most commonly recommended lymphocyte-
depleting agent for induction therapy, particularly in patients with high immunological risk. Selection of induction therapy should
be guided by immunological risk stratification.

sections.title: Premedication for (S) Rabbit Antithymocyte Globulin (rATG)
sections.text:
Premedication should be administered 30 minutes to 1 hour before each dose of (S) rATG to reduce infusion-related reactions.
Administer:
D: paracetamol 1 g IV stat
         AND
A: chlorpheniramine 4 mg PO stat
         AND
C: pantoprazole 40 mg IV once daily
         AND
D: hydrocortisone 100 mg IV stat
         OR
D: methylprednisolone 125 mg IV stat
Administer a test dose of (S) rATG at 10 mL/hour for 10 minutes before giving the full daily dose. Follow institutional transplant
SOPs for rATG dilution and administration.

sections.title: Maintenance Immunosuppressive Medication
sections.text:
Maintenance immunosuppression after kidney transplantation is critical to prevent allograft rejection and ensure long-term graft
survival by using a combination of immunosuppressive agents tailored to balance efficacy and toxicity. The standard regimen
typically includes a calcineurin inhibitor (tacrolimus preferred), an antiproliferative agent (mycophenolate mofetil or
azathioprine), and corticosteroids, with mTOR inhibitors (sirolimus or everolimus) reserved for special circumstances.
Investigations
To be done on monthly basis
  •     Serum creatinine and Blood urea nitrogen
  •     Urinalysis
  •     Urine biochemistry (Urine dipstick)
  •     Serum Tacrolimus (12-h trough) sample taken preferably before the morning Tacrolimus dose or cyclosporine (12-h
        trough or 2-h post dose) levels according to patient’s regime

sections.title: Monitoring schedule for the Kidney Transplant Recipients (Routine)
sections.text:
Kidney transplant recipients have high risk of getting complications including surgical complications (first 3 months), frequent
infections (first six months) and complications related to immunosuppressive medications, including diabetic mellitus. Some of
the immunosuppressive medications have a narrow therapeutic window and have toxic effects, including nephrotoxicity.
Therefore, these patients need regular and frequent follow-up as indicated in the table below.

        suspicion arises.

sections.title: Acute Kidney Graft Rejection
sections.text:
Refers to an immune-mediated attack on the transplanted kidney, confirmed usually by biopsy and characterized by histologic
changes (e.g., T cell–mediated rejection or antibody-mediated rejection).
An acute rejection is clinically suspected in patients with increased serum creatinine, after the exclusion of other causes of graft
dysfunction. Other causes are generally excluded with a biopsy. Acute rejection should be treated after kidney biopsy unless
this will substantially delay treatment.

Clinical Presentation
  •    Occur within        the   first   six   months       after              •    Oliguria
       transplantation                                                         •    Graft pain and/or tenderness
  •    Fever                                                                   •    Worsening hypertension
  •    Malaise

Investigations
  •    Kidney biopsy which may be repeated if there is failure of treatment
  •    Serum creatinine and Blood Urea nitrogen
  •    KUB Ultrasound and Doppler USS of the kidney graft

sections.title: Cystic Kidney Disease
sections.text:
Acquired or hereditary disorders of the kidneys. Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease is a common cause of end stage
kidney disease. It is progressive and incurable condition.

Clinical Presentation
Kidney
  •    Nocturia, polyuria and frequency due to                         Extra-kidney manifestations
       concentration defect                                              •    Polycystic liver disease
  •    Hypertension                                                      •    Intracranial aneurysms
  •    Pain syndrome (infection, bleeding, stones, rupture               •    Cardiac – valvular heart disease
       or compression)
  •    Uremic manifestations

Diagnostic ultrasonographic criteria
 Age group                     Diagnostic criterion
 15–39 years                   ≥3 cysts, unilateral or bilateral
 40–59 years                   ≥2 cysts in each kidney
 ≥60 years                     ≥4 cysts in each kidney

Investigations
  •    Ultrasonography – KUB                                              •    MRI for detailed cyst detection, volume
  •    Serum creatinine                                                        measurement, monitoring progression, extra-renal
  •    Urinalysis – biochemistry and microscopy                                cysts, and aneurysms
  •    Genetic testing for those who want.to be donor                     •    CT scan – best for valuation of complications
       (family history)                                                        (stones, tumors), when MRI contraindicated or
                                                                               unavailable
                                                                          •    ALT, AST and bilirubin if using Tolvaptan
Non-Pharmacological Management
  •  Increase fluid intake >3 L in patients with eGFR ≥30 mL/min/1.73 m², unless contraindicated. For those with eGFR <30,
     individualized assessment is needed.
  •  Low-salt Diet: Recommended for all patients.
  •  Kidney transplantation when indicated; pre transplant nephrectomy may be needed for massively enlarged kidneys

Pharmacological Management
S: tolvaptan (PO) 45mg in the morning and 15mg 8 hours later (titrate to 90mg am and 30mg pm). pm dose should be taken
before 4pm

Pediatric Considerations
Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD) may be diagnosed in childhood, especially with family history or
genetic testing.

Screening: Ultrasound screening recommended in at-risk children, typically starting at age 15 or earlier if symptomatic.
MRI can be used for detailed assessment but is less commonly performed routinely in children.

Non-Pharmacological Management
Lifestyle: Encourage healthy diet, physical activity, and avoidance of nephrotoxins.

Pharmacological Management
Blood pressure management: Target blood pressure at or below the 50th percentile for age, sex, and height.

ACE inhibitors or ARBs are first-line agents for hypertension.
 Medicine                Initial Dose                Maximum Dose                                Frequency
 C: enalapril            0.08–0.2 mg/kg/day          0.6 mg/kg/day (maximum 40 mg/day)           1–2 divided doses
      OR
 C: lisinopril           0.07 mg/kg/day              0.6 mg/kg/day (maximum 40 mg/day)           Once daily
      OR
 B: captopril            0.3–0.5 mg/kg/dose          6 mg/kg/day (maximum 450 mg/day)            2–3 divided doses
      OR
 B: losartan             0.7 mg/kg/day               1.4 mg/kg/day (maximum 100 mg/day)          Once daily

  Note:
    •   Tolvaptan Evidence for long-term safety and efficacy in children is limited
    •   Considered only in selected pediatric patients with rapidly progressive disease,
    •   Dosing is weight-based and should be supervised by a pediatric nephrologist

Extrarenal Manifestations
Polycystic liver disease, intracranial aneurysms, and cardiac valvular abnormalities are common and should be screened for
based on clinical risk factors.
Intracranial aneurysm screening is recommended in patients with family history or high-risk features.

sections.title: Renal artery stenosis
sections.text:
Renal artery stenosis (RAS) is the narrowing of one or both renal arteries, most commonly due to atherosclerosis (especially
in older adults) or fibromuscular dysplasia (typically in younger patients, especially women).
If untreated, RAS can lead to resistant hypertension, chronic kidney disease (CKD), and end-stage kidney disease (ESKD).

Clinical Presentation
  •    Hypertension, which is resistant, refractory to                 •    Episodes of flash pulmonary oedema
       therapy with three or more drugs.                               •    Asymmetrical kidneys.
  •    Young onset hypertension with no family history                 •    Unexplained hypokalemia
  •    An acute rise in serum creatinine >30% after ACE-
       inhibitor or ARB use

Investigations
  •    Serum creatinine/BUN                                            •    Computer tomography angiography
  •    Urine protein creatinine ratio                                  •    Magnetic resonance angiography
  •    Urinalysis                                                      •    ACE-inhibitor Scintigraphy
  •    Duplex Doppler ultrasonography                                  •    Conventional arteriography

Non-Pharmacological Management
Revascularization (when >80% stenosis)

Pharmacological Management
A: Aspirin 75 mg orally once daily
ACE inhibitors or ARBs (refer to hypertension management section)

sections.title: Thrombotic Microangiopathy (TMA)
sections.text:
Thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA) is a pathological syndrome characterized by: Thrombocytopenia, Microangiopathic
haemolytic anaemia and Organ injury. Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a common manifestation due to glomerular microvascular
injury and occlusion. Early recognition and treatment are essential.

Clinical Presentation
  •    Haemolysis
  •    Ischaemic organ dysfunction
  •    Acute kidney injury (AKI)

Extrarenal manifestations may include:
  •    Pancreatitis
  •    Hepatitis
  •    Seizures
  •    Diarrhoea, vomiting, and abdominal pain
  •    Digital gangrene
  •

Investigations
  •    ADAMTS13 activity (>10% makes thrombotic                          •    Anti-double stranded DNA (anti-dsDNA)
       thrombocytopenic purpura [TTP] less likely)                       •    Antiphospholipid antibodies
  •    Bacterial culture/serology                                        •    Anti-Scl-70 antibodies
  •    HIV serology                                                      •    Kidney biopsy (where indicated)
  •    Antinuclear antibody (ANA)

Pharmacological Management
Identify and treat the underlying cause. Primary thrombotic microangiopathies include:
  •     Complement-mediated atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome (aHUS)
  •     Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) associated with reduced ADAMTS13 activity

S: Plasma exchange until ADAMTS13 results are available to exclude TTP, with or without immunosuppression.

sections.title: Reflux nephropathy
sections.text:
A chronic kidney disease characterized by renal scarring and interstitial fibrosis resulting from vesicoureteric reflux (VUR) and/or
recurrent urinary tract infections (UTIs), typically originating in early childhood. It is often associated with congenital
abnormalities of the urinary tract such as renal dysplasia and posterior urethral valves, leading to progressive loss of renal
function and hypertension."

Clinical Presentation
  •    Usually asymptomatic                                              •    Dysuria
  •    Hypertension                                                      •    Aching lumbar pain
  •    Frequency of micturition                                          •    Urinalysis shows leucocytes

Investigations
  •    Urine analysis– dipstick/biochemistry/microscopy                  •    MCUG- micturating cystourethrography
  •    Serum creatinine                                                  •    Serial imaging by Magnetic Resonance Imaging –
  •    Urine culture                                                          MR
  •    Ultrasonography – KUB                                             •    Renal biopsy
  •    Radionuclide DMSA scans

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •  If recurrent pyelonephritis occurs in an abnormal kidney with minimal function – Nephrectomy
  •  Hypertension may be cured by removal of a diseased kidney
  •  Severe reflux may be managed by ureteric reimplantation or sub trigonal injection of Teflon/polysaccharide
  •  Blood pressure targets: Children: ≤50th percentile for age, sex, and height Adults: <120/80 mmHg (or individualized
     based on comorbidities)

Pharmacological Management
Antibiotic Prophylaxis:
Adult: Not routinely recommended; treat UTIs promptly

Children: Recommended for high-grade VUR or recurrent febrile UTIs
Acute UTI Treatment:
Adult / Paediatric: Prompt appropriate antibiotics, Treat UTI as in section with Urinary tract infection.

Blood Pressure Control: use RAAS inhibitors;
Adult
B: Losartan: start 50 mg once daily, titrate up to 100 mg daily
Children
 Medicine                 Initial Dose                Maximum Dose                                    Frequency
 C: enalapril             0.08–0.2 mg/kg/day          0.6 mg/kg/day (maximum 40 mg/day)               1–2 divided doses
      OR
 C: lisinopril            0.07 mg/kg/day              0.6 mg/kg/day (maximum 40 mg/day)               Once daily
      OR
 B: captopril             0.3–0.5 mg/kg/dose          6 mg/kg/day (maximum 450 mg/day)                2–3 divided doses
      OR
 B: losartan              0.7 mg/kg/day               1.4 mg/kg/day (maximum 100 mg/day)              Once daily

Proteinuria Management: see section with proteinuria in adults consider SGLT2i

sections.title: Contrast Induced Nephropathy (CIN)
sections.text:
Contrast induced nephropathy (CIN), which is also known as Contrast Induced Acute Kidney Injury may occur after
administration of iodinated contrast material, which is called contrast-induced nephropathy. Common contrast based studies
resulting in CIN include CT scan, MRI and coronary angiography. Contrast induced acute kidney injury is usually characterized
by rapid recovery of renal function.

Clinical Presentation
  •    Early mild increase in serum creatinine that is generally observed within 24-48 hours after the iodinated contrast
       exposure and that is usually mild. Serum creatinine starts to decline within 3-7days of exposure
  •    No oliguria, patients with CIN are passing urine normally and if it occurs develop immediately. Oliguria and more severe
       elevation of creatinine may develop in patients with moderate to severe CKD.
  •    Urinalysis may show sediments consistent with acute tubular necrosis.
  •    Other manifestations of reduced GFR including hyperkalaemia, acidosis and hyperphosphataemia

Investigations
  •    All patients scheduled for contrast studies should have serum creatinine performed before the study and 24-48hours
       after contrast study
  •    For patients with raised creatinine
       > Serial creatinine should be performed until 7 days
       > Potassium, sodium, phosphorus, calcium and urinalysis
       > Kidney ureters and bladder ultrasound

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •  Identify all at risk patients; diabetic mellitus, heart failure, patients with CKD
  •  Withdrawal of nonessential potentially nephrotoxic medications (e.g., NSAIDs, diuretics, aminoglycosides, amphotericin,
     platins, zoledronate, and methotrexate) in people with AKI or eGFR <30 ml/min per 1.73 m2 for 24–48 hours before
     contrast study
  •  For people with AKI or an eGFR <30 ml/min per 1.73 m2, stop metformin restart 48 hours later only if GFR remains
     stable
  •  withholding RAASi in people at risk for 48 hours before elective contrast-enhanced CT restart 48 hours later only if GFR
     remains stable
  •  Encourage adequate hydration prior to study
  •  Use lower possible dose of contrast (<125 ml)
  •  Use low osmolar (iohexol, ioversol) or iso-osmolar (iodixanol) contrast media
  •  Prophylactic peri contrast hemodialysis has been shown to be potentially harmful and is not recommended.

Pharmacological Management
Fluid administration should be used if there are no contra-indications. Normal saline should be administered before and
continued for few hours after the study

Outpatients:
A: sodium chloride 0.9% ,3mL/kg over one-hour pre-procedure and 1-1.5mL/kg/hour during and for four to six hours’ post-
procedure, with administration of at least 6mL/kg post-procedure

Inpatients
A: sodium chloride 0.9%, 1mL/kg/hour for 6-12hours pre-procedure, intra-procedure, and for 6- 12hours post-procedure

 Note: Patient with severe CIN may need to undergo haemodialysis if there is no improvement within 7days

sections.title: Urinary Tract Infection (UTI)
sections.text:
Urinary tract infections may involve the upper or lower urinary tract. Infections may be complicated or uncomplicated.
Uncomplicated cystitis is a lower UTI in a non-pregnant woman of reproductive age and who has a normal urinary tract. All
other UTIs should be regarded as complicated. The commonest causative pathogens for UTIs irrespective of the group of
patients involved in Tanzania are Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumonia, Proteus spp. and Staphylococcus aureus.

   Note:
     •   Differentiation of upper from lower urinary tract infection in young children is not possible on clinical grounds
     •   Upper UTI is a more serious condition and requires longer and sometimes intravenous antimicrobial treatment.
     •   Special considerations should be given in the following groups of patients: children, pregnant women, elderly (>60
         years) and other individuals with functional or structural abnormalities in the urinary tract.

Table 21.30: Clinical Presentation of Urinary Tract Infections
  Type of UTI                                       Clinical Presentation
  Lower UTI (Cystitis)                              • Suprapubic pain/tenderness
                                                    • Dysuria

                                                    • Urgency

                                                    • Occasionally haematuria
                                                    • Temperature ≥38°C
  Upper UTI (Pyelonephritis)                        • Flank pain/tenderness
                                                    • Pyuria
                                                    • Occasionally haematuria
                                                    • Temperature ≥38°C
                                                    • Vomiting
  Catheter-Associated UTI (CAUTI)                   Presence of symptoms and signs of cystitis or pyelonephritis in a person
                                                    whose urinary tract is currently catheterized or who had a urinary catheter
                                                    in place within the previous 48 hours.
  Urosepsis                                         Features of cystitis or pyelonephritis plus two or more of the following:
                                                    • Temperature >38°C or <36°C
                                                    • Tachycardia >90 beats/minute
                                                    • Tachypnoea >20 breaths/minute
                                                    • WBC count >12,000/mm³ or <4,000/mm³
                                                    • Confusion
                                                    • Hypotension
                                                    • Other evidence of organ dysfunction
Investigations
   •   Quantitative or semi-quantitative urinalysis (high protein, low sugar, nitrites positive, leukocyte esterase positive, and
       low pH) and Urine microscopy (>8–10 WBC/HPF) may be suggestive of UTIs.
   •   Quantitative urine culture (growth of at least 104 or 105 colony forming units of bacteria/ml of urine) and antimicrobial
       sensitivity testing. Concomitant urine and blood cultures are indicated in case of urosepsis.
   •   Urinary LAMM – in patients with suspected to have genitourinary TB
   •   Ultrasound (kidney and pelvis) to exclude stones or structural abnormalities in patients with recurrent UTI

  Note: Positive WBC counts on urinalysis or urine microscopy + compatible 2 or more Clinical Presentations supported by
  urine culture in centers where this test is available.

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •  Ensure adequate hydration
  •  Voiding of urine whenever an urge to micturate occurs; or after sexual intercourse in adults.
  •  Removal of indwelling bladder catheter (where indicated)
Pharmacological Management

Analgesics in severe dysuria and flank pain
Adults
A: paracetamol (PO) 500-100 mg every 6-8 hours.
Children:
A: paracetamol (PO) 15 mg/kg/dose 4–6 hourly when required to a maximum of 4 doses per 24 hours;

Uncomplicated Cystitis                                               Complicated Cystitis

daily for 5 days                                                     daily for 7 days

Treatment of Urinary Tract Infection (UTI) in Children

General Principles

sections.title: Urology Disorders
sections.text:
Are diseases that affect urinary system including urinary incontinence, urolithiasis, benign prostatic hyperplasia, prostate
cancer.

sections.title: Hematuria
sections.text:
Hematuria is the presence of blood in the urine, either visible (gross hematuria) or microscopic. It is a clinical sign indicating
possible underlying pathology in the urinary tract or systemic disease. Prompt evaluation and appropriate management are
essential to identify treatable causes and prevent complications.

Clinical Presentation
  •    Gross hematuria: Visible red or cola-colored urine, often alarming to patients.
  •    Microscopic hematuria: Detected on urinalysis without visible discoloration.
  •    Associated symptoms may include dysuria, flank pain, fever, urinary frequency, urgency, or clots in urine

Table 21.31: Initial Assessment and Diagnosis
 Assessment Component         Details/Parameters to Assess            Purpose/Notes
 History                      Duration and quantity of                Determine onset, severity, and progression
                              haematuria
                              Associated urinary symptoms             Identify infection, inflammation, or obstruction
                              (pain, burning, frequency)
                              History of trauma,                      Assess iatrogenic or traumatic causes
                              instrumentation, or
                              catheterization
                              Past urinary tract infections or        Evaluate common infectious causes (context-specific)
                              schistosomiasis exposure
                              Medication history                      Identify drug-induced bleeding or interactions
                              (anticoagulants, herbal
                              medicines)
                              Risk factors for malignancy             Stratify risk and urgency of investigation
                              (age >40 years, smoking,
                              occupational exposure)
 Physical Examination         Vital signs (including features         Assess haemodynamic stability and severity
                              of anemia or shock)
                              Abdominal and flank                     Suggest stones, infection, or obstruction
                              tenderness
                              Palpation for bladder distension        Detect urinary retention or tumours
                              or masses
                              Genital examination                     Identify local sources of bleeding or infection

                              leukocytes, nitrites)                   disease

                                                                      malignancy risk factors

Supportive Care
  •  Maintain adequate hydration to help flush the urinary tract.
  •  Monitor vital signs and haemoglobin levels in cases of significant bleeding.
  •  Blood transfusion only if clinically indicated (e.g., severe anaemia or haemodynamic instability).
  •  Provide pain management using paracetamol or NSAIDs where appropriate.

Refer patients for specialist care in the following situations:
  •    Persistent or recurrent haematuria with no clear                 •    Severe anaemia or haemodynamic instability due

       retention or obstruction.                                             intervention.

  •    Educate on personal hygiene and prevention of                    •    Encourage early health-seeking behavior when

  •    Promote awareness of schistosomiasis prevention,                 •    Counsel on medication adherence and follow-up

21.11.2 Prostatitis
It is an inflammation of the prostate usually secondary to bacterial infection caused by urinary or STI pathogens

Clinical Presentation
  •    Perineal, sacral or suprapubic pain Dysuria and Urinary frequency
  •    Varying degrees of obstructive symptoms which may lead to urinary retention
  •    Sometimes fever

Investigations
Urine analysis, Urine culture

Pharmacological Management
Acute bacterial prostatitis
In men < 35 years or if there are features of associated urethritis (STI regimen):

S: cefixime (PO) 400mg as a single dose
          THEN
A: doxycycline (PO) 100mg 12hourly for 7days

In men > 35 years or if there is associated cystitis:
A: ciprofloxacin (PO) 500 mg 12hourly for 14days

Referral to Urologist if:
  •   No response to treatment                                          •    High fever
  •   Urinary retention                                                 •    Chronic/relapsing prostatitis

   Note:
     •   Avoid unnecessary use of broad-spectrum or reserve antibiotics at primary care level
     •   Educate patients on medication adherence and the importance of follow-up.

sections.title: 3 Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH)
sections.text:
Benign prostatic hyperplasia is a noncancerous (benign) growth of the prostate gland. Management of BPH depends on severity
of symptoms according to International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS)

Clinical Presentation
  •    Obstructive symptoms: weak, intermittent stream and urinary hesitancy
  •    Irritative (frequency, nocturia and urgency) voiding symptoms.
  •    Digital Rectal Examination reveals a uniform enlargement of the prostate with smooth surface and firm in consistence.
       The median sulcus is also palpable
  •    Urinary retention with a distended bladder may be present in the absence of severe symptoms, therefore it is important
       to palpate for an enlarged bladder during examination.
  •    Pelvic or transrectal USS confirms the prostate enlargement
  •    Prostatic specific antigen levels are within normal range
  •    Symptoms should be graded by the IPSS – international prostate symptom score into mild, moderate and severe.

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •  Patients with mild symptoms should be put under watchful waiting (change of lifestyle and regular follow up). Reduce
     fluid intake especially in the evening, avoid caffeinated drinks
  •  Patients with severe symptoms should undergo surgery, transurethral resection of the prostate for prostate weighing up
     to 75g and those weighing more than 75g should undergo open prostatectomy
  •  For patients presenting with urinary retention, insert a urethral catheter as a temporary measure while patient is
     transferred to hospital
  •  Remove drugs that prevent urinary outflow e.g. tricyclics and neuroleptics.

Pharmacological Management
Patients with moderate symptoms according to IPSS should be put under medical therapy unless opt for surgery.
Medical treatment of BPH includes alpha-adrenergic blocker or 5 alpha- reductase inhibitor or a combination of both

Adrenergic Alpha Blockers:
D: tamsulosin (PO) 0.4mg 24hourly
         OR
D: alfuzosin (PO) 10mg 24hourly

5-alpha Reductase Inhibitors
D: finasteride (PO) 5mg 24hourly
          OR
S: dutasteride (PO) 0.5mg 24hourly

Anticholinergics
S: oxybutynin (PO) 5mg 8hourly for patients with persistent urgency despite above medications

  Note: All patients with BPH and associated complications like recurrent UTI, Haematuria, Kidney insufficiency, hernia and
  urinary stones need surgery and should be referred to centres where specialized care can be offered.
  Prostate Cancer has been posted in Oncology section

sections.title: Cryptorchidism
sections.text:
Cryptorchidism is the absence of one or both testes from the scrotum due to failure of testicular descent. It is a common
congenital anomaly affecting approximately 1-4% of full-term male infants and is associated with risks of infertility, testicular
malignancy, and psychological impact if untreated.

Clinical Presentation
  •    Empty scrotum on one or both sides
  •    Asymmetrical or underdeveloped scrotum
  •    Non-palpable testis in scrotum
  •    Palpable testis in inguinal canal (some cases)
  •    Testis may be intra-abdominal in non-palpable cases
  •    Usually asymptomatic
  •    May be associated with inguinal hernia

Investigations
  •    Clinical examination (primary diagnostic method)
  •    Ultrasound of inguinal region and abdomen (if testis not palpable)
  •    MRI or diagnostic laparoscopy (Gold standard for non-palpable testes to confirm presence and location.)

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •  Orchidopexy (definitive treatment), Ideally performed between 6–12 months of age
  •  Laparoscopic exploration and orchidopexy for intra-abdominal testes
  •  Hernia repair if associated inguinal hernia is present

Pharmacological Management
  •  Hormonal therapy (e.g., hCG or GnRH) may be used in selected cases, but surgical correction remains the standard
     treatment
  •  No routine pharmacological cure; used only in specific specialist settings

Follow-up:
  •   Monitor testicular position and size postoperatively.
  •   Long-term surveillance for fertility and malignancy risks.

sections.title: Hypospadias
sections.text:
Hypospadias is a congenital malformation characterized by ectopic placement of the urethral meatus on the ventral side of the
penis, often accompanied by chordee (ventral curvature) and abnormal foreskin development. It can cause difficulties in
urination, sexual function, and fertility.
Early diagnosis and timely management of both conditions are essential to optimize outcomes, preserve fertility, and improve
quality of life.

Clinical Presentation

  •    Incomplete or “hooded” foreskin (dorsal prepuce)              •     Usually identified at birth during newborn
  •    Ventral penile curvature (chordee)                                  examination
  •    Abnormal urinary stream (spraying or downward                 •     Associated cryptorchidism may be present (in
       deviation)                                                          severe cases)
  •    Difficulty with standing urination in older children

sections.title: Phimosis
sections.text:
Inability to retract the foreskin over the glans penis.

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •  Gentle daily retraction and hygiene.
  •  Circumcision if conservative management fails or if recurrent infections/urinary obstruction.

Pharmacological Management
C: betamethasone 0.05% cream Apply thin layer to the preputial ring twice daily for 4–6 weeks
(Gentle foreskin retraction after application) (if not painful)
          OR
A: hydrocortisone 1% cream Apply twice daily 4–6 weeks
          AND
B: lidocaine topical 2% gel: apply before procedure; or infiltration as per procedure
          AND
A: paracetamol (PO) 10–15 mg/kg/dose orally every 6 hours as needed;
          OR
A: Ibuprofen: 5–10 mg/kg/dose orally every 8 hours as needed.

sections.title: Paraphimosis
sections.text:
Definition: Entrapment of retracted foreskin behind the glans, causing swelling and pain.

Non-Pharmacologic management
Emergency:
  •  Manual reduction after lubrication and local anesthesia.
  •  If manual reduction fails, dorsal slit or circumcision.

Pharmacological Management
Mainly Supportive:
Analgesics and antibiotics if infection is suspected.

B: lidocaine topical 2% gel: apply before procedure; or infiltration as per procedure
          AND
A: paracetamol (PO) 10–15 mg/kg/dose orally every 6 hours as needed;
          OR
A: ibuprofen: 5–10 mg/kg/dose orally every 8 hours as needed.
          AND
B: amoxicillin + clavulanic acid 625 mg (PO) every 8 hours for 5–7 days (adult); adjust for child weight.

sections.title: Hydrocele
sections.text:
Definition: Accumulation of fluid in the tunica vaginalis of the scrotum.

Non-Pharmacological Management
Observation:
  •   For small, asymptomatic hydroceles (especially in children).

Surgical:
  •    Hydrocelectomy is the definitive treatment.

Pharmacological Management
Mainly Supportive:
B: lidocaine topical 2% gel: apply before procedure; or infiltration as per procedure
          AND
A: paracetamol (PO) 10–15 mg/kg/dose orally every 6 hours as needed;
          OR
A: ibuprofen: 5–10 mg/kg/dose orally every 8 hours as needed.
          AND
B: amoxicillin + clavulanic acid 625 mg (PO) every 8 hours for 5–7 days (adult); adjust for child weight.

sections.title: Testicular Torsion
sections.text:
Definition: Twisting of the spermatic cord, compromising blood supply to the testis.

Non-Pharmacological Management
Surgical emergency.
  •    Immediate referral to surgical facility for detorsion and orchidopexy.

Pharmacological Management
Mainly Supportive:
B: lidocaine topical 1% infiltration as per procedure
          AND
A: paracetamol (PO) 10–15 mg/kg/dose orally every 6 hours as needed;
          OR
A: ibuprofen: 5–10 mg/kg/dose orally every 8 hours as needed.
          AND
B: ceftriaxone: 1–2 g IV once pre-operatively (adult); 50–80 mg/kg IV for children

sections.title: Varicocele
sections.text:
Introduction Varicocele is the abnormal dilation of the pampiniform venous plexus within the spermatic cord. It is most common
on the left side (90%) due to the anatomical entry of the left renal vein. It is a significant cause of preventable male infertility
and testicular atrophy.

Clinical Presentation
Usually asymptomatic but may present as a "bag of worms" sensation or a dull, aching pain in the scrotum that worsens with
standing. Physical Examination: Should be performed in both standing and supine positions. Use the Valsalva Maneuver to
accentuate dilated veins.
Grading: Grade 1: Palpable only with Valsalva.
          Grade 2: Palpable without Valsalva but not visible.
          Grade 3: Visible through the scrotal skin.

Differential Diagnosis
  •    Hydrocele: Transilluminates (Varicocele does not).                  •    Testicular Torsion: Acute, severe pain (Surgical
  •    Inguinal Hernia: Reducible mass with a cough                             emergency).
       impulse.                                                            •    Spermatocele: Cystic mass in the epididymis.

Investigations
  •    Scrotal Doppler Ultrasound: To confirm venous diameter >2.5mm and retrograde flow.
  •    Semen Analysis: To assess for oligospermia or decreased motility.

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •  Scrotal support
  •  Surgical (Varicocelectomy): Indicated for palpable varicocele with abnormal semen parameters, testicular atrophy, or
     chronic pain.
     Level B and C (District level): Diagnosis and referral.
     Level D (Regional): Inguinal or sub-inguinal ligation.
     Level S (Zona/ Special /National): Microsurgical varicocelectomy (Preferred).

Pharmacological Management
Analgesics for minor discomfort.

Adults
A: paracetamol 500 mg–1 g (PO) every 6–8 hours as                       Adults
needed                                                                  A: ibuprofen 400 mg PO every 8 hours as needed
Children:                                       OR                      Children
A: paracetamol 10–15 mg/kg/dose PO every 6 hours as                     A: ibuprofen 5–10 mg/kg/dose PO every 6–8 hours
needed

Follow-up
  •   Post-operative semen analysis every 3 months for 1 year.
  •   Monitor for post-surgical hydrocele or recurrence.

sections.title: Fournier’s Gangrene
sections.text:
Definition: Rapidly progressive necrotizing fasciitis of the perineum and genitalia.

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •  Emergency resuscitation (fluids, oxygen).
  •  Urgent surgical debridement.
  •  Wound care.

Pharmacological Management
Broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics

Adults
B: ceftriaxone 1–2 g IV once daily
Children:
B: ceftriaxone 50–80 mg/kg IV once daily
          AND
Adults and children:
A: gentamicin 5–7 mg/kg IV/IM once daily
          AND
Adults
A: metronidazole 500 mg IV every 8 hours
Children:
A: metronidazole 7.5 mg/kg IV every 8 hours

Supportive care: Analgesics for pain management

A: paracetamol 10–15 mg/kg/dose orally every 6 hours as needed
         OR
A: ibuprofen 5–10 mg/kg/dose orally every 8 hours as needed

Fluid Resuscitation
Administer intravenous fluids according to resuscitation protocols:
A: sodium chloride 0.9% (IV)
         OR
A: sodium lactate compound (IV)

Adjust fluid therapy based on haemodynamic status, urine output, and electrolyte balance.

sections.title: Male Incontinence
sections.text:
Definition: Involuntary leakage of urine in males.

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •  Bladder training,
  •  pelvic floor exercises.
  •  Surgical: Reserved for refractory cases

Pharmacological Management
Adults
S: oxybutynin 5 mg (PO) 2–3 times daily

Children ≥6 years:
S: oxybutynin 5 mg (PO) once daily, increase by 5 mg/week according to response and tolerability
          OR
Adults
S: tolterodine 2 mg (PO) twice daily
Adjust dose in renal or hepatic impairment

Pain Management
A: paracetamol 10–15 mg/kg/dose orally every 6 hours as needed
         OR
A: ibuprofen 5–10 mg/kg/dose orally every 8 hours as needed

sections.title: Obstructive uropathy
sections.text:
Obstructive uropathy contribute to the burden of CKD, obstruction may occur anywhere along the urinary tract. Causes of
obstruction vary based on the location of obstruction
  •    Obstruction within the kidney causing dilatation of individual calyces
  •    Obstruction at or distal to the renal pelvis causes diffuse caliectasis of hydronephrosis. Ureteral obstruction may result
       from stones, tumors, enlarged lymph nodes and retroperitoneal fibrosis
  •    Bladder tumors can obstruct one or both ureters or ureteric orifices

Clinical Presentation
Generally, patients present one or more of the following symptoms
  •    Pain                                                                •    Hematuria
  •    Change in urine output                                              •    Increased serum creatinine
  •    Hypertension

Investigations
  •    Urinalysis                                                          •    Intravenous pyelography
  •    Full blood count                                                    •    CT IVU
  •    Serum creatinine                                                    •    MRI
  •    KUB ultrasound                                                      •    Examination under anaesthesia

Non-Pharmacological Management
Taking adequate fluids 2L/day for patients with renal stones

Pharmacological Management
For Pain Relief
C: diclofenac (PO) 100mg as initial dose followed by 50mg 6-8hourly
          OR
C: morphine (IV/SC) 1-4mg 1-4hourly (may increase up to 10mg 4hourly as needed for acute pain

Referral of the patients
  •   The patient should be referred to the urologist for definitive treatment of the cause of obstruction
  •   Patient may need long term follow up if there is impaired renal function

sections.title: Female Sexual Dysfunction
sections.text:
Sexual dysfunction in women refers to sexual problems associated with personal distress and may take different forms including
lack of sexual drive, impaired arousal, failure to achieve orgasm or dyspareunia. Diagnostic criteria are reached when a sexual
problem is recurrent/ persistent and result in personal distress.
The causes of sexual dysfunction are multifactorial and may include psychological problem (depression or anxiety), relationship
conflicts, fatigue, stress, prior physical or sexual abuse, medications or physical problems that make sexual activity
uncomfortable (endometriosis, genitourinary symptoms of menopause).

Non-Pharmacological Management
Correction of contributing factor (genital lesion, systemic or hormonal factors and drugs e.g. SSRIs) Psychological therapies
Use of antidepressants

sections.title: Male sexual dysfunction
sections.text:
It is inability to attain and maintain an erect penis with sufficient rigidity for vaginal penetration and ability to ejaculate. Organic
causes include neurogenic, vasculogenic, endocrinological as well as many systemic diseases and medications.

Non Pharmacological Management
  •  Education counselling
  •  Consider the removal of drugs that may be associated with the problem.
  •  A change in lifestyle or medications may resolve the problem, e.g. advise cessation of smoking and alcohol abuse.

These disorders result from structural malformation or function of the genitourinary system that may lead to kidney impairment.
These disorders include diseases originating from the kidney and systemic diseases, which result in complications affecting the
kidney. Hypertension and diabetes mellitus are the commonest conditions causing complications in the kidney; therefore, all
patients with hypertension and diabetes mellitus should be regularly screened for kidney complications.

sections.title: Cancer Prevention, Screening, Early Detection and Registration
sections.text:
Cancer represents a unique public health opportunity. Unlike other non-Communicable diseases, it is possible to prevent most
cancers that prevail in Sub-Saharan Countries, including Tanzania, by intervening at both Primary and secondary levels of the
disease's natural history.

Primary prevention is mainly based on educating the public to modify their lifestyles (not limited to tobacco use, unhealthy diets,
physical inactivity, overweight, obesity, harmful alcohol use, etc) to avoid risk factors for cancer, as well as ensuring the
availability and affordability of prophylactic vaccines. Secondary prevention focuses on the availability of effective screening
programs that reduce the incidence of cancer and downstage it.

Early detection detects (or diagnoses) the disease at an early stage, when it has a high potential for cure (e.g., cervical or
breast cancer), reduces morbidity, improves quality of life, and increases survival due to good outcomes following treatment.

Key Interventions in Cancer Prevention

Primary Prevention
This is the most efficient and cost-effective form of cancer control. It involves preventive interventions that prevent a cancerous
process from developing. These can be through behavior change through health counseling, education, environmental controls,
or a biological mechanism, such as Vaccination.

Among the most important modifiable risk factors for cancer are: tobacco use; overweight and obesity; harmful alcohol use;
sexually transmitted human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, HIV/AIDS; air pollution, both outdoor and indoor; and occupational
carcinogens.

Public health education and promotion
Raising public awareness of risk factors for cancer and providing education on ways of avoiding and reducing exposure through
behavior change is essential. However, this is a long-term intervention and may be difficult to quantify. Community education
should also focus on raising awareness and knowledge of the benefits of early diagnosis, ways of detection, and screening.
These preventive measures should be highly promoted by also raising awareness of warning symptoms and signs of cancer
and taking prompt action, by the general public as well as physicians, nurses, and other health care providers, can have a
significant impact on the disease through early diagnosis and hence more effective management.

Tobacco control: Tobacco use causes an estimated 22% of cancer deaths. Age is the single most significant avoidable risk
factor for cancer mortality worldwide. Tobacco smoking causes many types of cancer, including cancers of the lung, esophagus,
larynx (voice box), mouth, throat, kidney, bladder, pancreas, stomach, and cervix. Over 70% of the lung cancer burden can be
attributed to smoking alone. Second-hand smoke (SHS), also known as environmental tobacco smoke, has been proven to
cause lung cancer in nonsmoking adults and expose children to cancer. Health workers should inform patients of the dangers
of smoking and encourage them to stop.

Healthy diets and physical activity: The incidence of Obesity is at an alarming rate, especially in developing countries like
Tanzania, where the adoption of unhealthy lifestyles is especially prevalent among people living in urban settings. There is
enough evidence that shows the link between overweight and obesity and many types of cancer, such as the esophagus,
colorectal, breast, endometrium, and kidney. Health care professionals should inform clients that regular physical activity,
combined with a healthy, balanced diet, prevents obesity and can reduce the risk of developing cancer.

Avoidance of alcohol use: little effort has been put into raising awareness of the effects of alcohol on cancer causation, even
though harmful (excessive) use of alcohol is a risk factor for many cancer types, including cancer of the oral cavity, pharynx,
larynx, esophagus, liver, colorectal, and breast.

The risk of cancer increases with the amount of alcohol consumed. Therefore, Health personnel should encourage their clients
to stop or moderate alcohol consumption. Avoidance of environmental pollution: Many African countries, including Tanzania,
are moving toward the Industrial Revolution, which goes hand in hand with increased environmental pollution.

Exposure to carcinogenic chemicals in the environment can occur through contaminated drinking water, pollution of indoor and
ambient air, and the contamination of food by chemicals such as aflatoxins or dioxins. Environmental carcinogens (aflatoxins,
asbestos, vehicle emissions, lead, ultraviolet (UV) light, and ionizing radiation) are also culprits. Indoor air pollution, such as
smoke from using charcoal and firewood in poorly ventilated houses, car fumes, and dust and garbage pollution, increases the
risk of lung cancer.

Prevention of Infections: More than 60% of Cancers that occur in Tanzania are Infectious diseases, which contribute a
significant proportion of cancer deaths. Viral hepatitis B and C cause cancer of the liver; human papillomavirus infection causes
cervical cancer; Helicobacter pylori increases the risk of stomach cancer. HIV/AIDS is associated with cancers, including
aggressive lymphoma subtypes, Kaposi’s sarcoma, anorectal cancer, and cervical cancer. In Lake Region, schistosomiasis

increases the risk of bladder cancer, and liver fluke increases the risk of cholangiocarcinoma. Preventive measures include
vaccination, prevention, and treatment of infection and infestation.

Vaccination
Approximately 60% of all cancers in Tanzania are attributed to infectious agents, including viruses and bacteria. Human
papillomaviruses (HPVs) is among the most important infections associated with cancers, which can cause most cervical and
anal cancers as well as a fraction of oral cancers; hepatitis B virus (HBV) and hepatitis C virus (HCV), which can cause liver
cancer, and Helicobacter pylori, which is a bacterium that can cause stomach cancer. Highly eff vaccines against HBV have
been available for several decades, and most countries include HBV vaccination in their childhood immunization programs;
vaccination is also highly effective in preventing infection with the HPV types that cause the majority of cervical cancers.

Hepatitis Vaccination is recommended for the general population and high-risk groups, such as healthcare workers, and can
be administered at all levels. The Vaccine is given in three doses over a period of six months. The second dose should be given
one month after the first dose, and the third dose should be given six months after the first dose.

HPV vaccination is recommended for girls between the ages of 9 and 14. The vaccine is given in two doses, six months apart.

Secondary Prevention
Early Detection and Cancer Screening
The main aim of cancer screening is to prevent death from cancer. Screening can also make using less severe treatment
methods possible if the cancer is detected early enough. Cervical, breast, skin, Prostate, and bowel cancer screening can
prevent the cancer from developing. In Tanzania, screening is recommended for Cervical, Breast, Prostate, skin, and bowel
cancer. However, only cervical cancer screening is offered as part of an organized program with adequate resources for high-
quality care. Efforts must be made to include other screening services for other cancers in organized screening programs.

Breast Cancer: Screening for breast cancer includes breast self-examination (BSE), clinical breast examination (CBE), and
breast imaging (mammogram and/or ultrasound scanning). BSE is recommended at day 10 of the menstrual cycle. For
postmenopausal women, a monthly breast self-examination (BSE) schedule should be established.

All patients with clinically suspicious lesions should have imaging as part of early detection. Mammogram is recommended for
women over 40 years, while ultrasound is the imaging for younger women. MRI may be used where possible for screening and
early detection in patients at high risk of breast cancer, such as those with BRCA1 & BRCA2 gene mutations.
For prevention and early detection, all women aged 25 years and above should be taught on breast self–examination and
advised to have regular physical checks with a health provider and a regular annual Mammography. They should also be
encouraged to exercise physically and properly diet.

Skin Cancer: Prevention or early detection is through frequent self–health check–ups or screening exercises and prompt
treatment of early skin lesions. For light-skinned people, avoid UV light, especially people with Albinism.

Colon: Colorectal cancers are usually asymptomatic until an advanced stage; hence, regular screening with an annual digital
rectal examination, stool for occult blood, and colonoscopy is recommended starting at 45 years of age.

Prostate: Routine screening is not recommended, but when done, it should begin with a PSA at age 50 if the life expectancy
is greater than 10 years. It is recommended that screening of the high-risk group should take place starting at age 45.

Cancer registration and surveillance
As a fundamental element of any cancer prevention strategy, Surveillance provides the foundation for advocacy and policy
development. This strategy will ensure national cancer data collection, monitoring, and reporting to facilitate cancer control
interventions, including establishing a population-based cancer registry. Currently, the country has established National
population-based cancer registries in four zones: the Lake Region (Bugando Medical Centre), the Northern Zone (KCMC), the
Southern Highlands (Mbeya Referral Hospital), the Central Zone (Benjamin Mkapa Hospital-Dodoma), and the Eastern Zone
(Ocean Road Cancer Institute - Dar es Salaam).

If patient is HIV positive or has mild renal impairment, consider 30 mg/m2 to max of 60 mg weekly.

Available preferred palliative chemotherapy drugs for metastatic, recurrent or persistent cancer after RT, given in single or
combination regimen include: cisplatin, paclitaxel, bevacizumab, carboplatin, docetaxel and gemcitabine.

S: carboplatin (IV) AUC 5–6 1-hour infusion day 1
          AND
paclitaxel (IV) 175 mg/m2 over 3hours on day 1
          AND
S: bevacizumab 15mg/kg repeat every 21 days for 4-6 cycles.

Alternatively
S: cisplatin 25mg/m2 (IV) infusion day 1over 2 hours
           AND
S: 5-Fluoruracil 1000mg/m2 over 22 hours every 21 days for 4-6 cycle.

Do FBC, urea and creatinine before each cycle of chemotherapy.

Follow up:
First visit at 4–6 weeks post treatment then 3–6 months in the first 2 years, there after yearly. *This follow-up schedule applies
to all malignancies with few exceptions*

  Note
    •  All patients suspected or confirmed to have cervical cancer should be referred to cancer-specialized centers for
       definitive management.
    •  All women aged 25 and above are advised to have regular cervical screening with VIA and VILI or a Pap smear
       annually for 3 years and then every 3 years.

sections.title: Endometrial Cancer
sections.text:
This is predominantly a disease of old women. Traditionally, EC is classified into Type I (estrogen-related, precursor: atypical
endometrial hyperplasia) and Type II (de novo, i.e., due to mutations, no precursor). Type I includes endometrioid (most
common), while other histologies are classified as type II (serous, clear cell carcinoma, and mucinous adenocarcinoma).

Risk factors
Risk factors for endometrial carcinoma include high BMI, hyperinsulinemia (diabetes), prolonged exposure to unopposed
estrogen (often related to nulliparity and infertility associated with PCOS or tamoxifen use, early age at menarche, and late age
at menopause), and hypertension.

Clinical Presentation
  •    Abnormal     uterine   bleeding,   especially   in              •    Symptoms of intraperitoneal disease (abdominal
       postmenopausal women. The bleeding can be                            distension, pelvic pressure, and pain) are similar to
       persistent intermenstrual bleeding or irregular or                   ovarian cancer
       infrequent heavy bleeding in women who are                      •    Pap smear: not designated to identify EC but may
       obese/PCOS or those using tamoxifen                                  occasionally show abnormal cervical pathology,
  •    Vaginal discharge                                                    i.e., atypical glandular cells of undetermined
  •    Thickened endometrium incidentally noted on USS                      significance (AGUS) or adenocarcinoma in situ.
       for other condition

Investigations
  •    FBC, LFT, Urea, Creatinine                                      •    Endometrial biopsy to confirm the diagnosis:
  •    Cancer Antigen 125 (CA 125)                                          Histological diagnosis should be made by sampling
  •    CXR                                                                  the endometrium: (office endometrial biopsy by
  •    Abdomen and Pelvis USS or transvaginal                               pipelle,    hysteroscopy-directed    biopsy,   or
  •    Abdomen and Pelvic CT scan                                           endometrial curettage)
  •    Pelvic MRI                                                      •    Cystoscopy, and /or sigmoidoscopy as clinically
                                                                            indicated
                                                                       •    PET/CT scan

Cytotoxic therapy for inoperable, metastatic or recurrent disease is given with palliative intent. Recommended regimens are;

sections.title: Cancer of the Vulva
sections.text:
Vulva cancer is predominantly a disease of older women. Squamous cell carcinoma is the most common histological type,
usually arising from premalignant lesions, such as vulva intraepithelial neoplasia (VIN). Risk factors contributing to the
development of VIN and later vulva cancer include HPV infection, immunosuppression, including infection with HIV, history of
genital warts, multiple sexual partners, and cigarette smoking.

Clinical Presentation
  •    Persistent itching in the vulva is often the earliest         •    Abnormal vulvar/vaginal bleeding—bleeding is due
       and most common symptom.                                           to ulceration or tumor involvement.
  •    Vulvar mass or lesion—a lump, wart, or ulcerated              •    Abnormal vulvar/vaginal discharge and may be
       or raised area.                                                    foul-smelling.
  •    Skin changes—thickening or discoloration (red,                •    Groin swelling—enlarged inguinal femoral nodes
       white, or dark spots)                                              indicate possible spread of advanced disease.

Investigations
  •    FBC, LFT, Urea, Creatinine, HIV test                          •    Cystoscopy and urethroscopy may be indicated for
  •    Pap smear of cervix and vagina                                     advanced stages
  •    CXR                                                           •    Biopsy—excisional if tumor ≤2 cm, incisional
  •    CT scan / MRI of the Abdomen and Pelvis                            wedge/punch biopsy.
  •    Colposcopy to determine presence of other lesions             •    PET/CT scan

sections.title: Vaginal Cancer
sections.text:
Majority are Squamous Cell Carcinoma, and are located in the upper posterior 1/3 of the vagina.

Risk factors: carcinoma in situ, HPV, chronic vaginal irritation, previous abnormal Pap smears, early hysterectomy, multiple
lifetime sex partners, early age at first intercourse, current smoker, in utero exposure to DES, partner with penile cancer.

Clinical Presentation
  •    Irregular vaginal bleeding or discharge (Often postcoital)
  •    Dysuria
  •    A lump or mass on the vaginal wall

Investigations
  •    FBC, LFT, Urea, Creatinine, HIV test                            •    Cystoscopy and urethroscopy may be indicated for
  •    Pap smear of the cervix                                              advanced stages
  •    CXR                                                             •    Biopsy of the vaginal lesion to confirm the diagnosis
  •    CT scan / MRI of the Abdomen and Pelvis                         •    PET/CT
  •    Colposcopy to determine the presence of other
       lesions

                                      • For recurrent disease: intracavitary (IC) brachytherapy to entire vaginal mucosa

sections.title: Gestational Trophoblastic Disease
sections.text:
Gestational trophoblastic diseases (GTDs) are a group of rare premalignant and malignant diseases characterized by their
origin in trophoblastic cells.
      i. Premalignant forms are complete hydatidiform mole (CHM), partial hydatidiform moles (PHM), and atypical placental site
        nodules (APSNs).
     ii. Malignant forms are called gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (GTN) and include invasive mole, choriocarcinoma,
        placental site trophoblastic tumor (PSTT), and epithelioid trophoblastic tumor (ETT).

sections.title: Premalignant gestational trophoblastic disease
sections.text:
Diagnostic criteria
abnormal vaginal bleeding or being asymptomatic and undergoing first trimester ultrasound (US), uterine enlargement
disproportionate to gestational age.

Investigations
  •    Serum B-hCG, FBP, blood             grouping    and             •    Pelvic and/or abdominal Ultrasound
       crossmatching                                                   •    CXR
  •    RFT, LFT                                                        •    PET CT scan
  •    Thyroid    function  tests  if     suspicious    of             •    MRI Brain
       hyperthyroidism TSH, T3, T4

Table 22.5: Management of Premalignant gestational trophoblastic disease
 Category                          Management
 Non-Pharmacological                     • Suction curettage under anesthesia
 Management                              • Ultrasound guidance may be used to ensure complete evacuation
                                         • Prepare and cross-match blood; transfusion may be required if indicated
                                         • Send evacuated tissue for histological examination
                                         • Hysterectomy may be considered in women with no desire for future fertility or
                                         when evacuation is unsafe/failed
 Pharmacological Management              A: oxytocin infusion: 10–40 IU in 1 L normal saline, titrated IV infusion during and
                                         after procedure once cervical dilatation is achieved to promote uterine contraction
                                         and reduce bleeding
                                          B: Recombinant Monoclonal anti-D Immunoglobulin (for Rh-negative women): 250
                                         IU (50 µg) IM within 72 hours of procedure (dose may vary by gestational age per
                                         protocol)

Follow-up: After suction curettage or hysterectomy, the patient should be followed up by measurement of B-hCG level at least
once every 2 weeks until normalized in 3 readings (defined as 3 consecutive normal assays), then monthly B-hCG levels until
levels are normal for 6 months. Provide a contraceptive method, preferably combined oral contraceptives.

sections.title: Malignant type (Gestational Trophoblastic neoplasia—GTN)
sections.text:
GTNs are highly sensitive to chemotherapy, with cure rates approaching 95%. Cure is possible even in metastatic disease. All
patients with GTN should be referred to a gynecologic oncologist for a careful pre-treatment evaluation (proper staging and risk
stratification) as well as for definitive management.

Clinical Presentation
  •    Abnormal vaginal bleeding                                        •    Metastatic symptoms, e.g., chest pain, hemoptysis,
  •    Uterine enlargement disproportionate to gestational                   jaundice, and seizures.
       age                                                              •    Persistently raising or plateauing β-hCG post molar
  •    Pelvic pain or pressure                                               pregnancy

Investigations
  •    Serum β-hCG level, LFT, RFT, Thyroid function                    •    Biopsy is avoided due to risk of significant
       tests if suspicious of hyperthyroidism                                hemorrhage. Histologic confirmation is not required
  •    Abdomen and Pelvis USS, CXR, and/or CT Scan                           for treatment of GTN. Review a uterine curettage or
  •    PET/CT scan                                                           other biopsy specimen if available prior to
  •    Brain MRI/CT                                                          treatment.

sections.title: Cancer of the Ovary
sections.text:
There are three (3) types of ovarian cancer. These are epithelial ovarian cancers, which develop from the ovarian epithelial
layer; germ cell tumors, which arise from the ovarian cortex; and sex cord stromal tumors, which arise from stromal cells within
the cortex. Management of the three histological types of ovarian cancer differs. Epithelial tumors comprise 90% of all ovarian
malignancies. Due to anatomical location, most patients present with advanced disease.

Risk factors
  •    The majority of ovarian cancers are sporadic, with                •    Nulliparity
       about 10% being hereditary.                                       •    Infertility
  •    Incessant ovulation                                               •    Diet –saturated fats
  •    Excess gonadotropin secretion, promoting high                     •    Obesity
       estrogen concentrations, which lead to epithelial                 •    Exposure to talc powder
       proliferation,    and,     possibly,    malignant                 •    Genetics account 10-12 %. A link with the breast
       transformation.                                                        cancer-associated genes BRCA1 and BRCA2, as
  •    Advanced age                                                           well as with HNPCC, is recognized.

Clinical Presentation
  •    Minimal or no symptoms in early stage
  •    Abdominal distension with palpable mass, pain and ascites are all late signs

Investigations
  •    Inspection and bimanual examination under                         •    Abdomen and Pelvis CT scan / MRI
       anesthesia (EUA) recto–vagina are mandatory to                    •    Histology of the Oophorectomy specimen or biopsy
       exclude primary disease or extension from other                        obtained at laparotomy
       sites such as cancer of the cervix                                •    Ascitic fluid/peritoneal and pelvic washing cytology
  •    FBC, RFT, LFT, CA 125 & CEA
  •    CXR
Table 22.9: Surgical Management of ovarian cancer
 Stage           Recommended Management
 Stage I–II      • Perform total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (TAH + BSO) AND omentectomy for
                 resectable tumors
                 • If complete tumor removal is not feasible → perform maximum debulking (cytoreductive) surgery, followed by
                 adjuvant chemotherapy
                 • Unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy may be considered only for Stage IA tumors with favorable histology (fertility
                 preservation option)
 Stage III       • Neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by surgery AND then adjuvant chemotherapy
 Stage IV        • Manage as Stage III (neoadjuvant chemotherapy → surgery → adjuvant chemotherapy) ± palliative care

Pharmacological Management
Adjuvant chemotherapy

Indicated in all patients at high risk, i.e., stage IC or II, high grade or clear cell cancers of any stage. Recommended regimens
are;
S: carboplatin (IV) AUC 6 1-hour infusion Day 1
          AND
S: paclitaxel (IV) 175 mg/m2 over 3 hours day1; repeat every 21days for 6 cycles.

For recurrent disease: give the same regimen if tumor is platinum sensitive (recurrence after 6 months since the last
chemotherapy cycle)

sections.title: Breast Cancer
sections.text:
Breast cancer is the second most common malignancy among women in Tanzania, with an incidence of 15%. It is the second
most common cause of death in women aged 45-55 years after cervical cancer. The incidence is expected to rise in recent
years due to screening programs around the country and increased awareness among the general population.

sections.title: Cancer of The Skin
sections.text: Skin cancers are classified into non melanoma and malignant melanoma.

sections.title: Non-melanoma Skin Cancers
sections.text:
Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) and squamous cell (SCC) are the most common non melanoma skin cancers. SCC is more
aggressive than BCC and has the potential to metastasis. The main cause of these skin cancers is overexposure to Ultraviolet
radiation. Risk factors include light-colored skin (e.g. albinism), previous burn and immunosuppression e.g. after transplant or
HIV infection

Prevention or early detection; is through frequent self–health check–up or screening exercise and prompt treatment of early
skin lesions. For light skinned people–avoid UV light especially people with Albinism.

Clinical Presentation
The most common warning sign of skin cancer is a change in the appearance on exposed areas of the skin, such as a new
growth or a sore that will not heal. Occasionally, such changes may appear on an old burn area.

Investigations
  •    None if the lesion is small                                       •   Biopsy – preferably excisional biopsy, where
  •    Local X-ray if bone involvement is suspected                          possible, for histology
  •    CXR                                                               •   CT or MRI is needed for suspected nodal and bone
                                                                             involvement.
                                                                         •   PET/CT when indicated

Management
Surgery is the primary treatment. Wide local excision that achieves negative surgical margins is adequate. For Node positive
BCC or SCC Resection with Lymph node dissection. Skin grafting may be required after surgery. Amputation is sometimes
done for palliation. Locally destructive methods such as curetting or cryotherapy may be employed.

Radiotherapy
Indication: Positive margin, high-grade disease, or inoperable tumour.
Dose: 60-66/ in 30-33 Fractions EBRT for Radical Treatment, 30Gy in 10 Fractions for palliative treatment

Pharmacological Management
S: 5-fluorouracil topical cream, apply every 12 -24 hours, for very superficial lesions or carcinoma in situ

Systemic chemotherapy is given during radiotherapy as a radiosensitizer.
S: cisplatin (IV) 40 mg/m2 to a maximum of 70 mg is given weekly during radiation therapy.

Metastatic or Unresectable disease SCC/BCC
S: cisplatin 25mg/m2 (IV) infusion day 1over 2 hours
           AND
S: 5-Fluorouracil 1000mg/m2 over 22 hours every 21 days for 4-6 cycles.

sections.title: Kaposi’s sarcoma (KS)
sections.text:
It is a malignant tumour of angio–formative cells usually starting from the skin but occasionally involving many other body
organs. Kaposi sarcoma can be primarily categorized into four types: epidemic of AIDS–related, immunocompromised, classic
or sporadic, and endemic (African). Here we have non-AIDS related (endemic) KS and AIDS related (epidemic) KS, where the
latter is more common, 80–85%.

Clinical Presentation
  •    KS presents as firm, dark brown nodules or plaques in the skin. Usually, more on the limbs
  •    It presents as widespread lymphadenopathy with or without skin lesions in young children and those with
       immunodeficiency.
  •    B symptoms (fever, sweating, and weight loss) are commonly associated with the epidemic type.

Investigations
  •    FBC, LFT, Urea & Creatinine, HIV test (if positive             •    Abdomen and Pelvis ultrasound, CT scan / MRI
       CD4 count and viral load)                                      •    Chest CT scan
  •    Immunohistochemistry (IHC) panel: KSHC 8 (HHV-                 •    Bronchoscopy and Endoscopy
       8)                                                             •    PET CT scan
  •    CXR                                                            •    Skin biopsy for histological confirmation

Staging of KS: Epidemic Kaposi sarcoma uses the AIDS Clinical Trials Group (ACTG) system, and for endemic/classical
Kaposi sarcoma uses the Mitsuyasu classification system.

Management:
 •   Treatment is palliative regardless of type and stage; hence, careful assessment and decision-making are required to
     choose the best palliative treatment.
 •   ARVs should be initiated in epidemic KS patients who have not started the treatment.
 •   The choice of palliation depends on the patient's Clinical Presentation and general condition.

Radiotherapy
Is the best palliative treatment in a symptomatic patient with local or extensive disease.
   •    8Gy single fraction for disease on limbs or lower half of the body
   •    6Gy single fraction for upper half of the body
   •    A dose of 9Gy/3Fractions or 22Gy/11 Fractions can be prescribed for lesions elsewhere.

Pharmacological Management

First-line palliative chemotherapy (generalized disease)

S: liposomal doxorubicin 20 mg/m² IV every 2–3 weeks for 6 cycles
          OR
S: doxorubicin (IV) 25 mg/m² over 30 minutes Day 1
          AND
S: bleomycin (IV) 10 IU/m² over 10 minutes Day 1
          AND
S: vincristine (IV) 1.4 mg/m² over 10 minutes (maximum 2 mg) Day 1, given every 21 days for 6–8 cycles
          OR
S: paclitaxel (IV) 100 mg/m² Day 1, given every 14 days for 6 cycles
          OR
S: docetaxel (IV) 75 mg/m² Day 1, given every 21 days for 6 cycles (for persistent or recurrent disease after ABV)

Relapsed/Refractory therapy

These agents are generally used as individual salvage options, not routinely combined together unless under specific specialist
protocols/clinical trials.

S: gemcitabine 1000 mg/m² IV every 2 weeks OR 1000 mg/m² IV on Days 1 and 8 every 21 days
          OR
S: bortezomib 1.6 mg/m² IV/SC on Days 1, 8, and 15 of each 28-day cycle
          OR
S: lenalidomide 25 mg PO daily for 21 days of each 28-day cycle
          OR
S: nivolumab 480 mg IV every 4 weeks for 6 months
          OR
S: pembrolizumab 200 mg IV every 3 weeks for up to 6 months

sections.title: Head and Neck Cancers
sections.text:
Cancers of the head and neck include the oral cavity, pharynx, larynx, nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, salivary glands, and
thyroid. Squamous cell carcinoma is the most common histological type of malignancy, but salivary gland tumors are mostly
adenocarcinoma.

Risk factors
Important etiological factors are smoking, excessive alcohol, viral infections (eg, HPV and EBV), genetic predisposition,
previous radiation exposure, and industrial chemicals.

sections.title: Nasopharyngeal Cancer
sections.text:
Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is the predominant tumor type arising in the epithelium of the nasopharynx.

Clinical Presentation:
Neck mass, unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus, nasal obstruction, epistaxis, and cranial nerve palsies

Investigations
  •    FBC, RFT, LFT, and HIV                                            •    Immunohistochemistry to further confirm the
  •    CXR                                                                    diagnosis
  •    Abdominal ultrasound                                              •    Preventive dental care and extractions should
  •    CT scan and/or MRI of the nasopharynx, skull base,                     occur 10-14 days before RT
       and neck                                                          •    Feeding tube (GFT) when indicated
  •    Nasopharyngoscopy                                                 •    Tracheostomy placement when indicated
  •    Endoscopic-guided biopsy of the primary tumor for                 •    Speech, swallow, and audiology evaluations when
       histology                                                              indicated
  •    PET CT

Management
Due to the deep location of the nasopharynx and its anatomic proximity to critical structures, radical surgery is typically not
used. The role of surgery is initially for biopsy for histological confirmation. It may also be used for management of the neck for
persistently enlarged lymph nodes.
Nasopharyngeal cancer is mainly treated by radiotherapy, either alone or in combination with chemotherapy.

sections.title: Laryngeal Cancer
sections.text:
Laryngeal cancer is one of the most common cancers of the head and neck. It is divided into three major anatomic regions;
supraglottis, glottis and subglottic.

Risk factors
It is predominantly found in men and mostly in those with history of tobacco smoking and alcohol intake.

Clinical Presentation
Hoarseness, pain, stridor, difficulty in breathing, otalgia, neck mass, odynophagia, cough.

Investigations

22.5.3 Hypopharyngeal Cancers
Hypopharyngeal cancer includes tumors arising from the pyriform sinus, posterior pharyngeal wall, post-cricoid region.

Risk factors
It is associated with tobacco use, alcohol consumption, and Plummer–Vinson syndrome.

Clinical Presentation
Dysphagia, odynophagia, change in speech (dysarthria), neck mass, referred otalgia, throat pain, weight loss, sensation of
mass in throat and hoarseness of voice.

Investigations
  •    FBC, RFT and LFT                                             •    Pathology: Definitive diagnosis is confirmed by
  •    CXR                                                               pharyngoscopy-guided biopsy of the primary tumor
  •    CT scan and/or MRI of the Head and Neck                      •    PET/CT scan

  •    Nasopharyngolaryngoscopy                                          occur 10-14 days before RT
  •    Esophagoscopy                                                •    Feeding tube (GFT) when indicated
  •    Bronchoscopy if clinically indicated                         •    Speech, swallow, and audiology evaluations when
                                                                         indicated

Radiation therapy is the mainstay of first-line local treatment for early stage hypopharyngeal carcinoma. For more advanced
disease, concurrent chemoradiation reduces the rate of distant metastasis, and improves local control.

sections.title: Salivary Gland Cancer
sections.text:
Salivary gland cancers arise from major or minor salivary glands in the head and neck region. The most common malignant
salivary gland tumors are mucoepidermoid carcinoma and adenocarcinoma.

Clinical Presentation
Depends on the primary site involved: Mass, pain, nerve palsies, neck mass

sections.title: Nasal Cavity and Paranasal Sinus Cancer
sections.text:
These tumors arise from the nasal cavity and the four paired paranasal sinuses (frontal, ethmoid, maxillary, and sphenoid).
Most common histological type is Squamous Cell Carcinoma (70%). Other histologies are Adenocarcinoma, adenoid cystic,
mucoepidermoid carcinoma, neuroendocrine, plasmacytoma, melanoma, lymphoma and sarcoma,

Clinical Presentation
Nasal obstruction, epistaxis, proptosis, double vision, cheek mass, loss of sensation of the cheek, and loosening or pain of the
teeth

sections.title: Oral Cavity Cancer
sections.text:
The oral cavity consists of the upper and lower lips, the gingivobuccal sulcus, the buccal mucosa, the upper and lower gingiva,
the retromolar trigone, the hard palate, the floor of the mouth, and the anterior two–thirds of the tongue. 90% of tumors are
squamous cell carcinoma. Less common tumors include minor salivary gland cancers (common in the hard palate and include
adenoid cystic carcinoma, mucoepidermoid carcinoma, and adenocarcinoma).

Risk factors
Risk factors include tobacco smoking, excessive consumption of alcohol, poor oral hygiene, prolonged focal denture irritation,
betel nut chewing, and syphilis.

Clinical Presentation
Non-healing ulcer, speech difficulty, hypersalivation, neck mass, dysphagia, and otalgia

Investigations
  •    FBC, LFT, RFT and HIV                                          •    Preventive dental care and extractions should
  •    CXR                                                                 occur 10-14 days before RT
  •    CT Scan and/or MRI of the Head and Neck                        •    Feeding tube (GFT) when indicated
  •    PET/ CT scan for Stage 3 and 4                                 •    Speech, swallow, and audiology evaluations when
