sections.title: Oropharyngeal Cancer
sections.text:
The oropharynx is located between the soft palate superiorly and the hyoid bone inferiorly. It has four walls: the soft palate,
tonsillar region, base of tongue, and pharyngeal wall. Tonsillar and pharyngeal tongue tumors are frequently initially recognized
by nodal metastases.

Risk factors: It is associated with tobacco use, alcohol consumption, and HPV.

Clinical Presentation
Sore throat, non-healing oropharyngeal ulcers, dysphagia, referred otalgia, hoarseness (with larynx invasion), odynophagia,
hot potato voice, impaired tongue movement, and protrusion.

Investigations:
  •    FBC, LFT, RFT, and HIV                                           •    Preventive dental care and extractions should
  •    CXR                                                                   occur 10-14 days before RT
  •    CT Scan and/or MRI of the Head and Neck                          •    Feeding tube (GFT) when indicated
  •    PET/CT Scan for Stage 3 and 4                                    •    Speech, swallow, and audiology evaluations when
  •    Mirror and fibre-optic endoscopic examination                         indicated
  •    Biopsy for histologic confirmation

Management:
Radiotherapy mainly treats oropharyngeal cancers in combination with chemotherapy. Surgery can be used in selected cases.

sections.title: Thyroid Carcinoma
sections.text:
Thyroid cancer is the most common endocrine malignancy in Tanzania. Histological types are medullary, anaplastic, and well-
differentiated thyroid cancer. Most of these cases are differentiated thyroid cancer, the commonest being the follicular subtype,
followed by the papillary subtype. Rare ones are Hurthle cell, a follicular variant of papillary thyroid carcinoma, tall cell, columnar,
solid, and clear cell. Females are mostly affected, the male-to-female ratio being 3:1. Follicular cells take up iodide ions,
including radioactive iodine (RAI).

Risk factors
  •    Radiation exposure, especially if exposed at age <10 years
  •    Iodine deficiency

Clinical Presentation
  •    Thyroid mass (Anterior neck mass), Obstructive symptoms (Stridor, hoarseness), laryngeal nerve palsy, dysphagia
  •    Metastatic symptoms such as weight loss, difficulty in breathing, bone pain/pathological fractures

Investigations
  •    Thyroid function tests (T3, T4, TSH), FBC, LFTs,                    •    Laryngoscopy/ bronchoscopy if airway invasion
       Urea & Creatinine, Serum calcitonin, Serum                          •    Biopsy or Fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC)
       thyroglobulin levels, CEA and Calcium                                    of a thyroid lesion
  •    Thyroid Scan                                                        •    Tracheostomy placement when indicated
  •    CXR                                                                 •    PET/CT scan for high-risk medullary and anaplastic
  •    Isotope bone scan                                                        thyroid carcinoma
  •    CT-Scan of the neck/ MRI (avoid iodinated contrast
       with CT, as this may preclude treatment with RAI for
       up to 6 months)

Surgery is the mainstay of treatment; lobectomy, total or near-total thyroidectomy. Radiotherapy is indicated in all cases of
anaplastic carcinoma.

sections.title: Esophageal Cancer
sections.text:
Histologically, there are two types: SCC and adenocarcinoma. Male to female ratio 4:1.

Risk factors
Tobacco and alcohol abuse are major risk factors for SCC, whereas obesity, gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), and
Barrett’s esophagus are the major risk factors for adenocarcinoma.

Clinical Presentation
Difficulty swallowing (dysphagia) is the most common symptom associated with weight loss and poor performance status.

Investigations
  •    FBC, LFT, Urea, Creatinine                                    •       Rigid            Oesophagoscopy          or
  •    Barium swallow and meal                                               Oesophagoduodenoscopy (OGD) and biopsy for
  •    Chest and Abdominal CT scan                                           histology
  •    PET/CT scan                                                   •       Bronchoscopy
  •    Abdominal USS                                                 •       Nutritional assessment and Gastrostomy tube
                                                                             placementtomy
Staging: TNM Staging system

Management: Surgery and radiotherapy
Surgery is a major component of treatment for resectable disease. Surgery and or radiotherapy may be curative in early
diseases. However, most patients present in late stages, hence the goal of treatment is to prolong survival and relieve
symptoms. Radiation (alone or in combination with chemotherapy) is given as a definitive, preoperative, postoperative therapy
or palliative setting.

sections.title: Pancreatic cancer
sections.text:
Most common type is of ductal origin. Cystadenocarcinomas, intraductal carcinomas, and solid and cystic papillary neoplasms
(also known as Hamoudi tumors) have a more indolent course. Acinar cell cancers and giant cell tumors are aggressive and
have poor survival. 5% are tumors of the endocrine pancreas – these tumors are rare, slow-growing, and have a long natural
history.

Risk factors
Known risks include tobacco use, alcohol abuse, a diet high in animal fat, ionizing radiation, chemotherapy, and exposure to 2-
naphthylamine and benzene. Also, hereditary mutations in BRCA1, BRCA2, Jeghers, and Lynch syndromes.

Clinical Presentation
Most common presenting symptoms: jaundice (common bile duct obstruction), weight loss (malabsorption from exocrine
dysfunction), diabetes (related to endocrine dysfunction), gastric outlet obstruction, and abdominal pain.

sections.title: Gastric Cancer
sections.text:
Gastric cancer is often diagnosed at an advanced stage. About 90–95% of the tumors are adenocarcinoma.

Risk factors
Risk factors include age, gender, genetic factors, smoking, salt-preserved food, a diet low in fruits and vegetables, infection
with H. Pylori, and Epstein-Barr Virus.

Clinical Presentation
  •    Epigastric pain worsened by food intake, early satiety
  •    Distal tumours may present with obstructive symptoms
  •    Occult of manifest bleeding may be a feature
  •    Other symptoms include epigastric mass, pallor, weight loss, supraclavicular nodes, hepatomegaly, periumbilical nodes

Investigations
  •    FBC, LFT, RFT, H. pylori                                       •    Barium meal (double contrast)
  •    Stool for occult blood                                         •    Abdomen and pelvis CT scan
  •    Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA)                                 •    PET/CT scan if clinically indicated
  •    IHC – Her 2 Status                                             •    Endoscopy and biopsy for histology
  •    CXR                                                            •    HER2-Neu testing if metastatic adenocarcinoma

Staging: TNM staging system

Management
Surgery is the primary treatment for early-stage gastric cancer. Total or partial gastrectomy is performed together with lymph
node dissection. Bypass surgery is done to relieve obstructive symptoms. Surgery is usually preceded by Chemotherapy
(Perioperative) or adjuvant chemoradiotherapy.

sections.title: Hepatocellular Carcinoma
sections.text:
Associated with chronic Hepatitis B/C infection.

Prevention
Vaccination for Hepatitis B/C. Cirrhosis, chronic liver disease, hereditary hemochromatosis, and aflatoxin B exposure are also
risk factors.

Clinical Presentation
  •    An arterial bruit and ascites may be present
  •    Right upper abdominal swelling and pain are often associated with weight loss, fever, and jaundice

Investigations
  •    FBC, LFT, RFT, Serum alpha-fetoprotein, HBsAg, HB core antibody, partial thromboplastin time (PTT). Bilirubin, albumin,
       Hepatitis B/C panels.
  •    CXR/ Chest CT
  •    Abdomen and Pelvis USS
  •    3-Phase Liver Protocol CT/MRI Scan with IV Contrast
  •    PET/CT
  •    Biopsy or FNAC of the Liver; not always needed If radiographic characteristics are diagnostic.

sections.title: Rectal Cancer
sections.text:
Histology: the commonest is adenocarcinoma 95%.

Risk factors
Risk factors include: inherited genetic syndromes, a diet high in red and processed meat, smoking and alcohol abuse, having
inflammatory bowel disease, type 2 diabetes, and obesity.

Screening
  •   Average risk persons (beginning age 40–75): colonoscopy 10 years.
  •   Family History (non-FAP/HNPCC): colonoscopy every 1–5 years, initiate at age 40 years or 10 years prior to earliest
      cancer diagnosis in the family.
  •   NPCC (lifetime colorectal cancer risk 10–70%, depending on mismatch repair status): colonoscopy every 1–2 years,
      initiate    at age 20–25 or 10 years younger than earliest cancer diagnosis in the family
Clinical Presentation
  •    Change in bowel habit, e.g., constipation or                     •    Abdominal mass with or without obstructive
       diarrhea, sense of incomplete bowel emptying.                         symptoms
  •    Rectal bleeding or blood in stool.                               •    Unexplained weight loss and other symptoms of
                                                                             advanced disease.

Investigations
  •    FBC, RFT, LFT, CEA                                               •    Sigmoidoscopy or Colonoscopy with Biopsy of the
  •    Stool for occult blood                                                lesion
  •    CXR/ Chest CT                                                    •    Abdomen and Pelvis CT-Scan
  •    Barium enema (double contrast)                                   •    MRI
  •    Abdomen and Pelvis USS                                           •    PET/CT
  •    Digital rectal examination

Staging: TNM staging system

Management
Surgery is the primary treatment for early disease. Hemicolectomy with lymph node dissection is commonly performed in colon
cancer. Give preoperative chemotherapy for locally advanced disease to shrink the tumor. Radiotherapy plays a role in rectal
tumors as neo-adjuvant, adjuvant, or palliative.

sections.title: Lung Cancer
sections.text:
Worldwide, lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer-related death. Approximately 85 %–90% of lung cancer cases are caused
by smoking. There are two main types of lung cancer: Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and small cell lung cancer (SCLC).
These two types have different prognosis and management approach.

sections.title: Carcinoma of the Prostate
sections.text:
The most common type of prostate cancer is adenocarcinoma (95 %). Tumours are stratified by T stage, Gleason score (GS),
and PSA into three prognostic groups of low, intermediate and high risk.
  •   Low risk: T1–T2a and PSA < 10 ng/ml and GS ≤ 6
  •   Intermediate risk: T2b or PSA 10 – 20 ng/ml or GS 7
  •   High risk: T2c–T4 or PSA > 20ng/ml or GS 8–10

Patient can be offered appropriate treatment options according to stage of disease, prognostic risk group and estimated survival
taking into account performance status and comorbidity.

Clinical Presentation
  •    May be asymptomatic in the early stages of the disease
  •    May present incidentally following examination for benign prostatic hypertrophy or elevated serum prostatic specific
       antigen (PSA)
  •    Prostatic symptoms are associated with advanced stages of the disease, which include: reduced potency, urinary
       frequency and nocturnal, poor stream, hesitancy and terminal dribbling
  •    Very often patients may present with bone pain including backache or pathological fracture
  •    Digital Rectal Examination (DRE) typically reveals a hard, irregular prostate. TURP is carried out to both confirm the
       diagnosis and also as part of the treatment (to relieve obstruction).

Screening for prostate cancer
Routine screening not recommended, but when done should begin with PSA and digital rectal examination at age 50 if life
expectancy is >10 years. It is recommended that screening of high-risk group should take place starting at age 45.

Investigations
  •    FBC, LFT, Urea, Creatinine, Serum PSA, ALP,                      •    Pelvic MRI in early-stage disease
       Testosterone                                                     •    PET/CT
  •    X-rays of the painful bone or spine                              •    Bone scan
  •    CXR                                                              •    Biopsy for histopathology
  •    Abdomen and Pelvis USS and or CT scan

Staging: TNM staging system

Management
Treatment depends on disease profile (Risk stratification) and patient factors as noted above. Options include:
  •   Watchful waiting                                                  •   Radiotherapy (curative or palliative)
  •   Active surveillance                                               •   Hormonal therapy (chemical vs surgical castration)
  •   Surgery (curative or palliative)                                  •   Chemotherapy

Surgery
Early stages (Low and Intermediate risk groups) can be treated with either radical prostatectomy or radical Radiotherapy with
cure intent. However, surgery may cause postoperative impotence and impaired urinary control. TURP is carried out to both
confirm the diagnosis and also as part of relieving obstruction.

Radiotherapy
Radical Radiotherapy for Adjuvant and definitive, EBRT up to 74 Gy/37 Fractions can be given using 3DCRT or IMRT
Techniques. Palliative radiotherapy is valuable to bone metastases, massive hematuria, spinal cord compression and brain
metastases

Hormonal Therapy
Hormonal manipulation is by surgical or medical castration. It is carried out in patients with locally advanced or metastatic
disease. Bilateral orchidectomy is a surgical hormonal manipulation and should not be regarded curative surgery.

Pharmacological Management
S: goserelin (SC) 3.6 mg every 4 weeks or 10.8mg every 12 weeks with/ without oral bicalutamide (PO) 50mg once daily
  Note
    •    Goserelin is not required after orchidectomy but patient may receive Bicalutamide.
    •    Treatment with goserelin and bicalutamide may be given up to 2 years depending on patient condition and Prostate Specific
         Antigen (PSA) levels

Chemotherapy
Recommended chemotherapy regimens for hormonal refractory prostate cancer are:
S: docetaxel (IV) 75mg/m2 2 hours’ infusion day 1 given every 21 days for 6 cycles. It is mainly reserved in hormonal refractory
prostate cancer.

For Bone metastases/osteolytic/tumour induced hypercalcemia are:
S: zolendronic acid (IV) 4mg over 15min given 4 Weekly

Metastatic disease
Lifelong ADT ± palliative RT ± bisphosphonates for hormone refractory disease. docetaxel and prednisone for androgen
independent disease can add Carboplatin if docetaxel not working to Castrate resistant prostate cancer patients.

Evaluation every 3 months (Check PSA level) Castrate resistant patients with rising PSA zoledronic acid should be given
monthly. These are given together with Ca2+ and Vitamin D supplements.

In Castrate resistant patients which did not respond to Docetaxel plus carboplatin and prednisolone, patients Abiraterone
acetate with prednisolone is an option (500mg OD taken with food is highly recommended)

S: abiraterone acetate (PO) 500mg one a day (Taken with food)
          OR
S: enzalutamide (PO) 160mg daily

sections.title: Urinary Bladder Cancer
sections.text:
Urinary bladder cancers are malignant tumors that commonly arise from the inner lining of the bladder or its connective tissue.
Common pathologies include transition cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, sarcomas and secondary
deposits.

Risk factors for bladder cancer include chronic irritation (schistosomiasis, irradiation, and catheterization), chemicals (aromatic
amines, aniline dyes, tobacco, analgesics) and genetic predisposition. Symptoms include blood in the urine, dysuria, Lower
urinary tract symptoms (LUTS), and low back pain.

Clinical Presentation
Symptoms include blood in the urine, pain with urination, and low back pain.

Investigations
  •    FBC, RFT, LFT, Alkaline phosphatase                               •    Cystoscopy with bladder mapping & Biopsy
  •    Urinalysis, Urine culture and sensitivity, Urine for              •    EUA
       cytology                                                          •    Bimanual examination
  •    CXR and /or CT chest                                              •    TURBT with random biopsies of normal appearing
  •    Bone scan                                                              mucosa to exclude CIS. (If trigone involved, biopsy
  •    Abdomen and Pelvis USS or CT scan                                      prostatic urethra)
  •    PET/CT

Staging: TNM staging system

Management
Treatment of Urinary bladder cancer depends on how deeply the tumor invades into the bladder wall.
Surgery: Several modalities that may extend from bladder preserving surgery–TURB; to radical cystectomy with urine diversion
depending bladder muscle invasion. Post operation patient may receive adjuvant chemo and/or radiotherapy

Chemotherapy
Chemotherapy in bladder cancer may be offered before surgery or after surgery. It may also be given concurrent with
radiotherapy or as palliative in inoperative tumor.

Recommended chemotherapy regimens for locally advanced and metastatic disease are;
S: gemcitabine (IV) 1000mg/m2 infusion over 30minutes day 1, 8 & 15
           AND
S: cisplatin (IV) 70mg/m2 infusion over 30mins day 2 given every 28 days for 6 cycles
           OR
MVAC regimen
S: methotrexate (IV) 30mg/m2 over 5 minutes day1, 15 & 22
           AND
S: vinblastine (IV) 3mg/m2 over 10 minutes day2, 15 & 22
           AND
S: doxorubicin (IV) 30mg/m2 over 15 minutes day2
           AND
S: cisplatin (IV) 70mg/m2 over 30mins day2

Radiotherapy
Radiotherapy may be given after bladder-preserving surgery or alone in small lesions with a dose up to 66Gy/33Fractions
concurrent with cisplatin. It is also commonly used as palliative therapy to control bleeding and or pain locally advanced and
metastatic disease. Palliative dose 30Gy/10Fractions or 20Gy/5Fractions

sections.title: Testicular Cancer
sections.text:
Testicular cancer types:
  •    Germ cell tumor (GCT, which accounts for >95% of testicular cancers) and pure seminoma (60% of GCT).
  •    Non-seminomatous germ cell tumors (NSGCT, 40% of GCT).
  •    Embryonal, yolk sac tumor, choriocarcinoma, teratoma, and mixed.
  •    Sex cord-stromal tumors.
  •    Sertoli cell, Leydig cell, granulosa cell, and mixed types.
  •    Others include lymphoma and embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma.

sections.title: Renal Cell Carcinoma
sections.text:
Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) constitutes 80–95% of primary renal neoplasms. There are four subtypes of RCC: clear cell (75–
85%), chromophilic/papillary (10–15%), chromophobic (5–10%), oncocytic (3–5%), and collecting duct (very rare). RCC is a
radioresistant tumor and has low response rates to cytotoxic chemotherapies, though targeted molecular agents and
stereotactic ablative radiotherapy are redefining the management of the disease.

Risk factors
Risk factors: tobacco, occupational exposure to cadmium/asbestos/petrols, obesity, acquired cystic disease of the kidney, and
phenacetin-containing analgesics exposure.

sections.title: Lymphomas
sections.text: The World Health Organization broadly classifies lymphomas into Hodgkin lymphoma (HL) and non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL).

sections.title: Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma
sections.text:
NHLs are a heterogeneous group of diseases which are mainly linked by their origin within the lymphoid system and its different
cellular components. They are -sub-classified based on the stage of maturation (immature vs. mature) and cell of origin [B cell,
T cell, or natural killer cell (NK) cell].

Clinical Presentation
  •    Peripheral Lymph node enlargement (commonest site-neck)
  •    Hepatomegaly and/or splenomegaly in advanced stages
  •    B-symptoms: Unexplained weight loss, fever, drenching night sweats
  •    Coughing, trouble breathing, or chest pain in case of Superior vena cava obstruction (SVCO)

Investigations
  •    CXR                                                              •    LDH, Urea, Electrolyte, Creatinine, Albumin,
  •    Chest and Abdominopelvic CT scan                                      Aspartate transaminase (AST), Bilirubin, Alkaline
  •    PET/CT                                                                phosphatase, Serum calcium, Uric acid, HIV
  •    FBC, differential, and film                                      •    Pregnancy test in females of hild–bearing age
  •    Bone marrow aspirate and trephine                                •    Hepatitis B and C
  •    Immunohistochemistry (IHC)                                       •    HIV status
                                                                        •    Tissue Biopsy for histopathology
                                                                        •    MUGA scan/ ECHO

  Note: Lumbar puncture and CSF cytology if there is CNS involvement in NHL associated with a high risk of CNS relapse, e.g.,
  Testicular, paranasal sinuses, extradural/paraspinal mass.

Staging: Ann Arbor classification.

NHL diseases are sensitive to both chemotherapy and radiotherapy

sections.title: Primary CNS Lymphoma
sections.text:
Standard chemotherapy regimens like CHOP are not effective, possibly due to poor penetration of the blood-brain-barrier (BBB).

Pharmacological Management
S: methotrexate (IV) 8mg/m2/day twice a week until remission is achieved

sections.title: Burkitt Lymphoma (BL)
sections.text:
Recommended chemotherapy regimens are:
S: CODOX-M AND IVAC (Magrath regimen- cyclophosphamide, vincristine, doxorubicin, methotrexate/ifosfamide, etoposide,
cytarabine) (IV)
         OR
S: CALGB 9251 (cyclophosphamide, prednisolone, ifosfamide, mesna, methotrexate, folinic acid, vincristine, cytarabine,
etoposide, dexamethasone and doxorubicin) (IV)
         OR
S: Hyper CVAD (cyclophosphamide, vincristine, doxorubicin and dexamethasone, methotrexate, cytarabine, folinic acid,
methylprednisolone and 6-mercaptopurine) (IV)
         OR
S: Dose-adjusted CHOP+ Etoposide (IV)

Aggressive T-cell lymphomas
Rare and more aggressive than DLBCL. First-line therapy is usually
S: CHOP with Etoposide (CHEOP) (IV)
           OR
S: cyclophosphamide (IV) day1 750 mg/m2 1-hour infusion AND doxorubicin (IV) 50 mg/m2 15 minutes’ infusion day 1 AND
vincristine (IV) 1.4 mg/m2 over 10 minutes (maximum 2mg) day1 AND prednisolone (PO) 100mg once a day, day 1–5 AND
etoposide 100mg/m2 (IV) day 1-day 3; repeat every 21 days for 6–8 cycles.

  Note
    •  For MALT lymphoma, eradication of Helicobacter pylori is essential. Splenectomy is recommended in splenic
       marginal zone lymphoma.
    •  Topical corticosteroids are indicated for localized or generalized skin involvement in mycosis fungoides. Systemic
       therapy is indicated for non-responders and Sezary syndrome.

These include S: retinoids, interferons and low dose methotrexate.
S: fludarabine AND Cyclophosphamide (FC) regimen is used as a second-line therapy for indolent B-cell lymphoma.

sections.title: Hodgkin’s disease (HD)
sections.text:
Hodgkin Lymphoma comprises about 30% of all lymphomas. The disease is characterized by scattered large multinucleated
Reed-Sternberg or mononuclear Hodgkin’s cells in an inflammatory background of a lymph node biopsy section.

Classified into two main types:
  •    Nodular lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin lymphoma–NLPHL
  •    Classical Hodgkin lymphoma–CHL, which is subdivided into:
             - Nodular sclerosis classical Hodgkin lymphoma–NSHL
             - Mixed cellularity classical Hodgkin lymphoma–MCHL
             - Lymphocyte–rich classical Hodgkin lymphoma–LRCHL
             - Lymphocyte–depleted classical Hodgkin lymphoma–LDHL

Clinical Presentation
  •    Enlarged painless lymph nodes in the neck or elsewhere
  •    B symptoms (weight loss, night sweats, and fever), pruritus, alcohol induced pain, general condition, throat, lymph nodes
       (site, number, size, consistency, mobility, matting), respiratory system, abdomen (liver, spleen, other masses), bone
       tenderness

Investigations
  •    CXR                                                           •    Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy (Not required in
  •    CT-Scan of neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis                        Stage I or II A)
  •    PET/CT                                                        •    Biopsy for histological diagnosis
  •    FBC, LFT, RFT, ESR, LDH, HIV Test                             •    MUGA scan / ECHO

As it is for NHL, HL diseases are sensitive to both chemotherapy and radiotherapy.

sections.title: Leukemia
sections.text:
The symptoms and signs are caused by: (i) bone marrow failure (e.g., anaemia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia); and (ii)
infiltration of organs (e.g. liver, spleen, lymph nodes, meninges, brain, skin or testes).

Investigations
  •    FBC, LFT, RFT, Coagulation indices
  •    Peripheral blood film
  •    Bone marrow aspiration and trephine biopsy
  •    Flow cytometry analysis, immunophenotyping, cytogenetic and molecular evaluation.
  •    ECHO/ECG for Cardiac function evaluation.

Management of acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL)
It is a medical emergency. Treatment should be initiated as soon as diagnosis is suspected based on cytologic criteria, before
definitive genetic, cytogenetic, or immunostaining confirmation is made.
All -trans - retinoic acid (ATRA) is added in all three phases of APL treatment. There is a high risk of developing DIC and
differentiation syndrome. Differentiation syndrome is treated with;

B: dexamethasone (IV) 10mg twice a day for 3 days or until symptoms resolve. Consider cessation of ATRA if symptoms are
severe

sections.title: Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL)
sections.text:
Pharmacological Management
The treatment of ALL is complex. The recommended regimens are, HYPER-CVAD/MTX-ARA-C Regimen which consists of
(cyclophosphamide/mesna/vincristine/ doxorubicin/dexamethasone/methotrexate/cytarabine/folinic acid) (IV)

sections.title: Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML)
sections.text:
Investigations:
Similar to other leukemia, plus BCR-ABL1 analysis by PCR or FISH for Ph chromosome analysis

Pharmacological Management
For BCR-ABL1 positive, first line treatment is Tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI)
Chronic phase: Characterized by blast cells < 10%.

S: imatinib (PO) 400mg once a day every day.

Accelerated phase: blasts 10 – 19%.
S: imatinib (PO) 600-800mg/day in 2 divided doses until the chronic phase is reached. Thereafter, continue with 400mg once
daily.

Blast crisis: Blast cells > 20%. If the patient was not on TKIs, treat as in accelerated phase. If patient was on TKIs, treat as
acute leukemia.

S: Second line TKIs include nilotinib, dasatinib, bosutinib and ponatinib (PO)
If BCR-ABL1 negative

D: hydroxyurea (PO) 40mg/kg daily. The dose ranges between 1mg and 3mg based on the WBC count.
  Note: Adequate hydration should be maintained. Blood transfusion is indicated based on the degree of anaemia

B: allopurinol (PO) 300mg 24hourly daily to prevent hyperuricemia.

sections.title: Chronic Lymphoid Leukemia (CLL)
sections.text:
Staging: RAI and Binet staging systems.

Pharmacological Management
S: chlorambucil (PO) 0.1mg/kg 24hourly for 2weeks, then rest for 2 weeks, repeat until remission is achieved.
          OR
S: fludarabine + cyclophosphamide + rituximab (FCR) regimen (IV)

If autoimmune haemolytic anaemia or autoimmune thrombocytopenia is present add
B: prednisolone (PO) 1mg/kg 24 once a day for 2 weeks

sections.title: Multiple myeloma and Plasmacytoma
sections.text:
Clinical features – CRAB: Features of hypercalcemia, renal impairment, features of anaemia, bone pain, recurrent infections
due to impaired antibody production, and bleeding tendencies and hyper viscosity syndrome in rare cases.

Investigations
  •    FBC plus diferRFT, LFT, Serum electrolytes, LDH                   •    Serum quantitative immunoglobulins, serum
  •    Peripheral blood smear                                                 protein electrophoresis and serum immunofixation
  •    Serum BUN, Calcium, uric acid                                          electrophoresis
  •    Bone marrow aspiration and trephine biopsy                        •    Skeletal survey by X-ray, CT scan or MRI
       including IHC and flow cytometry                                  •    ECHO
  •    FISH panel on bone marrow                                         •    Serum Beta2 microglobulin
  •    24 urine for total protein Bence Jones protein                    •    PET/CT scan

Staging: Revised International Staging System (RISS) Adopted by the International Myeloma Working Group

 Stage                     Treatment recommendations
 I or systemic             Observe or treat with systemic therapy
 smouldering
 SP – osseous              Involved field RT (≥30 Gy). Whole body MRI to look for additional sites of
                           disease
 SP – extraosseous         Involved field RT (≥45 Gy) alone, surgery alone, or surgery +
                           RT.
 II or III                 Chemo consists of a two- or three-agent combination of either alkylators, proteasome inhibitors,
                           immunomodulatory agents (lenalidomide/pomalidomide + prednisone/ dexamethasone +
                           bortezomib/carfilzomib), histone deacetylase
                           inhibitors, or newer monoclonal antibodies + bisphosphonate for
                           bone disease

                           Consider high-dose therapy followed by autologous stem-cell transplant.

                           Consider RT for palliation of local bone pain, prevention of pathologic fractures, or relief of spinal
                           cord compression

                           New MM with cord compression and significant end organ damage – start steroids and bortezomib
                           with RT to spine (hold lenalidomide until after RT)

                           Consider surgical consultation for impending fracture or spinal
                           cord involvement
Management
Radiotherapy is used for pain control of lytic lesions that are refractory to systemic therapy, treatment of spinal cord compression
from plasmacytoma and primary treatment of solitary plasmacytoma. Supportive treatment with blood transfusion, antibiotic,
hydration and analgesia when indicated.

Bisphosphonate therapy
S: zoledronic acid (IV) 4mg once monthly for 2 years

Recommended chemotherapy regimens include the following drugs in various combinations: Melphalan, Thalidomide,
Lenalidomide, Bortezomib, Cyclophosphamide, Prednisolone and Dexamethasone.
S: thalidomide (PO) 200mg 24hourly for 28days
          OR
S: lenalidomide (PO) 25mg 24hourly for 21days,
          AND
D: dexamethasone (PO) 40mg 24hourly on day 1, 8, 15, 22, repeats after every 4 weeks.
          OR
S: bortezomib (IV) 1.3mg/m2 24hourly AND dexamethasone (PO) 40mg 24 hourly WITH/WITHOUT cyclophosphamide (PO)
300mg/m2 all on day 1,8,15,22. Repeat every 4 weeks

sections.title: Meningiomas
sections.text:
Meningiomas are the second most common primary tumors of the meninges of the brain and constitute 30% of all intracranial
tumors. Commonest sites are cerebral convexity, parasagittal, and sphenoid
ridge.

Clinical Presentation
  •    Chronic headache
  •    Adult-onset seizures
  •    Inability to speak
  •    Loss of vision
  •    Focal neurological deficits

Investigations
  •    FBP                                                           •    CT/MR angiography
  •    Serum electrolytes                                            •    Histopathology studies
  •    CT Brain                                                      •    Digital substraction angiography (DSA) (4 Vessels
  •    MRI Brain                                                          Angiography) pri

Pharmacological Management
  •  Seizures: Give anticonvulsants.
  •  Brain edema: Give Dexamethasone

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •  Intracranial meningiomas are best managed with total excision following the principle of maximum safe excision (Refer
     to Simpson grading for intracranial meningiomas)
  •  Subtotal resection is associated with inferior outcome and higher recurrence rates.
  •  Preoperative embolization by DSA as initial treatment to embolize feeding vessels and decreasing intraoperative blood
     loss

Radiotherapy
  •   Radiotherapy is indicated in unresectable tumors, postoperative incomplete resection for WHO grade 1, and all grade
      2/3 tumors.
  •   Meticulous attention to operative notes is required, as well as to postoperative CT/MRI.

 Stage                                     Management
 Benign-appearing,            completely   Surgery (± preop angiography, embolization)
 resectable                                Definitive RT may achieve symptom relief and durable control for patients
                                           Observation can be considered for small, asymptomatic tumors
 Post op                                   WHO grade I GTR/STR: Observation? Consider
                                           RT if significant residual or symptomatic.
                                           WHO grade II GTR: Radiation?
                                           Grade II STR: 54–60 Gy/30 Fractions
                                           WHO grade III 60 Gy/30 Fractions?
 Inoperable                                RT Alone 60Gy/30 Fractions
 Recurrent, not previously radiated        Surgery
                                           Adjuvant RT 60Gy/30 Fractions

Follow up
  •   Follow up MRI is preferable than CT scan
  •   Follow up MR is a preferable test than CT scan WHO I
          i. Complete Resected-Annually for 5 years and then every 2years for 5 years
          ii. incomplete Resected-Annually indefinitely
  •   Small asymptomatic – 2years and 5years then discharge.
  •   WHO grade II
          i. Complete resected- Annually indefinitely
          ii. Incomplete resected Annually indefinitely
  •   WHO grade III (Malignant)
          i. Complete resected -3month to 6month for 2years then 6month indefinitely
          ii. Incomplete resected -3month

sections.title: Pituitary Tumors
sections.text:
Pituitary tumors constitute 10% of intracranial tumors. Morbidity is often due to mass effect and endocrine consequences,
including hyper -or hyposecretion of pituitary hormones.

Clinical Presentation
  •    Chronic headache                                                    >Male- erectile dysfunction, primary infertility,
  •    Loss of vision                                                      decreased libido
  •    Focal neurological deficits                                    •    Growth hormone excess (GH)
  •    Hormonal imbalances                                                 > Adult- Acromegalic features (Hands, feet, face),
  •    Prolactinomas                                                       high blood sugar, hypertension
       >Female -Mensural irregularity,        galactorrhea,                > Children- gigantism
       primary infertility, decrease libido                           •    ACTH excess- Obesity, Skin changes, muscles
                                                                           weakness
                                                                      •    TSH excess- Anxiety, weight loss, tachycardia

Investigations
  •    FBP, RFT, LFT                                                  •    Anterior pituitary hormones
  •    Prolactin                                                      •    CT / MRI Brain thin with contrast
  •    T3, T4, TSH                                                    •    CT/MR angiography
  •    LH, FSH, Testosterone                                          •    Visual field assessment
  •    FBS/glycosylated haemoglobin                                   •    Histopathology studies
  •    Echo and ECG

 Stage                             Management
 Nonfunctioning                    Surgery → (observation or RT) OR definitive RT alone
 pituitary tumours
 GH-secreting                      Surgery → observation → RT 45–50 Gy for recurrent GH
                                   elevation. Or, RT alone 45–50 Gy for inoperable patients.
 Prolactin-secreting               Observation OR medical management OR surgery vs. RT,
                                   individualize treatment based on symptoms, side effect profile, and patient preferences.
 ACTH-secreting                    Surgery → observation → RT 45–50 Gy for recurrent ACTH
                                   elevation.
                                   RT alone 45–50 Gy for inoperable patients.

 TSH-secreting                     Aggressive, always treat with postop RT 45-50Gy

Pharmacological Management
These should be treated initially with dopamine receptor agonist: Give:
C: bromocriptine (PO) 2.5mg 8 hourly
         OR
S: cabergoline (PO) 0.25mg once/twice a week (Titrate with prolactin levels checked 2 weekly, aim isto maintain PRL < 30ng/ml)

Cushing’s disease
Surgical management is recommended. Consider medicines that inhibit adrenocortical function only when surgery is not
possible:
S: metyrapone 250mg once a day (can be escalated based on response)

Acromegaly
Somatostatin analogues may be used to treat acromegaly.
S: octreotide (SC) 50–100 micrograms every 8 hours, titrated according to GH and IGF-1 response
          OR
S: octreotide LAR/SR 20 mg IM every 4 weeks (may be adjusted to 10–30 mg every 4 weeks based on response)

Efficacy is measured using clinical response defined as basal GH levels < 2.5 ng/ml, glucose- suppressed levels <1.5 ng/ml
and normalization of serum IGF-1 levels.

Surgical management of pituitary tumors
  •   This is the primary treatment for most symptomatic pituitary tumors, except for prolactinomas which may be managed
      medically if there is no urgent deterioration of vision.
  •   Trans-sphenoidal approach (endoscopic or microsurgical) is preferred as it is safer and better tolerated.
  •   Frequently subtotal especially in large tumors or tumors invading into cavernous sinuses. Hypopituitarism occurs post-
      operative in about 12% of patients.
Radiotherapy
Indicated post subtotal tumor resection, recurrent tumors, persistently elevated circulating hormone levels, and inoperable
patients.
Follow up MRI 3 months after surgery to assess residual tumor.

Radiotherapy is very effective for control of growth of pituitary tumors (>95%), but less effective for decreasing circulating
hormone levels in functional tumors.

Common complications
Diabetes Insipidus: is characterized by excessive urine output due to lack of ADH, usually immediate post-operative but may
be delayed. Patient will present with Polyuria, Polydipsia and some of them Polyphagia. In immediate post-operative period
you may consider fluid replacement (monitoring in input, output and serum electrolyte). Consider medical treatment if not
resolving

S: desmopressin (PO) 0.05mg 12 hourly daily (titrate based on response.
         OR
S: tolvaptan 7.5mg (PO) maximum dose 30mg in 24hr.

Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone Secretion (SIADH) is characterized by decreased urine output and
hyponatremia due to excessive ADH secretion, may occur early (first week) or late (2nd week) post operative. It’s important to
note that SIADH may occur in TBI, Brain tumors, CNS infections and some medications, treat the cause and manage
hyponatremia according the guideline on electrolyte imbalance section.

A: furosemide (PO/IV) 40mg Once or twice a day
          AND/OR
S: tolvaptan 7.5mg (PO) maximum dose 30mg in 24hr

Cerebral Salt Wasting(CSW): characterized by excessive urine sodium secretion and hyponatremia, usually immediate post-
operative. Manage hyponatremia with
C: sodium chloride 3% (hypertonic saline) (IV) 100–150 mL bolus (or as per severity), Repeat as needed until Na⁺ improves
          AND
D: fludrocortisone (PO) 0.05-0.1mg 12hourly daily.

Follow up
  •   There is significant risk of pituitary hypofunction after surgery or irradiation and this risk may occur up to 15 years later
      – the patients should be warned of the symptoms and be tested regularly.
  •   Patients treated with standard radiotherapy are unlikely to show an early response and would therefore be assessed at
      12 monthly intervals in terms of hormone levels and pituitary function.

sections.title: Gliomas
sections.text: Gliomas constitute the most common tumors of the brain affecting all age groups, with predilection to the adult population.

sections.title: Low-grade Gliomas (LGGs) Clinical Presentation
sections.text:
•    Seizures are common
  •    progressive neurologic symptoms depending on site of tumor

Investigations
  •    CT or MRI should be done in diagnosis of Gliomas.
  •    MR spectroscopy
  •    Diffusion tensor tractography (DTI)

Non- Pharmacological Management
Surgical management
Long term survival approaches 100% with complete removal. After partial resection, survival rates range from 80-90% at 5
years to 70-80% at 10 years and 50-60 % at 20 years.
Repeat the MRI scans at 3, 6, 12, 24 months to check for growth. If this is surgically resectable then repeat surgery should be
attempted

Radiotherapy
Dose for low grade gliomas: 1.8 Gy X 28 Fractions = 50.4 Gy (5 times per week). Concurrent and adjuvant use of Temozolomide
is indicated if available,
Pharmacological Management
S: temozolomide (PO) 75mg/m2 daily during RT and 150-200mg/m2 day 1-5 Monthly for 6 months.
If the hypothalamus /pituitary are in the RT field, then endocrine function should also be evaluated annually by T4 & TSH,
testosterone or FSH/LH.

Follow up
  •   CT scan immediate postoperative to assess resection.
  •   MRI recommended at 3months and then annually unless other clinical indications emergency.

sections.title: High Grade Gliomas (HGGs)
sections.text:
Anaplastic Astrocytoma (AA) and Glioblastoma Multiforme (GBM)

Clinical Presentation
Headache, Seizures are common, progressive neurologic symptoms depending on site and size of tumor.

Investigations
  •    FBP, Serum electrolytes,                                       •    MRI preferred investigation
  •    Histopathology studies                                         •    MR spectroscopy
  •    Immunohistochemistry studies: IDH,1 and IDH2,                  •    CT/MR angiography
       1p/19q codeletion, ATRX gene loss, MGMT.                       •    Functional MRI (fMRI)
  •    Ki-67, p53.                                                    •    PET/CT scan
  •    CT brain scan                                                  •    Intraoperative USS

Non-Pharmacological Management
Surgical management
  •   Complete excision of the tumor is essential for improved survival. Preoperative and intraoperative techniques to improve
      extent of resection in a safe manner (maximum safe resection) including brain mapping, use of intraoperative fluorescein
      guidance to expand resection margins and neuromonitoring techniques are advocated.
  •   Extent of resection is best assessed on post-op CT/MRI scans.
  •   Frozen section useful for a rapid and real-time histology diagnosis during the operation and this allow surgeons to make
      informed decision on extent of tumor removal, assess the margin, assess the margin and extent of tumor resection of
      which these have impact on surgical out come and overall mortality.
  •   Stereotactic brain biopsy/Neuronavigational using Brain lab indications:
            > CT/MRI- suggestive of high-grade glioma but Abscess, Metastasis and demyelinating disease
            > Tissue necessary for tumor grading of glioma
            > For Molecular testing for genetic mutations e.g. IDH, ATRX, EGFR) or epigenetic changes(methylation) which
            can influence treatment strategies
            > Suspicious PCNSL to differentiate it from glioma
            > Inoperable or eloquent area
            > Multifocal or diffuse infiltrative tumor

Radiotherapy
  •   Patients should be CT-planned, with contrast administration. 3mm to 5mm slices cuts from Vertex to Base of skull. Large
      volume PTV = should completely encompass enhancing lesion seen on pre-op T2/FLAIR scan, plus small (2cm) margin.
  •   Dose to LARGE VOLUME = 2.00 Gy X 23 Fractions = 46.00 Gy (5 times per week).
  •   Small volume PTV (PTV2) is based on Gd-enhanced T1 weighted image= enhancing lesion on pre-op scans +1- 2 cm
      margin.
  •   Dose to SMALL VOLUME = 2.00 Gy X 7 Fractions = 14.00 Gy
  •   Total dose 60Gy in 30 fractions.
  •   Other alternative radiotherapy fractionations can be used in elderly, more than 65 years of age are Hypo fractionation;
      40Gy/ 15 Fractions and 5Gy X 5 Fractions

Pharmacological Management
Seizures: Treat as per these guidelines Chapter 8 Nervous system disease conditions

 Note: Imaging techniques such as MR Spectroscopy may be indicated during follow up to distinguish tumor recurrence from
 post RT changes.

Chemotherapy
Concurrent chemotherapy + RT:
S: temozolomide (PO) 75 mg/m2 daily during RT, then 150-200mg/m2 give. n D1-D5 of a 28day cycle for 6 cycles after RT
Oral steroid/ Ondansetron should be taken half an hour prior to chemotherapy tablet on each day. Tablets must be taken 1st
thing in the morning on an empty stomach.

Prophylaxis for PCP pneumonia with
A: sulfamethoxazole + trimethoprim 480mg 12 hourly should be given during daily temozolomide treatment.
Recurrent disease
  •   Surgery plays an important role in selected patients- relieves symptoms, improves PS and QOL and reduces steroid
      requirement.
  •   Repeat radiotherapy can be considered, depending on size of lesion and previous dose.
  •   Palliation Chemotherapy may be the only modality available. Active regimens include BCNU, PCV, Temozolomide, and,
      more recently, Irinotecan and Bevacizumab.

Follow up
  •   A baseline scan should be done at 4 months’ post RT as a reference.
  •   Thereafter, scans are usually done at 6 months and annually, or if clinically indicated.
  •   High index of suspicion and testing if indicated for pituitary function for post RT hypopituitarism.

sections.title: Bone tumors
sections.text:
Primary bone tumors account for <0.2% of all cancers. 60% of the cases occur between 10 and 20 years of age (most active
age of skeletal growth). 80% of the cases in long bones until epiphyseal closure (then occur with the appendicular skeleton).
Lung metastases common in osteosarcoma, chondrosar- coma, malignant fibrous histiocytoma.

Investigations
  •    FBC, RFT, LFT, LDH urinalysis, ESR, alkaline                      •    In general, limb-sparing strategies are preferred,
       phosphatase,                                                           which may involve a combination of neoadjuvant
  •    Plain films (primary region)                                           chemo, RT, and surgery.
  •    CXR                                                               •    Input of an orthopedic surgeon is essential in
  •    CT and MRI (primary area and chest)                                    determining whether limb sparing is possible. Final
  •    Bone scan to evaluate for intramedullary skip                          limb function may
       metastases                                                        •    sometimes be better with a prosthesis than with a
  •    PET/CT scan                                                            partially resected and/or irradiated limb. In children,
  •    Incisional or percutaneous core biopsy treatment                       RT has added implications on limb growth and
       recommendations                                                        future function.

Management
 Pathology             Treatment recommendations                                       Dose             Follow up
 Osteosarcoma          •WLE, amputation vs. limb sparing surgery.                      Post-op:         Exam and imaging every
                       •Mastectomy for pulmonary, visceral metastases improves         R0 55–60 Gy      3–6
                       survival.                                                       R1 64–66 Gy      Months (including chest
                       •Neoadjuvant chemotherapy for high-grade, localized disease     R2 68–70 Gy      imaging) for 5 years,
                       or metastatic disease                                           Unresectable:    annually to 10 years
                       •Consider RT for positive margin, subtotal resection, or        60–70 Gy
                       unresectable

 Chondrosarcoma        •WLE is the primary treatment                                   Post-op:
                       •RT for inadequate margins, unfavourable location, palliation   60–70 Gy
                                                                                       Unresectable:
                                                                                       >70 Gy
 Chondroma             •WLE or en bloc resection is the primary treatment, followed    66–70       Gy
                       by RT                                                           standard
                       •RT alone for unresectable disease                              fractionation
                       •EGFR inhibitors can be added to surgery/RT for recurrent
                       disease
Pharmacological Management
Osteosarcoma
First line                                                            2nd line
Regimen 1                                                             Regimen 1
S: doxorubicin 25 mg/m²/day IV over 2 hours on Days 1–3               S: gemcitabine 675 mg/m² IV on Days 1 and 8
           AND                                                                  AND
S: cisplatin 75 mg/m² IV over 3 hours on Day 1                        S: docetaxel 75–100 mg/m² IV on Day 8
Repeat every 3 weeks for 6 cycles                                     Repeat every 3 weeks for 4–6 cycles
           OR                                                                   OR
                                                                      Regimen 2
Regimen 2                                                             S: carboplatin 400 mg/m²/day IV on Days 1–2
S: ifosfamide 1.3 g/m² IV on Days 1–3                                           AND
           AND                                                        S: ifosfamide 1,800 mg/m²/day IV on Days 1–3
S: doxorubicin (Adriamycin) 50 mg/m² IV on Day 1                                AND
