S: cisplatin 100 mg/m² IV divided over Days 1–3                                 AND
Repeat every 3 weeks for 6 cycles                                     S: etoposide 100 mg/m²/day IV on Days 1–3
                                                                      Repeat every 3 weeks for up to 6 cycles

sections.title: Soft tissue sarcoma
sections.text:
Frequency: MFH (20–30%), liposarcoma (10–20%), leiomyosarcoma (10–15%), fibrosarcoma (5–10%), synovial cell sarcoma
(5–10%), rhabdomyosarcoma (5–10%), malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor/malignant schwannoma (5%).
Rhabdomyosarcoma most common sarcoma in children. Approximately 10% have metastases at diagnosis. Extremity mainly
lung and retroperitoneal mainly liver.

Many sarcoma types harbor characteristic genetic aberrations, including single base pair substitutions, deletions and
amplifications, and translocations. For example, cKIT or PDGFRA activating mutation in GIST.

Risk factors
Genetics: NF-1, retinoblastoma, Gardner’s syndrome, Li-Fraumeni syndrome, and Carney Stratakis syndrome. Environmental
risk factors: ionizing radiation, herbicides, thorotrast, chlorophenols, vinyl chloride, and arsenic.

Investigations
  •    FBC, BUN/Cr, ESR, LDH                                        •    PET CT scan
  •    CT/MRI of primary, CT chest. If myxoid                       •    Incisional biopsy or core needle biopsy.
       liposarcoma, include CT abdomen because it                   •    Cytogenetic analysis of tissue to look         for
       frequently metastasizes to the retroperitoneum.                   characteristic chromosomal translocations.
  •    MRI brain for alveolar type.

Management
 Stage                        Treatment recommendations
 I Extremity                  Surgery alone, unless close (<1 cm) or +margin, re-resect or
                              post-op RT (60-66Gy).
 II-III Extremity             Pre-op RT (60-66Gy) then surgery or surgery then post-op RT.

                              Consider neoadjuvant/adjuvant chemo for large deep high-grade tumors.

                              For LR, amputation can salvage ∼75%

 IV                           For controlled primary, with ≤4 lung lesions and/or extended disease-free interval, consider
                              surgical resection and metastatectomy.
                              OR, best supportive care, chemo, and/or palliative surgery or RT.

 Unresectable                 Definitive RT (70-80Gy), chemo (Doxorubicin + ifosfamide), or chemoRT. Surgery if becomes
                              resectable.
 Retroperineal                Surgery then post-op EBRT 45–50 Gy.

                              Alternatively, pre-op RT +/– chemo then resection.

 GIST                        If resectable, surgery then imatinib.
                             If marginally or unresectable, imatinib then consider surgery then imatinib.
Pharmacological Management
AIM Regimen
S: doxorubicin 20-25 mg/m2 IV push on days 1-3
          AND
S: ifosfamide 2000-3000 mg/m2 IV push bolus 3 h on days 1-3
          AND
S: mesna 225 mg/m2 IV over 1 hour before ifosfamide and at 4 and 8 hour after ifosfamide. Repeat every 21-28 days for 6
cycles.

MAID Regimen
S: mesna 2.5 g/m2/day IV continuous infusion on days 1-4
          AND
S: doxorubicin 20 mg/m2/day IV continuous infusion on days 1-3
          AND
S: ifosfamide 2.5 g/m2/day IV continuous infusion on days 1-3
          AND
S: dacarbazine 300 mg/m2/day IV continuous infusion on days 1-3. Repeat every 21 days for 6 cycles.

AD Regimen
S: doxorubicin 15 mg/m2/day IV continuous infusion on days 1-4
         AND
S: dacarbazine 250 mg/m2/day IV continuous infusion on days 1-4. Repeat every 21 days for 6 cycles.

GD Regimen
S: gemcitabine 900 mg/m2 IV over 30-90 min on days 1 and 8
         AND
S: docetaxel 75-100 mg/m2 IV over 60 min on day 8; repeat every 21 days for 6 cycles.

sections.title: Oncological Emergencies
sections.text:
Important oncological emergencies include Hypercalcemia, Superior venous cava obstruction, Spinal cord compression, and
Neutropenic sepsis.

sections.title: Superior Vena Cava Syndrome (SVCS)
sections.text:
Superior vena cava syndrome (SVCS) is the clinical expression for obstruction of blood flow through the SVC. Malignancy
(90%) is the most frequent cause of SVC obstruction. SVC obstruction is a strong predictor of poor prognosis in patients with
non–small cell lung cancer. SVC obstruction in cancer patients can result from
  •    Extrinsic compression of the SVC
            >Lung Cancer (65%)
            >Lymphomas (15%)
            >Other cancers (10%)
  •    Intrinsic compression

Clinical Presentation
  •    Dyspnea                                                       •    Cough
  •    Headache                                                      •    Pemberton’s sign (development of facial flushing,
  •    Oedema and change in colour in the areas drained                   distended neck and head superficial veins,
       by SVC (examples–face and upper limb)                              inspiratory stridor, and elevation of the jugular
  •    Venous distension of the neck, upper chest, and                    venous pressure (JVP) upon raising both of the
       arms                                                               patient's arms above his/her head simultaneously,
                                                                          as high as possible (Pemberton's maneuver)

Investigations
  •    CXR                                                           •    Bronchoscopy
  •    CT scan Chest, Abdomen, and Pelvis                            •    Needle aspiration of a peripheral lymph node, or
  •    PET/CT                                                             mediastinoscopy
  •    Tissue diagnosis for the appropriate treatment                •    Sputum cytology
       modality                                                      •    Thoracentesis.

Non-Pharmacological Management
Treatment of SVC syndrome is divided into supportive and definitive therapy

Supportive measures
  •  Head elevation–To decrease the hydrostatic pressure and thereby the edema. No data are documenting the
     effectiveness of this maneuver, but it is simple and without risk.
  •  Glucocorticoid therapy (dexamethasone, 4 mg every 6 hours) to relieve inflammation and oedema (to be avoided before
     biopsy if lymphoma is suspected as steroid induced tissue necrosis might obscure the diagnosis)
  •  Loop diuretics (furosemide) are also commonly used, but it is unclear whether venous pressure distal to the obstruction
     is affected by small changes in right atrial pressure.

Definitive Therapy
  •    Radiation treatment to the malignant mass.
  •    Chemotherapy–in chemo sensitive cancers like lymphoma, germ cell tumours or small cell lung cancer
  •    SVC Stent–can be useful in cases of thrombosis and for patients not responding to cancer treatment
  •    Removal of central venous device.

 Note: It is advisable to avoid placement of intravenous lines in the arms so that fluid is not injected into the already
 compressed SVC.

sections.title: Hypercalcaemia
sections.text:
Hypercalcaemia refers to elevated calcium level in blood (normal range 2.2–2.6 mmol/L) that occurs in 10–20% patients with
advanced cancers (most commonly in cancer of the breast, kidney, lung, prostate, head and neck, and multiple myeloma)

Clinical Presentation
  •    Symptoms of hypercalcaemia include nausea, vomiting, constipation, polyuria and disorientation
  •    Psychiatric overtones (depression 30–40%, anxiety, cognitive dysfunction, insomnia, coma)
  •    Clinical evidence of volume contraction secondary to progressive dehydration may be apparent. Severe hypercalcaemia
       (above 3.75–4.0 mmol/L) is a medical emergency and a poor prognostic sign

Investigations
  •    Specific biochemistry like PTH,
  •    ECG to detect arrhythmias and
  •    Imaging with Bone Scan or PET–CT scan to identify metastatic bone disease.

Pharmacological Management
Treat the hypercalcaemia first and the cause later:
Hydration & dieresis:
A: sodium chloride (Normal saline) 1–2 litres over 2 hours with 30–40 mg of furosemide expands intravascular volume and
enhances calcium excretion.

In elderly and cardiac patients, the rate of hydration needs to be slower.

Bisphosphonates–via a complex mechanism inhibit osteoclasts and, in turn, both normal and pathological bone resorption.
Commonly used bisphosphonates are:

S: zolendronic acid (IV) infused as 4mg (IV) in 100 mL of Normal saline over 15 mins. Normalization of serum calcium occurs
in 4–10 days and lasts 4–6 weeks. Therefore, if re–treatment is required, dose is repeated after 7 days
          OR
S: ibandronate (IV) 6 mg over 2 hours’ infusion
  Note
     •   Bisphosphonates and denosumab cause increasing risk of osteonecrosis of jaw following extraction of teeth or oral
         surgical procedures. Therefore, a dental review may be necessary to make sure the necessary dental procedures are
         completed prior to commencing therapy
     •   Calcitonin – a thyroid hormone given 4–8 IU/kg IM or SC every 6–8 hours can bring about a rapid decline in calcium
         levels, however tachyphylaxis limits its utility.

sections.title: Spinal–cord Compression
sections.text:
Spinal cord compression can result from a myriad of both atraumatic and traumatic causes. The spinal column is vulnerable to
various compressive phenomena, such as the expansion of blood products, neoplastic disease, infectious collections, or
protrusion of bone or intervertebral disc within the limited area of the fat-filled spinal epidural space and meninges.

This topic focuses on atraumatic causes of spinal cord compression, including degenerative spondylosis with myelopathy,
metastatic disease of the spine, primary spinal cord malignancy, spinal epidural abscess, and spontaneous or iatrogenic spinal
epidural hematoma. (Traumatic spinal cord compression in chapter 18)

Clinical Presentation
  •    Myelopathy,                                                      •    Upper Motor Neurons findings
  •    Neurologic deficit(s)                                            •    Lower Motor Neurons Findings
  •    Back pain                                                        •    Gait disturbance
  •    Spastic urinary and rectal sphincter dysfunction

Investigations
  •    X-rays                                                           •    NCV
  •    CT scan                                                          •    EMG
  •    MRI neuroaxis                                                    •    Bone Marrow Aspiration Biopsy
  •    Bone scan                                                        •    CT /ultrasound-guided biopsy
  •    FBP

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •  Immobilizing the patient and obtaining urgent                      •    Radiotherapy: for patients who are not candidates
     investigations                                                          for upfront surgery.
  •  Bladder catheterization as appropriate.                            •    Palliative dose: 8Gy Single fraction or
  •  Physiotherapy                                                           20Gy/5Fractions or 30Gy/10 Fractions

Surgical Treatment
Spinal Cord Decompression and Spine stabilization

Pharmacological Management
 Indication                                    Medicine and Dose
 Reduce spinal cord edema                      B: dexamethasone 16 mg IV immediately, followed by 4 mg IV/PO every 6
                                               hours (total 16 mg/day), then taper according to clinical response
 Pain management (mild–moderate pain)          A: ibuprofen 400 mg PO every 8 hours after meals
                                                               OR
                                               C: diclofenac 50 mg PO every 8–12 hours after meals
 Gastric protection                            A: omeprazole 20–40 mg PO/IV once daily
                                                                OR
                                               C: pantoprazole 40 mg PO/IV once daily
 Neuropathic support                           C: vit B1, B6, B12 and Folic acid (FDC) once daily
 Severe pain                                   Epidural spinal analgesia as per anaesthesia/pain specialist protocol

 Note: All patients suspicious for spinal cord compression should be referred to a Neurosurgeon and radiation oncologist as
 soon as possible.

sections.title: Tumor Lysis Syndrome
sections.text:
The syndrome is mostly observed in cancers with a rapid proliferation index such as Burkitt’s lymphoma, acute lymphocytic
leukemia, acute non-lymphocytic leukemia, and less frequently, solid tumors of small-cell type, breast cancer, and
medulloblastoma.

Clinical Presentation
Clinically, the syndrome is characterized metabolically by the presence of hyperuricemia, hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia,
hypocalcemia, and acute renal failure.
  •     Work Up                                                       •    ECG.
  •     FBP, RFT, LFT, LDH                                            •    CXR
  •     Serum electrolytes phosphates and calcium                     •    CT-Scan.
  •     Urine pH and output                                           •    Abdomen and Pelvis USS

Pharmacological Management
 Indication                                  Medicine and Dose
 Prevention/treatment of                     B: allopurinol 300 mg PO/IV once daily
 hyperuricemia
 Urine alkalinization (if indicated)         D: sodium bicarbonate 100 mEq added to IV fluids over 24 hours for 48–72 hours
 Hyperkalemia with ECG changes               A: calcium gluconate 10% 10–30 mL IV over 5–10 minutes
 Hyperphosphatemia                           B: calcium carbonate 500–1500 mg PO every 8 hours with meals
 Symptomatic hypocalcemia                    A: calcium gluconate 10% 10–20 mL IV slow infusion
                                             B: ceftriaxone 2 g IV once daily
 Suspected febrile
                                                            OR
 neutropenia/opportunistic infection
                                             S: piperacillin + tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6–8 hours
 Suspected resistant gram-positive           S: vancomycin 15–20 mg/kg IV every 8–12 hours
 infection/MRSA
 Suspected fungal infection (persistent      C: fluconazole 400 mg IV/PO once daily
 neutropenic fever/high-risk patients)                      OR
                                             S: amphotericin B deoxycholate 0.7–1 mg/kg/day IV
 Neutropenia                                 S: filgrastim (G-CSF/Neupogen) 5 mcg/kg/day SC once daily until neutrophil
                                             recovery
 Nutritional support                         Total parenteral nutrition (TPN) if indicated

sections.title: Febrile Neutropenia
sections.text:
Applied only to the management of patients with:
  •    Fever and neutropenia as a result of a known or suspected malignancy or the use of chemotherapy
  •    Fever and neutropenia as a result of a bone marrow failure syndrome.
  •    Fever (or evidence of infection), who chemotherapy or have completed cancer therapy within 6 months, even though
       they are not neutropenic.

Investigations
FBP, LFT, RFT, Malaria screen, Urine analysis, Urine/blood/stool culture Serum Electrolytes, Throat Swab

Pharmacological Management
Antibiotic administration and Antipyretics and analgesics

Initial (first-line) and subsequent (second-line – deteriorating patients) empiric antibiotic selection.
Patients with no significant beta-lactam reactions:

S: piperacillin +tazobactam (FDC) (IV) 4 g piperacillin / 0.5 g tazobactam given every IV 6 hourly
             AND
C: Gentamicin 3-6mg/kg once daily. Deteriorating patients on first-line treatment with no history of anaphylaxis to Beta Lactams
(i.e. if history of rash only, can still use meropenem
             OR
S: meropenem (IV) 500mg 8 hourly
             AND
S: amikacin (IV) 15mg/kg/dose in 2-3 divided doses (or ciprofloxacin 200– 400 mg IV 12 hourly)
             AND
S: vancomycin 15 - 20mg/kg/dose 8 - 12 hourly

Patients with history of definite anaphylaxis to Beta Lactams
C: ciprofloxacin (IV) as above
          AND
D: metronidazole (IV) 500mg – 750mg dose 8 hourly
          AND
S: amikacin dose as above
          AND
S: vancomycin dose as above

Culture Negative Patients
First 48 hours
   •    If the patient had a single spike of fever (i.e., the patient’s temperature returns to normal within 4 hours of the initial
        fever), antibiotics may be discontinued.
   •    If the patient had more than a single spike of fever, antibiotics must be continued for at least 7 afebrile days. Also,
        consider the following.
   •    If the patient develops oral herpes or severe mucositis, commence IV Acyclovir.
   •    Obvious fungal infection – suspect candida – add fluconazole IV; suspect other fungal infection – add Amphotericin B
        IV.
   •    Diarrhoea and vomiting – culture stool and commence ciprofloxacin and metronidazole
   •    Signs of skin infection – add vancomycin
   •    No clinical focus but deteriorating rapidly or extremely unwell – consider adding vancomycin

   Note: If by day 5-7, the patient remains febrile, neutropenic, consider performing a fungal work-up, prior to commencing
   empiric appropriate antifungal treatment.

sections.title: Aggressive Disruptive Behaviors in Adults
sections.text:
Agitation may escalate to overt aggression and often manifests with restlessness, pacing, and loud or demanding speech.
Aggressive behavior includes verbally abusive language, specific verbal threats, intimidating physical behavior, and/or actual
physical violence to self, others or property. All agitation and aggression must be considered an emergency and violence
prevented wherever possible.

Causes:
  •  Physical: acute medical illness, delirium and its causes, epilepsy, intracerebral lesions, traumatic brain injury.
  •  Psychiatric: psychosis, mania, agitated depression, neurocognitive disorders, developmental disorders, severe anxiety.
  •  Substance misuse: alcohol, cannabis, methaqualone (mandrax) intoxication or withdrawal; stimulant (e.g. cocaine)
     intoxication; benzodiazepine withdrawal.
  •  Psychological factors: high levels of impulsivity and antagonism, hypersensitivity to rejection or insult, poor frustration
     tolerance and maladaptive coping skills all contribute to aggression and rage

In pregnant women: labour, obstetric complications, sepsis, organ failure as well as substances and mental disorders

Non-Pharmacological Management
Before starting pharmacological treatment, conduct a
structured assessment:
   •    Explore possible reasons for their distress
   •    Check for and address clinical or environmental causes (e.g., pain, delirium, or inappropriate care).
   •    Ensure the safety of the patient and those caring for them.
   •    Caution is needed with elderly and frail patients as they are vulnerable to falls and further injury if sedated.
   •    The use of physical restraint should only be employed when there is a need to protect the patient and surrounding
        people in an acute setting and it should be for as short time as possible with a constant monitoring of patients’ safety.
        Manual restraint may be necessary to administer medication.
        > Mechanical restraint: Only if absolutely necessary to protect the patient and others for as short a time as possible.
        > Document the type, sites and duration of any restraints used.
        > 15-minute monitoring: vital signs, the mental state, restraint sites, and reasons for use.
   •    As initial and ongoing management, offer psychosocial and environmental interventions to reduce aggressive and
        disruptive behavior.

De-escalation Techniques should be attempted first:
  •   Be calm, confident, kind, and reassuring.                        •    Do not argue, confront delusions, or touch the
  •   Maintain a submissive posture with open hands.                        patient.
  •   Do not turn your back on the patient; avoid direct               •    Set clear limits regarding behavior.
      eye contact.                                                     •    Take patient to quiet, calm area – do not leave
  •   Do not attempt to reason with the patient.                            unobserved

   Note: In Pregnant women:
     •    Never leave unattended.
     •    Use restraint sparingly, with care, if possible, with mother in a supported semi-seated position (not supine or prone).

Pharmacological Management
For cooperative patients

A: promethazine (PO) 25-50mg stat
         OR
C: diazepam (PO)10 mg stat
         OR
C: lorazepam (PO)4 mg stat

Uncooperative and severely agitated patients, if oral treatment fails after 30–60 minutes, OR If there is significant risk to the
patient and others, give

Parenteral treatment as follows:
B: haloperidol (IM) 2.5-5mg stat, repeat in 30-60minutes, if required. (Maximum dose: 20mg, within 24hours)
         AND
A: diazepam (IV/IM) 10mg stat. Repeat after 30–60minutes if needed. (maximum dose: 60mg per 24hours)
         OR
A: promethazine (deep IM) 25–50mg Repeat after 30–60minutes if needed. (Maximum dose: 100mg per 24hours.
         OR
C: lorazepam (IM) 1-4mg stat. Repeat after 30–60minutes if needed to a maximum dose of 12mg in 24hours
         OR
D: midazolam (IV/IM) 2-10mg stat
If haloperidol is unavailable,
A: chlorpromazine (deep IM) 25–50mg may be repeated as necessary 4 times in 24hours (Maximum dose: 2000mg per
24hours).

If patient is known to suffer from schizophrenia and is not neuroleptic naïve give:
S: zuclopenthixol acetate IM) 50–150 mg (Repeat after 2–3 days, if necessary.
Give a maximum of 3 repeat injections and should not be used for longer than 2 weeks. The maximum administered dose
should not exceed 400mg.

If patient develops acute dystonia give:
A: promethazine (deep IM) 25–50 mg 24hourly. In the elderly 25 mg (Maximum dose: 100mg per 24hours.
           OR
S: clonazepam (IM) 0.5 -4mg 24hourly
           OR
A: atropine (IM) 0.5 -2 mg when required

  Note
    •  Repeated doses of high potency antipsychotics may lead to the development of the life- threatening neuroleptic
       malignant syndrome. If suspected, stop antipsychotic, and institute supportive care.
    •  Elderly patients are at increased risk of respiratory depression and delirium from benzodiazepines, so they should be
       avoided as far as possible.
    •  Always monitor vital signs of sedated patients
    •  In giving Injection (IM) of Chlorpromazine, caution has to be taken and monitor BP every half an hour within
       administration period and every 4 hours for the next 24 hours, 6 hourly for the next days

sections.title: Delirium
sections.text:
Delirium or acute confusion state is a condition characterized by disturbance in attention accompanied with reduced awareness
of the environment; develops over a short period of time and fluctuates in severity.

Causes:
Think Delirium
  •    D rugs / Dehydration
  •    E electrolytes
  •    L evel of pain
  •    I nfection / Inflammation (post-surgery)
  •    R espiratory function (Hypoxia/Hypercapnia)
  •    I mpaction – constipation
  •    U rine retention (avoid catheters where possible)
  •    M etabolic disorder

Clinical Presentation
  •    Reduced awareness of the environment                            •   Disturbance in cognition
       > Inability to stay focused on a topic or to switch                 > Poor memory, particularly of recent events
       topics                                                              > Disorientation — for example, not knowing where
       > Getting stuck on an idea rather than responding                   you are or who you are
       to questions or conversation                                        > Difficulty speaking or recalling words
       > Being easily distracted by unimportant things                     > Rambling or nonsense speech
       > Being withdrawn, with little or no activity or little             > Trouble understanding speech
       response to the environment                                         > Difficulty reading or writing
                                                                           > Perceptual disturbance -Seeing things that don't
                                                                           exist (hallucinations)

  •    Behavioral changes                                              •   Emotional disturbances
       > Restlessness, agitation or combative behavior                     > Anxiety, fear or paranoia
       > Calling out, moaning or making other sounds                       > Depression
       > Being quiet and withdrawn — especially in older                   > Irritability or anger
       adults                                                              > A sense of feeling elated (euphoria)
       > Slowed movement or lethargy                                       > Apathy
       > Disturbed sleep habits                                            > Rapid and unpredictable mood shifts
       > Reversal of night-day sleep-wake cycle                            > Personality changes

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •  Control the acute disturbance.
  •  Patients who actively walk with symptoms of agitation or restlessness require close observation within a safe and
     reasonably closed environment.
  •  The least restrictive option should always be used when acting in the best interests of the patient to keep them safe from
     assessed risk.
  •  Firstly, attempts should be made to identify and remedy possible causes of agitation, e.g. pain, thirst, or a need for the
     toilet.
  •  Allowing the patient to walk will help promote and maintain functional ability and reduce the risk of pressure damage
     occurring.
  •  The use of restraint or Pharmacological Management should only be considered necessary in cases where the
     symptoms are considered to be threatening to the patient’s safety and that of others, or would result in the interruption
     of essential care, and should only be used as a final option
  •  Depending on the layout and nature of the ward, the medical and nursing team may need to consider what is in the best
     interest of the patient, using patient-centered therapy to frequently perform mental status examination
  •  Perform proper physical assessment as well as investigations in order to rule out or ascertain the underlying medical
     condition and treat accordingly

Pharmacological Management
Treat the underlying medical condition, if present. And any other presentations, symptomatically
Acute Management

B: haloperidol (IM) 5mg stat repeated in 30-60 minutes when required (Maximum dose: 20mg within 24 hours)
  •    Monitor vital signs and beware of acute dystonia and neuroleptic malignant syndrome
  •    Dosing may vary according to clinical circumstances
         AND
A: diazepam (IV) 10mg.
         OR
C: lorazepam (IM) 1-4mg.

Switch to oral route once containment is achieved.
  Note
     •    Benzodiazepines, especially diazepam IV, can cause respiratory depression. Monitor patients closely
     •    In the frail and elderly patient or where respiratory depression is a concern, reduce the dose by half
     •    The safest route of administration is oral followed by IM with the IV route having the highest risk of respiratory
          depression and arrest. Use the safest route wherever possible.
     •    Monitor vital signs closely during and after administration
     •    Use haloperidol instead of benzodiazepines in patients with respiratory insufficiency
     •    To avoid benzodiazepines toxicity, allow at least 15-30 minutes before repeating the IM dose

sections.title: Schizophrenia
sections.text:
It is a chronic mental disorder, characterized by disturbances in thought, emotions, drive, behavior and withdrawal from reality.

Clinical Presentation
Symptoms vary from patient to patient and from time to time. To diagnose Schizophrenia, the following criteria need to be met;
  •    Presence of 2 or more of the following symptoms over a 1-month period:
       a) Delusions
       b) Hallucinations
       c) Disorganized speech
       d) Disorganized behavior
       e) Negative symptoms
       (at least 1 of which must be a, b or c)
  •    Individual’s premorbid level of functioning is affected in several major domains of life.
  •    There must be continuous impairment over a period of at least 6 months, during which the individual might experience
       either active or residual symptoms.
  •    These symptoms must not be due to the effects of substance usage or an underlying medical condition

Assessment
Assessment includes thorough history taking, physical examination, mental state examination and investigations

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •  People with a first episode of psychosis are offered psychological interventions (family intervention and individual CBT)
     in conjunction with oral antipsychotics. CBT should be delivered on a one-to-one basis over at least 16 planned sessions
     > The re-evaluation of people's perceptions, beliefs or reasoning relates to the target symptoms
  •  Also include at least one of the following components:
     > People monitoring their thoughts, feelings or behaviors with respect to their symptoms or recurrence of symptoms
     > Promoting alternative ways of coping with the target symptom

       > Reducing distress
       > Improving functioning.

  •    Family intervention should:
       > Include the person with psychosis or schizophrenia if practical
       > be carried out for between 3 months and 1 year
       > Include at least 10 planned sessions
       > Take into account the whole family's preference for either single-family intervention or multi-family group intervention
       > Take into account the relationship between the main carer and the person with psychosis or schizophrenia
       > Have a specific supportive, educational or treatment function and include negotiated problem solving or crisis
       management work

Pharmacological Management
In acute attacks:
Treat like under section: Aggressive and Disruptive Behaviors in Adults.

For maintenance:
B: haloperidol (PO) 1.5-4.5mg 12hourly, increase by 1.5mg, every two weeks. Maximum dose 20 mg Daily
          OR
A: chlorpromazine (PO) 100–400mg 24hourly in divided doses
          OR
S: olanzapine (PO) 5–10mg titrate to maximum dose 20mg/24hours, given at night
          OR
S: aripiprazole (PO) Start 10 -15mg OD, Maximum dose 30mg OD
          OR
S: risperidone (PO) 1mg 12hourly then increase by 1mg every 2–3 days to 2–3mg 12 hourly. Maximum dose 6mg/day
          OR
S: quetiapine (PO) Start 25mg, then increase by 25mg over one week to a Maximum dose of 300mg-400mg in divided doses
a day

  Note:
    •   Titrate to maximum dose while monitoring dose-response to target symptoms against adverse effect
    •   The above medicines should not be given in combination
    •   The atypical antipsychotics have been shown to be comparatively more effective in treatment of negative symptoms
    •   High risk of tardive dyskinesia (age >50 years, female sex, prominent mood symptoms, cognitive or neurological
        disturbance e.g. intellectual disability, autistic spectrum, HIV-positive): avoid haloperidol and antiparkinsonian
        medicines; use chlorpromazine, risperidone or olanzapine at lowest doses possible

For patients who have poor compliance to oral medications and patient preference, give depot antipsychotics

C: fluphenazine decanoate (IM) 12.5 -50mg 2-4weekly, and monitor dose-response to target symptoms against adverse effect,
if necessary, dose may be tapered
            OR
S: zuclopenthixol decanoate (IM) 100-600mg 2-4weekly, and monitor dose-response to target symptoms against adverse
effect, if necessary, dose may be tapered
            OR
S: flupenthixol decanoate (IM) 20–40 mg every 4weeks, and monitor dose-response to target symptoms against adverse
effect, if necessary, dose may be tapered

  Note
    •  Give a test dose first. This is in view of the fact that depots are known to be long acting
    •  Giving a test dose helps to determine whether the patient is sensitive to the medication (either via development of
       EPSE or any adverse reactions to the oil base)
    •  Commence treatment with the lowest therapeutic dose
    •  Administer the depot at the longest possible duration
    •  Adjustment of dosages should be conducted after an adequate period of assessment

For treatment of resistant Schizophrenia, and recurrent suicidal behaviors in schizophrenic/schizoaffective patients;

S: clozapine (PO): Initial dose: 12.5–25 mg at night. Usual dose: 200–450 mg per day in divided doses. Maximum dose: 900
mg/day in divided doses

  Caution:
  Clozapine may cause:
    •   Neutropenia (3% of cases) and agranulocytosis (0.8% of cases):
        > Pre-treatment: Baseline normal white cell counts and absolute neutrophil count.
        > Monitor absolute neutrophil count regularly.
        > Withdraw clozapine and review medication if neutrophils <1.0 x109/L (general population).
    •   Myocarditis: highest risk in first two months of treatment. Monitor pulse, blood pressure, temperature; advise patient
        to report any palpitations, shortness of breath, chest pain, fever immediately.
    •   Seizures: risk increased at doses >450 mg/day. Manage as for epilepsy. Lamotrigine preferable as it is weight neutral
        and does not interfere with clozapine metabolism. Avoid carbamazepine because of possible myelosuppression and
        enzyme induction.
    •   Constipation: avoid anticholinergics; may require laxatives; prolonged discomfort may indicate intestinal obstruction.
    •   Weight gain, diabetes, dyslipidemia: Manage as per this STG:

Electroconvulsive Therapy (ECT)
ECT is an effective treatment for some types of severe mental illness. ECT uses an electric current to cause a seizure in the
brain and is one of the fastest ways to treat severe symptoms of mental illness. ECT is done with the informed consent of the
patient or following the patient's advance directives.
The procedure is done under anesthesia by a team of specialists with a prior comprehensive evaluation of patients for any
medical contraindication to ECT.

ECT is a safe and effective treatment with indications of its use in patients with schizophrenia including:
  •    Treatment-resistant schizophrenia                                 •    Presence of Suicidal behavior
  •    To augment pharmacotherapy                                        •    Severe agitation
  •    Management of catatonia                                           •    Clozapine-resistant schizophrenia

ECT should be administered 2 to 3 times a week for a total of 6-12 sessions.

Extrapyramidal side effects

Acute dystonia
A: promethazine (PO) 25-50mg 24hourly, until symptoms/signs subside
        OR
B: benzhexol (PO) 5mg 24hourly to12hourly, last dose before 1400 hours to avoid insomnia

Parkinsonism:
A: promethazine (PO) 25-50mg 24hourly, until symptoms/signs subside
        OR
B: benzhexol (PO) 5mg stat

Akathisia:
A: Propranolol (PO), 20-80mg 8 hourly. Monitor pulse and blood pressure
Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (NMS)
It is a syndrome caused by the use of high dose of antipsychotics; potent antipsychotics (e.g. haloperidol) and antipsychotics
that are given via the intravenous or intramuscular routes.

sections.title: Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (NMS)
sections.text:
It is a syndrome caused by the use of high dose of antipsychotics; potent antipsychotics (e.g. haloperidol) and antipsychotics
that are given via the intravenous or intramuscular routes.

Clinical Presentation
  •    Muscle rigidity,                                                •    Labile blood pressure,
  •    Fever,                                                          •    Tremor,
  •    Altered consciousness,                                          •    Incontinence,
  •    Mutism,                                                         •    Leukocytosis,
  •    Dysphagia,                                                      •    Laboratory evidence of muscle injury:
  •    Diaphoresis,                                                    •    Increase in creatinine kinase levels.
  •    Tachycardia,

Pharmacological Management
A: diazepam10 mg (IV) start.
         OR
C: lorazepam (IM/IV) 2 mg for immediate sedative or hypnotic action. If no response gives a second dose
         OR
C: bromocriptine (PO) 2.5 mg 8hourly

  Note
    •  NMS is a clinical emergency, it needs ICU care
    •  It is important to stop the antipsychotics immediately
    •  Supportive measures such as bed rest and controlling the hyperthermia by rapid cooling with the help of tepid water
       spray and via direct fluid replacement should be started immediately
    •  Consideration of ventilator support or intubation would be necessary if the patient has severe breathing difficulties

Referral: Refer to the next level in the following situations:
  •   First psychotic episode                                             •    Pregnant and lactating women
  •   High suicidal risk or risk of harm to others                        •    No response to treatment
  •   Children and adolescents                                            •    Intolerance to medications
  •   Elders                                                              •    Concurrent medical conditions or other

sections.title: Catatonia
sections.text:
Catatonia is a complex neuropsychiatric syndrome characterized by abnormalities in movement, behavior, and mental state.

Causes
  •  Schizophrenia
  •  Severe depressive disorder,
  •  Bipolar disorder,
  •  Organic disorders e.g. CNS infections, CNS tumor, cerebrovascular accident, severe intoxication of recreational drugs
     and lethal catatonia.

Clinical Presentation
  •    Ambitendency,                                                      •    Stereotypy,
  •    Automatic obedience,                                               •    Mannerism,
  •    Waxy flexibility / catalepsy,                                      •    Echolalia
  •    Negativism,                                                        •    Echopraxia.

Investigations
  •    FBP,                                                               •    CT,
  •    RFT,                                                               •    MRI,
  •    LFT,                                                               •    EEG,
  •    TFT,                                                               •    Urine and blood culture,
  •    Blood glucose,                                                     •    Syphilis screen,
  •    CK,                                                                •    HIV,
  •    Urine drug screen,                                                 •    Heavy metal screen,
  •    ECG,                                                               •    Auto-antibody screen and lumbar puncture.

Non-Pharmacological Management
Hydration, early mobilization, close monitoring, transferal to ICU if patient deteriorates.

Pharmacological Management
A: diazepam (IV/IM) 10-20mg 24hourly
         OR
C: lorazepam (IM) 2mg initially, then 2mg after 3hrs if no effect, maximum 24 mg/day

  Note: If benzodiazepine does not work after 1-2 days and symptoms are severe, ECT is an option

sections.title: Schizoaffective Disorder
sections.text:
DSM-5 Diagnostic criteria
For an individual to fulfill the diagnostic criteria, there must be the presence of solely hallucinations or delusions for at least 2
weeks in the absence of an affective episode, throughout the whole duration of the psychiatric illness. There must also have
an uninterrupted period where there are prominent affective symptoms concurrent with symptoms of schizophrenia. Individuals
should have symptoms fulfilling the diagnosis of an affective disorder for most of the duration of the illness.

DSM-5 has specified 2 subtypes of schizoaffective disorder, which are:
 •   Bipolar type - Whereby a manic episode is part of the entire course of the illness
 •   Depressive type - Whereby a major depressive episode is part of the entire course of the illness

Non-Pharmacological Management

  •  Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) for stabilized                        community        programs,    work assessment,
