sections.title: Stimulant withdrawal, including Cocaine and Amphetamine type stimulants (e.g. Methamphetamine)
sections.text:
Non-Pharmacological Management
These patients usually do not require admission, however beware of depression and assess suicide risk. Assess and monitor
for psychosis.

Pharmacological Management
No substitute drug available for detoxification. For severe anxiety, irritability and insomnia, give:
Benzodiazepines, short-term, e.g.:
C: diazepam (PO) 5–10mg 8hourly for 5–7 days (medication should be titrated according resolution)

Referral: Refer patients to specialized clinic.

Methaqualone (Mandrax/White pipe) withdrawal
Withdrawal can be dangerous and may lead to seizures or delirium. If withdrawal is symptomatic:
C: diazepam (PO), 5 mg 8 hourly. Reduce over 3–5 days depending on clinical response.

Cannabis withdrawal
Withdrawal is rarely dangerous or poorly tolerated.
Assess for other accompanying psychiatric disorders e.g. mood or psychosis.

sections.title: Benzodiazepine withdrawal
sections.text:
Benzodiazepine addiction may occur after only a few weeks of use. Withdrawal symptoms on abrupt dose reduction or cessation
includes anxiety, nervousness, irritability, depersonalization, delirium and seizures, increased sweating, sound sensitivity,
nausea, difficulty concentrating, myoclonus, tremor, weakness and fatigue. Gradual tapering of the benzodiazepine is
recommended to facilitate discontinuation.

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •  The therapeutic relationship between client and doctor is extremely important in initiating dose reduction.
  •  Confirm benzodiazepine dependence – ascertain usage, history of previous withdrawal symptoms; a urine screen may
     be necessary
  •  Establish full dosage of all benzodiazepines being taken, including those prescribed by other medical practitioners
  •  Take time to explain negative impact of ongoing benzodiazepine use, benefits of stopping, and concepts like tolerance
     and withdrawal
  •  Encourage the patient not to seek medication from other doctors.
  •  Evaluate and optimize management of comorbid substance use disorders, mental illness, and general health conditions.
  •  Avoid abrupt withdrawal of benzodiazepines; be prepared to take time. Negotiate each reduction with the patient.
     Individualize regular monitoring and motivation.
  •  Long-term follow-up with repeated motivation may be necessary to prevent relapse.

Pharmacological Management
Replace short-acting benzodiazepine with an equivalent diazepam (long-acting benzodiazepine) dose equivalent doses to
diazepam 5 mg are:
D: clonazepam (PO) 0.25–1 mg 24hourly
            OR
C: lorazepam (PO) 0.5 mg 24hourly
Higher doses may be required for patients who are dependent on both alcohol and benzodiazepines. Inpatient assessment and
initiation of benzodiazepine tapering may be warranted in these patients.

Reduction is done according to clinical response.
C: diazepam (PO).
Reduce daily dose every 1–2 weeks by 10 mg/day until a daily dose of 50 mg. Then reduce every 1–2 weeks by 5 mg/day until
a daily dose of 30 mg. Then reduce every 1–2 weeks by 2.5 mg/day until a daily dose of 20 mg. Then reduce every 1–2 weeks
by 1.25 mg/day until stopped.

If symptoms reappear, increase the dose a little and reduce dose over longer intervals. No more than one week’s duration of
therapy is generally issued at one time.

Opioid overdose

  Note: Initial doses of Naloxone above 2 mg can induce severe withdrawal, with the risk of vomiting and aspiration; very
  high doses above 10 mg may even be life threatening

Overdose Don’ts
 •   Do not leave the person alone by him/herself as they could stop breathing
 •   Do not induce vomiting or feed orally as the client may aspirate

Admit for continued observation for a minimum of 4 hours after administration of Naloxone. The client should be advised to
avoid using any opioids or other drugs that may cause CNS depression for at least 24 hours and to ensure they do not stay
alone during that period.

sections.title: Psychiatric Disorders Associated with Epilepsy
sections.text:
Epilepsy is a disorder of the brain characterized by an enduring predisposition to generate epileptic seizures and by the biologic,
cognitive, psychological, and social consequences of this condition. This association may reflect the anatomical and
neurobiological source of both epileptic seizures and the behavioral manifestations. Antiepileptic drugs (AEDs) can play a role
in the genesis of psychiatric symptoms; on the other hand, some psychotropic medications can lower the seizure threshold and
provoke epileptic seizures.

Clinical Presentation
Major depressive disorder, Bipolar mood disorder, Anxiety disorder, Psychoses, Suicidality

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •  Psychoeducation to the patient and the family                       •    Supportive group therapy
  •  Family therapy                                                      •    Occupational therapy

Pharmacological Management
A: carbamazepine (PO) 200-1000mg, in divided doses, per day (symptoms should be monitored and medication titrated
accordingly)
          OR
A: phenobarbitone (PO) 30-200mg, in divided doses, per day (symptoms should be monitored and medication titrated
accordingly)
          OR
C: sodium valproate (PO), 500-2000mg in divided doses, per day (symptoms should be monitored and medication titrated
accordingly)
          OR
S: Levetiracetam (PO), 500-1500mg,12hourly (depending on symptoms’ resolution)

If psychosis persists, give
B: haloperidol (PO) 0.75-4.5mg 12hourly. Maximum dose 20mg/day
          OR
S: olanzapine (PO) 5-10mg in divided doses, per day. Maximum dose 20mg/day (symptoms should be monitored and
medication titrated accordingly)
          OR
S: risperidone (PO) 0.5mg 12hourly then increase by 1mg every 2-3days to 2-3mg 12hourly. Maximum dose 16mg/day
                   OR
S: Aripiprazole (PO) 10-15 mg 24 hourly (titrating depending to individual response)

  Note:
    •   Postictal psychosis remits spontaneously even without treatment but that the use of effective neuroleptics may
        shorten the duration.
    •   Interictal psychosis is treated with antipsychotic drugs. Medications that lower the seizure threshold should be
        avoided.
    •   Atypical antipsychotic medications may have better profiles than typical antipsychotic medications.
    •   Medications that lower the seizure threshold should be avoided.
    •   The doses should be as minimal as possible

sections.title: Depressive symptoms/signs in patients with epilepsy;
sections.text:
Non-Pharmacological Management
  •  Psychoeducation to the patient and the family                     •   Supportive group therapy
  •  Family therapy                                                    •   Occupational therapy

Pharmacological Management
A: carbamazepine (PO) 200-1000mg, in divided doses,                            AND
per day (symptoms should be monitored and medication                A: amitriptyline 12.5-75mg (PO), nocte (symptoms should
titrated accordingly)                                               be monitored and medication titrated accordingly)
           OR                                                                  OR
A: phenobarbitone (PO) 30-200mg, in divided doses, per              S: fluoxetine 1 (PO) 0-20mg in divided doses, per day
day (symptoms should be monitored and medication                    (symptoms should be monitored and medication titrated
titrated accordingly)                                               accordingly)
           OR                                                                  OR
C: sodium valproate (PO) 500-2000mg in divided doses,               S: escitalopram (PO) 10-20 mg nocte (titrating according
per day (symptoms should be monitored and medication                to individual response)
titrated accordingly)

  Note:
    •   In the treatment of epilepsy-related depression, priority should be given to optimizing seizure control, since improved
        psychosocial functioning tends to accompany seizure remission
    •   Some anticonvulsant therapies, including sodium valproate, gabapentin, carbamazepine, and lamotrigine, also have
        antidepressant effects and may prove effective in treating depression in patients with epilepsy.
    •   Phenobarbitone is known to produce depression.

sections.title: Mania/hypomania in patients with epilepsy;
sections.text:
Non-Pharmacological Management
  •  Psychoeducation to the patient and the family
  •  Family therapy
  •  Supportive group therapy
  •  Occupational therapy

Pharmacological Management
A: carbamazepine (PO) 200-1000mg, in divided doses, per day
         OR
A: phenobarbitone (PO) 30-200mg, in divided doses, per day
         OR
A: sodium valproate (PO) 500-2000mg in divided doses, per day

  Note: Symptoms should be monitored and medication titrated accordingly

sections.title: Psychiatric Disorders in Pregnancy
sections.text:
In some women, pregnancy and motherhood increase their vulnerability to psychiatric conditions such as depression, anxiety
disorders, eating disorders, panic disorder, bipolar illness, and psychoses. These conditions are often underdiagnosed because
they are attributed to pregnancy- related changes in maternal temperament or physiology. In addition, such conditions are often
undertreated because of concerns about potential harmful effects of medication.

sections.title: Depression
sections.text:
Several risk factors and psychosocial correlates have been identified as contributing to depression during pregnancy, like;
Previous history of depression, discontinuation of medication(s) by a woman who has a history of depression, a previous history
of postpartum depression, and a family history of depression.

Several key psychosocial correlates may also contribute to depression during pregnancy: a negative attitude toward the
pregnancy, a lack of social support, maternal stress associated with negative life events, and a partner or family member who
is unhappy about the pregnancy. The relationship between maternal depression and early childhood problems may be part of
a sequence that starts with depressive symptoms during pregnancy.

Non-Pharmacological Management
Psychotherapies
  •   Cognitive behavioral therapy
  •   Interpersonal psychotherapy
  •   Education and support are also important, particularly as pregnancy is a unique experience for women, some of whom
      may not know what to expect.

Pharmacological Management
A: amitriptyline, (PO), 12.5–75 mg 24hourly at night, increase gradually to a maximum of 150 mg daily. {Elderly: Initially 12.5–
50 mg. Max. 75mg)
          OR
D: citalopram (PO) ,10-60mg 24hourly morning or evening and symptoms should be monitored, and medication to be tapered
          OR
S: fluoxetine (PO) 20-60mg 24hourly (morning)
          OR
S: escitalopram (PO) 10-20 mg nocte (titrating according to individual response)

 Note:
   •   Full disclosure of both the risk and benefits of various antidepressant medications should be made to the patient and,
       if possible, her partner prior to starting any Pharmacological management.
   •   Low doses of antidepressants should be considered when initiating medication.

sections.title: Panic Disorder
sections.text:
Some women may experience first-onset panic disorder during pregnancy. Women presenting with panic attacks for the first
time should be screened for thyroid disorder. The correlation between plasma levels of cortisol in the mother and in the fetus
may have implications for the developing fetal brain.

Non-Pharmacological management
  •  Cognitive behavioral therapy
  •  Supportive psychotherapy
  •  Relaxation techniques
  •  Sleep hygiene
  •  Dietary counseling

Pharmacological Management
Refer panic disorders

  Note:
    •   Full disclosure of both the risk and benefits of various antidepressant medications should be made to the patient
        and, if possible, her partner prior to starting any Pharmacological management.
    •   Low doses of antidepressants should be considered when initiating medication

sections.title: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder
sections.text:
Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is characterized by thoughts that cannot be controlled (obsessions) and repetitive
behaviors or rituals that cannot be controlled (compulsions) in response to these thoughts.

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •  Cognitive behavioral therapy
  •  Supportive psychotherapy
  •  Relaxation techniques
  •  Sleep hygiene
  •  Dietary counseling

Pharmacological Management
Refer to the specific section above

  Note: Treatments for GAD in pregnancy are the same as those in non-pregnant adults.

sections.title: Bipolar Mood Disorder
sections.text:
Non-Pharmacological Management
  •  Cognitive behavioral therapy
  •  Supportive psychotherapy
  •  Relaxation techniques
  •  Sleep hygiene
  •  Dietary counseling
Pharmacological Management
Refer to the specific section above

  Note:
    •   Decision whether to use mood stabilizers must be made following an assessment of risks and benefits.
    •   Low doses of mood stabilizers should be as low as possible
    •   Factors to consider include number and severity of previous episodes, level of insight, family supports, and the wishes
        of the woman
    •   Careful monitoring of psychological symptoms throughout the pregnancy is of paramount importance

sections.title: Schizophrenia
sections.text:
Non-Pharmacological Management
  •  Cognitive behavioral therapy
  •  Supportive psychotherapy
  •  Relaxation techniques
  •  Sleep hygiene
  •  Dietary counseling

Pharmacological Management
Treat as in the treatment of schizophrenia in non-pregnant woman

  Note:
    •   Women with a history of psychosis require close monitoring during pregnancy
    •   Psychosis during pregnancy can have devastating consequences for both the mother and her fetus, including failure
        to obtain proper prenatal care, negative pregnancy outcomes such as low birth weight and prematurity, and
        neonaticide or suicide
    •   Treatment of acute psychosis in pregnancy is mandatory and includes mobilization of supports, pharmacotherapy,
        and hospitalization
    •   Electroconvulsive therapy may be used for psychotic depression

sections.title: Post-partum psychosis
sections.text:
Post-partum psychosis (also called puerperal psychosis) is the most severe form of perinatal mental illness and carries a high
suicide risk or risk of infanticide if untreated
It is a syndrome associated with:
    •    Pregnancy or puerperium (commencing within about 6 weeks after delivery)
    •    Involves significant mental and behavioral features: including delusions, hallucinations, or other psychotic symptoms.
    •    Rapidly changing mood, disorientation, poor concentration, screaming or muteness and impaired memory of recent
         events
    •    Mood symptoms (depressive and/or manic) are also typically present.

Pharmacological Management
Puerperal psychosis in a psychiatric emergency that typically requires in-patient treatment. Ensure safety: Prevent patients
from harming themselves or others.
B: haloperidol (PO), 1.5-5mg stat OR (IM), 5mg. Maximum daily dosage of 20mg
          OR
A: chlorpromazine (PO), 100-200mg stat OR (IM):100-200mg stat. Max daily dose of 400mg
          OR
S: zuclopenthixol Acetate (IM), Adult: 50mg-150mg Stat.
          OR
S: olanzapine (PO), 2.5-10mg OR (IM): 2.5-10mg
          OR
S: aripiprazole (PO) 10-15 mg 24 hourly (titrating depending to individual response)

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •  Psychosocial support: Supportive care of the infant while his/her mother undergoes acute treatment. Individual and
     family psychotherapy is necessary to cope with stressors and improve self-esteem and confidence.
  •  Psychoeducation
  •  Referrals and Linkages: Refer to a mental health specialist for follow-up and maintenance treatment.

   Note: In other patients with post-partum psychosis, more investigations should be done, to rule out other pathologies

sections.title: Postpartum depression
sections.text:
Postpartum depression is a mood disorder that can affect individuals after childbirth.

Clinical Presentation
  •    Persistent feelings of sadness,
  •    Anxiety
  •    Fatigue
  •    Difficult to care for oneself or others.

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •  Psychotherapies
  •  Cognitive behavioral therapy
  •  Interpersonal psychotherapy
  •  Education and support are also important, particularly as pregnancy is a unique experience for women, some of whom
     may not know what to expect

Pharmacological Management
A: amitriptyline, (PO), 12.5–75 mg 24hourly at night, increase gradually to a maximum of 150 mg daily. {Elderly: Initially 12.5–
50 mg. Max. 75mg)
          OR
S: fluoxetine PO) 20-60mg (PO) 24hourly (morning)
          OR
S: escitalopram (PO) 10-20 mg nocte (titrating according to individual response)

sections.title: Autism Spectrum Disorder
sections.text:
Clinical Presentation
DSM-5 states that an individual diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder would have marked difficulties in terms of
communication and engagement with others across multiple social situations. These difficulties include:
   •   Difficulties with demonstrating appropriate behaviours in social contexts
   •   Difficulties associated with non-verbal communications used for social interactions
   •   Difficulties associated with failure to initiate or adapt to social interactions
In addition, the DSM-5 also requires the individuals to have characteristic repetitive behavioral patterns, such as repeated
stereotypical movements or Highly ritualized behavioral patterns. DSM-5 criteria specified that these behaviours must have
started since the early developmental period and has resulted in marked impairments in terms of functioning.

Assessment
  •  Detailed history from a caregiver and educational institutions.
  •  Vital signs and physical examination.
  •  Suicide risk assessment.
   Note: Despite exhibiting symptoms since childhood, autism spectrum disorder can sometimes be initially diagnosed in adulthood.

Investigations
   •     Baseline lab Investigations: FBC, LFT, RFT, VDRL, RBS, BS for M.P.s, HIV, TFT, Pregnancy Test,
   •     Specific test, e.g.(toxicology)
   •     Imaging (C.T. scan and MRI).
   •     Other investigations may be considered based on the patient’s presentation.
If a patient tests positive for any of the above tests, manage accordingly and refer where appropriate

Non-Pharmacological Management
For children
  •   Every pre-school child diagnosed with autism should have an individualized intervention plan that sets out the goals,
      type(s), frequency and intensity of intervention, in order to address particular developmental and educational needs
  •   An individualized intervention plan should consist of a variety of quality programs and activities. This includes attendance
      in comprehensive early intervention programs, programs targeting specific needs and also positive engagement with
      parents and/or caregivers
  •   Alternative-augmentative communication systems may be recommended for pre-school children with autism because
      the expanded (spoken or written) communication may stimulate speech acquisition in non-verbal children and enhance
      expression in verbal children.
  •   Visual strategies are useful interventions for children with autism because they offer visual support to communication,
      increase spontaneous imitation and socially communicative behaviour.
  •   Social skills programmes depend on the functioning level of the preschool child with autism and may include:
             > Assessment and teaching of social skills interaction in natural settings.
             > Provision of structure, visual cues and predictability.
             > Making abstract concepts more “concrete”.
             > Activities that enable purposeful and appropriate interaction with typically developing peers.
             > Goals focusing on fostering self-appreciation and self-esteem
For the parents
  •    Parents and caregivers should be encouraged to discuss the need for practical emotional support. This enables
       information to be provided, referrals made and support services made available
  •    Parents and caregivers are recommended to consult appropriate professionals when considering educational placement
       for their child with autism

Pharmacological Management
S: risperidone (PO). 0.5- 4 mg (For Tantrums, aggressive episodes, self-injurious behaviours, hyperactivity)
          OR
S: methylphenidate (PO), 5-15mg (immediate release) OR 18-36mg for extended release. (For comorbid hyperactivity)
          OR
B: haloperidol (PO), 1.5-20mg, (For Aggressive behaviour, irritability, and uncooperativeness)
          OR
S: aripiprazole (PO), 2-15mg, (For Irritability)
          OR
S: clozapine (PO), 25-400mg, (For Disruptive behavior)
          OR
S: venlafaxine (PO), 37.5-225mg, (For Aggression, self-injurious behaviour, and hyperactivity)
          OR
S: fluoxetine (O), 10-80 mg, (For Repetitive behaviors)
          OR
S: escitalopram (PO) 10-20 mg nocte (titrating according to individual response)

Pharmacological management in Autism should be symptomatic management depending on how the child is presenting, e.g.
comorbid with ADHD, psychosis or overstimulation

sections.title: Attention Deficit / Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)
sections.text:
DSM-5 states that an individual diagnosed with attention-deficit and hyperactivity disorder would have difficulties in terms of
functioning, mainly due to (a) inattention and/or (b) hyperactivity and impulsivity.

The DSM-5 states that these inattentive and/or hyperactivity and impulsivity symptoms must be present before the age of 12
years old. In addition, these symptoms must have resulted in impaired functioning in at least 2 different social situations.

Clinical Presentation
The DSM-5 requires the individual to fulfill at least 6 of the following signs and symptoms of inattention:
  •    Failing to pay close attention to details                           •    Reluctance to participate in tasks that involve much
  •    Concentration difficulties                                               attention
  •    Difficulties with sustaining attention at tasks                     •    Frequently loses important objects
  •    Daydreaming and does not seem to be able to                         •    Easily distractible
       follow normal conversations                                         •    Forgetfulness about daily activities.
  •    Difficulties with organization of tasks

The DSM-5 also specified that only 5 of the above signs and symptoms of inattention need to be fulfilled if individuals are 17
years of age and above.
DSM-5 also requires the individual to fulfil at least 6 of the following signs and symptoms of hyperactivity and
impulsivity:
  •    Moving about and unable to sit still                                 •   Impulsive and gives answers even before being
  •    Leaves seat even when required to remain seated                          asked to
  •    Climbs or runs about in inappropriate situations                     •   Having difficulties waiting for his/her turn
  •    Always having excessive energy and always on the                     •   Unable to carry out normal conversation due to
       move                                                                     frequent interruptions
  •    Chats excessively

Assessment
  •  Detailed history from a caregiver and educational                   •    Screen for comorbidities, e.g., Anxiety and
     institutions                                                             Depression
  •  Observation of symptoms                                             •    Routine blood work: FBC, LFTs, UECs, Thyroid
  •  Examination:     physical   and    mental   state                        Function Test, Calcium levels, Urinalysis
     examination                                                         •    EEG to rule out seizures
  •  Psychometric tools: conners comprehensive                           •    Imaging- CT scan or MRI brain
     behavioral rating scale

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •  Parent-training/ education programs
  •  Refer parents to educational programs to learn about ADHD, its management and coping strategy.
  •  For parents, the program should include individual or group-based parent-training/education programs.
  •  For children and youth with ADHD, the program should include CBT or social skill training.
  •  Offer training to the teachers on behavioral interventions in the classroom to help the child to cope with ADHD

Behaviour therapy
  •   Positive reinforcement of positive behaviour including reward system and praises. The parents can consider using a star
      chart to promote positive behaviour at home.
  •   Environmental modifications aim at improving attention e.g. placing the child in the front row of class, minimizing
      distractions etc.
  •   Combination of behaviour therapy and medication is better than medication alone.

Pharmacological Management
Age above six years:
CNS stimulants are used to improve the ability to sustain attention and academic sufficiency

S: methylphenidate 5mg to 10mg (PO) 12hourly taken after breakfast and after lunch.
         OR
S: methylphenidate extended-release (XL) 18-36mg (PO) 24hourly.
         OR
Non- stimulants,
S: Atomoxetine (PO) (0.5mg/kg 24hourly for the first three days and then increase to 1.2mg/kg according to the response).
Medications may also be used to manage comorbid conditions

sections.title: Anxiety disorders in children
sections.text:
Anxiety disorders in children are persistent fears or worries that disrupt their ability to participate in play, school, or typical age-
appropriate social situations.

Clinical Presentation
Common symptoms of anxiety disorders in children:
  •    Irritability                                                        •     Being tense or fidgety or using the toilet often
  •    Trouble sleeping or waking with bad dreams.                         •     Being too clingy, which is not age-appropriate.
  •    Restlessness                                                        •     Physical symptoms like fatigue, headaches, or
  •    Outbursts of anger                                                        stomachaches
  •    Difficulty concentrating

Types of Childhood Anxiety Disorders
 Anxiety Disorder   Clinical Manifestations / Diagnostic Features
 Separation         At least three of the following symptoms:
 Anxiety Disorder   • Recurrent excessive fear when anticipating or experiencing separation from major attachment
                    figures (e.g., parents/guardians)
                    • Excessive worry about losing a major attachment figure
                    • Persistent refusal to go to school or away from home
                    • Excessive fear of being alone or away from loved ones
                    • Recurrent nightmares involving separation themes
                    • Recurrent physical symptoms (e.g., headaches, abdominal pain) when separation occurs or is
                    anticipated
                    • Excessive fear or distress when away from parent’s/caregivers Additional criteria:
                    • Symptoms persist for ≥4 weeks
                    • Causes significant impairment in social, academic, or occupational functioning
 Selective Mutism • Consistent failure to speak in specific social situations where speaking is expected
                    • Symptoms persist for ≥1 month
                    • Failure to speak is not due to language barriers or lack of knowledge
                    • Not better explained by a communication disorder
                    • Child speaks normally in familiar settings but becomes mute in specific situations or around certain
                    people

Management of Anxiety Disorders in Children treatment plan that works best for the child and family should be developed with
a multidisciplinary approach. In the treatment of very young children, involving parents and other important caregivers is crucial,
and when appropriate, the school can also be included in the management process.

Non-Pharmacological Management
The Mainstay of treatment of mild to moderate anxiety disorders in children is psychotherapy. Various psychotherapeutic
interventions are effective, including:
   •   Cognitive behaviour therapy (CBT),                         •    Family therapy,
   •   Problem-solving therapy,                                   •    Relaxation techniques.
   •   Psychodynamic psychotherapy,

It's important to tailor the supportive therapy approach to each child's unique needs and consider the severity of their anxiety
symptoms. Additionally, involving parents and caregivers in the therapeutic process enhances the overall effectiveness of
anxiety management strategies for children

Pharmacological Management
Medication is only prescribed for severe anxiety. A combination of medication and psychotherapy has better outcomes than
either of the interventions alone

S: fluoxetine (PO), 10-40mg
           OR
S: escitalopram (PO) 10-20 mg nocte (titrating according to individual response)
           OR
S: sertraline (PO), 25-50mg 24hourly
           OR
S: venlafaxine (PO), 37.5-225mg 24hourly
           OR
A: amitriptyline (PO), 25-100mg 24hourly

 Note: Amitriptyline is not preferred unless its cost is a hindrance or where a child has side effects from the other options. In
 the same breadth, benzodiazepines are to be avoided due to the risk of addiction.

sections.title: Enuresis
sections.text:
Clinical Presentation
As per DSM-5
  •    Repeated voiding of urine into bed or clothes (whether involuntary or intentional)
  •    Behavior must be clinically significant as manifested by either a frequency of twice a week for at least three consecutive
       months or the presence of clinically significant distress or impairment in social, academic (occupational), or other
       important areas of functioning.
  •    Chronological age is at least 5 years of age (or equivalent developmental level).
  •    The behavior is not due exclusively to the direct physiological effect of a substance (such as a diuretic) or a general
       medical condition (such as diabetes, spina bifida, a seizure disorder, etc.).

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •  Fluid restriction at night especially 1 hour before the desmopressin dose until the next morning, or at least 8 hours after
     the dose. If child wakes up during the night, limit the amount that he or she drinks.
  •  Star chart: effective in one-third of cases
  •  Alarm: Child must wake up and urinate.

Pharmacological Management
A: amitriptyline (PO) 25mg nocte (medications should be titrated according to symptoms resolution)
          OR
C: imipramine (PO) 100mg nocte (medications should be titrated according to symptoms resolution)

sections.title: Oppositional Deviant Disorder
sections.text:
Oppositional defiant disorder (ODD) is listed in the DSM-5 under Disruptive, impulse-control, and conduct disorders and defined
as "a pattern of angry/irritable mood, argumentative/defiant behavior, or vindictiveness.
This behavior is usually targeted toward peers, parents, teachers, and other authority figures, including law enforcement
officials. Unlike Conduct Disorder (CD), those with ODD do not generally show patterns of aggression towards random people,
violence against animals, destruction of property, theft, or deceit

Clinical Presentation
Signs and symptoms
DSM-5, it states that a person must exhibit four out of the eight signs and symptoms to meet the diagnostic threshold for ODD.
These symptoms include:

  •    Often loses temper
  •    Is often touchy or easily annoyed                                     •     Often deliberately annoys others
  •    Is often angry and resentful                                          •     Often blames others for their own mistakes or
  •    Often argues with authority figures or, for children                        misbehavior
       and adolescents, with adults                                          •     Has been spiteful or vindictive at least twice within
  •    Often actively defies or refuses to comply with                             the past six months
       requests from authority figures or with rules

sections.title: Sleep-Wake Disorders
sections.text:
Sleep-wake disorders are changes in sleeping patterns or habits that can negatively affect health. The following are common
types of sleeping disorders: Insomnia disorder, Hypersomnolence disorder, Narcolepsy, Sleep-related breathing disorders,
Circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorders, Parasomnia and Substance/medication-induced sleep disorders.

sections.title: Insomnia
sections.text:
Insomnia refers to difficulty in getting to sleep or staying asleep, occurring at least three nights per week, is present for at least
three months, and occurs despite adequate opportunities for sleep.

Types of insomnia:
a) Transient or short-term insomnia
This type of insomnia often occurs in the aftermath of a stressful life event — for example, losing a loved one or going through
relationship issues. It can also happen if you work shifts or have jet lag. One might be unable to relax, experience disturbed
sleep, and may be unable to pinpoint any real reason for their inability to sleep.

b) Chronic insomnia
Chronic insomnia is characterized by experiencing non-restorative sleep, difficulty falling asleep and maintaining sleep for at
least one month, leading to daytime exhaustion. With chronic intermittent insomnia, one experiences a sleeping pattern with a
few nights of good sleep alternating with many nights of insomnia.

Causes
Poor sleep hygiene, Sleep-related breathing disorders, medical conditions, Disrupted sleep-wake schedule, Hormonal changes,
Limb movements during sleep, and Circadian rhythm disorder.

Clinical Presentation
  •    Inability to initiate sleep resulting in significant                  •     Difficulty falling asleep at night.
       distress or impairment.                                               •     Difficulty in paying attention, focusing on tasks, or
  •    Difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep.                                 remembering.
  •    Anxiety or depression commonly coexist with                           •     Not feeling well rested after a night’s sleep.
       insomnia.                                                             •     Increased errors or accidents.
  •    Waking up early in the morning.                                       •     Daytime tiredness or sleepiness

Diagnostic Criteria for Insomnia Disorder
 Criterion                           Description
 A. Sleep complaint                  Predominant complaint of dissatisfaction with sleep quantity or quality associated with one or
                                     more of the following:
                                     Difficulty initiating sleep (in children: difficulty initiating sleep without caregiver intervention)
                                     Difficulty maintaining sleep characterized by frequent awakenings or difficulty returning to
                                     sleep after awakening (in children: inability to return to sleep without caregiver intervention)
                                     Early-morning awakening with inability to return to sleep
 B. Functional impairment            Sleep disturbance causes clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational,
                                     educational, academic, behavioral, or other important areas of functioning
 C. Exclusion criteria               Insomnia is not better explained by another sleep-wake disorder and is not attributable to
                                     substances (e.g., drugs of abuse, medications), coexisting mental disorders, or medical
                                     conditions
Assessment
It is mainly done to rule out any physical or mental illness that would present with similar sleep disturbances.
    •   History taking, especially on the sleep schedule and sleep hygiene
    •   Mental status exam
    •   Vital signs and physical examination
    •   Suicide risk assessment

Investigations
  •    Baseline lab Investigations: FBC, LFT, RFT, VDRL, RBS, BS for MPs, HIV, TFT, Pregnancy Test.
  •    Specific test (toxicology).
  •    Imaging (CT scan and MRI).
Other investigations may be considered based on the patient’s presentation. If a patient tests positive for any of the above tests,
manage accordingly and refer where appropriate

Management of Insomnia
Insomnia management utilizes various interventions, including managing underlying conditions (for non-primary insomnia) and
psychosocial &pharmacotherapy interventions. Psychosocial interventions are the first line of treatment with CBT being the
most effective psychotherapeutic technique

Non-Pharmacological Management
 Intervention            Recommendation/Description
 Psycho-educational      Provide education on the relationship between thoughts, feelings, behaviours, and sleep as a
 interventions           core component of management
 Sleep hygiene education Promote healthy sleep habits to improve sleep initiation and maintenance
 Consistent sleep        Go to bed at the same time each night and wake up at the same time each morning, including
 schedule                weekends
 Sleep environment       Ensure the bedroom is quiet, relaxing, and maintained at a comfortable temperature
 optimization
 Reduce screen exposure Remove televisions, computers, smartphones, and other electronic devices from the bedroom
 Dietary modification    Avoid large meals, caffeine, and alcohol before bedtime
 Physical activity       Encourage regular daytime exercise to improve sleep quality
 Cognitive Behavioural   Identify and modify maladaptive thoughts, feelings, and behaviours contributing to insomnia;
 Therapy (CBT)           reframe misconceptions and promote healthy sleep practices

  Note: Psychosocial management is the mainstay of treatment for insomnia.

Pharmacological Management
Benzodiazepines are used in the acute management period, with a maximum duration of two weeks, as the drugs have a strong
propensity for addiction. They can also be used for a maximum of one week if used in combination with antidepressants to
allow for the antidepressant medication to take effect. Ensure to taper off the medication gradually when stopping.

C: diazepam 5–10 mg PO at night for a maximum of 2 weeks
         OR
C: lorazepam 1–2 mg PO at night for a maximum of 2 weeks
  Note: Short-acting benzodiazepines are often preferred for insomnia because they theoretically produce less next-day
  drowsiness, although many patients still experience these effects.
  Benzodiazepines should not be taken with alcohol or with opioids commonly found in prescription pain medications and
  cough syrups, as this can have serious side effects, including slowed or difficult breathing and even death.

Sedative antidepressants
These can be prescribed for more than four weeks and have a lower propensity to addiction. Therefore, they are used for long-
term management of insomnia in combination with other psychological interventions
Sedating antidepressants is a good option if the patient has comorbid depression and anxiety disorders; however, Avoid in the
elderly and patients with medical comorbidities. their use should be avoided in elderly persons and patients with medical
comorbidities.

A: amitriptyline (PO): initial dose 25mg, increase by 25mg weekly with a maximum of 50mg/day
          OR
S: zolpidem at 5-10mg at night. Suitable for long-term management of insomnia and usage by in-patients with multiple medical
comorbidities and older patients. It has fewer side effects compared to benzodiazepines and less addictive potential.

Antipsychotics
This is a good option if the patient has comorbid mood or psychotic symptoms.
S: quetiapine (PO) 50 mg nocte and increase by 25 mg every two days, titrated against response, a maximum dose of 100mg
per day.
          OR
S: aripiprazole (PO) 10-15 mg 24 hourly (titrating depending to individual response)
 Note: Combination pharmacotherapy may be used in certain situations where one mode of treatment is ineffective or side
 effects limit dose optimization for the initial medication. Combination medication should consider patient comorbidities and
 drug-drug interactions

Referral and Linkage
  •   To a psychiatrist in case of non-response to                       •    Linkage with community resource persons
      medication                                                         •    Refer to an occupational therapist to promote the
  •   Psychologist for other psychotherapy techniques                         person’s ability to fulfill their daily routines and roles.
  •   Refer to a social worker for social and economic
      assessment and support.

sections.title: Hypersomnolence disorder
sections.text:
Hypersomnolence disorder (hypersomnia), is a condition characterized by excessive daytime sleepiness and prolonged night
time sleep. It can be a symptom of other sleep disorders like narcolepsy or obstructive sleep apnea, but it can also exist as a
primary sleep disorder, like idiopathic hypersomnia

Clinical Presentation
  •    Excessive daytime sleepiness                                   •    Difficulty staying awake and alert
  •    Prolonged nighttime sleep                                      •    Cognitive impairment
  •    Sleep inertia                                                  •    Anxiety or irritability upon waking

Types of Hypersomnolence disorder
a) Idiopathic Hypersomnia: This is a primary sleep disorder where the cause is unknown.
b) Hypersomnia due to other conditions: It can be a symptom of other sleep disorders like narcolepsy, obstructive sleep apnea,
or medical/psychiatric conditions.
c) Hypersomnia due to medication or substance use: Certain medications and substance use can also lead to
hypersomnolence.

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •  Lifestyle adjustments: Maintaining a regular sleep schedule, optimizing sleep hygiene, and managing stress.
  •  Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia (CBT-I): This therapy can help improve sleep habits and reduce sleep-related
     anxiety.

Pharmacological Management
S: modafinil (PO) 200mg 24hourly, in the morning.
         OR
S: methylphenidate (PO), 20-30mg 12hourly or 8hourly and take 30 to 45 minutes before meals. Maximum dose is 60 mg per
day.

sections.title: Somatic Symptom Disorder
sections.text:
Clinical Presentation
As per DSM-5
  •    One or more somatic symptoms that are distressing or result in significant disruption of daily life.
  •    Excessive thoughts, feelings, or behaviors related to the somatic symptoms or associated health concerns as manifested
       by at least one of the following:
       > Disproportionate and persistent thoughts about the seriousness of one’s symptoms.
       > Persistently high level of anxiety about health or symptoms.
       > Excessive time and energy devoted to these symptoms or health concerns DSM-5 specified time duration of at least
       6 months of the presentations.

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •  Regular appointments: Patients diagnosed with                    •    Psychotherapy:
     somatic symptom disorder should have a fixed,                         > Self-help techniques
     regular physician whom they can seek help from                        > Supportive psychotherapy
     and be seen on a regular basis.                                       > Cognitive behaviour therapy (e.g. challenge
  •  Avoid unnecessary investigation but physical                          cognitive distortions, activity scheduling to enhance
     examination should be performed if new complaints                     physical activities).
     arise.                                                           •    Increase in social and occupational functioning
  •  Offer empathy to the sufferings experienced by the
     patient.

Pharmacological management
A: amitriptyline (PO) 25-50mg 24hourly (medications should be titrated according to symptoms resolution)
          OR
C: imipramine (PO) 100mg 24hourly (medications should be titrated according to symptoms resolution)
          OR
S: fluoxetine (PO) 10-20mg 24hourly (medications should be titrated according to symptoms resolution)
          OR
S: escitalopram (PO) 10-20 mg nocte (titrating according to individual response)

sections.title: Functional Neurological Disorder (formerly Conversion Disorder)
sections.text:
Clinical Presentation
As per DSM-5
  •    One or more symptoms of altered voluntary motor or sensory function.
  •    Clinical findings provide evidence of incompatibility between the symptom and recognized neurological or medical
       conditions.
  •    The symptom or deficit is not better explained by another medical or mental disorder.
  •    The symptom or deficit causes clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important
       areas of functioning or warrants medical evaluation

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •  Psycho-education                                                 •    Biofeedback: This uses sensors to help you see
  •  Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT): This is a                         how your body reacts to stress. It can help you learn
     treatment that shows how your thoughts, feelings                      to manage certain body functions to reduce
     and behaviors connect. It can help you spot                           symptoms.
     thoughts that trigger certain emotions, which can                •    Physical therapy: This may improve movement and
     then affect how you act and respond.                                  coordination. It also encourages better movement
  •  Psychodynamic therapy: This explores past trauma                      patterns and prevents muscle weakness.
     and     emotional    conflicts  throughout    your               •    Medication: This treatment may help if the patient
     development. It can help you understand how                           has depression, anxiety or chronic pain.
     symptoms may link to past events.
  •  Family therapy: Family therapy can help your loved
     ones understand the condition and offer support.

sections.title: Wernicke’s Encephalopathy
sections.text:
Wernicke’s Encephalopathy (WE) is an acute neuropsychiatric syndrome that results from thiamine deficiency. It is linked to
significant morbidity and mortality. If untreated, it can progress to Korsakoff Syndrome, which is characterized by a
disproportionate impairment in memory compared to other cognitive functions. Common causes include a staple diet of
unpolished rice, chronic alcohol abuse, malnutrition, recurrent vomiting and diarrhoea, gastrointestinal surgery, magnesium
deficiency, unbalanced nutrition, cancer, and chemotherapeutic treatments.

Clinical presentation
  •    May present with relatively non-specific Common symptoms or signs include:
  •    Ocular abnormalities
  •    Mental status changes (Delirium)
  •    Incoordination and gait ataxia
  •    Other symptoms include
  •    Hypotension and tachycardia
  •    Seizures
  •    Hearing loss
  •    Hypothermia
  •    Late-stage symptoms include Hyperthermia, Increased muscle tone, spastic paresis, Choreic dyskinesia, Coma

Management
C: thiamine hydrochloride 500mg dissolved in 100ml of NS given by infusion over 30 minutes, 8 hourly for 3 days.
If an effective response is observed,
          THEN
C: thiamine 250mg IV/IM daily for 5 days,

Prophylactic treatment in people with alcohol intoxication, severe alcohol withdrawal and people with poor diet and signs of
malnutrition:
C: thiamine 250mg IM once daily for 3-5 consecutive days.
          THEN
C: thiamine 100mg (PO)daily for at least 3 months.
Give Thiamine before or concomitantly with intravenous administration of glucose if WE is suspected, as glucose alone can
precipitate the disorder in thiamine-deficient individuals.

Management of vitamin b12 deficiency with neuropsychiatric symptoms
S: hydroxocobalamin (IM) 1mg 24hourly for 1 week, then weekly for 4 weeks, then monthly thereafter until maximum
improvement has occurred.
           OR
S: methyl cobalamin 500µgm (PO) 8hrly until maximum improvement has been observed. Stop if the underlying cause is
corrected.
           AND
A: folic acid (PO) 2mg once two weeks after starting treatment.

chapters.title: Nutrition Disorders

sections.title: Micronutrient Deficiencies
sections.text:
Micronutrient deficiency often termed as "hidden hunger" remains a critical public health challenge, despite the nation's steady
economic growth and its status as a "food basket" for East Africa. While the country produces a surplus of staple cereals like
maize and rice, a significant portion of the population suffers from a lack of essential vitamins and minerals necessary for
physical growth, cognitive development, and immune function.
The most micronutrient of public health importance in Tanzania includes; Iron, Vitamin A, Iodine, and Zinc. These deficiencies
disproportionately affect the most vulnerable segments of the population namely children under five and women of reproductive
age.

sections.title: Iron Deficiency Anaemia (IDA)
sections.text:
Iron deficiency anemia (IDA) typically develops gradually. As iron stores are depleted, the body’s ability to produce hemoglobin
the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen is compromised, leading to a variety of systemic symptoms.
Anaemia according to WHO is a condition in which the number of red blood cells or their oxygen-carrying capacity is insufficient
to meet physiologic needs, which vary by age, sex, altitude, smoking, and pregnancy status.

Table 24.1 Haemoglobin (Hb) levels (g/dl) and severity of anaemia at sea level
 Population group and age                     No anaemia       Mild anaemia Moderate anaemia                    Severe anaemia
 Children, 6-59 months                        11.0 and above 10.0-10.9         7.0-9.0                          <7.0
 Children, 5-11 years                         11.5 and above   11.0-11.4       8.0-10.9                         <8.0
 Children, 12-14 years                        12.0 and above   11.0-11.9       8.0-10.9                         <8.0
 Non-pregnant women (15 years and above)      12.0 and above   11.0-11.9       8.0-10.9                         <8.0
 Pregnant women                               11.0 and above   10.0-10.9       7.0-9.9                          <7.0
 Men, 15 years and above                      13.0 and above   11.0-12.9       8.0-10.9                         <8.0

Clinical Presentation
These symptoms arise because the body’s tissues are not receiving enough oxygen (hypoxia):
  •    Fatigue: The most common complaint; a persistent feeling of tiredness or lack of energy.
  •    Dyspnea on Exertion: Shortness of breath during physical activity.
  •     Palpitations: A sensation of a racing or irregular heartbeat as the heart pumps harder to compensate for low oxygen
       levels
  •    Pallor: Visible paleness, most easily observed in the conjunctiva (inner eyelids), mucous membranes, and nail beds.
  •    Dizziness or Lightheadedness: Often felt when standing up quickly.

Specific Features of Iron Deficiency
Certain physical signs are highly suggestive of iron deficiency specifically, rather than just general anemia:
  •    Koilonychia: Also known as "spoon-shaped nails," where the nails become thin, brittle, and concave.
  •    Glossitis and Stomatitis: A smooth, sore, or "beefy" red tongue and cracks at the corners of the mouth (angular cheilitis).
  •    Pica: A specialized craving for non-nutritive substances. Common forms include: Pagophagia: Craving and chewing ice;
       Geophagia: Craving dirt or clay.
  •    Plummer-Vinson Syndrome: A rare triad of IDA, esophageal webs, and dysphagia (difficulty swallowing).
  •    Restless Legs Syndrome (RLS): An irresistible urge to move the legs, often worsening at night.

Investigations
  •    Hemoglobin (Hb): The concentration of the oxygen-carrying protein. According to the WHO, anemia is generally defined
       as:
       > Men: <13 g/dL
       > Women (non-pregnant): <12 g/dL
       > Pregnant Women: <11 g/dL
  •    Hematocrit (Hct): The percentage of total blood volume made up of red blood cells (RBCs).
  •    Mean Corpuscular Volume (MCV): Measures the average size of RBCs. This is the most helpful value for classification:
       > Microcytic (Low MCV): Small cells; common in iron deficiency or thalassemia.
       > Normocytic (Normal MCV): Normal size; common in chronic disease or acute blood loss.
       > Macrocytic (High MCV): Large cells; common in B12 or Folate deficiency.

Non-Pharmacological Management
Dietary management (Refer FBDG & National Clinical Nutrition & Dietetics Guideline)
While diet alone is rarely sufficient to treat established anemia, it is crucial for maintaining levels once stores are restored.
  •    Encourage consumption of foods rich in iron, folate, proteins and other nutrients needed for blood production. This
       includes: green leafy vegetables such as spinach, amaranths, pumpkin leaves, sweet potato leaves etc.; citrus fruits
       such as passion fruits, lemon, oranges etc.; beetroots & rosella etc.
  •    Encourage consumption of Iron rich food: Found in animal products (red meat, poultry, fish etc). It is more easily
       absorbed by the body.
  •    Non-Heme rich food: Found in plant-based sources (legumes, leaf green vegetables, fortified cereals, nuts). Absorption
       is lower and more dependent on the presence of Vitamin C.
  •    Provide foods rich in Vitamin B12, folate, Vitamin E and C
  •    Reduce intake of beverages that contain phenolic compounds and tannin such as tea leaves, wheat brans.
  •    Encourage consumption of fortified food rich in Iron & folate such as fortified wheat and maize flour and bio fortified food
       such as High-Iron Beans (HIB) etc.

Pharmacological Management
Supplementation with iron and folic acid or Multiple Micronutrient Supplementation (MMS)

Iron and Folic Acid supplementation:
For Pregnant Women (Daily Use)
A: ferrous Sulfate (PO) 200mg (60 mg elemental iron
           AND
 A: folic Acid 0.4mg 24hourly for at least 90 consecutive days during pregnancy

For Post Natal women
A: ferrous Sulfate (PO) 200mg (60 mg elemental iron
           AND
A: folic acid 0.4mg 24hourly for at least 90 consecutive days during pregnancy

Multiple Micronutrient Supplementation (MMS)
A: multiple micronutrient supplement (MMS) 1 tablet PO once daily

Maternal anemia and micronutrient deficiencies are primary drivers of adverse pregnancy outcomes, notably low birth weight
(LBW), small-for-gestational-age (SGA) births, prematurity, and neonatal mortality.

Evidence, both globally and locally indicates that MMS significantly enhances maternal nutritional status and birth outcomes

Table 24.2 Description of the type of MMS that is recommended in Tanzania (One tablet components).
 Component                               Chemical entity                   Amount
 Vitamin A                               Retinyl acetate                   800 mcg RAE
 Vitamin C                               Ascorbic acid                     70 mg
 Vitamin D                               Cholecalciferol                   5 mcg (200 IU)
 Vitamin E                               Alpha tocopheryl succinate        10 mg α-TE
 Vitamin B₁                              Thiamine mononitrate              1.4 mg
 Vitamin B₂                              Riboflavin                        1.4 mg
 Vitamin B₃                              Niacinamide                       18 mg NE
 Vitamin B₆                              Pyridoxine HCl                    1.9 mg
 Folic acid                              Folic acid                        680 mcg DFE (400 mcg)
 Vitamin B₁₂                             Cyanocobalamin                    2.6 mcg
 Iron                                    Ferrous fumarate                  30 mg
 Iodine                                  Potassium iodide                  150 mcg
 Zinc                                    Zinc oxide                        15 mg
 Selenium                                Sodium selenite                   65 mcg
 Copper                                  Cupric oxide                      2 mg

Recommended use of MMS
a) For supplementation (Pregnant women without anemia)

MMS recommended has 30mg of elemental Iron and should be provided daily for all pregnant women.
A: multiple micronutrient supplement (MMS) 1 tablet 24hourly for 12 weeks post childbirth.

b) Women with high risk for neural tube disease (NTD):
The group of women who require higher dosage of folic acid include – Women with a history of neural tube disease in previous
pregnancy, women who themselves had neural tube disease, family history of neural tube disease, and women who are using
anti-folate medication e.g. Sodium valproate for epilepsy.

A: folic acid (PO) 5mg 24hourly for 90 days prior to conception
           OR
A: folic acid (PO) 5mg 24hourly for the first 12 weeks of pregnancy
          OR
A: folic acid (PO) 400mcg 24hourly

c) Use of MMS in pregnant women with sickle cell disease (SCD)
Folic acid supplementation is essential due to increased red blood cell turnover.
   •   Iron should only be given if iron deficiency is confirmed by laboratory testing, due to the risk of iron overload.
   •   MMS/Iron supplementation should NOT be used routine.
   •   It is recommended to use folic acid 5 mg daily for pregnant women with sickle cell disease.

d) Use of MMS for Anemia Prophylaxis during Post-Partum Period
Providing MMS during breastfeeding, has the potential to influence breastmilk micronutrient composition, infant growth,
maternal cognition, and maternal and infant micronutrient status.
   •   Post-delivery women should continue with 1tablet of MMS 24hourly for 6 to 12 weeks, but it can be extended up to
       6months.
   •   Postpartum anemic patient should continue with 24hourly tablet of MMS with additional prescription of iron tablet from
       other available iron tablets that can provide elemental Iron of 30 to 90mg per day to meet a demand of 60 to 120mg/day
       until hemoglobin of 11g/dl is reached

For treatment of anaemia refer Haematology chapter 3

sections.title: Iodine Deficiency Disorders (IDD)
sections.text:
Clinical Presentation
  •    Goitre enlarged thyroid gland from over activity.
  •    Hypothyroidism - dry skin, weight gain, puffy face, frequent constipation, and lethargy from under-active thyroid
  •    Hyperthyroidism - exophthalmia, rapid pulse, and weight loss from over-active thyroid

sections.title: Vitamin A Deficiency (VAD)
sections.text:
Clinical presentation
  •    Night blindness or inability to see in the dark
  •    White foamy patches on the eye (Bitot’s spot) or conjunctival and corneal dryness
  •    Keratomalacia or wrinkling and cloudiness of cornea
  •    Corneal ulceration or the cornea becomes soft and bulges

Investigations
Common indicators of VAD used for population surveys/assessments
  •    Clinical eye signs (Exophthalmia)
  •    Serum Retinol Concentration

Table 24.5 Serum Retinol Concentration
Public Health Importance      Serum or plasma retinol: <0.70 µmol/l in preschool-age children or pregnant women
Mild                                > 2% - < 10%
Moderate                            > 10% - < 20%
Severe                              > 20%

Non-Pharmacological Management
Dietary consumption of vitamin-A rich foods
Recommended to use animal source Vitamin A and plant source vitamin A (Provitamin A)

a) Animal Sources: Liver (glandular meats), eggs, whole milk, small fish (sardines/dagaa) etc. Contains "Retinol," which is
highly bioavailable and easily absorbed.

b) Plant sources: dark leaf green vegetables such as Amaranth (mchicha), pumpkin leaves (majani ya maboga), sweet potato
leaves (matembele), and cassava leaves (kisamvu) etc.
      > Biofortified Crops such as Vitamin A Maize and Orange Sweet Potatoes.
      > Orange/Yellow Plants such as Orange-Fleshed Sweet Potatoes (OFSP), carrots, ripe mangoes, and pawpaw.
c) Fortified food: oil fortified with vitamin A (consider food fortification logo).

Pharmacological Management

Vitamin A supplementation/prophylaxis
a) Under-five children supplementation (6 – 59 months)
A: retinol (vitamin A) (PO) 6 monthly up to the age of 5years.

b) Postnatal Supplementation
Postnatal mothers are eligible for a one-time -dose Vitamin A supplement (200,000 IU) within 4 to 8 weeks after delivery.

For children 6- 59months and children refer to table 24.4

For adults (except women of reproductive age)
A: retinol (vitamin A) (PO) 200,000 IU stat.

In case of Exophthalmia and Measles:
For infants < 6 months’ give
A: retinol (vitamin A) (PO) 50,000IU immediately on diagnosis repeat next day and on day 1

For infants 6-11months
A: retinol (vitamin A) (PO) 100,000IU immediately on diagnosis repeat next day and on day

For children 12-59 months
A: retinol (vitamin A) (PO) 200,000IU immediately on diagnosis repeat next day and on day

For all adults except women of reproductive age
A: retinol (vitamin A) (PO) 200,000IU immediately on diagnosis repeat next day and on day

For exophthalmia or Bitot’s sport for women of reproductive age
A: retinol (vitamin A) (PO) 10,000IU 24hourly for 4weeks

 Children who received a prophylactic dose within the previous month should not receive the treatment dose of vitamin A.

sections.title: Zinc Deficiency
sections.text:
Zinc deficiency is particularly prevalent among children under five and is a major contributor to stunting and recurrent infections.

Non-Pharmacological Management
Dietary management (Refer FBDG & Clinical Nutrition & Dietetics guideline)
  •    Animal Proteins: Small fish (dagaa), poultry, and liver are the most "bioavailable" sources (easiest for the body to use).
  •    Legumes: Beans and lentils (though these should be soaked or fermented to reduce phytates and improve zinc uptake).
  •    Pumpkin Seeds: A locally available and highly potent plant source of zinc.
  •    Food Fortification: fortification of wheat and maize flour with zinc (consider food fortification logo).
  •    Biofortified crops; Zinc bio-fortified beans

Pharmacological Management
In Management of Diarrhea: Zinc is a mandatory part of the "Integrated Management of Childhood Illness" (IMCI) protocol.

Children 6 months to 5 years:
A: zinc sulfate (PO) 20 mg 24hourly for 10–14 days.

Infants under 6 months:
A: zinc sulfate (PO) 10 mg 24hourly for 10–14 days.

sections.title: Overnutrition
sections.text:
Overweight and Obesity (Adiposity Based Chronic Disease - ABCD)
Obesity is a chronic disorder of excessive accumulation of fat in the body, whereas overweight refer to the excess amount of
body weight in all tissues.

Management of Obesity and Overweight
Aim of nutritional management is to:
  •    Achieve and maintain ideal body weight by bringing about gradual weight loss
  •    Correct fault food habits

Table 24.12 Nutrition Assessment
 Assessment Domain               Parameters/Components                     Interpretation/Purpose
 Anthropometric Assessment       Body Mass Index (BMI)
                                 Overweight                                25–29.9 kg/m²
                                 Obesity Class I                           30–34.9 kg/m²
                                 Obesity Class II                          35–39.9 kg/m²
                                 Obesity Class III                         ≥40 kg/m²
                                 Waist Circumference (WC)                  Assesses central obesity risk
                                 Men                                       >94 cm = Increased risk; >102 cm = Substantially
                                                                           increased risk
                                 Women                                     >80 cm = Increased risk; >88 cm = Substantially

                                 Men                                       ≥0.90
                                 Women                                     ≥0.85
                                 Children (Weight-for-Height)

                                 Obesity                                   > +3 SD
 Biochemical Assessment          Fasting blood glucose, HbA1c              Assess diabetes risk
                                 Lipid profile (Total cholesterol, LDL,    Assess dyslipidaemia/cardiovascular risk
                                 HDL, triglycerides)
                                 Liver function tests (ALT, AST, GGT)      Assess for non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD)
                                 Thyroid function tests (TSH, T3, T4)      Rule out hypothyroidism

                                 Vitamin B12)

                                 Chronic diseases                          Identify comorbidities

                                 Physical signs                            e.g., acanthosis nigricans, joint problems
 Dietary Assessment              24-hour dietary recall                    Assess recent food intake
                                 Food Frequency Questionnaire (FFQ)        Assess usual intake over time
                                 Eating pattern assessment                 Evaluate snacking, eating out, high-calorie
                                                                           foods/drinks

Table 24.13: Nutrient–Drug Interactions
 Medicine/Class                             Nutrient Interaction/Effect
 Metformin                                  Decreased absorption of vitamin B12 and folic acid
 Orlistat                                   Reduced absorption of fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) and beta-carotene
 Calcium and Vitamin D supplementation      Risk of low bone mineral density if inadequate intake
 Diuretics                                  May cause potassium and magnesium depletion
 Metoprolol (Beta-blockers)                 May mask hypoglycaemia symptoms and alter glucose metabolism

Non-Pharmacological Management
Dietary Management (Refer FBDG & National Clinical Nutrition & Dietetics Guideline)
Lifestyle-first approach remains the core of obesity management in Tanzania.
  •    Control total energy intake based on individual
  •    assessment by limiting energy intake from total fat and simple sugars.
  •    Put the client on a weight reduction diet regime of 30-25kcal/kg /day.
  •    High fiber, restricted fat diets based on individual assessment is recommended
  •    Offer nutrition education and counseling to the clients with emphasis on weight management, fat diets and other
       unhealthy practices in weight control
  •    Recommend suitable exercise program and encourage physical activity for gradual weight loss
  •    Recommend support systems for the clients who need behavior modification

  Note
    •  A maximum reduction of 1000kcal daily is required to lose about 1kg a week and a reduction. Drastic reduction of
       calorie intake is however not advisable.
    •  Diet adjustments should be gradual as such people experience excessive appetite. Use of appetite suppressants is
       not recommended

Table 24.14 Nutritional Management
  Nutrients              Nutritional Goal                 Recommendation
  Fat                    20–35% of total calorie intake   Choose lower-fat alternatives- Include monounsaturated & polyunsaturated
                                                          fats
  Protein                0.9 g/kg/day                     Include protein to enhance satiety and meet needs - opt for lean meats,
                                                          skinless poultry, fish, eggs, legumes, tofu, low-fat dairy
  Carbohydrates          45–65% of total calorie intake   Switch to whole grains - Choose low energy dense foods- Prefer foods with
                                                          lower kcal/100g
  Fiber                  20–35 grams per day              Increases satiety- Include legumes, fruits, vegetables, whole grains
  Sugar &                <10% of total calorie intake     Limit added sugars- Choose low-calorie beverages, Water is best, Limit
  Beverages                                               alcohol consumption

Table 24.15 Recommended strategies in weight management
  Strategy Area                   Component                       Details/Recommendations
                                  16:8 Method                     Eat within an 8-hour window; fast for 16 hours daily
  Intermittent Fasting            5:2 Method                      Eat normally 5 days/week; fast 2 days/week (~500 kcal on
                                                                  fasting days)
  Dietary Modifications           Portion Control                 Reduce portion sizes; follow National Food-Based Dietary
                                                                  Guidelines
  Education & Counseling          Nutrition Education             Teach balanced eating, label reading, managing emotional
                                                                  eating, meal planning
  Behavioral Strategies           Behavior Change Support         Set realistic goals, self-monitor, build support systems,
                                                                  address barriers

                                                                  capabilities
  Monitoring & Follow-up          Ongoing Evaluation              Regularly assess progress, reassess goals, and adjust
                                                                  nutrition care plan as needed

Bariatric surgery
Bariatric Surgery Treatment indications and approach consideration. Surgery for obesity should be considered as a treatment
of last resort after dieting, exercise, psychotherapy, and drug treatments have failed.
   •     Metabolic and bariatric surgery (MBS) is recommended for all individuals with a body mass index (BMI) higher than 35
         kg/m2, regardless of the presence, absence, or severity of comorbid conditions.
   •     Metabolic and bariatric surgery (MBS) should be considered for individuals who have metabolic disease and a BMI
         between 30 and 34.9 kg/m2
   •     Metabolic surgery should be a recommended option to treat type 2 diabetes mellitus in appropriate surgical candidates
         with class III obesity (BMI ≥40 kg/m2), regardless of the level of glycemic control or complexity of glucose-lowering
         regimens, as well as in patients with class II obesity (BMI 35.0-39.9 kg/m2) with inadequately controlled hyperglycemia
         despite lifestyle and optimal medical therapy
   •     Metabolic surgery should also be considered to be an option to treat type 2 diabetes in patients with class I obesity (BMI
         30.0-34.9 kg/m2) and inadequately controlled hyperglycemia despite optimal medical treatment by either oral or
         injectable medications (including insulin)
   •     Consider bariatric surgery in "carefully selected" patients with a body mass index (BMI) higher than 40 kg/m2 who have
         severe comorbidities (e.g., nonalcoholic fatty liver disease [NAFLD]) or in those with a BMI higher than 50 kg/m2 who
         have milder comorbidities

Surgical options
Types of bariatric surgery include the following:
  •   Correct fault food habits Restrictive procedures (e.g., adjustable gastric banding, sleeve gastrectomy)
  •   Restrictive procedures with some malabsorption (e.g., Roux-en-Y gastric bypass)
  •   Malabsorptive procedures with some restriction (e.g., biliopancreatic diversion with duodenal switch)
  •   Bariatric surgery can be performed either via an open approach or via a laparoscopic approach. The laparoscopic
      approach has become the more popular one.

Provide the rest of energy 60% from carbohydrates which should be mainly in complex form; starches and dietary fiber. Limit
simple forms like sugars

Minerals and Vitamins
Provide adequate amount of essential nutrients like minerals and vitamins to maintain a good nutrition status
Generally, increase intake of the following food:
  •    Vegetables such as broccoli, mushroom, zucchini, cabbage, lettuce, cucumber
  •    Fruits such as pineapple, cherimoya, peach, grapefruit
  •    Tubers such as sweet potatoes
  •    Low fat milk
  •    Diuretic foods such as celery, apples, watermelon (diuretic drugs are not recommended)

Pharmacological Management
Refer to Chapter 19 - Endocrine and Metabolic disease conditions

 Note: Pharmacotherapy is considered only for BMI ≥ 30 kg/m² (or ≥ 27 with comorbidities like diabetes or hypertension) and
 when lifestyle changes alone fail

sections.title: Nutrition Management for Infectious Diseases
sections.text:
Nutritional Management in TB, HIV and AIDS

Refer to National Guideline for Nutritional Care & Support of People Living with HIV and Nutrition Implementation Guideline for
MDR-TB Patients in Tanzania
  •    Maintain and improve nutrition status of a person               •    Improve performance of immune system.
       living with HIV/ AIDS thus delay the progression                •    Replenishment of nutrient losses incurred during
       from HIV to AIDS related diseases.                                   infection.
  •    Ensure adequate intake of all nutrients thus                    •    Minimizing symptoms of malabsorption.
       preventing development of nutritional deficiencies.             •    Regeneration of glycogen stores.
  •    Preservation of lean body mass.                                 •    Maintain laboratory values within normal limits.
  •    Maintain body weight and fitness.

  Note: Control side effects due to medication and monitor drug – nutrient interaction

Table 24.18: Side Effects related to TB drugs and food intake recommendations to minimize them.
 Medicine         Food Recommendation                                 Avoid                Common Side
                                                                                           Effects/Considerations
 Rifampicin       Take 1 hour before or 2 hours after meals           Alcohol; antacids    Nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite
                                                                      within 1 hour
 Isoniazid        Take 1 hour before or 2 hours after meals;          Alcohol              May interfere with nutrient metabolism;
                  give Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) 10 mg daily                                 peripheral neuropathy
 Ethambutol       May be taken with food                              Alcohol              Gastrointestinal discomfort; visual
                                                                                           disturbances
 Streptomycin     Increase fluid intake                               —                    Taste changes, nausea
 Pyrazinamide     May be taken with food                              Alcohol              Nausea, hepatotoxicity, joint pains
 Ethionamide      Take with or after meals; supplement with Vitamin   Alcohol              Abdominal discomfort, nausea
                  B6
 Ofloxacin        Take 2 hours before or after food                   Antacids, milk       Gastrointestinal upset
                                                                      products
 Cycloserine      Supplement with Vitamin B6                          Alcohol              Neurological side effects, irritability
Nutrient Requirements and Dietary Management in TB, HIV and AIDS Patients

Energy
Most patients with chronic tuberculosis, HIV and AIDS are malnourished, energy needs are increased in order to minimize
weight loss and achieve a desirable weight. An additional 300- 500 kcal (35 -40 kcal per ideal body weight) is recommended.
This will help in protein sparing.

Protein
An intake of 1.2- 1.5 g of protein per kg body weight is required to generate serum albumin levels per day, due to tissue wasting
and repair of worn-out tissues.

Fats/ oils
These should provide 25-30% or less of the total energy requirements of an individual.

Vitamins and minerals
The body should be provided with liberal amounts of vitamins and minerals. In TB conversion of beta carotene to retinol is
affected in the intestinal mucosa. The client should be supplemented with vitamin A (as per the National Vitamin A
supplementation schedule) and encouraged to eat vitamin A rich food. Patients on isoniazid should ideally be supplemented
with 10mg of pyridoxine B6 daily since the drug inhibits its absorption. Additional amounts of vitamin C is recommended in the
diet to facilitate healing of lesions. Other antioxidants (Vit A, C, and E, folic acid, zinc and selenium) neutralize free radicals and
prevent the production of peroxides from lipids.

Water
At least 8 glasses or more of safe drinking water per day

sections.title: Dumping Syndrome.
sections.text:
It is a rapid gastric emptying occurs when food especially sugar moves from stomach into small bowel too quickly.

Nutritional implications
Loss of nutrients, Weight loss.

Aims of nutrition management

  •   Prevent weight loss

sections.title: Critical Care Nutrition Support
sections.text:
The goal of nutrition management is to preserve lean body mass

Oral Nutrition Supplement
Oral nutritional supplements (ONS) should be used whenever possible to meet patient’s needs, when dietary counseling and
food fortification are not sufficient to increase dietary intake and reach nutritional goals.

Enteral and Parenteral Nutrition
Where nutritional requirements cannot be met orally or, expected to be impossible >3 days or expected to be below half of
energy requirements for >1week, enteral nutrition (EN) should be administered. This should be assessed on a case-by-case
basis and the long-term impact of nutrition deficit considered.

Parenteral nutrition (PN)
Parenteral nutrition (PN) should be considered when EN is not indicated or unable to reach targets over 3-7 days despite use
of appropriate management strategies, and calorie and protein delivery is consistently <50% of prescribed targets.
Supplemental PN should be considered after other measures to improve EN have been attempted or insertion of a post-pyloric
enteral feeding tube is deemed unsafe and calorie and protein intake remain significantly less than prescribed targets (i.e. <50%
over a 3-7day period)

Parenteral Feeds
Total Parenteral Nutrition (TPN) is a life-sustaining medical treatment that bypasses the normal digestion process, delivering a
complete nutrient mix directly into the bloodstream through a central vein. It is used when the gastrointestinal tract is non-
functional or inaccessible.

Table 24.23: Nutrition Composition
TPN is a complex "all-in-one" admixture (often called a 3-in-1 or TNA) tailored to a patient’s specific metabolic needs.
 Component                    Contents                                        Function
 Macronutrients               Dextrose (carbohydrates), amino acids           Provide energy and prevent muscle wasting
                              (protein), lipid emulsions (fat)

                                                                              carrier
