 indicated)                                                                   reduce gastric acid secretion

                           wear gloves

                           lipids) OR 0.22-micron filter for 2-in-1
                           formulations

                           alcohol/chlorhexidine for at least 15

                           infusion pump; do not gravity infuse

                           mL/hour) and titrate as ordered

 TPN should only be used when clearly indicated and requires close monitoring for complications such as infections, electrolyte
 disturbances, liver dysfunction, and hyperglycaemia.

Indications                                                          Contraindications
  •    Non-functional GI tract: Short bowel syndrome,                  •   Functional GI tract: If the "gut works, use it" (Enteral
       severe malabsorption, or paralytic ileus.                           nutrition is always preferred).
  •    Severe Bowel Obstruction: Intestinal blockages that             •   Hemodynamic Instability: Severe shock or

  •    Gastrointestinal Fistulas: High-output fistulas                 •   Short-term use: If the patient is expected to resume
       where feeding would prevent healing.                                eating within 5 days.
  •    Severe Malnutrition: Pre-operative support for                  •   Terminal Illness: When the prognosis does not
       patients who cannot eat for >7 days.                                warrant invasive nutritional support.
  •    Critical Illness: Severe pancreatitis or intractable            •   Inability to gain venous access: Lack of central line
       vomiting/diarrhea.                                                  capability.

TPN Dosage
The dosage for Total Parenteral Nutrition (TPN) is a highly individualized process.
For adults, it is calculated based on ideal body weight (IBW), while for children, it is based on actual weight in kilograms and
their specific developmental stage.

Adult TPN Dosage (General Guidelines)
Adult requirements focus on maintaining lean body mass and providing enough energy for metabolic stress without
"overfeeding," which can damage the liver.

Pediatric TPN Dosage (Age-Dependent)
Children have much higher metabolic demands per kilogram than adults because they require nutrients for both maintenance
and rapid growth.

Gastrointestinal Disorders
sections.text:
Inflammatory Gastroduodenal Disorders (Peptic ulcer diseases, Gastritis, gastroenteritis)
Peptic Ulcers: These are ulcers of the stomach or duodenum or both. Commonly caused by infection e.g. H Pylori and mucosal
injuries (acid, NSAID, iatrogenic) they increased risk of bleeding and perforation. Gastritis: inflammation of the lining of the
stomach. It can develop suddenly (acute gastritis) or gradually over time (chronic gastritis).
Gastroenteritis: Is the inflammation of the stomach and small intestines, often caused by viral, fungal, or bacterial infections,
leading to diarrhea, vomiting, and abdominal pain.

Risks factors
Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) infection, Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), smoking, alcoholism, stress, people
older than 60 years, prior peptic ulcer and radiation treatments

sections.title: Hepatic Disorders
sections.text:
Group of disorders that damages the liver and impair its functions. They can be caused by viruses, drugs, alcohol, or inherited
conditions. The common ones are hepatitis, acute liver failure, Liver Cirrhosis, fat liver disorders and can be caused by viruses,
toxic substances and injuries.

Hepatitis
Hepatitis is an inflammation of the liver that is caused by a variety of infectious viruses and noninfectious agents leading to a
range of health problems, some of which can be fatal.

Risk factors: Risk factors vary by type of hepatitis

sections.text:
Cardiovascular disease is a class of diseases that affect the heart and blood vessels (arteries and veins). It is one of the major
leading causes of death globally.
Common examples of cardiovascular disease include; coronary heart disease (CHD)/coronary artery disease (CAD)/ ischemic
heart disease (IHD), Myocardial infarction (MI) and Hypertension

sections.text:
1.Acute kidney injury (AKI)
It represents an abrupt reduction in glomerular filtration rate (GFR), resulting in the reduced ability of the kidney to excrete
metabolic wastes with dysregulation of fluid, electrolytes, and acid-base homeostasis.

Nutrition diagnosis
  •    Altered nutrition-related lab values related to                   •     Risk for electrolyte imbalance related to renal
       impaired kidney function as evidenced by                                dysfunction and altered excretion as evidenced by
       hyperkalemia (serum potassium 6.0 mEq/L) and                            hypokalemia (serum potassium 3.1 mEq/L)
       hyperphosphatemia (serum phosphorus 6.8                                 following diuretic use.
       mg/dL).                                                           •     Excessive fluid intake related to inappropriate
  •    Fluid retention related to oliguria secondary to AKI                    hydration management in AKI as evidenced by
       as evidenced by edema, weight gain of 3 kg in one                       pulmonary edema and serum sodium dilution.
       week, and elevated blood pressure.                                •     Food and nutrition-related knowledge deficit related
  •    Inadequate energy intake related to poor appetite                       to unfamiliarity with AKI dietary modifications as
       and nausea from AKI as evidenced by oral intake                         evidenced by patient-reported uncertainty about
       below 50% of estimated needs and 5% weight loss                         low-potassium foods.
       in one week.

Drugs nutrient interactions
  •   Furosemide: causes urinary loss of potassium, zinc, magnesium, calcium, sodium dehydration.
  •   Thiazide Diuretics cause nausea, anorexia, hyponatremia, hypokalemia, hyperuricemia, hyperglycemia.
  •   Spironolactone: causes hyperkalemia, dry mouth, nausea, vomiting, gastritis, diarrhea.
  •   Aluminium hydroxide suspension: causes constipation, Aluminium toxicity, increased thiamine requirements,
      impaired iron and folate absorption.
  •   Sevelamer Hydrochloride: causes increased calcium absorption if taken with calcium, diarrhea, nausea, vomiting,
      dyspepsia, peripheral oedema, decrease LDL, increase HDL.
  •   Calcium: causes constipation, increased Ca-P product, hypercalcemia, calcium citrate increases Aluminium absorption,
      nausea and vomiting.

2. Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) or Chronic renal failure (CRF)
It is defined as decreased kidney function of estimated Glomerular Filtration Rate (eGFR) of < 60 mL/min per 1.73 m2, or
markers of kidney damage, or both, in a period of at least 3 months, regardless of the underlying cause.

Drugs nutrient interactions
  •   Furosemide causes urinary loss of potassium, zinc, magnesium, calcium, sodium dehydration.
  •   Thiazide Diuretics cause nausea, anorexia, hyponatraemia, hypokalaemia, hyperuricemia, hyperglycaemia.
  •   Spironolactone causes hyperkalemia, dry mouth, nausea, vomiting, gastritis, diarrhea.
  •   Aluminium hydroxide suspension causes constipation, Aluminium toxicity, increased thiamine requirements, impaired
      iron and folate absorption.
  •   Sevelamer Hydrochloride causes increased calcium absorption if taken with calcium, diarrhea, nausea, vomiting,
      dyspepsia, peripheral oedema, decrease LDL, increase HDL.

1. Nephritic Syndrome
Nephritic syndrome is a disorder of the glomerular (clusters of microscopic blood vessels in the kidneys with small pores through
which blood is filtered). It is characterized by body tissue swelling (oedema), high blood pressure, proteinuria, azotemia,
decreased urine output and the presence of red blood cells in the urine.

Nutritional assessment
Anthropometric Data: Monitor body weight and changes for signs of fluid retention or malnutrition.

2. Renal transplant
A kidney transplant is a surgical procedure to place a kidney from a live or deceased donor into a person whose kidneys no
longer function properly.

Nutrient-drug interactions
  •   Mycophenolate mofetil can cause diarrhea, constipation, nausea & vomiting
  •   Tacrolimus may cause increased blood sugar (glucose) levels, nausea and diarrhea.
  •   Cyclosporin (Neural /S& immune) may cause potassium (K+) retention & increase blood K+ levels, increases blood
      lipids levels e.g. cholesterol & triglycerides, & increased blood. May cause nausea & vomiting. It is recommended that
      this medication is taken with food.
  •   Prednisone may increase loss of vitamin K, vitamin C, selenium and zinc. Also, may increase the loss of vitamin B6,
      leading to breakdown and loss of protein.

Nutrition management for recipient post-transplant
  •    The diet prescription is based on the kidney functions as indicated by the following: urine output, serum creatinine, blood
       urea nitrogen (BUN), potassium and phosphorus
  •    NPO for 8 hours first day after operation
  •    Initially clear liquids within 24 hours, are given to the patient during the early post-operative period, and then progresses
       to semi solid then regular foods as tolerated.
  •    Finally, the patient is placed on an essentially normal diet.

chapters.intro:
Nutrition disorders can be caused by an insufficient intake of food or certain nutrients, or by inability of the body to absorb and
use nutrients, or by over consumption of certain foods.
This chapter serves as an essential component of the Standard Treatment Guidelines (STG), focusing on the comprehensive
management of nutrition-related disorders. Malnutrition, in all its forms including undernutrition (wasting, stunting, underweight),
micronutrient deficiencies (Iron Deficiency Anaemia – IDA, Vitamin A Deficiency - VAD, Iodine Deficiency Disorder - IDD) and
overnutrition (overweight and obesity), representing a significant public health challenge with far reaching implications for
individual health outcomes and national development.
The primary objective of this chapter is to provide healthcare professionals with evidence-based guidance for the prevention,
early detection, diagnosis, and management of common nutrition disorders. It aims to standardize approaches to nutritional
assessment, intervention, and monitoring, ensuring that patients receive timely, appropriate, and effective care.
By adhering to the principles and recommendations outlined herein, healthcare providers will be better equipped to improve
nutritional status, enhance treatment outcomes, and ultimately contribute to a healthier population.

chapters.title: Poisoning

sections.title: Acute Alcohol Intoxication
sections.text:
Is a clinically harmful condition that usually follows the ingestion of a large amount of alcohol

Clinical Presentation
  •    Confusion, Vomiting, Seizures.                                     •    Skin that looks blue, gray or pale.
  •    Slow breathing (fewer than eight breaths a minute).                •    Low body temperature (hypothermia).
  •    Irregular Breathing                                                •    Trouble staying conscious or awake

Non-pharmacological Management
  •  Airway assessment and observation of the development of respiratory function should be done.
  •  Prevent aspiration by placement of the patient in a lateral position).

Refer the Mental Health Chapter 23 for other psychological management

Pharmacological Management
For dehydration or electrolyte imbalance:
A: sodium chloride 0.9% IV infusion according to hydration status and electrolyte requirements.

If hypoglycemia is present: then correct with
C: dextrose 50% IV, 25 g stat (50 mL IV bolus)
          OR
B: dextrose 10% IV infusion as clinically indicated.

For patients with alcohol use disorder, malnutrition, or altered mental status:
C: thiamine injection 100 mg IV/IM stat, then 100 mg IV/IM/PO once daily
           AND
A: folic acid 1 mg IV/PO once daily
           AND/OR
A: magnesium sulfate 1–2 g IV infusion stat (repeat based on serum magnesium levels)
           AND/OR
B: multivitamin injection IV once daily according to product formulation.

For nausea and/or vomiting:
D: ondansetron 4–8 mg IV/PO every 8–12 hours as needed
         OR
B: metoclopramide 10 mg IV/PO every 8 hours as needed.

For severe agitation or violent behavior:
B: haloperidol 2.5–5 mg IM/IV stat, repeat as needed

  Note:
    •   Prolonged vomiting can lead to hyponatremia; this should not be corrected too rapidly since it can induce a central
        pontine myelinolysis
    •   Depending on the severity of the intoxication and complications e.g. Wernicke encephalopathy, alcoholic hepatitis,
        or dysrhythmias, patients may have to be admitted to the hospital for further treatment
    •   Call the Poison Control Centre at a Toll-free phone number 0800112031 for information.

Management of Ingested Poisons
Ingested toxins are suspected in any patient with signs and symptoms irrespective of reported dose ingested.

Clinical Presentations
  •    General clinical features: Nausea, vomiting, drowsiness, blurred vision, and dizziness
  •    Central Nervous System toxicity: Altered level of consciousness, convulsions, acute confusion and coma,
  •    Renal Toxicity: Acute kidney injury/failure and papillary necrosis
  •    Metabolic derangement: Metabolic acidosis, respiratory acidosis, hypoglycemia.
  •    Allergic reactions: Urticaria, angioedema, anaphylaxis
  •    Haematological toxicity: Aplastic anaemia, agranulocytosis

Non-Pharmacological Management
Gastric decontamination – Functional removal of an ingested toxin from the gastrointestinal tract to reduce absorption. This
may include:

1. Gastric evacuation:
Forced emesis is not recommended and is highly discouraged.
Gastric lavage is not routinely recommended and should only be considered in life-threatening poisoning when:
      >Poison was ingested within 30 minutes to 1 hour, AND
      >No safer alternative decontamination method is available.

2. Intragastric binding:
Use of single-dose or multiple-dose activated charcoal may be considered depending on the poison ingested, timing of
ingestion, and contraindications. Limitations should be assessed before use.

3. Enhanced gastrointestinal transit:
Whole bowel irrigation may be considered in selected cases. Routine use of cathartics is not recommended.

Contraindications to Gastric Lavage:
  •   An unprotected airway in an unconscious patient increase aspiration risk
  •   Ingestion of corrosives or petroleum products e.g. kerosene,
  •   Bowel obstruction
  •   Bowel perforation
  •   GI bleeding
  •   Identify the specific agent and remove or adsorb it as soon as possible.

  Note
    •  Treatment is most effective if given as quickly as possible after the poisoning event, ideally within 1 hour.
    •  If the patient has swallowed kerosene, petrol, or petrol-based products (note that most pesticides are in petrol-based
       solvents) or if the patient’s mouth and throat have been burned (for example with bleach, toilet cleaner or battery
       acid) do not vomit the patient but give water orally? Never use salt as an emetic as this can be fatal.

Pharmacological Management
A: charcoal, activated (PO) single dose (if available) within one hour of ingestion and do not induce vomiting; given by mouth
or NG tube according to the dosage below:
Children below one year: 1g/kg Children 1-12 years of age: 25–50g
Adolescents and adults: 25–100g
         AND
A: sodium lactate compound (ringer’s lactate)(IV) 30ml/kg 2liters for 24hours if Shock is present
         OR
A: sodium chloride 0.9% (IV) 30ml/kg 2liters for 24hours if Shock is present

  Note: Toxins for which multiple doses of activated charcoal are indicated includes Carbamazepine, Dapsone, Digoxin,
  Paraquat, Phenobarbitone, Quinine, Slow-release preparations such as theophylline, Amanita phalloides fungus, Multiple
  doses may also be considered in life threatening overdose of other drugs (e.g. tricyclic antidepressants).

Content mixing:
  •   Mix the charcoal in 8–10 times the amount of water, e.g. 5g in 40 ml of water.
  •   If possible, give the whole amount at once; if the child has difficulty in tolerating it, the charcoal dose can be divided.
  •   If charcoal is not available, then induce vomiting but only if the patient is conscious by rubbing the back of the patient
      throat with a spatula or spoon handle;

Referral: Consider transferring patient to next referral level hospital, where this can be done safely, if the patient is:
  •   Unconscious or deteriorating conscious level
  •   Burns to mouth and throat
  •   Severe respiratory distress
  •   Cyanosed
  •   Heart failure

sections.title: Food Poisoning
sections.text:
Food poisoning, also called foodborne illness, is illness caused by eating contaminated food. Infectious organisms including
bacteria, viruses, and parasites or their toxins are the most common causes of food poisoning as listed in the table. Large
intestine and small intestine have an intermediate incubation from about 1 to 3 days.

Large intestine
Infections of the large intestine or colon can cause bloody, mucous diarrhea associated with crampy abdominal pain.
   •    Campylobacter spp, is the common one cause of food-borne disease
   •    Shigella spp contaminate food and water and cause dysentery (severe diarrhea often containing mucus and blood).
   •    Salmonella spp infections often occur because of poorly or undercooked cooked and/or poor handling of the chicken
        and eggs. In individuals with weakened immune systems, including the elderly, the infection can enter the bloodstream
        and cause potentially life- threatening infections.
   •    Vibrio parahaemolyticus can contaminate saltwater shellfish and cause a watery diarrhea.

Small Intestine Infection
Diarrhea due to small bowel infection tends not to be bloody, but infections may affect both the small and large intestine at the
same time.
  •    E. coli (enterotoxigenic) is the most common cause of traveler's diarrhea. It lacks symptoms such as fever or bloody
       diarrhea.
  •    Vibrio cholerae, often from contaminated drinking, water produces a voluminous watery diarrhea resembling rice-water.
  •    Viruses such as Norwalk, rotavirus and adenovirus tend to have other symptoms associated with an infection including
       fever, chills, headache, and vomiting.
  •    Botulism is caused by Clostridium botulinum toxin and may present with fever, vomiting, mild diarrhea, numbness, and
       weakness leading to paralysis.

sections.title: Shellfish poisoning
sections.text:
Shellfish poisoning occurs when oysters, clams, scallops, or mussels) are eaten by humans. shellfish poisonings fall into four
groups based on the specific toxins or chemicals that poison humans it includes:
  •     Amnesic shellfish poisoning (ASP)
  •     Diarrheal shellfish poisoning (DSP)
  •     Neurotoxic shellfish poisoning (NSP)
  •     Paralytic shellfish poisoning (PSP)

Clinical presentation
  •    Permanent short-term memory loss, brain damage, death (by Amnesic shellfish causative being domoic acid)
  •    Diarrhea, nausea, vomiting (Diarrheal shellfish by okadaic acid, azaspiracid)
  •    Slurred speech, nausea, vomiting (Neurotoxic shellfish caused by brevetoxins)
  •    Paresthesias, coordination loss, speech defects, nausea, vomiting, death (Paralytic shellfish caused by saxitoxin,
       neosaxiton and gonyautoxins I to IV

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •  Oral charcoal may be used to patients that are seen early after ingestion of large amounts of food
  •  Resuscitation and stabilization refer to EMD Chapter 1

Pharmacological Management
There is no specific antidote for shellfish poisoning.

For dehydration due to vomiting/diarrhea:
A: oral Rehydration Salts (ORS) PO for mild dehydration
         OR
A: sodium chloride 0.9% IV infusion
         OR
A: sodium lactate compound (ringer’s lactate) IV infusion for moderate to severe dehydration.

For nausea/vomiting:
D: ondansetron 4–8 mg IV/PO every 8 hours as needed
         OR
B: metoclopramide 10 mg IV/PO every 8 hours as needed

Severe respiratory paralysis may require mechanical ventilation/supportive ICU care.

sections.title: Herbal Poisoning
sections.text:
Investigations
  •    Basic blood count, renal function, liver function, and electrocardiogram
  •    Heavy metal screening if suspected or if symptoms are non-specific
  •    Analysis methods exist for some herbal toxins only—Colchicine (HPLC, GCMS), tropane alkaloids (GCMS, oxalate
       (GCMS), vinca alkaloids (HPLC), cardioactive steroids (immunoassay)—check with the Poison Control Centre for
       Toxicology test.

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •  Ask specifically regarding the use of such products and a matched clinical feature using the above Toxidrome
  •  Secure sample for identification
          > Actual herbs or product used
          > Prescription or packaging
  •  Good resuscitative, symptomatic, and supportive care
  •  Instruct patients and family to stop using the product
  •  Consider outpatient monitoring of renal function, liver function, and blood counts
  •  Report case to regulating authority
  •  Report unusual cases to the National Poison Control Center via a Toll-free phone 0800112031

Pharmacological Management
Activated charcoal may be administered in acute ingestion of herbal toxins if: Presentation is within appropriate time window

A: charcoal, activated PO/NG
Adults: 50 g PO/NG stat
Children: 1 g/kg PO/NG (maximum 50 g)
Use only if ingestion is recent (usually ≤1 hour) and airway is protected and Airway is protected

For shock or severe dehydration due to vomiting/diarrhea:
A: sodium lactate compound (ringer’s lactate)(Ringer’s lactate) IV infusion
         OR
A: sodium chloride 0.9% IV infusion
30 mL/kg IV bolus initially, then continue fluid resuscitation up to 2 liters within first 24 hours, guided by clinical response.

sections.title: Management of Skin Contamination
sections.text:
•    Remove all clothing and personal effects and thoroughly flush all exposed areas with copious amounts of running water
       running for:
       > 5-minutes for non-irritants or mild irritants
       > 15-20 minutes for moderate to severe irritants and chemicals that cause acute toxicity if absorbed through the skin
       > 30 minutes for most corrosives
       > 60 minutes for strong alkalis (e.g., sodium, potassium or calcium hydroxide)
  •    Use non-abrasive soap and water for oily substances
  •    Attending staff should take care to protect themselves from secondary contamination by wearing gloves and apron
  •    Removed clothing and personal effects should be stored safely in a see-through plastic bag that can be sealed, for later
       cleansing or disposal.

sections.title: Management of Eye Contamination
sections.text:
Non-Pharmacological Management
  •  Immediately irrigate the affected eye with clean                      •    Continue irrigation for an additional 30 minutes if
     running water for 15–20 minutes, ensuring that                             symptoms persist or ocular pH remains abnormal.
     contaminated runoff does not enter the unaffected                     •    Remove contact lenses if present.
     eye.                                                                  •    Perform thorough eye examination where possible,
  •  Evert the eyelids and ensure all conjunctival                              including:
     surfaces are adequately irrigated.                                         > Visual acuity assessment
  •  For acid or alkali exposure, irrigate t54he eye with                       > Fluorescein staining to assess corneal injury
     copious amounts of water OR normal saline for at                           > Examination for retained foreign material
     least 30 minutes, then reassess.

Pharmacological Management
To facilitate irrigation where severe blepharospasm or pain limits eye opening:
C: tetracaine hydrochloride ophthalmic 0.5% eye drops, 1–2 drops into affected eye stat prior to dexamethasone

Referral: Urgently refer to an ophthalmologist if:
  •   Significant conjunctival injury                                      •    Chemical burns from strong acids/alkalis
  •   Corneal ulceration or corneal burns                                  •    Retained foreign body
  •   Persistent pain                                                      •    When further ophthalmic evaluation cannot be
  •   Reduced visual acuity                                                     performed

sections.title: Management of Inhaled Poisoning
sections.text:
Non-Pharmacological Management
  •  Remove the patient from the source of exposure immediately and move to fresh air.
  •  Ensure rescuers avoid exposure to toxic fumes/gases.
  •  Thoroughly ventilate the contaminated area.
  •  If vomiting occurs, place the patient in the recovery position (head turned to the side) to prevent aspiration.
  •  Initiate cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) if there are signs of cardiac arrest.
  •  Contact National Poison Control Centre: 0800 112031 for further guidance.

Monitor for delayed respiratory complications such as: Upper airway edema, Bronchospasm, Chemical pneumonitis, delayed
pulmonary edema (observe for 24–48 hours where indicated)

Pharmacological Management
Table 25.6: Oxygen therapy: Administer oxygen and titrate according to pulse oximetry:

 Mild hypoxia/distress           Nasal cannula                         2–6 L/min (24–40% oxygen)
 Moderate hypoxia/distress       Face mask/Venturi mask                6–10 L/min (24–50% oxygen)

 Apnea/respiratory arrest        Bag-valve-mask ventilation            10–15 L/min (~100% oxygen)

Target oxygen saturation:
94–96% in most patients
88–92% in patients with Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease

                                                  OR
                                    A: epinephrine (adrenaline) 0.3–0.5 mg IM (1:1000 solution), may be repeated every 5–
                                    15 minutes if severe airway edema/anaphylaxis is suspected

 (≥12 years)                        dose: 2 mg

 Corticosteroids are not routinely recommended. Consider only in:
   •    Significant airway inflammation
   •    Reactive airway disease
   •    Severe chemical pneumonitis (specialist guidance recommended)

sections.title: Corrosive Compounds Poisoning
sections.text:
Examples: sodium hydroxide (drain/oven cleaners), potassium hydroxide, acids, bleach, disinfectants.

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •   Assess airway, breathing, and circulation immediately.
  •   Remove contaminated clothing if dermal exposure occurred.
  •   If ingestion is recent and patient is fully conscious with intact airway reflexes: Give small amounts of water OR milk
      (100–200 mL in adults; age-appropriate amounts in children) for dilution.
  •   Avoid large-volume dilution.
  •   Do NOT induce vomiting.
  •   Do NOT perform gastric lavage.
  •   Do NOT administer activated charcoal (ineffective and may interfere with endoscopy).
  •   Keep patient nil per mouth if severe pain, drooling, vomiting, or suspected perforation.

Pharmacological Management
 Clinical Condition             Management
 Hypoxia/respiratory distress   Administer oxygen therapy according to oxygen saturation and severity of respiratory distress
 Pain                           A: Paracetamol 1 g PO/IV every 6–8 hours as needed OR appropriate analgesia based on severity
 Severe pain                    C: Morphine 2.5–5 mg IV slowly as needed

Surgical / Specialist Review
Urgently arrange surgical/gastroenterology review for suspected:
  •    Esophageal burns                                          •   Persistent vomiting
  •    Esophageal rupture                                        •   Severe chest pain
  •    Gastrointestinal perforation                              •   Severe abdominal pain
  •    Mediastinitis                                             •   Hematemesis
  •    Peritonitis
Upper GI endoscopy may be required within 12–24 hours depending on severity.

sections.title: Petroleum Compounds Poisoning
sections.text:
Examples: kerosene, gasoline, turpentine, paraffin, paint thinners, petrol

Clinical Presentation
 System                         Clinical Presentation

                                pneumonitis, pulmonary edema
 Other Findings                 Characteristic smell of paraffin/petroleum products
 Central Nervous System         Headache, dizziness, euphoria, restlessness, ataxia, convulsions, encephalopathy, coma
 (CNS)

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •   Remove patient from source of exposure immediately.
  •   Remove contaminated clothing.
  •   Wash exposed skin thoroughly with soap and water.
  •   If eye exposure occurs, irrigate with clean water for at least 15–20 minutes.
  •   Do NOT induce vomiting.
  •   Do NOT perform gastric lavage unless under specialist toxicology advice for exceptional circumstances.
  •   Observe for aspiration pneumonitis and respiratory deterioration.

sections.title: Kerosene (Paraffin) Poisoning
sections.text:
Kerosene poisoning commonly affects children. The primary target organ is the respiratory system, and aspiration leads to
chemical pneumonitis which may be bilateral and interstitial.
Vomiting after ingestion is associated with increased risk of aspiration pneumonitis. CNS symptoms are usually secondary to
hypoxia.

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •   Immediately remove the child from the source of                  •    Provide respiratory support: Intubation and
      exposure.                                                             mechanical ventilation if severe hypoxia,
  •   Ensure airway patency and maintain ABC as first                       respiratory distress, or reduced consciousness.
      priority.                                                        •    Do NOT perform gastric lavage routinely due to
  •   Remove contaminated clothing and wash skin                            high risk of aspiration pneumonitis.
      thoroughly with soap and water.                                  •    Gastric lavage may only be considered:
  •   Monitor oxygen saturation using pulse oximetry                        > If a large ingestion occurred within 1 hour, and
      where available.                                                      > Airway is protected by expert endotracheal
  •   Administer supplemental oxygen if hypoxia or                          intubation.
      respiratory distress is present.

Pharmacological Management
Supportive fluid therapy (ONLY if shock or significant dehydration is present):
A: sodium lactate compound (ringer’s lactate)(Ringer’s Lactate) IV infusion 30 mL/kg IV bolus stat,
          OR
A: sodium Chloride 0.9% IV infusion 30 mL/kg IV bolus stat,
         THEN
Reassess, may continue guided fluid replacement up to 2 L over 24 hours in adults, or weight-based maintenance in children.

  Note:
    •   There is no evidence supporting the routine use of corticosteroids in kerosene (paraffin) poisoning; therefore, they
        are not recommended.
    •   No specific antidote exists for kerosene poisoning.
    •   Antibiotics are not routine (only if secondary bacterial infection develops)
    •   Mainstay of treatment is supportive respiratory care
    •   Hypoxia is the main cause of CNS symptoms

sections.title: Organophosphorus and Carbamate Compounds Poisoning
sections.text:
Organophosphates and carbamates are insecticides that inhibit cholinesterase, causing accumulation of acetylcholine and
leading to cholinergic toxicity.
Examples
Organophosphates: Malathion, Parathion, TEPP, mevinphos
Carbamates: carbaryl, methiocarb

Exposure occurs via ingestion, inhalation, or dermal absorption.

Clinical Presentation
 System / Toxicity Type                   Clinical Features
 Muscarinic effects (SLUDGE /             Salivation, lacrimation, urination, diarrhea, emesis, bronchorrhea, bronchospasm,
 DUMBBELLS)                               bradycardia, miosis
 Nicotinic effects                        Muscle fasciculations, weakness progressing to paralysis
 Central Nervous System (CNS)             Confusion, convulsions, coma
 Severe / Respiratory complications       Pulmonary oedema, respiratory depression, respiratory failure

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •   Immediately remove patient from exposure source.
  •   If dermal exposure: remove clothing and wash skin thoroughly with soap and water.
  •   If ocular exposure: irrigate eyes with clean water or normal saline.
  •   Do NOT induce vomiting (risk of aspiration due to hydrocarbon solvents).
  •   Give oxygen if SpO₂ < 90%
  •   Gastric decontamination (NG aspiration) Consider: NG aspiration ONLY in severe ingestion AND when airway is secured
      (intubated patient)
  •   Avoid decontamination procedures if airway is not protected due to risk of aspiration and worsening respiratory failure
  •   Monitor: Respiratory rate, Heart rate, Level of consciousness, Chest secretions (auscultation).
Pharmacological Management
 Treatment Category                     Management
 Atropine (First-line antidote for      A: atropine
 muscarinic symptoms)                   Adults: 5 mg IV bolus stat, repeat every 5–10 minutes until atropinization achieved:
                                        • Dry chest secretions
                                        • HR > 80 bpm
                                        • SBP > 80 mmHg
                                        • Pupils no longer pinpoint
                                        • Dry axillae
                                        Paediatrics: 0.05 mg/kg IV, then double dose every 5–10 minutes until
                                        atropinization

 (Organophosphate poisoning only)       minutes May repeat once or twice if required Maintenance infusion: 10–20
                                        mg/kg/hour IV infusion

                                        failure develops
 Charcoal, activated                    A: charcoal, activated PO/NG stat
 (decontamination)                      Adults: 50 g single dose
                                        Children: 1 g/kg (maximum 50 g)
                                        Only if ingestion occurred within 1 hour AND airway is protected
  Note:
    •     Atropine is life-saving and titrated to clinical endpoint (not fixed dose).
    •     Pralidoxime is indicated only in organophosphate poisoning (not carbamates in most cases).
    •     Early airway protection is critical in severe poisoning.
    •     Decontamination must never delay resuscitation.

sections.title: Paracetamol Poisoning
sections.text:
It is the commonest taken drug overdose. The toxic dose is highly variable. In general, the recommended maximum daily dose
for healthy adults is 4 grams.

Chronic excessive alcohol consumption and Isoniazid can induce CYP2E1, antiepileptics including carbamazepine, phenytoin,
and barbiturates induces CYP enzymes thus increasing the potential toxicity of Paracetamol.

Supportive care is essential in paracetamol toxicity. Immediate assess the patient's airway, breathing, and hemodynamic status

Clinical Presentation
  •    Phase-1: 0.5–24 hours after ingestion: asymptomatic, to nonspecific symptoms (anorexia, nausea, vomiting and
       malaise). Pallor, diaphoresis
  •    Phase-2: 18–72 hours after ingestion: Right upper quadrant abdominal pain, anorexia, nausea and vomiting, Tender
       right upper quadrant, tachycardia, hypotension and oliguria.
  •    Phase-3: 72–96 hours after ingestion: all of the above and jaundice, coagulopathy, hypoglycemia and hepatic
       encephalopathy, Acute Renal failure.
  •    Phase-4: 4th day to 3weeks after ingestion: patient who survive critical illness in phase 3, have complete recovery.

Investigations
  •    Liver Function Test - Liver transaminases ALT, AST,              •    ABG,
       ALP, Prothrombin Time (PT) with INR (International               •    LFTs,
       Normalization Ratio)                                             •    Full   Blood     Picture    (Leukocytosis       and
  •    Serum Glucose                                                         thrombocytopenia)
  •    Renal Function Test: Electrolytes, BUN, Creatinine               •    Coagulation studies (PT and PTT)
  •    ABG-Arterial Blood Gas

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •   Resuscitation
  •   In adults, the initial treatment for paracetamol overdose is gastrointestinal decontamination.
  •   Usually there is no immediate threat to the airway, breathing and circulation with paracetamol poisoning
  •   Correct hypoglycemia (Give glucose or sugar or honey)
  •   If within 1 hour of ingestion of 150mg/kg or more paracetamol give activated charcoal, if available.

Pharmacological Management
 Treatment Category                           Management
 Gastrointestinal decontamination             A: charcoal, activated 1 g/kg PO (maximum 50 g), given if within 1–2 hours of
                                              ingestion AND airway is protected
 First-line antidote (N-acetylcysteine        C: n-acetylcysteine (IV) Adults: 150 mg/kg in 200 mL 5% dextrose over 20 min,
 regimen)                                     THEN 50 mg/kg in 500 mL over 4 hours, THEN 100 mg/kg in 1 L over 16
                                              hours Children <20 kg: 150 mg/kg in 3 mL/kg 5% dextrose over 15 min, THEN 50
                                              mg/kg in 7 mL/kg over 4 hours, THEN 100 mg/kg in 14 mL/kg over 16 hours
                                              Severe poisoning: may repeat 100 mg/kg over additional 24 hours
 Alternative antidote                         S: methionine Use if patient is conscious, not vomiting, OR when N-
                                              acetylcysteine is not available or poorly tolerated <6 years: 1 g PO every 4 hours
                                              for 4 doses ≥6 years: 2.5 g PO every 4 hours for 4 doses

  Note: Syrup of ipecac is contraindicated in inducing vomiting to control paracetamol overdose because the vomiting it
  induces delays the effective administration of activated charcoal and oral acetylcysteine

sections.title: Acetylsalicylic Acid and other Salicylates Poisoning.
sections.text:
Clinical Presentation
 Stage                                                Clinical Features
 Early (Initial) features                             • Tinnitus and hearing impairment (classic early sign)
                                                      • Nausea and vomiting
                                                      • Hyperventilation (primary respiratory alkalosis → “acidotic breathing”
                                                      appearance) • Fever (especially in children)
                                                      • Dizziness and lightheadedness
                                                      • Dehydration
 Late / Severe features                               • Confusion, agitation, delirium, bizarre behavior
                                                      • Ataxia (unsteady gait)
                                                      • Coma
 Signs of severe toxicity (end-organ                  • Seizures
 involvement)                                         • Non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema
                                                      • Cerebral edema
                                                      • Rhabdomyolysis
                                                      • Acute kidney injury
                                                      • Severe metabolic acidosis

Investigations
  •    Arterial blood gases (ABG): mixed respiratory                       •    Blood glucose (hypoglycemia may occur,
       alkalosis + metabolic acidosis                                           especially in children)
  •    Serum electrolytes: Na⁺, K⁺, HCO₃⁻ (also Ca²⁺,                      •    Renal function tests
       Mg²⁺ if severe)                                                     •    Liver function tests (in severe poisoning)
  •    Serum salicylate concentration (serial levels                       •    ECG (arrhythmias, conduction abnormalities)
       important)

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •   Immediate ABC stabilization                                          •    Maintain adequate hydration
  •   Charcoal, activated 1 g/kg (max 50 g) if within 1                    •    Avoid acidifying agents
      hour (consider extended window in large ingestions                   •    Early referral to intensive care if moderate–severe
      or modified-release preparations)                                         poisoning
  •   Continuous monitoring: Vital signs, Neurological
      status, Blood glucose (regular monitoring, not fixed
      6-hourly in severe cases)

Pharmacological Management
 Indication/Condition                    Management
 Fluid resuscitation / dehydration       A: sodium chloride 0.9% (IV): 20 mL/kg bolus over 15–30 minutes if
                                         hypotensive/dehydrated, then continue maintenance/replacement fluids to maintain urine
                                         output of 1–2 mL/kg/hour
 Hypoglycemia (Adults)                   C: dextrose 50% (IV): 50 mL bolus (25 g glucose),
                                                   THEN
                                         A: dextrose 5% infusion IV according to blood glucose monitoring
 Hypoglycemia (Children)                 B: dextrose 10% (IV): 2–5 mL/kg bolus, followed by maintenance dextrose-containing fluids
                                         according to blood glucose monitoring
 Urinary alkalinization / metabolic      D: sodium bicarbonate (IV): 1–2 mEq/kg slow IV bolus, followed by infusion prepared by
 acidosis (moderate–severe               adding 150 mEq sodium bicarbonate (3 ampoules of 50 mL of 8.4%) in 1 litre of 5%
 poisoning)                              dextrose, infuse at 150–250 mL/hour (adjust according to clinical status) to maintain urine
                                         pH 7.5–8.0 and serum pH 7.45–7.55

 Indication/Condition                Management
 Hypokalemia                         C: potassium chloride (IV): 20–40 mEq added to each litre of IV fluid OR 10–20 mEq/hour
                                     IV infusion depending on serum potassium level and ECG monitoring
 Seizures                            A: diazepam (IV): 0.15–0.2 mg/kg (maximum 10 mg) slow IV, may repeat once after 5–10
                                     minutes
                                               OR
                                     C: lorazepam (IV): 0.1 mg/kg (maximum 4 mg) slow IV, may repeat once if needed

  Note: Hemodialysis is required if the concentration exceeds 700mg/liter or in presence of severe metabolic acidosis

sections.title: Iron Poisoning
sections.text:
Symptoms appear at doses greater than 20mg/kg. Iron levels above 350–500µg/dL are considered toxic, and levels over
1000µg/dL indicate severe iron poisoning. Iron pills can look like candy to children. Intentional overdose can occur among
adults, but is rare.
 Parameter                       Description
 Toxic dose of elemental iron    • <20 mg/kg: Usually non-toxic
                                 • 20–60 mg/kg: Mild to moderate toxicity
                                 • >60 mg/kg: Severe toxicity likely
                                 • >120 mg/kg: Potentially fatal poisoning
 Serum iron levels               • 350–500 micrograms/dL: Toxic
                                 • >500 micrograms/dL: Severe toxicity
                                 • >1000 micrograms/dL: Life-threatening poisoning
 Common cause                    • Iron tablets may resemble candy and are a common cause of accidental poisoning in
                                 children
 Adult exposure                  • Intentional overdose in adults is uncommon

Clinical Presentation
 Stage                     Clinical Features
 Stage I (0–6 hours)       Nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, hematemesis, melena/black stools
 Stage II (6–24 hours)     Apparent clinical improvement (latent phase)
 Stage III (12–48 hours)   Shock, metabolic acidosis, GI hemorrhage, hypotension, altered mental status, seizures
 Stage IV (2–5 days)       Hepatic failure
 Stage V (2–8 weeks)       Gastric outlet obstruction/bowel scarring (rare)

Investigations
  •    Serum iron level (4–6 hours post ingestion)                    •    Liver function tests
  •    Serum electrolytes                                             •    Renal function tests
  •    Blood glucose                                                  •    Full blood count
  •    Arterial blood gas                                             •    Abdominal X-ray (may show radiopaque tablets)

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •   ABC stabilization
  •   IV fluids if dehydrated/shocked
  •   Whole bowel irrigation may be considered for large ingestion or visible tablets on X-ray
  •   Routine gastric lavage is generally NOT recommended unless:
      > Massive ingestion
      > Presentation within 1 hour
      > Airway protected

Pharmacological Management
Moderate poisoning
D: deferoxamine (IM) 50 mg/kg every 4–12 hours

Severe poisoning
D: deferoxamine (IV infusion) 15 mg/kg/hour

Continue until:
  •   Clinical improvement
  •   Serum iron normalizes
  •   Resolution of metabolic acidosis
  •   Urine color returns from “vin rose” to normal

sections.title: Carbon Monoxide Poisoning
sections.text:
Carbon monoxide (CO) is a colorless, odorless gas produced by incomplete combustion of organic compounds. Exposure
commonly occurs in private residences due to: Improper use of gasoline-powered generators, Indoor use of charcoal for
cooking/heating, Faulty heating systems, House fires, Poor ventilation.

Clinical Presentation
Mild to Moderate Poisoning
  •     Headache                                                      •    Flu-like symptoms
  •     Dizziness                                                     •    Blurred vision
  •     Weakness                                                      •    Chest pain
  •     Nausea/vomiting                                               •    Shortness of breath

Severe Poisoning
  •   Confusion                                                       •    Cardiac arrhythmias
  •   Loss of consciousness                                           •    Coma
  •   Seizures                                                        •    Death

  Note: Patients may appear “pink” or have normal pulse oximetry readings despite significant hypoxia.

Investigations
  •    Complete clinical assessment and detailed                      •    Serum electrolytes
       exposure history                                               •    Carboxyhemoglobin level (if available)
  •    Identification of probable exposure source/risk                •    ECG (if chest pain or arrhythmias suspected)
       factors
  •    Arterial blood gases (ABG)

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •   Remove patient from exposure source immediately
  •   Ensure airway, breathing, and circulation (ABC stabilization)
  •   Administer 100% oxygen via non-rebreather mask or bag-valve mask at 10–15 L/min until symptoms resolve and
      carboxyhemoglobin levels normalize
  •   Continuous cardiac monitoring if severe poisoning
  •   Perform CPR if patient is unconscious and pulseless
  •   Consider urgent referral for hyperbaric oxygen therapy (if available) in severe poisoning:
      > Loss of consciousness
      > Severe neurological symptoms
      > Pregnancy
      > Significant cardiac ischemia
      > Severe metabolic acidosis

Table 25.8: Carbon Monoxide Elimination Half-Life
 Oxygen Therapy                                                           Approximate Carbon Monoxide Half-Life
 21% oxygen at normal atmospheric pressure (room air)                     4–6 hours (approximately 5 hours 20 minutes)
 100% oxygen at normal atmospheric pressure (non-rebreather mask)         60–90 minutes (approximately 1 hour 20 minutes)
 100% hyperbaric oxygen (2–3 atmospheres absolute)                        15–30 minutes

  Note
    •    Administration of 100% oxygen significantly accelerates dissociation of carbon monoxide from hemoglobin.
    •    Hyperbaric oxygen therapy should be considered in severe poisoning (e.g., loss of consciousness, neurological
         symptoms, pregnancy, severe acidosis, cardiac ischemia).
     •   Public Health Prevention Measures should be done e.g. ensuring proper ventilation

sections.title: Opioid Poisoning
sections.text:
Opioid poisoning occurs following excessive exposure to opioids due to: Substance abuse, Unintentional overdose, Intentional
overdose, Therapeutic medication errors, Neonatal exposure (maternal opioid use during delivery), and Palliative/terminal care
dosing errors
Common opioids involved include: Codeine, Diamorphine, Dihydrocodeine, Fentanyl, Heroin, Loperamide, Methadone,
Morphine, Opium, or Tramadol. These may be taken alone or in combination with other sedatives.

Risk Factors for Toxicity
  •   People with opioid use disorder
  •   Social vulnerability/disadvantaged populations
  •   Previous opioid exposure for pain treatment
  •   Concurrent alcohol use
  •   Concurrent sedative use (e.g., benzodiazepines)

Clinical Presentation
 Type                                           Clinical Features
 Early/Acute toxicity                           • Drowsiness
                                                • Nausea/vomiting
                                                • Slurred speech
 Severe toxicity (classic opioid toxidrome)     • Respiratory depression/bradypnea
                                                • Reduced level of consciousness/coma
                                                • Pinpoint pupils (miosis)
                                                • Hypotension
                                                • Bradycardia (tachycardia may occur in hypoxia but is not classic)
 Chronic toxicity/adverse effects               • Constipation
                                                • Loss of appetite
                                                • Nausea/vomiting

Investigations
  •    Full blood count                                                 •    Arterial blood gas
  •    Pregnancy test (where appropriate)                               •    Blood glucose
  •    Liver function tests (ALT/AST)                                   •    ECG (recommended in all suspected overdoses,
  •    Renal function tests (urea, creatinine)                               especially Methadone overdose due to QT
  •    Creatine         kinase         (if     prolonged                     prolongation)
       immobilization/rhabdomyolysis suspected)

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •   Assess and secure airway                                          •    Administer supplemental oxygen
  •   Provide assisted ventilation if required                          •    Continuous pulse oximetry and cardiac monitoring
  •   Intubate patients unable to protect airway

Pharmacological Management
1. hypo-ventilating patient with spontaneous ventilation

Adults and children >20 kg
B: naloxone (IV) 0.4–0.5 mg initially, repeat every 2–3 minutes and titrate upward until respiratory rate ≥12 breaths/min and
adequate ventilation is achieved. Maximum cumulative dose typically 10 mg.
Children <20 kg
B: naloxone (IV) 0.01 mg/kg initially (maximum 2 mg/dose); may increase to 0.1 mg/kg if inadequate response.

 Note
   •     Before administering Naloxone, ensure airway support and provide 100% oxygen or assist ventilation using a bag-
         valve-mask in patients with respiratory depression or apnea until adequate spontaneous breathing resumes.
    •    Usual initial dose of Naloxone: Adults: 0.4–2 mg IV, Children: 0.1 mg/kg IV (maximum 2 mg per dose)
    •    In suspected chronic opioid users, Naloxone should be administered slowly and titrated carefully to avoid
         precipitating acute withdrawal and sudden return of severe pain: Start with 0.04–0.1 mg IV, Repeat every 1–3
         minutes as needed until adequate ventilation is restored
    •    The goal of Naloxone therapy is restoration of adequate respiratory function, not necessarily full consciousness.
    •    Onset of action is usually within 1–2 minutes IV, with peak response occurring within 3–8 minutes.
    •    Repeat doses may be required if signs of opioid toxicity persist or recur, particularly with long-acting opioids such as
         Methadone or Buprenorphine.
    •    Some patients may require continuous naloxone infusion due to the shorter half-life of Naloxone compared with long-
         acting opioids.
    •    Patients with Buprenorphine toxicity may show incomplete response to standard naloxone doses and may require
         higher doses, prolonged monitoring, and ventilatory support.
    •    Monitor for recurrent respiratory depression after initial reversal.
    •    Observe for acute opioid withdrawal symptoms in opioid-dependent patients.

2. Patients with apnea

Newborn with apnea secondary to maternal opioid exposure
B: naloxone (IV/IM) 0.01 mg/kg (maximum 0.4 mg/dose)
Children <20 kg
B: naloxone (IV) 0.1 mg/kg (maximum 2 mg/dose), repeat doses or continuous infusion as required
Adults and children >20 kg
B: naloxone (IV) 0.2–2 mg initially, titrate to clinical response

3. Life-threatening opioid toxicity

Children <20 kg
B: naloxone (IV) 0.1 mg/kg (maximum 2 mg/dose)
Adults and children >20 kg
B: naloxone (IV) 2 mg initially
> Repeat dose every 2–3 minutes until respiratory function improves.
> If a maximum cumulative dose of 10 mg is reached without improvement, consider alternative diagnoses or co-ingestants.
> Continuous infusion may be required for recurrent toxicity, especially with long-acting opioids such as Methadone or
   Buprenorphine.
 Note
     •   In neonates exposed to maternal opioids, rapid reversal with high doses of Naloxone may precipitate acute opioid
         withdrawal, which can be severe and potentially life-threatening. Therefore:
         > Use low initial doses of Naloxone
         > Recommended dose: 0.01 mg/kg IV/IM
         > Titrate cautiously based on respiratory response
     •   Supportive airway management and ventilation remain essential.

Further management of Psychiatric Management of Opioid Toxicity refer Mental Disorders Chapter 23

sections.title: Heavy Metal Poisoning
sections.text:
This includes mercury, arsenic, cadmium, copper, lead poisoning and thallium
The management of heavy metal toxicity depends on the specific metal, route of exposure and length of time between exposure
and clinical presentation of symptoms

sections.title: Lead Poisoning
sections.text:
Lead is a heavy metal with no physiological role in the human body. Common sources include: Lead-based paint and paint dust
(especially older buildings), Contaminated water pipes, Industrial exposure, Batteries, Traditional cosmetics/herbal remedies
Contaminated soil. Lead poisoning often develops gradually over months to years and may cause irreversible toxicity.

Clinical Presentation
 Population Group     Clinical Features
 Newborns             Prematurity , Low birth weight , Slowed growth.

 Children                 Developmental delay, Learning difficulties, Irritability, Loss of appetite, Weight loss, Fatigue,
                          Abdominal pain, Vomiting, Constipation, Hearing loss, Seizures, Pica, Reduced IQ,
                          Anxiety/depression, ADHD-like symptoms.
 Adults                   Hypertension, Joint/muscle pain, Memory/concentration difficulties, Headache, Abdominal pain ,
                          Mood disorders, Reduced sperm count, Miscarriage/stillbirth/prematurity, Anemia, Fanconi
                          syndrome, Wrist drop

Investigations
  •    Blood lead level (BLL)                                           •    Liver function tests (ALT/AST)
  •    Free erythrocyte protoporphyrin (FEP)                            •    Renal function tests (creatinine, BUN)
  •    Erythrocyte protoporphyrin (EP)                                  •    Imaging studies as indicated: Abdominal X-ray,
  •    Full blood count                                                      Chest X-ray, Bone X-ray.

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •   Remove source of lead exposure                                    •    Monitor cardiovascular status
  •   Community/environmental assessment                                •    Monitor neurological status
  •   Maintain adequate hydration and urine output                      •    Assess renal and hepatic function

Pharmacological Management
(Chelation Therapy)
 Blood Lead Level / Clinical Status       Management
 25–44 micrograms/dL(symptomatic          D: penicillamine (PO) 30–40 mg/kg/day for 1–6 months, administer 2 hours before
 or persistent exposure)                  or 3 hours after meals
 45–69 micrograms/dL                      D: succimer (PO) 10 mg/kg every 8 hours for 5 days, followed by 10 mg/kg every
                                          12 hours for 14 days
 >70 micrograms/dL OR                     D: dimercaprol (deep IM) 3–5 mg/kg every 4 hours for 48 hours, followed by dose
 encephalopathy                           adjustment based on clinical response
                                                   AND
                                          D: calcium disodium EDTA (ethylene diamine tetra-acetic acid)
                                          (IV infusion) 10–20 mg/kg/day divided every 8–12 hours for 5 days

sections.title: Mercury Toxicity
sections.text:
Mercury in all forms is toxic. Poisoning may result from: Mercury vapor inhalation, Accidental or intentional mercury injection,
Dermal absorption, Ingestion of mercury-containing compounds, or Consumption of contaminated seafood containing
methylmercury (organic mercury).

Clinical Presentation
 Type of Mercury             Clinical Features
 Inorganic Mercury           Ash-gray mucous membranes, Hematochezia, Severe abdominal pain, Foul breath, Metallic
                             taste, Stomatitis, Gingival irritation, Loosening of teeth, Hypovolemic shock, Acute kidney
                             injury/renal tubular necrosis
 Organic Mercury             Visual disturbances (scotomata, visual field constriction) , Ataxia, Paresthesia (early sign) ,
 (Methylmercury)             Hearing loss , Dysarthria, Mental deterioration, Tremors, Movement disorders, Paralysis, Death
                             (severe exposure)

Laboratory Investigations
  •   Blood mercury levels                                             •    Toenail mercury level (chronic exposure)
  •   Urine mercury levels                                             •    CSF mercury level (selected severe neurological
  •   Full blood count                                                      cases)
  •   Renal function tests                                             •    Plain abdominal X-ray (if ingestion suspected)
  •   Hair mercury level (chronic exposure)

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •   Remove patient from source of exposure
  •   Maintain Airway, Breathing and Circulation (ABC)
  •   Administer oxygen if required
  •   Copious skin irrigation if dermal exposure occurred
  •   Routine gastric lavage is not recommended, may be considered only in selected cases of recent significant ingestion,
      when mercury is visible on abdominal imaging and the airway is protected.
  •   Hemodialysis may be required in severe renal failure
  •   Surgical/endoscopic removal may be required for retained mercury in the gastrointestinal tract

Pharmacological Management
(Chelation Therapy)
 Clinical Scenario         Management
 Recent ingestion          A: charcoal, activated (PO) may be considered in ingested poisons, though effectiveness
                           in mercury poisoning is limited
 Mild–moderate mercury     D: succimer (DMSA) (PO) 10 mg/kg every 8 hours for 5 days, followed by 10 mg/kg every
 poisoning                 12 hours for 14 days (maximum 500 mg/dose)
 Severe acute inorganic    D: dimercaprol (deep IM) 5 mg/kg stat, then 2.5 mg/kg IM every 12 hours for 10 days
 mercury poisoning

 Note: Surgical or endoscopic intervention may be required to remove mercury retained/lodged in the gastrointestinal tract
 (e.g., intestine or colon), particularly when spontaneous passage fails or ongoing absorption is suspected.

sections.title: Prevention of Poisoning
sections.text:
Educate patients and caregivers on do’s and don’ts for prevention of poisoning.

Do’s                                                               Don’ts
  •    Keep medicines and poisons in properly labeled                •    Do not leave containers open
       containers and out of reach of children                       •    Do not transfer chemicals or medicines into
  •    Use containers with child-resistant caps                           unlabeled or inappropriate containers
  •    Consult the Material Safety Data Sheet (MSDS) for             •    Do not remove labels from medicine or chemical
       chemical handling and safety information                           products
  •    Keep all products in their original containers                •    Do not store tablets in alternative containers such
  •    Read medicine labels carefully to avoid medication                 as purses, envelopes, or bags
       errors                                                        •    Do not refer to medicines as “sweets” or candy
  •    Contact the Poison Information Centre for                     •    Do not take medicines in front of children, as they
       guidance: 0800112031                                               may imitate the behavior

sections.title: Alcohol Intoxication
sections.text: Management of alcohol intoxication see mental health conditions on chapter 23.

sections.title: Bites and Stings
sections.text:
Most serious sting-related reactions are caused by insects of the order Hymenoptera, particularly: Bees, Wasps and Ants.
Other arthropods/venomous creatures that may also cause bites or stings include: Spiders, Scorpions, Centipedes, Millipedes.

Clinical Presentation
Localized pain at the bite/sting site, Swelling, Redness, Itching. Severe reactions may include: Generalized urticaria,
Angioedema, Wheezing, Difficulty breathing, Hypotension, Anaphylaxis.

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •   Clean the affected area with soap and water to                  •   Apply a cold compress/cold pack wrapped in cloth
      remove contaminants                                                 to reduce pain and swelling
  •   If a stinger is present (e.g., bee sting), remove it            •   Avoid scratching to prevent skin breakdown and
      gently by scraping with a fingernail, card, or gauze                secondary infection
  •   Avoid using tweezers because they may squeeze
      additional venom into the wound

Pharmacological Management
 Indication                         Management
 Pain and inflammation              A: ibuprofen (PO) Adults: 400–800 mg every 8 hours for 3 days
                                    Children: 10 mg/kg every 8 hours (maximum 400 mg/day) for 3 days
 Moderate inflammatory              A: prednisolone (PO) 2 mg/kg/day as a single daily dose (maximum 80 mg/day) for 5
 reaction/severe local swelling     days
 Allergic symptoms (first-          A: chlorpheniramine (PO)
 generation antihistamine)          • <6 years: 1 mg every 4–6 hours as needed (maximum 6 mg/day)
                                    • 6–12 years: 2 mg every 4–6 hours as needed (maximum 12 mg/day)
                                    • >12 years/adults: 4 mg every 4–6 hours as needed (maximum 24 mg/day)
 Non-sedating antihistamine         C: loratadine (PO)
                                    • 2–5 years: 5 mg once daily (syrup)
                                    • ≥6 years/adults: 10 mg once daily

 Note:
   •   In case of severe Allergic reaction like anaphylaxis, manage according to Chapter 1: Approach To Patients With
       Emergency Conditions
   •   For Centipedes Ensure your patient’s tetanus vaccination is up to date.

sections.title: Bee and Wasps Sting
sections.text:
Bee venom contains multiple toxins including hemolytic enzymes, neurotoxic factors, histamine, and lytic peptides. Wasp
venom contains substances such as hyaluronidase and serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine).

Prevention of Complications After Sting
  •   Move victim to a safe area to prevent additional stings
  •   Remove stinger promptly if present (scrape gently using card/gauze/fingernail)
  •   Wash affected area with soap and water
  •   Apply cold compress/ice pack wrapped in cloth
  •   Apply Hydrocortisone 0.5–1% cream, calamine lotion, or baking soda paste for local irritation

Clinical Presentation
 Type                               Clinical Features

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •   Assess airway, breathing, and circulation
  •   Remove stingers carefully
  •   Elevate affected limb
  •   Clean wound
  •   Monitor for anaphylaxis

   •   Patients with multiple stings should be observed for at least 24 hours for delayed systemic toxicity.
   •   Healthy adults: observe if there are >50 stings, Children: observe if there are >1 sting per kilogram body weight or if
       there are systemic symptoms/anaphylaxis
   •   Any patient with: Respiratory distress, Hypotension, Anaphylaxis, Rhabdomyolysis, Hemolysis or Renal impairment
       should be admitted and closely monitored regardless of the number of stings.

sections.title: Scorpion Sting (Envenoming)
sections.text:
Scorpion stings can cause severe local pain and systemic toxicity. Children are at higher risk of severe envenoming and death
compared to adults.

Clinical Presentation
 System/Type                    Clinical Features
 Local effects                  Severe pain at sting site , Paresthesia at or near sting site
 Neurological / cranial         Paresthesia distant from sting site , Blurred vision , Nystagmus / roving eye movements ,
 effects                        Tongue fasciculations , Dysphagia , Dysphonia , Restlessness Tremors or involuntary
                                jerking movements ,Tetanus-like muscle rigidity
 Autonomic effects              Tachycardia or bradycardia, Hypertension or hypotension , Excess salivation and
                                lacrimation, Urinary and fecal incontinence , Sweating
 Severe / systemic effects      Pulmonary edema , Cardiogenic shock , Hyperthermia , Rhabdomyolysis , Multi-organ
                                failure, Death (usually due to cardiogenic shock or pulmonary edema)

Grading of Envenomation
 Grade        Clinical Features
 Grade I       Local pain ± mild paresthesia at sting site
 Grade II      Local pain and paresthesia extending proximal to sting site
 Grade III     Cranial nerve involvement (excess salivation, visual disturbance, nystagmus) and/or neuromuscular
               dysfunction (tremors, muscle spasms, abnormal posturing) ± autonomic dysfunction
 Grade IV      Severe systemic toxicity including pulmonary edema, rhabdomyolysis, hyperthermia, cardiogenic shock, and
               multi-organ failure

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •   Ensure airway, breathing, and circulation (ABC)
  •   Provide oxygen therapy
  •   Keep patient calm to reduce sympathetic stimulation
  •   Continuous monitoring of: Oxygen saturation, Heart rate, Respiratory rate and Blood pressure.
  •   Early recognition and management of pulmonary edema or shock

Pharmacological Management

 Local wound care                              Clean sting site with normal saline
 Fluid resuscitation                           A: sodium lactate compound (ringer’s lactate)(IV) as required (approx.

 III–IV)                                       30 minutes Initial: 1 vial infused over 10 minutes, observe for response
                                               for 60 minutes Repeat remaining vials (up to total 3 vials) at 30-minute
                                               intervals if symptoms persist

 Severe pain (rescue analgesia)                C: morphine (IV/IM) titrated according to severity
 Local anesthetic for severe localized pain    A: lidocaine 1% infiltration at sting site
 Severe cardiovascular/respiratory             Prepare for airway support, intubation, and intensive care monitoring

chapters.intro:
Poison is any substance (liquid, solid, gas), that is harmful to the body, when ingested, inhaled, injected or absorbed through
the skin. There is a variability of the clinical presentation and poisonings vary by nature of poison, victims’ age group, intention,
geographic region, and level of economic development. Poisons can be classified according to whether the chemical is metallic
versus nonmetallic, organic versus inorganic, or acidic versus alkaline.
Common Poisons
The common poisoning in our settings are:
  •   Household agents:
      > Chemicals e.g. detergents, Kerosene, Disinfectants and bleach
      > Pesticides e.g. Organophosphate, malathion (insecticide), nuvan top and rat poison.
      > Medicines e.g. Acetylsalicylic Acid, Paracetamol, Anticonvulsants (carbamazepine), Hematinic (Iron and Vitamins),
  •   Major tranquilizers and herbal products
  •   Foods e.g. Mushroom, infected foods
General Principles of Management of Poisoning
In managing a patient who has been exposed to toxins holistic approach should be considered.
 Note
   •  A low respiratory rate with decreased oxygen saturations may indicate hypoventilation. A normal saturation does not
      exclude hypercarbia or indeed hypoxia in carbon monoxide poisoning. If in any doubt, arterial blood gases should be
      measured. Tachypnoea can be seen with metabolic acidosis (e.g. tricyclics, methanol), anxiety, and stimulant drug
      overdose and as an early feature of salicylate poisoning (respiratory alkalosis).
   •  Supplementary oxygen via facemask should be given to all patients initially, taking account of pulse oximetry (noting
      the limitations described above).
   •  Many drugs exhibit cardiovascular toxicity hypotension and or cardiac arrhythmias in overdose (e.g. tricyclics, b-
      blockers, digoxin, lithium). ECG should be recorded, intravenous access established and initial fluid resuscitation given
      as appropriate
   •  General examination may give corroborating evidence of significant ingestions or clues in unknown overdoses (SSRIs,
      tricyclics, phenothiazines) have serotonergic or anticholinergic effects with pupil dilatation, and extrapyramidal
      movements, whilst opioid type drugs will cause sedation and pin point pupils.
   •  Temperature, blood glucose (low in b-blocker, ethanol poisoning)
   •  Weight is important in identifying a toxic dose against the weight and may guide treatment, for example in paracetamol
      overdose.
   •  Examination for injury (intentional or un-intentional self-harm) suggest appropriate methods for treatment, or the
      presence of other substances such as alcohol.
   •  If clinical condition allows, an assessment of the patient’s mental state should be made.
Resuscitation and stabilization which is key to every poison refer to EMD Chapter 1
Airway, breathing and circulation should be reassessed and treated accordingly as a priority. Refer Approach to patient with
Emergency conditions chapter 1.
