chapters.title: Rheumatological Disorders

sections.title: Inflammatory Arthritis
sections.text:
Inflammatory arthritis refers to a group of diseases characterized by inflammation of the joints, including:
   •   Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)                                        •   Reactive Arthritis
   •   Psoriatic Arthritis (PsA)                                        •   Enteropathic Arthritis (associated with IBD)
   •   Axial Spondyloarthritis

sections.title: Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
sections.text:
RA is a chronic, systemic autoimmune disease that primarily affects synovial joints, causing symmetrical inflammation, pain,
and progressive joint deformity. It often involves the hands and feet, but any synovial joint may be affected. Extra-articular
manifestations (such as those affecting the skin, heart, lungs, and eyes) can also occur.

Clinical Presentation
  •    Symmetrical joint swelling, stiffness, and pain
  •    Morning stiffness >30 minutes
  •    Fatigue and general malaise
  •    Extra-articular signs (e.g., nodules, lung or eye involvement)
  •    Small and large joint tenderness, swelling, stiffness, pain on motion, deformity, and functional limitation.

Investigations
  •    CBC: anemia of chronic disease, thrombocytosis, or leukopenia (may occur with Felty's syndrome or DMARD toxicity).
  •    ESR and CRP: used both for diagnosis and monitoring disease activity and treatment response. Serologic tests: RF:
       Positive in ~70–80% of RA cases; less specific. Anti-CCP: More specific for RA; indicates a risk of severe erosive
       disease and extra-articular disease.
  •    Imaging
       > X-ray (hands, wrists, feet): Shows swelling, osteopenia, joint narrowing, and erosions. Chest X-ray to rule out ILD or
       TB
       > Ultrasound (US): Detects synovitis, effusion, and erosions earlier than X-ray.
       > CT: Used for suspected atlantoaxial subluxation, preoperative cervical spine planning, or unclear MRI findings.
       > MRI: More sensitive, identifying bone marrow edema and early erosions.

Diagnosis
RA is classified by ACR/EULAR 2010 criteria with a score ≥6/10 based on joints, serology, inflammation markers, and symptom
duration.

Treatment consideration
  •   Assess disease activity using the Disease Activity Score in 28 joints (DAS28), Clinical Disease Activity Index (CDAI),
      and Simplified Disease Activity Index (SDAI)
  •   Monitor and adjust treatment every 3 months
  •   Follow a treat-to-target strategy with tight control
  •   Aim for low disease activity or remission within 6 months

Non-Pharmacological Management:
  •   Education
  •   Physical therapy
  •   Occupational therapy
  •   Lifestyle: Smoking cessation, Healthy diet & weight control, Psychosocial support.

Pharmacological Management

1. Disease-modifying anti-rheumatic Drugs (DMARDs)
DMARDs are the cornerstone of RA treatment. They should be started as soon as the diagnosis is made.

a). Conventional Synthetic DMARDs (csDMARDs)
All patients with active rheumatoid arthritis should be initiated on methotrexate as first-line therapy unless there are
contraindications or intolerance

S: methotrexate (PO) Start with 10–15 mg/week; increase by 5 mg every 2–4 weeks, depending on the response, up to a
maximum of 20-25mg/week.
           AND
A: folic acid (PO) 5 mg weekly, taken a day before methotrexate. For severe toxicity, give daily (except on methotrexate day)
           OR
S: leflunomide (PO) 10–20 mg 24hourly.
           OR
S: hydroxychloroquine (PO) 200–400mg 24hourly, (usually 5 mg/kg/day, max 400 mg/day).
           OR
D: sulfasalazine (PO) 500 mg twice daily initially; increase by 500 mg every week to target 2–3 g/day in divided doses
maintenance dose 1–1.5 g twice daily.

If the response is inadequate, step-up combination therapy of csDMARDs is advised.

 Note:
   •     Hydroxychloroquine: Annual eye exam after 5 years or earlier if high risk.
   •     Methotrexate: Split dose or subcutaneous if poorly tolerated.
   •     Sulfasalazine: Avoid sulfa allergy.
   •     Triple therapy: Combines methotrexate, sulfasalazine, and hydroxychloroquine; leflunomide may be used as an
         alternative to methotrexate.
    •    Methotrexate & leflunomide: Contraindicated in pregnancy and breastfeeding. Avoid leflunomide in women planning
         pregnancy.

b). Biologic DMARDs (bDMARDs)
In moderate-to-severe RA not controlled by csDMARDs, adding a bDMARD or tsDMARD is preferred.

S: rituximab (IV) 1000 mg on days 1 and 15; may repeat every 6 months or based on response.
           OR
S: adalimumab (SC) 40 mg subcutaneously every other week (may increase to weekly if needed)
           OR
S: tocilizumab (IV) 4mg/kg every other 4 weeks may increase to 8mg/kg (Max 800mg/dose)

c). Targeted Synthetic DMARDs (tsDMARDs)
JAK inhibitors are used after the failure of csDMARDs or bDMARDs.
S: tofacitinib (PO) 5 mg12hourly.

2. Glucocorticoids
Used for short-term (< 3 months) control and as bridging therapy.

A: prednisolone (PO) 5–15 mg/day orally (4-6 weeks). Gradually reduce over weeks to months, depending on the response
          OR
D: methylprednisolone (IV/IM) 500–1000 mg daily for 1–3 days for severe flares.
          OR
S: triamcinolone acetonide: deep IM 10–40 mg monthly or IA in case only 1-2 joints are affected

3. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory Drugs (NSAIDs)
Used for symptom control only (do not modify disease course).

A: Ibuprofen (PO) 400–800 mg 8 hourly                                         OR
          OR                                                        S: ketoprofen (PO) 75mg 8 hourly
C: diclofenac (PO) 50mg 8-12hourly                                            OR
          OR                                                        S: ketoprofen gel 2.5% apply 6 hourly
A: piroxicam (PO) 20mg 24hourly                                               OR
          OR                                                        A: diclofenac gel 1% apply 6 hourly
D: meloxicam (PO) 7.5–15 mg 24hourly

  Note: In patients at high risk of NSAID-related gastrointestinal complications, co-administration of a PPI should be
  considered to reduce the risk of PUD and UGB

Surgical management
is indicated when medical treatment fails to relieve pain, maintain function, or prevent deformity.

Peripheral joint care:
  •   Joint replacement
  •   Synovectomy
  •   Tendon repair or transfer
  •   Arthrodesis

Cervical Spine Involvement
  •   Atlantoaxial subluxation should be routinely monitored in long-standing RA; surgery is indicated in cases of instability
      with neurological symptoms.
  •   Basilar invagination (BI) may occur due to ligamentous and bony weakening. Surgical management includes
      decompression and stabilization via C1–C2 fusion or craniovertebral fusion, depending on severity.

Perioperative and Postoperative Considerations
  •   Biologics and JAK inhibitors should be temporarily withheld perioperatively based on the risk of infection and the
      complexity of the procedure.
  •   Postoperative rehabilitation is crucial for optimizing functional recovery, particularly after joint replacement or tendon
      procedures.

Special Considerations in RA Treatment
  •   Subcutaneous Nodules: Use methotrexate for active disease; switch DMARD if nodules worsen
  •   Heart Failure (HF) (NYHA III/IV): Prefer non-TNF bDMARDs or tsDMARDs over TNF inhibitors if csDMARDs fail or HF
      develops.
  •   Pulmonary Disease: MTX is acceptable in mild, stable lung disease or incidental findings.
  •   Lymphoproliferative Disorder: Rituximab is preferred if there is a history of treated lymphoproliferative disease.
  •   Hepatitis B:
      > HBsAg-positive: Use rituximab with prophylactic antivirals.
      > Core Ab positive only: Monitor viral load and LFTs.
  •   NAFLD: MTX is safe if LFTs are normal and no advanced fibrosis
  •   Cardiovascular disease: Tofacitinib is contraindicated in patients with a history of myocardial infarction, stroke, or HF.

sections.title: Psoriatic Arthritis (PsA)
sections.text:
PsA is a chronic inflammatory arthritis that is usually seen in patients with psoriasis, although it may predate skin involvement,
which can be subtle. It typically presents as seronegative oligoarthritic, with features such as distal joint involvement, arthritis
mutilans, or inflammation of joints, spine, entheses, nails, and skin.

Clinical Presentation
  •    Joints: Asymmetric, DIP, spine, severe deformity (mutilans)
  •    Dactylitis: Swollen “sausage” digits with PIP synovitis
  •    Enthesitis: Tender tendon insertions
  •    Skin/Nails: Psoriasis, nail pitting/onycholysis
  •    Other: Fatigue, stiffness, joint swelling, and tenderness on exam

Investigations
  •    ESR, CRP (sometimes normal)
  •    RF and anti-CCP (usually negative)
  •    HLA-B27 for those with suspected axial involvement.
  •    X-rays: First-line; show erosions, new bone, pencil-in-cup, ankylosis, asymmetric sacroiliitis.
  •    Ultrasound: Shows synovitis, enthesitis, tenosynovitis; Doppler detects active inflammation
  •    MRI: gold standard test for sacroiliitis and spinal involvement

Diagnosis
PsA is diagnosed using CASPAR criteria, requiring inflammatory joint, spine, or enthesis involvement plus ≥3 points from
clinical, lab, or imaging features.

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •   Weight reduction                                                   •    Stress reduction
  •   Skin care (avoid trauma)                                           •    Smoking cessation
  •   Physical therapy                                                   •    Alcohol reduction

Pharmacological Management
1.Non-Steroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drugs (NSAIDs)
  •   For mild peripheral arthritis, enthesitis, or axial symptoms without poor prognostic factors.
  •   Relieve symptoms but don’t prevent damage.
  •   Not for monotherapy in moderate-to-severe disease

A: Ibuprofen (PO) 400–800 mg 8 hourly                                D: meloxicam (PO) 7.5–15 mg 24 hourly
          OR                                                                  OR
C: diclofenac (PO) 50 mg orally 8–12 hourly                          S: ketoprofen (PO) 75mg 8 hourly
          OR                                                                  OR
A: diclofenac gel 1% apply 6 hourly                                  S: ketoprofen (PO) 50mg 6 hourly
          OR                                                                  OR
A: piroxicam (PO) 20 mg 24 hourly                                    S: ketoprofen gel 2.5% apply 6 hourly
          OR

  Note: In patients at high risk of NSAID-related gastrointestinal complications, co-administration of a PPI should be
  considered to reduce the risk of PUD and UGB

2. Conventional Synthetic DMARDs (csDMARDs)
S: methotrexate (PO) A first-line csDMARDs is especially effective in patients with skin and nail involvement. 15–25 mg once
weekly.
           AND
A: folic acid (PO) 5mg weekly, taken a day before methotrexate. For severe toxicity, give daily (except on methotrexate day)
           OR
D: sulfasalazine: (PO) 500mg 12hourly initially; increase by 500 mg every week to target 2–3 g/day in divided doses
           OR
S: leflunomide (PO) 10mg 24 hourly, increase to 20mg 24hourly

3. Biologic DMARDs (bDMARDs)
Used in moderate-to-severe PsA, poor prognosis, or inadequate csDMARDs response.
S: adalimumab (SC) 40mg every 2 weeks.

4. Targeted Synthetic DMARDs (tsDMARDs)
Patients who have failed or are intolerant to bDMARDs.
S: tofacitinib (PO) 5mg 12 hourly

Surgical Treatment
Surgery in PsA is used for severe joint damage or deformity, including synovectomy, joint replacement, Tendon repair or
transfer, and Arthrodesis.

  Note
    •    Avoid oral steroids in active psoriasis to prevent flares.
    •    Start DMARDs or biologics early in the erosive disease stage.
    •    Monitor with DAPSA, PASI, and HAQ-DI to guide treatment.

sections.title: Axial Spondyloarthritis
sections.text:
A chronic inflammatory rheumatic disease that primarily affects the sacroiliac joints and spine, leading to pain, stiffness, and
progressive fusion of the axial skeleton, resulting in reduced spinal mobility.
It is usually classified as:

1.Non-radiographic axSpA (nr-axSpA): No structural damage seen on X-ray. MRI may show active inflammation of the sacroiliac
joints (SIJ)
2.Radiographic axSpA / Ankylosing Spondylitis (AS): Structural damage to SIJ visible on X-ray (per modified New York criteria).
Progressive spinal fusion may occur.

Clinical Presentation
  •    Back pain >3 months, <45 yrs onset, improves with
       activity, worse at rest                                       •    Uveitis (red, painful eye)
  •    Night pain, buttock pain                                      •    Associated diseases: Psoriasis, IBD
  •    Spinal stiffness, ↓ decreased mobility                        •    Fatigue, weight loss
  •    Peripheral features: arthritis (asymmetric, lower             •    Rare: heart (aortic regurgitation), lung (apical
       limbs), Enthesitis (heel, Achilles), Dactylitis                    fibrosis)
       (sausage digits)

Investigations
Laboratory Tests
  •    HLA-B27: Positive in ~80–90% of AS cases
  •    CRP / ESR: May be elevated in active disease
  •    CBC: May show mild anemia of chronic disease
  •    RF and anti-CCP: Typically, negative; helps rule out RA

Imaging
  •   Pelvic X-ray: Sacroiliitis (unilateral or bilateral)
  •   MRI of sacroiliac joints: Detects early inflammation (bone marrow edema)
  •   Spine X-ray/MRI: Shows syndesmophytes or vertebral fusion in advanced disease
  •   Eye exam: If anterior uveitis is suspected
  •   ECG/Echocardiogram: If cardiac involvement is suspected

Diagnosis
AS is diagnosed based on the ASAS 2009 criteria, which require either the presence of sacroiliitis on imaging, accompanied
by at least one clinical feature of spondyloarthritis, or HLA-B27 positivity, accompanied by at least two clinical features.

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •   Daily spinal extension and mobility exercises                  •    Smoking cessation (smoking worsens radiographic
  •   Structured physical therapy programs                                progression)
  •   Postural training to prevent kyphosis                          •    Encourage physical activity, avoid prolonged rest or
                                                                          immobilization

Pharmacological Management
1.Non-Steroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drugs (NSAIDs)
First-line therapy: NSAIDs — effective for controlling pain and stiffness; used continuously or on-demand based on symptom
severity and response

A: Ibuprofen (PO) 400–800 mg 8 hourly                                       OR
          OR                                                       S: Ketoprofen (PO) 75 mg 8 hourly
C: diclofenac (PO) 50 mg 8 hourly /Diclofenac gel 1% apply                  OR
6 hourly                                                           S: Ketoprofen (PO) 50 mg every 6 hourly
          OR                                                                OR
A: Piroxicam (PO) 20mg 24 hourly                                   S: Ketoprofen gel 2.5% topical, apply to affected area 6
          OR                                                       hourly
D: Meloxicam (PO) 7.5–15 mg 24 hourly

2. Biologic DMARDs (bDMARDs)
If NSAIDs are insufficient, biological DMARDs are recommended. Conventional DMARDs have no proven efficacy in axial
spondyloarthritis and are not routinely recommended.

S: adalimumab (SC) 40 mg SC every two weeks

Surgical Treatment
Indicated for severe deformity, neurologic compromise, or failed medical therapy.
   •    Corrective osteotomy: For severe kyphosis (e.g.,              •    Decompression: For cord or nerve compression
        chin-on-chest).                                                    (e.g., cauda equina).
   •    Spinal fusion/stabilization: For unstable fractures in        •    Hip replacement: For advanced hip damage;
        the fused spine.                                                   commonly needed in axSpA

sections.title: Reactive Arthritis (ReA)
sections.text:
RA is a sterile inflammatory arthritis that occurs 1–4 weeks after an extra-articular infection, most commonly involving the
gastrointestinal (e.g., Salmonella, Shigella, Yersinia, Campylobacter) or genitourinary tract (especially Chlamydia trachomatis).

Clinical Presentation
  •    Arthritis: Asymmetric oligoarthritis (knees, ankles),              •    Eye: Conjunctivitis, uveitis (can threaten vision)
       axial spine, sacroiliitis                                          •    Skin/Mucosa:       Oral      ulcers,    keratoderma
  •    Enthesitis & Dactylitis: Common (heel, Achilles,                        blennorrhagicum, nail dystrophy
       sausage digits)                                                    •    Systemic: Fatigue, fever, weight loss
  •    Genitourinary: Urethritis, cervicitis, prostatitis,
       circinate balanitis

Investigations
  •    Inflammatory markers: ESR and CRP may be                           •    Joint aspiration: Sterile inflammatory fluid (rule out
       elevated                                                                sepsis)
  •    CBC: May show leukocytosis, anemia                                 •    Imaging: X-ray: May show late sacroiliitis or
  •    Infection screen: Urine/genital PCR: Chlamydia                          periostitis
       and Stool culture: GI pathogens                                    •    MRI: Detects early sacroiliitis/enthesitis
  •    HLA-B27: Positive in ~50%, linked to severe
       disease

Diagnosis
Diagnosis is supported by the exclusion of other causes of arthritis (e.g., septic arthritis, crystal arthropathy)

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •   Rest during acute inflammation                                      •    Nutritional support, especially if enteric infection led
  •   Physical therapy to maintain joint function and                          to weight loss or malabsorption
      mobility                                                            •    Patient education on the self-limiting nature in most
  •   Safe sexual practices (e.g., condom use to prevent                       cases and possible chronicity in some cases
      STI-related recurrence)

Pharmacological Management
1.Non-Steroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drugs (NSAIDs)
First-line therapy: NSAIDs — effective for controlling pain and stiffness; used continuously or on-demand based on symptom
severity and response
                                                                      D: meloxicam (PO) 7.5–15mg 24 hourly
A: ibuprofen (PO) 400–800 mg orally 3 times daily                              OR
           OR                                                         S: ketoprofen (PO) 75mg 8 hourly
C: diclofenac (PO) 50 mg 8 hourly /Diclofenac gel 1% apply                     OR
6hourly                                                               S: ketoprofen gel 2.5% apply 6hourly
           OR                                                                  OR
A: piroxicam (PO) 20mg 24hourly                                       S: dexketoprofen (PO) 25mg 8 hourly
           OR

2. Glucocorticoids
A: prednisolone (PO) 5–10 mg 24 hourly, short course for polyarthritis or enthesitis
          OR
S: triamcinolone acetonide (deep IM) 10–40 mg monthly for persistent monoarthritis or IA 20-40mg in the affected joint

3. Antibiotic therapy: Indicated only if evidence of ongoing infection, especially Chlamydia
A: doxycycline (PO) 100 mg 12hourly for 7–14 days

4. Conventional Synthetic DMARDs (csDMARDs): for chronic or refractory cases
D: sulfasalazine (PO) 500 mg 12hourly initially; increase by 500 mg every week to target 2–3 g/day in divided doses. Especially
for patients with persistent arthritis >3–6 months
           OR
S: methotrexate (PO) 15–25mg weekly. May be used if sulfasalazine is ineffective or in patients with extensive peripheral
arthritis
           AND
A: folic acid (PO) 5mg weekly (except on Methotrexate day)

sections.title: Enteropathic Arthritis (Associated with IBD)
sections.text:
Enteropathic arthritis is a seronegative spondyloarthritis associated with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). It can involve both
the axial skeleton (spine and sacroiliac joints) and the peripheral joints, and may also present with enthesitis or dactylitis.

Clinical Presentation
  •    Peripheral arthritis: Asymmetric, large joints, Type 1: <5 joints, flares with IBD, Type 2: >5 joints, not linked to IBD activity
  •    Axial arthritis: Sacroiliitis, spondylitis,
  •    Enthesitis (Achilles ' heel), Dactylitis (sausage digits),
  •    Uveitis and Skin: erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum
  •    IBD symptoms: Diarrhea, abdominal pain, bleeding, weight loss

Investigations
  •    ESR and CRP: Often elevated in both IBD and active arthritis
  •    Colonoscopy or gastrointestinal imaging (such as MRI/CT enterography or fluoroscopic barium studies) is used to
       confirm the diagnosis of IBD or to assess disease activity.
  •    X-ray / MRI: sacroiliac joints for early axial involvement and late changes
  •    HLA-B27: May be positive, especially in those with axial involvement
  •    Autoantibodies: RF and anti-CCP negative (to rule out RA)

Diagnosis
There is no specific classification criterion; however, diagnosis is based on the presence of confirmed IBD (Crohn’s disease or
ulcerative colitis), clinical features of arthritis, and the absence of RF and anti-CCP antibodies.

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •   Physical therapy: Improves mobility and function, especially in axial involvement
  •   Nutritional support: Address malnutrition or deficiencies associated with IBD
  •   Management of underlying IBD: Control of intestinal inflammation often improves joint symptoms

Pharmacological Management
1.Non-Steroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drugs (NSAIDs) may ease joint symptoms but can worsen IBD. Use the lowest effective
dose briefly. Prefer COX-2 inhibitors for lower GI risk.
D: meloxicam (PO) 7.5–15mg 24hourly (selective at lower dosages)
          OR
C: celecoxib (PO) 100-200mg 12 hourly
          OR
S: etoricoxib (PO) 30–60 mg 24 hourly

2.DMARDs for Peripheral Arthritis:
D: sulfasalazine (PO) 500 mg 12 hourly initially; increase by 500 mg every week to target 2–3 g/day in divided doses
           OR
S: methotrexate (PO)15–25 mg once weekly. Used more in Crohn’s disease than ulcerative colitis; helpful if peripheral arthritis
coexists
           AND
A: folic acid (PO) 5mg weekly (except on methotrexate day)

3. Biologic Therapy (for moderate-to-severe disease or axial involvement):
S: adalimumab (SC) 40mg every two weeks

4. Glucocorticoids
A: prednisolone (PO) 5–10 mg 24 hourly . A short course may help during flares
          OR
S: triamcinolone acetonide (deeply IM) 10–40 mg monthly for persistent monoarthritis or IA in case only 1-2 joints are affected.

sections.title: Crystal Arthropathies
sections.text:
Crystal arthropathies are caused by the deposition of crystals in joints or periarticular tissues, resulting in inflammation and
tissue damage. The most common types include:
   •    Gout (Monosodium urate crystals)
   •    Calcium Pyrophosphate Dihydrate Deposition Disease (CPPD)

sections.title: Gout
sections.text:
A metabolic disease characterized by recurrent attacks of acute arthritis due to monosodium urate (MSU) crystal deposition,
typically affecting men and postmenopausal women.

Clinical Presentation
  •    Acute gout attack: sudden, severe joint pain and                 •   Monoarthritis (usually one joint at a time) is rarely
       swelling, often at night                                             polyarticular or RA-like in late stages or the elderly.
  •    Most       commonly         affects    the    first              •   Tophaceous deposits (chronic cases)
       metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint (podagra)                        •   Fever may occur in severe cases
  •    It can also involve ankles, knees, and elbows                    •   Associated with CKD, obesity, HTN, diabetes, and
                                                                            CVD

Investigations
  •    Serum uric acid (note: may be normal during acute                •   Ultrasound: crystals, double contour signs
       attacks)                                                         •   Joint X-rays (look for erosions and tophi)
  •    ESR/CRP (elevated during attacks)                                •   Joint fluid aspiration (gold standard if feasible):
  •    Renal function (before initiating urate-lowering                     needle-shaped crystals with negative birefringent
       therapy)

Diagnosis : The 2015 ACR/EULAR Gout Classification Criteria define gout as present when the total score is ≥8 points, based
on clinical, laboratory, and imaging domains.

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •   Modify your diet by avoiding purine-rich foods (e.g.,             •   Weight loss in overweight/obese patients
      red meat, organ meats, shellfish), limiting alcohol—              •   Exercise: low-impact, regular physical activity
      especially beer and spirits—and eliminating sugary                •   Avoid triggers: Acetylsalicylic acid, thiazide
      drinks.                                                               diuretics, excessive alcohol
  •   Encourage hydration by drinking 2–3 liters of water
      per day.

Pharmacological Management

Acute Gout Attack
1.Non-Steroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drugs (NSAIDs): First-line therapy:

A: ibuprofen (PO) 400–800mg 8 hourly for 3days
          OR
C: diclofenac (PO) 50mg orally 12 hourly or 8hourly for 3days
          OR
A: diclofenac gel 1% apply 6 hourly
          OR
A: piroxicam (PO) 20mg 24 hourly for 5 days
          OR
D: meloxicam (PO) 7.5–15 mg 24 hourly
          OR
S: ketoprofen (PO) 75 mg 8 hourly
          OR
S: ketoprofen (PO) 50 mg every 6 hourly
          OR
S: ketoprofen gel 2.5% topical, apply to affected area 6 hourly

2.Anti-inflammatory agents
D: colchicine (PO) 1mg start then 0.5 mg 12hourly (low dose better tolerated)

3. Glucocorticoids
A: prednisolone (PO) 20–40mg/day 24 hourly, taper over 7-10 days
          OR
S: triamcinolone acetonide (deeply IM) or IA 10–40mg for monoarticular involvement

Chronic Tophaceous Gout

1. Urate-Lowering Therapy (ULT)
Usually, treatment is started 2–4 weeks after the flare subsides, but in some cases, it can be initiated during the acute attack.

B: allopurinol (PO) Start at 100mg 24 hourly. Titrate every 2–5 weeks by 100 mg to achieve serum urate <6 mg/dL.
          OR
S: febuxostat (PO) 40–80mg 24 hourly: alternative in allopurinol intolerance or renal impairment (where available)

2. Prophylaxis During Initiation or Titration of ULT

D: colchicine 0.5mg 12hourly or 24 hourly for 3–6 months
  Note:
   •    Indication to start ULT: ≥2 gout flares per year, Presence of tophi (clinical or imaging evidence).
   •    Chronic gouty arthritis or radiographic joint damage
   •    Chronic kidney disease (stage ≥2)
   •    History of uric acid kidney stones
   •    Serum urate level >9 mg/dL (≈540 µmol/L)First gout attack in high-risk patients

sections.title: Calcium Pyrophosphate Dihydrate Deposition Disease (CPPD)
sections.text:
Inflammatory arthritis is caused by the deposition of calcium pyrophosphate crystals in joint cartilage and soft tissues.

Clinical Presentation
  •    Acute arthritis: Sudden joint pain, swelling, warmth             •    Spinal: Crowned dens syndrome (neck pain,
       (knees, wrists, shoulders); may mimic gout or                         stiffness, fever)
       infection.                                                       •    Associated with: Metabolic disorders (e.g.,
  •    Chronic form: Resembles OA or RA; stiffness, pain,                    hyperparathyroidism, hemochromatosis)
       limited motion (knees, wrists, MCPs, hips, spine)
  •    Asymptomatic: Chondrocalcinosis on imaging

Investigations
  •    Synovial fluid: Rhomboid, positively birefringent                •    CT/MRI: For spinal involvement (e.g., crowned
       crystals; inflammatory                                                dens)
  •    X-ray: Chondrocalcinosis, OA-like changes                        •    Blood   tests: ↑ESR/CRP;     check    calcium,
  •    Ultrasound: Crystal deposits; no double contour                       phosphate, magnesium, iron, PTH for metabolic
                                                                             causes
Non-Pharmacological Management
  •   Rest the affected joint during flares                             •    Initiate physiotherapy post-flare to restore mobility
  •   Apply ice packs to reduce swelling                                •    Educate patients about the chronic nature of CPPD

Pharmacological Management
Acute Pseudogout Attack

1. Non-Steroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drugs (NSAIDs): First-line therapy:
A: ibuprofen (PO) 400–800mg 8 hourly for 3days.                              OR
          OR                                                       S: ketoprofen 75 mg (PO) every 8 hours
C: diclofenac (PO) 50mg 12 hourly                                           OR
          OR                                                       S: ketoprofen 50 mg (PO) every 6 hourly
A: piroxicam (PO) 20mg 24 hourly for 3-5days                                OR
          OR                                                       S: ketoprofen gel 2.5% topical, apply to affected area 6
D: meloxicam (PO) 7.5–15mg 24 hourly for 3-5days.                  hourly.

2. Anti-inflammatory agents
D: colchicine (PO) 1mg start then 0.5mg 2–3x/day (low dose better tolerated)

3. Glucocorticoids
A: prednisolone (PO) 20–40 mg 24 hourly, taper over 7-10 days.
          OR
S: triamcinolone acetonide (IA) 10–40mg for monoarticular involvement

Prevention
D: colchicine prophylaxis: 0.5 mg 12hourly or 24hourly for patients with frequent attacks
Treat underlying metabolic disorders (e.g., correct magnesium deficiency, treat hypothyroidism)

  Note: Urate-lowering therapies used in gout are not effective in CPPD

sections.title: Connective Tissue Diseases (CTDs)
sections.text:
CTDs include systemic autoimmune disorders such as:                    •    Sjogren's Syndrome
  •   Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE)                               •    Mixed Connective Tissue Disease (MCTD)
  •   Systemic Sclerosis (SSc)                                         •    Dermatomyositis/Polymyositis

sections.title: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE)
sections.text:
SLE is a chronic autoimmune disease marked by autoantibodies (e.g., ANA, anti-dsDNA), multisystem involvement, and a
relapsing-remitting course. It mainly affects women of childbearing age.

Clinical Presentation
 Category/System                          Clinical Features
 Classic presentation                     Fever , Joint pain (arthralgia/arthritis), Rash (commonly seen in women of
                                          childbearing age)
 Pattern of onset                         Variable onset , Can affect any age group or gender
 General manifestations                   Fatigue, Fever , Weight loss, Arthralgia
 Musculoskeletal manifestations           Arthritis, Myalgia, Avascular necrosis
 Dermatological manifestations            Malar rash, Discoid rash, Photosensitivity
 Renal manifestations                     Nephritis, Renal failure
 Neurological manifestations              Seizures, Psychosis
 Respiratory manifestations               Pleurisy, Pleural effusion, Interstitial lung disease (ILD), Pulmonary hypertension
 Cardiovascular manifestations            Pericarditis , Myocarditis
 Gastrointestinal manifestations          Nausea , Abdominal pain
 Hematological manifestations             Anemia, Leukopenia , Thrombocytopenia
 Children                                 More rash, More seizures, More fever
 Adults                                   More joint involvement, More lung involvement
 Family history                           Positive family history may support suspicion in suggestive cases

Investigations:
  •    CBC:      may      show     anemia,    leukopenia,              •    Anti-Ro/SSA, Anti-La/SSB, Anti-U1 RNP
       thrombocytopenia                                                •    Urinalysis, Creatinine: Assess renal involvement
  •    ESR/CRP: ESR raised; CRP may be normal unless                   •    Complement (C3, C4): Often decreased during
       infection or serositis                                               active disease
  •    ANA: Screening test (sensitive but not specific)                •    Renal        Biopsy:        Recommended         for
  •    Anti-dsDNA, Anti-Sm: Specific for SLE                                diagnosis/classification of lupus nephritis
  •    Antiphospholipid antibodies at baseline and after               •    Chest x-ray, ECHO, and abdominal USS for
       12 months for all high-risk patients                                 serositis

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •   Sun protection: Avoid triggers of skin flares                    •    Vaccination: Especially pneumococcal, influenza
  •   Patient education: Disease course, treatment                     •    Routine monitoring: BP, renal, hematologic, CVD
      adherence                                                             risk

Pharmacological Management
Treatment is guided by: Severity of disease, such as SLEDAI-2K, Organ system involvement, Activity vs. damage or Patient
comorbidities

1.Baseline Therapy for All Patients
S: hydroxychloroquine 200–400mg 24hourly (usually 5 mg/kg/day, max 400 mg/day).: All SLE patients unless contraindicated

Benefit: Reduces flares, improves survival, lowers thrombotic risk, and improves lipid profile and glucose tolerance

2. Nonsteroidal Anti-inflammatory Drugs Indication: For mild musculoskeletal pain or serositis

C: diclofenac (PO) 50 mg orally 2–3 times daily/Diclofenac          S: ketoprofen 75 mg PO every 8 hours
gel 1% apply 4 times daily                                                   OR
          OR                                                        S: ketoprofen 50 mg PO every 4 hourly
A: piroxicam (PO) 20mg 24hourly                                              OR
          OR                                                        S: ketoprofen gel 2.5% topical, apply to affected area
D: meloxicam (PO) 7.5–15mg 24 hourly                                6 hourly
          OR

3. Corticosteroids: Used to control inflammation rapidly, especially in flares.
 Steroid type                                Dosage formulation                      Use
 Low dosage                                  A: prednisolone ≤7.5 mg/day             Mild disease (e.g., skin, joint symptoms)
 Moderate-dose                               A: prednisolone 10–30 mg/day            Moderate disease (e.g., serositis, cytopenia)
 High-dose / Pulse Therapy                   A: prednisolone 1–2 mg/kg/day orally,   Severe or life-threatening disease (e.g.,
                                             D: methylprednisolone 500–1000          lupus nephritis, CNS lupus, severe
                                                mg/day × 3 days                      thrombocytopenia or hemolytic anemia,
                                                                                     myocarditis, alveolar hemorrhage)

4.Conventional Immunosuppressants: Used as steroid-sparing agents or for organ-threatening disease

 Indication                                                      Management
 Moderate disease; maintenance of LN                             S: azathioprine (PO) 1-2 mg/kg/day
 Arthritis, skin disease                                         S: methotrexate (PO) 15-25 mg/week
 Lupus nephritis (especially class III/IV/V), pneumonitis,       S: mycophenolate mofetil (PO)
 vasculitic ulcers, thrombocytopenia, acute hemolytic            Induction: 2-3 g/day; Maintenance: 1-2 g/day
 anemia
 Induction: Severe organ involvement (renal, CNS, cardiac        S: cyclophosphamide 500-1000 mg/m² monthly × 6
 tamponade), then maintain with MMF/Azathioprine

5. Biologic Therapies: Reserved for patients with refractory or severe SLE or those who are intolerant to conventional therapy.
S: rituximab IV 1000 mg × 2 doses, 2 weeks apart (Repeat based on clinical response)

Adjunctive Medications in SLE Management
  •   Acetylsalicylic acid (low-dose): Used to prevent thrombosis in patients with antiphospholipid antibodies.
  •   Antihypertensives (ACE inhibitors or ARBs); Indicated in protein uric renal disease to reduce proteinuria and preserve
      kidney function.
  •   Statins are prescribed to reduce cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk.
  •   Calcium/Vitamin D + Bisphosphonates: Recommended for patients on long-term corticosteroid therapy to prevent
      osteoporosis.
  •   Antimicrobials (e.g., TMP-SMX): Used for Pneumocystis Jirovecii pneumonia (PJP) prophylaxis in patients receiving
      high-dose steroids or cyclophosphamide.
  •   Apply sunscreen with a minimum SPF of 50 before going outside in the sun.

Neonatal lupus (NL)
NL is a passively acquired autoimmune condition in newborns caused by the transplacental transfer of maternal
autoantibodies—mainly anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB, and less commonly anti-U1 RNP—crossing the placenta (usually after
12–16 weeks of gestation); it is not true SLE in the baby.

Most commonly seen in mothers with: SLE, Sjögren's syndrome, Undifferentiated connective tissue disease. Sometimes the
mother is asymptomatic but antibody-positive
 Domain                      Details
 Clinical Presentation       • Skin rash – annular/periorbital rash, usually resolves by 6–8 months
                             • Photosensitivity
                             • Congenital heart block – usually complete and may be permanent
                             • Hepatitis
                             • Cytopenias (usually self-limiting)
 Investigations              • ECG – assess for congenital heart block
                             • Complete blood count (CBC)
                             • Liver function tests (LFTs)
                             • Anti-Ro/SSA antibody test
                             • Anti-La/SSB antibody test
 Management                  • Skin rash → Sun protection
                             • Mild topical corticosteroids for rash
                             • Congenital heart block → Pacemaker insertion if severe/symptomatic
                             • Future pregnancy prevention → Hydroxychloroquine + fetal echocardiography between 16–
                             26 weeks’ gestation

sections.title: Systemic Sclerosis (SSc)
sections.text:
Systemic sclerosis (scleroderma) is a chronic autoimmune disease marked by skin and organ fibrosis, vasculopathy, and
autoimmunity. It causes tissue thickening and can affect the skin, lungs, kidneys, and heart.

Clinical Presentation
  •    Skin: Skin thickening (sclerodactyly), Raynaud’s                 •    Gastrointestinal: Reflux, dysphagia, bloating, Small
       phenomenon, digital ulcers, pitting, telangiectasia,                  intestine     bacterial     overgrowth      (SIBO),
       calcinosis, tight mask-like face, and skin pigment                    malabsorption,     weight     loss,   and     faecal
       changes                                                               incontinence
  •    Vascular: Raynaud’s, nailfold capillary changes,                 •    Lung: ILD (diffuse type) and pulmonary
       and pulmonary hypertension (limited type)                             hypertension (limited type)
  •    Musculoskeletal: Joint pain/stiffness, muscle                    •    Renal: Scleroderma renal crisis (hypertension, AKI)
       weaknesses and tendon rubs                                       •    Cardiac: Pericarditis, arrhythmias, and myocardial
                                                                             fibrosis

Investigations:
  •    ANA, anti-centromere, anti-Scl-70, Anti-RNA                      •    Chest X-ray, HRCT for ILD
       polymerase III                                                   •    Echocardiogram for pulmonary hypertension
  •    Serum creatinine and urinalysis, blood pressure

Diagnosis
SS is classified using the ACR/EULAR 2013 criteria, where a total score of ≥9, based on weighted clinical, vascular, serological,
and organ involvement features, is required for diagnosis.

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •   Avoid cold to prevent Raynaud’s—keep hands and feet warm.
  •   Use moisturizers to maintain skin hydration and to avoid cracking.
  •   Physiotherapy helps preserve joint mobility and counteract skin tightening, especially in the hands

Pharmacological Management
                                                                             OR
1. Raynaud's phenomenon prevention                                   S: mycophenolate Mofetil (PO) 1g–1.5 g 12hourly
A: nifedipine: (PO) 20–120mg 24hourly (extended-release              Pulmonology consultation is advised
formulation)
                                                                     4. Renal crisis (emergency)
2. Gastroesophageal reflux (GERD)                                    C: enalapril (PO) 5–40mg 24 hourly (divided doses)
A: omeprazole (PO) 20–40mg 24 hourly                                           OR
           OR                                                        C: lisinopril (PO) 5–40mg 24hourly. Nephrology
C: pantoprazole (PO) 40 mg 24 hourly                                 consultation is advised
           OR
S: esomeprazole (PO) 20–40mg 24 hourly                               5. Skin and Joint involvement
3. Interstitial lung disease (ILD)                                   S: methotrexate (PO) 15–25 mg weekly
                                                                               OR
S: cyclophosphamide: 500–1000mg/m² every 4 weeks                     S: azathioprine (PO) 1–2 mg/kg 24hourly
(intravenous infusion)

sections.title: Sjögren’s Syndrome
sections.text:
Sjögren’s syndrome is a chronic autoimmune disease characterized by dry eyes (xeropthalmia) and dry mouth (xerostomia),
resulting from lymphocytic destruction of the salivary and lacrimal glands. It may occur as a primary condition (primary Sjögren’s
syndrome) or in association with other autoimmune diseases such as RA and SLE, viral infections such as HIV and Epstein–
Barr virus, and primary biliary cirrhosis (secondary Sjögren’s syndrome).

Clinical Presentation
  •    Dry eyes (gritty, red)                                        Extra glandular manifestations
  •    keratoconjunctivitis sicca                                      •    Fatigue,    arthralgias,  myalgia,         Raynaud’s
  •    Dry    mouth       (swallowing   difficulty,   dental                Phenomena
       decay/caries, tongue fissure)                                   •    Skin: Dryness, purpura
  •    Salivary gland swelling (esp. parotid)                          •    Lungs: Cough, ILD
                                                                       •    Kidneys: Tubular acidosis
                                                                       •    Nerves: Neuropathy
                                                                       •    Blood: Anemia, leukopenia
                                                                       •    B cell Lymphoma (MALT lymphoma)
Investigations:
  •    ANA: Often elevated in autoimmune diseases; not                •    Schirmer’s test: Confirms dry eyes by measuring
       specific.                                                           tear production.
  •    Anti-Ro/SSA and Anti-La/SSB: Key markers; Anti-                •    Salivary gland biopsy: Confirms the disease biopsy
       Ro/SSA is most common.                                              shows lymphocytic infiltration

Diagnosis
SS is classified by ACR/EULAR 2016 criteria when the total score is ≥4 in a symptomatic patient without exclusion criteria

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •   Artificial tears/saliva: Relieve dry eyes and mouth.            •    Hydration: Frequent fluid intake; sugar-free gum
  •   Dental hygiene, including brushing, flossing, and                    stimulates saliva
      regular dental check-ups, helps prevent decay and               •    Avoid: Tobacco, cannabis, caffeine, Cola drink
      infection.

Pharmacological Management
1. Dry Mouth
D: pilocarpine (PO) 5 mg, 8 hourly for dry mouth.

2. Fatigue or arthralgia
S: hydroxychloroquine (PO) 200–400mg 24 hourly

3. Systemic involvement, such as Vasculitis or other systemic manifestations
A: prednisolone (PO) 0.5-1 mg/kg/ 24hourly
          OR
S: methotrexate: 10–25mg weekly
          OR
S: azathioprine: 1.5–2.5 mg/kg/day

sections.title: Dermatomyositis / Polymyositis
sections.text:
Dermatomyositis (DM) and polymyositis (PM) are inflammatory myopathies causing proximal muscle weakness. DM is marked
by distinctive skin rashes (e.g., Gottron’s papules, heliotrope rash), whereas PM lacks skin involvement. Both may lead to
significant functional impairment.
                                                                           Gottron's papules are red or violet, flat-topped,
                                                                           scaly lesions that appear symmetrically over joint
                                                                           extensor surfaces—typically the knuckles, elbows,
                                                                           knees, and ankles

                                                                           A heliotrope rash is a distinctive reddish-purple or
                                                                           lilac discoloration of the upper eyelids and
                                                                           periorbital region, often associated with DM, an
                                                                           autoimmune inflammatory myopathy.

                                                                    Clinical Presentation
                                                                      •    Proximal muscle weakness: Symmetric, gradual
                                                                           onset
                                                                      •    Skin signs (DM only): Heliotrope rash, Gottron’s
                                                                           papules, photosensitive rash
                                                                      •    Systemic: Fatigue, fever, weight loss
                                                                      •    Lungs: ILD, cough, dyspnea
                                                                      •    Joints: Arthralgia, non-erosive arthritis
                                                                      •    Myalgia
                                                                      •    Raynaud’s phenomenon
                                                                      •    Dysphagia: Esophageal weakness
                                                                      •    ↑ Malignancy risk i.e Colon, lung, breast and
                                                                           ovarian cancers (mainly in DM)
Investigations
  •    CK: Elevated in active disease.                                •    EMG: Shows myopathic changes.
  •    AST and ALT: Mildly raised from muscle injury.                 •    Muscle biopsy: Confirms inflammation.
  •    ANA: Often positive, but non-specific.                         •    Chest CT imaging: for ILD
  •    Myositis-specific antibodies: Anti-Jo-1 (ILD), Anti-           •    Malignancy screening: Essential in DM—age- and

Diagnosis
DM and PM are classified using the 2017 EULAR/ACR criteria with a score of ≥6.7 (with biopsy) or ≥8.7 (without biopsy) in
patients without exclusion criteria.

Non-Pharmacological Management
Physiotherapy: Essential for managing weakness, preventing atrophy, and improving strength and flexibility.

Pharmacological Management

1. High-dose Corticosteroids: First-line treatment.
A: prednisone (PO) Starting at 0.5–1 mg/kg/day, tapering as the patient improves.

2. Immunosuppressants: Used as adjunctive therapy or steroid-sparing strategies.

S: methotrexate (PO) 10–25 mg weekly
          OR
S: azathioprine (PO) 1.5–2.5 mg/kg 24 hourly
          OR
S: hydroxychloroquine (PO) 200–400mg 24hourly. Used for skin involvement in DM
          OR
S: cyclophosphamide (IV) 500–1000 mg/m² every 4 weeks

Immunoglobulin Intravenous (IGIV): For severe or refractory cases, it is often used in life-threatening DM or PM or with
significant skin involvement.

3. Biologics
S: rituximab (IV) 1000mg × 2 doses, 2 weeks apart (Repeat based on clinical response. For refractory cases or overlap
syndromes (e.g., lupus).

Treatment Considerations:
  •   Monitor muscle strength, creatine kinase, or CK, and skin rash to guide treatment.
  •   Long-term: Use physiotherapy and monitor for complications like ILD and malignancy.

sections.title: Mixed Connective Tissue Disease (MCTD)
sections.text:
MCTD is an overlap syndrome with features of SLE, systemic sclerosis, and polymyositis. It is defined by high titers of anti-U1
RNP antibodies, distinguishing it from other CTDs.

Clinical Presentation
  •    SLE: Malar rash, photosensitivity, oral ulcers.                •    Polymyositis: Muscle weakness, ↑CK.
  •    SSc: Skin thickening, Raynaud’s.                               •    Raynaud’s: Common and may be an early feature.

Investigations
  •    ANA (Antinuclear Antibody): Positive in most cases.            •    Anti-DNA antibodies may be present, especially if
  •    Anti-U1 RNP: High titer confirms the diagnosis.                     SLE features are prominent.
  •    CBC: To assess for anemia, thrombocytopenia, or                •    Echocardiogram:      Assesses       pericarditis  or
       leukopenia.                                                         pulmonary hypertension.
  •    Creatine Kinase (CK): Elevated in cases with                   •    PFTs: Evaluate interstitial lung disease or
       muscle involvement (polymyositis).                                  pulmonary hypertension.
  •    ESR/CRP: To assess inflammation levels.                        •    Urinalysis: Screens for renal involvement, including
                                                                           lupus nephritis.

Diagnosis: MCTD is diagnosed clinically, based on overlapping features of multiple CTDs and high anti-U1 RNP antibody
levels.

Non-Pharmacological Management
  •   Educate on flare triggers and early symptom recognition.
  •   Emphasize sun protection, especially in patients with SLE features.
  •   Encourage regular follow-ups to monitor disease activity and complications.

Pharmacological Management
The management of MCTD involves a combination of corticosteroids, disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs), and
targeted therapies aimed at alleviating symptoms.

1.High-dose Corticosteroids: First-line treatment.
A: prednisone: Starting at 0.5–1 mg/kg/day, tapering as the patient improves.

2. Immunosuppressants: Used as adjunctive therapy or in steroid-sparing strategies.
S: methotrexate (PO) 10–25 mg weekly
          OR
S: azathioprine: 1.5–2.5 mg/kg/day
          OR
S: hydroxychloroquine (PO) 200–400mg 24hourly. Used for SLE involvement
          OR
S: cyclophosphamide (IV) 500–1000 mg/m² every 4 weeks

sections.title: Managing Systemic Vasculitis
sections.text:
Vasculitis is a group of disorders characterized by inflammation of blood vessels, resulting in damage to the vessel and organ
involvement. It is classified by vessel size (large, medium, small) or by mechanism (e.g., immune complex–mediated, ANCA-
associated)

26.5 Hypermobility and Associated Connective Tissue Disorders
Hypermobility refers to excessive joint movement beyond the normal range, often associated with connective tissue disorders
such as Joint Hypermobility Syndrome (JHS) and Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome (EDS). Symptoms include joint pain, instability,
dislocations, and soft tissue injury. Co-existing neurodivergent features are common. Management focuses on symptom control,
functional improvement, and the prevention of complications. The Beighton Score is commonly used for assessing joint
hypermobility

  •   Physical Therapy: Strengthen supporting muscles, improve coordination and posture; use bracing or orthotics if needed.

  •   Occupational Therapy: Adapt daily activities and ergonomics to reduce joint stress

sections.title: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA)
sections.text:
Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA) refers to a group of inflammatory joint disorders that begin before the age of 16 and last for
more than 6 weeks. It is characterized by chronic inflammation of the synovium, which can lead to joint destruction, deformity,
and functional impairment. The cause of JIA is not fully understood, but it involves genetic and environmental factors that trigger
an autoimmune response in genetically predisposed children.

Diagnosis and classification of JIA
Clinical assessment: Joint swelling, pain, and stiffness lasting over 6 weeks.

Management
Treatment focuses on controlling inflammation, relieving symptoms, and preventing joint damage.

  •   Physical Therapy: Strengthening, proprioception, posture, bracing/orthotics.
  •   Patient Education: Joint protection, posture, ergonomics, balanced exercise.
  •   Occupational Therapy: Task modification and assistive devices to reduce joint strain.

4. Glucocorticoids
A: prednisolone (PO) 10–40 mg/day, taper over 7-10 days. Prednisone for acute flare-ups or severe systemic features.

Surgical Management
Orthopedic surgery, including joint replacement, may be needed for deformities, contractures, instability, or severe joint
destruction unresponsive to conservative treatment.

sections.title: Fibromyalgia
sections.text:
Fibromyalgia is a chronic pain syndrome characterized by widespread musculoskeletal pain lasting ≥3 months, associated with
fatigue, sleep disturbance, and cognitive dysfunction.
It is a disorder of central pain processing (central sensitization) rather than peripheral inflammation.

Diagnosis
The 2016 Revised ACR Fibromyalgia Diagnostic Criteria assist in diagnosing fibromyalgia. Tender point examination is no
longer required; diagnosis is based on the Widespread Pain Index (WPI) and Symptom Severity Score (SSS) with symptoms
present for at least 3 months.

Investigations
Laboratory testing should be limited to excluding alternative diagnoses when clinically indicated.
  •    ESR and CRP
  •    CK levels
  •    Thyroid function testing
  •    Vitamin D testing may be considered in selected patients.
  •    Autoimmune serology should not be ordered routinely unless clinical suspicion exists.

Management
Fibromyalgia management should be multimodal and individualized, prioritizing non-pharmacological therapy first, with
medications added for persistent moderate to severe symptoms.

Non pharmacological management
  •   Patients should receive structured education about the condition.
  •   Regular graded aerobic exercise and Strength training is strongly recommended.
  •   Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT).
  •   Encourage sleep hygiene measures.
  •   Stress reduction strategies.

Pharmacological Management
S: duloxetine (PO) 30mg-60mg 24 hourly
          OR
A: amitriptyline (PO) 25mg 24 hourly

chapters.intro:
Rheumatological disorders, also known as rheumatic diseases, comprise a diverse group of conditions that primarily affect the
joints, bones, muscles, tendons, ligaments, and connective tissues. Many are driven by autoimmune and inflammatory
processes, often leading to multi-organ involvement.
These diseases are usually chronic, may cause long-term disability, and often require multidisciplinary care. Management
involves immunosuppressive therapy, including corticosteroids, conventional DMARDs, and biological agents. Accurate
diagnosis and thorough assessment are crucial for guiding safe and effective treatment.
Before initiating DMARDs or biologics, it is essential to conduct liver and renal function tests, a chest X-ray, and screen for
tuberculosis, HIV, and hepatitis B and C to rule out latent infections and ensure the safety of treatment.

 Maximum loading dose          Up to 50 mg/kg within 24 hours
 Maintenance therapy           A: phenobarbitone 5 mg/kg/day IV/PO, started 12–24 hours after last loading dose

 Note:
   •     Stabilize first (airway, breathing, circulation, glucose)
   •     Phenobarbitone is first-line anticonvulsant, Avoid diazepam in neonates.
   •     Always treat underlying cause (e.g., infection, hypoxia, metabolic disturbance)
   •     Maintain strict monitoring of neurological and systemic status

sections.title: Neonatal Sepsis
sections.text:
This is a serious systemic condition of infectious origin occurring in the first month of life. Neonatal sepsis is classified as early-
onset or late onset.

Early-onset neonatal sepsis
It is diagnosed in the first 3 days and caused by pathogens in the mother’s genital tract.

27.2 Risk factors and clinical indicators for early-onset neonatal sepsis
 Category               Red Flags (High Risk – urgent admission        Non–Red Flags (Warning signs – close
                        & evaluation)                                  observation & assessment)
 Risk factors           > Suspected or confirmed infection in twin
 (maternal / perinatal)  (multiple pregnancy)
                        > Previous baby with Group B Streptococcal
                         (GBS) infection
                        > Maternal GBS colonization or bacteriuria
                        > Unexplained preterm birth <37 weeks
                        > Prolonged rupture of membranes >18 hours
                        > Pre-labour rupture of membranes >24 hours
                        > Intrapartum fever >38°C
                        > Clinical diagnosis of chorioamnionitis
 Clinical indicators       > Need for cardiopulmonary resuscitation (at        > Altered behaviour or responsiveness
 (neonatal                   birth)                                            > Hypotonia (floppiness)
 presentation)             > Apnoea                                            > Refusal/poor feeding
                           > Seizures                                          > Vomiting, high gastric aspirates, abdominal
                           > Signs of shock                                      distension
                           > Requirement for mechanical ventilation            > Abnormal heart rate (tachycardia or
                           > Respiratory distress beginning after 4 hours        bradycardia)
                           of age (suggests pathology rather than              > Signs of respiratory distress (mild/moderate)
                           transition)                                         > Central cyanosis or low oxygen saturation
                                                                               > Jaundice within 24 hours of birth
                                                                               > Temperature <36°C or >38°C (not
                                                                                 environmental cause)
                                                                               > Unexplained bleeding
                                                                               > Abnormal blood glucose (hypoglycemia or
                                                                                 hyperglycemia)

 Note:
 Red flags → immediate admission, full sepsis work-up, and urgent management
 Non–red flags → close monitoring, reassessment, and early intervention if progression occurs

Neonate ≤ 3days to be investigated for sepsis and started on antibiotics:
  •   Those with any red flag risk factor or clinical indicator
  •   Those with 2 or more none red flag risk factor or clinical indicator

Investigations
For early onset neonatal sepsis
  •    Full Blood picture (FBP)                                            •    Random blood glucose (RBG)
  •    Blood culture and sensitivity                                       •    Lumbar puncture (in case of CNS signs)
  •    C-reactive protein (CRP)                                            •    Chest X-ray (in case of respiratory signs)

Pharmacological Management

Management of early-onset neonatal sepsis
Start antibiotics immediately (do not wait for results)
A: ampicillin (IV) 50 mg/kg 12 hourly for 5 – 7 days
          AND
A: gentamicin (IV) 5 mg/kg (3mg/kg for LBW neonates) 24hourly for 5 – 7 days
  •     Provide other supportive care as indicated by the neonate’s condition
  •     Close monitoring of vitals - respiratory rate, temp, SPO2, heart rate, RBG, BP and urine output

Late-onset neonatal sepsis
Late-onset sepsis is diagnosed after 3 days of age and is horizontally acquired from the environment and the people handling
the neonate.

Table 27.3 Clinical indicators of possible late-onset neonatal sepsis
 System/Category Clinical Signs (Warning signs)                                Severe Clinical Signs (Emergency signs)
 CNS                   • Parent/caregiver concern of behavioral change         • Reduced movement
                       • Appears ill to healthcare provider (lethargy)         • Convulsions (ongoing or recurrent)
                       • Weak, high-pitched or continuous cry                  • Not waking or not staying awake when
                       • Seizures                                               aroused
                       • Inactive or reduced responsiveness
                       • Bulging fontanelle
 Respiratory           • Fast breathing ≥60 breaths/min                        • Severe chest indrawing
                       • Grunting                                              • Apnoea
                       • Oxygen saturation <90% in room air or increased       • Fast breathing >60 breaths/min
                         oxygen requirement                                     (persistent/worsening)
                                                                               • Increasing oxygen requirement
 Circulation           • Persistent heart rate >160 bpm or <100 bpm            • Capillary refill time >3 seconds
                         (unexplained)                                          (marked/prolonged)
                       • Capillary refill time >3 seconds (sternum)
 Skin                  • Mottled or ashen appearance                           • Central cyanosis (severe/persistent)
                       • Central cyanosis                                      • Sclerema
                       • Non-blanching rash
                       • Sclerema
 Other                 • Temperature >38°C or <36°C (non-environmental         • Not feeding at all
                         cause)                                                • Unexplained bleeding
                       • Poor feeding                                           (significant/persistent)
                       • Abdominal distension
                       • Unexplained bleeding

Investigations
As described for early-onset sepsis Plus:
  •    Lumbar puncture if there is no contraindication
  •    Urinalysis and culture
  •    Electrolytes
  •    Consider ABG (some babies have inborn error of metabolism and mistaken for sepsis)

Pharmacological Management
Late-onset neonatal sepsis:
  •    All neonates with signs suggestive of sepsis need to be admitted for close observation
  •    After taking samples for investigation commence antibiotics immediately

B: ampicillin + cloxacillin (FDC) (IV) 100 mg/kg 12hourly for 5 – 7 days
        AND
A: gentamicin (IV) 5mg/kg 24hourly for 5 – 7day

 Note:
   •   Monitor vitals continuously for neonates with severe clinical signs
   •   Repeat septic markers (CRP) after 48hours of antibiotics
   •   For treatment guidance regularly review the clinical condition and investigation results of the neonate

When to consider changing antibiotics to the next line for neonate with sepsis
 •    If there is deterioration
 •    If no clinical improvement after 48 hours of treatment
 •    If culture results indicate resistance to current antibiotics

  Note:
  1st line antibiotics are:
    •     ampicillin + gentamicin (early onset sepsis)
    •     ampicillin + cloxacillin(FDC) + gentamicin (late onset sepsis)

  2nd line antibiotics
  cefotaxime or ceftriaxone or ciprofloxacin)

sections.title: Care of a low-birth-weight Neonate
sections.text:
Low Birth Weight neonates (LBW) are at higher risk of early growth retardation, infections, developmental delay, impaired
respiration, difficulty in feeding, poor body temperature regulation and death. The smaller the neonate, the higher the risk.

Table 27.4: Classification of Low-birth weight in neonates
 Category                                         Birth Weight
 Extremely Low Birth Weight (ELBW)                    <1000 g
 Very Low Birth Weight (VLBW)                         1000 g – <1500 g
 Low Birth Weight (LBW)                               1500 g – ≤2500 g

Non-Pharmacological Management
 Area                          Management
 1. Thermal Control                     • Maintain neonatal temperature 36.5°C – 37.5°C
                                        • Maintain room temperature 25°C – 28°C
                                        • Use radiant warmers with servo control mode
                                        • Ensure correct placement of temperature probe (right side, ~3 cm below right
                                        costal margin)
                                        • If probe failure → use manual mode and monitor axillary temperature every 15–30
                                        minutes
                                        • In cold environments use heaters; in hot environments use air conditioning
                                        • Rewarm hypothermic neonates slowly (0.5°C/hour) to avoid complications
                                        • Promote skin-to-skin contact (Kangaroo Mother Care)
 2. Feeding and Fluid Management        • Start with Minimal Enteral Feeding (MEF / trophic feeds) when appropriate
                                        • Gradually advance feeds based on tolerance
                                        • Monitor feeding tolerance and abdominal distension
                                        • Use enteral feeding whenever possible before IV nutrition
 3. Monitoring and Support              • Monitor temperature, weight, and feeding tolerance
                                        • Observe for signs of infection (treat only if indicated)
                                        • Monitor for respiratory distress and hypoglycemia

 Note: Non-pharmacological care is the cornerstone of LBW management, especially thermal regulation, feeding support,
 and close monitoring.

Pharmacological Management
 Therapeutic Area Indication                             Management
 1. Antibiotic         LBW neonates with sepsis          A: ampicillin 50 mg/kg (IV) every 12 hours (may be adjusted to every
 therapy               risk criteria or suspected        8 hours in severe cases depending on protocol)
 (empirical)           infection                                   AND
                                                         A: gentamicin 5 mg/kg IV once daily (24-hourly) for 5–7 days, guided
                                                         by clinical response and culture results
 2. Total Parenteral   Neonates unable to tolerate       D: Neonatal/paediatric Total Parenteral Nutrition (TPN)
 Nutrition (TPN)       or receive adequate enteral
                       feeding
 3. TPN indications    Gastrointestinal failure or       • Gastrointestinal anomalies (gastroschisis, congenital
                       inability to feed enterally        diaphragmatic hernia, esophageal/intestinal atresia)
                                                         • NPO neonates with no expected enteral feeds within 72 hours
                                                         • Short bowel syndrome
 4. Early TPN          Risk-based early nutritional      • <28 weeks (<1000 g): if no adequate feeds within 24 hours
 initiation criteria   support                           • 28–32 weeks (1000–1500 g): if no adequate feeds within 3 days
                                                         • >32 weeks (>1500 g): if no adequate feeds within 5 days

 Note:
   •     Ampicillin + Gentamicin remains first-line empirical therapy for suspected neonatal sepsis
   •     Duration is typically 5–7 days, adjusted by clinical and microbiological response
   •     TPN is indicated when enteral feeding is not possible or significantly delayed
   •     Early nutrition improves survival and growth outcomes in LBW neonates

Figure 27.1: Feeding modality/options in the first few days of life

Calculate the total fluid intake (TFI) using birth weight then minus the amount of milk required for that day (if it exceeds trophic
feed), and give the remaining amount as IV fluids over 24 hours.

Table 27.5: Total fluid requirement according to Birth weight and postnatal age
  Day of Life            Weight < 1 kg            Weight 1 – < 1.5 kg                              Weight ≥ 1.5 kg
 Day 1              100 mL/kg/day                80 mL/kg/day                        60 mL/kg/day
 Day 2              120 mL/kg/day                100 mL/kg/day                       80 mL/kg/day
 Day 3              140 mL/kg/day                120 mL/kg/day                       100 mL/kg/day
 Day 4              160 mL/kg/day                140 mL/kg/day                       120 mL/kg/day
 Day 5              160–180 mL/kg/day            160 mL/kg/day                       140 mL/kg/day
 Day ≥6             160–180 mL/kg/day            160–180 mL/kg/day                   150–160 mL/kg/day

Things to consider when giving IV fluids
  •   Type of fluid in the first 48 hours of life is Dextrose 10%
  •   After 48 hours of life:
      > 4/5 (80%) of total volume will be dextrose 10% the remaining 1/5 (20%) iv sodium chloride or sodium lactate
      > IV fluids should be given as a continuous infusion for 24 hours NOT bolus (preferably use an infusion pump if
      available).
      > Consider to stop IV fluid if neonate can take 2/3rd of total fluid required enterally and maintains normal RBG.

Apnoea of Prematurity
Apnoea of Prematurity is defined as a pause in breathing ≥20 seconds, or a shorter pause associated with bradycardia,
cyanosis, or oxygen desaturation in preterm neonates due to immature respiratory control.

Caffeine citrate should be given to all preterm neonates until reaching 34 weeks GA or 1.5 kg, and if there have been no apnoeic
episodes after CPAP discontinuation for at least 5 days.

B: caffeine citrate (IV/PO) – loading dose 20 mg/kg stat, then maintenance 5 – 10 mg/kg/day

Complications of LBW

Table 27.6: Complications of Low -Birth Weight Broadly categorized into short-term (neonatal period) and long-term
(beyond the neonatal period).
  Short-term complications (Neonatal period)          Long-term complications (Beyond neonatal period)
  Hypothermia and hyperthermia                        Developmental delay
  Hypoglycaemia and hyperglycaemia                    Anaemia of prematurity
  Respiratory distress syndrome                       Retinopathy of prematurity
  Apnoea of prematurity                               Bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD)
  Infections                                          —
  Hyperbilirubinaemia (jaundice)                      —
  Vitamin K deficiency bleeding                       —
  Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA)                      —
  Intraventricular haemorrhage (IVH)                  —

sections.title: Respiratory Distress Syndrome (RDS)
sections.text:
Respiratory Distress Syndrome (RDS) is caused by deficiency of pulmonary surfactant in immature lungs, commonly affecting
preterm neonates born at <34 weeks’ gestational age.

Clinical Presentation
  •    Tachypnea (respiratory rate >60 breaths/minute)              •    Apnoea (in severe cases)
  •    Chest wall indrawing                                         •    Diminished breath sounds
  •    Intercostal retractions                                      •    Cyanosis
  •    Grunting

Investigations/Monitoring
  •    Oxygen saturation monitoring (pulse oximetry)                •    Blood gas analysis (where available)
  •    Random blood glucose (RBG)                                   •    Chest X-ray (where available, if diagnosis is
  •    Temperature monitoring                                            uncertain)

Table 27.7: Management of Respiratory Distress Syndrome (RDS)
 Management Category                 Intervention     Details/Criteria
 Non-Pharmacological Management         1.Continuous        Initiate CPAP with:
                                        Positive Airway     • FiO₂: 30%
                                        Pressure (CPAP)     • PEEP: 6 cmH₂O Adjust FiO₂ and PEEP according to
                                                            severity of respiratory distress and oxygen saturation.
                                        2.Thermal care      Maintain normal body temperature through:
                                                            • Kangaroo Mother Care (intermittent skin-to-skin contact
                                                            where appropriate)
                                                            • Radiant warmer/incubator if indicated
                                        3.Nutrition and     • Start enteral feeding if stable
                                        fluid support       • If unable to feed, initiate IV fluids as per neonatal fluid
                                                            guidelines
                                        4.Monitoring        Monitor:
                                                            • Temperature
                                                            • Blood glucose
                                                            • Respiratory status
                                                            • Oxygen saturation
 Pharmacological Management             D: Surfactant       Administer if ALL of the following are present:
                                                            • Silverman Andersen Score (SAS) ≥7
                                                            • FiO₂ requirement ≥40%
                                                            • PEEP requirement ≥7 cmH₂O to maintain oxygen
                                                            saturation ≥90%

                                                            D: Beractant 100 mg/kg (4 mL/kg) intratracheally as a single
                                                            dose via endotracheal tube; may repeat every 6 hours if
                                                            required to a maximum of 4 doses
                                                                      OR
                                                            D: Poractant alfa 200 mg/kg intratracheally as an initial dose
                                                            via endotracheal tube, followed by 100 mg/kg intratracheally
                                                            after 12 hours if required; maximum 3 doses

Post-administration care: Continue CPAP after surfactant administration where appropriate and monitor oxygen saturation,
respiratory effort, and need for repeat dosing.

  Note:
  Surfactant administration should only be performed at Level D facility (Regional Referral Hospital) and above by trained
  healthcare providers.

 Advanced Respiratory         Mechanical ventilation   Consider mechanical ventilation if: Severe respiratory distress:
 Support                                               • SAS ≥7
                                                       • Requires FiO₂ ≥50%
                                                       • Requires PEEP ≥8 cmH₂O
                                                       • Persistent oxygen saturation <90% after second dose of
                                                       surfactant
                                                       OR
                                                        Recurrent apnoea: More than two episodes within 24 hours

Table 27.8: Neonatal Referral Care

 Indications for Referral     Refer promptly to a      • Advanced respiratory support is unavailable
                              higher-level facility    • Surfactant therapy is required but unavailable
                              when:                    • Mechanical ventilation is required

                              facility                 • District Hospital and above: Sick neonates and/or neonates <1.8
                                                       kg

                                                       • Perform physical examination

                                                       • Conduct relevant investigations

                                                       guidelines
                                                       • Insert NGT for decompression where indicated

                           care                  • Keep airway patent
6. Management During                             • Monitor pulse rate, respiratory rate, and oxygen saturation

chapters.intro:
Common neonatal conditions are a major cause of illness and death in the first 28 days of life. Early recognition and prompt
management are essential to improve survival and prevent complications.
Assessment begins with rapid identification of emergency signs including respiratory distress, apnoea, shock, convulsions,
severe bleeding, hypothermia, poor feeding, and altered consciousness. Immediate management should follow the principles
of airway, breathing, circulation, correction of hypoglycemia, and thermal protection.
A focused history should include maternal risk factors, antenatal and intrapartum events, gestational age, birth weight, feeding
history, and any history of delayed cry or resuscitation. Physical examination should assess vital signs, respiratory status,
hydration, jaundice, signs of infection, congenital abnormalities, and neurological status.
Investigations are guided by clinical findings and may include blood glucose, full blood count, C-reactive protein, blood culture,
serum bilirubin, electrolytes, and relevant imaging.
Management involves supportive care (warmth, oxygen, fluids, nutrition, and glucose correction) and specific treatment for
conditions such as neonatal sepsis, neonatal jaundice, respiratory distress syndrome, birth asphyxia, and neonatal seizures.
Continuous monitoring and follow-up are essential for early detection of complications and improved outcomes.
